layers: {"core": "In a series RL circuit driven by a step voltage, the current rises as i(t) = (V/R)(1 − e^(−tR/L)). One time constant τ = L/R is the moment the exponent reaches −1, so the current has climbed to (1 − 1/e) ≈ 63.2% of its final value V/R. It is defined in terms of current because the inductor's state variable is current, not voltage.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "The time constant of an RL circuit is defined by the rise of current through the inductor, not voltage. The voltage across the inductor actually starts at the full applied value and decays toward zero, while the resistor voltage merely tracks the current.", "why_tempting": "The RC definition is stated in terms of capacitor voltage reaching 63.2%, and it is easy to carry that wording over to the RL case without noticing that the roles of voltage and current swap."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "36.8% (1/e) is the fraction remaining in a decay, not the fraction reached in a build-up; and in any case the RL constant is defined on current, not voltage.", "why_tempting": "Both 63.2% and 36.8% appear in time-constant questions; this option combines the wrong quantity with the decay percentage."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "After one τ the current has built up to 63.2% of maximum, leaving 36.8% still to go. 36.8% is the value a decaying quantity falls to, not the value a rising one reaches.", "why_tempting": "It picks the right variable (current) but inverts the rise/decay percentages, which is the most common slip in this family of questions."}], "concept": "When a voltage V is switched across a series L and R, Kirchhoff gives V = L di/dt + iR. The solution is i(t) = (V/R)(1 − e^(−t/τ)) with τ = L/R. Physically, the inductor generates a back EMF that initially cancels the applied voltage entirely, so at t = 0 the current is zero and all of V appears across L; as current grows, iR takes a larger share and di/dt shrinks, so the approach is exponential. The dimensional check is useful: henries divided by ohms is (V·s/A)/(V/A) = seconds. Compare with RC, where τ = RC and the state variable is capacitor voltage. In both cases one τ means the gap to the final value has shrunk by a factor of e, which is where 63.2% comes from.", "worked_example": "Take L = 10 mH and R = 100 Ω with a 12 V step. τ = L/R = 0.010/100 = 100 μs. Final current I = V/R = 120 mA. At t = 100 μs: i = 120 mA × (1 − e^(−1)) = 120 × 0.632 = 75.9 mA. At t = 200 μs: 120 × (1 − e^(−2)) = 120 × 0.865 = 103.8 mA. At t = 500 μs (5τ): 120 × 0.9933 ≈ 119.2 mA, which is the usual engineering definition of fully settled.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the time constant is always about voltage reaching 63.2%. Correction: it is about the state variable of the energy-storage element. For a capacitor that is voltage; for an inductor it is current. The inductor voltage goes the other way, decaying from V toward zero.", "link": "section 1", "mnemonic": "L stores current, C stores voltage: the time constant tracks whatever the element stores.", "edge_cases": "The 63.2% figure assumes a pure step into an ideal L and R. Real inductors have winding resistance that adds to R and shortens τ, and core saturation makes L current-dependent so the rise is no longer a clean exponential."}

{"core": "In an RC charging circuit, v_C(t) = V(1 − e^(−t/RC)). The product RC is the time constant τ, and at t = τ the capacitor voltage has reached 1 − e^(−1) ≈ 63.2% of the supply. So the interval described is one time constant.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "\"Exponential period\" is not a defined quantity in circuit theory. The exponential has no period; it is a monotonic curve characterised by its time constant.", "why_tempting": "The charging curve is exponential, so a name containing that word sounds plausible, and \"period\" is a familiar timing term from AC work."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "An \"exponential rate of one\" is not a standard term. The rate of charging is set by 1/τ, and the exponent equals −1 at t = τ, but nobody names the interval that way.", "why_tempting": "The exponent does equal 1 in magnitude after one τ, so the phrase has a grain of truth that makes it feel technical."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "\"Time factor\" is a made-up label. The established term for RC (and L/R) is time constant, symbol τ, measured in seconds.", "why_tempting": "It is close in wording to time constant and was written to catch learners who recognise the shape of the right answer but not the exact term."}], "concept": "Charging a capacitor through a resistor: the current is i = (V − v_C)/R, and i = C dv_C/dt, which gives the first-order equation RC dv_C/dt + v_C = V. Its solution is v_C(t) = V(1 − e^(−t/RC)). The time constant τ = RC has units of seconds (ohms × farads = (V/A)(A·s/V)). It is the time at which the remaining gap to the final voltage has shrunk by a factor of e. Because the charging current is proportional to that gap, the same τ governs the current decay i(t) = (V/R)e^(−t/RC). Multiples matter: 2τ gives 86.5%, 3τ gives 95.0%, 5τ gives 99.3%, which is the practical settle point used in timing circuits, power-supply soft-start and RC filter step response.", "worked_example": "R = 10 kΩ, C = 100 nF, V = 5 V. τ = 10 000 × 100 × 10^(−9) = 1 ms. At t = 1 ms, v_C = 5 × 0.632 = 3.16 V. The initial charging current is 5/10 000 = 0.5 mA and at t = 1 ms it has fallen to 0.5 × 0.368 = 0.184 mA. By t = 5 ms the capacitor is at 4.97 V, effectively charged.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a capacitor is \"charged\" after one time constant. Correction: one τ is only 63.2% of the way; the exponential never quite reaches the supply voltage, and the usual rule of thumb is that 5τ (99.3%) counts as fully charged.", "link": "section 1", "mnemonic": "One tau, two-thirds there (63.2% is just under two-thirds).", "edge_cases": "The simple RC law assumes the source has zero internal resistance and the capacitor is ideal. Electrolytics with significant ESR and leakage, or a source with its own output resistance, add to R and lengthen the effective τ."}

{"core": "The current in a series RL circuit rises as i(t) = I_max(1 − e^(−tR/L)). The time L/R is the time constant, and at t = L/R the current has reached 63.2% of I_max. That interval is called one time constant.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "\"Time factor\" is not a term used for L/R or RC. The quantity is a constant of the circuit (it does not depend on the applied voltage), which is why it is called the time constant.", "why_tempting": "The phrase resembles the correct term and the question is testing exact vocabulary rather than physics."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A \"rate\" would have units of 1/seconds, whereas the quantity asked about is a time in seconds. There is no standard term called exponential rate for this interval.", "why_tempting": "The curve is exponential and learners sometimes think of 1/τ as a rate, so a name built from those words sounds reasonable."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "An exponential function has no period; \"exponential period\" is not a defined concept. Period belongs to repeating waveforms, not to a single transient.", "why_tempting": "It borrows the vocabulary of AC analysis (period) and attaches it to the right curve shape."}], "concept": "For an inductor, v_L = L di/dt. Applying a step voltage V to L in series with R gives V = L di/dt + iR, a first-order linear equation whose solution is i(t) = (V/R)(1 − e^(−t/τ)) with τ = L/R. At t = 0 all of V is across the inductor because its back EMF opposes any sudden change in current; as current builds, the resistor drop grows and the inductor voltage shrinks, so the current growth slows. The time constant is the time it would take to reach the final current if the initial slope continued unchanged, which is another way to see why it is independent of V. Note the inverse relationship to RC: more resistance makes an RC circuit slower but an RL circuit faster, because R is in the denominator of L/R.", "worked_example": "A 2.2 mH choke in series with 22 Ω across a 12 V supply: τ = 0.0022/22 = 100 μs. I_max = 12/22 = 545 mA. After 100 μs: 545 × 0.632 = 345 mA. If you doubled R to 44 Ω, τ would halve to 50 μs even though the final current also halves to 273 mA; the circuit settles faster because the resistor dissipates the inductor's stored energy more quickly.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: larger resistance always slows a transient. Correction: that is true for RC (τ = RC) but inverted for RL (τ = L/R); the mnemonic is that in an RL circuit the resistor is what lets the inductor's current settle.", "link": "section 1", "mnemonic": "RC multiplies, L/R divides.", "edge_cases": "When the circuit is opened rather than closed, the inductor tries to maintain its current and the back EMF can rise to hundreds of volts; the decay time constant is then L divided by the much larger resistance of the arc or flyback path."}

{"core": "A capacitor discharging through a resistor follows q(t) = Q_0 e^(−t/RC), and because v = q/C the voltage follows the same curve. At t = RC the stored charge has fallen to e^(−1) ≈ 36.8% of its initial value, so the interval described is one time constant.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "\"Discharge period\" is not a defined term. A discharge is a one-way exponential with no period; it is characterised by its time constant.", "why_tempting": "It describes the situation (a discharge) using a timing word (period) and so reads naturally to someone who has not memorised the proper term."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "There is no quantity called a discharge factor. The ratio 1/e that the charge falls to is simply what happens after one time constant.", "why_tempting": "The 36.8% ratio could be called a factor in casual speech, and this option mimics the structure of the correct phrase."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "\"Exponential discharge of one\" is invented wording. The exponent is −1 at t = τ, but the interval itself is the time constant.", "why_tempting": "The exponent genuinely has magnitude one at this point, which gives the phrase a superficial correctness."}], "concept": "Discharging: with no source, the loop equation is R dq/dt + q/C = 0, giving q(t) = Q_0 e^(−t/RC). Charge, capacitor voltage and discharge current all share this exponential because they are proportional to one another (v = q/C, i = v/R). The time constant τ = RC is the time for any of them to fall to 1/e of the starting value. The same τ governs charging; the difference is only whether you measure the fraction reached (63.2%) or the fraction remaining (36.8%), and the two numbers sum to 100%. Extending: after 2τ the residue is 13.5%, after 3τ 5.0%, after 5τ 0.67%. This is the basis of bleeder-resistor sizing in high-voltage supplies and of RC timing in monostables.", "worked_example": "A 470 μF filter capacitor charged to 400 V with a 100 kΩ bleeder: τ = 100 000 × 470 × 10^(−6) = 47 s. After 47 s the voltage is 400 × 0.368 = 147 V, still dangerous. After 2τ = 94 s it is 54 V; after 3τ = 141 s it is 20 V. Sizing a bleeder means choosing R so that 3τ to 5τ is a tolerable wait, while keeping its continuous dissipation V²/R acceptable.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: after one time constant the capacitor is mostly empty. Correction: it still holds 36.8% of its charge and 36.8% of its voltage, which for a high-voltage cap can be lethal; stored energy (½CV²) is still 13.5% of the original.", "link": "section 1", "mnemonic": "Charge-up reaches 63.2, discharge leaves 36.8; both add to 100.", "edge_cases": "Energy decays faster than voltage because it goes as V². After one τ the voltage is at 36.8% but the energy is at only 13.5%."}

{"core": "Back EMF (counter EMF) is the voltage an inductor develops in response to a changing current, v = −L di/dt, with polarity that opposes the change producing it. It is a voltage, and it opposes the applied EMF, so A is the only correct description.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "EMF is a voltage by definition, not a current. The back EMF produces an effect on current, but it is itself measured in volts.", "why_tempting": "Because the back EMF limits the rise of current, learners sometimes think of it as an opposing current rather than an opposing voltage."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "There is no relationship of the form R times C percent. RC is a time constant in seconds and has nothing to do with the magnitude of an inductive back EMF, which depends on L and di/dt.", "why_tempting": "It sprinkles in R and C from the neighbouring time-constant questions to look like a formula."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A current cannot equal a voltage; they are different quantities with different units. Back EMF is a voltage, and it opposes rather than equals the applied EMF (except momentarily at t = 0 in an ideal RL step).", "why_tempting": "At the instant a voltage is applied to an inductor the back EMF does equal the applied EMF in magnitude, which can be misremembered as a general statement, and the option also confuses current with voltage."}], "concept": "Faraday's law says a changing magnetic flux through a coil induces an EMF, and Lenz's law fixes its sign: the induced EMF drives current in the direction that opposes the change in flux. For a self-inductance L carrying current i, the flux linkage is Li, so v_L = L di/dt. When current tries to increase, the inductor's terminal voltage rises in the polarity that opposes the source; when current tries to decrease, the polarity flips and the inductor becomes a source itself, trying to keep current flowing. This is why an RL circuit's current cannot jump, why switching off a relay coil produces a high-voltage spike, and why a DC motor draws less current once it is spinning (its rotating armature generates a back EMF that subtracts from the supply). The same mechanism gives inductive reactance X_L = 2πfL in AC circuits: the faster the current changes, the larger the opposing voltage.", "worked_example": "A 100 mH coil has its current ramped from 0 to 2 A in 10 ms. Back EMF = L di/dt = 0.1 × (2/0.010) = 20 V, opposing the supply. If the circuit is then opened in 10 μs, di/dt = 2/10^(−5) = 200 000 A/s and the inductor tries to produce 0.1 × 200 000 = 20 000 V, which is why a flyback diode or snubber is needed across relay coils and why ignition coils work at all.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: back EMF is a current that flows backwards. Correction: it is a voltage generated by the inductor's own changing flux; its polarity opposes any change in current, which makes the current rise gradually on switch-on and spike the voltage on switch-off.", "link": "section 1", "mnemonic": "Lenz: inductors hate change in current, capacitors hate change in voltage.", "edge_cases": "In a motor the back EMF is proportional to speed, not di/dt, so a stalled motor has no back EMF and draws its full locked-rotor current; this is the same physics (Faraday) but a different mechanism than the self-inductance case."}

{"core": "Charging follows v_C = V(1 − e^(−t/τ)). At t = 2τ the exponent is −2, e^(−2) = 0.1353, so the capacitor is at 1 − 0.1353 = 0.8647, or 86.5% of the supply voltage.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "36.8% is e^(−1), the fraction remaining after one time constant of a discharge. It is neither a charging value nor a two-time-constant value.", "why_tempting": "It is one of the famous time-constant numbers and appears in nearly every question of this type."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "63.2% is the charge level after one time constant, not two. After the second τ the remaining gap (36.8%) shrinks by another factor of e to 13.5%, giving 86.5%.", "why_tempting": "Learners who memorise only the single-τ figure pick it reflexively, or they double 63.2% and realise that exceeds 100% so retreat to the known number."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "95% is the charge level after three time constants (1 − e^(−3) = 0.950), not two.", "why_tempting": "The multi-τ table is easy to shift by one row; 95% is the next entry after 86.5%."}], "concept": "The exponential charging curve has a simple compounding property: each time constant removes a fraction (1 − 1/e) of whatever gap remains to the final value. After 1τ the gap is e^(−1) = 36.8%; after 2τ it is e^(−2) = 13.5%; after 3τ, 5.0%; after 4τ, 1.8%; after 5τ, 0.67%. The charged fraction is 100% minus the gap: 63.2%, 86.5%, 95.0%, 98.2%, 99.3%. The same ratios apply to RL current build-up with τ = L/R. This is worth internalising as a table because the exam asks it in several forms (charging, discharging, one or two τ), and because it tells you in practice how long an RC timer, a soft-start or a filter must wait to be considered settled.", "worked_example": "V = 10 V, R = 1 kΩ, C = 1 μF, so τ = 1 ms. At t = 2 ms: v_C = 10 × (1 − e^(−2)) = 10 × (1 − 0.1353) = 8.65 V, i.e. 86.5%. Check by steps: after 1 ms the gap is 3.68 V; after another τ that gap becomes 3.68 × 0.368 = 1.35 V, so v_C = 10 − 1.35 = 8.65 V.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: two time constants means twice 63.2%. Correction: the exponential compounds on the remaining gap, so each τ closes 63.2% of what is left; two τ gives 86.5%, never 126%.", "link": "section 1", "mnemonic": "63, 86, 95, 98, 99: one number per tau."}

{"core": "A discharging capacitor follows v_C = V_0 e^(−t/τ). At t = 2τ, v_C = V_0 e^(−2) = 0.1353 V_0, so the capacitor has fallen to 13.5% of its starting voltage.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "63.2% is the fraction reached during charging after one τ. In a discharge after two τ, 86.5% has been lost and 13.5% remains.", "why_tempting": "It is the headline time-constant number and learners often reach for it without checking whether the question is charge or discharge."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "36.8% is the residue after one time constant of discharge. After a second time constant that residue is multiplied by e^(−1) again, giving 13.5%.", "why_tempting": "Right curve, wrong number of time constants; it is the off-by-one-row error."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "86.5% is the charging level after two τ, equivalently the amount discharged after two τ. The question asks what remains, which is the complement, 13.5%.", "why_tempting": "It is the correct two-τ figure for the opposite question, and the exam deliberately pairs these two items."}], "concept": "The discharge equation comes from R dq/dt + q/C = 0, giving q = Q_0 e^(−t/RC); voltage and current scale identically. Each time constant multiplies the remaining value by 1/e = 0.368. So after 2τ the residue is 0.368² = 0.135, after 3τ it is 0.050, after 5τ it is 0.0067. The charging and discharging tables are complements of each other: charged fraction after nτ equals 1 − (discharge residue after nτ). Keeping both in mind lets you answer any variant by computing e^(−n) once. This matters for bleeder design, for how quickly a sample-and-hold droops, and for understanding why an AC coupling capacitor's low-frequency cutoff is set by the same RC.", "worked_example": "A 10 μF capacitor charged to 100 V discharges through 47 kΩ: τ = 47 000 × 10^(−5) = 0.47 s. After 0.94 s (2τ): v = 100 × e^(−2) = 13.5 V. Step by step: after 0.47 s it is 36.8 V; after another 0.47 s it is 36.8 × 0.368 = 13.5 V. The remaining stored energy is ½ × 10^(−5) × 13.5² ≈ 0.9 mJ versus 50 mJ initially.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: discharge after two time constants leaves 2 × 36.8% or 100% − 2 × 36.8%. Correction: the residue compounds multiplicatively, 0.368 × 0.368 = 0.135, so 13.5% remains.", "link": "section 1", "mnemonic": "Discharge residues: 37, 13.5, 5, 2, 0.7 percent for 1 to 5 tau."}

{"core": "τ = RC = 470 × 10³ Ω × 100 × 10^(−6) F = 47 s. Ohms times farads gives seconds directly, so no further conversion is needed.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "4700 s would need a capacitor of 10 mF or a resistor of 47 MΩ. It is the answer with the powers of ten mishandled by a factor of 100.", "why_tempting": "470 × 100 looks like 47 000 and sloppy exponent bookkeeping can land two decades high."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "470 s is ten times too large; it would correspond to 1 mF rather than 100 μF.", "why_tempting": "Writing 100 μF as 10^(−3) instead of 10^(−4) is an easy slip when μ (10^(−6)) is combined with 100."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "0.47 s is a hundred times too small, corresponding to 1 μF with 470 kΩ.", "why_tempting": "Treating 100 μF as roughly 1 μF, or dropping the kilo prefix on the resistor and keeping the micro on the capacitor, gives this."}], "concept": "The RC time constant is simply the product of resistance and capacitance: τ = RC, in seconds when R is in ohms and C in farads. Dimensionally, Ω × F = (V/A) × (A·s/V) = s. The most reliable method on the exam is to express both values in scientific notation, multiply mantissas, and add exponents: 470 kΩ = 4.7 × 10^5, 100 μF = 1.0 × 10^(−4), product 4.7 × 10^1 = 47. A handy shortcut: kΩ × μF gives milliseconds, MΩ × μF gives seconds, kΩ × nF gives microseconds. With 470 kΩ × 100 μF that is 47 000 ms = 47 s. The physical meaning is that this circuit takes 47 s to charge to 63.2% or discharge to 36.8%, and roughly 4 minutes (5τ) to be fully settled, which is a slow bleeder.", "worked_example": "R = 470 kΩ = 4.7 × 10^5 Ω. C = 100 μF = 1.0 × 10^(−4) F. τ = 4.7 × 10^5 × 1.0 × 10^(−4) = 4.7 × 10^(5 − 4) = 4.7 × 10 = 47 s. Shortcut check: 470 kΩ × 100 μF = 47 000 ms = 47 s. Full settle (5τ) ≈ 235 s.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: time constants need a 2π or a 1/x somewhere, like reactance formulas. Correction: τ = RC is a bare product; the only work is getting the metric prefixes right.", "link": "Formula-sheet trainer", "mnemonic": "kilo-ohms times microfarads equals milliseconds.", "edge_cases": "At 47 s this is in the range where electrolytic leakage current (effectively a parallel resistance of a few MΩ or less) can noticeably shorten the measured discharge time compared with the ideal RC calculation."}

{"core": "τ = RC = 470 × 10³ Ω × 470 × 10^(−6) F = 220.9 s, which rounds to 221 s. Ohms times farads is seconds, so the result is already in the right unit.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "470 s would require the product of mantissas to be 47.0 rather than 4.7 × 4.7 = 22.09; it comes from forgetting to multiply the two 470s and just carrying one of them through.", "why_tempting": "Both components have the value 470, and it is easy to write the familiar number down as the answer."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "221 000 s is a thousand times too large, equivalent to using 470 mF or 470 MΩ.", "why_tempting": "The mantissa (221) is right, so a learner who got the digits but mis-added exponents by three will pick it."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "47 000 s is neither the right mantissa nor the right exponent; it looks like 470 × 100 with the prefixes dropped.", "why_tempting": "It is a large round number assembled from the digits in the question."}], "concept": "τ = RC with R in ohms and C in farads gives seconds. In scientific notation: R = 4.7 × 10^5, C = 4.7 × 10^(−4), so τ = 4.7 × 4.7 × 10^(5 − 4) = 22.09 × 10 = 220.9 s. The prefix shortcut kΩ × μF = ms gives 470 × 470 = 220 900 ms = 220.9 s. The spread of distractors (470, 221, 221 000, 47 000) is designed to catch exponent errors rather than arithmetic ones, so the discipline of writing each value as mantissa × 10^n and adding exponents is the whole skill being examined. Physically, a 221 s time constant means this RC network would take about 18 minutes (5τ) to settle, which is why high-value bleeders across large capacitor banks need to be chosen deliberately.", "worked_example": "R = 470 kΩ = 4.7 × 10^5 Ω. C = 470 μF = 4.7 × 10^(−4) F. Mantissas: 4.7 × 4.7 = 22.09. Exponents: 5 + (−4) = 1. τ = 22.09 × 10^1 = 220.9 s ≈ 221 s. After 221 s a charged capacitor would be at 36.8% of its initial voltage; after 5τ ≈ 1105 s (18.4 min) it is at 0.67%.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: when both components have the same number, the time constant is that number. Correction: τ is a product, so equal mantissas square (4.7² = 22.09) and the exponents must still be added.", "link": "Formula-sheet trainer", "mnemonic": "Mantissas multiply, exponents add.", "edge_cases": "A real 470 μF electrolytic may have a −20/+50% tolerance, so the measured τ could sit anywhere from roughly 180 s to 330 s; the exam value is the nominal one."}

{"core": "τ = RC = 470 × 10³ Ω × 220 × 10^(−6) F = 103.4 s, which matches 103 s. Ohms times farads gives seconds directly.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "470 000 s would be the resistor value in ohms copied as if it were the answer; it ignores the capacitor entirely.", "why_tempting": "A learner who thinks τ is dominated by the larger-looking number may just write down 470 k."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "470 s is the resistor's kilohm value with the wrong unit attached, not the RC product. The actual product is 4.7 × 2.2 × 10^1.", "why_tempting": "The number 470 appears in every question of this set, and it is tempting to reuse it as an answer."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "220 s is the capacitor value in microfarads mislabelled as seconds. The true answer scales 220 by 0.47.", "why_tempting": "Picking the other component's number is the mirror of choosing 470; both skip the multiplication."}], "concept": "τ = RC in seconds for ohms and farads. Scientific notation: R = 4.7 × 10^5, C = 2.2 × 10^(−4). Multiply mantissas (4.7 × 2.2 = 10.34) and add exponents (5 − 4 = 1), giving 103.4 s. Using the kΩ × μF = ms shortcut: 470 × 220 = 103 400 ms = 103.4 s. These three questions (100, 220 and 470 μF with 470 kΩ) share one method and differ only in the mantissa product; recognising the pattern (47, 103, 221 s) lets you sanity-check any of them. The practical takeaway is that large electrolytic banks with high-value bleeders take minutes to discharge, and the 5τ full-settle time here is over eight minutes.", "worked_example": "R = 470 kΩ = 4.7 × 10^5 Ω. C = 220 μF = 2.2 × 10^(−4) F. 4.7 × 2.2 = 10.34. 10^5 × 10^(−4) = 10^1. τ = 10.34 × 10 = 103.4 s ≈ 103 s. Charging from 0 V with a 50 V source, the capacitor reaches 31.6 V at 103 s and 43.2 V at 207 s.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the time constant is set by whichever component is bigger. Correction: τ is the product of both, and both prefixes must be converted; neither 470 nor 220 on its own is the answer.", "link": "Formula-sheet trainer"}

{"core": "Skin effect is the tendency of alternating current to concentrate near a conductor's surface, in a layer whose depth δ = √(ρ/(πfμ)) shrinks as frequency rises. So as frequency increases, RF current flows in a thinner surface layer, raising the effective AC resistance.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Skin depth is inversely proportional to the square root of frequency, so lowering frequency makes the current layer thicker, not thinner. At DC the current fills the entire cross-section.", "why_tempting": "It is the correct statement with the frequency direction flipped, the classic inverted-relationship distractor."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Skin effect is an electromagnetic phenomenon caused by induced eddy currents inside the conductor, not a thermal one. Heating does raise resistance via the temperature coefficient of copper, but that is a different and separate effect.", "why_tempting": "RF conductors do get warm, and the word surface in the question suggests surface heating to someone guessing."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Thermal effects do not decrease a conductor's impedance (copper resistance rises with temperature), and skin effect is not thermal in origin anyway.", "why_tempting": "It pairs with C as a thermal explanation and has the wrong direction too; it catches anyone eliminating on surface vocabulary alone."}], "concept": "An alternating current produces a changing magnetic field inside the conductor itself. That changing field induces eddy currents (Faraday's law) which, by Lenz's law, oppose the current at the centre and reinforce it near the surface. The net effect is a current density that decays exponentially from the surface inward with a characteristic skin depth δ = √(ρ/(π f μ)), where ρ is resistivity and μ the permeability. For copper, δ ≈ 66/√f mm with f in Hz, so about 0.66 mm at 10 kHz, 21 μm at 10 MHz and 6.6 μm at 100 MHz. Because only a thin annulus carries current, the effective resistance is R_AC ≈ ρ l/(2π r δ) for a round wire of radius r when r is much greater than δ, which grows as √f. This is why RF conductors are silver-plated or made of tubing (the centre is wasted anyway), why Litz wire helps at LF and MF but not VHF, and why coil Q is limited by conductor loss at HF.", "worked_example": "A 1 mm diameter copper wire at 14 MHz: δ = 66/√(14 × 10^6) mm = 66/3742 = 0.0176 mm = 17.6 μm. The conducting annulus area is ≈ 2π r δ = 2π × 0.5 × 0.0176 = 0.0553 mm², versus the full cross-section of 0.785 mm². R_AC/R_DC ≈ 0.785/0.0553 ≈ 14, so one metre of this wire (R_DC ≈ 0.022 Ω) shows about 0.31 Ω at 14 MHz. Doubling the frequency to 28 MHz raises that by √2 to about 0.44 Ω.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: skin effect is about the surface heating up or the insulation conducting. Correction: it is magnetic self-induction inside the metal pushing current outward; the heating is a consequence of the raised resistance, not its cause.", "link": "section 1", "mnemonic": "Higher frequency, thinner skin: δ ∝ 1/√f.", "edge_cases": "Skin effect only matters when the conductor dimension exceeds the skin depth. Below roughly a few kHz in ordinary wire, δ is larger than the wire radius and R_AC ≈ R_DC. In ferromagnetic conductors (steel) the high μ makes δ tiny even at audio frequencies, which is why steel wire is a poor RF conductor unless copper-clad."}

{"core": "Skin effect is the name for the concentration of alternating current near a conductor's surface; it arises from eddy currents induced by the conductor's own changing magnetic field, and it becomes pronounced at RF where the skin depth is a tiny fraction of the wire radius.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "\"Layer effect\" is not a recognised term in electromagnetics. The phenomenon is universally called skin effect, after the surface skin that carries the current.", "why_tempting": "The current does flow in a layer, so the invented name describes the result and can fool a learner who has not seen the proper term."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The piezoelectric effect is the generation of voltage by mechanical strain in certain crystals (quartz, some ceramics). It is the basis of crystal oscillators and has nothing to do with current distribution in a wire.", "why_tempting": "It is a real effect from the same syllabus area (components) and sounds technical enough to be a plausible guess."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Resonance is the condition where inductive and capacitive reactance cancel in a tuned circuit. It affects impedance versus frequency but does not describe where inside a conductor the current flows.", "why_tempting": "Resonance and skin effect both become important at RF, so the association is loose but real."}], "concept": "Inside a conductor carrying AC, the current creates a magnetic field that also changes with time. By Faraday's law this induces circulating eddy currents within the metal; by Lenz's law they oppose the current in the centre and add to it near the surface. The result is a current density that falls off exponentially from the surface with skin depth δ = √(ρ/(π f μ)). For copper, δ ≈ 66/√f mm (f in Hz): about 0.02 mm at 14 MHz. Consequences: AC resistance rises roughly as √f, hollow tubing conducts RF as well as solid rod of the same outside diameter, plating with a better conductor (silver) on the surface lowers loss, and surface finish and corrosion matter at VHF and above. Skin effect is also why coaxial cable's shield current flows on its inner surface and any common-mode current flows on its outer surface, and why a thick copper strap, not a round wire, is the preferred RF ground conductor.", "worked_example": "Compare 1 m of 2 mm diameter copper wire at DC and at 7 MHz. R_DC = ρ l/A = 1.72 × 10^(−8) × 1/(π × 10^(−6)) ≈ 5.5 mΩ. At 7 MHz, δ = 66/√(7 × 10^6) = 0.025 mm, so the effective area is 2π × 1 mm × 0.025 mm = 0.157 mm² and R_AC ≈ 1.72 × 10^(−8)/(0.157 × 10^(−6)) ≈ 0.11 Ω, twenty times the DC value.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: skin effect means current flows on the outside of the insulation or jacket. Correction: it flows in the outermost layer of the metal itself; the insulation remains a non-conductor.", "link": "section 1", "edge_cases": "Litz wire (many individually insulated strands woven so each takes turns at the surface) beats skin effect up to a few MHz, but above that interstrand capacitance defeats it; at HF and VHF the cure is larger diameter, tubing, or silver plating."}

{"core": "Because of skin effect, RF current density is highest at the conductor's surface and decays exponentially inward with skin depth δ = √(ρ/(πfμ)). At HF and above, δ is tens of micrometres in copper, so essentially all the current flows along the surface.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "The centre of a conductor is where RF current density is lowest. Eddy currents induced by the conductor's own field cancel the current there, leaving the core effectively unused at RF.", "why_tempting": "At DC the current is uniform across the whole cross-section, and the intuitive picture of current flowing through the middle of a wire is hard to shake."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Current is the motion of charge in the metal; it does not flow in a magnetic field. The magnetic field is a consequence of the current, and the field inside the conductor is actually what pushes the current outward.", "why_tempting": "The question set discusses fields around conductors, so an option mixing current and field language can seem like it is saying something sophisticated."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "The magnetic field surrounding the conductor carries energy, but it does not carry conduction current. Current flows in the metal, specifically in its surface layer.", "why_tempting": "Energy does propagate in the fields around a transmission line rather than in the metal, and that true fact about energy can be confused with where the current is."}], "concept": "Skin effect comes from the interaction of the current with its own magnetic field. The time-varying field inside the conductor induces an electric field that opposes the current near the axis and assists it near the surface, giving a current density J(r) ∝ e^(−(a − r)/δ) for a wire of radius a. Skin depth δ = √(ρ/(π f μ)) = 66/√f mm for copper (f in Hz), so at 1 MHz δ = 66 μm and at 144 MHz δ = 5.5 μm. Beyond about three skin depths the current is negligible, so a conductor much thicker than 3δ gains nothing from its interior. Practical implications: AC resistance scales with √f and inversely with circumference rather than area; wide flat strap and large-diameter tubing are the low-loss choices; plating must be at least a few δ thick to help; and in coax, the centre conductor's surface and the shield's inner surface are the only metal that matters for differential-mode loss.", "worked_example": "A 6 mm copper tube with 0.5 mm wall at 30 MHz: δ = 66/√(3 × 10^7) = 0.012 mm = 12 μm. The wall (500 μm) is over 40 skin depths thick, so the tube behaves identically to a solid 6 mm rod and the inside wall carries essentially nothing. Swapping to solid rod would add weight and cost with no reduction in RF loss.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a thicker solid conductor always has proportionally lower RF resistance. Correction: only the outer skin conducts, so RF resistance depends on surface perimeter and skin depth; doubling the diameter halves R_AC rather than quartering it as it would at DC.", "link": "section 1", "mnemonic": "RF rides the rim.", "edge_cases": "Surface condition matters because the current is confined there: a rough, oxidised or corroded surface can raise loss noticeably at VHF/UHF even though the bulk conductor is unchanged."}

{"core": "The thin surface layer is a direct consequence of skin effect: the conductor's own changing magnetic field induces eddy currents that cancel current in the interior and reinforce it at the surface, confining RF current to a skin of depth δ = √(ρ/(πfμ)).", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Heating of the interior does not redirect current; temperature slightly raises resistivity everywhere but produces no radial redistribution. The cause is electromagnetic induction, not thermal.", "why_tempting": "The idea that a hot interior pushes current outward is an intuitive but false mental model that the word surface invites."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The RF resistance of a conductor is greater than its DC resistance, not less, precisely because the current is squeezed into a smaller effective area. The option has the comparison backwards and also describes a result, not a cause.", "why_tempting": "A learner who remembers that something changes between RF and DC resistance but not which way will find this plausible."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Self-inductance does give a conductor inductive reactance, but reactance is not resistance and does not by itself confine current to the surface. The internal part of that inductance is involved in the mechanism, but the option misnames the effect and conflates reactance with resistance.", "why_tempting": "It contains a true-sounding fragment (conductors have inductance) and uses AC resistance loosely, which is close to how skin effect is sometimes described informally."}], "concept": "Consider a round wire carrying an AC current. Ampère's law gives a circumferential magnetic field inside the wire that grows with radius; because the current alternates, that internal field changes with time. Faraday's law then produces an induced electric field along the wire axis that is strongest at the centre and opposes the drive there, while it has the opposite sign near the surface. The net current density becomes J(r) ≈ J_s e^(−(a − r)/δ), decaying inward from the surface value J_s with skin depth δ = √(ρ/(π f μ)) = √(2ρ/(ωμ)). The dependence on ρ and μ explains why silver (lower ρ) is better than copper, why aluminium's higher ρ gives a deeper skin and higher loss, and why steel's high μ gives an extremely shallow skin and very high RF loss. The effective resistance of a wire with a much larger than δ is R_AC ≈ ρ l/(2π a δ), which exceeds R_DC = ρ l/(π a²) by a factor a/(2δ).", "worked_example": "For a 2 mm diameter copper wire (a = 1 mm) at 28 MHz: δ = 66/√(2.8 × 10^7) = 0.0125 mm. R_AC/R_DC = a/(2δ) = 1/(2 × 0.0125) = 40. If the same wire were aluminium (ρ about 1.6 times copper), δ is √1.6 = 1.26 times deeper but ρ is 1.6 times higher, so R_AC is 1.6/1.26 ≈ 1.27 times that of copper, which is why aluminium tubing elements are acceptable but not quite as low-loss.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: RF resistance is lower than DC resistance because the current has a shortcut along the surface. Correction: the surface path has far less cross-sectional area than the whole wire, so RF resistance is higher, rising roughly with the square root of frequency.", "link": "section 1", "edge_cases": "The exponential profile and the R_AC ≈ ρ l/(2π a δ) approximation assume a much greater than δ. For thin wires at low frequency where a is comparable to δ the full Bessel-function solution is needed and R_AC approaches R_DC smoothly."}

{"core": "A conductor's resistance to RF differs from its DC resistance because skin effect confines RF current to a thin surface layer of depth δ = √(ρ/(πfμ)), reducing the effective cross-section and raising the resistance roughly as √f.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Good insulation does not conduct at RF. Dielectrics do have loss at RF (dielectric heating), but that is a separate parallel loss mechanism in the insulation, not a change in the conductor's own resistance.", "why_tempting": "Dielectric loss in coax and insulators is a real RF phenomenon, so a learner may transfer it to the conductor question."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "There is no Hertzberg effect in circuit theory or electromagnetics; it is an invented name.", "why_tempting": "It sounds like an eponymous physical effect (Hertz is a real name from radio history), so it has a veneer of authority."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Ordinary metallic conductors are linear: voltage is proportional to current at any frequency. Non-linearity (as in diodes or saturating cores) produces harmonics and mixing, not a frequency-dependent resistance of a wire.", "why_tempting": "Non-linear devices are discussed elsewhere in the Advanced syllabus, and the term is a convenient catch-all for anything that behaves differently at RF."}], "concept": "At DC, current spreads uniformly over a conductor's cross-section and R = ρ l/A. As frequency rises, the conductor's own changing magnetic field induces eddy currents that oppose flow in the interior, so current migrates to the surface with an exponential profile of characteristic depth δ = √(ρ/(π f μ)). The effective area becomes roughly the perimeter times δ, so for a round wire of radius a (a much greater than δ) the ratio R_AC/R_DC ≈ a/(2δ), which grows with √f. This is the principal reason copper losses in coils, feedlines and antenna elements increase with frequency; combined with dielectric loss it sets cable attenuation versus frequency. In coil design it caps the achievable Q and motivates large-diameter wire or tubing, silver plating, and at LF, Litz construction. It also explains why ground straps for RF should be wide and flat (large perimeter) rather than thick and round.", "worked_example": "A 20 m dipole made of 2 mm copper wire has R_DC ≈ 0.11 Ω for its 10 m total length. At 14 MHz, δ = 66/√(1.4 × 10^7) = 0.0176 mm; R_AC/R_DC = 1/(2 × 0.0176) ≈ 28, so the wire's RF resistance is about 3 Ω. Against a 73 Ω radiation resistance that is a 4% loss (about 0.18 dB), acceptable; at 1 mm diameter it would roughly double.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a wire's resistance is a fixed property measured with an ohmmeter. Correction: the ohmmeter value is the DC resistance; at RF the effective resistance is higher and frequency-dependent because of skin effect, and that is the value that sets RF loss.", "link": "section 1", "edge_cases": "Proximity effect, where the fields of adjacent turns in a coil push current to one side of each conductor, adds to skin effect and can raise coil resistance several times above the single-wire skin-effect prediction."}

{"core": "Capacitance, the ability to store charge per volt applied, is measured in farads: C = Q/V, so one farad stores one coulomb at one volt. The coulomb measures the charge itself, not the ability to store it.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "The coulomb is the unit of electric charge (the Q in C = Q/V), not of the capacity to store it. A capacitor's ability is the ratio of charge to voltage, which is the farad.", "why_tempting": "The question mentions storing charge, and the coulomb is the charge unit, so a literal reading pulls toward it."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The watt is a unit of power (energy per second). A capacitor stores energy (joules, E = ½CV²) but power is a rate, and neither is the measure of charge-storage ability.", "why_tempting": "Energy storage and power are easily conflated, and watts are the most familiar electrical unit."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "The volt measures potential difference, the V in C = Q/V. A given capacitor can be charged to many different voltages; the voltage does not describe its ability to hold charge.", "why_tempting": "Capacitor ratings always carry a voltage figure, so volts feel like a capacitor property."}], "concept": "Capacitance is defined by C = Q/V: the charge that accumulates on the plates per volt of potential difference. One farad equals one coulomb per volt. For a parallel-plate capacitor C = ε A/d, so capacitance is a geometric and material property (plate area, spacing, dielectric permittivity), independent of the voltage applied. The stored energy is E = ½CV² = Q²/(2C) joules, which is what links capacitance to the energy-in-fields questions nearby. Because a farad is enormous, practical values are μF, nF and pF; the reactance X_C = 1/(2πfC) in ohms converts capacitance to its effect in AC circuits. Keeping the four units straight (coulomb for charge, farad for capacitance, volt for potential, joule for energy) is the whole point of this item.", "worked_example": "A 100 μF capacitor charged to 25 V holds Q = CV = 100 × 10^(−6) × 25 = 2.5 mC of charge and E = ½ × 10^(−4) × 25² = 31 mJ of energy. Doubling the voltage doubles the charge (5 mC) but quadruples the energy (125 mJ); the capacitance stays 100 μF throughout because it is a property of the device, not of its state.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: coulombs measure how much a capacitor can store. Correction: coulombs measure the charge actually present; the capacitor's ability to store charge per volt is capacitance in farads, and the same capacitor holds different charge at different voltages.", "link": "section 1", "mnemonic": "Farad = coulomb per volt.", "edge_cases": "The energy a capacitor can safely store is limited by its voltage rating (dielectric breakdown), so two capacitors of equal farads can differ enormously in usable stored energy."}

{"core": "A current in a wire produces a magnetic field circling the conductor (Ampère's law), and if the current varies, the changing magnetic field is accompanied by an electric field; the general description of the field surrounding a current-carrying wire is therefore an electromagnetic field.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Skin effect is a redistribution of current inside the conductor, not a field outside it. It does not extend into the surrounding space.", "why_tempting": "Skin effect is discussed in the neighbouring questions and mentions the conductor's surface, which sounds like something near the wire."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "An electrostatic field arises from stationary separated charge, as between capacitor plates. A current, by definition, is moving charge, and its characteristic field is magnetic; a wire carrying current without a net charge imbalance has no electrostatic field.", "why_tempting": "Voltage is needed to drive the current, and voltage is associated with electric fields, so the leap to electrostatic is natural but misses that the question is about the current."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "The conduction electrons stay inside the metal; they do not form a cloud around the wire. The wire remains electrically neutral overall.", "why_tempting": "Picturing current as electrons may suggest electrons spilling out, but it is their motion within the metal that creates the field."}], "concept": "Ampère's law states that a current I produces a magnetic field of strength B = μ₀ I/(2π r) at distance r from a long straight wire, with field lines forming closed circles around the conductor. If the current is time-varying, Faraday's law means the changing B is linked to a changing E, and the combined, coupled fields are the electromagnetic field; at RF, and at distances beyond about λ/2π, part of this field detaches and propagates as a radiated wave. Energy is stored in the magnetic field at a density of B²/(2μ₀) per unit volume, which is where an inductor's ½LI² comes from. The question's phrasing is deliberately general: for DC the field is purely magnetic, for AC it is electromagnetic, and electromagnetic is the term that covers both.", "worked_example": "A 10 A DC current in a straight wire gives B = 4π × 10^(−7) × 10/(2π × 0.01) = 2 × 10^(−4) T at 1 cm, about four times the Earth's field; a compass placed there deflects. Replace the DC with 10 A at 7 MHz and the same magnetic field now oscillates, inducing voltage in any nearby loop and, together with the accompanying electric field, radiating energy. Wind the wire into a coil and the field inside adds up, giving inductance.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a wire carrying current is surrounded by an electric (electrostatic) field. Correction: moving charge produces a magnetic field; the electrostatic field belongs to separated static charge. Only when the current changes does an electric field accompany the magnetic one, making the field electromagnetic.", "link": "section 1", "mnemonic": "Charge at rest: electric field. Charge in motion: magnetic field. Changing motion: electromagnetic.", "edge_cases": "Very close to an antenna (the near field, within about λ/2π) the electric and magnetic components are not in the fixed 377 Ω ratio of a radiated wave; the magnetic field dominates near a current maximum and the electric field near a voltage maximum."}

{"core": "The magnetic field around a conductor forms closed circles around it, and its sense is given by a hand rule. Taking electron flow (negative to positive) as the current direction, the left-hand rule applies: thumb along electron flow, fingers curl in the field direction. The field is circumferential, never parallel or antiparallel to the current.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "The magnetic field is not isotropic; it has a definite circular orientation around the conductor, and reversing the current reverses it. \"All directions\" would describe a scalar quantity, not a vector field.", "why_tempting": "Field lines do surround the wire on every side, which can be misread as pointing in all directions."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The magnetic field is always perpendicular to the current that produces it (B ∝ I × r̂, a cross product). It wraps around the wire in circles rather than running along it.", "why_tempting": "It is natural to assume a field produced by a current would share its direction, as the electric field does inside the conductor."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "For the same reason as C, the field cannot be antiparallel to the current; it is circumferential. Reversing the current reverses the sense of rotation, not the axis.", "why_tempting": "Lenz's law teaches that induced effects oppose their cause, and this option borrows that intuition where it does not apply."}], "concept": "The Biot-Savart law and Ampère's law give the magnetic field of a straight conductor as concentric circles with magnitude B = μ₀I/(2πr). Direction follows a hand rule, and which hand depends on the current convention. With conventional current (positive to negative), grasp the wire with the right hand, thumb along the current, and the fingers curl with the field. With electron flow, which is opposite, the same geometry requires the left hand. ISED's bank frames current as electron flow, so the keyed answer is the left-hand rule. The physics is identical either way: the field is a cross product of current direction and the radial vector, so it is always tangential to circles around the wire. For a coil, the same rule applied to each turn shows that the fields of all turns add along the axis inside the solenoid, giving the north pole at the end the fingers point toward.", "worked_example": "Hold a vertical wire with electrons flowing upward. Point the left thumb up: the fingers curl counter-clockwise when viewed from above, so a compass placed north of the wire would deflect toward the west. Apply the right-hand rule with conventional current flowing downward (thumb down): fingers also curl counter-clockwise from above. Same field, two bookkeeping conventions.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the hand rule is a fact about nature and only one hand can ever be right. Correction: the hand encodes the current convention; left for electron flow, right for conventional current; both describe the same circumferential field.", "link": "section 1", "mnemonic": "Left for electrons, right for conventional; either way, thumb is current and fingers are field.", "edge_cases": "Many engineering texts use conventional current and therefore state the right-hand rule; if a different exam or textbook keys it as right-hand, check which current direction it assumes before deciding it conflicts."}

{"core": "Energy held in an electrostatic field (a charged capacitor, ½CV²) or an electromagnetic field (a current-carrying inductor, ½LI²) is stored energy that can be recovered later; energy stored by virtue of configuration or state rather than motion is potential energy.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Kinetic energy is energy of motion of mass. Although inductor energy is sometimes compared to momentum by analogy, the energy in a field is stored in the field configuration itself and is classified as potential energy.", "why_tempting": "The inductor-as-mass analogy (current resists change like mass resists acceleration) can lead to labelling magnetic energy as kinetic."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Ampere-joules is not a unit of energy or anything else; it combines a current and an energy into a meaningless product. Energy is measured in joules alone.", "why_tempting": "Attaching an electrical unit to joules makes it sound like a special electrical energy unit."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Joule-coulombs is likewise not a physical unit. Joules per coulomb would be volts, but joule times coulomb has no meaning.", "why_tempting": "Both joule and coulomb appear in capacitor formulas, so the pairing seems related to stored charge."}], "concept": "A capacitor stores energy in the electric field between its plates: E = ½CV² = ½QV, with energy density ½εE² per unit volume of dielectric. An inductor stores energy in the magnetic field of its coil: E = ½LI², with energy density B²/(2μ) per unit volume. In both cases nothing is moving in the mechanical sense; the energy resides in the stressed field and is released when the field collapses (the capacitor drives a discharge current, the inductor drives a current through its back EMF). That makes it potential energy in the thermodynamic sense: it depends on the state of the system and is fully recoverable in the ideal case. The continuous exchange of energy between the electric field of C and the magnetic field of L is exactly what a resonant LC circuit does at f = 1/(2π√(LC)), and the losses in R are where that stored energy leaks away as heat, which is the origin of Q.", "worked_example": "A 1 μF capacitor at 100 V stores ½ × 10^(−6) × 100² = 5 mJ. Connect it to a lossless 1 mH inductor: a quarter-cycle later the capacitor is at 0 V and all 5 mJ is magnetic, so ½ × 10^(−3) × I² = 5 mJ gives I = √10 = 3.16 A peak. The exchange repeats at f = 1/(2π√(10^(−3) × 10^(−6))) = 5.03 kHz. Add 1 Ω of series resistance and each cycle loses a little of the 5 mJ as heat; the potential energy is what the resistor consumes.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a current-carrying inductor's energy is kinetic because current is charge in motion. Correction: the drift motion of electrons carries negligible kinetic energy; the ½LI² is stored in the magnetic field configuration and is potential energy, recoverable when the field collapses.", "link": "section 1", "mnemonic": "Fields hold potential: ½CV² in E, ½LI² in B.", "edge_cases": "The field-energy picture also explains where the energy goes when an inductor is open-circuited abruptly: the field cannot vanish instantly, so the energy forces a voltage spike high enough to arc or to be absorbed by a snubber."}

{"core": "A charged capacitor has equal and opposite static charges on its plates; between them is a uniform electric field E = V/d set up by that stationary charge, which is by definition an electrostatic field. No current crosses the dielectric and no magnetic field exists while the charge is constant.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A magnetic field requires moving charge (current). With the capacitor holding a steady charge, there is no current and therefore no magnetic field between the plates.", "why_tempting": "Inductors and capacitors are taught as a pair, and the magnetic field of the inductor can be transposed onto the capacitor by mistake."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Excess electrons sit on the negative plate's surface; they do not occupy the space between the plates. The dielectric is an insulator with no free electron cloud.", "why_tempting": "Picturing charge storage as electrons filling the gap is a common mental image, but the electrons stay on the metal."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "In a charged capacitor at rest no conduction current flows through the dielectric; if it did, the capacitor would be discharging through a leaky insulator. Current flows in the external circuit only while the charge is changing.", "why_tempting": "During charging and discharging, current does flow in the leads, and the displacement current concept can blur the picture of what happens between the plates."}], "concept": "When a capacitor is charged, charge +Q accumulates on one plate and −Q on the other. Static charge produces an electric field; between parallel plates it is nearly uniform with magnitude E = V/d, pointing from the positive to the negative plate. The dielectric polarises in that field, which is what raises C above its vacuum value (C = εA/d). The energy ½CV² is stored in this field with density ½εE². Because the charges are stationary there is no magnetic field; one appears only transiently while the charge is changing, and Maxwell's displacement current (ε dE/dt) is the term that keeps Ampère's law consistent in the gap during that interval. In practice, the electric field strength E = V/d is what dielectric breakdown ratings limit, which is why high-voltage capacitors need thicker dielectric or lower permittivity materials.", "worked_example": "A capacitor with plate spacing 0.1 mm charged to 50 V has an internal field E = 50/0.0001 = 500 kV/m. If the dielectric is a polyester film rated at about 200 MV/m, there is a wide margin; raise the voltage to 25 kV on the same spacing and the field reaches 250 MV/m, above breakdown, and the dielectric punctures. Nothing about this involves a magnetic field until the capacitor is connected and charge begins to move.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: current flows across the capacitor through the dielectric. Correction: the dielectric is an insulator; charge accumulates on the plates and what exists between them is an electrostatic field. Current appears only in the external circuit while the charge changes.", "link": "section 1", "mnemonic": "C: charge sits, E-field between. L: charge moves, B-field around.", "edge_cases": "Real dielectrics have a small leakage conductance, so a tiny current does cross the gap and a stored charge slowly decays; electrolytics are worst, film and ceramic capacitors much better."}

{"core": "The energy stored in an inductor's magnetic field is E = ½LI². {"core": "A resistor placed across a parallel tank adds a loss path, lowering Q = R/X_L, and since bandwidth is f₀/Q the response broadens. Designers add it deliberately when a wider, flatter passband or a more stable, less load-sensitive circuit is wanted.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A shunt resistor can only lower Q, never raise it, and it has no effect on skin effect, which is a property of the conductor and frequency.", "why_tempting": "Skin effect is a loss mechanism associated with Q, so a learner may conflate 'something to do with losses' with the resistor's purpose."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The resistor does lower Q, but in the ideal parallel model it does not change the resonant frequency, which depends only on L and C.", "why_tempting": "It gets the first half right, and the vague sense that 'damping shifts things' makes a frequency change seem plausible."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Adding a parallel resistance increases dissipation and lowers Q, which widens rather than narrows the bandwidth; the statement is inverted on both counts.", "why_tempting": "The series-Q formula X_L/R, where adding R lowers Q, is mentally confused with the parallel case, or the learner assumes that any added component must be 'improving' the circuit by sharpening it."}], "concept": "In a parallel tank the shunt resistor sees the full tank voltage and dissipates V²/R every cycle, so the loaded Q is Q = R/X_L; a lower R means more loss and lower Q. The half-power bandwidth is BW = f₀/Q, so lowering Q widens the passband. This is a legitimate design choice, not a defect: a wideband driver stage, an IF filter that must pass a full SSB or FM channel without ripple, or a frequency multiplier tank that should not be too sharp all benefit from a swamping resistor. A deliberately low Q also makes the circuit's response less dependent on the exact L and C values and on temperature drift, and it prevents a high-impedance tank from being pulled by small changes in the load. The cost is lower gain, since the resonant impedance drops to R in parallel with the tank's own equivalent loss resistance, and poorer rejection of off-channel signals. The resonant frequency f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)) is unaffected in the ideal model.", "worked_example": "Take a 7.1 MHz tank with X_L = 400 Ω and a coil good enough that unloaded Q is 150, giving an equivalent parallel loss resistance of about 60 kΩ and a bandwidth of 47 kHz. Shunting it with 4.7 kΩ gives a loaded R of about 4.35 kΩ, Q ≈ 4.35 kΩ / 400 Ω ≈ 10.9, and a bandwidth of 7.1 MHz / 10.9 ≈ 650 kHz, wide enough to cover the whole band without retuning. The impedance at resonance, and hence the stage gain, falls by roughly 14 times, which is the price paid.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: resistance always sharpens or always dulls a tuned circuit the same way regardless of where it sits. Correction: a series resistor lowers Q by X_L/R and a parallel resistor lowers Q by R/X_L; both lower Q, but the parallel case is the one where a larger resistance means less damping, and either way lower Q means wider bandwidth.", "link": "Reactance & Resonance", "mnemonic": "Swamp the tank, spread the band: a shunt resistor trades selectivity for width.", "edge_cases": "At VHF and above, a 'swamping' resistor may also be a parasitic suppressor; there it is often paralleled with a small coil so it damps only the unwanted high-frequency resonance while leaving the operating frequency tank lightly loaded."}

{"core": "Silicon and germanium are the two Group IV elements whose crystal lattices have a small band gap, so their conductivity sits between that of metals and insulators and can be tuned by doping; they are the elemental semiconductors on which diodes, transistors and ICs are built.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Galena is not an element; it is lead sulphide, a compound mineral. It served as the crystal in early cat's-whisker detectors but is not a modern semiconductor material.", "why_tempting": "Galena's historical role in crystal radios associates it with 'semiconductor' in amateur-radio lore, and germanium beside it is correct."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Galena is a compound, not an element, and bismuth is a semimetal that is not used as a semiconductor device material.", "why_tempting": "Both names sound exotic and 'semi-metallic', and bismuth really is sometimes described as a semimetal, which is a different concept."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Gold is a straightforward metal with no band gap; it is used for contacts and bonding wires in semiconductor packages, not as the semiconducting crystal.", "why_tempting": "Gold appears in device construction (gold-doped diodes, gold bond wires), so it is familiar from datasheets, and silicon is correct."}], "concept": "In a crystalline solid the allowed electron energies form bands; what distinguishes conductors, semiconductors and insulators is the gap between the filled valence band and the empty conduction band. Metals have overlapping bands and conduct freely; insulators have gaps of several electron-volts; silicon (about 1.1 eV) and germanium (about 0.67 eV) have gaps small enough that thermal energy promotes a few electrons across, giving a weak intrinsic conductivity that rises strongly with temperature. Both are Group IV elements with four valence electrons, forming a diamond-cubic lattice in which every atom shares covalent bonds with four neighbours; that structure is what makes substitutional doping with Group III or Group V atoms work. 'Both metallic and non-metallic' is the chemist's description of this intermediate behaviour. Germanium was used first because it is easier to purify, but silicon's larger gap gives lower leakage and higher operating temperature, and its stable native oxide makes planar fabrication possible, which is why it dominates today.", "worked_example": "Compare resistivities at room temperature: copper is about 1.7×10⁻⁸ Ω·m, pure silicon about 2.3×10³ Ω·m, and glass above 10¹⁰ Ω·m. Silicon sits roughly halfway between metal and insulator on a logarithmic scale, which is exactly the 'semi' in semiconductor. Dope that silicon with one phosphorus atom per million silicon atoms and its resistivity falls by several orders of magnitude, something no metal or insulator can be made to do.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: any material that was ever used in a radio detector (galena, carborundum) is a semiconductor element. Correction: the question asks for elements; galena is a compound, and the elemental semiconductors of practical electronics are silicon and germanium.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "Si and Ge, Group IV, four bonds each: the two elements that sit on the fence between metal and non-metal.", "edge_cases": "Compound semiconductors such as gallium arsenide, silicon carbide and gallium nitride matter at microwave and high-power frequencies, but they are compounds of two elements, not single elements, so they do not answer this question."}

{"core": "Gallium arsenide has an electron mobility several times higher than silicon and a semi-insulating substrate, so its transistors and diodes work at microwave frequencies where silicon and germanium devices run out of gain; its direct band gap also makes it useful for LEDs and lasers.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "At low frequencies silicon is cheaper, more mature and has lower leakage; GaAs offers no advantage there and costs far more.", "why_tempting": "A learner who remembers only that GaAs is 'special' may guess at either frequency extreme."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Bipolar transistors are overwhelmingly silicon; GaAs is mainly used for field-effect structures (MESFETs, HEMTs) and for heterojunction bipolar devices only in niche microwave work.", "why_tempting": "'Bipolar transistor' sounds like a general device category, and GaAs is indeed used in transistors, so the association seems safe."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "High-power circuits favour silicon and, more recently, silicon carbide and gallium nitride for their thermal conductivity and voltage rating; GaAs has poor thermal conductivity and is not a power material.", "why_tempting": "High performance is easily confused with high power, and GaAs is known as a high-performance material."}], "concept": "The frequency limit of a transistor is set by how fast carriers cross its active region, which depends on electron mobility and saturation velocity. In GaAs the conduction-band electrons have an effective mass much lower than in silicon, giving a mobility roughly five to six times higher and a higher peak velocity, so a GaAs FET of a given gate length has a transition frequency f_T several times that of a silicon device. GaAs can also be grown as a semi-insulating substrate, which reduces parasitic capacitance to the substrate and allows low-loss microstrip right on the chip, the basis of monolithic microwave ICs. These advantages matter from about 1 GHz upward, which is why GaAs devices appear in satellite LNAs, microwave transverters and cell-phone power amplifiers. The direct band gap, unlike silicon's indirect gap, lets electrons recombine by emitting photons efficiently, which is a separate reason GaAs and its alloys are used for LEDs and laser diodes.", "worked_example": "Suppose a silicon JFET has a transition frequency f_T of about 1 GHz and you need 10 dB of gain at 2.3 GHz. Since gain falls roughly 6 dB per octave above the point where it starts to roll off, the silicon device is at or below unity gain there. A GaAs MESFET with the same gate length but five times the electron mobility has an f_T in the 5 GHz range and still has usable gain at 2.3 GHz, with a lower noise figure because less drain current is needed to achieve the required transconductance.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: GaAs is simply a 'better silicon' and would be used everywhere if it were cheaper. Correction: GaAs wins specifically where carrier speed and substrate isolation matter, that is at microwave frequencies and in optoelectronics; for low-frequency, high-power or dense digital circuits silicon's thermal properties, oxide and maturity make it superior.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "GaAs is for GHz.", "edge_cases": "Since this question was written, silicon-germanium bipolar and gallium-nitride HEMT devices have taken over parts of the microwave and power-microwave markets, but GaAs remains the classic answer and is still dominant in low-noise and handset PA applications."}

{"core": "P-type material is made by doping with a trivalent acceptor such as boron, which leaves a missing bond (a hole) in the lattice; holes become the majority carrier and free electrons, being the minority carrier, are fewer than in the intrinsic crystal.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "'Bipolar' describes a device structure (a transistor using both carrier types), not a kind of doped material.", "why_tempting": "The word appears constantly in semiconductor discussion and sounds like a material classification."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A superconductor is a material with zero resistance below a critical temperature, not a doped semiconductor, and it has an abundance of mobile carriers, not a deficit.", "why_tempting": "It is listed as an exotic conductor category alongside the others and a learner may treat the question as 'which material type is odd'."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "N-type material is doped with donor atoms and has more free electrons than the intrinsic crystal, the opposite of what the question asks.", "why_tempting": "The N stands for negative and electrons are negative, so a learner who inverts the question's wording ('fewer' versus 'more') picks it."}], "concept": "An intrinsic silicon crystal has equal, small numbers of free electrons and holes generated thermally, with n·p = n_i². Substituting a Group III atom such as boron, aluminium or gallium for a silicon atom provides only three valence electrons for four bonds; the unfilled bond is a hole that neighbouring valence electrons can hop into, so the hole moves through the lattice as a positive mobile charge. Each acceptor atom contributes one hole, so the hole concentration p is about equal to the acceptor density N_A, and because the product n·p must remain n_i², the free-electron concentration n = n_i²/N_A falls far below its intrinsic value. That is the precise sense in which P-type material has fewer free electrons than pure silicon: doping does not remove electrons from the crystal, it fills the conduction band's thermal electrons into the new acceptor sites. The P stands for positive, naming the sign of the majority carrier.", "worked_example": "Intrinsic silicon at room temperature has n_i ≈ 1×10¹⁰ cm⁻³ electrons and the same number of holes. Dope it with boron at N_A = 1×10¹⁶ cm⁻³. Then p ≈ 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ and n = n_i²/p = 10²⁰/10¹⁶ = 10⁴ cm⁻³. The free-electron population has dropped by a factor of a million relative to the intrinsic crystal while holes have risen by a million; electrons are now the minority carrier.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: P-type doping adds positive charges to the crystal, making it electrically positive overall. Correction: the crystal stays neutral; the acceptor atoms become fixed negative ions and the mobile holes balance them. 'P' refers to the sign of the mobile majority carrier, not a net charge.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "P for Positive holes, from a three-valent (one short) acceptor.", "edge_cases": "The n·p = n_i² relation holds only in thermal equilibrium; under forward bias or illumination both carrier populations are driven above their equilibrium values, which is exactly what makes diodes conduct and photodiodes respond."}

{"core": "N-type material is doped with pentavalent donor atoms such as phosphorus or arsenic; each contributes a fifth valence electron that is not needed for bonding and is easily freed, so the crystal has far more free electrons than intrinsic silicon or germanium.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "P-type material is doped with acceptors and has fewer free electrons than the intrinsic crystal; its majority carriers are holes.", "why_tempting": "Simple letter confusion, or inverting the question's 'more' into 'fewer', swaps the two doping types."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "'Bipolar' names a transistor structure that uses both electrons and holes, not a category of doped material.", "why_tempting": "It is a ubiquitous semiconductor word and could be misread as 'material with two kinds of carrier'."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A superconductor is a zero-resistance state in certain metals and ceramics at cryogenic temperatures; it is not a doped semiconductor and the question concerns doping.", "why_tempting": "It is the most conductive-sounding option, and 'more free electrons' invites a guess at the strongest conductor."}], "concept": "A Group V donor atom in a silicon lattice uses four of its five valence electrons for covalent bonds with its neighbours; the fifth is bound to the donor only by a weak Coulomb attraction, roughly 0.045 eV in silicon, so at room temperature nearly every donor is ionised and its electron is free in the conduction band. The electron concentration n therefore approximately equals the donor density N_D, typically 10¹⁴ to 10¹⁹ cm⁻³, versus an intrinsic n_i of about 10¹⁰ cm⁻³ in silicon. Because n·p = n_i² at equilibrium, the hole concentration drops to n_i²/N_D, making holes the minority carrier. The donor atoms are left as fixed positive ions, so the material is still electrically neutral overall; the N refers to the negative sign of the mobile majority carrier. Conductivity σ = q(n·μ_n + p·μ_p) rises enormously because n has increased by many orders of magnitude, and since electron mobility is higher than hole mobility, N-type material of a given doping is more conductive than P-type at the same density.", "worked_example": "Dope silicon with phosphorus at N_D = 1×10¹⁵ cm⁻³. Then n ≈ 10¹⁵ cm⁻³, a hundred-thousand-fold increase over n_i ≈ 10¹⁰, and p = n_i²/n = 10²⁰/10¹⁵ = 10⁵ cm⁻³. With μ_n ≈ 1350 cm²/V·s the resistivity is about 1/(1.6×10⁻¹⁹ × 10¹⁵ × 1350) ≈ 4.6 Ω·cm, compared with about 2.3×10⁵ Ω·cm for the intrinsic crystal.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: an N-type crystal carries a net negative charge because extra electrons were added. Correction: each extra electron came with a donor nucleus carrying an extra proton, so the crystal is neutral; N describes the sign of the mobile carriers, not the net charge of the material.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "N for Negative electrons, from a five-valent (one extra) donor.", "edge_cases": "At very high doping (degenerate, above about 10¹⁹ cm⁻³) the simple picture breaks down, the Fermi level enters the conduction band and the material behaves almost like a metal; this is deliberately used for ohmic contacts and for tunnel diodes."}

{"core": "P-type material is doped with trivalent acceptors that leave vacant bonding sites; those vacancies, holes, behave as mobile positive charges and vastly outnumber free electrons, so holes are the majority carrier.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Protons are bound in atomic nuclei and are not mobile in a solid crystal; nothing in semiconductor conduction involves free protons.", "why_tempting": "Holes act like positive charges and protons are the positive particle a learner knows, so the two are easily conflated."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Neutrons have no charge and are bound in nuclei; they cannot carry current at all.", "why_tempting": "Listed alongside protons and electrons it looks like a legitimate particle choice for a learner guessing among subatomic names."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Free electrons are the minority carrier in P-type material; they are the majority carrier in N-type.", "why_tempting": "Electrons are the only carrier in metals and the familiar one from Basic-level theory, so a learner may assume they carry current everywhere."}], "concept": "A hole is not a particle but the absence of an electron in a covalent bond, which the lattice treats as a mobile positive charge: when a neighbouring valence electron moves into the vacancy, the vacancy appears to move the other way. In P-type silicon the acceptor density N_A sets the hole concentration p ≈ N_A, while the electron concentration is suppressed to n_i²/N_A by the equilibrium relation n·p = n_i². Majority carriers dominate conduction in the bulk; minority carriers matter at junctions, where they are injected across the depletion region and control diode and transistor behaviour. Hole mobility in silicon (about 480 cm²/V·s) is less than electron mobility (about 1350 cm²/V·s), so P-type material of a given doping is somewhat more resistive than N-type, and PNP transistors are slower than NPN of comparable geometry. The sign convention follows directly: a current of holes moving left is physically the same as a current of electrons moving right, and conventional current points with the holes.", "worked_example": "Thought experiment: apply a field across a P-type bar. Valence electrons hop into adjacent holes against the field, so each hole steps along the field direction. If a bar carries 10 mA and the hole density is 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ in a 1 mm² cross-section, the hole drift velocity is I/(q·p·A) = 0.01/(1.6×10⁻¹⁹ × 10²² m⁻³ × 10⁻⁶ m²) ≈ 6 m/s, a quite real and measurable motion of the vacancies even though no positive particle moves.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a hole is a positively charged particle, perhaps a proton, moving through the crystal. Correction: a hole is a vacancy in the valence bonding; its motion is the collective motion of bound electrons, but it carries charge, momentum and an effective mass just like a particle, so treating it as a positive carrier is exact for circuit purposes.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "P-type, Positive holes; N-type, Negative electrons.", "edge_cases": "The Hall effect confirms the hole picture: a P-type sample develops a Hall voltage of the opposite sign to an N-type sample, which would be impossible if only electrons were moving."}
