{"core": "N-type material is doped with pentavalent donors whose fifth valence electron is loosely bound and thermally freed into the conduction band; those free electrons outnumber holes by many orders of magnitude and are the majority carrier.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Holes are the minority carrier in N-type material; they are the majority carrier in P-type.", "why_tempting": "Swapping the letters, or reasoning that 'N' means 'no electrons', inverts the answer."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Protons are locked in atomic nuclei and never move as current carriers in a solid.", "why_tempting": "A learner thinking in terms of 'positive and negative particles' may reach for the proton as the positive counterpart to the electron."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Neutrons are uncharged and bound in nuclei; they can neither move freely in a crystal nor carry charge.", "why_tempting": "It appears as one of three subatomic particles and may be chosen by a learner guessing among particle names."}], "concept": "Substituting a Group V atom (phosphorus, arsenic, antimony) into the silicon lattice supplies one more valence electron than the four bonds require. That electron sits in a shallow donor level a few hundredths of an electron-volt below the conduction band, so at room temperature it is essentially always freed. The electron concentration n is then about equal to the donor density N_D, and the hole concentration is suppressed to n_i²/N_D by the mass-action law. The crystal remains neutral because each freed electron leaves a fixed positive donor ion. Conduction in the bulk is dominated by these electrons, with conductivity σ ≈ q·n·μ_n; their higher mobility compared with holes is why N-channel FETs and NPN transistors generally offer better high-frequency performance than their P-type counterparts. Minority holes in N-type material still matter: they are what is injected from a P region under forward bias and what constitutes the leakage current in reverse bias.", "worked_example": "If N-type silicon is doped at N_D = 5×10¹⁵ cm⁻³ then n ≈ 5×10¹⁵ cm⁻³ and p = n_i²/n = (10¹⁰)²/(5×10¹⁵) = 2×10⁴ cm⁻³. The ratio of majority to minority carriers is 2.5×10¹¹; for practical purposes the material conducts entirely by electrons. If the temperature rises so that n_i doubles, p quadruples but n is unchanged, which is why minority-carrier leakage is so strongly temperature dependent while majority-carrier conduction is not.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the N in N-type means the material has a net negative charge or has had electrons pumped into it from outside. Correction: the extra electrons came from the donor atoms built into the crystal; N labels the sign of the majority mobile carrier, and the crystal as a whole is neutral.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "Donors give, so N-type has extra electrons; acceptors take, so P-type has holes.", "edge_cases": "In germanium the intrinsic carrier density is about a thousand times higher than in silicon, so at the same doping level the minority-carrier population and hence the leakage are far larger, which is one reason germanium devices were abandoned for most purposes."}

{"core": "Pure, undoped silicon has very few thermally generated carriers at room temperature (about 10¹⁰ per cm³ against 5×10²² atoms), giving a resistivity in the hundreds of kΩ·cm; for practical purposes it behaves as an insulator until doping or heat supplies carriers. Among the four options, 'an insulator' best describes its intrinsic electrical behaviour, which is the point the examiners want made.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "'Semiconductor' names the material class, but the question asks how silicon behaves in its pure form; intrinsic silicon is so poorly conducting that it functions as an insulator, and only doping brings out the useful semiconducting behaviour.", "why_tempting": "Silicon is the archetypal semiconductor, so this is the reflexive answer; the question is deliberately probing the difference between the material class and its undoped behaviour."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A conductor has a partially filled band and carriers of order 10²² per cm³; intrinsic silicon has twelve orders of magnitude fewer and conducts negligibly.", "why_tempting": "Silicon is used to make things that conduct and switch, so a learner may assume the raw material is itself a conductor."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Superconductivity is a zero-resistance state found in certain metals and compounds below a critical temperature; silicon is not a superconductor under any normal condition.", "why_tempting": "It is the most impressive-sounding option and may be picked as 'the special property of silicon' by a learner who has heard both words together."}], "concept": "Intrinsic silicon has a band gap of about 1.1 eV, and the probability of an electron being thermally excited across it scales roughly as exp(−E_g/(2kT)); at 300 K that gives an intrinsic carrier density n_i of about 10¹⁰ cm⁻³, which is a vanishingly small fraction of the atoms. Resistivity ρ = 1/(q·n_i·(μ_n + μ_p)) works out to roughly 2×10⁵ Ω·cm, which is insulator territory compared with the few μΩ·cm of a metal. The semiconducting character is latent: it emerges when doping adds carriers (raising conductivity by many orders of magnitude), when temperature rises (n_i roughly doubles every 8 to 10 °C in silicon), or when light creates electron-hole pairs. This is why the exam's phrasing distinguishes 'pure silicon' from 'semiconductor devices': the raw crystal is a good insulator, and controllable conductivity is engineered into it. Germanium, with its smaller 0.67 eV gap, has n_i about a thousand times higher and is a noticeably poorer insulator when pure.", "worked_example": "Estimate the resistance of a 1 cm cube of intrinsic silicon: ρ ≈ 2.3×10⁵ Ω·cm, so R = ρ·L/A = 2.3×10⁵ × 1/1 ≈ 230 kΩ. Now dope it with boron at 10¹⁶ cm⁻³: ρ ≈ 1/(1.6×10⁻¹⁹ × 10¹⁶ × 480) ≈ 1.3 Ω·cm, so the same cube is about 1.3 Ω. A factor of nearly 200,000 from one part in five million of impurity is the whole basis of semiconductor engineering.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: silicon is a semiconductor, so it must be moderately conductive in any form. Correction: 'semiconductor' describes a material whose conductivity can be controlled; in its pure, cold state that conductivity is so low that it is an insulator, and devices only work because doping and junctions are added.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "Pure silicon is a blank slate: it insulates until you dope it.", "edge_cases": "Strictly, physicists class intrinsic silicon as a semiconductor by its band structure regardless of its resistivity; the exam's answer reflects engineering behaviour at room temperature, and the companion question A-002-001-010 uses the same convention."}

{"core": "A semiconductor is a material whose conductivity lies between that of conductors and insulators and, crucially, can be switched between those extremes by doping, temperature, light or applied voltage; that controllable dual behaviour is its defining property.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "N-type describes a doped semiconductor whose majority carriers are electrons; it is a subcategory, not the name of the material class, and it is not itself 'sometimes an insulator'.", "why_tempting": "N-type is a term from the same vocabulary and a learner may think any doped material counts as the answer."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "P-type names hole-majority doped material, a subcategory of semiconductor, not the general class the question describes.", "why_tempting": "Like N-type, it is a familiar label from the same topic and sounds like a kind of 'conductor'."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "'Intrinsic' describes an undoped semiconductor; 'intrinsic conductor' is not a standard term and does not capture the sometimes-conducting, sometimes-insulating behaviour.", "why_tempting": "The word intrinsic is genuinely used in semiconductor physics, so the phrase sounds authoritative."}], "concept": "Band theory explains the dual behaviour. In a semiconductor the valence band is full and the conduction band empty at absolute zero, separated by a modest gap of around 0.5 to 3 eV, so with no excitation the material cannot conduct and behaves as an insulator. Thermal energy, photons or impurity atoms can place electrons in the conduction band or holes in the valence band, and then the material conducts; the number of carriers, and hence the conductivity, spans many orders of magnitude depending on these conditions. A PN junction exploits this further: under reverse bias the depletion region is swept of carriers and the device is an insulator, under forward bias carriers flood across and it is a conductor. That voltage-controlled switching between the two states, within one piece of material, is what distinguishes a semiconductor from a resistor that merely has a middling resistance. Silicon and germanium are the elemental examples; gallium arsenide, silicon carbide and others are compound semiconductors.", "worked_example": "A silicon diode illustrates the dual nature in one component. Reverse biased at 10 V it passes perhaps 10 nA, an effective resistance of 1 GΩ: an insulator. Forward biased at 0.7 V it passes 100 mA, an effective resistance of 7 Ω: a conductor. The same crystal has changed its behaviour by eight orders of magnitude solely because of the applied voltage.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a semiconductor is simply a material with a resistance somewhere between copper and glass, like a carbon resistor. Correction: the defining feature is that its conductivity is variable and controllable; a fixed mid-range resistance is not semiconduction.", "link": "section 2", "edge_cases": "A thermistor made of a semiconducting oxide shows the same dual nature through temperature alone, dropping from megohms when cold to ohms when hot, which is why NTC thermistors are built from semiconductors rather than metals."}

{"core": "Silicon is a Group IV element with a 1.1 eV band gap and a diamond-cubic crystal that accepts substitutional dopants; it is the material from which the vast majority of diodes, transistors and integrated circuits are made.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Copper is a metal with overlapping bands and about 10²² free electrons per cm³; its conductivity cannot be modulated by doping, so it is a conductor, not a semiconductor.", "why_tempting": "Copper is the most familiar electrical material and is used for traces and wires in every semiconductor assembly."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Sulphur is a molecular, non-crystalline insulator with a large band gap; it is not used as a semiconductor substrate.", "why_tempting": "Sulphur does appear in semiconductor compounds (lead sulphide, cadmium sulphide) and in early galena detectors, so the association exists."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Tantalum is a refractory metal; it is used for the electrodes of tantalum electrolytic capacitors, not as a semiconducting crystal.", "why_tempting": "Tantalum is a component material seen on parts lists alongside semiconductors, so it is a plausible-looking distractor."}], "concept": "A useful semiconductor needs three things: a band gap small enough that thermal or applied energy can create carriers but large enough that leakage is controllable at operating temperature; a crystal lattice in which impurity atoms of adjacent valence can substitute for host atoms and contribute carriers; and a practical means of growing, purifying and processing it. Silicon satisfies all three, with the bonus of a stable, insulating native oxide (SiO₂) that enables planar processing and MOS gates. Germanium works too but its smaller band gap gives higher leakage and a lower maximum junction temperature, and it lacks a good native oxide. Metals such as copper and tantalum fail the first criterion outright because they have no band gap; insulators such as sulphur fail because their gap is too large and their structure does not support controlled doping. Compound semiconductors such as gallium arsenide and silicon carbide are engineered to shift the band gap and mobility for specialised uses, but elemental silicon remains the workhorse.", "worked_example": "Thought experiment: try to make a transistor out of copper. With 8×10²² free electrons per cm³ already present, adding a dopant at 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ changes the carrier count by one part in ten million, so no junction, depletion region or gate field can switch it. In silicon the same dopant raises the carrier density from 10¹⁰ to 10¹⁶ cm⁻³, a millionfold change, and a few volts across a junction can deplete or flood a region entirely. The band gap is what makes the material controllable.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: any element that shows up in electronic components is a semiconductor material. Correction: only elements with a suitable band gap and dopable crystal structure qualify; silicon and germanium are the elemental semiconductors, while copper, tantalum and sulphur play other roles (conductor, capacitor electrode, compound ingredient).", "link": "section 2"}

{"core": "Undoped silicon has an intrinsic carrier density of only about 10¹⁰ cm⁻³ at room temperature, giving a resistivity around 2×10⁵ Ω·cm; it conducts so poorly that in practice it is a good insulator until impurities are added to supply carriers.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A tuned circuit is a combination of inductance and capacitance, not a property of a material; the question is about the electrical nature of pure silicon.", "why_tempting": "It is an electronics term placed among the options to catch a learner skimming for familiar words."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "An inductor is a component that stores energy in a magnetic field; a block of pure silicon is not an inductor and the question concerns conductivity.", "why_tempting": "Another component name that may be chosen if the learner does not read the question as asking about conductive behaviour."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A conductor has free carriers of order 10²² cm⁻³; intrinsic silicon has roughly a trillion times fewer and has an effective resistance that is enormous by comparison.", "why_tempting": "Silicon is known as the basis of electronics and a learner may assume the raw material conducts well."}], "concept": "In an intrinsic semiconductor every carrier must be thermally generated across the band gap, and the number created scales roughly as T^(3/2)·exp(−E_g/(2kT)). For silicon's 1.1 eV gap this gives about 10¹⁰ cm⁻³ electrons and an equal number of holes at 300 K; with mobilities of 1350 and 480 cm²/V·s that is a resistivity of about 2.3×10⁵ Ω·cm. Doping replaces this feeble thermal supply with a fixed population of carriers set by the impurity concentration, and the resistivity can then be anything from about 10⁻³ Ω·cm (heavily doped, nearly metallic) to tens of Ω·cm (lightly doped), under the designer's control. The practical consequences follow: intrinsic or very lightly doped regions are used where an insulating or high-resistance layer is needed, for example the I layer of a PIN diode or the drift region of a high-voltage device, and heavy doping is used for contacts and low-resistance paths. The word 'usually' in the question acknowledges that temperature or light can make pure silicon conduct, but under ordinary conditions it insulates.", "worked_example": "A 10 mm × 1 mm × 1 mm bar of intrinsic silicon has R = ρ·L/A = 2.3×10⁵ Ω·cm × 1 cm / 0.01 cm² ≈ 2.3×10⁷ Ω, or 23 MΩ. Heat it to about 100 °C and n_i rises roughly a hundredfold, dropping R to a few hundred kΩ, still a poor conductor. Dope the same bar with phosphorus at 10¹⁷ cm⁻³ and R falls to about 0.1 Ω·cm × 1/0.01 ≈ 10 Ω.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: because silicon conducts in a transistor, pure silicon must be a decent conductor. Correction: the conduction in a transistor comes from doped regions and injected carriers; the pure crystal has almost no carriers and insulates.", "link": "section 2", "edge_cases": "At elevated temperature the intrinsic carrier density grows exponentially and can eventually exceed the doping level, at which point a doped region 'goes intrinsic' and the device loses its junctions; this sets the maximum junction temperature of silicon devices at roughly 150 to 200 °C."}

{"core": "Doping means deliberately introducing trace amounts of impurity atoms, typically a few parts per million or less, of a valence different from the host (Group III or Group V for silicon) to supply holes or free electrons and thereby set the crystal's conductivity and carrier type.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Protons cannot be added to a crystal as free particles; adding protons to nuclei would change the element entirely, which is not what doping does.", "why_tempting": "Doping creates positive carriers (holes) in P-type material and the proton is the familiar positive particle, so a learner may link the two."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Although dopant atoms become ionised once in the lattice, doping is not the addition of free ions; the impurity is introduced as neutral atoms that substitute for host atoms during crystal growth, diffusion or implantation.", "why_tempting": "In ion implantation the dopant is accelerated as an ion beam, and the fixed donor or acceptor sites are often called ions, so the word has a real but secondary connection."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Free electrons cannot be stored in a crystal in significant numbers; injecting electrons would make the crystal strongly negatively charged. N-type material gains electrons only because each comes paired with a donor nucleus.", "why_tempting": "The outcome of N-type doping is more free electrons, so the cause and the effect are easy to confuse."}], "concept": "A pure semiconductor crystal has equal, tiny numbers of electrons and holes. Replacing a small fraction of the host atoms with impurities of a different valence changes this: a Group V donor such as phosphorus brings one surplus valence electron that is freed into the conduction band, making N-type material; a Group III acceptor such as boron is one electron short, creating a hole, making P-type material. Because the dopant sits substitutionally in the lattice, each impurity atom contributes exactly one carrier, so the carrier concentration equals the dopant concentration and the conductivity σ = q·N·μ is set precisely by how much impurity is added. The quantities are minute, often one dopant per 10⁶ to 10⁸ host atoms, which is why the starting silicon must be purified to better than one part in 10⁹ before doping is meaningful. Doping is also what creates junctions: a P region adjacent to an N region in the same crystal forms the depletion layer whose asymmetric conduction underlies every diode and transistor. The crystal remains electrically neutral throughout, because each mobile carrier is balanced by a fixed ionised dopant atom.", "worked_example": "Silicon has about 5×10²² atoms per cm³. Doping with boron to 5×10¹⁶ cm⁻³ means one boron atom per million silicon atoms. That trace changes the hole density from 10¹⁰ to 5×10¹⁶ cm⁻³ and the resistivity from about 2×10⁵ Ω·cm to about 0.3 Ω·cm, a change of nearly a million times from an impurity level that a chemist would describe as 99.9999% pure silicon.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: doping means injecting charge (electrons or ions) into the crystal to make it conductive. Correction: doping is the substitution of neutral impurity atoms into the lattice; the carriers are released by those atoms once in place, and the crystal stays neutral.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "Dope with atoms, not with charge: the impurity brings its own carrier.", "edge_cases": "Unintentional impurities such as gold or iron create deep levels in the band gap that trap carriers and shorten lifetime; that is sometimes done on purpose (gold doping for fast switching diodes) but it is a different mechanism from the shallow donor and acceptor doping that sets carrier type."}

{"core": "A Zener diode is operated in reverse breakdown, where a large change in current produces only a tiny change in voltage across it; that near-constant reverse voltage, set by the doping and junction design, is the property exploited for voltage references and shunt regulators.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A voltage-dependent junction capacitance is the defining property of a varactor diode; every reverse-biased diode has some, but it is not what a Zener is built or used for.", "why_tempting": "Both devices are reverse-biased in normal use, so a learner may muddle which reverse-bias property belongs to which."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Constant current under varying voltage describes a current-regulator diode (a JFET with gate tied to source) or a current source; a Zener's current varies freely while its voltage stays fixed, which is the opposite behaviour.", "why_tempting": "It is the dual of the correct statement with current and voltage swapped, a classic inverted-ratio distractor."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Negative resistance, where current falls as voltage rises, is the property of a tunnel diode or Gunn device; a Zener in breakdown has a very low positive dynamic resistance.", "why_tempting": "Breakdown sounds like an abrupt, unusual region of the curve and a learner may associate any sharp knee with negative resistance."}], "concept": "In reverse bias a PN junction normally passes only a small leakage current until the field in the depletion region becomes high enough to break down. Two mechanisms exist: Zener breakdown, in which the field is strong enough for valence electrons to tunnel directly across a very thin depletion layer (dominant below about 5 V, heavy doping), and avalanche breakdown, in which accelerated carriers knock loose further pairs in a chain reaction (dominant above about 6 V, lighter doping). Both produce a steep current rise at a well-defined reverse voltage V_Z. The slope of the breakdown curve is the dynamic resistance r_z = ΔV/ΔI, typically a few ohms to a few tens of ohms, so a current swing of tens of milliamps moves the voltage by only tens of millivolts. In a shunt regulator a series resistor R_s drops the excess supply voltage, and the Zener absorbs whatever current the load does not take; the output stays at V_Z as long as the Zener current remains above its knee. Power dissipation P = V_Z × I_Z must be respected, and the temperature coefficient is negative for Zener-mechanism parts and positive for avalanche parts, crossing near zero at about 5.6 V.", "worked_example": "Design a 5.6 V shunt regulator from a 12 V supply for a 20 mA load. Choose a Zener current of 10 mA at full load so the total through R_s is 30 mA: R_s = (12 − 5.6)/0.030 ≈ 213 Ω, use 220 Ω. If the load disconnects, all 29 mA flows in the Zener: P = 5.6 × 0.029 ≈ 0.16 W, so a 400 mW part is adequate. With r_z = 10 Ω the output shifts by only 10 × 0.020 = 0.2 V between no load and full load, illustrating constant voltage under varying current.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a Zener diode is a special kind of forward-conducting diode with a higher threshold. Correction: it is used in reverse breakdown; its forward behaviour is that of an ordinary silicon diode, and the regulated voltage appears only when the cathode is positive with respect to the anode.", "link": "section 4", "mnemonic": "Zener: reverse it, and it holds its voltage.", "edge_cases": "Below about 3 V the breakdown knee becomes soft and the dynamic resistance rises to hundreds of ohms, so low-voltage Zeners regulate poorly; band-gap reference ICs are preferred there. Above about 6 V the avalanche mechanism dominates and the device is still called a Zener by convention."}

{"core": "A varactor (varicap) diode is operated in reverse bias so that its depletion layer widens with increasing voltage; since the depletion layer acts as the dielectric of a capacitor, the junction capacitance falls as the reverse voltage rises, giving a voltage-controlled capacitance.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A Schottky diode is valued for its fast switching and low forward drop; its capacitance is deliberately made small and is not the exploited property.", "why_tempting": "Schottky diodes are used at VHF and UHF, where capacitance matters, so the two 'RF diode' types can be confused."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "A Zener diode exploits a constant reverse breakdown voltage; while it has junction capacitance like any diode, that is not its defining or useful characteristic.", "why_tempting": "Both Zener and varactor are reverse-biased in normal operation, so the two reverse-bias properties get swapped."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A silicon-controlled rectifier is a four-layer latching switch triggered by a gate pulse; it is a power-control device with no role as a variable capacitor.", "why_tempting": "It is the most complex-sounding device in the list and may be chosen by a learner who associates 'controlled' with 'variable'."}], "concept": "A reverse-biased PN junction has a depletion region of width W that grows roughly as the square root of the total junction voltage (built-in potential plus applied reverse bias) for an abruptly doped junction. The depleted region contains no mobile carriers and behaves as an insulator sandwiched between two conducting regions, so the junction has a capacitance C_j = εA/W. Because W increases with reverse voltage, C_j decreases: for an abrupt junction C_j ∝ (V_bi + V_R)^(−1/2), and hyperabrupt doping profiles are engineered to give a steeper law, approaching C ∝ V^(−2), which makes a tank's resonant frequency vary nearly linearly with control voltage. Typical varactors offer a few picofarads to a few hundred picofarads over a 2 to 30 V range with capacitance ratios of 3:1 to 10:1 or more. Applications include voltage-controlled oscillators in PLL synthesisers, electronic tuning of filters, automatic frequency control, and frequency modulation by applying the audio to the varactor bias. The diode must stay reverse biased at all times, so the RF swing must be kept well below the DC bias, and the varactor's Q (set by its series resistance) limits the Q of any tank it tunes.", "worked_example": "A VCO tank uses L = 1 μH with a varactor giving 30 pF at 2 V and 10 pF at 20 V. At 2 V: f = 1/(2π√(1×10⁻⁶ × 30×10⁻¹²)) ≈ 29.1 MHz. At 20 V: f = 1/(2π√(1×10⁻⁶ × 10×10⁻¹²)) ≈ 50.3 MHz. A 3:1 capacitance ratio gives a √3 ≈ 1.73:1 frequency ratio, confirming the square-root law from f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)).", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a varactor's capacitance increases with voltage, as more voltage somehow stores more charge. Correction: more reverse voltage widens the depletion layer, which is the dielectric gap, so capacitance decreases with increasing reverse voltage; the relationship is inverse.", "link": "Reactance & Resonance", "mnemonic": "More reverse volts, wider gap, less capacitance.", "edge_cases": "Every diode is a varactor to some degree; the junction capacitance of a Schottky mixer diode or a rectifier limits its high-frequency performance, and the voltage dependence of a transistor's collector-base capacitance is a classic source of unwanted FM in oscillators and distortion in amplifiers."}

{"core": "A Schottky diode is a metal-semiconductor junction that conducts by majority carriers only, so it has no minority-carrier storage, switches in picoseconds and has a low forward drop; those properties make it the standard choice for mixers and detectors at VHF, UHF and microwave frequencies.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Balanced mixers are used in SSB generation and frequency conversion, not FM generation, which is done by varying an oscillator's frequency; the option misattributes the mixer's role.", "why_tempting": "Schottky diodes really are used in balanced mixers, so the first half of the statement rings true and the FM error can slip past."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A voltage-variable capacitance in an AFC circuit is the role of a varactor diode, whose junction capacitance is deliberately exploited; a Schottky diode is designed to minimise capacitance.", "why_tempting": "AFC is a receiver function and Schottky diodes are receiver components, so the association is loose but plausible."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "A constant-voltage reference is a Zener diode function; a Schottky diode's reverse breakdown is comparatively low and soft, and it is not used as a regulator.", "why_tempting": "A learner who has confused the diode types may match 'hot-carrier' with the power-supply context by elimination."}], "concept": "In a Schottky (hot-carrier) diode a metal such as platinum or titanium silicide contacts N-type silicon or GaAs. Current flows when majority electrons in the semiconductor have enough energy to surmount the metal-semiconductor barrier, typically 0.2 to 0.4 V, and once in the metal they are simply more metal electrons; no minority carriers are injected into the semiconductor, so there is no stored charge to sweep out when the diode turns off. The absence of reverse-recovery time means the diode follows signals into the tens of GHz, and the low barrier gives a sharp exponential curve near zero bias, which is what a mixer or envelope detector needs: mixing relies on the diode's nonlinearity to multiply the RF and LO signals, and the conversion loss and noise figure depend on how little drive is wasted overcoming the forward drop. Small junction area keeps capacitance to a fraction of a picofarad. Compared with a PN diode, which stores minority carriers and has a 0.6 to 0.7 V knee, the Schottky is faster and more sensitive; compared with a point-contact diode, it is far more rugged and reproducible.", "worked_example": "Compare detector sensitivity: an envelope detector must rectify a 20 mV peak RF signal. A silicon PN diode with a 0.6 V knee barely conducts and the detector output is in the microvolt range. A Schottky with a 0.25 V barrier operates in its square-law region at this level and gives a usable output; biasing it with a few microamps lowers the effective threshold further. For a 1296 MHz mixer the Schottky's sub-picofarad capacitance and absence of recovery time mean the diode can switch at the LO rate, whereas a PN diode's stored charge would smear the switching and raise conversion loss by many dB.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: all diodes rectify equally well and the choice between types is about current rating. Correction: at VHF and above the limiting factors are minority-carrier storage and junction capacitance; the Schottky's majority-carrier conduction removes storage entirely, which is why it dominates RF mixing and detection.", "link": "section 6", "mnemonic": "Hot carriers, no storage: Schottky for speed.", "edge_cases": "Schottky diodes have higher reverse leakage and lower breakdown voltage than PN diodes of similar size, so in power rectification they are limited to low-voltage, high-current roles such as switching supplies and reverse-polarity protection; their RF use is a separate strength."}

{"core": "Forward current dissipates power in the diode (P ≈ V_F × I_F plus I²R in the bulk), raising the junction temperature; above a limit, typically 150 to 175 °C for silicon, the crystal's properties degrade and it fails, so the maximum forward current rating is set by the junction temperature that the package and heatsinking can hold.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Peak inverse voltage is the maximum reverse voltage before breakdown; it concerns the reverse-biased condition and says nothing about how much forward current the device can carry.", "why_tempting": "PIV is the other headline diode rating, so a learner recalling 'the two ratings' may pick it without checking which applies."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The forward voltage is the drop across the conducting diode (about 0.7 V for silicon); it is a consequence of current, not a limit on it, and it rises only slowly with current.", "why_tempting": "Forward voltage appears in the power calculation and in every datasheet, so it is easy to mistake a factor for a limit."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Back EMF is a voltage induced by a collapsing magnetic field in an inductor; it relates to why diodes are placed across relay coils, not to what limits the diode's forward current.", "why_tempting": "Flyback diodes across inductive loads are a common diode application, so 'back EMF' is a familiar phrase in diode contexts."}], "concept": "A conducting diode dissipates P = V_F·I_F, where V_F is roughly 0.7 V for silicon at modest current and rises with the I·R_s drop in the bulk material at high current. That heat flows from the junction through the die, package and leads to the ambient with a thermal resistance θ_JA (junction to ambient), so the junction temperature is T_J = T_A + P·θ_JA. Silicon junctions are rated for a maximum T_J of about 150 to 175 °C; beyond that, intrinsic carrier generation becomes comparable to the doping, leakage soars, the junction can no longer block reverse voltage, and localised hot spots cause thermal runaway and metallurgical damage. The manufacturer's maximum forward current rating is therefore the current at which P·θ_JA raises T_J to its limit for a stated mounting and ambient temperature, which is why the same die has a higher current rating in a larger package or on a heatsink, and why datasheets derate current against case or ambient temperature. Surge ratings (I_FSM) are higher because a brief pulse does not have time to heat the junction fully. Germanium devices have a lower maximum T_J, around 85 to 100 °C, which is part of why they were superseded.", "worked_example": "A diode in a TO-220 package has θ_JA = 60 °C/W in free air and a maximum T_J of 150 °C. At 40 °C ambient the allowed dissipation is (150 − 40)/60 ≈ 1.8 W. With V_F ≈ 0.9 V at high current, the sustainable forward current is about 1.8/0.9 = 2 A. Bolt it to a heatsink bringing θ_JA to 10 °C/W and the allowance rises to 11 W, or about 10 A at a V_F of 1.1 V: same diode, five times the current, purely because the junction temperature is held down.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a diode's current rating is a fixed property of the silicon like its PIV. Correction: it is a thermal rating; the die would pass far more current if it could be kept cool, and the number on the datasheet is tied to a specific package, mounting and ambient temperature.", "link": "section 4", "mnemonic": "Current makes heat, heat kills junctions: the limit is temperature.", "edge_cases": "At very high current, current crowding at the edge of the die and the resistance of the bond wires set additional limits, and in pulse applications the surge rating rather than the thermal rating applies; both are still ultimately about keeping local temperature below the damage threshold."}

{"core": "The two ratings that define a rectifier diode's safe operating envelope are the maximum average forward current, limited by junction heating, and the peak inverse voltage, the largest reverse voltage it can block without breakdown; exceeding either destroys the device.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Capacitance is a parameter that matters for RF and switching performance but it is not a maximum rating that bounds safe operation; a diode is not damaged by having too much capacitance.", "why_tempting": "Junction capacitance is listed on datasheets and matters for varactors and RF diodes, so it looks like a key specification."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Maximum reverse current is a leakage specification (a few microamps at rated PIV), a performance figure rather than a limit; the current that must be rated is the forward current the diode carries in use.", "why_tempting": "Pairing 'reverse current' with 'peak inverse voltage' sounds consistent, both being reverse-bias quantities, which disguises that one is a rating and the other a characteristic."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Neither reverse current nor capacitance is a limiting rating; both are measured characteristics that describe performance within the safe region.", "why_tempting": "It sounds technical and both terms appear on every diode datasheet, so it can pass as the 'advanced' answer."}], "concept": "A junction diode has two failure modes and a rating for each. In the forward direction, current produces dissipation V_F·I_F that raises the junction temperature; the maximum forward current (I_F(AV) for average, I_FSM for surge) is the level at which the junction reaches its thermal limit for a specified package and ambient. In the reverse direction, the depletion layer must sustain the full applied voltage; when the field becomes high enough, avalanche or Zener breakdown occurs and, unless the current is limited as in a Zener diode, the resulting dissipation destroys the junction. The peak inverse voltage (PIV, also PRV or V_RRM) rating is the maximum reverse voltage the device will withstand. In a power supply the PIV seen by each diode depends on the circuit: a half-wave or full-wave centre-tap rectifier with a capacitor-input filter subjects each diode to about twice the peak secondary voltage, while a bridge subjects each to about one peak. Designers apply a safety margin on both ratings, commonly derating PIV by half and keeping forward current well below the maximum for the expected heatsinking, and add transient protection because line spikes can exceed the steady-state PIV.", "worked_example": "A full-wave centre-tapped supply uses a 24 V-0-24 V RMS secondary with a capacitor-input filter and delivers 1 A DC. Peak voltage per half is 24 × √2 ≈ 34 V. Each diode sees PIV ≈ 2 × 34 = 68 V, so a 100 V part gives margin and a 200 V part is better against transients. Each diode conducts on alternate half cycles with an average current of about 0.5 A, but capacitor-input filters draw brief high-peak pulses, so a 1 A or 3 A rated diode is prudent. Those two numbers, PIV and forward current, are the whole selection.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the important diode numbers are forward voltage drop and capacitance because they appear in every circuit calculation. Correction: those are characteristics; the ratings that define whether the diode survives are maximum forward current (thermal) and peak inverse voltage (breakdown).", "link": "section 4", "mnemonic": "A diode has two walls: too much current forward, too much voltage backward.", "edge_cases": "For switching supplies a third parameter, reverse recovery time, becomes a practical limit because slow recovery causes heating and EMI even within the current and PIV ratings; and for Zener diodes the reverse 'limit' is deliberately exceeded and the real rating is power dissipation."}

{"core": "Semiconductor diodes are classified structurally by how the rectifying barrier is formed: a junction diode has a p-n (or metal-semiconductor) interface grown or diffused across the whole die, while a point contact diode forms its barrier where a sharp metal whisker presses on a semiconductor surface. Those two construction methods are the two main categories.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "An electrolytic device is a capacitor technology (an oxide dielectric formed electrochemically on aluminium or tantalum), not a diode structure. It has polarity, but it stores charge rather than rectifying.", "why_tempting": "Electrolytic capacitors are polarized and marked with + and −, so a learner can confuse polarity with rectification."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "A vacuum diode rectifies by thermionic emission from a heated cathode in an evacuated envelope; it is not a semiconductor at all, so it cannot be a category of semiconductor diode.", "why_tempting": "Vacuum diodes were the original rectifiers and many texts introduce diodes historically, so the term sits next to point contact in memory."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Point contact is a legitimate category, but electrolytic is a capacitor construction, so this pair is half right and therefore wrong.", "why_tempting": "Pairing the one familiar true term with a polarized-sounding partner reads plausibly if you only recognize point contact."}], "concept": "Every diode needs a potential barrier that lets carriers cross easily in one direction and poorly in the other. In a junction diode that barrier is the depletion region of a p-n junction formed inside the crystal by doping, giving a relatively large junction area; large area means high current capability but also large junction capacitance, C_j ∝ A/W where W is the depletion width. In a point contact diode a sharp tungsten or gold whisker touches an n-type crystal (classically germanium) and a tiny rectifying region forms under the tip, giving an extremely small contact area and therefore picofarad-or-less capacitance. The trade is current handling against speed: large-area junctions for power rectification, point contacts (and their modern descendant, the Schottky barrier) for detection and mixing at RF and microwave frequencies. This structural split is the frame for the rest of the diode subsection: PIN, Zener, varactor and Schottky diodes are all variations on where and how the barrier is built.", "worked_example": "Compare a 1N4007 power rectifier (junction, die area on the order of a square millimetre, C_j around 15 pF at reverse bias) with a 1N34A point contact germanium diode (C_j under 1 pF). At 100 MHz the reactance X_C = 1/(2πfC) is roughly 106 Ω for 15 pF but about 1.6 kΩ for 1 pF, so RF signal leaks straight through the big junction's capacitance while the point contact still behaves like a switch. That is why structure, not just material, defines the category.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: diodes are categorized by material (silicon versus germanium) or by application (rectifier versus detector). Correction: the structural categories are junction and point contact; material and application are separate axes that cut across both.", "link": "section 2", "edge_cases": "Modern practice has largely replaced the whisker point contact with the Schottky (hot carrier) diode, which is a metal-semiconductor junction fabricated lithographically; it gives point-contact-like capacitance with junction-diode ruggedness and repeatability. The exam still uses the classic two-way split."}

{"core": "A point contact diode has a tiny rectifying area and therefore very low junction capacitance, so it can follow the envelope of an RF signal without the capacitance shorting the signal around it. That makes it the natural choice as an RF detector (demodulator) and mixer, not as a power or regulation device.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A constant voltage source is the job of a Zener or avalanche diode operated in reverse breakdown; a point contact diode has a soft, poorly defined reverse characteristic and would make a terrible reference.", "why_tempting": "Diodes do have a roughly fixed forward drop (about 0.3 V for germanium), and a learner may generalize that into voltage regulation."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "The contact area is minuscule, so current capacity is a few tens of milliamps and reverse breakdown is low; a high-voltage rectifier needs a large-area junction with a wide depletion region.", "why_tempting": "Point contact diodes are rectifiers in the sense that they conduct one way, so the word rectifier makes the option look right."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A constant current source is built from a transistor or a current-regulator diode (a JFET with gate tied to source); nothing about a point contact diode's exponential I-V curve holds current constant.", "why_tempting": "Swapping voltage for current in a reference-source answer is a classic distractor pattern."}], "concept": "An RF detector must rectify at the carrier frequency and let the low-frequency envelope through. Any diode has a junction capacitance C_j in parallel with its ideal switch; the capacitive reactance X_C = 1/(2πfC) falls with frequency, and once X_C is comparable to the diode's dynamic resistance the signal bypasses the rectifying action. Point contact diodes achieve C_j well under 1 pF because the whisker contact is only micrometres across, and germanium's low forward knee (about 0.2 to 0.3 V) means small signals are detected with little loss. The same low-capacitance, fast-switching behaviour makes them useful as mixers, where the nonlinearity of the I-V curve multiplies the RF and local oscillator signals to produce sum and difference frequencies. The detector output is the envelope; low-pass filtering with an RC whose time constant sits between the carrier period and the modulation period recovers the audio.", "worked_example": "Design check for a simple envelope detector at 7 MHz carrier, 3 kHz audio. Pick a load of 10 kΩ. The RC time constant must satisfy 1/f_carrier << RC << 1/f_audio, i.e. 0.14 μs << RC << 330 μs. Choosing C = 1 nF gives RC = 10 μs, which sits comfortably in the window. If the diode itself had 15 pF of junction capacitance, X_C at 7 MHz would be about 1.5 kΩ, a sizeable shunt across a source of a few hundred ohms; with a point contact diode's 0.5 pF, X_C is about 45 kΩ and the detector behaves as intended.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: all diodes are interchangeable one-way valves, so any diode detects RF. Correction: junction capacitance and forward knee voltage set the usable frequency and sensitivity, and the point contact structure minimizes both, which is why it is specifically the RF detector choice.", "link": "section 6", "mnemonic": "Point contact: pinpoint area, pinpoint capacitance, picks out the envelope.", "edge_cases": "Schottky diodes have replaced germanium point contacts in most new designs and in microwave mixers, and at low signal levels a square-law detector response (output proportional to input power) applies rather than linear envelope detection."}

{"core": "A PIN diode has a thick intrinsic (undoped) layer between its p and n regions, which makes it behave at RF as a resistor whose value is set by DC bias rather than as a rectifier. Forward bias floods the I layer with carriers and gives a low RF resistance (switch closed); zero or reverse bias leaves it depleted and high impedance (switch open), so the common use is as an RF switch or attenuator.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Although the wide I region does give a high reverse breakdown voltage, the PIN diode's slow carrier recombination makes it a poor rectifier above audio frequencies; high-voltage rectification uses ordinary junction or avalanche rectifiers.", "why_tempting": "A wide depletion region does mean high breakdown voltage, so a learner who knows that fact half-reasons toward rectifier duty."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Voltage references rely on a sharp reverse breakdown knee (Zener or avalanche); the PIN diode is designed to avoid breakdown and has no regulating characteristic.", "why_tempting": "Reference-source options recur across the diode questions and look like generic safe answers."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Nothing in the PIN structure limits current; its forward I-V is a normal diode exponential at DC. Current regulation needs a transistor or current-regulator diode.", "why_tempting": "Same confusion as the constant-voltage option, with voltage and current swapped."}], "concept": "At DC a PIN diode is a normal diode. At frequencies well above 1/(2πτ), where τ is the carrier lifetime in the intrinsic layer (often 0.1 to several microseconds), the stored charge cannot be swept out within one RF cycle, so the diode stops rectifying and the I layer simply presents a resistance R_s ≈ K/I_bias, falling from kilohms at zero bias to under an ohm at tens of milliamps. The thick I layer also gives very low capacitance when reverse biased, on the order of 0.1 to 1 pF, so the open state has high isolation. A PIN diode therefore acts as a current-controlled variable resistor at RF: in series it makes a switch (transmit/receive switching in transceivers, band-filter selection), and in a pi or tee network it makes an electronically variable attenuator for AGC and ALC. Because it does not rectify at RF, it adds little distortion even with large signals, unlike a varactor or ordinary diode.", "worked_example": "Suppose a PIN diode has R_s ≈ 50 Ω·mA / I_bias. At 10 mA forward bias R_s ≈ 5 Ω; placed in series in a 50 Ω line the insertion loss is about 20·log10(50/(50 + 5/2)) ≈ 0.4 dB. At zero bias with C = 0.3 pF the reactance at 30 MHz is 1/(2π·30e6·0.3e-12) ≈ 17.7 kΩ, giving isolation of roughly 20·log10(17.7k/100) ≈ 45 dB. One diode plus a bias tee has replaced a relay.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: PIN diodes are high-performance rectifiers because of their wide intrinsic region. Correction: the wide I region is precisely what prevents rectification at RF; it turns the device into a bias-controlled resistor, which is why it switches and attenuates RF instead.", "link": "section 5", "mnemonic": "PIN: Pass It or Not — a bias-controlled RF switch.", "edge_cases": "At frequencies below roughly 1/(2πτ) a PIN diode does start to rectify and distort, so a device chosen for VHF switching may misbehave at low HF; thin-I-layer parts have short lifetimes and lower usable frequency limits."}

{"core": "A Zener diode is operated reverse biased at its breakdown voltage, where a very large change in current produces only a tiny change in voltage across it. Placed across a load with a series resistor it holds the load voltage nearly constant, which is voltage regulation.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Voltage is a potential difference, not a quantity that can be dissipated; power is dissipated. The Zener does dissipate power (V_Z·I_Z) as a side effect, but its purpose is to fix the voltage, not to burn it off.", "why_tempting": "The series dropping resistor does dissipate the excess, and learners merge the resistor's role with the diode's."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A Zener regulator actually draws more current as the source voltage rises, shunting excess through itself to keep the node voltage constant; it does not limit or reduce current.", "why_tempting": "Any device in a circuit looks like it might be restricting something, and the series resistor limits current, inviting the mix-up."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "A Zener cannot supply or multiply current; it is a passive sink in a shunt regulator. Current increase is a transistor or amplifier function.", "why_tempting": "Direct inversion of the previous option; a learner guessing between the current options has a coin flip."}], "concept": "In reverse breakdown the diode's I-V curve becomes nearly vertical: the dynamic resistance r_z = ΔV/ΔI can be a few ohms. Below about 5 V the mechanism is true Zener tunnelling (negative temperature coefficient); above about 6 V it is avalanche multiplication (positive coefficient), and near 5.6 V the two cancel, giving the most temperature-stable references. A shunt regulator is a series resistor R_s from the raw supply V_in to the Zener node, with the load in parallel with the diode. Kirchhoff gives I_s = (V_in − V_Z)/R_s = I_Z + I_L, so as the load draws more, the Zener draws less, and the node stays at V_Z as long as I_Z stays above its knee current. Line regulation is approximately r_z/(R_s + r_z) and load regulation is about r_z in series with the load, which is why a small r_z matters. The same breakdown behaviour used in reverse makes the Zener a clamp and transient absorber.", "worked_example": "Regulate 12 V down to 5.1 V for a load that draws 0 to 40 mA. Choose a minimum Zener current of 5 mA, so the series resistor must pass 45 mA at full load: R_s = (12 − 5.1)/0.045 ≈ 153 Ω; use 150 Ω. At no load all 46 mA flows through the Zener, so P_Z = 5.1 V × 0.046 A ≈ 0.23 W; a 1 W Zener is comfortable. If r_z is 5 Ω, a 1 V rise in V_in shifts the output by only about 5/(150 + 5) ≈ 32 mV.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the Zener acts in series like a resistor that drops the excess voltage. Correction: it sits in parallel with the load and fixes the node voltage; the series resistor does the dropping and the Zener absorbs whatever current the load does not take.", "link": "section 4", "mnemonic": "Zener: Zero change in Voltage — it is a voltage clamp, not a current gate.", "edge_cases": "Zener regulators waste power at light load and have poor regulation versus three-terminal or bandgap regulators; in modern designs the Zener is used as a reference for an error amplifier rather than as the regulator itself."}

{"core": "Power is voltage times current, and the Zener's voltage is pinned at 10 V in breakdown, so I = P/V = 50 W / 10 V = 5 A at maximum dissipation.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "50 A would be 50 A × 10 V = 500 W, ten times the rating; this is the watt figure copied across without dividing by the voltage.", "why_tempting": "The number 50 is in the question, and under exam pressure it gets reused as the answer."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "0.05 A × 10 V = 0.5 W, a hundred times too small; this comes from dividing the wrong way or mishandling a decimal place.", "why_tempting": "Small milliamp-scale Zener currents are familiar from low-power regulator circuits, so a small number feels normal."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "0.5 A × 10 V = 5 W, one tenth of the rating; a factor-of-ten slip in the division.", "why_tempting": "5 and 0.5 look alike when scribbled, and 0.5 A is a typical rectifier current value."}], "concept": "In breakdown the Zener holds V_Z almost constant, so the dissipation relation reduces to P_Z = V_Z × I_Z and the maximum current is I_Z(max) = P_max / V_Z. Because V_Z is fixed, power handling and current handling are the same spec expressed two ways, and a 50 W, 10 V part is physically a large stud-mount or TO-3 device that must be heatsunk. The dissipation rating is a thermal limit: junction temperature T_j = T_ambient + P·θ_JA must stay below the maximum (typically 150 to 175 °C), and θ_JA depends heavily on the heatsink. In a shunt regulator the worst case for the Zener is no load, when the full series current flows through it, so a design should check P_Z at minimum load and maximum input voltage. A slightly higher V_Z (within tolerance, often ±5%) raises dissipation at the same current, so use the upper tolerance limit for a conservative check.", "worked_example": "P = V × I, so I = P / V = 50 W / 10 V = 5 A. Cross-check: 5 A × 10 V = 50 W. If the part's V_Z tolerance is ±5%, V_Z could be 10.5 V, and then 5 A gives 52.5 W, so a conservative design would cap current at 50/10.5 ≈ 4.76 A. Dissipating 50 W at θ_JC = 1 °C/W plus a heatsink of 1.5 °C/W in a 40 °C enclosure puts the junction at 40 + 50 × 2.5 = 165 °C, right at the limit, which shows why maximum rating is a boundary and not an operating point.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a Zener's current is set by its wattage alone, so a 50 W part passes 50 A. Correction: power is the product of V and I; at a fixed Zener voltage the current is P/V, and the fixed-voltage behaviour is exactly what makes this division valid.", "link": "Ohm's Law & Power", "edge_cases": "Ratings assume a 25 °C case or lead temperature; the next question covers derating, and the real usable current is lower in any practical enclosure."}

{"core": "A Zener's power rating is a thermal limit set by the maximum junction temperature. The rated power at 25 °C assumes the full temperature rise from ambient to that limit is available; as ambient rises that headroom shrinks, so the allowable dissipation must be derated and is less.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Any increase in ambient reduces the temperature difference available to carry heat out of the junction, which can only reduce the permissible power, never raise it.", "why_tempting": "Zeners above about 6 V have a positive temperature coefficient of voltage, and a learner may conflate a slightly rising V_Z with rising capability."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Only an ideal device with infinite thermal conductance would be independent of ambient; real packages have a thermal resistance, so dissipation and ambient trade off linearly.", "why_tempting": "Datasheets print a single headline wattage, which suggests a fixed number that does not move."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "This is the inverse of reality; heat flows out of the junction only because it is hotter than its surroundings, and a hotter surrounding reduces that flow.", "why_tempting": "Semiconductors conduct better when warm, and that true fact about carriers gets misapplied to power handling."}], "concept": "Heat flow is analogous to current: P = (T_j − T_a)/θ_JA, where θ_JA is the junction-to-ambient thermal resistance in °C/W. The datasheet rating is P_max = (T_j(max) − 25)/θ_JA. At a higher ambient T_a the allowed power becomes P(T_a) = (T_j(max) − T_a)/θ_JA, a straight line falling to zero at T_a = T_j(max). Manufacturers express this as a derating factor in mW/°C above 25 °C (or above 50 or 75 °C for some packages). Two other effects compound the problem: the breakdown voltage of avalanche-type Zeners rises with temperature (roughly +0.05 to +0.1 %/°C), so a fixed current dissipates slightly more power; and leakage current rises. The thermal picture is the same one that governs transistor SOA curves and power supply pass-element derating, so understanding it here pays off across sections 2 and 4.", "worked_example": "A 1 W Zener in a DO-41 package with T_j(max) = 175 °C has θ_JA = (175 − 25)/1 = 150 °C/W, which corresponds to a derating of 1/150 ≈ 6.7 mW/°C. In a 70 °C enclosure, P_allowed = (175 − 70)/150 = 0.70 W. If the diode is a 10 V part, its safe current drops from 100 mA to 70 mA. With the enclosure at 100 °C the limit is only 0.5 W, half the headline rating.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the power rating on the datasheet is a fixed property of the part. Correction: it is the dissipation that keeps the junction at its limit with a 25 °C reference temperature; every degree of ambient above that reduces the allowable power by the derating factor.", "link": "section 4", "mnemonic": "Hotter room, less room: ambient up means allowed watts down.", "edge_cases": "Some datasheets rate at a 25 °C lead or case temperature with leads soldered close to the body; mounted on long leads or on a board with poor copper the effective θ_JA is far worse than the datasheet number, so real-world derating is often steeper than the printed curve."}

{"core": "Alpha (α) is the common-base current gain, defined as the ratio of collector current to emitter current, α = ΔI_C / ΔI_E. Since nearly all the emitter current reaches the collector, α is slightly less than 1.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A bipolar transistor has no gate; gate is a field-effect transistor terminal. The control electrode of a BJT is the base.", "why_tempting": "FET and BJT terminology gets interleaved in the syllabus, and gate and base both mean the control input."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "ΔI_C/ΔI_B is beta, the common-emitter current gain, a number typically in the tens to hundreds, not alpha.", "why_tempting": "Beta is the gain figure most hobbyists meet first (h_FE on a multimeter), so it is the default for any gain question."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "ΔI_B/ΔI_C is the reciprocal of beta, a tiny fraction with no standard name; it is the ratio written upside down.", "why_tempting": "Inverting a ratio is the easiest distractor to generate and the easiest to fall for when reading quickly."}], "concept": "In a BJT the emitter injects carriers into the thin base; most diffuse across to the collector and a small fraction recombine in the base, exiting as base current. Kirchhoff at the device gives I_E = I_C + I_B. Alpha measures the fraction of emitter current that makes it to the collector: α = I_C / I_E, typically 0.95 to 0.998. Beta measures collector current per unit base current: β = I_C / I_B. Dividing the KCL equation by I_C gives 1/α = 1 + 1/β, so β = α/(1 − α) and α = β/(1 + β). Alpha is the natural gain figure for the common-base configuration, where the emitter is the input and the collector the output, so the current gain is less than unity and the stage gains only in voltage and power. Alpha is set by base width and doping (base transport factor times emitter injection efficiency), so a thinner base pushes α closer to 1 and β much higher.", "worked_example": "Take a transistor with β = 100 and base current 50 μA. Then I_C = β·I_B = 5.00 mA and I_E = I_C + I_B = 5.05 mA. Alpha = I_C/I_E = 5.00/5.05 = 0.990. Check with the formula: α = β/(1 + β) = 100/101 = 0.990. Doubling β to 200 only moves α to 200/201 = 0.995: large beta changes are tiny alpha changes.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: alpha, like beta, is a large amplification factor. Correction: alpha is a fraction just under 1 because the collector can never receive more current than the emitter supplies; the large number is beta.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "Alpha: Almost one, collector over emitter. Beta: Big, collector over base.", "edge_cases": "At very high collector currents or high frequencies α falls (high-level injection, base transit time), so the small-signal α quoted at a given bias point is not constant across the operating range."}

{"core": "Beta (β, or h_FE / h_fe) is the common-emitter forward current gain, the ratio of collector current to base current: β = ΔI_C / ΔI_B. It is the large gain figure, typically 20 to several hundred.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "ΔI_C/ΔI_E is alpha, the common-base gain, a number just below unity; it is the other named ratio, not beta.", "why_tempting": "Alpha and beta are introduced together and both are collector current over something, so the denominators get swapped."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A BJT has no gate terminal, and base current compared with a non-existent current is meaningless; gate belongs to the FET family.", "why_tempting": "Terminology bleed from FET questions in the same section."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "ΔI_B/ΔI_E = 1 − α, the fraction of emitter current lost to the base; it is a small number with no standard letter and is not a gain.", "why_tempting": "Any ratio of the three terminal currents looks like a candidate definition if the learner has not fixed which current is the input."}], "concept": "The base is the control input in a common-emitter amplifier and the collector is the output, so the current gain of that stage is I_C/I_B = β. Physically, the base current is only the small recombination and reverse-injection loss while the collector collects the bulk of the emitter's carriers, so a small base current steers a much larger collector current. Beta is related to alpha by β = α/(1 − α); because α is close to 1 the denominator is tiny and β is large and very sensitive to small changes in α. That sensitivity is why β varies widely between units of the same part number (often 2:1 or worse), with temperature, and with collector current, and why good bias design (emitter degeneration, voltage divider bias) makes the operating point independent of β. DC beta (h_FE) uses total currents; small-signal beta (h_fe) uses increments, which is what the question's change-of-current wording describes.", "worked_example": "A 2N3904 at I_C = 10 mA has a datasheet h_FE between 100 and 300. With I_B = 50 μA the collector current could be anywhere from 5 mA to 15 mA, a 3:1 spread. If alpha is 0.990, β = 0.990/0.010 = 99; if alpha creeps to 0.995, β = 0.995/0.005 = 199. A half-percent change in alpha doubled beta, which is the mathematical reason beta is unreliable as a design constant.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: beta is a fixed, precise transistor constant you can design around. Correction: beta is a large ratio derived from 1/(1 − α), so tiny physical variations swing it widely; circuits are designed to be insensitive to it.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "Beta = Base in, Big out: collector current divided by base current.", "edge_cases": "At very low and very high collector currents β drops off (the datasheet h_FE versus I_C curve is a hump), and above the transition frequency f_T the current gain has fallen to unity, so the DC beta says nothing about RF gain."}

{"core": "An NPN transistor conducts when its base is driven positive relative to the emitter, forward-biasing the base-emitter junction; conventional current then flows into the collector (held positive) and out of the negative emitter. The polarity described, negative emitter, positive collector, positive base, is exactly NPN operation.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A triode's terminals are cathode, grid and plate, and it conducts when the grid is made less negative relative to the cathode; it has no emitter, collector or base.", "why_tempting": "A triode is also a three-terminal amplifier with a positive plate and a control electrode, so the functional analogy invites the wrong pick."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A PNP transistor needs its emitter positive and collector negative, and it turns on when the base is pulled negative relative to the emitter; the polarities in the question are backwards for PNP.", "why_tempting": "NPN and PNP are mirror images and the learner has a 50/50 chance of inverting the polarity rule."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A varactor is a two-terminal diode used reverse biased as a voltage-variable capacitor; it has no base and no transistor action.", "why_tempting": "It is another semiconductor term from the same section, present as a filler option."}], "concept": "A BJT amplifies by forward biasing one junction (base-emitter) and reverse biasing the other (base-collector). In an NPN device the emitter is n-type and injects electrons into the p-type base when V_BE is about +0.6 to +0.7 V; the reverse-biased collector-base junction's field sweeps those electrons into the collector. Electrons flow emitter to collector, so conventional current flows collector to emitter, which matches the question's negative emitter and positive collector. A PNP device swaps every doping and every polarity: emitter positive, base pulled below the emitter, collector most negative, and the carriers are holes. The transfer relation is I_C ≈ I_S·exp(V_BE/V_T) with V_T ≈ 26 mV at room temperature, so a 60 mV increase in V_BE raises I_C by about ten times; that exponential is why bias voltage, not base current, is the physically fundamental control and why V_BE is nearly constant in practice.", "worked_example": "Wire an NPN as a switch: emitter to ground (negative), collector through a 1 kΩ load to +12 V. With the base at 0 V no current flows. Drive the base to +5 V through 10 kΩ: I_B = (5 − 0.7)/10k ≈ 0.43 mA, and with β = 100 the transistor wants 43 mA, more than the load can supply, so it saturates and the collector falls to about 0.2 V, passing roughly 11.8 mA. Swap in a PNP with the same wiring and nothing conducts, because the emitter-base junction is reverse biased.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: NPN and PNP are interchangeable as long as the base gets a signal. Correction: the sign of the base drive relative to the emitter and the supply polarity must match the device type; NPN wants a positive base and positive collector relative to the emitter.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "NPN: Not Pointing iN — the emitter arrow points out, and the base goes positive to turn it on.", "edge_cases": "The question describes conventional current direction; electron flow is the reverse, emitter to collector in the NPN. Either description is fine as long as the junction biasing rule, forward BE and reverse BC, is applied consistently."}

{"core": "In the common-base configuration the emitter is the input and the collector is the output, so the forward current gain of the stage is I_C/I_E, which is the definition of alpha. Alpha is therefore the common-base forward current gain, a value just under unity.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Common-base stages have substantial voltage gain, but alpha specifically relates currents, not voltages; voltage gain depends on the collector load and emitter input resistance, not on a device constant.", "why_tempting": "Common base is known for high voltage gain, so a learner associates its named parameter with voltage."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Reverse current gain would be the ratio with the transistor driven backwards (collector as emitter), a different and much smaller parameter (reverse alpha, α_R) used in the Ebers-Moll model, not what alpha normally denotes.", "why_tempting": "The hybrid-parameter set includes a reverse transfer term (h_rb), making reverse sound like a legitimate alternative."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Reverse voltage gain (h_r) describes how output voltage feeds back to the input; it is a tiny feedback ratio and has nothing to do with alpha.", "why_tempting": "Both reverse and voltage appear in the h-parameter vocabulary that surrounds this topic."}], "concept": "Each BJT configuration names the terminal common to input and output. In common base, signal enters at the emitter, leaves at the collector, and the base is grounded for AC. The current gain is α = I_C/I_E < 1, so the stage does not amplify current; it amplifies voltage because the input impedance at the emitter is very low (about r_e = 26 mV/I_E) while the collector drives a high load impedance, so A_v ≈ R_L/r_e. The reverse-biased collector-base junction also isolates output from input, giving low reverse transfer and excellent stability at VHF and UHF, which is why common-base (and its FET cousin common-gate) stages appear in RF amplifiers and in the upper half of cascode circuits. In h-parameter language alpha is h_fb, the forward current transfer ratio with b for the common-base connection.", "worked_example": "A common-base stage biased at I_E = 2 mA has r_e ≈ 26 mV/2 mA = 13 Ω of input resistance. With α = 0.99 and a 1 kΩ collector load, output current is 0.99 × input current, so current gain is 0.99, but voltage gain is approximately α·R_L/r_e = 0.99 × 1000/13 ≈ 76. Power gain is the product, about 75, all delivered without any current amplification.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a gain parameter must be greater than one, so alpha cannot be a current gain. Correction: forward current gain is just output current over input current; for common base that ratio is alpha, less than one, and the stage's useful gain comes from the impedance transformation.", "link": "section 2", "edge_cases": "Because the emitter input impedance is so low, common-base stages are often matched to a 50 Ω source with a step-down transformer; the configuration's low input impedance makes it less useful at audio where high input impedance is wanted."}

{"core": "The ratio of a change in collector current to the change in base current that caused it is the common-emitter current gain, named beta (β) and listed on datasheets as h_FE or h_fe.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Gamma is not a standard BJT gain symbol; in semiconductor physics it sometimes denotes emitter injection efficiency, a component of alpha, not a terminal current ratio.", "why_tempting": "It is the third Greek letter and looks like the next item in an alpha-beta-gamma series."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Delta is the symbol for change itself (ΔI_C), not a named transistor parameter; it appears in the definition but is not the quantity.", "why_tempting": "The question's wording involves changes in current, so the symbol for change feels relevant."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Alpha is collector current over emitter current, the common-base gain, a value just under one; it uses the wrong denominator.", "why_tempting": "The standard confusion of this subsection: alpha and beta are both collector current over an input current."}], "concept": "In common-emitter operation the base is the input and the collector the output, and the device parameter linking them is β = ΔI_C/ΔI_B. Physically the base current is the small loss term (recombination in the base plus holes injected back into the emitter in an NPN), while the collector current is the main electron flux that crossed the base, so the ratio is large. Beta's relation to alpha, β = α/(1 − α), shows that a base transport factor of 0.99 gives β ≈ 99 and 0.995 gives β ≈ 199. The two subscript conventions matter: h_FE (capital) is DC beta I_C/I_B at a bias point, while h_fe (lower case) is small-signal beta ∂I_C/∂I_B, and the two differ when the curve is nonlinear. The question's change of current phrasing is the small-signal definition. Beta also sets the input resistance of a common-emitter stage, r_π = β·r_e = β·26 mV/I_C, tying this parameter into amplifier design.", "worked_example": "Measure a transistor at two bias points: I_B = 20 μA gives I_C = 2.4 mA, and I_B = 30 μA gives I_C = 3.9 mA. Small-signal beta is ΔI_C/ΔI_B = (3.9 − 2.4) mA / (30 − 20) μA = 1.5 mA / 10 μA = 150. DC beta at the second point is 3.9 mA / 30 μA = 130. Both are called beta; the first is h_fe and the second is h_FE.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: alpha is the primary transistor gain because it comes first alphabetically. Correction: beta is the collector-over-base ratio used in common-emitter and common-collector design; alpha is the collector-over-emitter fraction for common base.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "Beta pairs with Base: ΔI_C over ΔI_B.", "edge_cases": "Beta falls with frequency; it is flat up to the beta cutoff frequency f_β = f_T/β and then rolls off at 6 dB per octave, reaching 1 at f_T, so a DC beta of 150 can be only 5 at a few hundred MHz."}

{"core": "Alpha is defined as collector current divided by emitter current, and the configuration in which the emitter is the input and the collector is the output is common base. Alpha is therefore the forward current gain specified for the common-base connection.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "In common collector (emitter follower) the base is the input and the emitter is the output, so its current gain is I_E/I_B = β + 1, not alpha.", "why_tempting": "Common collector is the least-discussed configuration and gets picked as the unfamiliar option that might hide the trick."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Common gate is a field-effect transistor configuration; a BJT has no gate, so no BJT parameter is specified for it.", "why_tempting": "Common gate is the FET analogue of common base, so a learner who knows that analogy may reach for it."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Common emitter uses the base as input and collector as output, so its current gain is β = I_C/I_B; alpha is not the parameter of that stage.", "why_tempting": "Common emitter is the default amplifier configuration, and the learner may assume the first-named parameter belongs to it."}], "concept": "The three BJT configurations are named for the terminal shared by input and output: common base (emitter in, collector out), common emitter (base in, collector out), and common collector (base in, emitter out). The current gain of a configuration is simply its output current over its input current, so each configuration has its own figure: α = I_C/I_E for common base, β = I_C/I_B for common emitter, and β + 1 = I_E/I_B for common collector. All three are tied together by I_E = I_C + I_B. Beyond current gain, the configurations differ in input impedance (lowest for common base, highest for common collector), voltage gain (common collector about 1, the others high) and phase (common emitter inverts). Alpha being just under 1 is the signature of common base and it is why that stage's usefulness lies in impedance transformation and isolation rather than current amplification.", "worked_example": "With I_B = 10 μA and I_C = 1.00 mA, I_E = 1.01 mA. Common-base gain α = 1.00/1.01 = 0.990. Common-emitter gain β = 1.00/0.010 = 100. Common-collector gain I_E/I_B = 1.01/0.010 = 101 = β + 1. Each number is the same transistor viewed from a different pair of terminals.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: alpha and beta are two properties of the transistor independent of how it is wired. Correction: they are the same device's current gain measured for different input-output terminal pairs, and alpha belongs to the common-base pair, emitter in and collector out.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "Alpha and base both start near the beginning: alpha is the common-Base gain.", "edge_cases": "In the hybrid-parameter notation the letter subscript gives the configuration: h_fb is alpha (b for base), h_fe is beta (e for emitter), h_fc is the common-collector gain. Datasheets usually only print h_FE and you convert."}

{"core": "Beta relates collector current to base current, so it is the parameter for the configurations where the base is the input terminal: common emitter (output at the collector, gain β) and common collector (output at the emitter, gain β + 1, which is governed by beta).", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Common gate is a FET configuration; a BJT has no gate, so no BJT gain is specified for it, and the pairing fails on that term alone.", "why_tempting": "Common emitter is correct and common gate sounds like a legitimate configuration to the learner who mixes device families."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Common base uses the emitter as input and is characterized by alpha, not beta; common collector is correct but the pair is wrong.", "why_tempting": "Each option in this question contains one correct configuration, so a half-remembered answer can land anywhere."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Common emitter is a beta configuration, but common base is the alpha configuration; this pairs the two different gain figures.", "why_tempting": "Common base and common emitter are the two most-discussed configurations, so they look like the natural pair."}], "concept": "The deciding question is which terminal drives the transistor. Whenever the base is the input, the controlling quantity is base current and the device gain is beta. In common emitter the output is taken from the collector, so A_i = I_C/I_B = β and the stage also gives voltage gain and inverts phase. In common collector the output is taken from the emitter, so A_i = I_E/I_B = (I_C + I_B)/I_B = β + 1; the voltage gain is slightly under 1 and the stage is used as a buffer because its input impedance is roughly (β + 1)·(r_e + R_E), high, and its output impedance is low. Both stages therefore inherit beta's large value and beta's variability, which is why both need bias stabilization. The common-base stage is the odd one out: emitter driven, gain alpha, input impedance only r_e. Knowing which parameter belongs to which stage lets you predict input impedance, current gain and phase behaviour from a schematic without calculation.", "worked_example": "An emitter follower with β = 120 and a 1 kΩ emitter resistor at I_E = 5 mA: r_e = 26 mV/5 mA ≈ 5 Ω, so input resistance ≈ 121 × (5 + 1000) ≈ 122 kΩ and current gain ≈ 121. Reconfigure the same transistor as common emitter with the same bias: current gain 120, input resistance ≈ β·r_e = 120 × 5 ≈ 600 Ω (plus any unbypassed emitter resistance). Both numbers come straight from beta.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: beta only applies to the common-emitter amplifier because that is where it is usually introduced.
