Correction: beta governs every configuration in which the base is the input, which includes common collector; only common base, driven at the emitter, uses alpha.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "If the Base is the input, Beta is the gain: common Emitter and common Collector.", "edge_cases": "Some texts quote the common-collector current gain as simply beta, treating β + 1 ≈ β; for large beta the distinction is academic, but the exact relation matters when deriving input impedance of an emitter follower."}

{"core": "A PNP transistor has a p-type emitter and collector with an n-type base; it conducts when the emitter is positive relative to the collector and the base is pulled negative relative to the emitter, forward-biasing the emitter-base junction. Those are exactly the polarities described.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A varactor is a two-terminal reverse-biased diode used as a voltage-variable capacitor; it has no emitter, collector or base.", "why_tempting": "It appears in the same component list and is a three-syllable semiconductor word."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "An NPN requires a negative emitter, positive collector and a base driven positive; the question's polarities would reverse bias its emitter-base junction and it would stay off.", "why_tempting": "Mirror-image confusion: NPN is the more common device, and the learner may not flip all three polarities."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A triode uses cathode, grid and plate; it conducts with a positive plate and a grid driven less negative, and its terminals do not match emitter, collector and base at all.", "why_tempting": "A triode is a three-terminal controlled conductor, so the analogy is tempting if the terminal names are not checked."}], "concept": "In a PNP transistor the majority carriers are holes. Forward biasing the emitter-base junction (emitter about 0.6 to 0.7 V above the base) injects holes from the p-type emitter into the thin n-type base; the reverse-biased collector-base junction, with the collector most negative, sweeps those holes into the collector. Conventional current therefore flows into the emitter and out of the collector, which is the positive-emitter, negative-collector arrangement in the question. The device is the exact complement of the NPN: every doping type, every junction polarity and every current direction is reversed, and the governing equation is the same, I_C ≈ I_S·exp(V_EB/V_T). PNP devices are convenient for high-side switching (emitter at the positive rail, load to ground) and for complementary push-pull output stages where an NPN sources and a PNP sinks, which is the basis of class B and AB audio and modulator stages.", "worked_example": "High-side switch: PNP emitter to +12 V, collector through a 100 Ω load to ground. Base left at +12 V through a pull-up: V_EB = 0, off. Pull the base to ground through 4.7 kΩ: I_B ≈ (12 − 0.7)/4.7k ≈ 2.4 mA, and with β = 100 the device saturates, the collector rises to about 11.8 V, and roughly 118 mA flows through the load. Substitute an NPN in the same socket and it never turns on because its emitter would be the most positive terminal.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: NPN and PNP differ only in symbol arrow direction and are otherwise wired the same. Correction: a PNP needs the opposite supply polarity and the opposite base drive, with the emitter the most positive terminal and the base pulled below it to conduct.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "PNP: Pointing iN Proudly — the emitter arrow points in, and the base goes negative to turn it on.", "edge_cases": "Historically PNP germanium transistors dominated early designs (hence older schematics with negative ground); modern silicon practice favours NPN for most tasks because electron mobility gives better high-frequency performance, with PNP used where polarity demands it."}

{"core": "From I_E = I_C + I_B with α = I_C/I_E and β = I_C/I_B, dividing I_E = I_C + I_B by I_C gives 1/α = 1 + 1/β = (β + 1)/β, so α = β/(1 + β).", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "β(1 + β) grows as β², giving a number in the thousands for a typical transistor; alpha must be a fraction below one.", "why_tempting": "Keeping the right pieces (β and 1 + β) but multiplying instead of dividing is an easy algebra slip."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "For any β above 1 this gives a negative number, which is physically impossible for a ratio of two currents flowing the same direction.", "why_tempting": "The minus sign appears in the companion formula β = α/(1 − α), and it gets carried over to the wrong relation."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "β/(1 − β) is negative for β > 1 and blows up at β = 1; it is the companion formula with alpha and beta swapped.", "why_tempting": "It has the same shape as the correct β = α/(1 − α), so a learner who memorized one formula may apply it in both directions."}], "concept": "The relationship comes entirely from current conservation at the transistor: I_E = I_C + I_B. Substituting I_B = I_C/β gives I_E = I_C(1 + 1/β) = I_C(β + 1)/β, and then α = I_C/I_E = β/(β + 1). The inverse follows the same way: from α, I_C = αI_E and I_B = I_E − I_C = (1 − α)I_E, so β = I_C/I_B = α/(1 − α). A sanity check that catches every wrong form is the limiting behaviour: as β → ∞, α → 1, and as α → 1, β → ∞. The denominator 1 − α is the fraction of emitter current that becomes base current, so beta is the ratio of the collected fraction to the lost fraction. This is also why beta is unstable: it is the ratio of a number near 1 to a number near 0, and a small shift in the base transport factor moves it enormously.", "worked_example": "Given β = 150: α = 150/(1 + 150) = 150/151 = 0.9934. Check the inverse: β = 0.9934/(1 − 0.9934) = 0.9934/0.0066 ≈ 150. Now test distractor A at β = 150: 150 × 151 = 22650, absurd for a current fraction. Distractor D's form is the only one that returns a value between 0 and 1 for every positive β.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: alpha and beta are independent datasheet numbers to be memorized separately. Correction: they are algebraically locked together by Kirchhoff's current law at the device, α = β/(1 + β), and either one determines the other.", "link": "Formula-sheet trainer", "mnemonic": "Alpha has the plus: α = β/(1 + β). Beta has the minus: β = α/(1 − α). Plus keeps alpha under one; minus makes beta blow up.", "edge_cases": "These relations assume the collector leakage current I_CBO is negligible; at high temperature with germanium devices the exact form is I_C = αI_E + I_CBO and the simple ratio formulas drift."}

{"core": "Common base has a current gain of alpha, just under 1, whereas common emitter and common collector are driven at the base and have current gains of β and β + 1, typically 20 to several hundred. Compared with common base, those two configurations therefore have high to very high current gain.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Doubling alpha (about 0.99) would give roughly 2, but common-emitter current gain is β = α/(1 − α), on the order of 100 for the same device, far more than double.", "why_tempting": "A learner who thinks of the configurations as mild variations rather than fundamentally different input terminals guesses a small factor."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Half of alpha would be about 0.5, meaning current loss; common emitter and common collector amplify current heavily, not attenuate it.", "why_tempting": "Inversion of the correct direction, chosen by someone who remembers there is a large ratio but not which way it goes."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Very low describes common base itself, whose current gain is below unity; the other two configurations are the opposite case.", "why_tempting": "The learner may anchor on common emitter's lower input impedance or common collector's unity voltage gain and misread low in the wrong dimension."}], "concept": "Current gain is output current over input current, and which terminal is the input decides everything. Common base is driven at the emitter, the terminal carrying the largest current, so output I_C can only be a fraction α ≈ 0.95 to 0.998 of the input. Common emitter and common collector are driven at the base, which carries only the recombination loss current, so output currents I_C and I_E are β and β + 1 times larger than the input. The ratio between the configurations is therefore about β/α ≈ β + 1, a factor of tens to hundreds. This does not make common base useless: its voltage gain is comparable to common emitter, its input is the low-impedance emitter (useful for 50 Ω matching), and its reverse isolation is far better, so it is preferred at VHF/UHF and as the upper device of a cascode. Power gain is the product of current and voltage gain, and common base still achieves good power gain through voltage gain alone.", "worked_example": "Transistor with α = 0.99, so β = 0.99/0.01 = 99. Current gains: common base 0.99, common emitter 99, common collector 100. Ratio of common emitter to common base: 99/0.99 = 100 = β + 1. A 10 μA input signal produces 9.9 μA out of a common-base stage but 990 μA out of a common-emitter stage from the same transistor.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a transistor has one current gain regardless of configuration. Correction: the gain depends on which terminal is the input; base-driven configurations multiply current by beta, while the emitter-driven common-base stage passes slightly less current than it receives.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "Base in, Big gain; Emitter in, Even (just under one).", "edge_cases": "At high frequencies common-emitter current gain falls to unity at f_T while common-base alpha stays near 1 up to a higher alpha cutoff frequency, so the gap narrows and common base can be the better RF choice despite the DC numbers."}

{"core": "Starting from I_E = I_C + I_B with I_C = αI_E, the base current is I_B = (1 − α)I_E, so β = I_C/I_B = αI_E/((1 − α)I_E) = α/(1 − α).", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "α/(1 + α) is at most 0.5 for any alpha below 1, which cannot represent a current gain of tens or hundreds; it has the wrong sign in the denominator.", "why_tempting": "It mirrors the correct alpha formula α = β/(1 + β), so a learner who remembers plus signs picks it."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "α(1 − α) peaks at 0.25 when α = 0.5 and is tiny near α ≈ 0.99 (about 0.01), the reverse of the explosive growth beta shows as alpha approaches 1.", "why_tempting": "The right two factors appear, so it looks like the answer with a product instead of a quotient."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "α(1 + α) is just under 2 for realistic alpha, nowhere near typical beta values of 50 to 300.", "why_tempting": "Another plus-sign variant; it only fails if the learner actually plugs in a number."}], "concept": "The derivation is the same current-conservation argument as for the alpha formula. Emitter current splits into the collected part αI_E and the lost part (1 − α)I_E that exits the base. Beta is the ratio of those two parts: β = α/(1 − α). Because alpha is close to 1 the denominator is a small difference of nearly equal numbers, so beta is numerically large and extremely sensitive: moving alpha from 0.990 to 0.995 halves the denominator and doubles beta. This sensitivity is the mathematical root of beta spread between transistors and beta drift with temperature and current, which in turn motivates bias designs that make the operating point depend on resistor values rather than on beta. The inverse α = β/(1 + β) confirms that even a huge beta pushes alpha only marginally closer to 1. A quick plausibility test for any proposed formula: plug in α = 0.99 and expect a result near 100.", "worked_example": "Given α = 0.985: β = 0.985/(1 − 0.985) = 0.985/0.015 ≈ 65.7. Check: I_E = 1 mA gives I_C = 0.985 mA and I_B = 0.015 mA; I_C/I_B = 65.7. Now test the distractors at α = 0.985: B gives 0.985/1.985 ≈ 0.50; C gives 0.985 × 0.015 ≈ 0.015; D gives 0.985 × 1.985 ≈ 1.96. Only the keyed formula yields a plausible transistor gain.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: since alpha and beta are both gains, converting between them is a simple scaling. Correction: beta is alpha divided by the small fraction 1 − α, a nonlinear relation that makes beta explode as alpha nears unity.", "link": "Formula-sheet trainer", "mnemonic": "Beta = α over (1 minus α): the minus makes it big.", "edge_cases": "Including leakage, the exact DC relation is I_C = βI_B + (β + 1)I_CBO; for silicon at room temperature the leakage term is negligible, but for germanium or hot devices it can dominate the base current and the simple ratio misleads."}

{"core": "An enhancement-mode FET is built with no conducting channel between source and drain; the gate must be biased (positive for n-channel) to attract carriers and create, or enhance, a channel. With zero gate voltage there is no channel and no drain current, so the device is normally off.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A channel that blocks voltage through the gate is not a meaningful description; the gate of any FET is insulated or reverse biased and passes negligible current regardless of mode, and the channel is what conducts source to drain.", "why_tempting": "The option has the right vocabulary (channel, gate) arranged in a plausible-sounding sentence."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "A channel that conducts with zero gate voltage is the definition of a depletion-mode device, the opposite of enhancement.", "why_tempting": "This is the direct swap of the two modes and the most common error in the whole subsection."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Current does not flow through the gate in a MOSFET or reverse-biased JFET; the channel is between source and drain, so a channel to hinder gate current is a category error.", "why_tempting": "It contains the correct phrase without a channel, so a learner who remembers only that fragment may choose it."}], "concept": "In an n-channel enhancement MOSFET the source and drain are n+ regions in a p-type body with no n-type path between them; the gate is insulated by a thin oxide. Raising V_GS above the threshold voltage V_th attracts electrons to the surface of the p-type body under the gate, inverting it to n-type and forming a channel. Drain current then follows roughly I_D = K(V_GS − V_th)² in saturation and I_D ≈ 2K(V_GS − V_th)V_DS at small V_DS, so the device is a voltage-controlled resistor or current source, with transconductance g_m = 2K(V_GS − V_th). The gate draws no DC current, giving extremely high input impedance. Enhancement mode is the dominant type in modern power switching (the ubiquitous power MOSFET) and in CMOS logic, because a device that is off at zero gate voltage is safe and simple to drive from logic. Depletion mode, by contrast, has a built-in channel and is normally on.", "worked_example": "A logic-level n-channel MOSFET with V_th = 2 V and K = 0.5 A/V². At V_GS = 0 V the channel does not exist and I_D = 0. At V_GS = 5 V in saturation, I_D = 0.5 × (5 − 2)² = 4.5 A. In the ohmic region with V_DS small, R_DS(on) ≈ 1/(2K(V_GS − V_th)) = 1/(2 × 0.5 × 3) ≈ 0.33 Ω. Raising V_GS to 10 V drops R_DS(on) to about 0.125 Ω, which is why gate drive voltage matters for switching losses.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: all FETs conduct at zero gate bias and the gate only throttles them. Correction: that describes depletion mode; an enhancement-mode FET has no channel until the gate creates one, so it is off at zero bias and the gate turns it on.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "Enhancement: Empty until Energized — the gate must build the channel.", "edge_cases": "Enhancement MOSFETs have a body diode from source to drain that conducts if the drain goes below the source, and the thin gate oxide typically tolerates only ±20 V, so the device is not truly off against reverse drain voltage and gate overdrive is destructive."}

{"core": "A depletion-mode FET is fabricated with a conducting channel already present between source and drain, so drain current flows with zero gate voltage. Applying gate bias of the right polarity depletes the channel of carriers and reduces the current, which is why it is called depletion mode and is normally on.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A depletion device does have a channel, and current does not pass through the gate of any FET; this option is wrong on both points.", "why_tempting": "It recycles the phrase without a channel from the enhancement definition into the wrong mode."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A channel that blocks current at zero gate voltage is a contradiction for depletion mode; by definition the built-in channel conducts at zero bias.", "why_tempting": "The phrase has a channel is correct, and the learner may stop reading before the clause about blocking."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "No channel and no current at zero gate voltage is the enhancement-mode definition, the opposite case.", "why_tempting": "Straight swap of the two modes."}], "concept": "In a depletion-mode device (every JFET and the depletion-type MOSFET) the channel is doped into the silicon during manufacture, so at V_GS = 0 a drain current I_DSS flows. For an n-channel JFET, making the gate negative reverse biases the gate-channel junction and widens its depletion region, squeezing the channel; the drain current follows I_D ≈ I_DSS(1 − V_GS/V_P)² where V_P is the pinch-off voltage at which the channel closes completely. A depletion MOSFET behaves the same way but with an insulated gate, and it can additionally be driven positive to enhance the channel beyond I_DSS. Because the device is on at zero bias it is self-biasing: a source resistor R_S develops V_GS = −I_D·R_S automatically, which is the classic JFET amplifier arrangement and needs no gate supply. The transconductance g_m = 2I_DSS(1 − V_GS/V_P)/|V_P| sets the voltage gain A_v ≈ −g_m·R_D. Depletion devices are common in RF front ends, as constant-current sources, and as the pass element in some regulators that must start up with zero control voltage.", "worked_example": "An n-channel JFET with I_DSS = 10 mA and V_P = −4 V. At V_GS = 0: I_D = 10 mA, the channel is fully open. At V_GS = −2 V: I_D = 10 × (1 − 2/4)² = 10 × 0.25 = 2.5 mA. At V_GS = −4 V: I_D = 0, pinched off. To self-bias at 2.5 mA, choose R_S = 2 V/2.5 mA = 800 Ω with the gate returned to ground through a high-value resistor.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: an FET must be turned on by its gate the way a BJT must be turned on by base current. Correction: depletion-mode FETs are already on with no gate signal; the gate's job is to turn them down, and the bias design exploits that with a simple source resistor.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "Depletion: Default on, gate Drains it down.", "edge_cases": "Driving a JFET gate forward (positive for n-channel) turns the gate-channel diode on and loads the source, so JFET gate swing is limited to the reverse direction; a depletion MOSFET has no such limit and can be operated in both depletion and enhancement regions."}

{"core": "The MOSFET gate is separated from the channel by an oxide only tens of nanometres thick, which breaks down at a few tens of volts; with gate capacitance of only picofarads, a static charge of nanocoulombs is enough to exceed that. Built-in Zener diodes from gate to source clamp the gate voltage below the oxide breakdown so small static charges and overvoltages cannot puncture the insulation.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Overheating is governed by drain current and V_DS, not by the gate voltage staying within some window; a Zener clamp at ±15 to ±20 V does nothing to limit channel dissipation.", "why_tempting": "Keeping within specifications sounds responsible, and gate overdrive does increase current, so a thermal rationale seems adjacent."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The substrate (body) is tied to the source in most discrete devices and is not the vulnerable element; the fragile element is the gate oxide, so the diodes are gate to source.", "why_tempting": "Substrate is a term from the same device structure and sounds like the thing underneath that needs protecting."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "The protection diodes are normally non-conducting; they are not a reference and set no bias. Bias comes from external resistors and the operating point design, and the clamp voltage is well outside the normal gate operating range.", "why_tempting": "Zeners are taught primarily as voltage references, so a Zener in a gate circuit reads as a bias element."}], "concept": "A MOSFET gate is one plate of a capacitor whose dielectric is silicon dioxide of thickness t_ox; breakdown occurs at roughly 1 V per nanometre, so a 50 nm oxide fails near 50 V, and the datasheet V_GS(max) is typically ±20 V. The gate capacitance C_iss is small, a few picofarads for a small-signal device, so V = Q/C means a trivial charge produces a huge voltage: a person can carry 10 to 20 kV through a 100 to 200 pF body capacitance, and discharging even a fraction of that into picofarads exceeds breakdown instantly. Unlike a JFET or BJT, there is no junction to conduct the charge away; the oxide simply ruptures and the device is dead or degraded. Internal back-to-back Zener diodes from gate to source turn on at a voltage above the operating range but below oxide breakdown and shunt the charge safely, trading a small amount of added gate capacitance and leakage for ruggedness. Many dual-gate MOSFETs for RF receivers and most CMOS logic inputs use the same scheme.", "worked_example": "A small-signal MOSFET has C_iss = 5 pF and a 40 nm oxide breaking down near 40 V. The charge needed to reach breakdown is Q = CV = 5 pF × 40 V = 0.2 nC. A fingertip at a modest 2 kV with 150 pF body capacitance holds 300 nC, 1500 times that amount. A gate-source Zener pair clamping at 15 V limits the gate to 15 V while absorbing the pulse; its current for a 1 μs, 300 nC event is about 0.3 A, well within what a small protection diode survives.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the protective Zener regulates or biases the gate during normal operation. Correction: it is inactive during normal operation and exists only to clamp transient overvoltage, especially static discharge, below the level that punctures the gate oxide.", "link": "section 2", "edge_cases": "The protection diodes add capacitance and can slightly raise noise and reduce the very highest input impedance, so some low-noise and high-impedance devices omit them and rely entirely on handling precautions; power MOSFETs often have no internal gate Zener and need an external gate clamp or series resistor."}

{"core": "FET and CMOS devices have insulated gates with very high input impedance and tiny capacitance, so a static charge delivered to the gate has no path to leak away and produces a voltage that can exceed the oxide breakdown and permanently puncture it. They therefore require antistatic handling: grounded wrist straps, conductive mats and packaging, and shorted leads until installed.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Semiconductor junctions are diffused regions inside a crystal, not welded joints; mechanical fragility of the die is not the issue, and bipolar devices built the same way need no special handling.", "why_tempting": "Micro-welded sounds like a plausible manufacturing detail and the word susceptible appears in the correct answer."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "FET leads are the same kind of metal as any other component's; there is nothing unusually delicate about them mechanically.", "why_tempting": "Small packages do have fine leads, so a learner may generalize a real but minor handling concern into the reason."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Ordinary packaged FETs are opaque and not photosensitive; light sensitivity is a property of phototransistors, photodiodes and exposed-die devices in clear packages.", "why_tempting": "Some semiconductors are light sensitive, and old glass-cased diodes do respond to light, so the fact is real but misapplied."}], "concept": "The gate of a MOSFET is a capacitor plate over an oxide tens of nanometres thick; the gate of a JFET is a reverse-biased junction with very low leakage. Either way the input is almost perfectly insulating, so any charge deposited on it stays there and V = Q/C applies with C in the picofarad range. Static electricity generated by walking on carpet or sliding out of a chair can reach 10 to 30 kV on a human body, stored on roughly 100 to 200 pF; even a small fraction transferred to a 5 pF gate exceeds the 20 to 50 V oxide limit. The failure is a physical puncture of the oxide that leaves a conductive path, giving a dead device or, worse, a degraded one that fails later. CMOS integrated circuits are particularly exposed because every input is a MOSFET gate. Mitigation keeps all parts of the system at the same potential and provides a slow discharge path: a 1 MΩ-series wrist strap, dissipative mats, conductive foam or shorting clips on leads, grounded soldering iron tips, and leaving devices in their packaging until insertion.", "worked_example": "A technician charged to 5 kV with a body capacitance of 150 pF carries Q = CV = 0.75 μC. Touching a MOSFET gate whose capacitance to source is 5 pF, even if only 0.1% of the charge transfers (0.75 nC), produces V = 0.75 nC / 5 pF = 150 V, several times the oxide limit. A wrist strap with 1 MΩ to ground discharges the body with a time constant RC = 1 MΩ × 150 pF = 0.15 ms, so the operator is at ground potential long before touching the part.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: electrostatic discharge only matters for obviously sensitive parts, and a device that still works after handling was undamaged. Correction: ESD damage to gate oxide is often latent, degrading the part so it fails in service; the precaution is about charge that you cannot feel, since discharges below about 3 kV are imperceptible but already far above the oxide limit.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "FET gates are Fragile to Electrostatic Touch.", "edge_cases": "Many modern MOSFETs and all CMOS logic include on-chip protection diodes that survive routine handling, so the real-world risk is lower than for 1970s parts, but power MOSFET gates without internal clamps and high-impedance analog front ends remain genuinely vulnerable."}

{"core": "An FET's gate is either an insulated electrode (MOSFET) or a reverse-biased junction (JFET), so it draws essentially no input current and presents a very high input impedance, megohms to gigohms. A bipolar transistor's input is a forward-biased base-emitter junction that must be supplied with base current, giving a comparatively low input impedance of hundreds of ohms to a few kilohms.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Input impedance is a property of the device's input structure (insulated or reverse-biased gate versus forward-biased junction) and is characterized at any reasonable supply voltage; the supply does not change which is higher.", "why_tempting": "It sounds cautious and engineering-minded, and impedances do depend on bias current, so a learner may think the comparison is undefined."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "This reverses reality: the forward-biased base-emitter junction of a BJT is the low-impedance input, and the non-conducting gate of an FET is the high one.", "why_tempting": "Straight inversion for a learner who remembers there is a big difference but not which direction."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The two differ by several orders of magnitude; a BJT input of about 1 kΩ versus an FET input of 100 MΩ or more is not the same by any measure.", "why_tempting": "Both are three-terminal amplifiers and the learner may assume their small-signal models are interchangeable."}], "concept": "A BJT is a current-controlled device: the base-emitter junction is forward biased, and the small-signal input resistance is r_π = β·V_T/I_C, where V_T ≈ 26 mV. At I_C = 1 mA with β = 100, r_π ≈ 2.6 kΩ, and it falls further at higher currents. An FET is voltage controlled: a JFET gate is a reverse-biased p-n junction with leakage of picoamps to nanoamps, giving an effective input resistance of hundreds of megohms, and a MOSFET gate is insulated by oxide, with leakage in the femtoamp range. At DC and audio frequencies the FET input is therefore effectively open, and it is the input capacitance (a few pF) rather than any resistance that defines the input impedance at RF, Z_in ≈ 1/(2πfC_iss). This difference decides the application: FETs for high-impedance sources such as crystal microphones, pH probes, antenna whips in active antennas, sample-and-hold circuits and oscilloscope probes; BJTs where a low source impedance is available and their higher transconductance per milliamp is wanted.", "worked_example": "A 100 kΩ source drives an amplifier input. With a BJT common-emitter stage at I_C = 1 mA, β = 100, r_π ≈ 2.6 kΩ, so the input sees a voltage divider delivering only 2.6/(100 + 2.6) ≈ 2.5% of the signal. With a JFET whose gate leakage is 1 nA at 10 V (10 GΩ equivalent) and a 1 MΩ gate return resistor, the input is essentially 1 MΩ, delivering about 91% of the signal. At 10 MHz the JFET's 5 pF C_iss gives about 3.2 kΩ of reactance, so the advantage shrinks at RF.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: all transistors load their source similarly, so the choice between FET and BJT is only about gain or noise. Correction: the BJT's forward-biased input junction loads the source heavily while the FET's gate loads it almost not at all, which is often the deciding factor in input-stage design.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "FET: Few Electrons Taken at the gate; BJT needs Base current.", "edge_cases": "At VHF and above, both devices' input impedances are dominated by capacitance and Miller effect, and the high-resistance advantage of the FET disappears; conversely, BJT input impedance can be raised to megohms with a Darlington or bootstrapped emitter follower."}

{"core": "A JFET has a conducting channel with a source at one end and a drain at the other, controlled by a gate that forms a reverse-biased junction with the channel. Its three terminals are gate, drain and source.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Emitter, base 1 and base 2 are the terminals of a unijunction transistor (UJT), a relaxation-oscillator device, not a field-effect transistor.", "why_tempting": "The UJT appears in the same component section and also has three terminals with unusual names."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Emitter, base and collector are the bipolar junction transistor's terminals; a JFET has no forward-biased junction and no emitter or collector.", "why_tempting": "BJT terminals are learned first, and a learner may map them one-to-one onto any three-terminal device."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Two gates plus a drain describes a dual-gate MOSFET minus its source; a JFET has one gate and must have a source.", "why_tempting": "Dual-gate MOSFETs are common in receiver RF and mixer stages, so two gates sounds like a real device, and it is, just not a JFET."}], "concept": "A JFET is a bar of doped semiconductor, the channel, with ohmic contacts at each end: the source, where majority carriers enter, and the drain, where they leave. Along the channel sits a region of opposite doping, the gate, which forms a p-n junction with the channel. The gate is operated reverse biased, so the junction's depletion region extends into the channel and narrows the conducting path without the gate drawing current. Increasing reverse bias widens the depletion region, reducing I_D from I_DSS toward zero at pinch-off V_P, following I_D ≈ I_DSS(1 − V_GS/V_P)². Functionally the terminals map onto the BJT as source to emitter, gate to base and drain to collector, which helps when reading schematics, but the physics differs: the JFET is voltage controlled with no input current, has a square-law rather than exponential transfer curve, and is symmetric enough that source and drain can often be swapped. The terminal names carry over to MOSFETs, which add a fourth body or substrate connection, usually tied internally to the source.", "worked_example": "Reading a common-source amplifier: the input signal goes to the gate, the source is tied to ground through a self-bias resistor R_S (bypassed by a capacitor for AC), and the output is taken from the drain across R_D. With I_DSS = 8 mA, V_P = −3 V and R_S = 330 Ω, the self-bias point solves I_D = 8(1 − I_D·0.33/3)², giving about I_D ≈ 3.5 mA and V_GS ≈ −1.15 V. Output voltage gain is approximately −g_m·R_D; with g_m ≈ 3.3 mS and R_D = 2.2 kΩ, A_v ≈ −7.3.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: all three-terminal transistors use emitter, base and collector. Correction: those are BJT terms tied to junction injection; field-effect devices use source, gate and drain because carriers flow through a channel whose width the gate controls electrostatically.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "FET terminals follow the water: carriers Spring from the Source, pass the Gate, and exit at the Drain.", "edge_cases": "Some JFETs are truly symmetric and the datasheet does not distinguish source from drain; others are optimized with a lower-capacitance drain end, so swapping them works but degrades high-frequency performance."}

{"core": "A JFET is classified by the doping of its channel: an n-channel JFET conducts by electrons through n-type material with a p-type gate, and a p-channel JFET conducts by holes through p-type material with an n-type gate. Those are the two basic types, with opposite supply and gate polarities.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Silicon versus germanium is a material choice, not a device type; practically all JFETs are silicon and the type distinction is about channel polarity.", "why_tempting": "Material is the classic two-way split for diodes and early transistors, so the learner may reuse it here."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Power rating is a continuum of ratings for the same device type, not a structural category; JFETs in particular are almost all small-signal parts.", "why_tempting": "Power transistors and small-signal transistors are sold as separate families, so it feels like a classification."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "MOSFET and GaAsFET are other families of field-effect transistor, with an insulated gate or a gallium-arsenide Schottky gate respectively; neither is a type of junction FET.", "why_tempting": "They are both FETs, and the learner may read the question as asking for FET types in general rather than JFET types."}], "concept": "In an n-channel JFET the channel is n-type silicon, carriers are electrons, the drain is operated positive relative to the source, and the p-type gate is held at or below the source potential so the gate-channel junction stays reverse biased. A p-channel JFET is the complement: p-type channel, hole conduction, drain negative relative to source, and the n-type gate held at or above the source. The transfer law is the same, I_D = I_DSS(1 − V_GS/V_P)², with the signs of V_GS and V_P reversed. Electron mobility in silicon is about three times hole mobility, so for the same geometry an n-channel device has higher transconductance, higher I_DSS and better high-frequency performance, which is why n-channel JFETs dominate RF front ends and low-noise audio stages; p-channel parts exist mainly for complementary circuits and positive-rail current sources. This channel-polarity split runs through the whole FET family: MOSFETs are likewise n- or p-channel, and in each case the gate polarity that turns the device on or off follows from the channel type.", "worked_example": "Compare the same circuit built both ways. N-channel: drain to +12 V through R_D, source to ground through R_S, gate returned to ground; self-bias gives V_GS negative, say −1.5 V with I_D = 2 mA. P-channel: drain to −12 V (or source to +12 V with drain toward ground), gate returned to the source rail side; self-bias gives V_GS = +1.5 V at the same 2 mA. Every voltage changes sign and the device behaves identically otherwise.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: FET type refers to the construction family (JFET, MOSFET, GaAsFET). Correction: within the junction FET family the two basic types are defined by the channel's doping, n-channel or p-channel, which sets the carrier type and all operating polarities.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "N-channel: Negative gate pinches, positive drain pulls. P-channel: everything flipped.", "edge_cases": "Because hole mobility is lower, a p-channel JFET with matching I_DSS needs a wider channel and has higher capacitance, so complementary FET pairs are never perfectly matched the way complementary BJT pairs can be approximated."}

{"core": "In an n-channel depletion-type MOSFET the current carriers are electrons flowing through a built-in n-type channel, and the gate operates by depleting that channel of electrons. Electron conduction is therefore the signature of n-channel depletion operation.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A p-channel device conducts by holes, not electrons, so p-channel depletion is the wrong carrier type even though the mode matches.", "why_tempting": "Depletion is the correct mode, and the learner may miss that the carrier type pins the channel type."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "P-channel enhancement is wrong on both counts: hole conduction and a channel that must be induced rather than built in.", "why_tempting": "Enhancement MOSFETs are the ones most learners have handled, so enhancement is a familiar word to reach for."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "There is no q-channel; semiconductor channels are n-type (electron) or p-type (hole) only.", "why_tempting": "It looks like the next letter in a series and is a pure nonsense filler that a rushed reader may not reject."}], "concept": "The channel type of any FET names the majority carrier: n-channel means an n-type channel where electrons carry the current from source to drain, p-channel means a p-type channel carrying holes. The mode names whether that channel exists at zero gate bias: depletion means it was diffused in during manufacture and the gate's job is to thin it, enhancement means the gate must induce it. An n-channel depletion MOSFET therefore has an n-type channel between n+ source and drain regions on a p-type substrate, conducts I_DSS at V_GS = 0, is reduced toward pinch-off by negative V_GS (which repels electrons from the channel and depletes it), and can be driven above I_DSS by positive V_GS (which attracts more electrons, enhancing it). Its transfer curve I_D = I_DSS(1 − V_GS/V_P)² is identical to a JFET's except that it extends into positive V_GS. Electron conduction with a built-in channel is the dual-gate RF MOSFET found in classic receiver front ends and mixers, where the second gate provides AGC.", "worked_example": "An n-channel depletion MOSFET with I_DSS = 6 mA and V_P = −3 V. V_GS = −1.5 V: I_D = 6(1 − 0.5)² = 1.5 mA, electrons partially depleted from the channel. V_GS = 0: I_D = 6 mA. V_GS = +1 V: I_D = 6(1 + 1/3)² ≈ 10.7 mA, the channel enhanced beyond its built-in conductivity. The carriers are electrons throughout; only their number in the channel changes.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: depletion and enhancement describe the carrier type. Correction: the carrier type is fixed by the channel doping (n gives electrons, p gives holes); depletion versus enhancement only describes whether the channel is present at zero gate bias.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "N for Negative carriers (electrons), P for Positive carriers (holes); the mode is a separate axis.", "edge_cases": "Depletion-mode MOSFETs are far less common than enhancement types in modern catalogues and are mostly found in RF small-signal and some high-voltage start-up circuits, so the exam's symmetry between the four variants is more complete than the marketplace."}

{"core": "An n-channel enhancement MOSFET has n+ source and drain in a p-type body with no built-in channel; a positive gate voltage above threshold attracts electrons to the surface and creates an n-type inversion layer. Conduction is by electrons through that induced channel, so electron conduction corresponds to n-channel enhancement.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A p-channel enhancement device induces a hole channel under a negative gate, so its carriers are holes, not electrons.", "why_tempting": "The mode matches, and the carrier-to-channel mapping is the fact most often dropped."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "P-channel depletion uses holes in a built-in channel, wrong on both the carrier and the mode.", "why_tempting": "It is the complete complement of the correct answer, a plausible-looking pick for a learner who has the mapping inverted."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "No q-channel exists; channels are n or p only.", "why_tempting": "Filler option that a learner eliminating quickly might skip past without rejecting."}], "concept": "An n-channel enhancement MOSFET is the device inside most power switches, CMOS logic and modern RF amplifiers. With V_GS = 0 the p-type body separates the two n+ regions by back-to-back p-n junctions and no current flows. When V_GS exceeds the threshold V_th the gate's electric field pushes holes away from the oxide interface and pulls electrons in, inverting the surface to n-type; this inversion layer is the channel and electrons flow through it from source to drain under a positive V_DS. Current follows I_D = K(V_GS − V_th)² in saturation. The p-channel complement works identically with a negative gate voltage pulling holes into an n-type body to form a p-type channel. Because an n-channel device is off at zero bias, conducts with a positive gate relative to the source, and has electron mobility on its side, it is the preferred switch in nearly every application; p-channel enhancement devices are used mainly for high-side switching where a gate pulled below the positive rail is convenient.", "worked_example": "Thought experiment: take an n-channel enhancement MOSFET with V_th = 2 V and ground the source. At V_GS = 1 V there is no inversion layer and I_D is nanoamps of leakage. Step V_GS to 3 V and electrons populate the surface; with K = 0.2 A/V², I_D = 0.2 × 1² = 0.2 A in saturation. Reverse the test on a p-channel part: V_GS = +3 V does nothing; V_GS = −3 V induces holes and the same magnitude of current flows, carried by holes, with V_DS negative.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: enhancement MOSFETs have a channel that the gate merely opens wider. Correction: the enhancement device has no channel at all until the gate inverts the body surface; the electrons that conduct are attracted there by the gate field and vanish when it is removed.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "Positive gate pulls in electrons: n-channel enhancement.", "edge_cases": "The induced channel's mobility is lower than bulk silicon because electrons scatter at the oxide interface, and at high V_GS the channel resistance stops falling; this is why R_DS(on) curves flatten above about 10 V of gate drive."}

{"core": "A p-channel depletion MOSFET has a built-in p-type channel between p+ source and drain regions, so holes carry current at zero gate bias and the gate reduces current by depleting them. Hole conduction with a pre-existing channel is p-channel depletion.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "There is no q-channel; the only channel types are n (electron) and p (hole).", "why_tempting": "A nonsense filler that reads like a legitimate category to a learner scanning for unfamiliar terms."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "N-channel depletion conducts by electrons; the mode is right but the carrier is wrong.", "why_tempting": "Depletion is the matching mode, and the learner may not have internalized that holes imply p-type."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "N-channel enhancement is wrong on both counts: electrons as carriers and no built-in channel.", "why_tempting": "It is the most common MOSFET type in practice, making it a reflexive choice."}], "concept": "The carrier type and the channel type are the same fact: holes are the majority carriers of p-type semiconductor, so hole conduction means a p-type channel. In a depletion device that channel is present at V_GS = 0, giving I_DSS, and for a p-channel part the gate depletes it by going positive relative to the source, repelling holes from the channel region; going negative enhances it by attracting more holes. The drain is operated negative relative to the source so holes drift from source to drain, and conventional current flows source to drain, out of the drain. The transfer characteristic has the same form as every other depletion-mode FET, I_D = I_DSS(1 − V_GS/V_P)², with V_P positive for p-channel. Hole mobility is roughly one third of electron mobility in silicon, so p-channel depletion devices have lower transconductance and higher on-resistance for the same size, which is why they are uncommon; they appear where a normally-on device referenced to a positive rail is needed.", "worked_example": "P-channel depletion MOSFET with I_DSS = 4 mA and V_P = +2.5 V, source at +12 V, drain through a load toward ground. At V_GS = 0 (gate at +12 V): I_D = 4 mA of holes flowing source to drain. Raise the gate to +13.25 V so V_GS = +1.25 V: I_D = 4(1 − 0.5)² = 1 mA. Raise it to +14.5 V (V_GS = +2.5 V): pinched off, I_D ≈ 0. Pull the gate to +11 V (V_GS = −1 V): I_D = 4(1 + 0.4)² ≈ 7.8 mA, enhanced.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: holes are a property of the mode, so depletion devices conduct by holes and enhancement devices by electrons. Correction: carriers are set by channel doping alone; a p-channel device conducts by holes whether it is depletion or enhancement type.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "Holes live in P-type: hole conduction always means P-channel.", "edge_cases": "The four-way matrix in the exam (n/p times depletion/enhancement) is logically complete, but commercially p-channel depletion MOSFETs are rare; the question is testing the mapping, not a device you are likely to buy."}

{"core": "A p-channel enhancement MOSFET has p+ source and drain in an n-type body with no channel at zero bias; a gate driven negative relative to the source attracts holes to the surface and induces a p-type channel. Hole conduction through an induced channel is p-channel enhancement.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "N-channel depletion is the exact opposite: electron carriers and a built-in channel.", "why_tempting": "A learner with the mapping fully inverted lands here with confidence."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "N-channel enhancement induces an electron channel with a positive gate; the mode matches but the carriers are electrons, not holes.", "why_tempting": "It is the familiar power-switch MOSFET, and enhancement is the correct mode."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "There is no q-channel; the only possibilities are n-type (electrons) and p-type (holes).", "why_tempting": "Filler option that survives a quick scan because it sounds like a category."}], "concept": "The p-channel enhancement MOSFET is the complement of the ubiquitous n-channel enhancement device. Its body is n-type, its source and drain are p+ regions, and at V_GS = 0 the two p-n junctions block current in both directions. When V_GS falls below a negative threshold (say −2 V), the gate field repels electrons and accumulates holes at the oxide interface, inverting the surface to p-type and forming a channel. Holes then flow from source to drain under a negative V_DS, so conventional current enters the source (the most positive terminal) and leaves the drain. The saturation current obeys I_D = K(V_GS − V_th)² with both V_GS and V_th negative. The practical attraction is high-side switching: with the source tied to the positive supply, pulling the gate toward ground turns the device on, which is easy to drive from a microcontroller without a level shifter or charge pump. The penalty is lower hole mobility, so for the same on-resistance a p-channel device needs about three times the die area of an n-channel one and has correspondingly higher capacitance.", "worked_example": "High-side switch with a p-channel enhancement MOSFET, V_th = −2 V, K = 0.3 A/V², source at +12 V, drain to a 24 Ω load to ground. Gate at +12 V: V_GS = 0, no channel, load off. Gate pulled to 0 V: V_GS = −12 V, well beyond threshold, so the device is in its ohmic region; with R_DS(on) ≈ 1/(2 × 0.3 × 10) ≈ 0.17 Ω the load gets about 11.9 V and 0.5 A, carried by holes through the induced channel.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a MOSFET is turned on by a positive gate voltage regardless of type. Correction: the gate must be driven in the direction that attracts the channel's carriers, positive for electrons (n-channel) and negative for holes (p-channel); a p-channel enhancement device turns on with its gate below its source.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "Negative gate gathers holes: p-channel enhancement.", "edge_cases": "Like its n-channel counterpart, a p-channel enhancement MOSFET contains a body diode (drain to source in the conducting direction of the n-body/p-drain junction) that conducts if the drain is pulled above the source, so it cannot block reverse voltage in a high-side switch."}

{"core": "An SCR is a four-layer PNPN device with three connections: the anode on the outer p-layer, the cathode on the outer n-layer, and the gate on the inner p-layer next to the cathode. Current flows anode to cathode once the gate triggers it.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Base, collector and emitter are bipolar transistor terminals; the SCR can be modelled as two interlocked transistors but its external terminals are named for its rectifier-like behaviour.", "why_tempting": "The two-transistor equivalent model uses these names internally, and the learner may surface them."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Gate, source and sink is not a real device terminal set; source and drain are FET terms and sink is a circuit role, not a terminal.", "why_tempting": "Gate is correct, and source-sink sounds like a current path."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Gate (or emitter), base 1 and base 2 belong to the unijunction transistor, a device often used to trigger SCRs but structurally different.", "why_tempting": "UJTs and SCRs appear together in phase-control circuits, so their terminal names get mixed."}], "concept": "The SCR is a rectifier that stays off until commanded. Its PNPN stack has three junctions: J1 between anode p and the first n, J2 the central blocking junction, and J3 between the gate p-layer and the cathode n-layer. With anode positive, J1 and J3 are forward biased but J2 is reverse biased and blocks; the device is in its forward blocking state. A pulse of gate current into the gate (positive relative to the cathode) injects carriers across J3, which flood J2 and collapse its barrier, and the device latches on. In the two-transistor model the inner layers form a PNP and an NPN cross-connected so that each one's collector drives the other's base; once the loop gain α_PNP + α_NPN reaches 1, regeneration holds the device on with no further gate drive. The gate therefore only initiates conduction; turning off requires reducing anode current below the holding current, which in AC circuits happens every half cycle. The anode-cathode terminals carry the load current, which can be hundreds of amps, while the gate needs only milliamps for microseconds, giving enormous power gain in a single device.", "worked_example": "A 600 V, 25 A SCR with a gate trigger current of 20 mA and gate trigger voltage of 1.5 V is placed in series with a 10 Ω heater on 120 V AC. A gate pulse of 1.5 V at 20 mA delivered for 10 μs (energy about 0.3 μJ) at the 60° point of the positive half cycle turns it on, and roughly 12 A peak flows anode to cathode for the remaining 120° of that half cycle; the SCR turns off at the zero crossing because current falls below the holding current. One milliwatt-scale gate pulse controls over a kilowatt.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the SCR gate behaves like a transistor base that modulates current continuously. Correction: the gate is a trigger only; once the anode-cathode path latches, the gate loses control and the device conducts fully until anode current is interrupted.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "ACG: Anode in, Cathode out, Gate to fire.", "edge_cases": "Some SCRs can also be triggered unintentionally by a fast rising anode voltage (dV/dt triggering through J2's capacitance) or by excessive temperature, so snubbers across the device are standard in inductive and noisy circuits."}

{"core": "An SCR is a bistable latch: it is either blocking (off, non-conducting, passing only leakage) or latched on (conducting like a forward-biased diode). There is no stable intermediate state, so the two stable operating conditions are conducting and non-conducting.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "The two-transistor equivalent has NPN and PNP parts that conduct together, not alternately; they are a single regenerative loop, not two separate states.", "why_tempting": "The two-transistor model is taught alongside the SCR and the learner may think each transistor represents a state."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "An SCR does not oscillate; it switches and latches. Quiescent is a bias term for linear amplifiers, not a thyristor state.", "why_tempting": "Oscillators and SCR relaxation circuits (with a UJT) are sometimes discussed together, inviting the mix-up."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "An SCR is a rectifier and does not conduct in reverse; with cathode positive it blocks until reverse breakdown, which is a failure mode, not an operating condition.", "why_tempting": "A triac does conduct in both directions, and the learner may transfer that property to the SCR."}], "concept": "Bistability comes from positive feedback inside the PNPN structure. Modelling it as a PNP (anode-side) and an NPN (cathode-side) transistor, the NPN's collector current is the PNP's base current and vice versa. The anode current is I_A = (α_NPN·I_G + I_leak)/(1 − α_NPN − α_PNP). While both alphas are small (low current), the denominator is near 1 and the device is off with only leakage flowing: the non-conducting state. A gate pulse raises current, alphas rise with current, and as α_NPN + α_PNP approaches 1 the denominator goes to zero and the current runs away until limited by the external circuit: the conducting state, where the device acts like a forward-biased diode with about 1 to 2 V drop. The on state is self-sustaining as long as anode current exceeds the holding current I_H; the off state is self-sustaining as long as the gate is not triggered and V_AK stays below the breakover voltage. This latching makes the SCR ideal for crowbar overvoltage protection in power supplies, phase-control dimmers and controlled rectifiers, and makes it unsuited to linear control, which needs a device with a continuum of stable operating points.", "worked_example": "Crowbar thought experiment: an SCR sits across a 13.8 V supply output with a Zener-triggered gate set to fire at 15 V. Normally the SCR is non-conducting and draws microamps. If a regulator fails and the output climbs past 15 V, the gate fires, the SCR snaps into the conducting state within a microsecond, drops the rail to about 1.5 V and blows the input fuse. Removing the gate signal changes nothing; only interrupting the anode current (the fuse) returns it to non-conducting.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: an SCR, like a transistor, has a linear region where it partially conducts under gate control. Correction: regenerative feedback forces it into one of two states, fully off or fully on, and the gate can only move it from off to on.", "link": "section 4", "mnemonic": "SCR: Snap, Conduct, Remain — two states, no in-between.", "edge_cases": "During the microseconds of turn-on the device does pass through a high-dissipation transition where only part of the die is conducting; the datasheet di/dt limit exists because that transient state is destructive if current rises faster than the conducting area spreads."}

{"core": "Once triggered, the SCR's central blocking junction collapses and the anode-to-cathode path behaves like a single forward-biased silicon p-n junction: low dynamic resistance, a forward drop of roughly 1 to 2 V, and current limited only by the external circuit. Its characteristics are therefore similar to a junction diode.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A varactor is operated reverse biased as a voltage-variable capacitor; a conducting SCR is forward biased and resistive, nothing like a tunable capacitor.", "why_tempting": "Varactor is a prominent diode type in the section and gets picked as a familiar name."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "A PIN diode's defining property is RF behaviour as a bias-controlled resistor with a thick intrinsic layer; the SCR has no intrinsic layer and is used at power frequencies.", "why_tempting": "Both are multi-layer devices with a letter-string name, so they feel structurally related."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A Schottky diode has a metal-semiconductor barrier with a low forward drop of about 0.3 V and no minority-carrier storage; a conducting SCR has a higher drop (about 1 to 2 V) and heavy minority-carrier storage, so the match is poor.", "why_tempting": "Both conduct forward current, and the learner may think any fast diode qualifies."}], "concept": "The SCR is PNPN; its name says it is a rectifier, and once gated it rectifies exactly like a diode made from the outer P and N layers with the middle junction shorted out by the carrier flood. The on-state I-V curve is that of a p-n junction in series with a small bulk resistance: V_AK ≈ V_j + I·R_bulk, typically 1.2 V at rated current for a medium device and higher for high-voltage parts because of their thicker, more lightly doped blocking layers. The device blocks in reverse like a diode as well, since J1 and J3 are reverse biased with cathode positive; reverse blocking capability is one of the SCR's defining differences from a triac. The analogy also carries the diode's thermal and recovery behaviour: on-state dissipation is V_AK × I_avg, and turning off requires the stored charge to recombine, giving a turn-off time t_q of tens of microseconds during which forward voltage must not be reapplied or the device re-latches without a gate signal. In a controlled rectifier, each SCR is simply a diode that waits for permission.", "worked_example": "Thought experiment: replace one of the two diodes in a full-wave centre-tapped rectifier with an SCR gated at the start of each positive half cycle. The output waveform is identical to the all-diode version, because once gated the SCR conducts exactly like the diode it replaced, with perhaps 0.5 V more drop. Delay the gate pulse by 90° and the SCR still conducts like a diode, but only for the last half of each half cycle, halving the average output: that is phase control, a diode with a timed on switch.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: an SCR in conduction behaves like a saturated transistor with a collector-emitter drop of a few hundred millivolts and gate-controlled current. Correction: it behaves like a forward-biased junction diode, with a diode's forward drop and a diode's indifference to its control terminal once on.", "link": "section 4", "mnemonic": "Gated on, it is just a diode: Silicon Controlled Rectifier means a rectifier with a permission switch.", "edge_cases": "The on-state drop of an SCR is higher than that of a single diode because current must traverse three junctions' worth of silicon; at high currents this adds measurable loss compared with a Schottky or ordinary rectifier."}

{"core": "An SCR resembles a forward-biased silicon rectifier only after it has been gated on: the gate pulse collapses the central blocking junction and the anode-cathode path latches into a low-resistance, diode-like forward conduction. Before gating it blocks forward voltage; the gated-on state is the diode-like condition.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "An SCR cannot be gated off; the gate has no control once the device is latched, and in the off state the device blocks forward voltage, the opposite of a forward-biased diode.", "why_tempting": "Symmetry suggests the gate can toggle both ways, and gate turn-off thyristors (GTOs) do exist, blurring the distinction."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "An SCR is not used as a signal detector; it has large junction area, heavy carrier storage and a trigger threshold that make it useless for demodulation.", "why_tempting": "Detector is a diode application, and the question is about diode-like behaviour."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "During the switching transition the device passes through a high-impedance, high-dissipation region as the conducting area spreads; it does not look like a forward-biased diode until the transition completes.", "why_tempting": "Switching transition sounds technically specific and is a real phase of SCR operation."}], "concept": "The SCR has three regions of its forward characteristic. In forward blocking (anode positive, no gate signal) the central junction J2 is reverse biased and only microamps of leakage flow; the device looks like an open circuit up to its forward breakover voltage. When a gate current I_GT is injected, carriers from the cathode junction flood J2, the two-transistor loop gain reaches unity, and the device enters forward conduction, the third region, where its I-V curve is that of a forward-biased silicon rectifier with about 1 to 2 V drop and a small dynamic resistance. Conduction persists without gate current as long as anode current stays above the holding current I_H. The gate's influence is therefore a one-way, one-time event per conduction interval: it determines when conduction starts, and in an AC circuit the natural current zero determines when it stops. This asymmetry is the heart of phase-control dimmers, controlled rectifiers for variable DC supplies, and crowbar protection, where a single short gate pulse commits the device to conduct until the circuit itself removes the current.", "worked_example": "Measure a small SCR on a curve tracer with 12 V on the anode through 100 Ω. Gate open: anode current is about 10 μA, V_AK ≈ 12 V, the device is a blocking junction. Apply a 5 mA gate pulse for 20 μs: V_AK drops to about 1.1 V and I_A = (12 − 1.1)/100 ≈ 109 mA, persisting after the gate pulse ends. Reduce the anode supply until I_A falls below the 5 mA holding current: the device snaps back to blocking. Only in the middle measurement did it resemble a forward-biased rectifier.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: an SCR is a diode with a gate that can turn it on and off. Correction: it is a diode that is held off until gated on; turn-off is achieved only by reducing anode current below holding, not by the gate.", "link": "section 4", "mnemonic": "Gate on, diode on; gate off, nothing changes.", "edge_cases": "Variants exist that relax this rule: the gate turn-off thyristor (GTO) can be switched off with a large negative gate pulse, and MOS-controlled thyristors behave similarly, but a plain SCR cannot be gated off."}

{"core": "An SCR is a four-layer semiconductor with alternating doping, P-N-P-N from anode to cathode, giving three p-n junctions. The outer P is the anode, the outer N the cathode, and the gate connects to the inner P layer.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "NPPN would have two adjacent p-layers forming no junction between them, so it would be only a two-junction NPN structure; it cannot latch.", "why_tempting": "It is a four-letter string with the right letters, and a learner who remembers four layers but not the alternation may pick it."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "PNNP likewise merges the two inner layers into one and has only two junctions; it is a PNP transistor with a thick base, not a thyristor.", "why_tempting": "Same four letters, differently arranged."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "PPNN is just a single p-n junction with extra material on each side, electrically a diode.", "why_tempting": "A learner thinking SCR equals rectifier equals p-n may choose the arrangement that most resembles a diode."}], "concept": "Thyristor action requires three junctions in series with alternating polarity, which is exactly what P-N-P-N provides. Label the junctions J1 (anode P to N1), J2 (N1 to P2) and J3 (P2 to cathode N2). With anode positive J1 and J3 are forward biased but J2 is reverse biased and blocks. The regenerative behaviour comes from viewing the stack as two overlapping transistors sharing their middle layers: the top three layers P-N1-P2 are a PNP and the bottom three N1-P2-N2 are an NPN, with N1 serving as the PNP's base and the NPN's collector, and P2 serving as the NPN's base and the PNP's collector. Gate current into P2 is base current for the NPN, whose collector current pulls base current from the PNP, whose collector current feeds back into P2. Once the sum of the two alphas reaches unity the loop sustains itself and J2 is flooded with carriers, losing its blocking ability; that is the on state. The same P-N-P-N stack with a second gate structure gives the triac (two antiparallel SCRs in one die) and with no gate the four-layer diode (Shockley diode) that breaks over on voltage alone.", "worked_example": "Trace the layers for a small SCR: anode contact on P1 (heavily doped), N1 (lightly doped, thick, sets forward blocking voltage, perhaps 50 μm for 600 V), P2 (the gate layer, moderately doped), N2 (heavily doped cathode). Blocking voltage is set almost entirely by the thickness and doping of N1 across J2, the way a rectifier's rating is set by its lightly doped side. Reversing the device (cathode positive) reverse biases J1 and J3, so it blocks in reverse too, consistent with it being a rectifier.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the SCR is a three-layer device like a transistor with an extra terminal. Correction: it has four alternating layers and three junctions; the extra junction is what allows the regenerative latch that a three-layer transistor cannot produce.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "Pancake stack: P-N-P-N, anode on top, cathode at the bottom, gate taps the lower P.", "edge_cases": "Real SCRs often include cathode shorts (small regions where the gate P layer is shorted to the cathode metal) to reduce dV/dt sensitivity and leakage-induced triggering at high temperature, a refinement of the ideal four-layer picture."}

{"core": "The SCR's control terminal is the gate, connected to the inner p-layer adjacent to the cathode. A small current pulse into the gate relative to the cathode triggers the device from blocking into conduction, which is the only control the SCR offers.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "The anode is the main positive terminal that carries the load current into the device; raising anode voltage can cause breakover, but that is a limit, not a control input.", "why_tempting": "Anode is the terminal most associated with the SCR's rectifier identity, and voltage on it does affect triggering."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "The cathode is the main negative terminal and the return for both load current and gate current; it is a reference, not a control element.", "why_tempting": "The gate signal is applied with respect to the cathode, so the cathode's name appears in trigger specifications."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "An SCR has no emitter; that term belongs to bipolar transistors and vacuum tubes.", "why_tempting": "In the two-transistor model the cathode layer acts as the NPN's emitter, and the term leaks into the SCR vocabulary."}], "concept": "The gate is the base of the cathode-side NPN transistor in the two-transistor model of the PNPN stack. Injecting gate current I_G forward biases the gate-cathode junction J3, launching electrons from the cathode into the gate p-layer; most are collected across the blocking junction J2 into N1, where they act as base current for the anode-side PNP, whose collector current returns to the gate layer and reinforces the original injection. Triggering requires the gate current to exceed I_GT (milliamps to tens of milliamps) for long enough that anode current rises above the latching current I_L; after that the gate can be removed. The gate controls only the turn-on instant; it cannot modulate the on-state current and cannot turn the device off. Gate sensitivity varies with temperature (I_GT falls when hot) and gate-cathode resistors are often added to desensitize the device against noise and leakage. Isolated gate drive (pulse transformer or optocoupler) is standard in AC phase control, since the gate must be driven relative to a cathode that may be at line potential.", "worked_example": "Half-wave phase-control dimmer on 120 V AC with a 100 Ω load. A trigger circuit delivers a 50 mA, 20 μs gate pulse at a delay of 4.2 ms after each positive zero crossing (about 90°). At that moment the anode is at the 170 V peak; the SCR fires, drops to 1.5 V, and passes about 1.7 A falling to zero over the remaining 4.2 ms. Average load power is roughly half of full-wave rectified maximum. Shifting the gate pulse earlier or later is the only knob; nothing about the gate drive amplitude changes the on-state behaviour once I_GT is exceeded.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the gate of an SCR, like a FET gate or a transistor base, is a proportional control. Correction: the gate is a trigger whose job ends the instant the device latches; control of power is achieved by timing the trigger, not by varying it.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "The Gate opens the gate and then steps aside.", "edge_cases": "Driving the gate negative relative to the cathode while the device is on does not turn a conventional SCR off and can damage the gate junction; only GTO thyristors are designed for negative gate turn-off."}

{"core": "Thyristors are the family of four-layer, three-junction PNPN semiconductor switches that latch on when triggered and stay on until current is interrupted. The SCR is the basic unidirectional member of that family, alongside the triac, diac, GTO and four-layer diode.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A phase-locked loop is a feedback control system (phase detector, loop filter, VCO) used for frequency synthesis and demodulation; it is a circuit, not a semiconductor device family.", "why_tempting": "PLL is another acronym from the Advanced syllabus and shares the letter L with latching concepts in a learner's memory."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Varactors are reverse-biased diodes used as voltage-variable capacitors in tuners and VCOs; they have two layers and no switching action.", "why_tempting": "Varactor appears in the same component subsection and has a similar-sounding technical name."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Varistors (MOVs) are voltage-dependent resistors made of sintered zinc oxide, used to clamp surges; they are not junction devices and do not latch.", "why_tempting": "Varistor is one letter away from varactor and both relate to overvoltage situations, as does the SCR crowbar."}], "concept": "The thyristor family is defined by the regenerative PNPN structure: once the internal transistor pair's loop gain reaches unity the device switches from high impedance to low impedance and remains there without further control input. The members differ in how they are triggered and in conduction direction. The SCR is unidirectional with a cathode-side gate. The triac integrates two antiparallel SCR structures with a single gate to control AC in both directions. The diac is a gateless, bidirectional breakover device used to deliver trigger pulses to triacs. The four-layer (Shockley) diode is a gateless unidirectional breakover device. The GTO adds a gate that can also turn the device off with a large negative pulse. All share the same key parameters: forward breakover voltage, gate trigger current, holding current, latching current, dV/dt and di/dt limits, and turn-off time t_q. Thyristors handle the highest power levels of any semiconductor (kilovolts and kiloamps in HVDC converters) because their on-state is a flooded diode with very low loss, at the cost of having no linear control and only line-commutated turn-off in simple circuits.", "worked_example": "Family tree by behaviour: apply +10 V and a gate pulse to an SCR and it latches, conducting one way. Apply −10 V with the same gate pulse and it blocks. Repeat on a triac and it latches either way, so it can switch AC. Remove the gate and increase the voltage across a diac: at about 30 V it breaks over and conducts in either direction until current drops, which is why it is used to fire a triac at a controllable phase angle. Every one of these is a PNPN latch; only the trigger method and polarity differ.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: an SCR is a special kind of diode or transistor. Correction: it belongs to a distinct device family, thyristors, defined by four-layer regenerative latching; diodes and transistors have no self-sustaining on state.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "Thyristor is the Tribe; SCR, triac, diac and GTO are the members.", "edge_cases": "In modern power electronics IGBTs and MOSFETs have displaced thyristors for most switching below a few hundred kilowatts because they can be turned off from the gate; thyristors remain dominant in very high power line-commutated converters and in simple AC phase control."}

{"core": "An SCR is a latching switch: once its gate fires it conducts heavily and stays on until anode current is removed, which is exactly the behaviour a crowbar needs. When a regulator fails and the output rises past a set point, a Zener or comparator fires the gate, the SCR shorts the supply rail and either blows the fuse or trips the current limit before the load sees the overvoltage.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A Class C stage needs a device that turns off every cycle as the drive falls; an SCR cannot be turned off by its gate and would latch on the first positive half-cycle.", "why_tempting": "Both SCRs and Class C stages conduct in short pulses, so the idea of a pulsed device feels adjacent."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "A microphone preamp needs a small-signal linear device with gain; an SCR has no linear region, it is either blocking or saturated.", "why_tempting": "SCRs are silicon three-terminal devices with a control electrode, superficially like a transistor."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "SWR detection uses a directional coupler and small-signal diodes to rectify forward and reflected samples; a latching power switch has no role there.", "why_tempting": "The word rectifier in SCR suggests a detector or rectifying role."}], "concept": "The SCR is a four-layer PNPN thyristor. Below its breakover voltage it blocks in both directions with no gate signal. A short gate pulse injects carriers into the inner junction, the two internal transistor sections drive each other into saturation, and the device latches with a forward drop of about 1 to 1.5 V. It stays on until anode current falls below the holding current, regardless of the gate. A crowbar circuit exploits this: a sense network (typically a Zener plus a small resistor, or a dedicated crowbar IC) fires the gate when V_out exceeds V_trip, the SCR places a near short across the output, and the upstream fuse, breaker or foldback limiter removes power. Because the SCR carries a huge surge for a few milliseconds, it is specified by its peak surge current I_TSM rather than continuous rating. This protects expensive loads such as a transceiver from a pass-transistor short in a linear supply.", "worked_example": "Take a 13.8 V linear supply with a 2N3055 pass stage that fails collector-to-emitter shorted, so the raw 20 V appears at the output. A 15 V Zener in series with a 100 Ω gate resistor conducts once V_out exceeds about 15.7 V (Zener plus gate-cathode drop), giving roughly (20 − 15.7)/100 ≈ 43 mA of gate current, far above the few mA a 25 A SCR needs. The SCR latches within microseconds, the output collapses to about 1.5 V, the 20 A fuse carries the fault current and opens within tens of milliseconds, and the radio never saw more than a brief spike.", "misconception": "The trap is believing an SCR is just a diode with a gate that can be modulated like a transistor. In fact gate control is one-way: it can only turn the device on, and removing gate drive does nothing. That latching behaviour is useless for amplification but ideal for a protective device that must stay faulted until power is cycled.", "link": "section 4", "mnemonic": "Crowbar: throw a steel bar across the rails and let the fuse decide.", "edge_cases": "A crowbar must trip faster than the load's overvoltage tolerance but slower than switching noise, so a small gate capacitor or deliberate delay is added to avoid nuisance trips. In modern switch-mode supplies the SCR crowbar is often replaced by a latching shutdown of the controller, but the SCR remains the classic answer and still appears in linear bench supplies."}

{"core": "The SCR is the only listed device whose three terminals are named anode, cathode and gate. The anode and cathode name the main current path, like a diode, and the gate is the trigger electrode that turns it on.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A bipolar transistor has emitter, base and collector; its control terminal passes a continuous current, not a trigger pulse.", "why_tempting": "Three terminals, one of which controls conduction, matches the SCR pattern superficially."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "A FET has source, gate and drain (plus sometimes a substrate lead). It shares the word gate but has no anode or cathode.", "why_tempting": "The gate terminal name is shared with the SCR, so a learner may lock onto that word alone."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A triode has a cathode, a control grid and a plate (anode), so it has two of the three names but the control element is a grid, not a gate.", "why_tempting": "Anode and cathode are classic tube terms, and a triode is indeed a three-electrode device."}], "concept": "Terminal naming tracks device physics. Two-terminal rectifiers inherit anode and cathode from vacuum tube and electrochemical convention: conventional current enters the anode and leaves the cathode. The SCR keeps those names because its main path is a rectifier, and adds a gate on the P layer next to the cathode. Injecting gate current into that junction turns on the inner NPN section, which drives the outer PNP section, which in turn supplies more base current to the NPN, a regenerative loop that latches. Bipolar transistors use emitter, base and collector because carriers are emitted, cross a base region, and are collected. FETs use source, gate and drain because carriers flow from source to drain through a channel whose width the gate field controls. Triodes use cathode, grid and plate. Knowing which family a name belongs to lets you decode an unfamiliar schematic quickly.", "worked_example": "Picture a 12 V lamp in series with an SCR anode, cathode to ground. Nothing flows. Touch a 1 kΩ resistor from +12 V to the gate for an instant: about 10 mA of gate current fires the device and the lamp lights. Remove the resistor and the lamp stays lit. Now briefly open the anode circuit or short anode to cathode so current drops below the holding value, and the lamp goes out and stays out. The three terminals you manipulated are anode, cathode and gate.", "misconception": "The trap is that any three-terminal silicon device with a gate must be a FET.
