The SCR borrows the word gate but its other two terminals are rectifier terminals, and its gate is a trigger, not a continuous control.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "SCR = a rectifier (anode, cathode) with a doorbell (gate).", "edge_cases": "The TRIAC, a bidirectional cousin, uses main terminal 1, main terminal 2 and gate because current can flow either way, so anode and cathode would be meaningless. A gate turn-off thyristor (GTO) keeps the SCR names but can also be switched off by a negative gate pulse."}

{"core": "Once gated on, an SCR is a saturated PNPN structure that behaves like an ordinary silicon rectifier in forward conduction: low forward drop of roughly 1 to 1.5 V, current limited only by the external circuit, and it blocks when the anode goes negative.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A reverse-biased rectifier passes only leakage current; the gated-on SCR passes full load current with a small drop, the opposite behaviour.", "why_tempting": "Inverting the bias direction is the simplest confusion between the SCR's blocking state and its conducting state."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "A forward-biased PIN diode acts as a current-controlled RF resistor with slow recovery, used as an attenuator or switch at RF; the SCR has no such controllable resistance and is a hard on switch.", "why_tempting": "Both are forward-biased multi-layer silicon devices used as switches."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A reverse-biased Schottky diode is an open circuit with low capacitance; the conducting SCR is nearly a short.", "why_tempting": "Schottky devices are associated with fast switching, and SCR switching speed may bring them to mind."}], "concept": "The SCR's I-V curve has three regions. In forward blocking (anode positive, no gate) only leakage flows until the forward breakover voltage V_BO. In reverse blocking it behaves like a reverse-biased diode up to V_RRM. In the on state, reached by gate triggering or breakover, the two internal transistors are in saturation so all three junctions are forward biased and the device looks like a single forward-biased PN junction plus a little bulk resistance: V_AK ≈ 1 to 1.5 V, roughly constant over a wide current range. Power dissipation in conduction is therefore P ≈ V_AK × I_avg just as for a rectifier diode. The key difference from a diode is memory: the SCR will not return to blocking until current falls below I_H, the holding current. In AC circuits this happens naturally at every zero crossing, which is why SCRs make simple phase-controlled rectifiers.", "worked_example": "An SCR phase-controls a 120 V RMS, 60 Hz heater drawing 10 A. Once fired each positive half-cycle it drops about 1.2 V. Conduction loss ≈ 1.2 V × 10 A × 0.5 (half-wave duty) ≈ 6 W, so a heatsink is needed, the same calculation you would do for a 10 A rectifier diode. At the negative half-cycle current reverses, falls below I_H (say 20 mA), and the SCR reverts to blocking until the next gate pulse.", "misconception": "The trap is thinking a triggered SCR behaves like a resistor whose value depends on gate drive, as a transistor would. Gate drive sets only whether it fires; after that the forward characteristic is a diode-like fixed drop independent of the gate.", "link": "section 2", "edge_cases": "At very high di/dt the SCR can be damaged because conduction starts near the gate and spreads across the die at finite speed, so power SCRs need series inductance; and a fast dv/dt on the anode can falsely trigger the device through junction capacitance (snubber networks prevent this)."}

{"core": "The SCR is built from four alternating semiconductor layers, P-N-P-N, giving three junctions. The anode connects to the outer P, the cathode to the outer N, and the gate to the inner P layer.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A Zener diode is a single PN junction doped heavily so it breaks down at a controlled reverse voltage; it has two layers, not four.", "why_tempting": "Zeners and SCRs both appear in overvoltage protection circuits, so they are mentally filed together."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "A PIN diode is P-type, intrinsic (undoped) and N-type: three layers, with the intrinsic region giving it RF resistance control and slow carrier lifetime.", "why_tempting": "The three letters P-I-N look like a layer sequence and the learner may miscount or misread I as another doped layer."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A Schottky diode is a metal-to-N-semiconductor junction with no P layer at all; its low forward drop comes from majority-carrier conduction.", "why_tempting": "It is a diode listed alongside the others, and diode family questions encourage guessing."}], "concept": "Think of the PNPN stack as two transistors sharing layers: the top P-N-P (anode, N1, P2) is a PNP whose collector is the inner P layer, and the bottom N-P-N (N1, P2, cathode N2) is an NPN whose collector is the inner N layer. Each transistor's collector feeds the other's base. With no gate current the loop gain α1 + α2 is below unity and the device blocks. A gate pulse raises the NPN current, its collector pulls base current from the PNP, the PNP collector feeds the NPN base, and when α1 + α2 reaches 1 the loop regenerates and latches. The layer count explains the other devices too: a Zener is PN, a PIN is P-I-N (three layers, two with doping), a Schottky is metal-N, a bipolar transistor is NPN or PNP (three layers), a DIAC is a symmetrical three-layer trigger, and a TRIAC is effectively two PNPN paths in antiparallel.", "worked_example": "Model an SCR as a 2N3906 PNP and a 2N3904 NPN: tie the PNP collector to the NPN base, the NPN collector to the PNP base, PNP emitter is the anode, NPN emitter is the cathode, and the NPN base is the gate. Put a 1 kΩ load from +9 V to the anode. Nothing flows. Tap the gate to +9 V through 10 kΩ for an instant and the pair latches with about 8 mA through the load and roughly 0.8 V across the stack. Disconnect the 9 V momentarily and it resets. You have built a PNPN device from two three-layer devices, which is exactly how the layers are counted.", "misconception": "The trap is treating every diode-like component as a two-layer PN junction. The SCR's defining feature is the extra pair of layers that create the regenerative loop; without four layers there is no latching.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "PNPN: two transistors holding hands, each one keeping the other awake.", "edge_cases": "The discrete two-transistor model latches more easily than a real SCR because small-signal transistors have high beta; real SCRs are doped so the sum of alphas stays well below one until triggered, giving useful dv/dt immunity."}

{"core": "A Class A stage is biased at the midpoint of its linear region so the device conducts continuously, for all 360 degrees of the input cycle. Output current never reaches cutoff, which gives the best linearity at the cost of efficiency.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Exactly 180 degrees of conduction defines Class B, where the device is biased right at cutoff and reproduces only half the waveform.", "why_tempting": "Half-cycle conduction is the next class in the sequence and the numbers are easily swapped."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Conduction between 180 and 360 degrees is Class AB, biased slightly above cutoff to remove crossover distortion in push-pull stages.", "why_tempting": "A learner may remember that Class A conducts more than half the cycle and stop short of the full 360."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Less than 180 degrees is Class C, where the device is biased below cutoff and conducts only in brief pulses at the waveform peaks.", "why_tempting": "Class C is associated with RF transmitters, and the learner may mix up which class is the transmitter one."}], "concept": "Amplifier class is defined by the conduction angle, the portion of the input cycle over which the device passes current. In Class A the quiescent bias point sits near the middle of the load line, so the signal swings the current up and down around a standing DC value without ever reaching zero: conduction angle 360 degrees. The price is that the device dissipates its full quiescent power even with no signal; the theoretical maximum efficiency is 25 percent with a resistive load or 50 percent with a transformer or inductor load. The benefit is that the transfer function is used only in its most linear region, so harmonic and intermodulation distortion are lowest. Class A is standard for small-signal receiver front ends, IF stages, audio preamps and low-level driver stages where distortion matters more than heat.", "worked_example": "Bias a transistor at V_CE = 6 V, I_C = 10 mA from a 12 V supply with a 600 Ω collector load. Quiescent dissipation is 6 V × 10 mA = 60 mW continuously. Drive it with a sinusoid that swings the collector current from 1 mA to 19 mA: the current never hits zero, so conduction is the full 360 degrees. Output power is at most (6 V peak)² / (2 × 600 Ω) ≈ 30 mW while the supply delivers 12 V × 10 mA = 120 mW, so efficiency is 25 percent at best, the classic Class A number.", "misconception": "The trap is assuming the device must at some point stop conducting for amplification to happen. In Class A it never does; the output is a scaled copy of the input riding on a DC standing current, and the output coupling network strips the DC.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "A for All of the cycle.", "edge_cases": "Class A efficiency can approach 50 percent with an inductive or transformer load because the collector can swing to nearly twice the supply voltage, but it never exceeds that bound."}

{"core": "Class A has the highest linearity because the device conducts for the whole cycle while operating in the centre of its transfer curve; it never passes through cutoff, so there is no crossover or clipping distortion from the bias scheme itself.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Class C conducts in pulses of less than half a cycle; its output is a train of current spikes and only the tank circuit reconstructs a sinewave, so it is the least linear class.", "why_tempting": "Class C is the class most often discussed in RF amplifier questions, so it may be guessed as the best for something."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Class AB conducts slightly more than 180 degrees; in push-pull it is quite linear but there is still a small nonlinearity near the handover between devices.", "why_tempting": "Class AB is the usual compromise for SSB linears and may be remembered as the linear class."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Class B conducts exactly half a cycle; at the zero crossing both devices of a push-pull pair are near cutoff and the output shows crossover distortion.", "why_tempting": "Push-pull Class B produces a full sinewave from two half-cycle devices, which can look like full linearity."}], "concept": "Distortion arises wherever the transfer characteristic I_out versus V_in is curved. A bipolar transistor follows I_C ≈ I_S exp(V_BE/V_T) and a FET follows a square law, so both are nonlinear, but the curvature is gentlest in the middle of the usable range and worst near cutoff. Class A keeps the operating point in that middle region at all times. As bias moves toward cutoff (AB, then B), the device spends part of the cycle in the most curved region or fully off, and two devices must hand over to each other; any mismatch between the two halves or the exponential knee introduces crossover distortion rich in odd harmonics. Class C abandons linearity entirely. The ordering of linearity, A better than AB better than B better than C, is exactly the reverse of the efficiency ordering, and that trade-off is the central idea of this subsection.", "worked_example": "Imagine driving a single transistor with a 1 kHz sinewave and watching the collector waveform. Biased Class A at mid-supply, the output is a clean inverted sinewave; THD maybe 1 percent. Lower the bias toward cutoff so the bottom of the swing clips: the negative half-cycle flattens and a spectrum analyzer now shows strong second harmonic. Lower it below cutoff so only the peaks conduct and you have narrow pulses with harmonics stronger than the fundamental. Nothing changed but the bias, and linearity went from best to worst.", "misconception": "The trap is believing push-pull Class B or AB is just as linear as Class A because the output waveform looks complete. The seam between the two devices is a real nonlinearity, and single-ended Class A avoids it altogether.", "link": "section 2", "edge_cases": "Negative feedback can make a Class AB stage measure as linear as an open-loop Class A stage, which is why audio hi-fi and SSB linears use AB with feedback; the question is about the intrinsic class behaviour without feedback."}

{"core": "Class AB is biased just above cutoff so the device conducts for slightly more than half the cycle but well short of the full cycle: more than 180 degrees but less than 360.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Full-cycle conduction is Class A, biased at the centre of the load line.", "why_tempting": "The A in AB suggests the learner should answer as if it were Class A."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Less than 180 degrees is Class C, biased below cutoff so only the signal peaks turn the device on.", "why_tempting": "A learner thinking AB is slightly worse than B may push the angle in the wrong direction."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Exactly 180 degrees is Class B, biased at the cutoff threshold.", "why_tempting": "The B in AB suggests the half-cycle Class B value."}], "concept": "Class AB sits between A and B on the bias axis. A small quiescent current (a few percent of peak) keeps the device slightly on at zero signal, so the exponential knee of the transistor's V_BE curve is already past when the signal arrives. The device conducts for about 190 to 240 degrees in typical designs. In a push-pull pair each half conducts a little past the zero crossing so the two halves overlap, filling in the crossover notch that pure Class B leaves. Efficiency is a little lower than Class B, perhaps 50 to 65 percent at full drive versus the 78.5 percent theoretical maximum for B, and far above Class A. This is why almost every SSB linear amplifier, whether tube or solid-state, runs in AB: the mode preserves the amplitude envelope that SSB needs while keeping heat manageable. Bias is set by monitoring idle current and adjusting a Zener, diode string or a VBE multiplier.", "worked_example": "A 50 V, 100 W solid-state linear is set for 200 mA idle current per device. With no drive it dissipates 50 V × 0.2 A = 10 W per device, enough to be slightly on. Apply a sinewave whose negative excursion would push the device 20 mV below the knee; the device stays on through roughly 200 degrees of each cycle rather than switching off at exactly 180. The 20-degree overlap on each side of the crossover is what removes the notch.", "misconception": "The trap is treating AB as a vague middle ground rather than a defined range. It is defined by conduction angle between 180 and 360, and in practice it is close to the 180 end, not the middle.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "AB: A Bit more than half.", "edge_cases": "Idle current in a solid-state AB stage drifts with temperature because V_BE falls about 2 mV per degree C; without a thermally coupled bias diode the stage can creep toward Class A and thermally run away."}

{"core": "Class B is biased exactly at cutoff, so the device conducts only while the input drives it above that threshold: exactly one half of the cycle, 180 degrees.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Conduction under 180 degrees means the bias is below cutoff, which defines Class C.", "why_tempting": "Both B and C conduct for a fraction of the cycle and are easy to confuse."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "More than 180 but less than 360 defines Class AB, biased slightly above cutoff.", "why_tempting": "A learner who knows AB is just above B may pick the AB range for B."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Full-cycle conduction is Class A.", "why_tempting": "Simple sequence error: if A is 360 and C is less than 180, the learner may not recall B's exact value."}], "concept": "With the operating point placed at the cutoff point of the load line, positive input half-cycles pull the device into conduction and negative half-cycles leave it off. The output current is a half-wave rectified copy of the input. A single-ended Class B stage is therefore only usable with a resonant tank that supplies the missing half-cycle through flywheel action, or in push-pull where a second device handles the other half. The appeal is efficiency: there is no quiescent current, so dissipation is proportional to signal. The ideal push-pull Class B efficiency is π/4 ≈ 78.5 percent at full sinusoidal drive. The downside is crossover distortion because each device must traverse the nonlinear knee near V_BE ≈ 0.6 V as it turns on. The Fourier series of a half-wave rectified sine contains a DC term, the fundamental at half amplitude, and even harmonics, which is why push-pull (cancelling even harmonics) pairs so naturally with Class B.", "worked_example": "A push-pull Class B stage on ±12 V rails drives an 8 Ω load to a full 12 V peak swing, so I_pk = 1.5 A. Load power = V_pk² / (2R) = 12² / 16 = 9 W. Each rail supplies a half-sine of current for its own 180 degrees, whose average is I_pk/π ≈ 0.477 A, so each rail delivers 12 V × 0.477 A ≈ 5.73 W and the two together ≈ 11.46 W. Efficiency = 9 / 11.46 ≈ 78.5 percent, which is exactly π/4. Each device conducted for precisely its own half-cycle and was off for the other half.", "misconception": "The trap is thinking Class B cannot be used for RF because it clips half the wave. A tank circuit or push-pull pair restores the missing half, and Class B push-pull is a legitimate linear RF mode once crossover distortion is tolerated or feedback is applied.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "B: Both halves split Between two devices.", "edge_cases": "True Class B is rare in practice because the crossover notch is audible or produces splatter; most stages labelled Class B are actually run with a trickle of bias and are really AB."}

{"core": "Class C is biased below cutoff so the device remains off until the input signal peaks drive it on; current flows in short pulses lasting less than half a cycle, typically 90 to 150 degrees.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Exactly 180 degrees of conduction is Class B, biased at cutoff rather than below it.", "why_tempting": "Class B and C are neighbours and both conduct for part of the cycle."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Between 180 and 360 degrees is Class AB, biased slightly above cutoff.", "why_tempting": "A learner may recall that Class C is the most extreme class and overshoot in the wrong direction."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Full-cycle conduction is Class A, the opposite end of the bias range.", "why_tempting": "Simple reversal of the sequence from A to C."}], "concept": "With the grid, base or gate biased negative beyond cutoff (for a tube, often by grid-leak self-bias; for a transistor, zero or reverse base bias), the device turns on only when the input exceeds the cutoff threshold near the positive peak. The output current is a narrow pulse train at the drive frequency. That pulse train is rich in harmonics, so a Class C stage must work into a high-Q parallel resonant tank: the tank's flywheel effect stores energy from each pulse and delivers a sinusoidal voltage at the fundamental, while rejecting the harmonics. Efficiency can reach 75 to 85 percent because the device conducts only when its voltage is near minimum, so V × I dissipation is small. The output amplitude does not track input amplitude linearly, so Class C cannot amplify AM or SSB, but it is ideal for constant-envelope signals (CW, FM, FSK) and for frequency multipliers, where the tank is tuned to a harmonic of the drive.", "worked_example": "Drive a Class C transistor stage with a 7 MHz sinewave of 2 V peak while the base sits at −0.5 V bias. The base crosses the 0.65 V turn-on threshold when the input exceeds +1.15 V, i.e. for sin(θ) > 0.575, which happens between θ ≈ 35° and 145°, a conduction angle of about 110 degrees. The collector current is a 110-degree pulse once per cycle; the tank tuned to 7 MHz with Q of 12 converts those pulses into a clean carrier and attenuates the 14 MHz second harmonic by roughly 20 dB before the low-pass filter.", "misconception": "The trap is assuming a Class C amplifier distorts the output waveform. The device current is severely distorted, but the resonant tank restores a sinewave, so the transmitted signal is clean for constant-envelope modes.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "C: Clipped to a Crest, Cleaned by the tank.", "edge_cases": "Narrowing the conduction angle raises efficiency but lowers power output for a given device, because less charge is delivered per cycle; practical designs settle around 120 degrees as the compromise."}

{"core": "Class C has the highest efficiency because the device conducts only in brief pulses near the point where its voltage is lowest, so very little power is dissipated in the device itself; practical efficiencies of 75 to 85 percent are typical.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Class A burns full quiescent power regardless of signal and tops out at 25 or 50 percent efficiency.", "why_tempting": "A might be assumed best at everything since it is the first and most linear class."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Class AB has some idle current and conducts a bit beyond half the cycle, so its efficiency is below Class B, typically 50 to 65 percent.", "why_tempting": "AB is the class used in most high-power linears, so a learner may assume it is the most efficient practical choice."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Class B reaches a theoretical 78.5 percent but conducts for a full half-cycle, including the region where device voltage is high, so it is less efficient than Class C.", "why_tempting": "The 78.5 percent Class B figure is well known and seems high."}], "concept": "Efficiency η = P_out(RF) / P_in(DC). Dissipation in the active device is the time average of v(t) × i(t). An amplifier is most efficient when current flows only while the device voltage is near its minimum, which happens at the peak of the output swing in a resonant stage. Class A has current flowing all the time, including when device voltage is high. Reducing the conduction angle progressively restricts current to the low-voltage portion of the cycle, so efficiency climbs: A (25 to 50 percent) < AB (50 to 65) < B (78.5 max) < C (80 plus). The cost of reducing conduction angle is a loss of linearity and a loss of gain, because the output fundamental component of a narrow pulse is smaller than that of a half sine. The ultimate extension of this idea is the switching classes (D, E, F), where the device is either fully on or fully off and efficiencies above 90 percent are possible.", "worked_example": "A 12 V Class C stage delivers 5 W into its tank while drawing an average 0.5 A: P_in = 12 × 0.5 = 6 W, η = 5/6 ≈ 83 percent, device dissipation 1 W. The same transistor run Class A for 5 W output would need a quiescent power of at least 20 W (η ≤ 25 percent), dissipating 15 W or more and needing a large heatsink. Same device, same output; the only difference is where in the cycle current is allowed to flow.", "misconception": "The trap is confusing efficiency with gain or output power. Class C has the lowest gain of the four and needs the most drive, but converts DC to RF with the least waste heat.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "Efficiency climbs A to C; linearity falls A to C.", "edge_cases": "Class C efficiency only holds with a properly tuned high-Q tank; into a mistuned or resistive load the pulses are not recovered and both efficiency and output collapse. Switching classes D and E exceed Class C but are outside the four listed."}

{"core": "CW, RTTY and FM are constant-envelope modes that carry no amplitude information, so the nonlinearity of a Class C stage does them no harm, and Class C gives the highest efficiency of the four listed classes.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Class AB sacrifices efficiency to preserve amplitude linearity, which these modes do not need; it would waste heat for no benefit.", "why_tempting": "AB is the familiar final-amplifier class for SSB rigs and multi-mode transceivers."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Class B is more efficient than AB but still conducts a full half-cycle and is beaten by Class C on efficiency.", "why_tempting": "The 78.5 percent theoretical figure for Class B is memorable."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Class A is the least efficient class and is used only where linearity dominates, never for a high-power constant-envelope final.", "why_tempting": "A learner may assume the cleanest class is always the best choice for a transmitter."}], "concept": "The choice of amplifier class is a match between the signal's information content and the amplifier's distortion. An AM or SSB signal carries information in its envelope, so the final must reproduce amplitude faithfully and must run Class A or AB. CW is a keyed carrier of fixed amplitude, FM encodes information purely in instantaneous frequency, and RTTY (FSK) is a two-tone frequency shift; in each case the envelope is constant during transmission and any amplitude nonlinearity merely changes the overall level, which the operator sets anyway. Class C, with its pulse conduction and tank-circuit reconstruction, preserves frequency and phase perfectly while distorting amplitude, so it is a free lunch for these modes. The practical result: FM handhelds and mobiles, CW-only transmitters and FM repeater amplifiers run Class C for cool operation and long battery life, while multi-mode rigs that must also do SSB run AB and accept the heat.", "worked_example": "A 2 m FM mobile delivering 50 W from 13.8 V: in Class C at 80 percent efficiency it draws 50/0.8/13.8 ≈ 4.5 A and dissipates 12.5 W in the final. The same 50 W in Class AB at 55 percent would draw 50/0.55/13.8 ≈ 6.6 A and dissipate 41 W, more than three times the heat, for an FM signal that would sound identical. If instead the mode were SSB, the Class C stage would flatten the voice envelope into splatter across the band.", "misconception": "The trap is believing a transmitter final must always be linear. Linearity is only needed when the modulation lives in the envelope; frequency and phase modes tolerate Class C and benefit from its efficiency.", "link": "section 5", "mnemonic": "Constant envelope, Class C.", "edge_cases": "AFSK RTTY generated as audio tones into an SSB transmitter is actually an SSB signal and must go through a linear amplifier; only true FSK keying of the carrier qualifies for Class C."}

{"core": "Class A is the least efficient because the device carries its full quiescent current for the whole cycle, dissipating power continuously even with no input; the theoretical ceiling is 25 percent with a resistive load or 50 percent with a transformer or tuned load.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Class C is the most efficient of the four, conducting only in narrow pulses where device voltage is low.", "why_tempting": "A learner may invert the ordering and assume the most distorting class is also the most wasteful."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Class B has zero quiescent current and a theoretical maximum of 78.5 percent, much better than A.", "why_tempting": "Crossover distortion gives Class B a poor reputation that can bleed into the efficiency question."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Class AB has a small idle current but is still far more efficient than Class A, typically 50 to 65 percent at full drive.", "why_tempting": "AB is the compromise class and may be guessed as the worst of both worlds."}], "concept": "In Class A the DC supply delivers V_cc × I_Q continuously. With a resistive collector load, the maximum undistorted output swing is V_cc/2 peak, so P_out(max) = (V_cc/2)² / (2R_L) while P_in = V_cc × I_Q with I_Q = V_cc/(2R_L); the ratio works out to exactly 25 percent. With an inductor or transformer in the collector the DC drop across the load is zero, the collector can swing from 0 to 2V_cc, and the ceiling doubles to 50 percent. Either way the input power is the same whether the signal is present or not, so at low drive efficiency collapses toward zero. This is why Class A is reserved for small-signal stages where the absolute dissipation is tiny, or for high-end audio where heat is accepted as the price of linearity. The ranking A < AB < B < C for efficiency is the mirror image of the linearity ranking.", "worked_example": "A Class A audio stage from 12 V with a 1 kΩ collector resistor is biased at I_Q = 6 mA, so V_CE = 6 V and P_in = 72 mW constantly. The largest clean output swing is 6 V peak into the 1 kΩ load: P_out = 6² / (2 × 1000) = 18 mW. Efficiency = 18/72 = 25 percent at full drive and only 0.25 percent if the signal is reduced to 0.6 V peak. The transistor dissipates about 36 mW at idle and the resistor another 36 mW, all of it heat.", "misconception": "The trap is assuming efficiency only matters at high power. Class A is inefficient at every drive level, which becomes a real battery-life and thermal problem in anything beyond a small-signal stage.", "link": "section 2", "edge_cases": "Some RF low-noise amplifiers deliberately run Class A at a few milliamps where the inefficiency is irrelevant and the linearity protects against intermodulation from strong adjacent signals."}

{"core": "Class C has the poorest linearity because the device is biased below cutoff and conducts only in narrow pulses at the signal peaks; the device current bears no proportional relationship to the input waveform and the output amplitude does not track input amplitude.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Class AB conducts slightly over half the cycle with a small idle current that smooths the crossover; it is the standard linear mode for SSB amplifiers.", "why_tempting": "AB is a compromise class and may be guessed as compromised on linearity too."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Class A is the most linear class: the device stays in the centre of its transfer curve for the whole cycle.", "why_tempting": "A learner who has flipped the ordering of classes will pick the wrong end."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Class B has crossover distortion but in push-pull still reproduces the envelope roughly proportionally; it is far more linear than Class C.", "why_tempting": "Class B's crossover notch is a well-known distortion mechanism and could be mistaken for the worst case."}], "concept": "Linearity means the output envelope is a scaled copy of the input envelope: V_out = k × V_in over the useful range. Class C breaks this in two ways. First, conduction only begins when the drive exceeds the cutoff threshold, so small inputs produce no output at all: the transfer curve has a dead zone. Second, the conduction angle itself changes with drive level, so the fundamental component extracted by the tank varies in a strongly nonlinear way with input amplitude. The tank circuit cleans the harmonics out of the frequency spectrum, which is why constant-envelope signals survive, but it cannot restore amplitude information that the dead zone and variable conduction angle have destroyed. An SSB or AM signal through a Class C stage emerges with its envelope flattened and distorted, generating intermodulation products that splatter across adjacent channels. The linearity ranking A > AB > B > C is the exact mirror of the efficiency ranking, and the exam tests both directions.", "worked_example": "Feed a two-tone SSB test signal (1 kHz and 1.5 kHz at equal amplitude) through a Class C stage. The envelope of a two-tone signal swings from zero to twice the single-tone amplitude at a 500 Hz rate. During the envelope troughs the drive falls below the cutoff threshold and the stage produces nothing; at the crests it saturates. The output envelope becomes a flattened pulse train at 500 Hz instead of a smooth sinusoidal beat, and the spectrum shows third-order products at 500 Hz and 2 kHz offsets only 10 to 15 dB below the tones, versus 30 dB or better from a Class AB stage.", "misconception": "The trap is thinking that because the Class C tank output is a clean sinewave the amplifier is linear. Spectral purity at one amplitude is not linearity; linearity is about faithfully following changes in amplitude, which Class C cannot do.", "link": "section 5", "edge_cases": "A Class C stage can be made to carry amplitude information by modulating its collector or plate supply voltage (high-level AM), because output amplitude tracks supply voltage nearly linearly even though it does not track drive."}

{"core": "Class A is defined by conduction over the full 360 degrees of the input cycle; the device is biased at the midpoint of its linear region and never reaches cutoff.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Class C conducts for less than half the cycle, biased below cutoff.", "why_tempting": "Class C is the familiar transmitter class and may be the first one to come to mind."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Class AB conducts for more than half but less than the full cycle, biased just above cutoff.", "why_tempting": "The A in AB suggests full-cycle behaviour."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Class B conducts for exactly half the cycle, biased at cutoff.", "why_tempting": "Push-pull Class B produces a full output waveform, which can be mistaken for full-cycle conduction by one device."}], "concept": "This is the inverse of the usual question: given the conduction angle, name the class. The mapping is A = 360 degrees, AB = between 180 and 360, B = 180, C = less than 180. Each step down the list moves the quiescent operating point closer to and then below cutoff. Full-cycle conduction means the standing current is large enough that the negative half of the signal only reduces it, never stops it. Physically the transistor's collector current swings symmetrically about I_Q, the output coupling capacitor or transformer removes the DC component, and the load sees an amplified replica. Class A is used wherever a single device must reproduce the whole waveform on its own: receiver RF and IF stages, mixers, audio preamps and low-level transmitter drivers. It is the reference against which the other classes trade linearity for efficiency.", "worked_example": "Set a JFET common-source stage with V_DD = 15 V, R_D = 1.5 kΩ, biased at I_D = 5 mA so V_DS = 7.5 V. Apply a 0.2 V peak gate signal with g_m = 10 mS: drain current swings ±2 mA, from 3 mA to 7 mA, never zero. Drain voltage swings 7.5 ± 3 V. Conduction was continuous through all 360 degrees, so by definition the stage operated in Class A.", "misconception": "The trap is associating the class letters with quality or power rather than conduction angle. The letters are a shorthand for bias point: A means never off, C means mostly off.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "A is All, B is Both halves split, C is Chopped.", "edge_cases": "Driving a Class A stage too hard pushes it into cutoff or saturation on peaks; it then no longer meets the 360-degree definition and its distortion rises sharply, so headroom matters."}

{"core": "Only Class C is biased below cutoff, so its device conducts for less than half the cycle, in pulses that occur only around the positive peaks of the drive.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Class AB conducts for more than 180 degrees because its bias keeps the device slightly on at zero signal.", "why_tempting": "AB is sometimes loosely described as near Class B, which could suggest less than half a cycle."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Class A conducts for the whole cycle.", "why_tempting": "A simple reversal of the class ordering."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Class B conducts for exactly 180 degrees, not less.", "why_tempting": "B and C are adjacent and both involve the device being off for part of the cycle."}], "concept": "Conduction angle is the span of the input cycle during which device current is nonzero. Place the bias below the cutoff threshold by a margin V_m; the device turns on only when the input instantaneous value exceeds V_m. For a sinusoid of peak V_p the conduction angle is θ_c = 2 × arccos(V_m / V_p), which is less than 180 degrees whenever V_m > 0. Deeper bias or smaller drive narrows the pulse. The resulting current pulse has a fundamental component that the tank extracts and a set of harmonics it rejects; the ratio of fundamental to DC rises as the pulse narrows, which is why efficiency rises, but the absolute fundamental falls, which is why gain and output drop. Class C is therefore paired with high drive, a high-Q tank and constant-envelope modes. The same mechanism is used in frequency multipliers by tuning the tank to the second or third harmonic, where the narrow pulse's harmonic richness becomes an asset.", "worked_example": "A tube Class C stage with cutoff at −50 V on the grid is biased at −100 V (twice cutoff) and driven with 150 V peak. The grid crosses cutoff when the drive exceeds +50 V, i.e. when sin(θ) > 1/3. θ_c = 2 × arccos(50/150) = 2 × 70.5° ≈ 141 degrees of conduction. Increase the bias to −150 V and θ_c = 2 × arccos(100/150) ≈ 96 degrees; the pulse narrows, efficiency climbs and output power falls.", "misconception": "The trap is assuming the amplifier class is set by the device or circuit topology. It is set purely by the bias point relative to cutoff; the same transistor in the same circuit can run A, AB, B or C depending on how the base is biased.", "link": "section 2", "edge_cases": "In many Class C transistor stages the bias is not a fixed negative voltage but zero or self-generated by rectified drive across an RF choke and resistor, so the conduction angle changes with drive level and the operating point shifts if drive is lost."}

{"core": "A FET gate is a reverse-biased junction or an insulated electrode that draws essentially no current, so the FET itself presents an extremely high impedance; the input impedance seen by the source is therefore set almost entirely by the external gate biasing resistors.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "The source-to-substrate path is a reverse-biased or tied-off junction that plays no part in the signal input circuit of a common-source stage.", "why_tempting": "Substrate connections appear on MOSFET symbols and sound like a hidden resistance."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Source-to-drain resistance is the channel, which sets the output side behaviour, not what the input signal sees at the gate.", "why_tempting": "The channel resistance is the parameter the gate controls, so it is easy to confuse the controlled quantity with the controlling input."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Drain-to-substrate is another reverse-biased junction with no connection to the gate input.", "why_tempting": "Any pairing of terminal names sounds plausible if the learner is guessing from vocabulary."}], "concept": "In a JFET the gate-channel junction is reverse biased and passes only nanoamps of leakage; in a MOSFET the gate is separated from the channel by an oxide and the DC input resistance is on the order of 10¹² Ω. Whatever the FET's own input resistance, it is in parallel with the bias network: for a simple self-biased JFET stage a single gate resistor R_G to ground, often 100 kΩ to 10 MΩ; for a MOSFET a divider R1 and R2. Since R_G is many orders of magnitude smaller than the gate leakage resistance, Z_in ≈ R_G (or R1 ∥ R2). At RF the picture changes: the gate-source capacitance C_gs and the Miller-amplified gate-drain capacitance C_gd add a reactive component X_C = 1/(2πfC) that can dominate above a few MHz. The contrast with a bipolar common-emitter stage is the point: there Z_in ≈ R1 ∥ R2 ∥ (β × r_e), and the transistor's own input resistance matters.", "worked_example": "A 2N3819 JFET common-source stage uses a 1 MΩ gate resistor and 1 kΩ source resistor bypassed by 100 μF. Gate leakage is about 1 nA at 10 V, equivalent to roughly 10¹⁰ Ω. Z_in at audio = 1 MΩ ∥ 10¹⁰ Ω ≈ 1 MΩ, set entirely by R_G. Swap R_G for 100 kΩ and Z_in drops to 100 kΩ; nothing about the FET changed. At 10 MHz with C_gs = 6 pF plus Miller capacitance of about 15 pF, X_C ≈ 1/(2π × 10⁷ × 21 × 10⁻¹²) ≈ 760 Ω, which now swamps the resistive network.", "misconception": "The trap is quoting the FET's famous high input impedance as the stage input impedance. The device is nearly ideal, so the designer's external resistors, not the device, decide what the source sees.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "FET gate: the resistor you choose is the input you get.", "edge_cases": "At VHF and above, input impedance is dominated by gate capacitance and lead inductance rather than the bias network, and matching networks or neutralization are used instead of simply picking a large resistor."}

{"core": "A FET drain acts as a current source with very high dynamic resistance, so the output impedance of a common-source stage is essentially that current source in parallel with the drain load resistor, and since r_d is much larger than R_D, the output impedance is approximately R_D.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "The gate supply voltage sets the bias point, affecting g_m slightly, but it is not an impedance and does not set what the next stage sees at the drain.", "why_tempting": "Bias voltages do influence operating point, so a learner may think they define output characteristics."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "The input impedance belongs to the gate side; a FET is unilateral to a good approximation, so what happens at the gate does not appear at the drain as an impedance.", "why_tempting": "Confusing input and output sides, or assuming impedances reflect through the device as in a transformer."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "The drain supply voltage determines headroom, not impedance; a stiff supply rail is an AC ground.", "why_tempting": "Supply voltage appears in the output circuit, so it may be mistaken for an output parameter."}], "concept": "Looking back into the drain of a FET in saturation, you see the device's output resistance r_d = 1/g_ds, typically tens to hundreds of kΩ, in parallel with whatever load resistor is connected from drain to the supply rail (which is an AC ground via the bypass capacitor). Z_out = R_D ∥ r_d ≈ R_D when r_d >> R_D. The voltage gain of the stage is A_v = −g_m × (R_D ∥ r_d ∥ R_L), so R_D also sets gain, and raising R_D for more gain raises output impedance in step. This matters for driving the next stage: a 10 kΩ output impedance into a 1 kΩ load loses most of the gain. If the drain load is a tuned circuit instead of a resistor, Z_out becomes the tank's resonant impedance in parallel with r_d, and the stage gains frequency selectivity at the cost of bandwidth. The parallel with the bipolar common-emitter stage is exact: there Z_out ≈ R_C.", "worked_example": "A common-source stage has R_D = 4.7 kΩ and a JFET with r_d = 50 kΩ and g_m = 4 mS. Z_out = 4.7k ∥ 50k = (4.7 × 50)/(4.7 + 50) ≈ 4.3 kΩ. Unloaded gain A_v = −4 mS × 4.3 kΩ ≈ −17. Connect a 4.7 kΩ following stage: effective load = 4.3k ∥ 4.7k ≈ 2.25 kΩ and gain falls to −9. Change R_D to 10 kΩ: Z_out ≈ 8.3 kΩ and unloaded gain ≈ −33, but the loaded gain into 4.7 kΩ is only −12. R_D governs both numbers.", "misconception": "The trap is treating the FET as a voltage source with low output impedance like an emitter follower. In common-source configuration the drain is a current source, so the output impedance is high and set by the load resistor, not the device.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "Common source: drain resistor drives the output impedance.", "edge_cases": "With a constant-current source as the drain load, R_D is effectively infinite and Z_out becomes r_d itself, which gives very high gain but makes the stage extremely sensitive to loading."}

{"core": "A Darlington pair cascades two emitter followers (or a follower driving a common emitter) so the current gains multiply, β_total ≈ β1 × β2; that multiplied gain raises the input impedance by the same factor and lowers the output impedance when used as a follower.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Darlingtons have very high input impedance, not low; the base of the first transistor only has to supply the second transistor's base current divided by β1.", "why_tempting": "Low input impedance is a bipolar trait in common-base, and the learner may generalize it."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Darlingtons deliver high output current (they are used as power drivers); low output current is the opposite of their purpose, and high mutual impedance is not a defined advantage.", "why_tempting": "The phrase low output impedance is correct, and the rest is plausible-sounding jargon."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Mutual inductance is a transformer property with no relevance to a transistor pair, and Darlingtons are not notably stable, since their slower turn-off and higher V_BE drop can cause issues.", "why_tempting": "Mutual conductance (g_m) is a real transistor parameter and mutual inductance sounds similar."}], "concept": "In a Darlington, transistor Q1's emitter feeds Q2's base directly, both collectors are tied together. Q2's base current is Q1's emitter current, so I_C(total) ≈ β1 × β2 × I_B1. A pair of transistors each with β = 100 yields an effective β of about 10,000. Because input resistance of an emitter follower is roughly β × (r_e + R_E), the Darlington follower's input impedance is β1 × β2 × R_E, often in the megohm range, while its output impedance as a follower is approximately R_source/(β1 × β2) plus two r_e terms, very low. The penalties: two base-emitter drops in series (about 1.2 to 1.4 V), a higher saturation voltage (around 0.8 to 1 V) because Q2 cannot saturate while Q1 is driving it, and slower switching because Q2's base has no low-impedance path to discharge. For audio, the combination of high gain, high input impedance and low output impedance is exactly what a buffer or power driver wants.", "worked_example": "A Darlington emitter follower with β1 = β2 = 100 drives an 8 Ω speaker load through R_E = 8 Ω. Input resistance ≈ β1 × β2 × R_E = 10,000 × 8 Ω = 80 kΩ, so a 1 kΩ source preamp sees almost no loading. Output impedance ≈ (1 kΩ)/10,000 plus about 2 × 26 mV/I_E; at 500 mA that is 0.1 Ω + 0.1 Ω ≈ 0.2 Ω, which drives the speaker stiffly. A single transistor would present only 800 Ω input impedance and need 5 mA of base current instead of 50 μA.", "misconception": "The trap is thinking a Darlington simply doubles the gain or just adds a second stage of voltage gain. The gain multiplies, and it is current gain that multiplies; voltage gain of the follower is still slightly below unity.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "Darlington: betas multiply, so input goes up and output goes down.", "edge_cases": "Integrated Darlingtons (TIP120 family) include internal base-emitter resistors to speed turn-off, and some audio designs use a Sziklai (complementary feedback) pair instead because it has only one V_BE drop and better linearity."}

{"core": "In a common-base stage the signal enters the emitter and leaves the collector; raising the emitter voltage reduces V_BE, cuts collector current, and the collector voltage rises, so input and output move together and are in phase.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A 90-degree lag would require a reactive transfer element; the transistor is a resistive controlled current source and introduces no quadrature shift at mid-band.", "why_tempting": "Phase shifts of 90 degrees are familiar from reactance questions and get transplanted onto amplifier questions."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A 90-degree lead is likewise a reactive effect, not produced by a resistive amplifier stage.", "why_tempting": "Same confusion with RC and LC phase relationships."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "A 180-degree inversion occurs in common-emitter stages where the input drives the base; in common-base the input drives the emitter and the sign reverses twice, giving no inversion.", "why_tempting": "Common-emitter inversion is the most memorized transistor fact and gets applied to every configuration."}], "concept": "Phase relationship in each configuration follows from which terminal receives the signal. Collector current depends on V_BE = V_B − V_E. In common-base the base is AC-grounded and the input drives the emitter: a positive input raises V_E, lowers V_BE, lowers I_C, lowers the drop across R_C, and the collector (output) rises. Positive in, positive out, so zero phase shift. In common-emitter the input raises V_B, raises V_BE, raises I_C, and the collector falls: inversion. In common-collector the emitter follows the base: in phase. Common-base is used at RF because the grounded base acts as a shield between input and output, nearly eliminating the Miller feedback capacitance and allowing stable high-frequency gain without neutralization. Its current gain is slightly under unity (α ≈ 0.99) but its voltage gain is high, and it is the natural choice for a cascode upper device or a low-impedance antenna-driven preamp.", "worked_example": "Common-base stage: R_C = 2.2 kΩ, I_C = 2 mA, so r_e ≈ 26 mV / 2 mA = 13 Ω. Apply +10 mV to the emitter. Since the base is fixed, V_BE drops 10 mV, emitter current falls by 10 mV / 13 Ω ≈ 0.77 mA, collector current falls by about the same, and the collector voltage rises by 0.77 mA × 2.2 kΩ ≈ +1.7 V. Positive input gave positive output: in phase, with voltage gain ≈ R_C / r_e ≈ 170.", "misconception": "The trap is believing every transistor amplifier inverts. Only the configuration whose input is on the base and output on the collector inverts; common-base and common-collector are non-inverting.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "Only the common emitter flips the signal.", "edge_cases": "At frequencies approaching f_T the transit time through the base adds a real phase lag, and stray reactances in the circuit can shift the phase away from zero, so in-phase is a mid-band statement."}

{"core": "The emitter input of a common-base stage looks into the forward-biased base-emitter junction with a dynamic resistance r_e ≈ 26 mV / I_E, typically a few ohms to tens of ohms, while the collector output is a high-impedance current source loaded by R_C; the input impedance is therefore very low compared with the output.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "The difference is orders of magnitude, ohms versus kilohms, not slight.", "why_tempting": "Hedged answers feel safer when the learner is unsure of direction."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Very high input impedance describes the FET gate or a Darlington follower, not an emitter being driven directly.", "why_tempting": "Common-base has high output impedance, and the learner may transpose the two."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "The input is not higher than the output at all; the emitter is the lowest-impedance input node of any bipolar configuration.", "why_tempting": "Same hedging instinct as option A, in the wrong direction."}], "concept": "The base-emitter junction is an exponential diode, and its small-signal resistance seen from the emitter is r_e = V_T / I_E with V_T ≈ 26 mV at room temperature. In common-base this diode is the input: Z_in ≈ r_e, with no β multiplication because the base current flows out of the grounded base rather than being supplied by the source. By contrast common-emitter sees β × r_e and common-collector sees β × (r_e + R_E). The output of a common-base stage is the collector, a current source with dynamic resistance in the hundreds of kΩ, shunted by R_C, so Z_out ≈ R_C, typically kΩ. The impedance ratio Z_out/Z_in of several hundred is what gives common-base its large voltage gain, A_v ≈ R_C / r_e, despite current gain of only α. The very low input impedance is an asset when the source is itself low impedance, such as a 50 Ω antenna feed, a mixer output or the collector of a common-emitter device in a cascode.", "worked_example": "Bias a common-base stage at I_E = 1 mA with R_C = 3.3 kΩ: Z_in ≈ 26 mV / 1 mA = 26 Ω, Z_out ≈ 3.3 kΩ, ratio about 127. Driven from a 50 Ω source, the input divider delivers 26/(50 + 26) ≈ 34 percent of the source voltage to the emitter, and the stage then provides R_C / r_e ≈ 127 of voltage gain, net about 43. Raising I_E to 5 mA lowers Z_in to 5 Ω, making it an even better match to a very low source and a worse one to 50 Ω.", "misconception": "The trap is applying the Basic-level rule that transistor inputs are high impedance. That rule is for the base; driving the emitter bypasses β entirely and exposes the raw junction resistance.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "Emitter in, ohms in.", "edge_cases": "Z_in = r_e is the room-temperature small-signal value; it scales with absolute temperature and falls with emitter current, and any unbypassed resistance in the base lead adds (R_B/β) to it."}

{"core": "In a common-emitter stage the input drives the base and the output is taken from the collector; a rising base voltage increases collector current, which increases the drop across the collector resistor and pulls the collector voltage down, so the output is inverted, 180 degrees out of phase with the input.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A 90-degree lead needs a reactive element in the signal path; a resistively loaded transistor at mid-band provides none.", "why_tempting": "Phase angles of 90 degrees are familiar from capacitive and inductive circuits."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A 90-degree lag is likewise a reactance effect, not an amplifier-configuration property.", "why_tempting": "Same reactance confusion."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "In-phase output belongs to common-base and common-collector stages; common-emitter is the one configuration that inverts.", "why_tempting": "A learner may remember that one configuration inverts and misassign which one."}], "concept": "Collector current follows I_C ≈ β × I_B, or equivalently I_C = I_S × exp(V_BE / V_T). Output voltage is V_C = V_CC − I_C × R_C. Raise V_B by a small amount: V_BE rises, I_C rises, and V_C falls. The transfer is V_out = −g_m × R_C × V_in where g_m = I_C / V_T, so the gain carries a negative sign that represents the 180-degree inversion. This inversion is the reason a common-emitter stage can oscillate if a feedback path from collector to base adds another 180 degrees of shift from reactive components: the total loop becomes positive feedback. It is also why a two-stage common-emitter amplifier is non-inverting overall, and why negative feedback in a single common-emitter stage can be applied simply with a resistor from collector to base. The FET common-source stage inverts for the same reason with g_m replaced by the FET transconductance.", "worked_example": "Common-emitter stage with R_C = 4.7 kΩ biased at I_C = 1 mA, so g_m = 1 mA / 26 mV ≈ 38 mS. Collector sits at V_CC − 4.7 V. Apply +5 mV at the base: I_C increases by 38 mS × 5 mV = 0.19 mA, the collector drop grows by 0.19 mA × 4.7 kΩ ≈ 0.9 V, and the collector voltage falls by 0.9 V. Input went up, output went down, gain ≈ −180: a 180-degree phase relationship.", "misconception": "The trap is thinking inversion means a time delay of half a cycle. It is an instantaneous sign reversal; the output waveform is a mirror image, which for a sinewave is indistinguishable from a 180-degree shift but applies equally to a square wave or an impulse.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "Base up, collector down.", "edge_cases": "The clean 180 degrees holds only in the mid-band; coupling capacitors add phase lead at low frequencies and the Miller capacitance adds phase lag at high frequencies, so the real shift drifts away from 180 toward the band edges, which matters for feedback stability."}

{"core": "In a common-collector (emitter follower) stage the output is taken from the emitter, which sits one diode drop below the base and tracks it directly; the output rises when the input rises, so the two are in phase.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A 180-degree inversion occurs only when the output is taken from the collector in a common-emitter stage; the emitter follows the base rather than opposing it.", "why_tempting": "Transistor inversion is the most memorized phase fact and is wrongly generalized."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "A 90-degree lead requires a reactive element; the follower is a resistive stage with essentially zero phase shift.", "why_tempting": "Confusion with reactance phase relationships."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A 90-degree lag likewise does not arise from a resistively loaded transistor.", "why_tempting": "Same reactance confusion."}], "concept": "In the emitter follower the collector is tied to the supply rail (AC ground), the input drives the base, and the load is in the emitter. The emitter voltage is V_E = V_B − V_BE, and since V_BE changes very little (a few mV for large current changes because of the exponential relationship), V_E tracks V_B nearly one-for-one: voltage gain A_v = R_E / (R_E + r_e) ≈ 0.99, non-inverting. There is no R_C to create an inverting voltage drop. The stage's value lies in impedance transformation, not gain: Z_in ≈ β × (R_E ∥ R_L + r_e), which is high, and Z_out ≈ r_e + R_source/β, which is low. This makes the follower the standard buffer between a high-impedance source (a detector, a crystal filter, an oscillator tank) and a low-impedance load, and the output stage of most audio amplifiers. The in-phase property also means a follower can be inserted into a feedback loop without changing the loop's polarity.", "worked_example": "Emitter follower: R_E = 1 kΩ, I_E = 5 mA, β = 150, driven from a 10 kΩ source. r_e = 26 mV / 5 mA ≈ 5 Ω. A_v = 1000 / 1005 ≈ 0.995. Apply a +1 V step at the base: the emitter rises by +0.995 V, in phase. Z_in ≈ 150 × 1005 ≈ 150 kΩ, so the 10 kΩ source is barely loaded; Z_out ≈ 5 Ω + 10 kΩ/150 ≈ 72 Ω. The signal was not amplified, it was made stiff.", "misconception": "The trap is assuming a stage with no voltage gain is useless. The follower's job is to convert impedance levels while leaving the voltage and phase untouched, and that is often the most important stage in a signal chain.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "Follower: the emitter follows the base, same direction, same phase.", "edge_cases": "An emitter follower driving a capacitive load can oscillate at VHF because its output impedance becomes negative-real at high frequencies; a small series base resistor or ferrite bead is the usual cure."}

{"core": "A source follower takes its input at the gate and output at the source, with the drain tied to the supply rail, so the drain is the terminal common to input and output: it is the common-drain configuration.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Common mode is not an amplifier configuration; it describes a signal appearing equally on both inputs of a differential amplifier.", "why_tempting": "It begins with common and sounds like a configuration name."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Common gate has the input on the source and output on the drain; it is the FET analogue of common base, not a follower.", "why_tempting": "The source is involved in both source follower and common gate, inviting a mix-up."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Common source has input at the gate and output at the drain and provides inverting voltage gain; the source is grounded or bypassed, not used as the output.", "why_tempting": "The word source appears in both names, and common source is the most common FET stage."}], "concept": "Configuration names follow which terminal is shared, at AC, between the input loop and the output loop. For a FET: common source (input gate, output drain, high inverting voltage gain), common drain or source follower (input gate, output source, gain just under unity, non-inverting, high Z_in, low Z_out), and common gate (input source, output drain, non-inverting, very low Z_in). In the source follower the drain goes straight to V_DD, which the supply bypass capacitor makes an AC ground, hence common drain. The output at the source sits at V_G − V_GS and tracks the gate: A_v = g_m R_S / (1 + g_m R_S). Output impedance is approximately 1/g_m in parallel with R_S, a few hundred ohms for a typical JFET, far lower than the gate side's megohms. This is the FET counterpart of the emitter follower and is used to buffer crystal oscillators, high-impedance detectors and active antennas where the source must not be loaded.", "worked_example": "A JFET source follower with g_m = 5 mS and R_S = 2.2 kΩ: A_v = (5 mS × 2.2 kΩ)/(1 + 11) = 11/12 ≈ 0.92, non-inverting. Z_out ≈ (1/g_m) ∥ R_S = 200 Ω ∥ 2.2 kΩ ≈ 183 Ω. Z_in is the 1 MΩ gate resistor. Driving it from a 100 kΩ crystal detector and into a 1 kΩ load, the follower delivers about 0.92 × 1000/1183 ≈ 0.78 of the input voltage with negligible loading on the detector, where a direct connection would have delivered 1/101 of it.", "misconception": "The trap is naming the configuration after the terminal where the output appears. The name refers to the terminal that is common to both ports, which is the one tied to AC ground, so the source follower is common drain.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "Follower names the output, common names the ground: source follower = common drain.", "edge_cases": "Because g_m of a JFET is modest, a source follower's gain is noticeably below unity and its output impedance is higher than a bipolar follower's; a current-source load in place of R_S brings gain closer to one."}

{"core": "Common source and common emitter both take the input on the control terminal (gate or base), ground the reference terminal (source or emitter), and take the output from the collecting terminal (drain or collector); both give inverting voltage gain and are the general-purpose gain stage of their families.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Common collector is the emitter follower, whose FET analogue is common drain, a unity-gain buffer.", "why_tempting": "Collector and drain both receive the carriers, so a learner may pair the names by terminal function rather than by which is grounded."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Common base corresponds to common gate, the configuration with the input on the emitter or source.", "why_tempting": "Base and gate are the control terminals, so the names seem to pair, but in both configurations the control terminal is grounded rather than driven."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Common mode is a differential amplifier term, not a single-transistor configuration.", "why_tempting": "It fits the naming pattern of the other options."}], "concept": "The three FET terminals map onto the three bipolar terminals by function: gate ↔ base (control), source ↔ emitter (carrier origin, reference), drain ↔ collector (carrier destination, output). Each configuration is named for the AC-grounded terminal, so the mapping of configurations follows directly: common source ↔ common emitter, common drain ↔ common collector, common gate ↔ common base. Common source and common emitter share every important property: input on the control terminal, output on the collecting terminal, voltage gain A_v = −g_m × R_load with phase inversion, moderate output impedance set by the load resistor, and susceptibility to Miller effect because the inverted output couples back to the input through C_gd or C_cb. The differences are quantitative: the FET input impedance is set by the bias resistor rather than β × r_e, and the FET's g_m is usually lower than a bipolar's at the same current, so common-source gain is typically smaller.", "worked_example": "Compare two stages at 1 mA with a 4.7 kΩ load. Bipolar common emitter: g_m = I_C / V_T = 1 mA / 26 mV ≈ 38 mS, A_v ≈ −38 mS × 4.7 kΩ ≈ −180. JFET common source: g_m ≈ 3 mS at 1 mA, A_v ≈ −3 mS × 4.7 kΩ ≈ −14. Both invert, both have Z_out ≈ 4.7 kΩ, both suffer Miller multiplication of their feedback capacitance by (1 + |A_v|). Same circuit role, same topology, different numbers.", "misconception": "The trap is mapping configurations by the terminal that sounds similar rather than by the terminal that is grounded. Gate and base are both control terminals, but common gate and common base are the configurations where that control terminal is grounded, not driven.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "Source is emitter, drain is collector, gate is base; the configuration name follows.", "edge_cases": "A MOSFET common-source stage with its source tied to the substrate behaves like the JFET version, but if the substrate is at a different potential the body effect adds a second transconductance term that the bipolar analogy does not have."}

{"core": "Common drain is the source follower: input at the gate, output at the source, drain at AC ground. Its bipolar counterpart has input at the base, output at the emitter, collector at AC ground, which is the common collector or emitter follower.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Common base is the bipolar analogue of common gate, with the input applied to the emitter or source.", "why_tempting": "The learner may be cycling through configurations without a clear terminal map."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Common mode is a differential-amplifier term describing identical signals on both inputs, not a single-device configuration.", "why_tempting": "Pattern-matching on the word common."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Common emitter corresponds to common source, the inverting gain stage.", "why_tempting": "Common emitter is the default bipolar stage and tends to be chosen when the mapping is unclear."}], "concept": "The functional map is gate ↔ base, source ↔ emitter, drain ↔ collector, and configurations are named for the terminal common to input and output at AC. Common drain and common collector are therefore the same circuit idea in two technologies: a follower. Both have voltage gain slightly below unity and non-inverting, high input impedance, low output impedance, and both are used as buffers and output drivers. The FET version has the higher input impedance (set by the gate resistor, often megohms) because the gate draws no current, while the bipolar version usually has the lower output impedance (r_e + R_s/β, often under 10 Ω) because bipolar g_m is higher at a given current. Neither suffers the Miller effect because the output is in phase with the input and the feedback capacitance sees almost no voltage across it; this makes followers excellent isolation stages between a sensitive oscillator and a varying load.", "worked_example": "Take a 10 MHz crystal oscillator whose tank is 20 kΩ at resonance and which must drive a 50 Ω mixer port. A common-drain JFET buffer with a 1 MΩ gate resistor loads the tank by 2 percent and presents about 200 Ω at its source. Follow that with a common-collector bipolar stage at 10 mA (r_e ≈ 2.6 Ω) to reach a few ohms, then a resistive pad to 50 Ω. Each follower is non-inverting, so the oscillator phase is preserved and no stage adds the Miller capacitance that would pull the crystal frequency.", "misconception": "The trap is matching common drain to common emitter because emitter and drain are both non-control terminals. The correct pairing is by role: drain and collector are both the carrier-collecting terminal that gets tied to the supply in a follower.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "Drain is the FET's collector; common drain is common collector.", "edge_cases": "Both followers can show a negative input resistance at VHF when loaded capacitively and may oscillate; a series gate or base resistor of 50 to 100 Ω damps this in both technologies."}

{"core": "Common gate grounds the gate at AC, drives the source and takes the output from the drain; the bipolar equivalent grounds the base, drives the emitter and takes the output from the collector, which is the common-base configuration.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Common emitter corresponds to common source, where the control terminal is driven, not grounded.", "why_tempting": "Default-stage bias: common emitter is the first bipolar circuit learned."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Common mode is a differential amplifier concept with no single-transistor equivalent.", "why_tempting": "It sounds like a configuration name."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Common collector is the emitter follower, matching common drain, with output on the emitter or source rather than the collector or drain.", "why_tempting": "Both common gate and common collector are less common stages, and a learner may swap the two remaining names."}], "concept": "With gate ↔ base, source ↔ emitter and drain ↔ collector, grounding the control terminal in each family gives common gate and common base. Both share the defining traits of this topology: very low input impedance (about 1/g_m for the FET, r_e for the bipolar), high output impedance set by the drain or collector load, non-inverting voltage gain of about g_m × R_load, and current gain near unity. Most importantly, both put the grounded control terminal between input and output as an electrostatic shield, so the drain-gate or collector-base capacitance no longer feeds output back to input. That removes the Miller effect and makes the stage stable at VHF and UHF without neutralization. Common-gate and common-base stages therefore appear as the upper device of a cascode, as low-noise amplifiers fed from a 50 Ω antenna where the low input impedance is a match rather than a liability, and as the output stage of a diode mixer where the IF port is also low impedance.", "worked_example": "A common-gate JFET LNA with g_m = 20 mS has Z_in ≈ 1/g_m = 50 Ω, a direct match to coax with no transformer. With a 10 MHz drain tank of 2 kΩ resonant impedance, voltage gain ≈ 20 mS × 2 kΩ = 40, non-inverting. The equivalent common-base bipolar stage at I_E = 0.5 mA has r_e ≈ 52 Ω, nearly the same input impedance, and with the same tank gives gain ≈ 2000/52 ≈ 38. The two circuits are interchangeable in function.", "misconception": "The trap is assuming the control terminal must always be the input. In the common-gate and common-base topologies the control terminal is the fixed reference and the input is injected at the source or emitter, which is what makes the stage non-inverting and Miller-free.", "link": "section 6", "mnemonic": "Gate grounded, base grounded: same shield, same job.", "edge_cases": "The low input impedance of common gate and common base is a current-dependent quantity, so the stage must be biased with the match in mind; it also provides no reverse isolation at DC, only at AC, so bias networks must still be decoupled."}

{"core": "An op-amp is a very high gain, DC-coupled differential amplifier designed so that its open-loop gain is so large that the circuit's actual behaviour is dictated by the external feedback network; the designer sets gain, bandwidth and function with the parts around it, not inside it.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Raising an FM transmitter's output to a legal limit is a job for an RF power amplifier; an op-amp is a small-signal device unrelated to transmitter output power.", "why_tempting": "The word amplifier and a mention of amateur signals make it sound like a radio application."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "An op-amp is hardware, not software; the historical name comes from analog computers where the device performed mathematical operations such as summing and integrating, not from a program subroutine.", "why_tempting": "Operational suggests a computing operation, and modern learners associate that with code."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "An op-amp is differential, not single-ended audio, and its defining feature is that external components, not internal ones, set its characteristics; this option inverts both key properties.", "why_tempting": "It copies most of the correct wording and only swaps two details, which is how the distractor catches a learner who skims."}], "concept": "Inside, an op-amp is a differential input pair feeding a high-gain voltage amplifier and a low-impedance output stage, all direct coupled so it works down to DC. Open-loop gain A_OL is typically 10⁵ to 10⁶. Because A_OL is enormous, applying negative feedback through external resistors forces the differential input voltage toward zero (the virtual short), and the closed-loop gain depends only on the feedback ratio: A_CL = A_OL / (1 + A_OL × β) ≈ 1/β when A_OL × β >> 1. The same chip therefore becomes an inverting amplifier, a non-inverting amplifier, a summer, an integrator, a differentiator, a comparator or an active filter purely by changing the feedback network. For amateur use the op-amp is the workhorse of audio stages: microphone preamps, CW and SSB audio filters, AGC amplifiers, keyers and meter drivers. Its DC coupling also makes it the standard for instrumentation such as SWR bridge amplifiers and power-supply error amplifiers.", "worked_example": "Take an op-amp with A_OL = 100,000 and wire it non-inverting with R_f = 99 kΩ and R_g = 1 kΩ, so β = 1/100. Exact closed-loop gain = 100,000 / (1 + 100,000 × 0.01) = 100,000 / 1001 ≈ 99.9. The ideal 1/β value is 100. Swap in a different op-amp with A_OL = 1,000,000 and the gain becomes 99.99. The device changed by a factor of ten and the circuit gain changed by 0.1 percent: the external resistors are in charge.", "misconception": "The trap is thinking an op-amp has a fixed gain like a transistor stage. Its open-loop gain is deliberately huge and unspecified; the usable gain exists only once feedback is applied, and that gain is a ratio of external parts.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "Op-amp: the chip supplies the gain, the resistors decide how much to use.", "edge_cases": "The feedback-sets-everything rule weakens as frequency rises: A_OL rolls off at 20 dB per decade, so once A_OL × β approaches 1 (near the gain-bandwidth limit) the op-amp's internal characteristics reassert themselves and the closed-loop gain falls."}

{"core": "The ideal op-amp draws no input current (infinite input impedance), delivers any output current without voltage droop (zero output impedance), amplifies the differential input without limit (infinite gain), and does so equally at every frequency (flat response); these four idealizations are what make the feedback analysis exact.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Zero input impedance would load the source completely and infinite output impedance could drive nothing; both are reversed.", "why_tempting": "The two impedance words are simply swapped, which a learner can miss when scanning for the gain and bandwidth terms."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Zero input impedance would short the signal source; the ideal input is an open circuit.", "why_tempting": "Zero output impedance is correct, and the repeated zero can slip past."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Infinite output impedance means the output cannot deliver current, so no load could be driven; the ideal output is a perfect voltage source.", "why_tempting": "Infinite input impedance is correct, and a learner may assume both impedances should be infinite for an ideal device."}], "concept": "The ideal model exists because it lets you analyse any feedback circuit with two rules. Infinite input impedance means no current enters either input terminal, so all current in the input resistor must flow through the feedback resistor. Infinite gain with negative feedback means the differential input voltage must be zero, otherwise the output would be infinite, so the inverting input sits at the same potential as the non-inverting input (the virtual short, or virtual ground when the non-inverting input is grounded). Zero output impedance means the output voltage is independent of load. Flat frequency response means these rules hold at all frequencies. Real devices approximate the model: input impedance of 10⁶ Ω for bipolar inputs to 10¹² Ω for FET inputs, output impedance of tens of ohms open loop reduced to milliohms by feedback, open-loop gain of 10⁵ to 10⁶ at DC falling at 20 dB per decade, and the response flat only up to the gain-bandwidth product divided by the closed-loop gain.", "worked_example": "Inverting amplifier with R_in = 10 kΩ, R_f = 100 kΩ, 0.5 V input. Rule 1 (virtual ground): the inverting input is at 0 V, so current through R_in = 0.5 V / 10 kΩ = 50 μA. Rule 2 (no input current): all 50 μA flows through R_f, so V_out = −50 μA × 100 kΩ = −5 V. Rule 3 (zero output impedance): V_out stays −5 V whether the load is 1 kΩ or open. The whole analysis used nothing but the four ideal properties.", "misconception": "The trap is thinking an ideal amplifier should have high impedance everywhere. An amplifier's input should not load its source (high Z) and its output should not be loaded by the next stage (low Z); the two requirements are opposite.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "In like a voltmeter, out like a battery: infinite in, zero out.", "edge_cases": "The ideal model also assumes zero offset voltage, zero bias current, infinite slew rate and infinite common-mode rejection; the rest of this subsection introduces offset voltage as the first of these real-world departures."}

{"core": "With open-loop gain so large that the input differential is forced to zero, the closed-loop gain depends only on the ratio of the external feedback resistors, A_CL ≈ 1/β, where β is the fraction of the output fed back to the inverting input.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Internal junction capacitances affect open-loop bandwidth and stability, but with feedback applied they do not set the mid-band gain.", "why_tempting": "Miller capacitance does limit gain in discrete transistor stages, and the question looks like it might be about internal transistors."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The internal load of an output stage affects open-loop gain, which feedback deliberately makes irrelevant.", "why_tempting": "Collector load sets gain in a single-transistor stage, a rule the learner carries over from the previous subsection."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Supply voltage sets the output swing limits and nothing about the gain ratio; within the supply rails the gain is the same at 5 V or 15 V.", "why_tempting": "A learner may think more supply voltage gives more gain, confusing headroom with amplification."}], "concept": "Consider the general feedback equation A_CL = A_OL / (1 + A_OL β). When A_OL β >> 1 the 1 in the denominator vanishes and A_CL → 1/β. For a non-inverting amplifier β = R_g / (R_g + R_f) so A_CL = 1 + R_f / R_g; for an inverting amplifier A_CL = −R_f / R_in. Neither expression contains any op-amp parameter. This is the whole point of negative feedback: it trades the enormous but poorly controlled and temperature-dependent open-loop gain for a smaller, precise gain set by resistor ratios, which can be 0.1 percent parts. The same substitution gives feedback its other benefits: input impedance multiplied by (1 + A_OL β) for the non-inverting case, output impedance divided by it, distortion divided by it, and bandwidth extended by it, which is why gain × bandwidth is constant. The feedback network can contain capacitors or inductors instead of resistors, and then 1/β becomes a frequency-dependent transfer function, which is how the same op-amp becomes an integrator or a filter.", "worked_example": "Non-inverting amplifier, R_f = 47 kΩ, R_g = 4.7 kΩ: A_CL = 1 + 47/4.7 = 11.
