Correction: it is a resonator, so it is inherently a narrow band-pass or notch device, and its size scales with wavelength, confining it to VHF and up.", "link": "Reactance & Resonance", "mnemonic": "Cavity: a quarter wave in a can, only narrow and only when the wave is short.", "edge_cases": "Cavities also resonate at odd multiples of f_0 and at higher-order waveguide modes, so a 2 m cavity passes energy near 438 MHz too; a separate low-pass or a second cavity is needed when those spurious responses matter."}

{"core": "A quarter-wave coaxial cavity is a shorted transmission-line stub one quarter wavelength long. At 50 MHz the free-space wavelength is λ = c/f = 300/50 = 6 m, so a quarter wave is about 1.5 m; the inner conductor and can are air-dielectric, so there is no significant velocity-factor shortening.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "0.6 m is a quarter wave at about 125 MHz, or one tenth of a wavelength at 50 MHz; a stub that short presents a modest inductive reactance, not a high-Q parallel resonance.", "why_tempting": "Students remember that solid-dielectric coax has a velocity factor near 0.66 and shorten the stub, but an air cavity has VF ≈ 1."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "2.4 m is 0.4 λ at 50 MHz, past the quarter-wave point where the shorted stub has turned capacitive and is heading toward a series resonance at a half wave.", "why_tempting": "8 ft is roughly a quarter wave at 10 m (28 MHz), so a 10 m band figure may be remembered instead."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "3.7 m is about 0.62 λ at 50 MHz, beyond the half-wave series resonance; it is not a quarter-wave resonator for this band.", "why_tempting": "12 ft is roughly the length of a 7 MHz quarter-wave vertical scaled wrongly, or a half-wave at 40 MHz; it looks like an antenna number."}], "concept": "A transmission line shorted at one end and measured a length l from the short presents Z_in = j · Z_0 · tan(2πl/λ). When l = λ/4 the tangent goes to infinity and the open end looks like a very high impedance parallel resonance; that is the operating point of a coaxial cavity. Physical length is therefore l = λ/4 = c/(4f), with c ≈ 3×10⁸ m/s, multiplied by the velocity factor of whatever fills the line, which for an air cavity is essentially 1.0. The diameter (10 cm here) does not set the frequency; it sets Z_0 and the Q, since a larger can has more surface and lower loss. A small variable capacitor at the open end lowers the resonant frequency slightly and lets the builder trim a cavity that was cut a little short, which is why practical cavities are often a few percent shorter than the exact quarter wave. The same stub mathematics underlies quarter-wave matching sections, bazooka baluns and the notch stubs used on feedlines.", "worked_example": "λ = 300 / 50 MHz = 6.0 m. Quarter wave = 6.0 / 4 = 1.5 m, about 5 ft. Check the alternative: with foam coax of VF 0.8 the length would be 1.2 m, and with solid polyethylene VF 0.66 it would be 0.99 m; only the air-filled 1.5 m value matches the answer list. For a 2 m cavity at 146 MHz the same arithmetic gives 300/146/4 ≈ 0.51 m, which is why 2 m duplexer cans are about half a metre tall, and 70 cm cans about 17 cm.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: coax-style structures always need the 0.66 velocity factor applied. Correction: velocity factor comes from the dielectric; an air-spaced cavity has VF close to 1, so the quarter wave is nearly the free-space value.", "link": "Wavelength ↔ Frequency", "mnemonic": "300 over MHz gives metres; divide by 4 for a quarter-wave can.", "edge_cases": "Cavities are often built deliberately short (say 0.2 λ) and loaded with a capacitor at the open end; the capacitance resonates with the stub's inductive reactance, so real cans may be noticeably less than 1.5 m at 50 MHz."}

{"core": "A helical resonator is a quarter-wave resonator whose inner conductor is coiled into a helix inside a shielded can; it gives cavity-like selectivity (Q of several hundred to a thousand) in a package small enough to fit in a VHF/UHF receiver front end, where it rejects strong out-of-band signals before they can overload the first stage or create spurious mixer products.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A diplexer is a frequency-splitting network that routes two different bands to or from one port, for example letting a dual-band antenna feed separate 2 m and 70 cm radios. It is a pair of complementary filters with broad passbands, not a narrow preselector against overload.", "why_tempting": "It contains filters and is installed in the antenna path, and the name is one letter from duplexer."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "A directional coupler samples a small, known fraction of forward or reflected power for measurement; it has no selectivity and does nothing to reduce the level of unwanted signals reaching the receiver.", "why_tempting": "It is another front-end accessory found in the same block of a station diagram."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A duplexer is the set of cavities that lets a repeater transmit and receive simultaneously on one antenna. It solves transmitter-into-own-receiver isolation at a fixed pair of frequencies, not general front-end overload from arbitrary strong signals, and it is a large external assembly, not a front-end component.", "why_tempting": "Duplexers are built from cavities and do protect a receiver from a strong signal, so the function overlaps on the surface."}], "concept": "At VHF a lumped LC tank with wire-wound coils achieves a Q of perhaps 100 to 200, and parasitic capacitance limits what can be built; a full quarter-wave cavity has Q in the thousands but is half a metre long at 2 m. The helical resonator sits between them: wind the quarter-wave inner conductor into a coil of a few turns, put it in a shielded box roughly the coil's diameter, ground one end and leave the other open, and the structure behaves as a slow-wave transmission line whose electrical length is a quarter wave but whose physical length is a few centimetres. Unloaded Q scales roughly with the can size (Q_u ≈ 50 · D · √f with D in inches and f in MHz as the old rule of thumb), so a 2.5 cm can at 146 MHz gives Q_u around 600. Two or three resonators coupled through apertures in the shield walls give a band-pass with a few hundred kHz to a few MHz bandwidth and 60 dB or more of rejection a few MHz away. Placed ahead of the first RF stage or mixer, this keeps paging transmitters, broadcast FM and nearby repeaters out of the stages whose nonlinearity would otherwise generate intermodulation and desensitisation, which are the overload and spurious responses the question refers to.", "worked_example": "Imagine a 2 m receiver with a 20 dB wideband preamp and a mixer whose third-order intercept is +10 dBm. A 152 MHz pager at −10 dBm at the antenna arrives at the mixer at +10 dBm, sitting right at the intercept point, so intermod products land everywhere in the band. Insert a 3-section helical filter centred on 146 MHz with 2 MHz bandwidth and 50 dB attenuation at 152 MHz: the pager now reaches the mixer at −40 dBm, and the third-order products, which fall 2 dB for every 1 dB of input reduction, drop by 100 dB. The wanted signals inside the passband lose only the filter's 1 dB insertion loss.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: any filter in the antenna line protects a receiver. Correction: protection from overload needs narrow selectivity close to the operating frequency with low loss, which at VHF/UHF calls for a resonator structure (helical or cavity), not the broad or non-selective devices listed as distractors.", "link": "section 6", "mnemonic": "Helical: a cavity with its inner conductor curled up to fit in the radio.", "edge_cases": "Helical resonators are hard to make useful much above 1 GHz (the coil shrinks to a pin) or below about 30 MHz (the can becomes large); at microwave, dielectric resonators or interdigital filters take over the same role."}

{"core": "A television channel is about 6 MHz wide, which at VHF is a passband of a few percent of centre frequency; that is too wide for a resonant cavity, whose Q of thousands confines it to a fraction of a percent, while Butterworth and Chebyshev are response shapes rather than VHF filter constructions. The structure that naturally gives a few-MHz passband at VHF is the helical resonator, which is not among the options, so the keyed answer is none of the other answers.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A cavity with loaded Q of 1000 at 200 MHz has a 3 dB bandwidth of only 200 kHz. To widen it to 6 MHz you would have to couple it so heavily that the Q and the rejection collapse, defeating the point of using a cavity.", "why_tempting": "Cavities are the VHF filter the syllabus emphasises, so VHF filter triggers cavity."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Butterworth names a mathematical response (maximally flat), not a physical VHF construction. A lumped Butterworth band-pass at 200 MHz with 6 MHz bandwidth needs loaded Q around 33 per section, which is achievable, but the option does not describe a device and the question is asking about a filter type as a construction.", "why_tempting": "It is a familiar filter name and nothing in the word forbids VHF use."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Chebyshev likewise names a response shape. It could be the alignment chosen for a helical or lumped band-pass, but it is not itself the filter type suited to the job, and lumped LC at VHF struggles with stray reactance and low coil Q.", "why_tempting": "Chebyshev's steep skirts sound attractive for channel selection."}], "concept": "The useful figure is fractional bandwidth, BW/f_0, and the loaded Q that implies, Q_L = f_0/BW. A 6 MHz channel at 200 MHz needs Q_L ≈ 33; at 60 MHz, Q_L ≈ 10. Each physical resonator technology has a natural Q range: lumped LC at VHF gives unloaded Q of 100 to 200 and is awkward because stray capacitance is comparable to the tuning capacitance; helical resonators give Q_u of 300 to 1000 in a few cubic centimetres and are easily loaded down to Q_L of 20 to 50; cavities give Q_u of several thousand and are meant to be used narrow. Since insertion loss rises as Q_L approaches Q_u (loss ≈ 20 · log₁₀(1/(1 − Q_L/Q_u)) dB for a single section), you want Q_u several times larger than Q_L but not hundreds of times larger, which is wasted size. That is why the helical resonator is the textbook choice for TV-channel-width VHF band-pass filters, and why none of the three named options fits: the cavity is too narrow, and the other two are alignment families rather than hardware.", "worked_example": "Target: pass 174 to 180 MHz (a 6 MHz channel, f_0 = 177 MHz), so Q_L = 177/6 ≈ 30. A helical resonator in a 25 mm square can has Q_u ≈ 700, so single-section loss ≈ 20 · log₁₀(1/(1 − 30/700)) ≈ 0.4 dB; a 3-section Chebyshev-aligned helical gives about 1.2 dB loss and 50 dB rejection 15 MHz away. A cavity with Q_u = 5000 coupled to Q_L = 30 would still work electrically but is a 40 cm can doing a job a matchbox can do, and the heavy coupling loops ruin its spurious-mode behaviour.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: cavity means the best VHF filter for any bandwidth. Correction: cavities are high-Q narrow devices; moderate-bandwidth VHF selectivity is the helical resonator's domain, and response-shape names like Butterworth and Chebyshev are not filter constructions at all.", "link": "section 2", "edge_cases": "At UHF and above, interdigital and combline filters (coupled quarter-wave lines on a common ground plane) take over the moderate-bandwidth role from helicals; at 6 MHz bandwidth they are the standard 70 cm and 23 cm band-pass designs."}

{"core": "The Butterworth's advantage is a maximally flat passband: its magnitude response has no ripple and its first 2n − 1 derivatives are zero at DC, so signals within the band are passed with uniform amplitude. The Chebyshev buys steeper skirts by giving exactly this flatness away.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Passband ripple in exchange for steeper skirts is the Chebyshev trade, the opposite of what the question asks.", "why_tempting": "It is the single most-tested sentence about Chebyshev filters, so it jumps out regardless of which filter the stem names."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "No practical selective filter can be made from inductors alone; a Butterworth ladder alternates series inductors with shunt capacitors or the dual.", "why_tempting": "Sounds like a parts-count advantage, and inductor-only reads as simpler."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "A capacitor-only network has no resonance and cannot form the higher-order roll-off the Butterworth polynomial requires.", "why_tempting": "Capacitor-only RC filters are familiar, and an RC-only active Butterworth does exist, which blurs the distinction, though that design still needs op-amp gain and resistors."}], "concept": "For an nth-order Butterworth, |H(jω)|² = 1/(1 + (ω/ω_c)^(2n)); for a Chebyshev, |H(jω)|² = 1/(1 + ε² · T_n²(ω/ω_c)). The Butterworth is a special case where the passband error polynomial is a single term, (ω/ω_c)^(2n), that is negligibly small until ω approaches ω_c; the Chebyshev spreads an equiripple error polynomial across the whole passband. Flatness matters when the filter sits in a signal path whose amplitude accuracy is part of the specification: an audio filter where a 1 dB bump at 2.5 kHz would colour speech, an IF filter where the AGC and S-meter should not depend on where in the passband a signal falls, or a measurement front end. The Butterworth also has gentler phase behaviour and less overshoot on a step than an equal-order Chebyshev, since its poles are farther from the jω axis. The penalty is that for the same stop-band requirement it needs more sections, with the attendant extra loss and cost.", "worked_example": "An audio low-pass for SSB speech with f_c = 3 kHz, 5th order. Butterworth: at 2.4 kHz the loss is −10 · log₁₀(1 + 0.8^10) ≈ −0.44 dB, and at 300 Hz it is essentially 0 dB, so the voice band is flat to within half a dB. A 1 dB-ripple Chebyshev of the same order would wobble the voice band by up to 1 dB in a pattern with several peaks between 300 Hz and 3 kHz, audible as a slightly hollow timbre, while attenuating 6 kHz by about 15 dB more. For audio quality the Butterworth is the better bargain.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: steeper is always better, so Chebyshev is the superior filter. Correction: each is optimal for a different criterion; Butterworth is the right choice when amplitude uniformity across the passband matters more than how fast the stop band is reached.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "Butterworth: flat as butter.", "edge_cases": "If delay flatness rather than amplitude flatness is the goal (data, pulses), a Bessel filter beats both; its amplitude response is softer than Butterworth but its group delay is nearly constant through the passband."}

{"core": "A Chebyshev response allows a specified amount of passband ripple and, in exchange, rolls off far more steeply than a Butterworth of the same order; that steeper skirt for the same number of components is its advantage.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Maximally flat passband is the Butterworth property; the Chebyshev passband is explicitly equiripple, not flat.", "why_tempting": "The two defining phrases are a matched pair and get swapped when the question stem flips which filter is being praised."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Capacitors alone cannot produce resonance or a steep multi-pole roll-off; Chebyshev ladders need both L and C, or an active RC equivalent with gain.", "why_tempting": "Sounds like a cost or simplicity advantage."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Likewise inductors alone give no selectivity. Both filter families use the same L-C ladder topology; they differ only in element values.", "why_tempting": "Inductor-heavy RF filters are common, so inductor-only seems plausible."}], "concept": "Both filters are all-pole ladders of the same shape; the difference is where the poles are placed. Butterworth poles lie on a circle, Chebyshev poles on an ellipse whose minor axis shrinks as ripple increases, bringing poles nearer the jω axis. Near-axis poles produce peaking (the ripple) and a faster fall-off beyond the corner. Quantitatively, for order n and ripple factor ε, the extra stop-band attenuation of a Chebyshev over a Butterworth, well past cutoff, is about 6(n − 1) + 20 · log₁₀(ε) dB; for a 5-pole, 1 dB-ripple design (ε ≈ 0.51) that is roughly 24 − 6 ≈ 18 dB more rejection at any given stop-band frequency. The practical consequence is that a required harmonic rejection or adjacent-channel rejection can be met with fewer sections, less insertion loss, and smaller size. The costs are the ripple itself, greater sensitivity of the response to component tolerance (the near-axis poles move visibly for small value errors), and a pronounced group-delay peak at the band edge.", "worked_example": "A 50 Ω transmitter low-pass must pass 14.35 MHz and attenuate the second harmonic at 28 MHz by at least 40 dB. Set f_c = 16 MHz, so 28 MHz is 1.75 × f_c. Butterworth, 5 poles: 10 · log₁₀(1 + 1.75^10) ≈ 24.4 dB, fails. Butterworth, 7 poles: ≈ 34 dB, still short. Chebyshev, 0.5 dB ripple, 5 poles: about 44 dB, passes with two fewer inductors. The 0.5 dB wobble across 0 to 16 MHz is invisible to the transmitter.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a Chebyshev filter is sharper because it uses better or more components. Correction: it uses the same component count; the sharpness comes purely from choosing pole positions that permit passband ripple.", "link": "section 2", "mnemonic": "Chebyshev: cheaper cliff, bumpy plateau.", "edge_cases": "If both passband and stopband ripple are acceptable, an elliptic (Cauer) filter beats the Chebyshev for steepness at the same order, because its transmission zeros near the band edge create a near-vertical skirt; many commercial transmitter low-pass filters are in fact elliptic."}

{"core": "A cavity filter is a physical resonator whose dimensions are a fraction of a wavelength; at audio and low RF the wavelength is tens to thousands of kilometres, so a cavity cannot be built. Elliptic, Chebyshev and Butterworth are response shapes realisable with lumped RC, LC or active components at any frequency.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "An elliptic (Cauer) filter is a mathematical alignment with ripple in both passband and stopband; it is routinely realised as an active op-amp filter at audio or as an LC ladder at LF and HF.", "why_tempting": "Elliptic is the least familiar of the three names and sounds exotic or microwave-only."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Chebyshev alignments are standard in audio active filters and in HF/LF lumped LC designs; nothing about the pole placement limits the frequency range.", "why_tempting": "The steep-skirt description sounds like a high-frequency property."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Butterworth filters are the default alignment for audio and instrumentation work; the response is defined by a polynomial, not by a physical structure, so it applies at any frequency.", "why_tempting": "Students may remember Butterworth from the IF or RF context and not from audio."}], "concept": "There are two independent axes in filter design. One is the response alignment: Butterworth, Chebyshev, Bessel, elliptic. These are polynomials that specify the transfer function and can be scaled to any corner frequency; the element values come from normalised tables multiplied by 1/(2πf_c · Z_0) for capacitors and Z_0/(2πf_c) for inductors. The other axis is the physical technology that realises the poles: RC-active at audio, LC at LF through VHF, crystals and ceramics at HF/VHF IF, helical resonators at VHF/UHF, cavities and striplines at UHF and microwave. A cavity is on the second axis and is a distributed resonator: its resonance occurs when a dimension equals a quarter or half wavelength. At 1 kHz, λ = 300 km, so a quarter-wave cavity would be 75 km long; even at 1 MHz it would be 75 m. Conversely, lumped alignments do work at VHF but become awkward because coil Q is low and stray reactance is comparable to the design values, which is why cavities and helicals take over there. The question is really asking which option is a wavelength-sized structure.", "worked_example": "Design a Butterworth low-pass at 3 kHz for a CW audio filter and at 30 MHz for a transmitter: same normalised prototype (for n = 3, Z_0 = 1 Ω, ω_c = 1 rad/s the elements are 1 F, 2 H, 1 F). Scale to 600 Ω at 3 kHz: C = 1/(2π · 3000 · 600) ≈ 88 nF, L = 2 · 600/(2π · 3000) ≈ 64 mH. Scale to 50 Ω at 30 MHz: C ≈ 106 pF, L ≈ 0.53 μH. Same alignment, four orders of magnitude apart in frequency, both buildable. Now try a cavity at 3 kHz: λ/4 = 25 km. Not buildable.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: Butterworth, Chebyshev, elliptic and cavity are four comparable kinds of filter. Correction: the first three are response shapes that can be built in any technology; a cavity is a technology whose size is tied to wavelength and is therefore limited to VHF and above.", "link": "Wavelength ↔ Frequency", "mnemonic": "Cavity needs a short wave to fit in a can; audio waves are kilometres long.", "edge_cases": "Mechanical and crystal filters are also physical resonators but their resonance is acoustic, with wavelengths in the millimetre range at a few hundred kHz, which is why they can be small at frequencies where an electromagnetic cavity would be enormous."}

{"core": "An oscilloscope draws the instantaneous waveform against a graticule, so the quantity you can read directly is a vertical distance between two features of the trace. For a sine wave the only two unambiguous features are the top and bottom of the excursion, and the span between them, peak-to-peak, needs no reference line and no computation.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "RMS is defined by an integral, V_rms = √((1/T)∫v²dt); a scope does not display it directly, and you obtain it only by reading peak-to-peak, halving, and multiplying by 0.707 (or by using a digital scope's measurement function, which performs that arithmetic for you).", "why_tempting": "RMS is the value most meters display and most specifications quote, so it feels like the natural amplitude to want."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "The average of a full sine cycle is zero; the half-cycle average, 0.637 V_p, is a derived quantity not visible on the trace.", "why_tempting": "Average sounds like a simple quantity, and moving-coil meters do respond to average."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Peak voltage requires knowing exactly where the zero line is. With AC coupling, trace position offsets, or any DC component, the zero reference is uncertain, so peak is less reliable than the top-to-bottom span.", "why_tempting": "Peak is half of peak-to-peak and the trace clearly has a peak, so it seems equally easy to read."}], "concept": "A scope measures the voltage as a function of time; everything else is derived. The relationships for a pure sine are: V_pp = 2 · V_p, V_rms = V_p/√2 = 0.707 · V_p = V_pp/(2√2) ≈ 0.354 · V_pp, and the half-cycle average V_avg = 2V_p/π = 0.637 · V_p. Peak-to-peak is the only one of these that is a difference between two visible points and is therefore immune to where the trace sits vertically, to AC-coupling baseline shifts, and to any superimposed DC. In practice you set the vertical sensitivity so the waveform fills most of the screen, count divisions from the lowest trough to the highest crest, and multiply by the volts per division and any probe attenuation. Measurement precision then comes from the graticule reading, typically a few percent. This is also why PEP measurements with a scope start from V_pp across the dummy load: PEP = V_pp²/(8R_L) folds the 2 and the √2 into one constant.", "worked_example": "A trace spans 6.8 divisions trough to crest at 5 V/div with a 10× probe: V_pp = 6.8 × 5 × 10 = 340 V. From that, V_p = 170 V and V_rms = 170 × 0.707 ≈ 120 V. If instead you tried to read the peak alone and the AC-coupled trace had drifted half a division above centre, you would read 3.9 divisions and get V_p = 195 V, a 15% error that the peak-to-peak reading never incurs.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a scope tells you RMS because that is the real voltage. Correction: a scope shows instantaneous amplitude versus time; peak-to-peak is what you read, and RMS is a calculation that assumes the waveform shape.", "link": "section 3", "mnemonic": "Scope reads top-to-bottom; everything else is arithmetic.", "edge_cases": "The 0.707 factor is only valid for a pure sine. For a square wave V_rms = V_p, for a triangle V_rms = V_p/√3, and for speech or noise there is no fixed ratio; peak-to-peak stays readable on the scope for all of them, which is exactly why it is the preferred scope quantity."}

{"core": "Halve the peak-to-peak value to get the peak, then multiply by 1/√2: 340 V_pp → 170 V_p → 170 × 0.707 ≈ 120 V RMS. This is the familiar 120 V mains waveform seen on a scope.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "300 V would require multiplying the peak-to-peak value by 0.88, which corresponds to no standard waveform ratio; it is above the peak value itself, which is impossible for an RMS figure since RMS can never exceed peak.", "why_tempting": "It is a round number near the given 340, inviting a guess."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "170 V is the peak value (V_pp/2), one step short of the RMS conversion; the 0.707 factor has not been applied.", "why_tempting": "Students sometimes remember divide by two as the whole conversion, especially since 170 is a clean number."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "240 V is 340 × 0.707, which applies the RMS factor to the peak-to-peak value directly without first halving it; equivalently it is the RMS of a sine with 340 V peak, not 340 V peak-to-peak.", "why_tempting": "It is also a familiar mains voltage, and the 0.707 factor was applied, just to the wrong quantity."}], "concept": "For a sinusoid v(t) = V_p · sin(ωt), the mean of v² over one cycle is V_p²/2 because sin² averages to one half. The RMS value is the square root of that mean, V_rms = V_p/√2 ≈ 0.707 · V_p. The oscilloscope gives peak-to-peak, which is 2V_p, so a single combined factor converts directly: V_rms = V_pp/(2√2) = V_pp/2.828 ≈ 0.354 · V_pp. The chain is therefore divide by 2, then multiply by 0.707, or equivalently multiply by 0.354 in one step. The reason 120 V mains has a 340 V peak-to-peak trace is this same chain in reverse: 120 × 1.414 = 170 V peak, 340 V peak-to-peak. Keeping the three quantities straight is the foundation for PEP calculations in the next subsection, where the same chain is applied before squaring and dividing by the load resistance.", "worked_example": "V_pp = 340 V. Step 1: V_p = 340/2 = 170 V. Step 2: V_rms = 170 × 0.7071 = 120.2 V ≈ 120 V. One-step check: 340 × 0.3536 = 120.2 V. Sanity check against the distractors: 170 is peak, 240 is 340 × 0.707 (factor applied to the wrong quantity), and 300 exceeds the peak, which RMS never can for any waveform.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: multiply whatever the scope shows by 0.707 to get RMS. Correction: the 0.707 factor applies to the peak value only; a peak-to-peak reading must be halved first.", "link": "Formula-sheet trainer", "mnemonic": "Half, then point-seven: pp → p → RMS.", "edge_cases": "The 0.707 factor assumes a pure sine. If the 340 V_pp waveform were a square wave the RMS would be 170 V, and for a triangle wave 98 V; always check the shape before converting."}

{"core": "The RMS (effective) value of an AC voltage is defined by its heating effect: it is the magnitude of the DC voltage that would dissipate the same average power in the same resistor. Option D states exactly that equivalence.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "The square root of the peak voltage is dimensionally meaningless (√volts) and numerically wrong; for a sine the RMS is the peak divided by √2, not the square root of the peak.", "why_tempting": "The words root and square appear in RMS, so taking a square root of something sounds right."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "It compares DC heating against the peak AC voltage, but the peak is reached only momentarily each cycle; the AC waveform heats less than a DC voltage equal to its peak. The equivalence must be with the AC waveform as a whole, not its peak.", "why_tempting": "It has the correct heating-equivalence structure and only substitutes peak for the waveform, an easy slip."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The square root of the average value is again dimensionally wrong and ignores the order of operations: RMS squares first, averages, then roots. The average of a full sine cycle is zero in any case.", "why_tempting": "It uses two of the three RMS operations, average and root, just in the wrong order and without the square."}], "concept": "Instantaneous power in a resistor is p(t) = v(t)²/R. Average power over a period T is P = (1/T)∫v²dt / R. Define V_rms such that P = V_rms²/R; then V_rms = √((1/T)∫v(t)²dt), the root of the mean of the square, hence the name. The definition is shape-independent and is what makes RMS the correct value to plug into Ohm's law and power formulas for any periodic waveform. For a sine, sin² averages to 1/2, so V_rms = V_p/√2. For a square wave of amplitude V_p the square is constant, so V_rms = V_p. For a triangle, V_rms = V_p/√3. The physical content is that heating depends on the square of voltage, so brief high peaks count disproportionately; a waveform with the same peak but narrower peaks (a higher crest factor, V_p/V_rms) delivers less power. This is why SSB with its high crest factor has a PEP far above its average power, and why a true-RMS meter is needed for non-sinusoidal signals.", "worked_example": "Apply 170 V peak sine to a 100 Ω resistor. Instantaneous peak power is 170²/100 = 289 W, but the average of sin² is 0.5, so the average power is 144.5 W. Which DC voltage gives 144.5 W in 100 Ω? V = √(144.5 × 100) = 120.2 V. So the RMS value is 120 V, and indeed 170/√2 = 120.2 V. Compare the trap in option B: a DC voltage equal to the 170 V peak would give 289 W, twice the actual heating.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: RMS is a mathematical trick for converting peak readings. Correction: RMS is a physical definition based on equal heating; the 0.707 factor is merely what that definition evaluates to for a sine wave.", "link": "Ohm's Law & Power", "mnemonic": "RMS: Root of the Mean of the Square, in that order from right to left.", "edge_cases": "Average-responding meters are calibrated to read RMS only for sine waves (they multiply the rectified average by 1.11). On a square wave they read about 11% high and on a narrow pulse train they read low; a true-RMS instrument actually computes the integral."}

{"core": "For a sinusoid the RMS value is the peak divided by √2: 20 V × 0.7071 = 14.14 V. The 100 Hz frequency is irrelevant to the ratio.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "16.38 V corresponds to no standard sine-wave ratio (it would be 0.819 × V_p); it is likely a decoy built from inverting 0.637 and 0.707 fragments.", "why_tempting": "It is between the average (12.7 V) and the peak, in a range where a guess might land."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "28.28 V is 20 × 1.414, the conversion in the wrong direction; it would be the peak of a 20 V RMS sine. RMS can never exceed peak.", "why_tempting": "Both 0.707 and 1.414 are on the formula sheet, and under pressure the multiplication direction is easy to flip."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "7.07 V is 20 × 0.707 × 0.5, which applies the halving step appropriate to a peak-to-peak reading to a value that is already peak; it is the RMS of a 20 V peak-to-peak sine.", "why_tempting": "The question gives a peak value, but the scope-measurement habit of halving first carries over."}], "concept": "The RMS value is defined by equal heating, V_rms = √(mean of v²). For v = V_p · sin(ωt), v² = V_p² · sin²(ωt) and the mean of sin² over any whole number of cycles is exactly 1/2, independent of frequency, so V_rms = V_p · √(1/2) = V_p/√2. The constants to carry are 1/√2 ≈ 0.7071 (peak to RMS) and √2 ≈ 1.4142 (RMS to peak). Frequency does not appear because sin² averages to one half whether the cycle takes 10 ms at 100 Hz or 70 ns at 14 MHz; the 100 Hz in the question is a distractor to test whether you know that. The three-way relationship among peak, peak-to-peak and RMS is the first thing to pin down before any AC power calculation, because power formulas assume RMS values and scope readings give peak-to-peak.", "worked_example": "V_p = 20 V. V_rms = 20/√2 = 20/1.4142 = 14.142 V. Check by heating: into 10 Ω the peak instantaneous power is 20²/10 = 40 W, the average is half that, 20 W, and the DC voltage giving 20 W in 10 Ω is √(20 × 10) = 14.14 V. Also note V_pp would be 40 V and V_avg (half-cycle) would be 20 × 0.637 = 12.7 V, neither of which is offered.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: RMS depends on frequency or on how the waveform is timed. Correction: for a given shape the RMS-to-peak ratio is a pure number; frequency only changes how fast the cycle repeats, not the mean of the square.", "link": "Formula-sheet trainer", "mnemonic": "Peak times point-seven-oh-seven; RMS times one-point-four-one-four. Smaller goes to RMS.", "edge_cases": "The 0.707 ratio holds only for a sine. For a sine with a DC offset, V_rms = √(V_dc² + V_p²/2), so a 20 V peak sine riding on 10 V DC has an RMS of √(100 + 200) ≈ 17.3 V."}

{"core": "Ohm's law and the power formulas hold for AC only when all quantities are expressed as RMS (effective) values, because those are the values that reproduce the DC heating relationships. For a sine wave RMS equals peak × 0.707, which is what option B states.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A correct description is present in the list (peak × 0.707 = RMS for a sine), so none of the above does not apply.", "why_tempting": "The other three look oddly specific and one of them might seem too narrow, making the escape option attractive."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The average of a full AC cycle is zero, and the half-cycle average (0.637 × peak) does not satisfy P = V²/R; using it understates power by about 19%.", "why_tempting": "Average sounds like the sensible representative value for a varying quantity, and moving-coil meters do respond to the rectified average."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Average × 1.414 is 0.637 × 1.414 ≈ 0.9 × peak, which matches no standard quantity; the 1.414 factor converts RMS to peak, not average to anything useful.", "why_tempting": "It contains a formula-sheet constant and the word average, a plausible-looking combination."}], "concept": "Ohm's law is linear, so it actually holds instant by instant for a resistor: v(t) = i(t) · R. That means it also holds for peaks, for peak-to-peak, and for RMS values, provided you use the same kind of value on both sides. What forces the choice of RMS is power: P = V · I = V²/R = I²R are quadratic, and the only single number that makes them give the true average power is the RMS value, by definition. Since engineering practice uses the same number for both Ohm's law and power, RMS is the standard currency of AC circuit work; meters are calibrated in it, mains is specified in it, and transmitter output power is computed from it. For reactive circuits the magnitudes still obey V_rms = I_rms · |Z|, while real power picks up the power-factor term P = V_rms · I_rms · cos φ. The sine-specific conversion is V_rms = 0.707 · V_p; for other waveforms the ratio differs, but the principle, use RMS in these formulas, is universal.", "worked_example": "A scope shows 28.3 V peak across a 20 Ω resistor. Peak current by Ohm's law is 28.3/20 = 1.415 A (valid: same kind of value both sides). Power from peaks, 28.3 × 1.415 = 40 W, is wrong; it is twice the true value. Convert to RMS: V = 28.3 × 0.707 = 20 V, I = 1.415 × 0.707 = 1.0 A, P = 20 × 1.0 = 20 W, which matches V_rms²/R = 400/20 = 20 W. Using half-cycle averages instead, 18 V × 0.9 A = 16.2 W, understates by 19%.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: any consistent pair of AC values works in Ohm's law and the power formulas. Correction: Ohm's law alone tolerates peak or RMS, but power requires RMS, so RMS is the convention for all AC calculations.", "link": "Ohm's Law & Power", "mnemonic": "AC formulas want the heating value: RMS, peak × 0.707.", "edge_cases": "In a reactive circuit V_rms × I_rms gives apparent power in volt-amperes; multiply by cos φ for real watts. The 0.707 factor is still correct for the sine magnitudes; it is the phase angle that adds the extra term."}

{"core": "Effective value is another name for RMS. For a sine wave the mean of sin² over a cycle is 1/2, so the RMS value is the maximum value divided by √2, which is 0.707 or 70.7% of the peak.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "An AC voltage equal to its own peak only momentarily cannot heat as much as a DC voltage held at that peak; the effective value must be less than the maximum for any waveform except a square wave.", "why_tempting": "Peak is the most visible number, and for a square wave 100% would actually be right."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "63.6% (more precisely 63.7%, 2/π) is the half-cycle average of a sine, the value a rectifier-fed moving-coil meter actually responds to. It is not the heating-equivalent value.", "why_tempting": "0.637 and 0.707 are both on the formula sheet and both relate average-ish quantities to peak."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "50% is the mean of sin² (the ratio of average power to peak instantaneous power), not the ratio of RMS voltage to peak voltage; the square root of 0.5 gives 0.707.", "why_tempting": "The factor one-half does appear in the derivation, just one square root earlier than the final answer."}], "concept": "Define the effective value as the DC value that produces the same average power in a resistor. For v = V_max · sin(ωt), p(t) = (V_max²/R) · sin²(ωt). Using sin²θ = (1 − cos 2θ)/2, the cosine term averages to zero over a cycle, leaving mean power = V_max²/(2R). Equate to V_eff²/R: V_eff = V_max/√2 = 0.7071 · V_max. The same derivation with current gives I_eff = 0.707 · I_max. Note the pattern in the distractors: 50% is the power ratio, 70.7% is its square root (the voltage ratio), and 63.7% comes from a different operation entirely, the average of |sin|, which is 2/π. Keeping these three separated is essential for the measurement section: RMS for heating and power, average for what a rectifier meter sees, and the form factor 0.707/0.637 = 1.11 that links the two on a sine-calibrated meter.", "worked_example": "A 100 V peak sine into 50 Ω. Peak instantaneous power = 100²/50 = 200 W. Average power = 200 × 0.5 = 100 W. Effective voltage = √(100 W × 50 Ω) = 70.7 V, which is 70.7% of the 100 V peak. Half-cycle average for comparison = 63.7 V; a DC supply of 63.7 V would give only 81 W, confirming that the average is not the effective value.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: effective and average are the same thing. Correction: effective (RMS) is defined by heating and equals 70.7% of peak for a sine; the rectified average is 63.7% of peak and is a different quantity used for meter movements.", "link": "Formula-sheet trainer", "mnemonic": "Seventy-point-seven heats; sixty-three-point-seven meters; fifty is the power fraction.", "edge_cases": "Only the sine gives 70.7%. Square wave 100%, triangle 57.7%, and for a sine with DC offset or for speech the figure must be computed from the actual waveform."}

{"core": "AC voltmeters are scaled in RMS because that is the value that plugs directly into power and Ohm's-law calculations and matches how AC supplies are specified. Even inexpensive average-responding meters have their scale factor adjusted (× 1.11) so that the needle reads the RMS value of a sine wave.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Peak is not what the scale reads; a peak-detecting meter would show 170 V on a 120 V mains outlet, which is not the convention. Some meters do use a peak detector internally, but their scale is divided by 1.414 so the displayed number is still RMS.", "why_tempting": "Peak is a physically obvious quantity and some RF probes do detect peaks."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "An instantaneous value changes continuously at the signal frequency; no mechanical or sampled meter could display it, and it would be useless as a single reading. That is the oscilloscope's job.", "why_tempting": "Instantaneous is the most literal meaning of what a voltage is at any moment."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Although many meters respond internally to the rectified average, the scale is deliberately calibrated 11% high so it displays RMS, not average, for a sine wave. A meter actually marked in average volts would read 108 V on a 120 V outlet.", "why_tempting": "It is true that the movement responds to average, so a student who knows the internals may pick the mechanism rather than the displayed quantity."}], "concept": "There are three common AC meter architectures. The average-responding meter rectifies the input and drives a d'Arsonval movement, whose deflection is proportional to the rectified average, 0.637 · V_p for a sine; the scale is multiplied by the form factor 1.11 (= 0.707/0.637) so it reads 0.707 · V_p, the RMS. The peak-responding meter charges a capacitor to V_p through a diode and divides the scale by 1.414. The true-RMS meter actually computes √(mean of v²), either thermally or with an analog or digital squaring circuit, and reads correctly for any waveform. All three are marked in RMS; they differ only in which waveforms they are accurate for. For a pure sine all three agree; for a square wave the average-responding meter reads 11% high and the peak-responding meter reads 41% high. That is why specifications state true-RMS when it matters, and why a scope is the right tool when the waveform shape is unknown.", "worked_example": "Connect three meters to a 120 V RMS sine (170 V peak, 108 V rectified average). Average-responding: movement sees 108 V, scale × 1.11 shows 120 V. Peak-responding: detector sees 170 V, scale ÷ 1.414 shows 120 V. True-RMS: computes 120 V directly. Now feed a 120 V peak square wave (true RMS 120 V). Average-responding: sees 120 V average, shows 133 V. Peak-responding: sees 120 V, shows 85 V. True-RMS: shows 120 V. Same scale label, three different answers.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the meter displays whatever its movement responds to. Correction: the scale is calibrated so the display is RMS for a sine; the internal response (average or peak) is hidden by the scale factor and only shows up as error on non-sinusoidal waveforms.", "link": "section 3", "mnemonic": "Meters are labelled for heating value: RMS.", "edge_cases": "Many true-RMS DMMs are AC-coupled, so they ignore a DC component; a 20 V peak sine on a 10 V offset reads 14.1 V rather than the true 17.3 V. Check the manual for AC+DC capability when it matters."}

{"core": "Effective value is the RMS value, and AC voltmeter scales are calibrated to display it, regardless of whether the meter's internal detector responds to the rectified average or the peak, because RMS is the value that works in power calculations and matches how AC sources are rated.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A meter scaled in peak volts would read 170 V on a 120 V outlet. Peak detectors exist inside some meters and RF probes, but the scale is divided by 1.414 so that the display is RMS.", "why_tempting": "Peak-reading RF probes and some scope-based measurements do produce peak values."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Peak-to-peak is an oscilloscope quantity, the span from trough to crest. No voltmeter is scaled in it; on a 120 V outlet it would read 340 V.", "why_tempting": "The previous subsection stresses that peak-to-peak is the easiest scope measurement, and that can bleed into meter questions."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "The rectified average (0.637 · V_p for a sine) is what the movement of a cheap meter physically responds to, but the scale is stretched by 1.11 so the display reads RMS. A meter marked in average volts would show 108 V on a 120 V outlet.", "why_tempting": "Knowing that the movement is average-responding makes this look like the technically honest answer."}], "concept": "The effective value of an AC waveform is the DC value that causes equal heating, V_eff = V_rms = √(mean of v²) = 0.707 · V_p for a sine. Meters are calibrated to display this because it is the quantity that makes P = V²/R and V = I · Z give correct results and because supplies and transformers are rated in it. The calibration is a scale-factor trick: an average-responding movement is marked with numbers 1.11 times larger than the average it senses, and a peak-responding detector with numbers 0.707 times smaller than the peak it holds. The trick is exact only for a sine. The form factor 1.11 and crest factor 1.414 are sine-wave constants; a square wave has form factor 1.0 and crest factor 1.0, so an average-responding meter over-reads it by 11% and a peak-responding meter under-reads it by 29%. True-RMS meters avoid the assumption by computing the mean square directly, which is why they are specified for measuring switching-supply ripple, audio, or any distorted waveform.", "worked_example": "A transformer secondary gives a 34 V peak-to-peak sine. Peak = 17 V, rectified average = 17 × 0.637 = 10.8 V, RMS = 17 × 0.707 = 12.0 V. A bench DMM on AC volts reads 12.0 V: if average-responding, 10.8 × 1.11 = 12.0; if peak-responding, 17 × 0.707 = 12.0; if true-RMS, 12.0 computed. Load it with 12 Ω and it dissipates 12²/12 = 12 W, confirming 12 V is the value you want for power.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the number on the dial is whatever the detector inside measures. Correction: the dial is always marked in effective (RMS) volts; the internal detector type only determines which non-sinusoidal waveforms the meter gets wrong.", "link": "section 3", "mnemonic": "Effective equals RMS equals what the dial says.", "edge_cases": "At RF, a diode probe on a DMM is typically a peak detector with a resistive divider that makes it read RMS for a sine; on an SSB signal its reading swings with the envelope and is not a meaningful RMS of the modulated signal."}

{"core": "By definition the RMS value of an AC waveform is the DC voltage that delivers the same average power to the same resistor; it is literally the heating-equivalent value, computed as the square root of the time-average of v².", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "An AC waveform only touches its peak momentarily, so its heating is less than a steady DC at the peak value; for a sine the AC heats only half as much as DC at the peak.", "why_tempting": "Peak is the largest number on the waveform and feels like the amount of voltage that is really there."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Peak-to-peak is twice the peak and four times too large in power terms; a DC voltage at the peak-to-peak value would heat eight times more than the sine does.", "why_tempting": "It is the quantity read most easily on a scope, so it is often the first number in hand."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "The full-cycle average of a symmetric AC wave is zero, and the half-cycle average (0.637 · V_p) understates heating because power depends on the square of voltage, which weights the peaks more than a linear average does.", "why_tempting": "Average is the intuitive summary of a varying quantity and is what a rectifier-and-movement meter physically responds to."}], "concept": "Power in a resistor is v²/R at every instant. Over a cycle the energy delivered is (1/R)∫v²dt, so average power is (1/R) × (mean of v²). The DC voltage V_dc that gives the same power satisfies V_dc² = mean of v², hence V_dc = √(mean of v²) = V_rms. The squaring is the key physical step: it makes the heating equivalence depend on the second moment of the waveform, not its first moment (average) or its extreme (peak). For a sine the result is V_p/√2; for a square wave it equals the peak; for an impulsive waveform with high crest factor it can be far below the peak. The same definition applies to current, I_rms = √(mean of i²), and the two combine as P = V_rms · I_rms for a resistor. This is why every AC power calculation, including transmitter output into a dummy load, is done with RMS values, and why PEP is defined via the RMS of the RF cycle at the envelope peak.", "worked_example": "A 50 Ω dummy load. Apply 100 V DC: P = 100²/50 = 200 W. Apply a 100 V peak sine: instantaneous power swings from 0 to 200 W and averages 100 W, half the DC case; the sine heats like 70.7 V DC (70.7²/50 = 100 W), its RMS. Apply a 100 V peak square wave: v² is always 10 000, P = 200 W, so its RMS is the full 100 V. Apply a 100 V peak, 10% duty pulse train: v² is 10 000 for 10% of the time, average 1000, P = 20 W, RMS = 31.6 V. Same peak, very different heating.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: an AC voltage of some peak value heats as much as DC of that peak value. Correction: heating tracks the mean of the squared voltage, and the equivalent DC is the RMS, which is below the peak for every waveform except a square wave.", "link": "Ohm's Law & Power", "mnemonic": "RMS is the DC that would make the resistor just as hot.", "edge_cases": "The equivalence holds for the power dissipated in a resistance. Into a reactive load the RMS current still sets I²R loss in the series resistance, but V_rms × I_rms is apparent power, not heat."}

{"core": "Multiply RMS by √2 to get the peak, then double it for peak-to-peak: 120 × 1.414 = 169.7 V peak, × 2 = 339.4 V peak-to-peak, which rounds to the 339.5 V option.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "204.8 V has no sine-wave relationship to 120 V RMS (it would be 1.707 × 120, i.e. adding 0.707 and 1 instead of multiplying by 2√2).", "why_tempting": "It lies between the peak and peak-to-peak values, in a plausible-looking range."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "84.8 V is 120 × 0.707, the result of applying the RMS-to-peak conversion backwards; it is smaller than the RMS, which no peak quantity can be.", "why_tempting": "0.707 is the first constant one reaches for, and the direction of the conversion is easy to flip."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "169.7 V is the peak value (120 × 1.414), one step short; the question asks for peak-to-peak, which is twice that.", "why_tempting": "The factor 1.414 was applied correctly, and 169.7 is a familiar mains peak figure, so it feels complete."}], "concept": "For a sinusoid V_rms = V_p/√2, so V_p = √2 · V_rms ≈ 1.414 · V_rms, and V_pp = 2 · V_p = 2√2 · V_rms ≈ 2.828 · V_rms. The three quantities form a ladder: RMS → (× 1.414) → peak → (× 2) → peak-to-peak, and the reverse: peak-to-peak → (÷ 2) → peak → (× 0.707) → RMS. The 120 V to 340 V_pp relationship is worth memorising as an anchor, because North American mains and a scope on a wall outlet (through a proper isolation transformer and high-voltage probe) give exactly this picture. The same ladder is the first step in every PEP problem, where the scope gives V_pp across the dummy load and the formula wants V_rms at the envelope peak. Note the useful shortcut constant 2√2 = 2.828 that converts RMS directly to peak-to-peak, and its reciprocal 0.354 going the other way.", "worked_example": "V_rms = 120 V. V_p = 120 × 1.4142 = 169.7 V. V_pp = 2 × 169.7 = 339.4 V, matching option B within rounding (120 × 2.828 = 339.4). Reverse check: 339.4/2 = 169.7; 169.7 × 0.7071 = 120.0 V. Also identify the distractors: 169.7 is peak, 84.8 is 120 × 0.707 (wrong direction), 204.8 is not a sine-wave quantity.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: converting RMS to peak-to-peak is a single multiplication by 1.414. Correction: 1.414 gets you to peak; peak-to-peak needs another factor of 2, for 2.828 overall.", "link": "Formula-sheet trainer", "mnemonic": "RMS to pp: one-four-one-four, then double it.", "edge_cases": "This applies to a symmetric sine with no DC component. If the waveform rides on a DC offset the peak-to-peak span is unchanged but the RMS rises, so the 2.828 ratio no longer holds."}

{"core": "RMS equals peak divided by √2 for a sine: 17 V × 0.7071 ≈ 12.0 V. The 17 V peak, 12 V RMS pair is the familiar 12.6 V transformer-secondary picture.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "24 V is 17 × 1.414, the conversion applied in the wrong direction; it would be the peak of a 17 V RMS sine. RMS is always less than or equal to peak.", "why_tempting": "1.414 and 0.707 sit side by side on the formula sheet and the direction is easy to reverse."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "34 V is the peak-to-peak value (2 × 17), a larger quantity than peak, not a smaller one.", "why_tempting": "Doubling is a reflex when peak and peak-to-peak are being juggled."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "8.5 V is half the peak, which is the RMS of a 17 V peak-to-peak sine, not a 17 V peak sine; the halving step belongs to peak-to-peak readings only.", "why_tempting": "The habit of halving a scope reading first gets applied to a value that is already peak."}], "concept": "The RMS of V_p · sin(ωt) is V_p/√2 because sin² averages to 1/2 over a cycle and the square root of 1/2 is 0.7071. This is a pure shape constant, independent of frequency and amplitude. The chain of conversions is peak-to-peak ÷ 2 = peak; peak × 0.707 = RMS; and the reverse, RMS × 1.414 = peak; peak × 2 = peak-to-peak. Spotting which quantity the question hands you is the whole skill: here it is peak, so only one operation is needed. A second sanity anchor is that RMS must be smaller than peak and larger than half of peak for a sine (since 0.5 < 0.707 < 1); that alone eliminates 24 V, 34 V and 8.5 V before any arithmetic. The practical relevance is power: a 17 V peak sine into 12 Ω gives 12²/12 = 12 W, not 17²/12 = 24 W, which is what you would compute from the peak.", "worked_example": "V_p = 17 V. V_rms = 17 × 0.7071 = 12.02 V ≈ 12 V. Heating check into 12 Ω: peak instantaneous power = 17²/12 = 24.1 W, average = 12.0 W, equivalent DC = √(12.0 × 12) = 12.0 V. Reverse: 12 × 1.414 = 17.0 V peak, 34 V peak-to-peak.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: whatever number the question gives must be halved before the 0.707 factor. Correction: halve only a peak-to-peak value; a peak value goes straight to 0.707.", "link": "Formula-sheet trainer", "mnemonic": "RMS sits between half the peak and the peak: 8.5 < 12 < 17.", "edge_cases": "A 12.6 V RMS filament transformer actually peaks at 17.8 V, and after a bridge rectifier and filter capacitor the DC is near that peak minus two diode drops (about 16.4 V), not 12.6 V; this is where the peak versus RMS distinction bites in power-supply design."}

{"core": "Peak-envelope power is defined as the average power over one RF cycle taken at the highest crest of the modulation envelope; it captures the instantaneous maximum output of a transmitter whose envelope varies, such as SSB or AM, and is the figure in which amateur transmitter power is normally specified.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Carrier power is the power of the unmodulated carrier alone. For SSB there is no carrier at all, and for AM the carrier is one quarter of the PEP at full modulation, so it is not the power at the envelope crest.", "why_tempting": "Carrier power is the traditional AM power rating and is what an average-reading meter shows with no modulation."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Full power is not a defined engineering quantity; it is colloquial language with no reference to the envelope or to the averaging interval.", "why_tempting": "It sounds like the maximum output and the question is about a maximum."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Mean power is the average over a time long enough to include many envelope cycles (the syllabus phrase is a period long compared with the lowest modulating frequency). For speech SSB it is typically a quarter to half the PEP; it is what a slow wattmeter displays, not the crest value.", "why_tempting": "Mean and average are what power meters read, and the definition also involves averaging, just over a different interval."}], "concept": "A modulated RF signal has two time scales: the RF cycle (tens of nanoseconds at HF) and the envelope, which follows the audio at millisecond scale. Averaging over one RF cycle removes the carrier oscillation but preserves the envelope; the result is the instantaneous envelope power P_env(t) = V_env(t)²/(2R_L), where V_env is the envelope's peak RF voltage at that moment. PEP is the maximum of P_env(t), reached at the crest of the loudest syllable or the top of the two-tone test envelope. Mean power averages P_env(t) over many envelope cycles. For a steady carrier the envelope is flat and PEP = mean. For a two-tone SSB test the envelope is a rectified sine and mean = PEP/2. For real speech the ratio is lower, often PEP/4 or less, because voice has a high peak-to-average ratio. The measurement recipe follows from the definition: capture the envelope peak voltage with an oscilloscope across a known resistive load, convert to RMS over that RF cycle (× 0.707), square, divide by R_L.", "worked_example": "An SSB transmitter under a two-tone test shows an envelope whose crests reach 200 V peak-to-peak on a 50 Ω dummy load. At the crest, V_p = 100 V, V_rms = 70.7 V, so PEP = 70.7²/50 = 100 W. Because the two-tone envelope averages half of its crest power, a thermal wattmeter reads 50 W mean. Switch to a steady carrier of the same 200 V_pp and both PEP and mean are 100 W. Switch to speech and the scope still flashes to 200 V_pp on syllable peaks (PEP 100 W) while the wattmeter wanders around 25 W.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: PEP is the power at the single highest instant of RF voltage. Correction: PEP averages over the full RF cycle at the envelope crest, so it uses the RMS of that cycle (V_p²/2R), not the instantaneous V_p²/R, which would be twice as large.", "link": "section 5", "mnemonic": "PEP: one RF cycle, at the top of the envelope.", "edge_cases": "With no modulation (CW key-down, FM, or an unmodulated AM carrier) the envelope is constant and PEP equals mean power, which is why a transmitter rated 100 W PEP delivers 100 W on CW but only 25 W of carrier on AM."}

{"core": "The recipe given, PEV × 0.707 to get RMS, square, divide by R_L, is the computation of peak-envelope power: PEP = (0.707 · PEV)²/R_L = PEV²/(2R_L). It takes the envelope's crest voltage and converts it to the average power of that RF cycle.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "ERP (effective radiated power) is transmitter power minus feedline loss plus antenna gain relative to a dipole; it involves decibel gain figures, not a voltage-squared-over-resistance calculation at the transmitter output.", "why_tempting": "It is another power term from the same part of the syllabus and also starts from transmitter output."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Power factor is the ratio of real to apparent power, cos φ, a dimensionless number between 0 and 1 that depends on phase angle, not on envelope voltage.", "why_tempting": "The word power appears and the question mentions a load, suggesting an AC power calculation."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "PIV (peak inverse voltage) is the maximum reverse voltage a rectifier diode must withstand; it is a voltage rating from the power-supply section and involves no squaring or load resistance.", "why_tempting": "It is a peak-voltage quantity with a three-letter acronym beginning with P, easily confused with PEV."}], "concept": "Power in a resistor from a sinusoidal voltage is P = V_rms²/R. At the crest of the modulation envelope the RF voltage is a sine of peak value PEV, so the RMS over that cycle is 0.707 · PEV and the power is (0.707 · PEV)²/R_L = 0.5 · PEV²/R_L. That is PEP by definition: the average power over one RF cycle at the envelope maximum. The 0.707 then squaring is equivalent to dividing PEV² by 2, and if the scope reading is peak-to-peak rather than peak the extra factor of 2² = 4 gives the compact form PEP = V_pp²/(8R_L). The procedure is the only practical way to measure PEP on a varying signal, because a thermal or diode wattmeter integrates over many envelope cycles and reports mean power; only an oscilloscope (or a fast peak-holding detector) can catch the crest voltage. The distractors are deliberately other P-acronyms from neighbouring sections, and the question is checking that the recipe is recognised as a power calculation on a sine-wave crest.", "worked_example": "Scope shows an envelope crest of 141 V peak (282 V peak-to-peak) across 50 Ω. RMS at the crest = 141 × 0.707 = 100 V. Square: 10 000 V². Divide by 50 Ω: 200 W PEP. Shortcut: 282²/(8 × 50) = 79 524/400 ≈ 199 W, same answer. A wattmeter on the same SSB signal would read perhaps 50 to 100 W depending on the modulation, which is the mean power, not the PEP.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: PEP is computed from the peak voltage directly as PEV²/R_L. Correction: the RMS over the crest cycle is what counts, so PEV must be reduced by 0.707 before squaring, giving half of PEV²/R_L.", "link": "Formula-sheet trainer", "mnemonic": "PEP: Point-seven, Exponent two, Per ohm.", "edge_cases": "The formula assumes a purely resistive load. Into a reactive antenna the voltage and current are out of phase and V²/|Z| overstates real power; that is why PEP is measured into a dummy load, not an antenna."}

{"core": "PEP is the average power during one RF cycle at the envelope crest, which for a sinusoidal RF cycle is the RMS voltage squared over the load: take the peak-envelope voltage, multiply by 0.707 to get RMS, square it and divide by R_L.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "RMS power is not a defined quantity in standard engineering use (power is already an average of v²/R); the phrase usually signals confusion between RMS voltage and average power. PEP is in any case the crest-cycle power, not a long-term average.", "why_tempting": "RMS is attached to so many AC quantities that RMS power sounds official."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "PEP is measurable and routinely measured, with an oscilloscope across a dummy load or with a peak-reading wattmeter; it is the standard basis on which SSB transmitters and amateur power limits are specified.", "why_tempting": "Because a slow wattmeter cannot show it on speech, PEP can seem like a theoretical construct."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Peak voltage × peak current is the instantaneous peak power of the RF cycle, V_p²/R, which is twice the PEP; it omits the averaging over the cycle that the definition requires.", "why_tempting": "P = V × I is Ohm's-law reasoning and using both peaks seems consistent, but power from peaks needs the factor of one half."}], "concept": "Define the envelope voltage V_env(t) as the peak RF voltage at each instant of the modulation. Average power over one RF cycle is then V_env²/(2R_L), since the RMS of a sine is its peak over √2. PEP is this quantity evaluated at the maximum of V_env, called PEV: PEP = (0.707 · PEV)²/R_L = PEV²/(2R_L). For an SSB signal driven by a single steady audio tone the envelope is flat and the output is a steady carrier at the offset frequency, so PEP equals mean power. With two equal tones the envelope varies from zero to PEV at the difference frequency, the mean power is PEP/2, and the scope shows the classic two-tone pattern used to check linearity. With speech the envelope is irregular and the mean is well below PEP. Because amplifiers distort at the envelope crest, PEP is the quantity that determines splatter and intermodulation, and it is the quantity to which transmitter specifications and power limits refer.", "worked_example": "Two-tone test, envelope crests at 316 V peak-to-peak on 50 Ω. PEV = 158 V. RMS at crest = 158 × 0.707 = 111.7 V. PEP = 111.7²/50 = 250 W. Peak × peak (option D) would give 158 × (158/50) = 499 W, double the true PEP. An average-reading wattmeter on this two-tone signal shows about 125 W.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: PEP is the product of peak voltage and peak current. Correction: that product is instantaneous peak power; PEP averages across the RF cycle, which halves it, equivalent to using the RMS voltage of the crest cycle.", "link": "Formula-sheet trainer", "mnemonic": "PEV, times point-seven, squared, over R.", "edge_cases": "Peak-reading wattmeters use a diode detector with a hold capacitor and are only approximately accurate on fast speech peaks; a scope remains the reference method, and the load must be resistive and known."}

{"core": "With a voltmeter reading the RMS RF voltage E across a known resistive load R, the power delivered is P = E²/R, the Ohm's-law power relation for a resistor; a voltmeter gives E, the load gives R, and no current measurement is needed.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "P = E · I · cos φ is the general AC power formula with power factor; it requires a current measurement and a phase angle. Into a resistive dummy load cos φ = 1 and no current is measured, so it is not the formula you use with only a voltmeter.", "why_tempting": "It is the most general and most correct-looking AC power equation."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "P = I · R is dimensionally volts, not watts (it is Ohm's law rearranged). The correct current form is P = I²R, and in any case the question specifies a voltmeter, not an ammeter.", "why_tempting": "It resembles both Ohm's law and the I²R power formula, missing only the square."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "P = E · I/R has units of amperes squared times ohms over ohms, i.e. not watts; it is a garbled mixture of P = EI and P = E²/R.", "why_tempting": "It contains all three familiar symbols and looks like a legitimate rearrangement."}], "concept": "The three equivalent power expressions for a resistor are P = E · I, P = I²R and P = E²/R, obtained by substituting Ohm's law into P = EI. Which one you use is dictated by which quantities you can measure: a voltmeter across a known load gives E and R, so P = E²/R. For RF this is the basis of the RF voltmeter plus dummy-load method, and E must be the RMS value of the RF voltage. An RF probe is typically a peak detector whose output is scaled by 0.707 so that the meter reads RMS for a sine; if instead you read peak with a scope, convert first (E_rms = 0.707 · E_p) or use P = E_p²/(2R). The dummy load must be resistive and its value known accurately, since any error in R passes straight into the power, and any reactance makes E²/R overstate real power because voltage and current are then not in phase. The same formula, evaluated at the envelope crest, becomes the PEP formula of the neighbouring questions.", "worked_example": "An RF voltmeter reads 70.7 V RMS across a 50 Ω dummy load. P = 70.7²/50 = 4998/50 ≈ 100 W. Check via the other forms: I = E/R = 1.414 A, P = EI = 70.7 × 1.414 = 100 W, P = I²R = 2.0 × 50 = 100 W. If the load were 0.5 Ω high at 50.5 Ω, the computed power would drop 1% to 99 W, showing how directly load accuracy matters.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: measuring power always requires measuring both voltage and current. Correction: with a known resistance, voltage alone suffices through P = E²/R; the resistor plays the role of the ammeter.", "link": "Ohm's Law & Power", "mnemonic": "Volts squared over ohms: the voltmeter-and-dummy-load formula.", "edge_cases": "At VHF and above the voltmeter probe's own capacitance and lead inductance can perturb the reading; a directional wattmeter or a calibrated attenuator plus power sensor is usually more trustworthy than a probe above 30 MHz."}

{"core": "PEP is the RF-cycle-average power at the envelope crest. The RMS over that cycle is 0.707 · PEV, and power is RMS squared over the load, so PEP = (0.707 · PEV)(0.707 · PEV)/R_L = PEV²/(2R_L).", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "V_p²/R_L is the instantaneous peak power of the RF cycle, twice the cycle average; it omits the 1/2 (the 0.707 squared) that converts peak to RMS.", "why_tempting": "P = V²/R is correct in form, and substituting the peak voltage feels natural when the quantity of interest is a peak power."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Multiplying by R_L instead of dividing gives units of V²·Ω, not watts; it is Ohm's-law algebra inverted.", "why_tempting": "A quick glance at a product of three symbols can pass as a power formula."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Applying 1.414 to PEV converts a value that is already peak as if it were RMS, giving (1.414 · PEV)²/R_L = 2PEV²/R_L, four times the correct PEP.", "why_tempting": "1.414 and 0.707 are paired on the formula sheet and the direction of the conversion is easily reversed."}], "concept": "At any instant of the modulation the RF carrier is a sine whose peak equals the envelope voltage. Averaging v²/R_L over one RF cycle gives V_env²/(2R_L), because the mean of sin² is one half; equivalently the RMS is V_env/√2 = 0.707 · V_env and P = V_rms²/R_L. PEP is this value at the maximum envelope, PEV. So PEP = (0.707 · PEV)²/R_L, which is what option A writes out as a product. If the scope is read peak-to-peak, V_pp = 2 · PEV and the formula becomes PEP = V_pp²/(8R_L). The constants 0.707², 1/2, and 1/8 are all the same physics appearing in different units of measurement. The formula applies to any envelope shape, since it only uses the crest; for a steady carrier it gives the same number as a wattmeter, for two-tone twice the wattmeter, and for speech several times the wattmeter. Measurement requires a resistive load whose value is known and a scope with enough bandwidth to show the RF cycle faithfully.", "worked_example": "PEV = 100 V across R_L = 50 Ω. 0.707 × 100 = 70.7 V RMS at the crest. 70.7 × 70.7 = 5000 V². 5000/50 = 100 W PEP. Compare the wrong forms: V_p²/R_L = 10 000/50 = 200 W (double); (1.414 · 100)²/50 = 20 000/50 = 400 W (quadruple); V_p² · R_L = 500 000 V²·Ω, not a power. Starting from the scope's 200 V_pp instead: 200²/(8 × 50) = 40 000/400 = 100 W, the same.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: because PEP is a peak quantity, use the peak voltage in V²/R. Correction: the peak refers to the envelope; within that crest RF cycle the power is still averaged, so the RMS of the cycle (0.707 × PEV) is what gets squared.", "link": "Formula-sheet trainer", "mnemonic": "PEP = (0.707 PEV)² / R; the 0.707 is non-negotiable.", "edge_cases": "The 0.707 factor presumes the RF cycle at the crest is a clean sine. A heavily flat-topped (clipped) transmitter produces a non-sinusoidal RF cycle with RMS closer to the peak, so a scope-based PEP slightly understates the true power while the harmonic content rises."}

{"core": "200 V peak-to-peak is 100 V peak; the RMS over the crest cycle is 100 × 0.707 = 70.7 V, and 70.7²/50 = 100 W PEP. The one-step form is PEP = V_pp²/(8R_L) = 40 000/400 = 100 W.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "400 W is 200²/(2 × 50), which treats the peak-to-peak reading as if it were peak; the halving step was skipped, inflating the answer by four.", "why_tempting": "The formula PEP = V_p²/(2R) is correct, but the scope number was substituted without converting peak-to-peak to peak."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "1000 W would require about 632 V peak-to-peak into 50 Ω; it does not follow from 200 V by any legitimate conversion.", "why_tempting": "It is a round kilowatt and the sort of number legal-limit discussions make familiar."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "200 W is 100²/50, the instantaneous peak power of the crest cycle: the peak-to-peak was halved correctly but the 0.707 RMS factor was not applied, so it is twice the PEP.", "why_tempting": "Halving the scope reading feels like the whole conversion, and V²/R then gives a clean number."}], "concept": "PEP is the RF-cycle-average power at the envelope crest. The scope gives the crest peak-to-peak voltage V_pp; the peak is V_pp/2; the RMS of that sine cycle is (V_pp/2)/√2; and P = V_rms²/R_L. Combining: PEP = (V_pp/(2√2))²/R_L = V_pp²/(8R_L). The 8 collects a 4 from halving-then-squaring and a 2 from the RMS conversion squared. Two common errors map directly onto two distractors: skipping the halving gives 4 × PEP, and skipping the 0.707 gives 2 × PEP. Keeping the 8 in the formula removes both opportunities for error, and a sanity anchor helps: 200 V_pp into 50 Ω is 100 W, 283 V_pp is 200 W, 400 V_pp is 400 W, 632 V_pp is 1 kW. Because power scales with the square of voltage, doubling V_pp quadruples PEP; that is why the 400 V_pp question in this subsection gives 400 W.", "worked_example": "V_pp = 200 V, R_L = 50 Ω. Long way: V_p = 100 V; V_rms = 100 × 0.7071 = 70.71 V; P = 70.71²/50 = 5000/50 = 100 W. Short way: 200² = 40 000; 8 × 50 = 400; 40 000/400 = 100 W. Current check: I_rms = 70.71/50 = 1.414 A; P = I²R = 2.0 × 50 = 100 W.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: PEP is the scope voltage squared over the load, with maybe a factor of 2 somewhere. Correction: from a peak-to-peak reading the divisor is 8R_L, which accounts for both halving to peak and converting peak to RMS.", "link": "Formula-sheet trainer", "mnemonic": "Scope to PEP: V_pp squared over eight R.", "edge_cases": "If the scope is AC-coupled and the trace clips at the screen edge, the crest is lost and PEP is understated; set the sensitivity so the whole envelope fits, and confirm the 50 Ω load is resistive at the operating frequency."}

{"core": "500 V peak-to-peak → 250 V peak → 250 × 0.707 = 176.8 V RMS at the crest → 176.8²/50 = 625 W PEP. Equivalently PEP = V_pp²/(8R_L) = 250 000/400 = 625 W.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "500 W does not follow from 500 V_pp into 50 Ω by any correct chain; it merely echoes the voltage number.", "why_tempting": "The coincidence of 500 V and a round 500 W invites a reflexive match."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "1250 W is 250²/50, the instantaneous peak power of the crest cycle; the halving to peak was done but the 0.707 RMS factor was omitted, doubling the PEP.", "why_tempting": "V²/R with the peak voltage is the most common single slip in this family of questions."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "2500 W is 500²/(2 × 50), which uses the peak-to-peak value where the peak belongs; the result is four times the true PEP.", "why_tempting": "The formula V_p²/(2R) is right, but the scope reading was plugged in without halving."}], "concept": "The oscilloscope shows the full RF excursion, trough to crest, at the envelope maximum: V_pp. Peak is V_pp/2 and the RMS of that sinusoidal RF cycle is V_pp/(2√2). PEP, the cycle-average power at the crest, is V_rms²/R_L = V_pp²/(8R_L). Because PEP is quadratic in voltage, a 2.5× increase in V_pp (200 V to 500 V) raises PEP by 6.25× (100 W to 625 W), and the distractor set is built from the two classic omissions: miss the 0.707 and you get 2× (1250 W); miss the halving and you get 4× (2500 W). Keeping the eight in the denominator prevents both. Note what the 625 W figure means physically: at the crest the RF current is 176.8/50 = 3.54 A RMS, 5 A peak, and the instantaneous power swings between zero and 1250 W within each RF cycle; 625 W is the average over that cycle.", "worked_example": "V_pp = 500 V, R_L = 50 Ω. V_p = 250 V. V_rms = 250 × 0.7071 = 176.8 V. V_rms² = 31 250 V². PEP = 31 250/50 = 625 W. One-step: 500² = 250 000; 8 × 50 = 400; 250 000/400 = 625 W. Reverse check: 625 W into 50 Ω needs V_rms = √(625 × 50) = 176.8 V, V_p = 250 V, V_pp = 500 V.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: peak power uses the peak voltage in V²/R. Correction: PEP averages over the RF cycle at the crest, so the voltage to square is the RMS of that cycle, 0.707 × the peak.", "link": "Formula-sheet trainer", "mnemonic": "V_pp squared, over eight R: 500 squared over 400 is 625.", "edge_cases": "A 10× scope probe rated for 300 V may be overstressed by a 500 V_pp signal, and the probe's capacitance can detune the measurement at higher HF; use a proper high-voltage RF probe or a calibrated sampling tap."}

{"core": "An unmodulated carrier has a constant envelope, so the power averaged over one RF cycle is the same at every instant; the crest value and the long-term mean coincide, and PEP equals the average reading, 1060 W.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "530 W would be half the average; the factor of one half belongs to the two-tone SSB case (mean = PEP/2) applied in reverse, or to confusing peak and RMS. For a steady carrier there is no such ratio.", "why_tempting": "Students remember that PEP and average differ by a factor of two in some SSB test and apply it the wrong way."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "2120 W doubles the average, which would be correct for a two-tone SSB signal whose wattmeter reads 1060 W, but not for an unmodulated carrier whose envelope never varies.", "why_tempting": "The two-tone rule PEP = 2 × mean is a familiar formula-sheet fact and the stem mentions PEP and average together."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "1500 W has no computational relationship to 1060 W; it is a decoy drawn from a round legal-limit-style number.", "why_tempting": "It is a familiar power figure from regulatory discussions and sounds like a cap."}], "concept": "PEP is the average power over one RF cycle at the maximum of the modulation envelope. Mean power is the average over a span long compared with the modulation period. The two differ only when the envelope varies. For an unmodulated carrier, CW key-down, or FM (constant envelope by nature), the envelope is flat, every RF cycle delivers the same energy, and PEP = mean. For AM at 100% modulation the envelope swings from 0 to 2 × carrier voltage, so PEP = 4 × carrier power and mean = 1.5 × carrier power. For a two-tone SSB test, mean = PEP/2. For speech SSB the mean is typically PEP/3 to PEP/5. The ratio PEP/mean is a property of the envelope shape, and an average-reading wattmeter (thermal, or diode-detector with a slow meter) reports the mean; to extract PEP from it you must know the modulation. The question tests whether you recognise that for a steady carrier there is nothing to convert.", "worked_example": "Wattmeter reads 1060 W on a steady carrier into 50 Ω. Envelope is flat, so PEP = 1060 W. The scope would show V_rms = √(1060 × 50) = 230 V, V_pp = 651 V, constant. Now key the same transmitter with two-tone SSB adjusted so the scope crests still reach 651 V_pp: PEP stays 1060 W, but the wattmeter drops to 530 W. With speech it would drop further, to perhaps 250 to 350 W, while PEP remains 1060 W.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: PEP is always larger than average power. Correction: PEP equals average whenever the envelope is constant; it exceeds the average only when modulation makes the envelope vary.", "link": "section 5", "mnemonic": "Flat envelope: PEP and average are the same number.", "edge_cases": "A peak-reading wattmeter on a steady carrier reads the same as its average mode; if the two modes disagree on a supposedly unmodulated carrier, the carrier has hum or ripple modulation and the envelope is not actually flat."}

{"core": "400 V peak-to-peak → 200 V peak → 200 × 0.707 = 141.4 V RMS at the crest → 141.4²/50 = 400 W PEP.
