The trace closes on itself only when the frequencies are in a rational ratio f_y / f_x = p/q in lowest terms, and over one full period the y signal reaches its maximum p times while the x signal reaches its maximum q times. Each y maximum is a point where the figure touches the top edge, so there are p loops along the top (tangent to a horizontal line); each x maximum touches a side, so there are q loops along a side (tangent to a vertical line). The counting rule is therefore f_y / f_x = (tangencies to a horizontal line) / (tangencies to a vertical line). For 150/100 = 3/2: three loops along the top edge, two along the side. Historically this was the way to measure an unknown audio frequency against a calibrated oscillator before counters were affordable, and it is still a vivid demonstration of phase and frequency relationships. If the ratio is irrational or slowly drifting, the figure rotates or writhes, which itself is a sensitive indicator of a tiny frequency difference.", "worked_example": "f_x = 100 Hz, f_y = 150 Hz. Reduce: 150/100 = 3/2, so p = 3, q = 2. Common period: 1/50 s = 20 ms, during which x completes 2 cycles and y completes 3. Count: y hits its peak 3 times → 3 loops touching the top, x hits its peak 2 times → 2 loops touching the side. Check with the rule: f_y = f_x × (3/2) = 150 Hz. Consistent.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the loop count equals the frequency in hertz. Correction: loop counts give only the reduced ratio of the two frequencies, so you always need one known frequency to find the other.", "link": "section 3", "mnemonic": "Horizontal-line touches over vertical-line touches equals f_Y over f_X.", "edge_cases": "The phrase horizontal loops versus vertical loops is used inconsistently in textbooks; what is unambiguous is the tangency count, so always think in terms of how many times the figure touches the top edge versus the side edge."}

{"core": "An oscilloscope's horizontal axis is time, set by the sweep (time base), and its vertical axis is voltage, set by the deflection amplifiers. Measurement accuracy depends on the time base's accuracy, frequency response on the amplifiers' bandwidth, and faithful reproduction on their linearity, which is exactly the combination in option B.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "There is no such specification as tube face voltage increments; the graticule is a passive grid. Deflection amplifier voltages in isolation are not a limiting factor either; their linearity and bandwidth are.", "why_tempting": "The words tube face and deflection sound like genuine CRT terminology."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Output impedance of the deflection amplifier is an internal design detail that does not appear as a user-facing accuracy limit, and tube face frequency increments is meaningless.", "why_tempting": "Impedance is a real concern at the probe input, and the option borrows that credibility."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Time base accuracy and linearity are legitimate, but the option omits the deflection amplifiers entirely, which are what set frequency response, and substitutes a non-existent tube face specification.", "why_tempting": "Two-thirds of the option is correct, and linearity of the sweep is a genuine CRT-era concern."}], "concept": "A scope converts an input voltage to vertical deflection through an attenuator and vertical amplifier, and converts elapsed time to horizontal deflection through a sweep generator (the time base). Amplitude accuracy is therefore the gain accuracy and linearity of the vertical chain; a nonlinear amplifier compresses large signals and distorts the shape you are trying to inspect. Frequency response is the vertical amplifier's −3 dB bandwidth; a signal component above it is attenuated, and fast edges are slowed with rise time ≈ 0.35 / BW, so a 100 MHz scope cannot show a 3.5 ns edge faithfully. Time measurements depend on the sweep: its calibration accuracy sets how well you read period and frequency from the graticule, and its linearity determines whether a division near the left of the screen represents the same time as one near the right. On a digital scope the same ideas map to the ADC's sample clock accuracy (time base), the front-end bandwidth, and the ADC's linearity. Stability, meaning the ability to hold a steady display, depends on the trigger circuit and time base. None of this involves the screen face itself.", "worked_example": "A 20 MHz scope is used to look at a 10 MHz square wave. The 3rd harmonic at 30 MHz is already past the bandwidth, the 5th at 50 MHz is well down, so the display shows a rounded, nearly sinusoidal wave: a frequency-response limit, not a property of the signal. Measuring its period with a time base that is 3 percent off gives 103 ns instead of 100 ns, a time base accuracy limit. Swapping to a 200 MHz scope with a 0.5 percent time base fixes both.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the CRT screen or display contributes measurement error. Correction: the display only shows what the amplifiers and time base produce; accuracy and response are set by those analog chains.", "link": "section 3", "mnemonic": "Vertical amp for volts and bandwidth, time base for time.", "edge_cases": "The probe is part of the vertical chain: a 10:1 probe's own bandwidth and its compensation adjustment can degrade frequency response and amplitude accuracy below what the scope alone would deliver."}

{"core": "To see higher-frequency signals you need the vertical amplifier to pass them without attenuation and the horizontal sweep to run fast enough to spread a few cycles across the screen. Widening the vertical amplifier's bandwidth and raising the available horizontal sweep rate is what extends a scope's usable frequency range.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A crystal time base improves time accuracy, not bandwidth, and there is no vertical sweep rate; sweep is a horizontal function.", "why_tempting": "Crystal references improve accuracy in counters, and the option swaps the axis labels in a way that sounds symmetrical."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Again vertical sweep rate is not a scope parameter, and the horizontal amplifier's response only matters in X-Y mode; in normal operation it just has to follow the sweep ramp.", "why_tempting": "The option mentions amplifier frequency response, which is the right idea attached to the wrong axis."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Triggered sweep gives a stable display and a crystal time base gives accurate timing; neither raises the highest frequency the vertical channel can display.", "why_tempting": "Both are genuine scope improvements, just for stability and accuracy rather than frequency response."}], "concept": "The vertical channel carries the signal: attenuator, preamplifier, delay line and output amplifier driving the deflection plates or ADC. Its −3 dB bandwidth is the specification called scope bandwidth, and it fixes the fastest rise time the scope can show, t_r ≈ 0.35 / BW. To improve it you need faster transistors, lower stray capacitance, and careful compensation, which is why bandwidth is the main price driver. The horizontal channel in normal mode carries a linear ramp from the sweep generator; the faster the ramp (fewer ns per division), the more a high-frequency signal is spread out so individual cycles are resolvable. A scope with a 1 GHz vertical amplifier but a slowest sweep of 1 μs per division would show a 500 MHz signal as a solid band of 500 cycles per division, so sweep rate must keep pace with bandwidth. Triggering only stabilizes the picture and a crystal only improves the timing calibration; neither moves the frequency ceiling. On a DSO the equivalent of sweep rate is the sample rate, which must be at least a few times the bandwidth to avoid aliasing.", "worked_example": "A 20 MHz scope with a fastest sweep of 0.1 μs per division displays a 20 MHz sine as 2 cycles per division, barely usable, and attenuates it 3 dB. Upgrading to a 100 MHz vertical amplifier alone makes the amplitude right but the sweep still crowds the cycles; adding a 10 ns per division sweep shows 0.2 cycles per division, a clean waveform with 5 divisions per cycle. Both changes together are the improvement the question describes.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the scope's time base determines what frequencies it can display. Correction: the vertical amplifier bandwidth limits the frequencies that reach the screen; the sweep only needs to be fast enough to spread them out.", "link": "section 3", "edge_cases": "On a digital scope, insufficient sample rate causes aliasing, where a 95 MHz signal sampled at 100 MS/s appears as 5 MHz; the bandwidth spec means little unless the sample rate is also adequate."}

{"core": "A dual-trace oscilloscope has two independent vertical channels sharing one time base, so the input and output waveforms of a circuit can be displayed one above the other against the same time axis, which is the straightforward way to compare them.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Putting the input on X and the output on Y gives a Lissajous figure or transfer curve, not two waveforms versus time; you can infer phase and linearity but you cannot see either waveform's shape.", "why_tempting": "X-Y mode is a legitimate two-signal technique, so it looks like a valid way to view two signals."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "The Z axis is intensity modulation; applying the output there would merely brighten or blank the trace and would not display its waveform.", "why_tempting": "Z input sounds like a third display dimension that could hold a second signal."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "This is the same X-Y arrangement as option A with the roles swapped; it still does not show both waveforms as functions of time.", "why_tempting": "Reversing the axes seems like it might change something, but the mode is identical."}], "concept": "A dual-trace scope uses an electronic switch to multiplex two vertical preamplifiers into one deflection system, either alternating full sweeps between channels (alternate mode, good at fast sweeps) or chopping rapidly between them within one sweep (chop mode, good at slow sweeps). Both channels are plotted against the same time base and the same trigger, so time relationships between the traces are preserved: you can read the delay through an amplifier, compare input and output amplitude for gain, see clipping or slew limiting appear on the output, and watch a logic signal's cause and effect. This is fundamentally different from X-Y mode, which plots one signal against the other with time eliminated; X-Y is the right tool for a transfer characteristic or a phase measurement via Lissajous ellipse, but not for seeing waveform shape. The Z input modulates beam intensity and is used for blanking or marking, not for displaying signals. Modern DSOs have four or more channels, but the principle is the same shared time base.", "worked_example": "Probe an audio amplifier: channel 1 on the input, 100 mV peak sine at 1 kHz; channel 2 on the output. The output shows 2.0 V peak with flattened tops, a gain of 26 dB and visible clipping. Switching to X-Y mode would show a diagonal line that bends over at the ends, confirming clipping, but you would no longer see that the clipping is asymmetric and only on the positive half, which the dual-trace view revealed immediately.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: any mode that accepts two signals lets you watch both signals. Correction: only dual-trace (multi-channel) mode shows two waveforms against time; X-Y mode shows their relationship with time removed.", "link": "section 3", "edge_cases": "In alternate mode at slow sweeps the two traces are drawn on different sweeps, so a one-shot event may appear on only one channel; use chop mode or a DSO's simultaneous sampling for single events."}

{"core": "An oscilloscope displays amplitude versus time. An FM signal's amplitude is constant, so the deviation, which is the swing in instantaneous frequency, is invisible on the trace; it requires a discriminator or deviation meter to convert frequency swing into something measurable. Frequency, DC level and complex-waveform amplitude are all readable directly.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Frequency is read directly by measuring one period against the calibrated time base and taking the reciprocal, or by a Lissajous comparison.", "why_tempting": "A counter is more precise, so a learner may conclude the scope cannot do it at all."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "With DC coupling a scope shows a steady deflection proportional to DC voltage; measuring DC and DC offsets is routine.", "why_tempting": "Scopes are thought of as AC waveform instruments, and AC coupling does hide DC, which may be remembered as a limitation of the whole instrument."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Displaying complex waveforms and reading their peak, peak-to-peak and envelope amplitudes is the scope's primary strength; a meter would only give an ambiguous average or RMS.", "why_tempting": "Complex sounds like it should be hard, but complexity of shape is exactly what the scope handles better than any meter."}], "concept": "The scope plots v(t). From that you can extract period (and hence frequency), amplitude in any form (peak, peak-to-peak, by graticule), DC offset (with DC coupling), rise time, duty cycle and envelope shape. What it cannot extract directly is information encoded in the instantaneous frequency of a constant-amplitude carrier. An FM signal v(t) = A cos(2π f_c t + β sin(2π f_m t)) has constant envelope A; on a scope at RF it is a solid band whose width never changes with modulation. The deviation Δf = β f_m lives in the phase argument, and to see it you need a frequency discriminator (slope detector, ratio detector, PLL) that converts frequency to voltage, or a spectrum analyzer that shows the Bessel sidebands, or a deviation meter that combines a discriminator with a calibrated peak detector. An indirect scope method does exist, the Bessel null, where a specific modulation index makes the carrier vanish, but that needs a spectrum display or a very selective receiver, not a plain time-domain trace, which is why the exam says the scope cannot determine deviation directly.", "worked_example": "Feed a 146.52 MHz FM transmitter's sampled output to a 200 MHz scope. With no modulation: a steady band 2 V peak-to-peak. Speak into the mic: the band is still 2 V peak-to-peak and visually identical, even though the frequency is swinging ±5 kHz. The scope shows no change because the information is in frequency, not amplitude. Route the same signal through a receiver's discriminator and the scope now shows the recovered audio, whose amplitude is proportional to deviation once the discriminator is calibrated.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: because frequency can be measured on a scope, frequency deviation can too. Correction: measuring a fixed frequency from a period is easy, but a 5 kHz swing on a 146 MHz carrier is a 0.003 percent change in period, invisible on the trace; deviation needs a frequency-to-voltage converter first.", "link": "section 5", "mnemonic": "Scopes see amplitude; FM hides in frequency.", "edge_cases": "Some digital scopes include a demodulation or FFT function; with FFT you can observe the Bessel sideband structure and infer deviation, but that is a spectrum measurement performed by the scope, not a direct reading from the time-domain trace."}

{"core": "Bandwidth is the vertical channel's −3 dB frequency: the highest frequency at which a sine wave is still displayed at roughly its true amplitude. Above it, signals are progressively attenuated, so the bandwidth defines the highest frequency the scope can usefully display.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Gain compression is a large-signal nonlinearity in the amplifier; it is unrelated to the small-signal frequency limit that defines bandwidth.", "why_tempting": "Both are vertical amplifier limitations, so they may seem connected."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Screen persistence is how long the phosphor keeps glowing after the beam passes; it affects how slow or single-shot events look, not the amplifier's frequency response.", "why_tempting": "Persistence does relate to seeing fast transients on an analog screen, which loosely ties it to high-frequency display in a learner's mind."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Time base accuracy governs how precisely time intervals are read on the horizontal axis; it has no effect on the vertical channel's frequency response.", "why_tempting": "Both bandwidth and time base involve frequency or time, and the earlier counter questions stressed the time base."}], "concept": "The vertical amplifier is a chain of stages each with some roll-off; its overall response falls at high frequency, and the −3 dB point (amplitude down to 70.7 percent, power to half) is the quoted bandwidth. The related figure is rise time, t_r ≈ 0.35 / BW for a Gaussian response, so a 100 MHz scope shows a step with about 3.5 ns rise even if the real edge is instantaneous. A rule of thumb for faithful display is to have bandwidth at least three to five times the fundamental for sine waves, and bandwidth covering at least the 5th harmonic for square waves. At exactly the bandwidth frequency the displayed amplitude is 30 percent low, so a 100 MHz sine on a 100 MHz scope reads 0.707 of its true value; the measured amplitude is only accurate well below the bandwidth. The spec is a property of the signal path (and the probe, which has its own bandwidth and can reduce the system figure), not of the display or sweep. In the DSO era bandwidth is paired with sample rate; both must be adequate.", "worked_example": "A 50 MHz scope measures a 50 MHz sine of true amplitude 1.00 V peak: displays about 0.71 V. The same scope on a 10 MHz sine: response is essentially flat, displays 0.99 V. On a 20 MHz square wave the 3rd harmonic (60 MHz) is already attenuated, so the corners round off and overshoot is hidden. These are all consequences of the single number, 50 MHz bandwidth.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a scope displays anything up to its bandwidth with full accuracy and nothing above it. Correction: the response rolls off gradually; amplitude error is already 30 percent at the bandwidth figure, so accurate measurement needs a wide margin.", "link": "Decibel Converter", "mnemonic": "Rise time ≈ 0.35 over bandwidth.", "edge_cases": "Many scopes with a bandwidth-limit switch (often 20 MHz) use it to reduce noise on low-frequency measurements; forgetting it is on makes a fast signal look slow and small."}

{"core": "With equal frequencies on X and Y, the Lissajous figure is an ellipse whose shape encodes phase. At 0 degrees the two signals rise and fall together, collapsing the ellipse to a straight diagonal line with positive slope; at 180 degrees they are opposed and the line has negative slope. Either way a straight diagonal line means 0 or 180 degrees.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A circle appears at exactly 90 degrees phase difference with equal amplitudes, when x = sin and y = cos trace x² + y² = 1.", "why_tempting": "The circle is the most memorable Lissajous shape and is often the first one taught, so it is easy to attach it to the wrong angle."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "A horizontal straight line means there is no vertical signal at all (Y input zero or disconnected), not a phase relationship between two signals.", "why_tempting": "A straight line is the right idea, but the orientation matters; a horizontal line carries no Y information."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "An ellipse indicates some phase difference other than 0, 90 or 180 degrees (or 90 degrees with unequal amplitudes); it is the general case, not the special case asked for.", "why_tempting": "Most phase angles produce an ellipse, so it feels like the safe answer."}], "concept": "In X-Y mode with x = A sin(ωt) and y = B sin(ωt + φ), eliminating t gives the ellipse equation x²/A² − 2xy cos(φ)/(AB) + y²/B² = sin²(φ). When φ = 0 the right side is zero and the equation factors to y = (B/A) x, a straight line rising to the right. When φ = 180 degrees, cos φ = −1 and the line is y = −(B/A) x, falling to the right. When φ = 90 degrees the cross term vanishes and the figure is an upright ellipse, a circle if A = B. For any other φ the ellipse is tilted. The phase can be read numerically from the ellipse: if the figure crosses the y axis at ±y_0 and its maximum y excursion is Y_max, then sin φ = y_0 / Y_max. This is how phase shift through a filter, amplifier or feedline was measured before dual-trace scopes with cursors, and it remains a quick way to check that two oscillators are locked (a stationary figure) or slightly off (a slowly rotating figure whose rotation rate equals the frequency difference).", "worked_example": "Apply the same 1 kHz signal to both X and Y: a 45-degree line with equal gains, confirming 0 degrees. Insert an RC network with f_c = 1 kHz in the Y path: the trace opens into a tilted ellipse; y_0 / Y_max measures 0.707, so sin φ = 0.707 and φ = 45 degrees, exactly the expected RC phase shift at its corner frequency. Now put an inverting amplifier in the Y path with no RC: the line flips to a negative slope, indicating 180 degrees.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a straight line on an X-Y display means one input is missing. Correction: a diagonal line means both inputs are present and exactly in or out of phase; only a horizontal or vertical line means one input is absent.", "link": "section 3", "mnemonic": "Line for lined up (0 or 180), circle for quarter turn (90).", "edge_cases": "The sin φ = y_0 / Y_max method cannot distinguish φ from 180 − φ; use the slope sign of the ellipse's major axis to tell which quadrant you are in."}

{"core": "For a Lissajous figure, f_vertical / f_horizontal equals the number of loops along a horizontal edge divided by the number along a vertical edge. Two loops horizontally and five loops vertically give f_v / 100 kHz = 2/5, so the unknown vertical frequency is 40 kHz.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "20 kHz would require a 1:5 ratio, meaning one loop along the top and five along the side; the figure has two along the top.", "why_tempting": "Dividing 100 kHz by the larger count of 5 is a natural first guess that ignores the second count."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "50 kHz corresponds to a 1:2 ratio, which would show one loop along the top and two along the side, not two and five.", "why_tempting": "Halving the known frequency is a tempting shortcut when one of the counts is 2."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "30 kHz would be a 3:10 ratio and would display three loops along the top and ten along the side.", "why_tempting": "It sits between the plausible answers and could arise from an arithmetic slip such as 100 × (5 − 2)/10."}], "concept": "In X-Y mode with f_x on the horizontal plates and f_y on the vertical, the closed figure repeats every common period. During that period the vertical signal reaches its peak p times, so the figure touches a horizontal line drawn along the top p times, and the horizontal signal peaks q times, touching a vertical line along one side q times. Since the two signals have the same elapsed time, f_y / f_x = p / q. The question's phrasing, five loops vertically and two loops horizontally, means five tangencies along a vertical edge (the x signal peaked five times) and two along a horizontal edge (the y signal peaked twice). Therefore f_y = f_x × 2/5. The important discipline is to attach each count to the axis of the signal whose peaks it represents: touches along the top count y peaks, touches along the side count x peaks. Compare with the 100 Hz / 150 Hz question in this section, where the unknown was higher than the reference and the ratio was 3:2; here it is lower, 2:5.", "worked_example": "f_x = 100 kHz (horizontal). Tangencies: horizontal edge 2, vertical edge 5. f_y = f_x × (horizontal tangencies / vertical tangencies) = 100 kHz × 2/5 = 40 kHz. Check: common period = 1/20 kHz = 50 μs; in 50 μs the 100 kHz signal completes 5 cycles (5 side touches) and the 40 kHz signal completes 2 cycles (2 top touches). Consistent.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the loop count on an axis gives that axis's frequency directly. Correction: the counts give a ratio, and the count along a given edge belongs to the signal on the other axis, since the figure touches the top each time the vertical signal peaks.", "link": "section 3", "mnemonic": "Top touches over side touches equals f_Y over f_X.", "edge_cases": "Ratios beyond about 10:1 produce figures too dense to count on an analog screen; in practice the method is limited to small integer ratios, and a frequency counter is used otherwise."}

{"core": "A 10:1 probe is a compensated attenuator: its 9 MΩ series resistor is paralleled by a small trimmer capacitor that must equal one-ninth of the scope's input capacitance plus cable capacitance for flat response. Input capacitance differs between scopes (and even between channels), so the probe must be re-compensated every time it is moved to a different oscilloscope.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Compensation is a property of the probe-scope pair, not of the signal; a sine wave at low frequency would not even reveal miscompensation. Square waves are used to check it because they contain high-frequency content.", "why_tempting": "Sine waves are the generic test signal and the learner may assume compensation relates to measuring them."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The high-value series resistor is already present inside the probe (9 MΩ for 10:1); compensation is the adjustment of the capacitor across it, not the addition of a resistor.", "why_tempting": "The probe does contain a large series resistance, so this option sounds like a description of the probe's construction."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A properly compensated probe is flat across all frequencies, so a varying signal frequency needs no readjustment; miscompensation would show up as frequency-dependent gain, which is the thing being avoided.", "why_tempting": "It inverts the logic: compensation makes the probe frequency-independent, so the learner may think it must be redone whenever frequency changes."}], "concept": "The probe tip resistor R_p = 9 MΩ and the scope input R_s = 1 MΩ form a 10:1 resistive divider at DC. At high frequency the scope's input capacitance C_s (typically 15 to 25 pF) plus the cable's capacitance shunt R_s, so the divider becomes capacitive and the ratio changes unless a compensating capacitor C_p across R_p satisfies R_p C_p = R_s C_s, that is, C_p = C_s / 9. When this holds the divider ratio is 10:1 at every frequency and the probe's time constants cancel. If C_p is too small, high frequencies are over-attenuated and a square wave shows rounded corners (undershoot); too large and they are under-attenuated, giving spikes (overshoot). Because C_s varies from scope to scope, and the cable is part of the probe, the only reliable practice is to connect the probe to the scope's calibrator square-wave output and trim C_p for flat tops each time the probe meets a new scope or channel. Input impedance of the compensated probe is 10 MΩ in parallel with about 10 to 15 pF, which is why 10:1 probes load circuits less than 1:1 probes do.", "worked_example": "Scope A input: 1 MΩ, 20 pF. Required C_p = 20/9 ≈ 2.2 pF; the probe is trimmed and shows a flat 1 kHz square wave. Move the same probe to scope B with 1 MΩ, 30 pF input: now C_p should be 3.3 pF, but it is still 2.2 pF, so the high-frequency divider ratio is 1 + 30/2.2 ≈ 14.6:1 instead of 10:1. The square-wave corners sag by about 30 percent and a 5 MHz sine reads 0.7 of true amplitude until the trimmer is readjusted.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a probe is a passive cable with a fixed 10:1 ratio. Correction: the ratio is only 10:1 at all frequencies when the probe capacitor matches the particular scope's input capacitance, so the probe is calibrated to a scope, not universal.", "link": "Series / Parallel R & C", "mnemonic": "New scope, new square wave, new trim.", "edge_cases": "At VHF the probe's ground lead inductance resonates with its tip capacitance and causes ringing that compensation cannot fix; use the shortest possible ground spring or a 50 Ω transmission-line probe instead."}

{"core": "An oscilloscope shows the RF envelope directly, revealing CW keying shape (clicks from too-fast edges), SSB flat-topping and splatter from over-drive, and hum or parasitics on the envelope. No other listed instrument shows the waveform itself, so the scope is the best choice for signal-quality checks.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A sidetone monitor lets you hear your own keying but is generated locally from the key line; it tells you nothing about the RF envelope's shape or the SSB waveform.", "why_tempting": "It is called a monitor and is used while transmitting CW, so it sounds like a quality-check tool."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A signal tracer and audio amplifier let you hear a demodulated signal; they can reveal gross distortion but cannot show the envelope shape, rise times or flat-topping with any precision.", "why_tempting": "Hearing the signal is a form of quality check, and these are legitimate troubleshooting tools."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "A field-strength meter indicates relative RF level and is useful for antenna checks; it averages the envelope and shows nothing about waveform quality.", "why_tempting": "It responds to the transmitted signal, so it seems like a monitoring device for what is actually going out."}], "concept": "Signal quality for CW means the shape of the keying envelope: rise and fall times of roughly 3 to 5 ms give a clean signal, while sub-millisecond edges spread energy into key clicks hundreds of hertz away. For SSB the concern is linearity: an over-driven linear stage flattens the envelope peaks, producing intermodulation products that splatter into adjacent channels. Both are envelope-domain phenomena, and the scope is the envelope instrument. Feed a sample of the transmitter output to the vertical input, set a sweep appropriate to the keying or voice rate, and the trace shows the RF band whose outline is the envelope. For a quantitative SSB check, the two-tone test applies two equal non-harmonically related audio tones; the ideal envelope is a clean series of sinusoidal lobes meeting at zero, and any flattening at the top or filling at the troughs indicates non-linearity. A trapezoid pattern, obtained by feeding audio to X and RF to Y, gives a linearity plot where straight edges mean a linear amplifier. The scope must have enough bandwidth to pass the carrier frequency, which is why HF transmitters are easy to check and VHF needs a faster scope or a sampling detector.", "worked_example": "Two-tone test of an SSB exciter at 14.2 MHz: 700 Hz and 1900 Hz tones at equal level. On a 100 MHz scope the envelope shows clean lobes crossing at zero with rounded peaks of 60 V peak-to-peak, meaning 60²/(8 × 50) = 9 W PEP into 50 Ω. Raise the mic gain by 6 dB: the lobe tops flatten and the crossing points no longer reach zero, a classic flat-topping signature. Back the drive off until the tops are round again; that is the maximum clean PEP.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: if the signal sounds good on the sidetone or on a nearby receiver, it is clean. Correction: audio monitoring cannot reveal envelope edge speed or peak flattening, which are what generate interference; only the envelope itself, seen on a scope, shows them.", "link": "section 5", "edge_cases": "A scope shows the envelope but not the spectrum; a modern spectrum display or SDR waterfall is better for quantifying splatter in dB, and ideally both are used together."}

{"core": "The scope must see the transmitter's actual RF output, but at a safe level and without disturbing the load, so the correct source is the final RF output sampled through a coupler, pickup loop, or high-impedance capacitive divider. Only that path shows the true envelope the antenna receives.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A nearby receiving antenna delivers an uncontrolled level that may overload the scope or be too small, picks up other signals, and adds multipath and antenna response that are not part of the transmitter's quality.", "why_tempting": "It seems convenient and non-invasive, and a field-strength style pickup does respond to the signal."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "A monitoring receiver's IF has passed through its own filters, AGC and possibly its own distortion; the envelope seen there reflects the receiver as much as the transmitter, and AGC in particular flattens the envelope you are trying to inspect.", "why_tempting": "An IF output is a tidy, controlled signal, and monitor receivers are real pieces of station equipment."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "The audio input is the signal before the modulator and power amplifier; it says nothing about linearity or keying shape in the RF stages, which is where the problems arise.", "why_tempting": "Checking the input is reasonable troubleshooting practice, but it cannot reveal faults downstream."}], "concept": "A sampling device is any arrangement that diverts a tiny, known fraction of the transmitter output to the instrument while the full power continues into the antenna or dummy load. Common forms: a directional coupler with 20 to 40 dB of coupling, a short pickup loop near the feedline, a capacitive divider across the line (a few picofarads in series with the scope's input), or a resistive tap across a dummy load. The sample preserves the envelope shape exactly because it is linear and frequency-flat over the band of interest, and it keeps the voltage within the scope's input rating; 100 W into 50 Ω is 100 V RMS, 283 V peak-to-peak, which a 10:1 probe can handle directly on a dummy load but which would be unsafe and mismatched if the scope were placed in the line. Any path through a receiver inserts filters, gain control and demodulation that change the envelope. A random antenna pickup inserts the channel and whatever else is on the air. The audio input is upstream of everything that can go wrong. The principle generalizes: measure a system at its output, sampled linearly, not through another nonlinear or band-limited system.", "worked_example": "Transmitter running 100 W into a dummy load, 70.7 V RMS across it. A 30 dB directional coupler delivers 100 mW to the scope (a 1000:1 power ratio, 31.6:1 voltage ratio), about 2.24 V RMS or 6.3 V peak-to-peak into 50 Ω at the scope, comfortably within range. Key the two-tone test and the envelope lobes appear at 6.3 V peak-to-peak; flat-topping would be visible as truncated lobes at exactly the same sampled scale.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the cleanest-looking signal source (an IF or audio line) gives the best measurement. Correction: the measurement must be of the transmitter's real output; convenience sources that have passed through other stages or the air show something other than the transmitter.", "link": "section 5", "edge_cases": "A capacitive divider's ratio changes with frequency unless its series capacitor is small compared with the scope's input capacitance; for consistent levels across bands a resistive or directional coupler sample is preferable."}

{"core": "At full scale the meter needs 40 μA through its 96 Ω coil, which drops 3.84 mV. The shunt must pass the remaining 960 μA at that same 3.84 mV, so R_shunt = 3.84 mV / 960 μA = 4 Ω.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "24 Ω would carry only 160 μA at 3.84 mV, giving a total of 200 μA full scale, not 1 mA; it results from dividing 96 by 4 instead of by 24.", "why_tempting": "96/4 = 24 looks like a tidy relationship between the given resistance and the multiplication factor."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "16 Ω would pass 240 μA, for a 280 μA full-scale range. It corresponds to dividing 96 by 6, a factor that appears nowhere in the problem.", "why_tempting": "It is a plausible-looking divisor of 96 that produces a small round number."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "40 Ω would pass only 96 μA, giving 136 μA full scale. It simply reuses the meter's 40 μA figure as a resistance.", "why_tempting": "The number 40 is in the question, and number-matching is a common exam reflex."}], "concept": "A moving-coil meter is a current instrument with a fixed full-scale current I_m and coil resistance R_m. To read a larger current I_total, a shunt resistor R_sh is placed in parallel so that most of the current bypasses the coil. Both branches see the same voltage, V = I_m R_m, so the shunt current is I_total − I_m and R_sh = I_m R_m / (I_total − I_m). Equivalently, with multiplication factor n = I_total / I_m, R_sh = R_m / (n − 1). Here n = 1 mA / 40 μA = 25, so R_sh = 96 / 24 = 4 Ω. The combined meter resistance becomes R_m in parallel with R_sh, which is 3.84 Ω, and its burden voltage at full scale is still only 3.84 mV, so the ammeter inserts very little resistance into the circuit, which is what you want. The same voltage-equality reasoning underlies voltmeter multipliers (series) and the loading concept in the next questions. Precision shunts are usually four-terminal to keep contact resistance out of the measurement.", "worked_example": "I_m = 40 μA, R_m = 96 Ω. V_fs = 40e-6 × 96 = 3.84e-3 V. Desired I_total = 1 mA = 1000 μA, so I_shunt = 1000 − 40 = 960 μA. R_sh = 3.84e-3 / 960e-6 = 4.00 Ω. Check via R_m / (n − 1): n = 1000/40 = 25, 96/24 = 4 Ω. Parallel combination: (96 × 4)/(96 + 4) = 3.84 Ω.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the shunt resistance is the meter resistance divided by the multiplication factor. Correction: it is divided by (n − 1), because the coil itself still carries one part of the n parts of current.", "link": "Series / Parallel R & C", "mnemonic": "Shunt = R_m over (n minus one).", "edge_cases": "At 4 Ω, a few milliohms of lead or switch contact resistance in series with the shunt is a measurable error; for high-current ranges with sub-ohm shunts this becomes the dominant accuracy limit, hence Kelvin connections."}

{"core": "A voltmeter is a current meter with a series multiplier chosen so that full-scale voltage drives exactly full-scale current. For 20 V and 1 mA the total resistance must be 20 V / 1 mA = 20 000 Ω; subtracting the 0.5 Ω coil leaves a series resistance of 19 999.5 Ω.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A shunt in parallel lowers the meter's resistance and extends its current range; it cannot make the instrument respond to 20 V, and 19.5 Ω would simply bypass almost all the current around the coil.", "why_tempting": "19.5 is 20 minus 0.5, so the subtraction looks like the right one applied to the wrong configuration."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "1 999.5 Ω in series would produce full scale at 2 V, not 20 V; it is off by a factor of ten.", "why_tempting": "A decimal-place slip in 20 / 0.001 gives 2000 instead of 20 000."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "The resistance value is right but the configuration is wrong: a 19 999.5 Ω shunt in parallel with 0.5 Ω would have no appreciable effect and the meter would still be a 1 mA ammeter.", "why_tempting": "Getting the arithmetic right and then choosing shunt because the earlier question was about shunts."}], "concept": "The moving-coil movement responds to current, I = V / R_total. To make full scale correspond to a chosen voltage V_fs, add a multiplier resistor R_mult in series so that R_total = R_m + R_mult = V_fs / I_m. Rearranged, R_mult = V_fs / I_m − R_m. The sensitivity of the resulting voltmeter is 1 / I_m ohms per volt, here 1000 Ω/V, and its input resistance on any range is sensitivity times the range, 20 kΩ on the 20 V range. That input resistance is what loads the circuit being measured; a 1000 Ω/V meter across a high-impedance divider will pull the voltage down noticeably, which is why 20 kΩ/V analog meters and 10 MΩ digital meters are preferred for electronics work. The contrast with the shunt problem is the configuration: series for voltage (add resistance, limit current), parallel for current (bypass current, keep voltage drop tiny). The coil resistance appears in both formulas but matters very little for voltmeters, as here where it is 0.0025 percent of the total.", "worked_example": "I_m = 1 mA, R_m = 0.5 Ω, V_fs = 20 V. R_total = 20 / 0.001 = 20 000 Ω. R_mult = 20 000 − 0.5 = 19 999.5 Ω. Check: 20 V / 20 000 Ω = 1.000 mA, full scale. Sensitivity = 1 / 0.001 = 1000 Ω/V, so on a 20 V range the meter presents 20 kΩ to the circuit.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: extending a meter's range always means adding a shunt. Correction: shunts extend current ranges; voltage ranges require a series multiplier, because the movement must be prevented from drawing more than its full-scale current at the higher voltage.", "link": "Ohm's Law & Power", "mnemonic": "Series for volts, shunt for amps.", "edge_cases": "For AC voltage ranges a rectifier precedes the movement and the multiplier is calibrated for sine-wave RMS; the same meter on a non-sinusoidal waveform reads incorrectly because the calibration assumes a specific form factor."}

{"core": "A 150 V meter with 150 000 Ω internal resistance draws 1 mA at full scale, so it is a 1000 Ω/V instrument. For 750 V full scale at the same 1 mA the total resistance must be 750 000 Ω; the added multiplier is 750 000 − 150 000 = 600 000 Ω.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "1 500 Ω would add only 1 percent to the existing resistance and move full scale from 150 V to 151.5 V; it is far too small.", "why_tempting": "It reuses the digits 150 with a smaller exponent, a classic order-of-magnitude slip."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "750 000 Ω is the total resistance required, not the added multiplier; the existing 150 000 Ω must be subtracted.", "why_tempting": "It is the correct intermediate result, and forgetting the subtraction is the most common error in this problem."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "1 200 000 Ω added to 150 000 Ω gives 1 350 000 Ω total, which corresponds to a 1350 V range, not 750 V.", "why_tempting": "It could come from multiplying the existing resistance by (5 + 3) or similar confusion of the range ratio."}], "concept": "The voltmeter's full-scale current is fixed by its movement and is found from the existing range: I_fs = V_range / R_internal = 150 / 150 000 = 1 mA. Any new range V_new needs a total resistance R_new = V_new / I_fs, and the multiplier to add in series is R_add = R_new − R_internal. A shortcut: since the resistance scales linearly with range, R_add = R_internal × (V_new / V_old − 1) = 150 kΩ × (5 − 1) = 600 kΩ. The sensitivity in ohms per volt stays 1000 Ω/V on every range, which means the loading on the circuit grows with the range selected: 750 kΩ on the 750 V range. This question tests the same series-multiplier principle as the 20 V problem, but starting from an existing voltmeter rather than a bare movement, so the internal resistance is already large and must not be ignored. Multipliers for high voltage ranges must also be rated for the voltage drop across them: 600 V across the added resistor here, which rules out ordinary quarter-watt parts on voltage rating grounds even though the power is only 0.6 W.", "worked_example": "I_fs = 150 V / 150 000 Ω = 1 mA. For 750 V: R_total = 750 V / 1 mA = 750 000 Ω. R_add = 750 000 − 150 000 = 600 000 Ω. Shortcut: ratio 750/150 = 5, R_add = 150 kΩ × (5 − 1) = 600 kΩ. Power in the multiplier at full scale: I² R = (1e-3)² × 600e3 = 0.6 W, with 600 V across it, so use a series string of high-voltage-rated resistors.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the multiplier equals the new range divided by the full-scale current. Correction: that gives the total resistance; the multiplier is the total minus the meter's existing internal resistance.", "link": "Ohm's Law & Power", "mnemonic": "Total first, then subtract what is already there.", "edge_cases": "At 750 V the voltage coefficient and leakage of the multiplier resistors matter, and a single carbon resistor can change value by a percent or more under that stress; precision high-voltage multipliers use several series metal-film parts."}

{"core": "Sensitivity describes how little current is needed to drive the meter to full scale; a 50 μA movement is more sensitive than a 1 mA movement. It is therefore an expression of the full-scale deflection current, option A.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "The coil resistance affects burden voltage and the shunt calculation, but two meters with the same resistance can have very different full-scale currents, so resistance does not define sensitivity.", "why_tempting": "Resistance appears in every meter calculation and feels like a fundamental property."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Loading effect is a consequence of the meter's resistance (for ammeters) or ohms-per-volt (for voltmeters) in a particular circuit; it is related to sensitivity but is a different quantity that depends on the circuit as well as the meter.", "why_tempting": "A sensitive meter loads less, so loading and sensitivity are correlated in practice."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "The shunt is an external component chosen for a given range; the movement's sensitivity exists before any shunt is added and does not change when a different shunt is fitted.", "why_tempting": "Shunts determine the ammeter's range, and range can be confused with sensitivity."}], "concept": "A moving-coil movement produces torque proportional to coil current, balanced by a spring; full-scale deflection occurs at a specific current I_fs set by the magnet strength, number of turns and spring stiffness. Sensitivity is this I_fs, quoted inversely: smaller full-scale current means higher sensitivity. For voltmeters the same property is expressed as ohms per volt, 1 / I_fs, so a 50 μA movement gives 20 000 Ω/V and a 1 mA movement gives 1000 Ω/V. High sensitivity is valuable because it lets you build low-range current meters directly and high-input-resistance voltmeters, both of which disturb the circuit under test less. The earlier questions in this subsection all start from I_fs: the shunt formula R_sh = I_fs R_m / (I_total − I_fs) and the multiplier formula R_mult = V_fs / I_fs − R_m. Loading is the downstream consequence: an ammeter's burden is I R_m, a voltmeter's loading is set by its ohms per volt times range in parallel with the circuit. Digital meters sidestep the issue with a fixed 10 MΩ input, but the analog concept is still tested because it explains why instruments disturb what they measure.", "worked_example": "Two movements: 40 μA/96 Ω and 1 mA/0.5 Ω. Sensitivity as voltmeters: 1/40e-6 = 25 000 Ω/V versus 1/1e-3 = 1000 Ω/V. Measuring the midpoint of two 100 kΩ resistors across 10 V (expected 5 V, source resistance 50 kΩ) on a 10 V range: the 25 kΩ/V meter presents 250 kΩ and reads 5 × 250/(250 + 50) = 4.17 V; the 1 kΩ/V meter presents 10 kΩ and reads 5 × 10/(10 + 50) = 0.83 V. The more sensitive movement, the one with the smaller full-scale current, loads far less.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a sensitive meter is one with low resistance. Correction: sensitivity is the smallness of the full-scale current; resistance is a separate parameter, and a sensitive movement often has a higher coil resistance because it has more turns of finer wire.", "link": "Ohm's Law & Power", "mnemonic": "Smaller full-scale current, more sensitive.", "edge_cases": "Very sensitive movements (10 to 50 μA) are fragile and easily damaged by overload; meter protection diodes across the coil are standard but can themselves introduce slight non-linearity near full scale."}

{"core": "Ohms-per-volt sensitivity is simply the reciprocal of the current that drives the meter movement to full scale: I_fs = 1 / S. For 20 kΩ/V that is 1 / 20 000 = 50 μA, so the instrument is built around a 50 microampere movement.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A 1 mA movement gives 1 / 0.001 A = 1000 Ω/V, twenty times less sensitive than the 20 kΩ/V stated.", "why_tempting": "1 mA is the classic cheap meter movement and 1000 Ω/V is the number many learners remember from Basic-era multimeters."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A 50 mA movement would give only 1 / 0.05 = 20 Ω/V; the question says 20 kΩ/V, a factor of 1000 away.", "why_tempting": "The digits 50 and 20 both appear; the unit prefix was dropped, which turns milliamps into microamps and 20 Ω/V into 20 kΩ/V."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "100 mA full scale corresponds to 1 / 0.1 = 10 Ω/V, a very insensitive movement that would load any circuit heavily.", "why_tempting": "Treating 20 kΩ/V as 20 000 and dividing by a convenient round number instead of taking the reciprocal."}], "concept": "A moving-coil voltmeter is a current meter with a series multiplier resistor. On any range, the total resistance is chosen so that the rated voltage pushes exactly the full-scale current through the movement: R_total = V_range / I_fs. Dividing both sides by V_range gives R_total / V_range = 1 / I_fs, which is the ohms-per-volt figure. It is constant across all ranges because every range is designed around the same movement current. The sensitivity therefore tells you two things at once: how little current the meter steals from the circuit under test, and how much the meter loads a high-impedance node. A 20 kΩ/V meter on its 10 V range presents 200 kΩ to the circuit; a 1000 Ω/V meter on the same range presents only 10 kΩ, which can badly drag down a divider made of 100 kΩ resistors. This is why FET-input and digital meters, with 10 MΩ or more input resistance regardless of range, replaced the ohms-per-volt specification for most work.", "worked_example": "Sensitivity S = 20 kΩ/V = 20 000 Ω/V. Full-scale current I_fs = 1 / S = 1 / 20 000 Ω/V = 5 × 10⁻⁵ A = 50 μA. Check the other direction: on the 50 V range the multiplier chain totals 50 V × 20 000 Ω/V = 1 MΩ, and 50 V / 1 MΩ = 50 μA, exactly full scale.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a higher ohms-per-volt number means a meter that needs more current to deflect. Correction: ohms-per-volt is the reciprocal of full-scale current, so a larger number means a more sensitive movement that draws less current and loads the circuit less.", "link": "Ohm's Law & Power", "mnemonic": "Ohms per volt is one over amps: big Ω/V, tiny μA.", "edge_cases": "The ohms-per-volt figure applies to DC ranges. AC ranges on an analog meter include a rectifier and are usually specified with a lower sensitivity, and the loading also becomes frequency dependent."}

{"core": "Sensitivity is total meter resistance divided by the full-scale voltage of the range in use: 150 000 Ω / 150 V = 1000 Ω/V. That corresponds to a 1 mA movement.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "100 000 Ω/V would require a 10 μA movement and a total resistance of 15 MΩ on the 150 V range, not 150 kΩ.", "why_tempting": "It looks like a plausible high-sensitivity figure and shares the leading digits with 150 000."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "10 000 Ω/V implies a 100 μA movement; on the 150 V range the series resistance would have to be 1.5 MΩ, ten times the stated value.", "why_tempting": "A slip of one decade when dividing 150 000 by 150."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "150 Ω/V would mean a 6.7 mA movement and a total resistance of only 22.5 kΩ on this range.", "why_tempting": "The number 150 appears twice in the question, so it is easy to just repeat it."}], "concept": "On a given range a moving-coil voltmeter is a current movement in series with a multiplier, and the design rule is R_total = V_range / I_fs. Rearranged, S = R_total / V_range = 1 / I_fs, in ohms per volt. The important consequence is that the input resistance of an analog meter scales with the range selected: R_in = S × V_range. A 1000 Ω/V meter is 150 kΩ on the 150 V range but only 10 kΩ on the 10 V range, so it loads low-voltage, high-impedance circuits much more than the big number suggests. When you measure a node fed through a resistance comparable to R_in, the meter and the source resistance form a divider and the reading drops; the error is R_source / (R_source + R_in). A learner strong in electronics should think of the meter as a shunt resistor that is briefly added to the circuit, and compute whether that shunt matters before trusting the reading.", "worked_example": "S = R_total / V_range = 150 000 Ω / 150 V = 1000 Ω/V. Full-scale current: I_fs = 1 / 1000 Ω/V = 1 mA. Loading check: measuring a 12 V node fed through 47 kΩ on the 15 V range gives R_in = 1000 × 15 = 15 kΩ, so the meter reads 12 × 15 / (47 + 15) = 2.9 V, a wildly low result caused purely by meter loading.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the input resistance of an analog voltmeter is a single fixed number like a DMM. Correction: the fixed number is ohms per volt; actual input resistance is that figure multiplied by the full-scale voltage of the selected range, and it falls on the lower ranges.", "link": "Ohm's Law & Power", "edge_cases": "A DMM or FET voltmeter has a fixed input resistance (typically 10 MΩ) on every range, so the ohms-per-volt idea does not apply and the loading error is usually negligible unless you probe multi-megohm nodes."}

{"core": "An ammeter movement has a small fixed full-scale current, so to read larger currents a low-value shunt resistor is placed in parallel with it. The shunt carries most of the current and the movement sees only a known fraction set by the current-divider ratio.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "The coil inductance has no bearing on DC current division; at DC an inductor is just its winding resistance.", "why_tempting": "Meter movements are coils, so inductance sounds like a relevant internal property."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Resonance is an AC phenomenon between L and C; it cannot change how a DC current splits between two paths.", "why_tempting": "Resonance is a strong Advanced-syllabus theme and the word internal makes it sound like a meter adjustment."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A series resistance only adds to the total loop resistance and reduces the current; it does not divert any current around the movement, so the meter still saturates at its original full-scale value.", "why_tempting": "Series resistance is exactly how a voltmeter range is extended, and learners cross the two rules."}], "concept": "A moving-coil meter is a current-measuring device with a full-scale current I_fs and an internal resistance R_m. To extend the range to I_total, a shunt R_sh is connected across the movement so that the two paths share the same voltage drop: I_fs × R_m = (I_total − I_fs) × R_sh. Solving, R_sh = I_fs × R_m / (I_total − I_fs). Because I_total is usually much larger than I_fs, R_sh ends up very small, often a milliohm-range strip of manganin whose resistance is stable with temperature. The combined meter-plus-shunt presents a very low resistance to the circuit, which is exactly what an ammeter should do to avoid disturbing the current it measures. The duality with the voltmeter case is worth internalizing: voltmeters want high resistance and get it with series multipliers; ammeters want low resistance and get it with parallel shunts. The same movement is the heart of both.", "worked_example": "Movement: I_fs = 1 mA, R_m = 50 Ω. Desired range: 1 A. R_sh = 0.001 A × 50 Ω / (1 A − 0.001 A) = 0.05 / 0.999 ≈ 0.05 Ω. At full scale the shunt carries 0.999 A, the drop across both paths is 0.001 × 50 = 50 mV, and the parallel combination is about 0.05 Ω, a near-ideal ammeter.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: adding resistance to a meter always extends its range. Correction: it depends on where it goes; a series resistor extends a voltmeter, a parallel shunt extends an ammeter, and putting one where the other belongs just ruins the reading.", "link": "Series / Parallel R & C", "mnemonic": "Shunt the amps, series the volts.", "edge_cases": "External shunts are usually specified by their drop at rated current (for example 50 mV at 100 A) and must be connected with separate sense leads so the lead resistance does not add to the tiny shunt value."}

{"core": "Switching to a higher voltage range inserts more multiplier resistance in series with the movement so that the larger input voltage still drives only the full-scale current. R_total = V_range / I_fs grows in proportion to the range.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Reducing a parallel resistance would divert more current around the movement, which is the ammeter range technique, and it would lower the input resistance, the opposite of what a voltmeter wants on a high range.", "why_tempting": "It mixes the shunt rule from ammeters with the vague idea that something should get smaller on a bigger range."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Adding a parallel path cannot limit the current through the movement when a larger voltage is applied; the movement would still be overdriven.", "why_tempting": "Parallel resistance is how ammeter ranges work, and learners swap the two rules."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Less series resistance would let more current flow for the same voltage, so the movement would peg at a lower voltage; that is what the lower range does.", "why_tempting": "An inverted sense of the relationship, perhaps thinking a higher range should be easier on the meter."}], "concept": "A multimeter on its voltage ranges is a current movement behind a chain of series multiplier resistors selected by the range switch. The required total is R_total = V_range / I_fs, so each higher range taps further along the chain, adding resistance. Because the full-scale current is the same on every range, the sensitivity in ohms per volt is constant and the input resistance climbs with the range: R_in = S × V_range. Physically, the extra series resistance drops the surplus voltage, leaving the same small full-scale voltage across the coil, typically tens of millivolts. On the current ranges the switch does the opposite job, selecting shunts in parallel. On resistance ranges it adds an internal battery and series limiting resistors. Understanding the switch as a resistor-network selector explains both why an analog meter loads circuits more on low ranges and why a meter set to a current range across a voltage source is a short circuit.", "worked_example": "Movement: 50 μA, 2 kΩ. On the 10 V range the chain must total 10 / 50 × 10⁻⁶ = 200 kΩ, so the multiplier is 198 kΩ. Switching to the 100 V range requires 2 MΩ total, so the switch adds another 1.8 MΩ in series. The coil still sees 50 μA × 2 kΩ = 0.1 V at full scale on both ranges.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a higher range means the meter tolerates more current. Correction: the movement always receives the same full-scale current; the range switch adds series resistance so that a larger applied voltage produces that same current.", "link": "Ohm's Law & Power", "mnemonic": "More volts, more series ohms.", "edge_cases": "Autoranging DMMs do the same thing electronically with a precision divider and an ADC, and present a constant input resistance (often 10 MΩ) because the divider's top resistor is in the input path on every range."}

{"core": "The range of an ammeter is increased by a shunt resistor in parallel with the meter movement, so the extra current bypasses the coil and only a known fraction reaches it. The meter and shunt together still sit in series with the circuit under test.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Resistance in series with the circuit under test changes the current you are trying to measure instead of changing how much of it the meter can handle.", "why_tempting": "Confuses modifying the measurement with modifying the instrument."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A resistor across the circuit under test alters the load and draws extra current from the source; it does nothing to protect or re-scale the meter movement.", "why_tempting": "Parallel is the right word but applied to the wrong element."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Series resistance with the meter raises its resistance and limits current through the whole loop, but the movement still pegs at its original full-scale current, so the range is unchanged.", "why_tempting": "Series resistance extends a voltmeter, and the two rules get crossed."}], "concept": "The current divider rule governs the shunt: with the movement (R_m) and shunt (R_sh) in parallel, the movement carries I_m = I_total × R_sh / (R_m + R_sh). Setting I_m equal to the full-scale current I_fs and solving for the shunt gives R_sh = I_fs × R_m / (I_total − I_fs). The ratio I_total / I_fs is the range multiplication factor, and for large factors R_sh ≈ R_m / factor. A good ammeter has very low total resistance so its insertion into a circuit barely changes the current; the shunt helps here too, because the parallel combination is lower than R_m alone. The shunt must dissipate nearly all of the power, I² × R_sh, and must hold its value as it warms, which is why manganin or constantan is used. This question is the dual of the voltmeter multiplier: the same movement becomes a voltmeter with series resistance and a wider-range ammeter with parallel resistance.", "worked_example": "Movement: I_fs = 100 μA, R_m = 1 kΩ. Target range 10 mA. R_sh = 100 × 10⁻⁶ × 1000 / (0.01 − 0.0001) = 0.1 / 0.0099 ≈ 10.1 Ω. Check: full-scale drop across the parallel pair is 100 μA × 1 kΩ = 0.1 V; shunt current is 0.1 V / 10.1 Ω ≈ 9.9 mA; total 10 mA. The ammeter now presents about 10 Ω to the circuit instead of 1 kΩ.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the shunt goes across the circuit being measured. Correction: the shunt goes across the meter movement only; the meter-plus-shunt pair is then inserted in series with the circuit like any ammeter.", "link": "Series / Parallel R & C", "edge_cases": "Multi-range ammeters often use a ring (Ayrton) shunt so that switch contact resistance never appears in series with the low-value shunt, which would otherwise introduce large errors during range changes."}

{"core": "The transmitter's output power is defined at its output connector, so the wattmeter belongs there. Any further along the line, feedline attenuation and mismatch loss reduce the forward power, and reflected power complicates the reading.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "At the feed point the meter reads what reaches the antenna after feedline loss and any matching losses, which is a measurement of delivered power, not transmitter output.", "why_tempting": "Delivered power to the antenna is what ultimately matters for signal strength, so it feels like the honest place to measure."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "A half-wavelength of line repeats the load impedance but still has attenuation and does nothing to make a directional coupler read more accurately; the reading simply includes that half-wave of loss.", "why_tempting": "Half-wave impedance repetition is a real transmission-line property and sounds like a calibration trick."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Measuring a half-wave back from the antenna sees the antenna impedance repeated but gives a reading degraded by the rest of the line between there and the transmitter.", "why_tempting": "Same half-wave repetition idea, applied at the antenna end instead."}], "concept": "A directional wattmeter samples forward and reflected waves with a coupler calibrated for a specific characteristic impedance. Its reading at any point equals forward power minus reflected power there, which is the net power flowing past that point. Along a lossy line the forward wave decays by the matched-line attenuation, and reflections add further loss, so the net power at the antenna is always less than at the transmitter: P_antenna = P_tx × 10^(−loss_dB / 10) when the line is matched, and lower still with SWR. If you want to characterize the transmitter, you must sample before those losses. There is a second, subtler reason: the coupler assumes the line is near 50 Ω. Right at the transmitter the rig's output network presents a 50 Ω source and, if the system is matched, the meter sees 50 Ω and reads correctly. If you place the meter where standing waves exist, the local impedance can differ from 50 Ω and some meters mis-read. Measuring at the connector, with a short jumper, minimizes both effects.", "worked_example": "Transmitter set to 100 W into 30 m of coax with 1.5 dB loss at 146 MHz. At the transmitter connector the meter reads 100 W forward. At the antenna end the forward power is 100 × 10^(−0.15) ≈ 70.8 W. If the antenna has an SWR of 2:1, the reflection coefficient is 1/3, reflected power is 70.8 × (1/3)² ≈ 7.9 W, and the net power into the antenna is about 63 W. Only the first reading describes the transmitter.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a wattmeter reads the same anywhere along a coax line. Correction: a wattmeter reads the net power passing its own location, which drops with every metre of lossy line and with mismatch, so transmitter output is measured only at the transmitter.", "link": "SWR & Impedance Match", "edge_cases": "For a very short, low-loss line at HF the difference may be a few percent, but at VHF/UHF with long runs of small coax the loss can exceed half the power, so the location of the meter changes the answer dramatically."}

{"core": "Amateur transmitters, coax, and accessories are standardized on a 50 Ω characteristic impedance, and RF wattmeters are calibrated with couplers and detectors designed for that line, so they read correctly only in a 50 Ω system.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "100 Ω is not a standard coax or station impedance; a 50 Ω calibrated coupler placed in a 100 Ω system would see a 2:1 mismatch and read incorrectly.", "why_tempting": "It is a round number and appears in balanced-line discussions and some antenna impedances."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "300 Ω is the impedance of twin-lead television ribbon and some balanced antenna feeds, not of the coaxial systems that wattmeters are built for.", "why_tempting": "300 Ω is a familiar feedline impedance from folded dipoles and TV ribbon."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "25 Ω appears when two 50 Ω loads are paralleled or at the feed point of some verticals, but it is not a system standard and no common wattmeter is calibrated for it.", "why_tempting": "It is exactly half of 50 and looks like a plausible alternative standard."}], "concept": "A through-line wattmeter contains a directional coupler, usually a small current transformer and a capacitive voltage sample, arranged so that the two samples cancel for a wave travelling in one direction and add for the other. The cancellation happens only when the ratio of voltage to current in the line equals the design impedance, V / I = Z_0 = 50 Ω. In a 50 Ω system a matched load produces zero reflected reading and the forward reading equals true power, P = V² / Z_0. If the same coupler is inserted into a line of different impedance, the voltage and current samples no longer balance, so the forward and reflected scales are both wrong even if that other line is perfectly matched internally. The 50 Ω choice itself is a compromise: for air-dielectric coax, minimum attenuation falls near 77 Ω and maximum power handling near 30 Ω, and 50 Ω sits between them. Once transmitters, coax, connectors, and test gear converged on that value, every measurement instrument followed.", "worked_example": "A matched 50 Ω load at 100 W has V_rms = √(P × Z_0) = √(100 × 50) ≈ 70.7 V and I_rms = √(P / Z_0) = √(100 / 50) ≈ 1.41 A, so V / I = 50 Ω and the coupler's samples cancel in the reverse direction. Put the same meter in a 300 Ω matched system at 100 W: V_rms = √(100 × 300) ≈ 173 V, I_rms ≈ 0.58 A, V / I = 300 Ω. The coupler's voltage sample is now 2.45 times larger relative to the current sample, so the reverse port no longer nulls and the meter reports a large false SWR and wrong power.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a wattmeter measures power the way a voltmeter measures volts, independent of the system around it. Correction: a directional wattmeter is an impedance-referenced instrument; its calibration assumes 50 Ω and is only valid in a 50 Ω line.", "link": "SWR & Impedance Match", "edge_cases": "Some laboratory instruments and television gear are built for 75 Ω; a 75 Ω meter in a 50 Ω system will indicate an SWR of 1.5:1 into a perfect 50 Ω load, which is a calibration artifact rather than a real mismatch."}

{"core": "A bridge rectifier conducts on both half-cycles and uses the entire secondary winding each time, so its average output is 0.9 × V_rms of the whole secondary. Half-wave gives 0.45 × V_rms, and a centre-tap circuit only uses half the winding at a time, so for the same total secondary voltage it also averages 0.45 × V_rms.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Half-wave rectification passes only one polarity, leaving a gap for half of every cycle, so the average is only V_pk / π ≈ 0.45 × V_rms.", "why_tempting": "It is the simplest circuit and some learners assume fewer diodes means less voltage drop and therefore more output."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "There is no such thing as a quarter-wave rectifier; a diode either conducts or blocks for a half-cycle, so this is a nonsense term.", "why_tempting": "Quarter-wave is a familiar antenna term and the pattern half, quarter, full looks like a series."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The centre-tap circuit alternates between the two halves of the secondary, so each conducting diode sees only half the total secondary voltage; its average output for the same total secondary voltage is 0.45 × V_rms, half that of the bridge.", "why_tempting": "It is a full-wave circuit and gives the same 120 Hz ripple as the bridge, so learners assume the output voltage must also be the same."}], "concept": "The average (DC) value of a rectified sine depends on how much of the waveform is used and how much of the transformer winding each conducting path spans. For a sine of peak V_pk, the full-wave rectified average is 2 × V_pk / π ≈ 0.637 × V_pk ≈ 0.9 × V_rms; the half-wave average is V_pk / π ≈ 0.45 × V_rms. The bridge applies the entire secondary across the load through two diodes on every half-cycle, so it earns the full 0.9 × V_rms. The centre-tap circuit is also full-wave in time, but each half-cycle uses only one half of the winding; if the whole secondary is V_rms end to end, each half is V_rms / 2 and the average is 0.9 × V_rms / 2 = 0.45 × V_rms. The trade-off is diode drops: the bridge has two diodes in series on each path, the centre-tap only one, which matters at low voltages but not at the hundreds of volts the question implies. With a capacitor input filter the no-load output rises toward V_pk for all of these, but the ranking by available voltage stays the same.", "worked_example": "Secondary 100 V_rms end to end, resistive load, no filter. Half-wave: V_avg = 0.45 × 100 = 45 V. Full-wave centre-tap: each half is 50 V_rms, V_avg = 0.9 × 50 = 45 V. Bridge: V_avg = 0.9 × 100 = 90 V. Subtracting diode drops (about 0.7 V each): half-wave ≈ 44.3 V, centre-tap ≈ 44.3 V, bridge ≈ 88.6 V. The bridge wins by a factor of two.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: all full-wave rectifiers give the same output for the same transformer. Correction: the centre-tap circuit uses only half the winding at a time, so for the same end-to-end secondary voltage the bridge delivers twice the average output.", "link": "section 4", "mnemonic": "Bridge uses the whole winding, both halves of the cycle: 0.9. Half of either gives 0.45.", "edge_cases": "If the centre-tap transformer is specified as 100-0-100 V, each half is 100 V_rms and its average output then matches a bridge on a 100 V secondary; always check whether the quoted voltage is per half or end to end."}

{"core": "With a capacitor input filter and no load, the capacitor charges to the secondary peak, 1.414 × V_rms, and holds it. On the opposite half-cycle the secondary swings to −1.414 × V_rms, so the diode sees the sum of the two: 2 × 1.414 ≈ 2.8 × V_rms.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "0.45 × V_rms is the average output of an unfiltered half-wave rectifier, not a reverse voltage; PIV is always at least the peak of the input.", "why_tempting": "0.45 is a memorized half-wave number and the question is about a half-wave supply."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "5.6 × V_rms would be four times the peak; nothing in a single-diode circuit stacks two full peaks on top of the capacitor voltage.", "why_tempting": "Doubling 2.8 again, or confusing this with the stresses in a voltage multiplier."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "1.4 × V_rms is the PIV for a half-wave rectifier with a resistive load and no capacitor, because the output falls to zero on the reverse half-cycle; the filter capacitor doubles it.", "why_tempting": "It is the peak of the AC waveform and feels like the obvious maximum voltage in the circuit."}], "concept": "Peak inverse voltage is the maximum reverse voltage the diode must block without avalanching. It is found by writing a loop equation at the instant the secondary is at its most negative: V_reverse = V_capacitor − V_secondary(min). With a capacitor input filter and little or no load current, the capacitor does not discharge between peaks, so V_capacitor ≈ +V_pk. At the negative peak V_secondary = −V_pk, so V_reverse = V_pk − (−V_pk) = 2 × V_pk = 2 × √2 × V_rms ≈ 2.83 × V_rms. Loading the supply lets the capacitor sag between peaks, which reduces the PIV slightly, but a safe design always assumes the no-load case because the supply will see it at power-up and whenever the load disconnects. The same reasoning underpins voltage doublers, which deliberately exploit the capacitor-plus-negative-peak sum.", "worked_example": "Secondary 120 V_rms, half-wave diode into a 100 μF capacitor, no load. V_pk = 120 × 1.414 ≈ 170 V, so the capacitor sits at +170 V. At the secondary's negative peak the anode is at −170 V while the cathode is at +170 V. Reverse voltage = 170 − (−170) = 340 V = 2.83 × 120. A 400 V rated diode is the minimum; 600 V gives margin for line surges.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a diode only needs to withstand the peak of the AC it rectifies. Correction: with a filter capacitor the output stays at the positive peak while the input goes to the negative peak, so the diode must block the sum, twice the peak.", "link": "section 4", "mnemonic": "Capacitor holds a peak, winding swings to a peak: the diode blocks both, 2.8 × RMS.", "edge_cases": "Transformer secondaries run higher than nameplate at light load and the mains can be 5 to 10 percent high, so the practical PIV at no load can exceed 3 × nominal V_rms; derate the diode accordingly."}

{"core": "In a centre-tap full-wave circuit the two diodes share a common cathode, so when one conducts it clamps the cathode to the peak of its half-winding while the other diode's anode sits at the negative peak of the opposite half. The reverse voltage is the full end-to-end secondary peak, 2 × √2 × V_rms(per half) ≈ 2.8 × V_rms, and it does not depend on whether a filter or load is present.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "0.636 is the ratio of average to peak for a full-wave rectified sine, a measure of output, not of the reverse voltage across a diode.", "why_tempting": "It is a famous rectifier constant and it appears in the same chapter."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "0.707 is the RMS-to-peak ratio of a sine wave; a reverse voltage below the input peak is impossible in any rectifier.", "why_tempting": "Another memorized sine-wave constant that looks like it belongs in a ratio question."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "1.4 × V_rms would be the PIV if only one half-winding's peak appeared across the diode, but the conducting diode ties the cathode to the opposite half's positive peak, adding another V_pk.", "why_tempting": "It is the correct PIV for a bridge rectifier and for an unfiltered half-wave circuit, so learners generalize it."}], "concept": "In the centre-tap circuit the two halves of the secondary are in series with the tap grounded, so their end voltages are always equal and opposite. When the top end is at +V_pk, the top diode conducts and the common cathode node is at about +V_pk (minus a diode drop). At that same instant the bottom end is at −V_pk, so the bottom diode has +V_pk on its cathode and −V_pk on its anode: reverse voltage = 2 × V_pk. This is true with a resistive load, with a choke input, or with a capacitor input, because the conducting diode always forces the common node to the peak regardless of what the load does afterward. Here V_rms refers to the voltage of one half of the secondary, the quantity normally quoted for a centre-tapped winding (for example 300-0-300 V). Compare the bridge, where each diode's reverse voltage is only one V_pk because the other diode in the same leg conducts and clamps the node; the centre-tap circuit pays for its single diode drop with double the PIV requirement.", "worked_example": "Transformer rated 250-0-250 V_rms. V_pk per half = 250 × 1.414 ≈ 354 V. When the top diode conducts, the common cathode is at +354 V and the bottom anode is at −354 V, so the bottom diode blocks 354 + 354 = 708 V ≈ 2.83 × 250. Diodes rated at 1000 V PIV are the sensible choice; 800 V leaves little margin for line surges.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: PIV only reaches twice the peak when a filter capacitor is present, as in the half-wave case. Correction: in the centre-tap circuit the second half-winding supplies the extra peak, so PIV is 2 × V_pk regardless of load or filter.", "link": "section 4", "mnemonic": "Centre-tap: one half conducts, the other half pushes back; the diode sees the whole winding.", "edge_cases": "If the transformer is specified end to end (500 V_rms total), the PIV is still about 1.4 × that total figure, which is the same 708 V; always identify which voltage the specification refers to before multiplying."}

{"core": "A bridge uses four diodes to steer current from a single, untapped secondary on both half-cycles, so it needs no centre tap. The centre-tap circuit needs the tap as the return point so that each half-winding can be used alternately with only two diodes.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "The bridge actually requires more diodes, four arranged across the winding, so it does not dispense with diodes on each leg.", "why_tempting": "The phrase diodes across each leg is a loose description of the centre-tap circuit and the two-diode count feels like something the bridge eliminates."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Both circuits produce the same pulsating 120 Hz output and both need filtering for any application that wants DC; the rectifier topology does not remove ripple.", "why_tempting": "Full-wave output looks smoother than half-wave and learners extend that to needing no filter."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "No common rectifier uses a tapped primary; the tap in the centre-tap circuit is on the secondary. The primary is simply connected across the mains in both designs.", "why_tempting": "Swapping primary for secondary is an easy mistake under exam pressure."}], "concept": "The centre-tap full-wave rectifier works by using the tap as a reference: on one half-cycle the upper half-winding drives current through the upper diode to the load and back to the tap; on the next half-cycle the lower half-winding and lower diode take over. This requires a winding with twice the voltage of the output you want and a third connection.
