The bridge instead treats the whole secondary as a floating source and uses two diodes per half-cycle to connect its momentary positive end to the load's positive rail and its negative end to the load's return. The winding is used fully on every half-cycle, so a given transformer gives twice the output voltage, and the diodes only need to block one peak rather than two. The cost is an extra pair of diodes and two forward drops per path instead of one. For low-voltage, high-current supplies the centre-tap arrangement's single diode drop can be worth the bulkier transformer; for everything else the bridge is the default.", "worked_example": "Design target: about 170 V peak DC from the mains. Centre-tap circuit: needs a 120-0-120 V secondary (240 V end to end) with two 400 V diodes. Bridge: needs a plain 120 V secondary with four 200 V diodes. Same output peak, same 120 Hz ripple, but the bridge transformer has half the secondary turns and no tap.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: full-wave rectification inherently needs a centre-tapped transformer. Correction: only the two-diode version does; the bridge achieves full-wave operation from an ordinary two-wire secondary by adding two diodes.", "link": "section 4", "mnemonic": "Two diodes, three wires. Four diodes, two wires.", "edge_cases": "In many switching supplies the opposite trade is made: a centre-tapped high-frequency secondary with two Schottky diodes is preferred precisely to avoid the second diode drop at high output currents."}

{"core": "The bridge applies the whole secondary across the load on each half-cycle, whereas the centre-tap circuit uses only one half of the winding at a time. For the same transformer, the bridge's peak and average outputs are therefore twice those of the centre-tap connection.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "The half-wave circuit uses the whole winding but only half the time; its peak equals the bridge's peak, but its average and filtered load capability are far lower, so it is not the same in any useful sense of output voltage.", "why_tempting": "Both circuits see the full secondary peak into a capacitor at no load, which can look like equal output."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "This inverts the ratio; the bridge does not use half the winding, the centre-tap circuit does.", "why_tempting": "Confusing which circuit uses half the winding."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Equal output would require the centre-tap circuit to use the full winding on each half-cycle, which it cannot do because the tap grounds the midpoint.", "why_tempting": "Both circuits are full-wave with 120 Hz ripple, so equal voltage seems natural."}], "concept": "Treat a secondary of V_rms end to end. The bridge's output peak is √2 × V_rms minus two diode drops, and its unfiltered average is 0.9 × V_rms. The centre-tap connection grounds the midpoint, so each diode delivers only √2 × (V_rms / 2) at the peak and the unfiltered average is 0.45 × V_rms. The ratio is exactly two. The flip side is the diode stress: the bridge diode blocks √2 × V_rms, while the centre-tap diode blocks the full end-to-end peak, 2 × √2 × (V_rms / 2) = √2 × V_rms, the same absolute number but twice its own output peak. The transformer utilization also differs: in a bridge the secondary carries current on every half-cycle, whereas in the centre-tap circuit each half-winding carries current only half the time, so for a given VA rating the bridge extracts more DC power. This is why designers reach for a bridge unless they specifically want the single-diode drop of the centre-tap arrangement.", "worked_example": "Transformer secondary 24-0-24 V (48 V_rms end to end). Centre-tap circuit: V_pk = 24 × 1.414 ≈ 34 V, filtered no-load output ≈ 33 V after one diode. Bridge across the full 48 V: V_pk = 48 × 1.414 ≈ 68 V, filtered no-load output ≈ 66.5 V after two diodes. The bridge delivers twice the voltage from the same iron.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the rectifier topology does not change the output voltage, only the ripple. Correction: topology determines how much of the winding is used per half-cycle, and the bridge uses all of it, doubling the output relative to the centre-tap circuit.", "link": "section 4", "edge_cases": "At output voltages of a few volts the two series diode drops of a bridge become a significant fraction of the output and the ratio falls below two; Schottky diodes or a centre-tap connection recover that loss."}

{"core": "A full-wave rectifier flips the negative half-cycles positive, producing one pulse per half-cycle, two per cycle. On 60 Hz mains that yields 120 pulses per second, so the fundamental ripple frequency is 120 Hz.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "60 Hz ripple is what a half-wave rectifier produces, one pulse per mains cycle; a full-wave circuit produces two.", "why_tempting": "The mains frequency is 60 Hz and it is natural to assume the ripple follows it directly."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "90 Hz is 1.5 times the mains frequency; no rectifier produces a non-integer multiple of its input frequency.", "why_tempting": "It sits between the two plausible values and looks like a compromise answer."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Rectification cannot produce a sub-harmonic; the output period can only be the input period or an integer fraction of it.", "why_tempting": "Confusing halving the waveform with halving the frequency."}], "concept": "Rectification is a nonlinear operation, so it generates harmonics. A half-wave rectifier passes every other half-cycle; the output repeats once per input period, so its fundamental ripple component is at f_mains and it also contains a large DC term plus harmonics at 2f, 3f and so on. A full-wave rectifier produces the absolute value of the sine, which repeats every half period; its spectrum contains DC, then components at 2f, 4f, 6f, with nothing at f or odd multiples. The lowest and largest AC component, 2f = 120 Hz on 60 Hz mains, is what the filter must attenuate, and because reactance scales with frequency, doubling the ripple frequency halves the required inductance or capacitance for the same ripple. The peak-to-peak ripple of a capacitor input filter under load is approximately ΔV ≈ I_load / (f_ripple × C), which shows the direct benefit of full-wave operation.", "worked_example": "Load 1 A, 10 000 μF capacitor. Half-wave, f_ripple = 60 Hz: ΔV ≈ 1 / (60 × 0.01) ≈ 1.67 V peak to peak. Full-wave, f_ripple = 120 Hz: ΔV ≈ 1 / (120 × 0.01) ≈ 0.83 V. Same capacitor, half the ripple, purely because there are twice as many recharge pulses per second.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: ripple frequency equals mains frequency. Correction: ripple frequency equals the number of rectified pulses per second, which is twice the mains frequency for any full-wave circuit (centre-tap or bridge).", "link": "section 4", "mnemonic": "Full-wave doubles the pulses: 60 in, 120 out.", "edge_cases": "A three-phase full-wave bridge gives 6 pulses per cycle, 360 Hz on 60 Hz mains, and much lower ripple amplitude; the general rule is f_ripple = pulses per cycle × f_mains."}

{"core": "A half-wave rectifier conducts on only one half-cycle, producing one pulse per mains cycle. On 60 Hz mains the output repeats 60 times per second, so the ripple fundamental is 60 Hz.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "90 Hz is not an integer multiple of 60 Hz and no rectifier produces it.", "why_tempting": "A number between the two memorized values that looks like it might be a trick."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "120 Hz ripple comes from a full-wave rectifier, which delivers two pulses per cycle; the half-wave circuit leaves a gap where the second pulse would be.", "why_tempting": "120 Hz is the number most often associated with power-supply hum and ripple, so it is reached for reflexively."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Dropping half the waveform does not halve the repetition rate; the surviving pulses still arrive once per full input cycle, at 60 Hz.", "why_tempting": "The word half invites halving the frequency instead of the duty."}], "concept": "The output of a half-wave rectifier is the input sine with its negative lobes removed. Its period is unchanged, one full mains cycle, because the next positive lobe arrives only after the missing negative one has passed. A Fourier view makes this concrete: the half-wave rectified sine contains a DC term of V_pk / π, a fundamental at f_mains with amplitude V_pk / 2, and even harmonics at 2f, 4f, and so on. The fundamental at 60 Hz is the dominant ripple term and it is the hardest for a filter to remove, since reactances are smallest at the lowest frequency. The gap in conduction also means the filter capacitor must hold the load for almost a full cycle between recharges, so for the same ripple a half-wave supply needs roughly twice the capacitance of a full-wave one, and the diode must deliver the entire charge in a single, narrow pulse each cycle. These are the reasons half-wave rectifiers are relegated to low-current bias and auxiliary supplies.", "worked_example": "A half-wave supply feeding 200 mA with a 2200 μF capacitor: ripple ≈ I / (f × C) = 0.2 / (60 × 0.0022) ≈ 1.5 V peak to peak at 60 Hz. The same capacitor in a full-wave circuit would see 0.2 / (120 × 0.0022) ≈ 0.76 V at 120 Hz. Listening to the output through an audio stage, the half-wave supply hums at the lower 60 Hz tone.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: all rectified supplies ripple at 120 Hz. Correction: ripple frequency is the pulse rate; half-wave gives one pulse per cycle and ripples at the mains frequency itself.", "link": "section 4", "edge_cases": "Because the half-wave circuit draws current from only one polarity, it puts a net DC component through the transformer secondary, which can partially saturate the core and increase heating; full-wave circuits avoid this."}

{"core": "A full-wave voltage doubler charges one capacitor on the positive half-cycle and a second on the negative half-cycle, then stacks the two in series. Using both halves of the AC wave gives it 120 Hz ripple and better regulation than a half-wave doubler, which charges only on one polarity.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Both types of doubler produce about 2 × V_pk at no load; the difference is in ripple and regulation, not in multiplying factor.", "why_tempting": "The word full suggests more of everything, and four times sounds like the next step in a multiplier series."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Power drawn is set by the load, not the rectifier topology; the doubler type changes efficiency only marginally through diode losses.", "why_tempting": "Full-wave circuits are more efficient in the sense of using the transformer better, which is misread as consuming less power."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Full-wave doublers are used at mains frequency in transformerless and high-voltage supplies; there is no high-frequency restriction.", "why_tempting": "Capacitor-based multipliers do work better at higher frequencies, so this option contains a grain of truth misapplied."}], "concept": "The full-wave doubler is two half-wave rectifiers of opposite polarity sharing one AC source. On the positive half-cycle, diode D1 charges C1 to +V_pk with respect to the common line; on the negative half-cycle, D2 charges C2 to V_pk the other way. C1 and C2 are in series across the output, so the no-load output is 2 × V_pk ≈ 2.83 × V_rms, and each capacitor is topped up once per cycle, 180 degrees apart, giving 120 Hz ripple. The half-wave doubler (a Villard cascade) instead charges a coupling capacitor to V_pk on one half-cycle and uses it as a floating offset so the second diode charges the output capacitor to 2 × V_pk on the other half-cycle; the output capacitor is recharged only once per cycle, so ripple is at 60 Hz and regulation is poorer. In both circuits each diode must block 2 × V_pk. Doublers trade current for voltage: the output current is less than half the transformer secondary current, so they suit high-voltage, low-current loads such as tube plate supplies.", "worked_example": "Transformer secondary 350 V_rms, full-wave doubler, no load. V_pk = 350 × 1.414 ≈ 495 V. C1 charges to +495 V, C2 to 495 V of the opposite sense, and the series pair delivers about 990 V. Each diode must withstand 2 × 495 = 990 V, so 1200 V or higher rated parts are needed. With a 50 mA load and 47 μF capacitors, each capacitor sags by roughly I × t / C = 0.05 × 0.00833 / 47 × 10⁻⁶ ≈ 8.9 V between recharges; because the two capacitors recharge alternately, the output ripple is at 120 Hz.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: full-wave in a doubler means it makes more voltage than a half-wave doubler. Correction: both make about twice the peak; full-wave refers to using both half-cycles, which improves ripple frequency and regulation, not the multiplication factor.", "link": "section 4", "mnemonic": "Full-wave doubler: two capacitors, two half-cycles, stacked.", "edge_cases": "The full-wave doubler's output is not referenced to either AC line, so it cannot be cascaded into a tripler the way the half-wave Villard circuit can; multipliers beyond two stages use the half-wave ladder."}

{"core": "A rectifier diode fails in two ways: reverse breakdown if the peak inverse voltage rating is exceeded, and junction overheating if the average forward current rating is exceeded. Those two ratings therefore set the design limits in every power supply.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Diodes are not specified by average power or average voltage; the reverse stress is a peak event and the forward stress is a current-driven thermal limit.", "why_tempting": "Power and voltage are the generic ratings for resistors and capacitors, so they feel universal."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Capacitive reactance is not a rating of a rectifier, and avalanche voltage is a property of the junction rather than a limit you design to; the design rating is PIV, with avalanche being what happens when you exceed it.", "why_tempting": "Avalanche sounds like a diode failure mode and junction capacitance is a real datasheet parameter."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "A diode has no load impedance rating, and peak voltage alone ignores the direction; the limiting voltage is specifically the reverse (inverse) one.", "why_tempting": "Peak voltage is half-right and load impedance sounds like a power-supply design parameter."}], "concept": "Reverse stress: a silicon rectifier's depletion region can only support a certain field before avalanche multiplication starts. The datasheet's repetitive peak reverse voltage V_RRM is the PIV limit; exceeding it drives large reverse current and, without current limiting, destroys the junction thermally. In rectifier circuits the PIV requirement ranges from 1.4 × V_rms (bridge, or unfiltered half-wave) to 2.8 × V_rms (capacitor-filtered half-wave, centre-tap full-wave) and higher in multipliers. Forward stress: the junction dissipates V_F × I_F, and the average forward current I_F(AV) rating is the current at which the junction reaches its maximum temperature with the specified mounting. Because capacitor input filters draw current in short pulses, the RMS and peak currents are several times the average; datasheets also give a non-repetitive surge rating I_FSM for the inrush at switch-on. Good practice derates both ratings by around 50 percent, which is why a 100 V supply commonly uses 400 V or 600 V diodes.", "worked_example": "Bridge rectifier from a 24 V_rms secondary feeding 2 A into a capacitor input filter. PIV per diode = 1.414 × 24 ≈ 34 V, so a 100 V part is comfortable. Each diode conducts on alternate half-cycles, so its average current is 1 A; choose a 3 A rated diode to cover the pulsed current and heating. Inrush into a 10 000 μF capacitor from a low-impedance transformer can reach tens of amps, so check I_FSM too.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a diode is specified mainly by its forward voltage drop. Correction: V_F matters for efficiency, but survival is set by two limits, the peak reverse voltage it must block and the average forward current it must carry without overheating.", "link": "section 4", "mnemonic": "PIV and I: how much it must block, how much it must pass.", "edge_cases": "Fast and ultrafast recovery diodes carry a third critical rating, reverse recovery time, which dominates in switching supplies; at mains frequency it is irrelevant."}

{"core": "High-voltage supplies string several diodes in series to reach the needed PIV. Parallel resistors force the steady reverse voltage to divide equally despite differing leakage currents, and parallel capacitors swamp the differing junction capacitances so fast transients and recovery spikes also divide equally.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Resistors and capacitors across the diodes carry negligible current in the forward direction and do not change the output voltage.", "why_tempting": "Any added resistor is associated with dropping voltage."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Current sharing is a problem for diodes in parallel, which is solved with small series resistors; across a series string every diode already carries the identical current.", "why_tempting": "Equalizing is the right idea but applied to current instead of voltage."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "The capacitors across the diodes are far too small (nanofarads) to filter anything, and they are not in the output path; smoothing is the job of the main filter.", "why_tempting": "Capacitors in a power supply are instinctively associated with filtering."}], "concept": "When diodes are connected in series, the total reverse voltage divides according to each diode's reverse resistance, which is set by its leakage current and varies widely between devices, even from the same batch. The leakiest diode takes the least voltage and the tightest diode may be driven past its PIV rating while the string as a whole is within limits. A resistor across each diode, chosen to pass several times the worst-case leakage, dominates the division and forces nearly equal shares: V_each ≈ V_total / n. This handles the slow, steady-state case. During the fast edge when the string switches from forward to reverse, the division is governed by the diodes' junction capacitances and their unequal reverse recovery times; the diode that recovers first momentarily sees the whole transient. A capacitor across each diode, large compared with the junction capacitance, equalizes the dynamic division and also absorbs line transients and transformer leakage-inductance spikes. Modern high-PIV avalanche-rated rectifiers often make the network unnecessary, but the engineering reason remains valid.", "worked_example": "A 3000 V supply using four 1000 V diodes in series. Without equalizing, if one diode has 5 μA leakage and the others 50 μA, the tight diode takes most of the 3000 V and fails. Add 470 kΩ across each: resistor current at 750 V is 750 / 470 000 ≈ 1.6 mA, 30 times the largest leakage, so each diode sits near 750 V. Add 10 nF across each to swamp the roughly 50 pF junction capacitance for the transient case.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: series diodes automatically share reverse voltage equally because they are identical parts. Correction: reverse leakage and junction capacitance vary enough between units that the string must be forced to share with external resistors and capacitors.", "link": "section 4", "mnemonic": "R for the slow share, C for the fast share.", "edge_cases": "The equalizing resistors dissipate continuous power and add to the supply's idle load; in the example each one dissipates about 1.2 W at full voltage, so they must be rated accordingly."}

{"core": "A full-wave rectifier passes the positive half-cycles and inverts the negative ones, so the load sees a train of identical positive half-sine pulses with no gaps. Two pulses per input cycle means the pulse rate is twice the input frequency.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Steady DC requires energy storage to fill in the valleys between pulses; with no filter the voltage falls to zero at every zero crossing of the input.", "why_tempting": "A rectifier is loosely described as converting AC to DC, so an unfiltered output is assumed to be DC already."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Rectification cannot produce a lower frequency, and the output is not sinusoidal; it has a DC component plus even harmonics of the input.", "why_tempting": "Confusing halving the waveform with halving the frequency."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Pulses at the input frequency describe a half-wave rectifier, which leaves a gap for every negative half-cycle.", "why_tempting": "The input is 60 Hz and the pulses obviously come from it, so same frequency seems safe."}], "concept": "With a purely resistive load the output voltage of a full-wave rectifier is v(t) = |V_pk × sin(2πft)| minus diode drops. The shape is a sequence of half-sine arches, each of duration 1 / (2f), touching zero at every zero crossing of the input. Its Fourier series has a DC term of 2 × V_pk / π, then components at 2f, 4f, 6f with decreasing amplitude; there is no component at f. The RMS of the full-wave output equals the RMS of the original sine, V_pk / √2, because squaring removes the sign, while the average is 0.637 × V_pk. The ratio of the AC content to the DC content, the ripple factor, is about 0.48 for an unfiltered full-wave output, versus 1.21 for half-wave. That large residual AC is why a filter follows every rectifier intended to make DC; the rectifier only makes the waveform unipolar, the filter makes it smooth.", "worked_example": "Input 120 V_rms at 60 Hz, bridge rectifier, 100 Ω resistive load. V_pk = 170 V, so the output is a series of 170 V peak half-sine pulses lasting 8.33 ms each, 120 per second. Average voltage 0.637 × 170 ≈ 108 V, average current ≈ 1.08 A, RMS voltage 120 V, so the resistor dissipates 120² / 100 = 144 W while the DC component accounts for only 108² / 100 ≈ 117 W. The remaining 27 W is ripple power.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a full-wave rectifier produces DC and the filter just cleans up some noise. Correction: the unfiltered output is a pulsating waveform that drops to zero 120 times per second; the filter is what turns that into usable DC.", "link": "section 4", "edge_cases": "With a capacitor across the load the picture changes completely: the diodes conduct only in short bursts near each peak, the output becomes a sawtooth riding near V_pk, and the diode current pulses become much larger than the load current."}

{"core": "A filter choke is specified by its inductance, which sets how well it opposes the ripple current, and by the DC current it can carry without saturating the core or overheating the winding. Both are needed because inductance of an iron-core choke falls as DC current magnetizes the core.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Power loss is a consequence of the winding resistance and core losses, not the primary specification; a choke is chosen for L and I first.", "why_tempting": "Chokes do get warm and losses do matter for efficiency, so it sounds like a rating."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Insulation voltage is a secondary rating that matters in high-voltage supplies, but it does not describe what the choke does in the filter.", "why_tempting": "In a high-voltage supply, breakdown of the choke insulation to the core is a real failure, so it appears important."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Reactance at any one frequency is derivable from inductance and adds nothing; 1000 Hz is also unrelated to the 120 Hz ripple the choke actually filters.", "why_tempting": "Reactance is the quantity that really blocks the ripple, and 1 kHz is a common audio test frequency."}], "concept": "The choke's job is to present a high impedance to the ripple and a low resistance to the DC. Its reactance at the ripple frequency is X_L = 2πfL, and the choke-capacitor pair acts as a voltage divider for ripple with attenuation roughly X_C / X_L = 1 / (4π²f²LC). More inductance means more attenuation. The DC current rating exists because an iron-core inductor's inductance depends on the core's permeability, and permeability collapses when the core saturates. Filter chokes have an air gap to allow substantial DC magnetization before saturation; the gap lowers the inductance per turn but keeps it stable up to the rated current. Beyond the rating, inductance drops sharply, ripple rises, and the winding may overheat. A choke marked 10 H at 200 mA may measure 15 H with no current and only 3 H at 400 mA. Swinging chokes exploit this deliberately, offering high inductance at light load for critical-inductance purposes and lower inductance at full load.", "worked_example": "Full-wave supply, 120 Hz ripple, choke 10 H at 300 mA DC, followed by 20 μF. X_L = 2π × 120 × 10 ≈ 7540 Ω; X_C = 1 / (2π × 120 × 20 × 10⁻⁶) ≈ 66 Ω. Ripple attenuation ≈ 66 / 7540 ≈ 0.0088, about 41 dB. If the load rises to 500 mA and the inductance collapses to 2 H, X_L falls to 1508 Ω and the attenuation degrades to 0.044, a loss of 14 dB of filtering.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a choke's inductance is a fixed number stamped on it. Correction: for an iron-core choke the inductance holds only up to its rated DC current; beyond that the core saturates and the inductance, and the filtering, fall away.", "link": "Reactance & Resonance", "mnemonic": "Henries and amps: how much it blocks, how much it can carry.", "edge_cases": "The winding's DC resistance is also significant; a 10 H choke might have 200 Ω of resistance, which drops 60 V at 300 mA and worsens regulation, so high-current designs favour lower inductance with heavier wire."}

{"core": "A choke input filter keeps the rectifier conducting continuously and delivers the average of the rectified wave, so its output barely changes with load. Combined with a full-wave rectifier, which supplies that average at 120 Hz with the least ripple to smooth, it gives the best regulation of the four.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Half-wave bridge is a contradiction in terms, a bridge is inherently full-wave; and a capacitor input filter has the poorest regulation because the capacitor charges to the peak at no load and sags steeply under current.", "why_tempting": "Bridge sounds modern and robust, and the nonsense qualifier may be skimmed over."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "A half-wave rectifier leaves a full half-cycle gap, so the choke must sustain current through that gap alone; the choke's current cannot stay continuous at reasonable inductances and regulation suffers.", "why_tempting": "It has the right filter type, and learners may not realize that choke input really needs full-wave pulses."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A capacitor input filter's output is set by the peak voltage minus a sag proportional to load current, so the output drops noticeably as current increases; its regulation is worse than choke input.", "why_tempting": "Full-wave with a capacitor is the most common hobby supply, so it is assumed to be the best."}], "concept": "Regulation describes how much the output voltage changes between no load and full load: regulation = (V_no-load − V_full-load) / V_full-load. In a capacitor input filter the capacitor charges to the peak of the secondary and is then discharged by the load between pulses; the diodes conduct in brief, high-current bursts that are limited by the transformer and diode resistance, so the output falls roughly linearly with load current and the no-load value is the full peak. A choke input filter instead places the inductor first, so the diodes conduct for the whole half-cycle, the current is a smooth DC with a small ripple, and the capacitor charges to the average of the rectified wave, 0.9 × V_rms, rather than the peak. Because the output is tied to the average rather than a peak-charge-and-decay process, it is nearly independent of load, provided the load current stays above the critical value that keeps the choke current continuous. A full-wave rectifier is required for this to work well: the choke needs pulses every half-cycle to keep current flowing. The price of the better regulation is a lower output voltage (0.9 versus 1.4 × V_rms) and the need for a bleeder to maintain the minimum current.", "worked_example": "Secondary 300 V_rms, 100 mA full load. Capacitor input: no-load output ≈ 424 V, full load perhaps 370 V after diode and transformer drops, regulation ≈ (424 − 370) / 370 ≈ 15 percent. Choke input with adequate inductance and a bleeder: no-load output ≈ 270 V, full load ≈ 260 V after the choke's resistance drop, regulation ≈ 4 percent. The choke input supply is 100 V lower but far stiffer.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the filter that gives the most voltage also gives the best regulation. Correction: the capacitor input filter gives the most voltage precisely because it chases the peak, and that peak-chasing is what makes its output sag under load; the lower-voltage choke input supply holds its value better.", "link": "section 4", "mnemonic": "Choke first for stiff; cap first for high.", "edge_cases": "Below the critical current the choke input filter behaves like a capacitor input filter and the output jumps toward the peak; a swinging choke or a bleeder resistor is used to keep it in the well-regulated region at light load."}

{"core": "With the capacitor directly across the rectifier, it charges to the peak of the secondary, so the output approaches 1.414 × V_rms. A choke input filter lets through only the average of the rectified wave, about 0.9 × V_rms, so the capacitor input filter delivers a markedly higher terminal voltage.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Regulation is the capacitor input filter's weak point; its output falls steeply with load because the capacitor discharges between the brief diode conduction pulses.", "why_tempting": "A higher voltage can be mistaken for a better voltage."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "The capacitor input filter produces much higher peak diode currents, because all the charge for a half-cycle must be delivered during the short interval near the peak when the secondary exceeds the capacitor voltage.", "why_tempting": "A capacitor is thought of as a gentle reservoir, so lower current sounds plausible."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "For a given choke and capacitor, the choke input arrangement gives better ripple attenuation under load; the capacitor input filter's ripple grows in proportion to load current.", "why_tempting": "Big capacitors are associated with smooth DC, so learners assume the capacitor-first order filters best."}], "concept": "In a capacitor input filter the capacitor is charged by the rectifier during the portion of each half-cycle when the secondary voltage exceeds the capacitor voltage. At light load it sits at nearly V_pk = √2 × V_rms and the diodes conduct for only a few degrees per pulse. As load increases, the capacitor discharges further between pulses, the conduction angle widens, and the average output falls; ripple under load is approximately I / (f_ripple × C). In a choke input filter the inductor's opposition to changes in current forces the diodes to conduct continuously, the voltage applied to the capacitor is the rectified wave's average, 2 × V_pk / π ≈ 0.9 × V_rms, and the choke's reactance divides down the ripple. The capacitor input filter therefore buys roughly 57 percent more voltage from the same transformer at the cost of poorer regulation, larger peak diode and transformer currents (the RMS secondary current can be 1.5 to 2 times the DC output), and higher transformer heating. For a solid-state supply where the transformer can be sized accordingly, the extra voltage usually wins; for high-power tube supplies that must hold voltage under keying, choke input often wins.", "worked_example": "Secondary 500 V_rms, full-wave rectifier. Capacitor input, light load: V_out ≈ 500 × 1.414 ≈ 707 V. Choke input, same transformer: V_out ≈ 500 × 0.9 = 450 V. The capacitor input filter yields 257 V more, a ratio of 1.57. At 200 mA the capacitor input output might sag to about 620 V while the choke input stays near 440 V.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the choke input filter gives more voltage because the choke stores energy and adds it to the output. Correction: the choke averages the rectified wave and holds the output to 0.9 × V_rms; only the capacitor input filter captures the peak.", "link": "section 4", "mnemonic": "Cap first: peak. Choke first: average.", "edge_cases": "Under heavy load the capacitor input advantage shrinks because the transformer's resistance and leakage inductance limit the peak charging current; with a small transformer the output can fall well below 1.2 × V_rms at full load."}

{"core": "A choke input filter forces continuous rectifier conduction and delivers the average of the rectified wave, so the output voltage changes very little between light and heavy load. Under a normal load it is the best-regulated of the common filter arrangements.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Ripple frequency is fixed by the rectifier, 60 or 120 Hz; the filter type does not change it.", "why_tempting": "Both filters and frequency appear in the same chapter, so the properties get mixed."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "The choke input filter's output is about 0.9 × V_rms, lower than the capacitor input filter's 1.4 × V_rms; high voltage is the capacitor input filter's advantage.", "why_tempting": "Reversing the two filters' signature properties."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "For a given L and C the choke input filter attenuates ripple more effectively under load than a capacitor input filter, so it gives a smaller percentage ripple, not a larger one.", "why_tempting": "Because the choke input output is lower, a learner might assume the ripple as a fraction must be higher."}], "concept": "In a choke input filter the inductor is the first element after the rectifier, so the current through the rectifier is the choke current, which cannot change abruptly. If the inductance exceeds the critical value, L_crit ≈ R_load / 1000 henries for 120 Hz ripple (with R_load in ohms), the current never falls to zero and the rectifier conducts throughout each half-cycle. The voltage at the choke's input is then the full rectified waveform, and the choke-capacitor combination passes its average, 0.9 × V_rms, while attenuating the AC components. Because the output is derived from an average rather than from a peak-charge process, changes in load current alter the output only through the resistive drops in the transformer, rectifier, and choke winding, which are small. The capacitor input filter, by contrast, starts at the peak at no load and sags as the load discharges the capacitor between increasingly short charging pulses, so its regulation is intrinsically worse. The qualifier normal load matters: above critical current the choke input filter is in its linear, well-regulated regime; at very light load it reverts toward peak charging.", "worked_example": "Load varies from 50 mA to 250 mA on a 400 V_rms supply. Capacitor input: output falls from roughly 550 V to 480 V, a 13 percent drop. Choke input with a 10 H choke (critical current for 10 H is about 400 V / (10 × 1000) ≈ 40 mA, so the whole range is above critical): output falls from about 358 V to 345 V as the choke's 50 Ω winding resistance drops an extra 10 V, a 3.6 percent change.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: regulation comes from the size of the filter capacitor. Correction: capacitor size sets ripple, not regulation; regulation is set by whether the output tracks the peak (capacitor input, poor) or the average (choke input, good) of the rectified wave.", "link": "section 4", "edge_cases": "A swinging choke, whose inductance is high at low current and lower at high current, extends the well-regulated region to lighter loads without needing a large bleeder current."}

{"core": "Power-supply filters are classified by the first element the rectifier sees: a choke input filter starts with a series inductor, a capacitor input filter starts with a shunt capacitor. That first element determines the output voltage, regulation, and rectifier current waveform.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Filters are named by their input element, and nearly every filter ends with a capacitor, so capacitor output does not distinguish anything.", "why_tempting": "It pairs the two component names and sounds like a complementary set."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Capacitor input is a real type, but choke output is not a recognized class; ending a filter with a series inductor would make the output impedance high and the regulation worse.", "why_tempting": "Half of this option is correct, which makes it look plausible."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Neither output term is used; the classification is about what the rectifier feeds into, not what the load connects to.", "why_tempting": "Symmetry with the correct answer, substituting output for input."}], "concept": "The behaviour of the entire supply hinges on the element immediately after the rectifier. If it is a shunt capacitor (capacitor input, also called a pi filter when a choke and second capacitor follow), the rectifier charges the capacitor to the peak of the secondary in short pulses; output approaches 1.4 × V_rms at no load, ripple is proportional to load current, peak diode currents are large, and regulation is poor. If it is a series inductor (choke input, an L-section filter), the inductor keeps the rectifier current continuous, the output settles at the average of the rectified wave, 0.9 × V_rms, ripple is attenuated by the ratio X_C / X_L, peak diode currents are modest, and regulation is good as long as the load exceeds the critical current. Any further sections of L and C added after the first element are refinements that reduce ripple further but do not change the classification. Knowing which type you are looking at tells you which set of formulas to apply and what PIV and current ratings the diodes need.", "worked_example": "Thought experiment: take a full-wave supply with a 300 V_rms secondary, a 10 H choke, and a 20 μF capacitor. Wire the choke first and the capacitor second: no-load output ≈ 270 V, diode current a smooth 120 Hz-rippled DC. Swap them so the capacitor is first and the choke follows: no-load output jumps to ≈ 424 V, diode current becomes narrow spikes several times the load current, and the output now sags more as load increases. Same parts, different filter type, different supply.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a filter with both a choke and a capacitor is just an LC filter and the order does not matter. Correction: the order is the whole point; the element the rectifier sees first dictates peak-charging versus averaging behaviour.", "link": "section 4", "mnemonic": "Named by what the rectifier meets first.", "edge_cases": "A resistor can substitute for the choke in low-current supplies (an RC pi filter); it is still a capacitor input filter because the capacitor comes first."}

{"core": "A bleeder draws a constant minimum current, so the supply never operates at true no load where the output would rise to its maximum. This narrows the voltage swing between light and full load, which is exactly what improved regulation means.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "The transformer's return is through its own winding connections; a resistor across the output has no role in completing the transformer circuit.", "why_tempting": "Bleeders are often drawn from the positive rail to ground, which looks like a return path."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The bleeder adds a current path and slightly increases total current drawn from the supply; it does not inhibit anything.", "why_tempting": "Resistors are thought of as limiting current."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A resistor across the output has no frequency selectivity and cannot reduce ripple; it slightly loads the filter but does not filter.", "why_tempting": "It sits in parallel with the filter capacitor, so it looks like part of the filter."}], "concept": "Regulation compares the no-load and full-load output voltages. In a capacitor input supply the no-load output is the full secondary peak; in a choke input supply, dropping below the critical current makes the output jump from the average toward the peak. In both cases the worst regulation figure comes from the extreme of zero load current. A bleeder resistor guarantees a baseline current, so the lightest condition the supply ever sees is bleeder current rather than zero. For a choke input supply the bleeder is chosen so that this baseline exceeds the critical current, I_crit ≈ V_out / (1000 × L) with L in henries, keeping the choke in continuous conduction and the output at 0.9 × V_rms at all times. For a capacitor input supply the bleeder simply sits on the load line somewhat below the peak, so the swing to full load is smaller in proportion. The primary function remains safety: discharging the filter capacitors after switch-off so the chassis is safe to work on. The bleeder can also serve as the top of a voltage-divider string for lower-voltage taps.", "worked_example": "Choke input supply, 400 V output, 8 H choke. Critical current ≈ 400 / (1000 × 8) = 50 mA. A 7.5 kΩ bleeder draws 400 / 7500 ≈ 53 mA and dissipates 400² / 7500 ≈ 21 W, so a 50 W resistor is appropriate. Without it, at no load the output would climb toward 1.414 / 0.9 × 400 ≈ 628 V; with it the no-load output stays near 400 V and regulation improves from roughly 57 percent to a few percent.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a bleeder is purely a safety component with no electrical effect while the supply runs. Correction: by setting a minimum load it also stabilizes the output against the no-load voltage rise, which is a genuine regulation improvement.", "link": "section 4", "mnemonic": "Bleed a little, hold the line.", "edge_cases": "The bleeder's dissipation is continuous and wasted, so in low-power or battery-fed supplies a much higher value is used purely for safety discharge and the regulation benefit is given up."}

{"core": "An inductor's impedance is Z = R_dc + j2πfL. At DC the reactive term is zero and only the small winding resistance remains, so DC passes freely; at the ripple frequency the reactance is large and the AC component is impeded.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "This describes a series capacitor, whose reactance is infinite at DC and small at high frequency, the exact opposite of an inductor.", "why_tempting": "Confusing which component blocks DC; both are reactive and the roles get swapped."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "An inductor's opposition grows with frequency, so it cannot impede DC and AC equally; the DC sees only the winding resistance.", "why_tempting": "The choke has measurable DC resistance, which may be mistaken for intentional impediment of DC."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "If the choke passed the AC component freely it would provide no filtering at all; the entire purpose is to oppose the ripple.", "why_tempting": "Thinking of a choke as just a piece of wire that conducts everything."}], "concept": "A series choke in the filter is a frequency-selective series element. Its inductive reactance, X_L = 2πfL, is proportional to frequency, so for the DC component (f = 0) the choke is simply its winding resistance, typically tens to a few hundred ohms, while for the 120 Hz ripple a 10 H choke presents about 7.5 kΩ. The following shunt capacitor has the opposite character: X_C = 1 / (2πfC) is infinite at DC and small at the ripple frequency. Together they form a frequency-dependent voltage divider: the DC component goes through the series choke and across the open capacitor to the load with only a resistive drop, while the ripple is divided by about X_C / X_L. The physical mechanism is Lenz's law: a changing current induces a back-EMF L × di/dt that opposes the change, so the choke resists the ripple's rapid rise and fall while a steady current induces nothing. This is the same L-C low-pass behaviour used in RF filters, just scaled to henries and microfarads for 120 Hz.", "worked_example": "Choke 10 H with 150 Ω winding resistance, 200 mA DC with a 120 Hz ripple component of 10 V_rms at its input, 16 μF capacitor after it. DC drop = 0.2 × 150 = 30 V, so the DC passes with a 30 V loss. For the ripple, X_L = 2π × 120 × 10 ≈ 7540 Ω and X_C ≈ 83 Ω, so the ripple at the output ≈ 10 × 83 / 7540 ≈ 0.11 V_rms. DC attenuated by a few percent, AC attenuated by about 37 dB.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a choke blocks DC the way a capacitor does. Correction: an inductor blocks change, not DC; it opposes the ripple's variations and lets the steady current through with only its winding resistance in the way.", "link": "Reactance & Resonance", "mnemonic": "Inductors oppose change; steady current is no change.", "edge_cases": "The choke's winding resistance drop is proportional to load current, which is the main source of the small remaining regulation error in a choke input supply, and it also dissipates I² × R as heat."}

{"core": "A choke input filter only behaves as designed when the choke current never drops to zero, which requires a minimum load current called the critical current. A bleeder resistor sized to draw at least that current guarantees it even when the external load is disconnected.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A full-wave bridge supplies the pulses the choke needs, but it does not draw any current itself; with no load the choke current still falls to zero.", "why_tempting": "Full-wave rectification is a genuine requirement of choke input filters and sounds like it addresses the same problem."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "An ammeter measures the current; it does not create one, and a meter in the output line draws nothing from the supply.", "why_tempting": "Monitoring the minimum current might be confused with maintaining it."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The output capacitor sits after the choke and its value affects ripple; it has no effect on whether the choke's DC current stays above the critical value.", "why_tempting": "Bigger capacitors are a reflexive fix for any filter problem."}], "concept": "In a choke input filter the rectifier feeds the inductor directly. The rectified wave has a DC component of 0.9 × V_rms and an AC component whose fundamental at 120 Hz has a peak amplitude of about 0.67 × V_rms. The choke passes the DC and converts the AC into a ripple current of roughly (0.67 × V_rms) / (2π × 120 × L). If that ripple current's peak exceeds the DC load current, the choke current tries to reverse, the diodes cut off, and the filter momentarily becomes a capacitor input filter with the output jumping toward the peak. The condition for continuous conduction is I_dc ≥ I_ripple peak, which simplifies to the familiar L_crit ≈ R_load / 1000 (L in henries, R in ohms, 120 Hz ripple) or equivalently I_crit ≈ V_out / (1000 × L). A bleeder resistor across the output sets a floor on I_dc so the inequality holds at all times. The alternative is a swinging choke whose inductance rises at low current, lowering the critical current automatically. Either way, the requirement is a design rule, not an optional refinement: a choke input supply without a minimum load has poor regulation and may overvoltage its capacitors.", "worked_example": "Supply: 350 V output, 6 H choke. I_crit ≈ 350 / (1000 × 6) ≈ 58 mA. Bleeder = 350 / 0.058 ≈ 6 kΩ; pick 5.6 kΩ for margin, giving 62.5 mA and dissipating 350² / 5600 ≈ 22 W, so a 50 W resistor. With this in place the choke stays in continuous conduction from no external load up to its rated current.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a choke input filter works at any load as long as the choke is big enough. Correction: it works only above a minimum current; the bleeder exists to provide that current when nothing else does.", "link": "section 4", "mnemonic": "No current, no choke action: bleed to stay above critical.", "edge_cases": "Below critical current the output rises from 0.9 toward 1.4 × V_rms, a 57 percent jump; capacitors chosen for the choke input voltage may be overvoltaged, which is why the bleeder is also a protective component."}

{"core": "The first choke and first capacitor of a choke input filter form a series L-C circuit driven by the rectifier's ripple. If their resonant frequency, f = 1 / (2π√(LC)), is near the ripple frequency, the ripple voltage across the capacitor is multiplied rather than attenuated, so these two parts must be chosen to keep resonance well below 120 Hz.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A resistor and an inductor cannot resonate; resonance needs both L and C. The bleeder sets the DC load and damps the circuit slightly but does not define the resonant frequency.", "why_tempting": "Both components are at the front of the filter and both matter for choke input behaviour."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Two capacitors with no inductor between them form no resonant circuit; they simply add in parallel at the ripple frequency.", "why_tempting": "Both capacitors do carry ripple current and sizing them is part of filter design."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The first choke and second capacitor are separated by the first capacitor, which shunts most of the ripple before it reaches the second section; the dominant series resonance is in the first L-C section.", "why_tempting": "Mixing the two stages of a two-section filter."}], "concept": "A choke input L-section is a series inductor feeding a shunt capacitor. Seen from the rectifier, the ripple source drives L and C in series, and the output is the voltage across C. The transfer ratio for the ripple fundamental is X_C / |X_L − X_C| when the winding resistance is small. Far above resonance, X_L dominates and the ratio collapses toward 1 / (4π²f²LC), which is the attenuation you want. At resonance, X_L = X_C and the ratio is limited only by the circuit resistance: Q = X_L / R, and the capacitor voltage becomes Q times the drive, so the ripple is amplified, the capacitor is overvoltaged, and the choke and rectifier carry large circulating current. The design rule is to keep f_res = 1 / (2π√(LC)) at no more than about half the ripple frequency, with many designers aiming for a quarter or less; in practice this means the product L × C (henries × microfarads) should be comfortably above about 20 for 120 Hz ripple. The same condition also ensures the ripple attenuation is good, so the two goals align.", "worked_example": "First choke 4 H, first capacitor 0.5 μF: f_res = 1 / (2π√(4 × 0.5 × 10⁻⁶)) = 1 / (2π × 0.00141) ≈ 113 Hz, almost on top of the 120 Hz ripple, so the ripple would be amplified by the circuit Q. Change the capacitor to 10 μF: f_res = 1 / (2π√(4 × 10 × 10⁻⁵)) ≈ 25 Hz, about a fifth of the ripple frequency, and the ripple is attenuated by roughly (25 / 120)² ≈ 0.04 instead.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: any L and C after the rectifier will reduce ripple. Correction: an L-C pair is a resonant circuit, and if its resonance lands near the ripple frequency it increases ripple; the first choke and first capacitor must be chosen so resonance is well below the ripple frequency.", "link": "Reactance & Resonance", "mnemonic": "L × C big enough that resonance lives below the ripple.", "edge_cases": "On 50 Hz mains the ripple is 100 Hz, so a filter designed with marginal L × C for 60 Hz systems moves closer to resonance; always check the product against the actual ripple frequency."}

{"core": "The first choke and first capacitor are in series across the rectifier's ripple output. If they are resonant near the ripple frequency, the impedance seen by the rectifier collapses to the small circuit resistance, drawing excessive peak current, and the resonant rise multiplies the voltage across the components, raising the diode's reverse stress.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "The first choke and second capacitor are not directly in series; the first capacitor sits between them and shunts the ripple. Also, parallel resonance would present a high impedance, which limits current rather than causing excessive peaks.", "why_tempting": "Parallel resonance is the other kind of resonance and the components named are real filter parts."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A choke on its own has no capacitance to resonate with at 120 Hz; its self-resonance from winding capacitance is far higher and irrelevant to ripple.", "why_tempting": "Tuned inductance sounds like a plausible technical phrase."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A shorted bleeder is a short across the output, which would overload the supply but has nothing to do with resonance or with PIV; it would reduce the output voltage, not raise it.", "why_tempting": "A failure mode that produces excessive current, which matches half the symptoms."}], "concept": "At the rectifier's output the ripple source has a low internal impedance (transformer resistance plus diode resistance). The first choke L and first capacitor C are in series across it. The series impedance is R + j(X_L − X_C); at f = 1 / (2π√(LC)) the reactances cancel and only R is left. The ripple current then becomes I = V_ripple / R, potentially many times the intended value, and that current flows through the diodes as sharp peaks superimposed on the DC. The resonant rise also means the voltage across the capacitor is Q × V_ripple, where Q = X_L / R, so the DC rail carries a large AC swing. When the swing on the output adds to the secondary's negative peak, the reverse voltage across the diodes exceeds the normal 2 × V_pk calculation and can breach their PIV rating. In other words, the same resonance mechanism that ruins the filtering also endangers the rectifier. Keeping the L-C product high enough that resonance is well below the ripple frequency avoids all of these effects together.", "worked_example": "First section 2 H and 1 μF: f_res = 1 / (2π√(2 × 10⁻⁶)) ≈ 113 Hz, essentially at the 120 Hz ripple. With a total series resistance of 100 Ω, Q = X_L / R = (2π × 120 × 2) / 100 ≈ 15. A 0.67 × V_rms ripple drive of 200 V would try to produce about 3000 V across the capacitor and a ripple current of 2 A peak through diodes meant for 200 mA. Increasing C to 20 μF drops f_res to about 25 Hz and removes the problem.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: resonance in a power-supply filter is only a ripple-quality issue. Correction: series resonance in the first L-C section also overloads the rectifier with peak current and exposes it to voltages beyond its PIV, so it is a reliability issue.", "link": "Reactance & Resonance", "edge_cases": "The transformer's leakage inductance and the diode's junction capacitance form a much higher-frequency resonance that produces ringing at each diode turn-off; that is addressed with snubbers, not with the filter's L and C values."}

{"core": "The choke input filter's 0.9 × V_rms output holds only while the choke current is continuous. If the bleeder fails open and the load is removed, the current falls below critical, the filter behaves as capacitor input, and the capacitor charges to the full secondary peak, 1.414 × V_rms. The capacitor must survive that case.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Resonance is a genuine design concern, but a properly designed filter, as the question states, has its resonance well below the ripple frequency; the margin addresses the no-load condition, not resonance.", "why_tempting": "Resonance causing high voltages is a neighbouring syllabus item and sounds like a reason for a safety margin."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Under heavy load the output voltage falls, not rises, because of resistive drops; high current does not create high voltage across the output capacitor.", "why_tempting": "Heavy load sounds like the stressful condition for a supply."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "With no load there is no current to speak of; the hazard under no load is voltage rise, not current rise.", "why_tempting": "Pairs the correct condition (no load) with the wrong quantity."}], "concept": "A choke input filter averages the rectified wave only when the inductor's current never reaches zero. Continuous conduction requires a DC load current above the critical value, I_crit ≈ V_out / (1000 × L). The bleeder is what normally guarantees that minimum. If the bleeder burns out, or is disconnected, and the external load is switched off, the choke current drops to zero during part of each cycle, the diodes cut off, and the capacitor is no longer held to the average. It is now charged directly to the peak of the secondary on each half-cycle, just as in a capacitor input filter, and sits at √2 × V_rms, a 57 percent increase over the 0.9 × V_rms design value. An electrolytic capacitor rated only for the nominal working voltage would be overvoltaged and could fail destructively. Rating the capacitor at the peak transformer voltage, with normal derating on top, covers the failure case at modest cost. The same reasoning applies at switch-on before a tube load warms up, which is another no-load interval.", "worked_example": "Secondary 500 V_rms, choke input, bleeder present: V_out ≈ 0.9 × 500 = 450 V, and a 500 V capacitor seems adequate. Bleeder fails open, load off: V_out rises toward 1.414 × 500 ≈ 707 V, and a 500 V capacitor is 40 percent overvoltaged. Rating the capacitor for the peak, 707 V, in practice an 800 V or two series 450 V units, survives the fault.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the filter capacitor only ever sees the supply's rated output voltage. Correction: in a choke input supply the output is held at 0.9 × V_rms only by continuous choke current; lose the minimum load and the capacitor sees the full peak.", "link": "section 4", "mnemonic": "Rate the cap for the peak, because the bleeder can die.", "edge_cases": "Mains voltage can run 5 to 10 percent high and a lightly loaded transformer's secondary exceeds nameplate, so the true worst case can be 10 to 15 percent above the computed peak; derating the capacitor further is prudent."}

{"core": "A linear regulator keeps the pass element in its active region and continuously adjusts its conduction, effectively varying its resistance, so that the output stays constant as the input voltage or load current changes. The control is proportional and continuous, not switched.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A ramp at the output would be gross ripple; a regulator's purpose is a flat output. Ramps appear internally in switching converters as the PWM timing waveform, not at any regulator's output.", "why_tempting": "Switching regulators do contain a sawtooth or triangle wave in their control loop."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Switching the pass transistor fully on and off is the defining feature of a switching regulator; a linear regulator deliberately avoids saturation and cut-off.", "why_tempting": "Both regulators use a pass transistor, so the distinction between proportional and switched operation is easy to lose."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "On-off control with a load-dependent duty cycle describes PWM switching regulation, the opposite of continuous linear control.", "why_tempting": "Duty cycle proportional to line and load sounds like regulation in general."}], "concept": "In a series linear regulator the pass transistor sits between the unregulated input and the load. A reference, usually a Zener or bandgap, sets the target; an error amplifier compares a sample of the output to the reference and drives the pass transistor's base or gate so that the output matches. If the input rises, the error amplifier reduces the transistor's drive, increasing its voltage drop, and the output stays put; if the load current rises, the drive increases to hold the output. The pass device therefore operates in its linear region throughout, with V_CE = V_in − V_out and dissipation P = (V_in − V_out) × I_load. Efficiency is approximately V_out / V_in, which is the price of this simplicity. The reward is a clean output with no switching noise, fast transient response, and no magnetics. A shunt regulator is also linear but places the variable element across the load; the conduction still varies proportionally rather than switching.", "worked_example": "A 7812-type regulator with V_in varying from 15 V to 20 V, load 1 A. Output stays at 12 V. Pass dissipation ranges from (15 − 12) × 1 = 3 W to (20 − 12) × 1 = 8 W, and efficiency ranges from 12 / 15 = 80 percent down to 12 / 20 = 60 percent. The same job done by a switching regulator at 90 percent efficiency would dissipate about 1.3 W regardless of input.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a regulator is a regulator; linear and switching just describe the package. Correction: linear regulation means proportional, continuous control of a pass element with dissipation equal to the dropped voltage times current; switching regulation means on-off control and energy storage, with much lower dissipation.", "link": "section 4", "mnemonic": "Linear: the pass transistor is a variable resistor. Switching: it is a switch.", "edge_cases": "Low-dropout (LDO) linear regulators can hold regulation with only a few hundred millivolts of headroom, but they are still linear, dissipating (V_in − V_out) × I, and some become unstable without a specified output capacitor ESR."}

{"core": "A switching regulator drives its control transistor fully on or fully off at a high frequency and adjusts the fraction of time it is on, the duty cycle, to hold the output constant. Because the switch is either saturated or cut off, it dissipates little power, which is the source of the high efficiency.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Proportional variation of a control element's conduction is the definition of a linear regulator; a switching regulator avoids the lossy linear region.", "why_tempting": "This is the correct answer to the companion question about linear regulators and the two get swapped."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Multiple outputs are a matter of transformer windings or additional stages and are available in both linear and switching supplies; they are not a defining characteristic.", "why_tempting": "Many commercial switching supplies do have several outputs."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "A ramp exists inside the PWM controller to set timing, but the output is filtered DC; a ramp at the output would be a failed regulator.", "why_tempting": "The internal sawtooth is well known and gets confused with the output waveform."}], "concept": "In a buck switching regulator the switch connects the input to an inductor for a fraction D of each period; while on, the inductor current ramps up and energy is stored in its field, and while off, a diode or synchronous switch lets the inductor deliver that current to the output capacitor and load. The averaged output is V_out = D × V_in for a buck, V_out = V_in / (1 − D) for a boost. The error amplifier compares the output to a reference and adjusts D, usually by comparing its output to the internal ramp, so a rising input or a heavier load produces a correspondingly shorter or longer on-time. Because the switch is either fully on (low V_CE or R_DS(on), low loss) or fully off (no current), the dominant losses are switching transitions, conduction resistance, and inductor and diode losses, giving efficiencies of 80 to 95 percent. The penalties are output ripple at the switching frequency, radiated and conducted noise that can land in the receiver, and the need for an inductor and careful layout. Switching frequencies of tens of kilohertz to several megahertz allow small magnetics compared with the 120 Hz filter chokes of a mains supply.", "worked_example": "Buck converter, V_in = 24 V, V_out = 12 V, load 2 A. Duty cycle D = 12 / 24 = 0.5, so with a 100 kHz clock the switch is on for 5 μs of each 10 μs period. If V_in rises to 30 V the controller trims D to 12 / 30 = 0.4, a 4 μs on-time. At 90 percent efficiency the losses are about 2.7 W, versus 24 W for a linear regulator doing the same job.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a switching regulator is a linear regulator that runs faster. Correction: the switching regulator never operates its transistor in the linear region; it chops the input and uses an inductor and capacitor to average the result, which is why its losses are so much lower.", "link": "section 4", "mnemonic": "Switcher: the question is how long it is on, not how hard it is on.", "edge_cases": "At very light loads many switchers drop into burst or pulse-skipping mode, and the output ripple and noise character change; this can produce birdies in a receiver that were absent at full load."}

{"core": "A Zener diode operated in reverse breakdown holds a nearly constant voltage over a wide range of current, so it provides the fixed reference against which the regulator compares its output. Everything else in the regulator exists to make the output track that reference.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "An SCR is a latching power switch used in crowbars and phase-control circuits; it has no stable voltage characteristic to serve as a reference.", "why_tempting": "SCRs appear in power-supply protection circuits so they feel related."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A varactor is a diode used for its voltage-dependent junction capacitance in tuning circuits; its voltage is whatever is applied to it, not a fixed value.", "why_tempting": "It is a diode with a special name, like the Zener, and shows up in the same chapter on semiconductors."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "An ordinary forward-biased junction diode drops only about 0.6 to 0.7 V and that drop varies with current and about −2 mV per degree Celsius; it is a poor, low-voltage reference compared with a Zener.", "why_tempting": "Forward diode drops are sometimes used as crude references in Basic-level circuits."}], "concept": "Below its breakdown voltage a reverse-biased Zener passes only leakage; at V_Z the junction breaks down by Zener tunnelling (below about 5 V) or avalanche multiplication (above about 6 V) and the current rises steeply while the voltage changes only slightly. The slope of that region is the dynamic impedance r_z, a few ohms for good references, so a current change ΔI produces only ΔV = ΔI × r_z of reference change. A series resistor from the unregulated input biases the Zener in this region; the regulator then uses an error amplifier to compare a divided-down sample of the output to V_Z and adjust the pass element. Zeners near 5.6 to 6.2 V have the smallest temperature coefficient because the negative coefficient of Zener tunnelling and the positive coefficient of avalanche roughly cancel, which is why precision references cluster there. Modern integrated regulators use a bandgap reference, which combines a forward diode's negative coefficient with a PTAT voltage to produce about 1.2 V with very low drift, but the role in the circuit is identical.", "worked_example": "Unregulated 20 V input, 6.2 V Zener with r_z = 5 Ω, series resistor 1 kΩ. Zener current ≈ (20 − 6.2) / 1000 ≈ 13.8 mA. If the input drifts to 24 V, the current rises to 17.8 mA and the reference moves by 4 mA × 5 Ω = 20 mV, about 0.3 percent, while the raw input moved 20 percent. Feeding this reference to an error amplifier that compares it with the output divided by two gives a 12.4 V regulated output that inherits only that 0.3 percent change.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the Zener diode is the regulator. Correction: in a linear regulator the Zener is only the reference; the pass transistor and error amplifier do the regulating, and the output quality depends on how well they track that reference.", "link": "section 4", "mnemonic": "Zener sets the target; the pass transistor hits it.", "edge_cases": "A bare Zener shunt regulator (Zener plus resistor across the load) does regulate on its own for small loads, but its output impedance is r_z and the series resistor wastes power, so it is used only for low-current bias supplies."}

{"core": "A series regulator places the control element in line with the load and draws from the source only the current the load actually needs plus a small overhead. A shunt regulator must draw its full design current at all times, dumping whatever the load does not use, so the series type makes far more efficient use of the primary source.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A constant current source holds current, not voltage, and is not a voltage regulator topology; it also delivers full current regardless of demand, which is the opposite of efficient utilization.", "why_tempting": "Constant sounds like regulated, and current sources are used inside regulators as biasing elements."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Shunt current source is not a standard regulator class, and anything shunt-connected across the load consumes power continuously rather than on demand.", "why_tempting": "Mixing the terms shunt and source makes it sound like an alternative topology."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A shunt regulator sits across the load and must sink the difference between the source's constant current and the load's demand; at light load it burns nearly all the power, so it is the least efficient option.", "why_tempting": "Shunt regulators present a constant load to the source, which is a different virtue that can be mistaken for efficiency."}], "concept": "The two linear topologies differ in where the variable element goes. In the series regulator the pass transistor is in series with the load; the current drawn from the source is I_load plus a few milliamps for the reference and error amplifier, and the pass dissipation is (V_in − V_out) × I_load. At light load the dissipation drops to almost nothing. In the shunt regulator a series resistor R_s feeds a node that is held at V_out by a transistor or Zener across the load; the source supplies I_s = (V_in − V_out) / R_s continuously, and the shunt element absorbs I_s − I_load. The resistor dissipates I_s² × R_s and the shunt element dissipates V_out × (I_s − I_load), so total input power is fixed at V_in × I_s regardless of load. When the load is a battery, a solar panel, or any source where every milliamp counts, the series regulator's on-demand draw wins decisively. The shunt regulator's strengths are different: inherent short-circuit tolerance (the series resistor limits current), a constant load presented to the source, and simplicity at low power.", "worked_example": "Source 15 V, regulated output 10 V, load varying 0 to 500 mA. Series regulator: at 100 mA load the source supplies about 105 mA, 1.6 W in; at 0 mA it supplies about 5 mA. Shunt regulator designed for 500 mA: R_s = 5 V / 0.5 A = 10 Ω, source always supplies 500 mA, 7.5 W in, whether the load draws 500 mA or nothing. At 100 mA load the series design draws one-fifth of the shunt design's power.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: all linear regulators are equally inefficient because they drop voltage resistively. Correction: the series regulator draws only what the load needs, so its loss scales with load; the shunt regulator draws its maximum current all the time, so its loss is greatest exactly when the load is lightest.", "link": "section 4", "mnemonic": "Series: pay for what you use. Shunt: pay the maximum always.", "edge_cases": "At full rated load the two topologies dissipate similar power; the series regulator's advantage is specifically at partial and light load, which is the normal operating condition for most equipment."}

{"core": "A shunt regulator draws a fixed total current from the unregulated source through its series resistor and diverts whatever the load does not take through the shunt element. The source therefore sees a constant current regardless of load changes, which is what this application needs.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A constant current source regulates its output current, not the load seen by the input; it is a different function and its draw from the input still varies with output conditions.", "why_tempting": "The word constant appears in both the option and the question."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "This is not a standard regulator class, and a current source across the load would fix the load current rather than presenting a constant load to the source.", "why_tempting": "It combines shunt, the right word, with current source, the wrong concept."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "The series regulator's input current equals the load current plus a small overhead, so the source sees a load that varies exactly as the output load varies, the opposite of constant.", "why_tempting": "The series regulator is the familiar, more efficient type and may be chosen by default."}], "concept": "The shunt regulator consists of a series dropping resistor R_s from the unregulated input to the output node, and a variable shunt element, a Zener, a transistor, or a transistor driven by an error amplifier, from that node to ground in parallel with the load. The node is held at V_out, so the resistor current is fixed at I_s = (V_in − V_out) / R_s as long as V_in is constant. The shunt element conducts I_shunt = I_s − I_load, rising when the load falls and vice versa. From the source's point of view nothing changes when the load changes: it delivers I_s into V_in at all times. This constant loading is valuable when the source itself behaves badly with a varying load, for example a high-impedance supply whose voltage would swing, a transformer winding that would shift the voltage on other windings, or a circuit whose stability depends on a steady drain. Shunt regulators are also inherently short-circuit proof, since R_s limits the current, and they can both sink and source current at the output node. The cost is continuous dissipation at the maximum design power, which is why they are kept to low-power roles.", "worked_example": "V_in = 12 V, V_out = 5 V, maximum load 100 mA, shunt regulator with R_s = 7 V / 0.12 A ≈ 58 Ω to give 120 mA total with 20 mA minimum in the shunt. At 100 mA load the shunt carries 20 mA; at 0 mA load it carries 120 mA and dissipates 0.6 W. The input supply delivers 12 V × 120 mA = 1.44 W in both cases, a constant load. A series regulator in the same role would present 12 V × (100 + 5) mA = 1.26 W at full load and 0.06 W at no load.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a shunt regulator wastes power, so it has no legitimate use. Correction: its constant input draw is a feature when the source needs a steady load, and its short-circuit immunity and bidirectional output are useful in reference and bias circuits.", "link": "section 4", "mnemonic": "Shunt: the source never notices the load.", "edge_cases": "The constant-load property holds only if V_in is constant; if the unregulated input ripples or sags, I_s follows it, so a shunt regulator's line regulation depends heavily on R_s and the dynamic impedance of the shunt element."}

{"core": "Remote sensing runs the error amplifier's feedback wires directly to the load terminals instead of to the regulator's own output pins. The regulator then corrects for the voltage dropped in the cables between it and the load, holding the voltage constant where it matters.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Comparing the input voltage to the reference is feed-forward from the wrong node; a regulator compares the output, and remote sensing specifies which point of the output.", "why_tempting": "It describes an error amplifier and a reference, which are real regulator parts, and the word input can be read loosely."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A connection outside the feedback loop is exactly the unregulated case; anything the loop does not see, it cannot correct, so the cable drop would remain.", "why_tempting": "Outside the loop sounds like remote, but the feedback must include the load, not exclude it."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "There is no inductive or wireless link in a regulator's feedback path; the sense lines are ordinary wires carrying a tiny current to the error amplifier.", "why_tempting": "Remote suggests wireless to someone thinking of radio."}], "concept": "A regulator holds constant whatever voltage its feedback divider samples. If the divider is attached at the regulator's output terminals, the voltage there is held, but the load at the far end of a cable sees V_load = V_out − I_load × R_cable. With a heavy load and thin or long leads, that drop can be a significant fraction of a volt and changes with current, so the load voltage is poorly regulated even though the regulator is working perfectly. Remote sensing adds a pair of sense wires from the load terminals back to the error amplifier's feedback input. The amplifier now compares the voltage at the load to the reference and raises the regulator's output by exactly the cable drop. Because the sense wires carry only microamps, their own resistance is irrelevant. The regulator must have enough headroom to supply the extra volts, and the loop gain and phase margin must tolerate the added cable inductance and the load capacitance. Bench supplies expose sense terminals for this reason; integrated regulators achieve the same effect by placing the feedback divider at the load.", "worked_example": "Regulator set to 13.8 V, load 20 A, 3 m of cable with 10 mΩ per metre each way, total loop resistance 60 mΩ. Cable drop = 20 × 0.06 = 1.2 V, so the load sees 12.6 V when sensed at the supply. With sense leads at the load, the error amplifier drives the supply output to 15.0 V and the load sees 13.8 V. The supply must have at least 1.2 V of extra headroom and dissipates an extra 24 W in the cable regardless.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a regulated supply delivers its rated voltage anywhere downstream. Correction: the supply regulates the point its feedback samples; everything between that point and the load is unregulated resistance, which remote sensing brings inside the loop.", "link": "section 4", "mnemonic": "Sense where you care, not where it is convenient.", "edge_cases": "If a sense lead opens, many supplies lose feedback and swing to maximum output; good designs tie the sense pins to the output through resistors so an open sense lead degrades to local sensing instead of a runaway."}
