{"core": "A three-terminal regulator is a complete closed-loop linear regulator integrated into one package with only input, output and common pins: inside are a bandgap or Zener-based voltage reference, an error amplifier that compares a scaled sample of the output against that reference, sensing resistors that set the sample ratio, and a series pass transistor that the amplifier drives to hold the output constant.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "The device produces one regulated output voltage, not three, and it regulates voltage rather than holding current constant; the three refers to pins, not outputs.", "why_tempting": "The word three is read as counting outputs, and constant-current sources are a neighbouring topic in the same section."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "There is a single error amplifier and a single sensing network in the standard architecture; multiplying them does not describe any common part and the three again refers to terminals.", "why_tempting": "It reuses real internal block names (error amplifier, sensing) and attaches the number three to them, which sounds plausible if you only half remember the block diagram."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "One output voltage only, and the current is whatever the load draws up to the device limit, so neither three voltages nor variable current describes the part.", "why_tempting": "Same mis-reading of three as a count of outputs, combined with the true fact that output current is load-dependent."}], "concept": "A linear series regulator is a negative-feedback loop. A reference V_ref (typically a bandgap of about 1.25 V in an LM317, or an internal Zener-plus-amplifier in a 78xx) feeds one input of an error amplifier; a resistive divider R1/R2 across the output feeds the other. The amplifier drives the base of a series pass transistor (often a Darlington) so that V_out × R2/(R1+R2) = V_ref, i.e. V_out = V_ref × (1 + R1/R2). Any disturbance that pulls V_out down reduces the sampled voltage, the amplifier raises the pass transistor drive, and V_out is restored; the loop gain divides the residual error. Integrating all of this on one die with only in, out and common pins is what makes it a three-terminal regulator; fixed types bury the divider internally, adjustable types bring the reference node out as the third pin so an external divider sets V_out. The pass element absorbs the entire input-output difference as heat, which is why these are linear rather than switching devices.", "worked_example": "Take an adjustable three-terminal regulator with V_ref = 1.25 V between its output and adjust pins. If R1 (output to adjust) = 240 Ω and R2 (adjust to ground) = 2.2 kΩ, then V_out = 1.25 × (1 + 2200/240) = 1.25 × 10.17 ≈ 12.7 V. Now imagine the load current steps up and V_out sags by 50 mV: the adjust-pin sample drops, the error amplifier sees the reference higher than the sample, pushes harder on the pass transistor, and the output recovers within microseconds. The same loop is inside a fixed 7812; the only difference is that R1 and R2 are on the die.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: three-terminal means three outputs or three internal amplifiers. Correction: the three are the input, output and common/adjust pins; internally it is a single complete feedback regulator (reference, error amplifier, sense divider, pass transistor).", "link": "section 4", "edge_cases": "Fixed three-terminal regulators need a minimum input-output headroom (dropout), roughly 2 V for a classic 7805 but under 0.3 V for LDO variants that use a PNP or PMOS pass element; the architecture is the same but the pass device changes."}

{"core": "A three-terminal regulator is specified by what it delivers: its regulated output voltage and the maximum output current it can source while staying in regulation and within its thermal limits. Together with the permissible input voltage range, those are the figures you design around.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A regulator has one nominal output voltage, not a maximum you choose, and no useful minimum output current rating exists for most parts; the limiting figure is maximum current.", "why_tempting": "Datasheets do list minimum load currents for some adjustable parts (a few mA to keep the reference biased), so a half-remembered footnote gets promoted to a headline spec."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "There is no minimum output voltage for a fixed regulator; the output is a single nominal value. Maximum current is correct but paired with a meaningless voltage spec.", "why_tempting": "Adjustable regulators do have a lowest settable output (equal to V_ref), which tempts the learner to generalize that to all three-terminal parts."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Output voltage is right, but the current figure that constrains a design is the maximum the device can supply, not a minimum; exceeding the maximum triggers current limiting or thermal shutdown.", "why_tempting": "Swapping maximum for minimum is an easy inversion when the learner recalls that some regulators need a minimum load to regulate properly."}], "concept": "Selecting a linear regulator is a three-sided problem. The input range sets the headroom: V_in must exceed V_out plus the dropout voltage at all times, including at the bottom of the ripple valley, but must not exceed the absolute maximum input rating. The output voltage is the fixed or adjustable value the part is built to hold. The maximum output current is bounded by two things: an internal current-limit circuit (often a sense resistor and a transistor that steals base drive from the pass element) and the thermal limit, since the pass transistor dissipates P = (V_in − V_out) × I_out. A 1 A part on a small heatsink may only manage 400 mA at a large differential before thermal shutdown, so the real usable current depends on dissipation, not just the nameplate. These three parameters tie directly into the next subsection on pass-transistor dissipation and into ripple and load regulation figures.", "worked_example": "You want 5 V at 800 mA from an unregulated 12 V supply. Check: V_in − V_out = 7 V of headroom, far above a 2 V dropout, so regulation is fine. Dissipation P = 7 V × 0.8 A = 5.6 W. A TO-220 regulator with junction-to-ambient of 50 °C/W in free air would rise 280 °C, so it must have a heatsink of a few °C/W, or you choose a lower input voltage. The three characteristics (input range, 5 V output, 1 A maximum) all passed, but the thermal consequence of the current rating is what actually shaped the design.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a regulator rated for 1 A will deliver 1 A under any conditions. Correction: the maximum current rating is only achievable when the dissipation (V_in − V_out) × I stays within thermal limits; the headline current, output voltage and input range must all be checked together.", "link": "Ohm's Law & Power", "edge_cases": "Adjustable regulators such as the LM317 do require a small minimum load (a few mA, usually supplied by the divider itself) so the reference stays biased; that is a design footnote, not one of the headline ratings."}

{"core": "Packaging the voltage reference, error amplifier, output-sensing resistors and transistors, and the series pass element all on one die with only input, output and common pins is exactly the definition of a three-terminal regulator.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A Zener regulator is just a series resistor and a Zener diode; it has a reference but no error amplifier, no sensing network and no pass element, so its regulation is limited by the Zener's dynamic resistance.", "why_tempting": "The Zener is the reference inside many regulators, so the learner conflates the simplest shunt regulator with the integrated series device that contains one."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "An op-amp regulator is a discrete implementation of the same loop using a separate op-amp, reference and external pass transistor; the blocks exist but are not in one package.", "why_tempting": "It is functionally the same architecture; the question hinges on the words in one package, which the discrete op-amp version fails."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A switching regulator does use a reference and error amplifier, but its power element is a switch driven by PWM through an inductor and catch diode, not a linear pass element, and it typically needs external L, C and diode.", "why_tempting": "Switching controllers also contain references and error amplifiers, and some are three-pin devices, so the feature list looks like a match if you skip the words pass element."}], "concept": "All closed-loop regulators share a signal path: reference → error amplifier → control element → output → sense divider → back to the amplifier. What distinguishes the categories is the control element and the level of integration. A Zener regulator has no loop at all; its output follows the Zener voltage plus I × r_z, where r_z is the diode's dynamic resistance, so load changes show up directly as output changes. A discrete op-amp regulator closes the loop with a separate amplifier and an external pass transistor and can achieve excellent regulation, but it is a board-level circuit. A switching regulator closes the loop by varying duty cycle D so that V_out ≈ D × V_in (buck), storing energy in an inductor; the pass element is a saturating switch, not a dissipative device. The three-terminal regulator takes the linear loop and integrates everything, including thermal and current protection, into a single component. Recognizing the component list in the question as the linear-loop block diagram, plus the phrase in one package, selects the integrated part.", "worked_example": "Compare load regulation for 100 mA to 500 mA load steps. Zener regulator with r_z = 5 Ω: ΔV = 0.4 A × 5 Ω = 2 V of droop, terrible. Three-terminal regulator with loop gain of about 1000 and the same effective open-loop output resistance: ΔV ≈ 2 V / 1000 = 2 mV. The difference is entirely the error amplifier and pass element the Zener design lacks, which is why the question's list of internal blocks points to the integrated regulator.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: any regulator containing a Zener or a reference is a Zener regulator. Correction: a Zener regulator is the open-loop shunt circuit; once a reference drives an error amplifier and a pass transistor inside one package, it is a three-terminal (linear series) regulator.", "link": "section 4", "edge_cases": "Modern three-terminal parts almost always use a bandgap reference rather than a true Zener, and LDO variants add a PNP or PMOS pass element with an external output capacitor whose ESR affects loop stability, something the classic 78xx never cared about."}

{"core": "Electronic (closed-loop) regulators divide into linear regulators, where a pass element operates in its active region and dissipates the input-output difference, and switching regulators, where the control element is switched fully on and off at high frequency and an LC network averages the result.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Non-linear is not a regulator category; every regulator's control law is arguably non-linear, and the term does not describe the switching architecture that is the actual second family.", "why_tempting": "If one category is called linear, the obvious opposite seems to be non-linear; it is a word-pairing guess rather than an engineering one."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Stiff describes a supply with low output impedance, which is a property any good regulator has; it is a description of performance, not a circuit family.", "why_tempting": "The question's phrase about holding voltage constant under large current changes is the definition of a stiff supply, so the adjective gets mistaken for a category name."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Switching is correct but non-linear is not a recognized class; the dissipative, continuously-conducting family is called linear.", "why_tempting": "A switching regulator is non-linear in operation, so the learner may think non-linear is a synonym and then needs a second category to pair it with."}], "concept": "In a linear regulator the pass transistor behaves as a variable resistor controlled by the error amplifier. The output is clean because nothing switches, but efficiency is η = V_out / V_in at best, and the dissipated power is (V_in − V_out) × I_load. In a switching regulator the control element is driven as a switch at tens of kHz to MHz; because a saturated switch has near-zero voltage across it and an open switch carries near-zero current, dissipation is small and efficiency of 85 to 95 percent is routine. The inductor and capacitor average the chopped waveform: for a buck converter V_out = D × V_in, for a boost V_out = V_in / (1 − D), and the error amplifier regulates by adjusting duty cycle D rather than a transistor's operating point. The price is switching ripple at the clock frequency and its harmonics, which is why the question frames the extremely low ripple case as the realm of the closed-loop (and usually linear) regulator, and why ham stations often follow a switcher with a linear post-regulator for sensitive receive stages.", "worked_example": "Supply 13.8 V at 20 A from a 24 V source. Linear: dissipation = (24 − 13.8) × 20 = 204 W, efficiency 13.8/24 = 58 percent, and a huge heatsink. Switching buck at D = 13.8/24 = 0.575 and 90 percent efficiency: input power = 276/0.9 = 307 W, loss about 31 W. Same regulated output voltage, same feedback principle, but one family throws away 204 W and the other 31 W, which is exactly why both categories exist.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the opposite of a linear regulator is a non-linear regulator. Correction: the two electronic regulator families are linear (dissipative pass element in its active region) and switching (pass element as an on/off switch with LC averaging).", "link": "section 4", "edge_cases": "Linear regulators themselves split into series and shunt types, and switchers into buck, boost, buck-boost and isolated topologies; the question asks for the two top-level categories only."}

{"core": "The integrated device that bundles a reference, high-gain error amplifier, temperature-compensated sensing resistors and transistors, and a series pass element behind only input, output and common pins is universally called a three-terminal regulator.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "No common regulator family is named by a 24-pin count; devices with that many pins are controllers or supervisors, not the simple integrated series regulator described.", "why_tempting": "Many ICs do come in 24-pin DIPs, and the long list of internal blocks suggests a complex, many-pinned part."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Six-terminal regulator is not a standard category; adding pins (enable, sense, bypass) exists on some LDOs but does not define the class the question describes.", "why_tempting": "Some precision regulators do expose extra pins for remote sense or noise bypass, so a learner who has seen such datasheets may over-count."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Nine-pin is not a regulator class; the term appears in tube-socket nomenclature (noval), not in regulator naming.", "why_tempting": "The numbers in the options are all plausible IC pin counts, so without recalling that the name derives from the minimum three connections, any could seem right."}], "concept": "The name reflects the minimum interface a series regulator needs: a node to take unregulated power in, a node to deliver regulated power out, and a common reference (ground for fixed parts, the adjust pin for adjustable ones). Everything else is internal. The temperature compensation mentioned in the question matters because V_out = V_ref × (1 + R1/R2) only holds if V_ref and the divider ratio are stable with temperature; integrating the sense resistors on the same die as the reference means they drift together and the ratio cancels, and a bandgap reference is designed so the positive tempco of a ΔV_BE term cancels the negative tempco of a V_BE term. The high-gain amplifier reduces load and line regulation errors by roughly the loop gain. The pass element is sized for the current rating and is usually a Darlington or power PNP/PMOS. Over-temperature and current-limit circuits are also included but do not add pins, which is why the three-pin interface survives even in modern parts.", "worked_example": "Thought experiment: build the same regulator discretely with a TL431 reference, an op-amp, two metal-film resistors and a TIP31 pass transistor. You will have at least eight external connections and the resistors will have a different tempco than the reference, so the output drifts perhaps 50 ppm/°C. Integrate all of it on one die with matched resistors and a bandgap, and the drift drops to around 10 ppm/°C while the pin count collapses to three. Same loop, but the integration both names the part and improves it.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: more internal functions must mean more pins. Correction: the internal reference, amplifier, sensing network and pass element all sit between the same three external nodes, so the device needs only input, output and common, hence three-terminal.", "link": "section 4", "edge_cases": "Some three-terminal regulators are sold in five-pin packages with enable or sense pins, and a TO-3 or TO-220 tab is often electrically the common or output pin, so count functional terminals, not package leads."}

{"core": "The pass transistor in a series regulator carries the full load current while standing off the difference between the unregulated input and the regulated output, so its dissipation is P = (V_in − V_out) × I_load, directly proportional to both the load current and the input-output differential.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Dissipation rises, not falls, with both load current and voltage differential; an inverse relationship would mean a heavily loaded regulator with large headroom runs cool, the opposite of reality.", "why_tempting": "Inverting a proportionality is the classic exam slip, and the learner may confuse the regulator's output impedance (which does fall with loop gain) with its dissipation."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "A Zener in a regulator sees a fixed reverse voltage equal to its rating and is a reference, not part of the power path; peak inverse voltage is a rectifier-diode rating and has nothing to do with pass-transistor heating.", "why_tempting": "Zener diodes and PIV are both power-supply vocabulary, so the option sounds like it belongs even though it mixes a reference-side diode with a rectifier-side specification."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Load voltage is held constant by the regulator and does not independently set dissipation; the variables that matter are current and differential, and the relationship is direct, not indirect.", "why_tempting": "It contains the correct phrase input/output differential and swaps in load voltage for load current, which is easy to miss when scanning."}], "concept": "In a series linear regulator the pass transistor is in series with the load, so the same current flows through both. Kirchhoff's voltage law puts V_CE = V_in − V_out across the transistor. Power dissipated in any element is V × I, giving P_pass = (V_in − V_out) × I_load. This is the fundamental efficiency limitation of linear regulation: efficiency η = P_out / P_in = V_out × I / (V_in × I) = V_out / V_in, independent of current. Note that V_in here is the instantaneous unregulated input, which includes ripple; at the ripple valley you need V_in,min ≥ V_out + V_dropout to stay in regulation, while at the ripple peak the dissipation is highest. Because the dissipation scales with current, heatsink design must use the worst-case load current and the highest expected line voltage. Shunt regulators invert this picture: their dissipation is highest at no load, since the shunt element absorbs the current the load is not drawing.", "worked_example": "A 13.8 V regulator fed from a rectifier-filter that sits at 20 V, delivering 5 A to a transceiver. P_pass = (20 − 13.8) × 5 = 6.2 × 5 = 31 W. Double the load current to 10 A: 62 W. Raise the line voltage so the input is 24 V at 10 A: (24 − 13.8) × 10 = 102 W. Each variable scales the heat linearly. A TO-3 transistor at 1.5 °C/W junction-to-case with a 0.5 °C/W heatsink and 25 °C ambient would reach 25 + 102 × 2 = 229 °C, far above the 150 °C limit, so the designer must reduce the differential, add pass transistors in parallel, or improve the heatsink.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the regulator's output voltage determines how hot it runs. Correction: heat is set by the voltage dropped across the pass transistor (input minus output) multiplied by the current through it; a lower output with the same input runs hotter, not cooler.", "link": "Ohm's Law & Power", "edge_cases": "At very low load the pass transistor dissipation falls toward zero, but the regulator's own quiescent current (a few mA at V_in) still produces a small constant loss; and in LDOs using a PNP pass element the base current adds to the dissipation at high load."}

{"core": "A feedback regulator can only correct what it measures; the output is held at the reference value, with minimum ripple and tightest regulation, precisely at the node the sampling divider or error amplifier senses, because any voltage drop between that node and the load lies outside the loop and is not corrected.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "The load is connected through wiring and connectors whose resistance drops voltage in proportion to current; unless the sense point is moved to the load (remote sensing) those drops are uncorrected.", "why_tempting": "Intuitively the regulator exists to serve the load, so the learner assumes the load terminals are where the specification is met."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "The pass transistor's emitter is usually close to but not identical with the sense node; any series element (current-sense resistor, fuse, output choke) between it and the sense point means the pass transistor output is not the regulated point.", "why_tempting": "In the simplest textbook circuit the sense divider is right at the pass transistor emitter, so the two points coincide and the distinction is invisible."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A transistor has no secondary winding; the phrase belongs to a transformer and describes no node in a regulator.", "why_tempting": "Power-supply vocabulary (secondary, pass transistor) is being recombined into a plausible-sounding but meaningless phrase."}], "concept": "Negative feedback forces the sensed quantity toward the reference. The loop sees V_sense = V_out,node × R2/(R1+R2) and drives the pass element until V_sense = V_ref, so the node where R1 attaches is held to V_ref × (1 + R1/R2) regardless of load, with residual error of roughly ΔV_open/(1 + A×β) where A is amplifier gain and β the divider ratio. Downstream of that node you have wire resistance R_w, connector resistance and sometimes a fuse; the load sees V_load = V_node − I_load × R_w, and the loop cannot know about that drop. Ripple behaves the same way: the loop cancels ripple at the sense node, but ripple current flowing through downstream impedance can reappear. This is the motivation for four-wire or remote sensing in bench and high-current supplies, where separate sense leads move the regulated node out to the load terminals. It also explains why a current-sense shunt should sit inside the loop or its drop will degrade regulation.", "worked_example": "A 13.8 V regulator senses at its own output terminals. The run to the radio is 3 m of 14 AWG two-conductor, about 8.3 mΩ/m per conductor, so round-trip R_w ≈ 6 m × 0.0083 = 0.05 Ω. At 20 A transmit current the drop is 20 × 0.05 = 1.0 V, so the radio sees 12.8 V on key-down and 13.8 V on receive: 1 V of load regulation error that the supply's datasheet 10 mV figure never mentions. Move the sense leads to the radio end and the supply raises its terminal voltage to 14.8 V on transmit, keeping 13.8 V at the radio.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a regulator holds its rated voltage everywhere on the output side. Correction: it holds the voltage only at the sensed node; everything between that node and the load is outside the loop and adds I × R drop and ripple the regulator cannot see.", "link": "section 4", "edge_cases": "Remote sensing introduces its own hazards: if a sense lead opens, the loop sees zero and drives the output to maximum, so practical supplies tie the sense pins to the output through resistors as a fallback."}

{"core": "The load resistance of a supply is defined as the output voltage divided by the total current the supply must deliver, and that total includes the bleeder resistor current because the bleeder is a permanent load on the output just like the external circuit.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Ideal is not a defined resistance in supply design; an ideal supply would have zero internal resistance, which is a different concept from the resistance the output sees.", "why_tempting": "The word ideal appears in discussions of ideal sources and Thevenin models, so it feels like supply vocabulary."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Rectifier resistance would refer to the forward resistance of the diodes, a small internal quantity, not the ratio of output voltage to drawn current.", "why_tempting": "Rectifier is a prominent supply component and the question is about a resistance in a supply, so component names feel like candidates."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Differential resistance is the slope dV/dI of a device curve, used for Zener dynamic resistance or a supply's output impedance; it is a small-signal slope, not V/I_total.", "why_tempting": "Output impedance of a supply is a differential quantity and is also computed from voltage and current, so the two ratios get confused."}], "concept": "From the supply's point of view every path from output to return is part of the load. R_load,effective = V_out / (I_external + I_bleeder). The bleeder is there for two reasons: it discharges the filter capacitors after switch-off for safety, and it provides a minimum load that keeps a capacitor-input filter from soaring toward the peak transformer voltage when the external load is removed. Both effects follow from that minimum current. The bleeder also factors into regulation arithmetic: the percentage regulation of a supply, (V_no-load − V_full-load)/V_full-load × 100, improves if the bleeder draws a meaningful fraction of full load, because the no-load point is no longer truly zero current. This contrasts with the supply's internal (Thevenin) resistance, which is dV/dI looking back into the terminals and is what you would call differential or output resistance.", "worked_example": "A 400 V supply feeds a 100 mA amplifier stage and has a 20 kΩ bleeder. Bleeder current = 400/20000 = 20 mA. Total current = 120 mA. Load resistance as defined here = 400 V / 0.120 A = 3333 Ω, not 400/0.1 = 4000 Ω. Bleeder dissipation = 400² / 20000 = 8 W, so a 20 W resistor is appropriate. If the amplifier is unkeyed, the supply still sees 20 kΩ, which limits the capacitor-input filter from rising to the transformer peak and also drains the capacitors in a few time constants once the mains is removed.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the bleeder is a parasitic that does not count as load. Correction: the bleeder is a constant load that the supply must furnish current to, so it is included in the total current used to define the load resistance and it sets the minimum-load condition for regulation.", "link": "Ohm's Law & Power", "edge_cases": "In regulated supplies with an active loop the bleeder's regulation role largely disappears, but its safety discharge role remains, and in a shunt regulator the shunt element itself plays the minimum-load part."}

{"core": "Static regulation describes how well a supply holds its output when the load resistance changes slowly or is held at a new steady value, so it is the steady-state figure measured after all transients have settled.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Active regulation would describe regulation by an active device (transistor loop) as opposed to passive filtering; it says nothing about the time scale of the load change.", "why_tempting": "Electronic regulators are active circuits, so active sounds like a regulation type rather than a description of hardware."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Analog regulation is not a defined term in supply specifications; it would at best distinguish linear from digital control and has no relation to long-term versus short-term load changes.", "why_tempting": "Analog versus digital is a familiar pairing, so it gets slotted in as an invented antonym."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Dynamic regulation is the complementary term for short-term, transient load changes, the response within microseconds to milliseconds of a step, not the long-term steady-state figure.", "why_tempting": "Static and dynamic are the actual pair, so the only risk is swapping them; dynamic sounds more impressive and gets picked by default."}], "concept": "Static regulation is quantified as load regulation = (V_no-load − V_full-load) / V_full-load × 100 percent, measured with DC loads after settling. It depends on the supply's DC output resistance: V_out = V_oc − I × R_out, so a lower R_out gives better static regulation. In an unregulated capacitor-input supply R_out is dominated by transformer winding resistance, rectifier drop and the capacitor's inability to hold the peak under load; in a closed-loop regulator R_out is the open-loop value divided by loop gain and can be milliohms. Dynamic regulation, by contrast, is the response to a load step faster than the loop or filter can follow, governed by the output capacitor's ability to supply charge, I = C × dV/dt, and by the loop's bandwidth. A supply can have excellent static regulation and poor dynamic regulation if its loop is slow and its output capacitor small, which is exactly the SSB and CW case treated in the following questions.", "worked_example": "Measure a 13.8 V supply at 0.5 A: 13.80 V. Increase the load to 20 A and wait a few seconds: 13.62 V. Static (load) regulation = (13.80 − 13.62)/13.62 × 100 = 1.3 percent, and the DC output resistance is 0.18 V / 19.5 A ≈ 9 mΩ. This number is independent of how fast the load changed; if the same step were applied in 10 μs and the output momentarily dipped to 13.0 V before recovering, that 0.8 V dip would be the dynamic regulation figure, a different measurement entirely.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: regulation is a single number. Correction: static regulation is the steady-state change for slow or sustained load changes (set by DC output resistance), while dynamic regulation is the transient response to fast changes (set by output capacitance and loop speed); the two are specified and improved separately.", "link": "section 4", "mnemonic": "Static = steady state (both start with st); dynamic = during the change."}

{"core": "Dynamic regulation is the supply's ability to hold its output during short-term, rapid changes in load current, such as the keying of a CW transmitter or the syllabic peaks of SSB, before the slower feedback loop and filter have time to respond.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Analog regulation is not a recognized specification term; it would describe the technology of the control loop, not the time scale of the disturbance.", "why_tempting": "It sounds technical and pairs naturally with digital, but neither word refers to a regulation category."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Active regulation would mean regulation by a transistor loop rather than passive filtering; it is a description of hardware, not of short-term versus long-term load behaviour.", "why_tempting": "A supply that responds quickly to load changes feels active, so the adjective gets mistaken for the technical term."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Static regulation is the steady-state figure for long-term or sustained load changes, the opposite time scale from the short-term changes the question asks about.", "why_tempting": "Static and dynamic are the real pair, and the question's phrasing about load resistance echoes the static-regulation definition, inviting the swap."}], "concept": "When load current steps from I1 to I2 in a time short compared with the regulator loop's response, the output capacitor must supply the difference. The instantaneous dip has two parts: an ESR step ΔV_ESR = ΔI × ESR, and a capacitive sag ΔV_C = ΔI × Δt / C over the time Δt until the loop or filter catches up. Dynamic regulation is therefore improved by lowering ESR, raising C, and widening the loop bandwidth. In an unregulated supply there is no loop at all and the capacitor plus transformer must ride through the step until the next rectifier conduction peak, which at 120 Hz is up to 8.3 ms away. For SSB, the envelope changes at syllabic rates of a few hertz to a few hundred hertz, and for CW the keying edges are a few milliseconds, so both demand good dynamic regulation; poor dynamic regulation shows up as a chirp on CW (frequency pulling as the oscillator supply sags on key-down) or as flat-topping and distortion on SSB peaks.", "worked_example": "An SSB amplifier draws 2 A idle and 20 A on voice peaks from a supply with 10,000 μF and 30 mΩ ESR, and the loop takes 1 ms to respond. ESR step: 18 A × 0.03 Ω = 0.54 V. Capacitive sag in 1 ms: ΔV = I × t / C = 18 × 0.001 / 0.01 = 1.8 V. Total momentary dip ≈ 2.3 V on a 13.8 V rail, which can trip low-voltage alarms and distort the first syllable. Raising C to 47,000 μF cuts the sag to 0.38 V and a low-ESR capacitor cuts the step to 0.1 V, improving dynamic regulation fivefold without touching static regulation.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: good steady-state regulation guarantees good performance on keyed or voice loads. Correction: fast load changes are handled by stored charge and loop speed, not DC output resistance; dynamic regulation is a separate figure governed by I = C × dV/dt and ESR.", "link": "Series / Parallel R & C", "mnemonic": "Dynamic = during the change; static = steady state."}

{"core": "Short-term load steps are supplied from the charge stored in the output capacitor until the loop or rectifier can respond, and since ΔV = I × Δt / C, a larger output capacitor produces a smaller voltage excursion for a given current step and duration, which is what better dynamic regulation means.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Increasing the bleeder resistance reduces bleeder current, which reduces the minimum load and makes the no-load voltage rise more, slightly worsening regulation; it does nothing to supply transient current.", "why_tempting": "The bleeder was just introduced as part of load regulation, so the learner reaches for it; also a bigger number sounds like more of a good thing."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "A larger choke opposes changes in current (V = L × di/dt), so when the load suddenly demands more current the choke resists delivering it and the output sags harder; chokes help ripple and static regulation in choke-input filters but hurt transient response.", "why_tempting": "Chokes improve regulation in choke-input filters, a true Basic-level fact that applies to static, not dynamic, regulation."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "The input (first) filter capacitor sits ahead of the choke or regulator and mainly sets ripple and peak charging current; its charge cannot reach the load quickly through the intervening series impedance, so it has little effect on transient response at the output.", "why_tempting": "A capacitor is the right component family, and in a plain capacitor-input filter the first capacitor is the output capacitor, so the distinction between input and output capacitor is easy to blur."}], "concept": "Model the supply during a fast load step as the output capacitor alone, because the regulator loop (or the next rectifier peak in an unregulated supply) is too slow to contribute. The capacitor relation i = C × dv/dt rearranges to ΔV = ΔI × Δt / C: the sag during the loop's response time Δt is inversely proportional to C. Add the ESR step ΔI × R_ESR and you have the complete first-order dynamic regulation model. The choke, by contrast, stores energy in current rather than voltage; its V = L × di/dt means a sudden demand for more current develops a voltage across the choke that subtracts from the output until the current ramps up, so a bigger choke worsens the transient. The bleeder only matters for the DC operating point. This is why high-current ham supplies, even switchers with fast loops, carry tens of thousands of microfarads at the output, and why adding a large low-ESR capacitor at the radio end of a long DC lead is an effective fix for keying-induced voltage dips.", "worked_example": "CW keying steps the load from 1 A to 15 A in under 1 ms; the regulator loop needs 500 μs to recover. With C = 4,700 μF: ΔV = 14 A × 500 μs / 4,700 μF = 14 × 0.0005 / 0.0047 ≈ 1.5 V dip. Replace with C = 22,000 μF: ΔV = 14 × 0.0005 / 0.022 ≈ 0.32 V. The static regulation (measured seconds later) is unchanged in both cases; only the dynamic figure improved, by the ratio of the capacitances.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: anything that improves ripple or static regulation also improves transient response, so a bigger choke must help. Correction: inductors resist current changes and worsen load-step response; only the output capacitor's stored charge (and low ESR) supplies fast current demands.", "link": "Series / Parallel R & C", "edge_cases": "Beyond a point, more capacitance hurts: the regulator loop may become unstable with very large output C, and the inrush charging current at switch-on stresses the rectifiers; practical designs balance C against ESR, loop phase margin and inrush limiting."}

{"core": "SSB and CW loads change current abruptly at syllabic and keying rates, and the output capacitor is the only element that can supply those current steps before the rectifier or loop responds; increasing the output capacitance reduces the momentary voltage dip ΔV = I × Δt / C and thereby improves dynamic regulation.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Capacitors in series combine as 1/C_total = 1/C1 + 1/C2, so the total capacitance falls below the smallest one; this reduces stored charge and worsens dynamic regulation.", "why_tempting": "Series stacking is used in high-voltage supplies to get a sufficient voltage rating, so the learner may remember series capacitors as a supply design technique and forget it lowers capacitance."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Reversing an electrolytic's polarity destroys its oxide dielectric, causing heavy leakage, heating and eventual venting or rupture; it does not increase capacitance.", "why_tempting": "It is phrased with enough detail to sound like a deliberate circuit trick, and a tired reader may skim over the words negative to positive."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A battery in series with the capacitor adds a DC offset and the battery's internal resistance into the charge path; it does not increase the capacitance available to the load, and a battery across the output (parallel) would be the only sensible way to add energy storage.", "why_tempting": "Batteries do stiffen supplies when floated in parallel, so the series/parallel distinction is the trap."}], "concept": "During the microseconds-to-milliseconds after a load step, the output capacitor acts as the voltage source. From Q = C × V, a current I drawn for a time Δt removes charge ΔQ = I × Δt and drops the voltage by ΔV = ΔQ / C. Doubling C halves the dip. Parallel capacitors add (C_total = C1 + C2) and also halve the effective ESR, which further reduces the ESR step ΔI × R_ESR, so paralleling several moderate capacitors is often better than one large one. Series capacitors do the reverse and are used only when a single part cannot withstand the voltage, with equalizing resistors across each to balance the DC split. For SSB the PEP-to-average ratio means current swings of ten to one at syllabic rates; a supply that sags on each peak flat-tops the envelope and generates splatter, so dynamic regulation is a spectral-purity issue, not just a voltage one. For CW the same sag can pull a VFO, producing chirp.", "worked_example": "A 50 V supply for a solid-state amplifier delivers 0.5 A idle and 12 A on SSB peaks; peaks rise in about 2 ms before the 120 Hz rectifier ripple refill arrives. With one 10,000 μF capacitor: ΔV = 11.5 A × 0.002 s / 0.01 F = 2.3 V. Parallel a second 10,000 μF: C = 20,000 μF, ΔV = 1.15 V, and ESR halves too. Put the same two in series instead: C = 5,000 μF and ΔV = 4.6 V, twice as bad as the original. The direction of improvement is unambiguous: increase (parallel) capacitance.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: more capacitors always means more capacitance. Correction: only parallel capacitors add; series connection reduces total capacitance and is used solely for voltage rating, so dynamic regulation improves with more parallel output capacitance.", "link": "Series / Parallel R & C", "edge_cases": "Very large output capacitance raises switch-on inrush current and can exceed the rectifier's surge rating, so supplies with tens of thousands of microfarads often include an NTC thermistor or relay-bypassed series resistor for soft start."}

{"core": "Four diodes arranged in a bridge steer both half-cycles of the transformer secondary current through the load in the same direction, producing full-wave rectified DC without a centre-tapped winding; that function is rectification.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Equalization refers to balancing voltage across series-connected capacitors or diodes with resistors; a bridge does not balance anything across the transformer, it converts AC to pulsating DC.", "why_tempting": "Equalizing resistors are a real supply technique and are often placed near the diodes in high-voltage designs, so the words co-occur."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Impedance matching between secondary and filter is not a function of the rectifier; the diodes are switches with near-zero forward impedance when conducting, and the filter's input impedance is set by its own L and C.", "why_tempting": "Matching is a pervasive concept in the Advanced syllabus (pi networks, feedlines), so it gets grafted onto any interface between two blocks."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A tuning network requires reactive elements (L and C) chosen for resonance; diodes are non-linear switches and nothing in a bridge resonates.", "why_tempting": "Four components in a diamond arrangement look superficially like a bridge circuit used for measurement or a balanced network, so the shape misleads."}], "concept": "In a bridge, on the positive half-cycle two diagonally opposite diodes conduct, routing current from the top of the secondary through the load and back to the bottom; on the negative half-cycle the other pair conducts and routes current through the load in the same direction. The output is full-wave, with ripple at twice the line frequency (120 Hz for 60 Hz mains), and the entire secondary winding is used on both half-cycles, giving better transformer utilization than a centre-tapped full-wave circuit, which uses only half the winding at a time. The costs are two diode drops in series (about 1.4 V for silicon) instead of one, and each diode must withstand a peak inverse voltage equal to the secondary peak, V_PIV ≈ 1.41 × V_rms, compared with 2.83 × V_rms per diode in the centre-tap circuit. With a capacitor-input filter the output approaches 1.41 × V_rms minus the two diode drops at light load. Bridge rectification is the front end of nearly every regulated supply, so this question is placing the first block in the chain: transformer → bridge → filter → regulator → load.", "worked_example": "A 12.6 V rms secondary feeds a bridge and a large capacitor. Peak = 12.6 × 1.414 = 17.8 V; subtract two silicon drops of about 0.7 V each: unloaded DC ≈ 16.4 V. Ripple frequency = 2 × 60 = 120 Hz. Each diode sees PIV ≈ 17.8 V, so 50 V diodes are ample. Had a centre-tapped 25.2 V transformer with two diodes been used for the same output, each diode would need to withstand about 35.6 V, and only half the winding would carry current at any instant.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a bridge of four diodes is some kind of balancing or matching network between transformer and filter. Correction: it is simply a full-wave rectifier that uses the whole secondary on both half-cycles without a centre tap; its only job is turning AC into pulsating DC.", "link": "section 4", "edge_cases": "At very low voltages (3.3 V or 5 V supplies) the two-diode drop of a bridge is a significant efficiency loss, which is why Schottky bridges or synchronous (MOSFET) rectification are used there."}

{"core": "Fuses are placed in the AC primary line before the transformer and often again in the DC output line, so they are the only components in a regulated supply that conduct alternating current at the input and direct current near the output while performing the same protective function in both places.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Capacitors in a supply are the filter elements and sit after the rectifier on the DC side; a capacitor by definition blocks DC and would not be placed in series in the primary line.", "why_tempting": "Capacitors do pass AC and block DC, so the learner may read the question as asking which component distinguishes AC from DC behaviour rather than which one is found in both locations."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Diodes are the rectifier and sit between the transformer and the filter; they are not placed before the transformer in the AC line and are not series elements before the output.", "why_tempting": "Diodes are the component that converts AC to DC, so a question mentioning both AC and DC seems to point at them."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Chokes are filter inductors on the DC side between rectifier and output; they are never placed in the mains primary of a typical supply.", "why_tempting": "A choke does conduct DC while opposing AC ripple, so the AC-and-DC phrasing can be misread as describing a choke's filtering behaviour."}], "concept": "Fuses are current-operated protective elements and do not care whether the current is AC or DC; a fusible link heats according to I² × R × t and melts when the integrated energy exceeds its rating. In a regulated supply the primary fuse protects against transformer or rectifier faults and against fire if the filter capacitor shorts, and is rated for the primary current plus inrush margin, typically with a slow-blow characteristic to survive the transformer magnetizing inrush and capacitor charging surge. The output fuse protects the regulator and wiring against a shorted load and is rated near the maximum DC output current, often fast-acting. Because DC arcs do not self-extinguish at a current zero the way AC arcs do, DC fuses carry a separate DC voltage rating that must be respected; a fuse rated 250 V AC may be rated for only 32 V DC. The question is really a block-diagram question: knowing that every other listed component lives in a single place in the chain while fuses appear at both ends.", "worked_example": "A 13.8 V 25 A supply draws about 25 × 13.8 / (0.8 × 120) ≈ 3.6 A rms from 120 V mains at 80 percent efficiency. Primary: 5 A slow-blow to ride through inrush. Secondary/output: 30 A fast fuse rated for at least 32 V DC. Both conduct continuously in normal operation, one carrying 60 Hz AC and the other smooth DC; both open on I² × t overload. No other component in the supply appears in both the AC input path and the DC output path.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the question is asking which component converts AC to DC. Correction: it asks which component is found conducting AC ahead of the transformer and DC ahead of the output, and only the protective fuses occupy both positions.", "link": "section 4", "edge_cases": "Fuses in the DC output of a regulated supply must be sized above the regulator's own current limit or they will never open, and their DC voltage rating must exceed the rail voltage because DC arcs are harder to interrupt than AC."}

{"core": "In the regulated-supply chain the electrolytic filter capacitor smooths the rectifier output into DC with residual ripple, and that filtered but unregulated DC is what feeds the voltage regulator, which removes the remaining ripple and holds the output constant.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Solid-state bypass circuit is not a block in a power supply; bypass capacitors shunt RF or audio around a stage and have no place between a filter and a regulator.", "why_tempting": "The regulator does contain solid-state devices and many supplies have bypass capacitors, so the phrase sounds like supply vocabulary."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "DC power delivery does not use impedance matching networks; the load is simply connected to the regulated output, and the regulator's low output impedance is what makes it a good voltage source.", "why_tempting": "Matching networks appear between every RF stage in the transmitter sections, so the learner applies the pattern to the supply."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A pi filter (C-L-C) is itself a filter stage; if present it precedes the regulator or forms the filter itself, and the question's single electrolytic filter capacitor output goes on to the regulator, not to another pi filter.", "why_tempting": "Pi filters are a legitimate supply filter topology, so it seems natural that one filter feeds another."}], "concept": "The regulated supply is a chain: transformer → rectifier → filter → regulator → load. The filter capacitor charges to near the rectified peak on each conduction pulse and discharges into the regulator between pulses, producing a sawtooth ripple of roughly V_ripple ≈ I_load / (f_ripple × C) for a capacitor-input filter, where f_ripple is 120 Hz for full-wave on 60 Hz mains. The regulator's job is to take that rippled DC and output a fixed voltage; its ripple rejection (often 60 to 80 dB for a three-terminal part) divides the residual ripple by a thousand to ten thousand. The design constraint tying the two blocks together is that the ripple valley V_peak − V_ripple must stay above V_out + V_dropout, or the regulator drops out of regulation at the bottom of every ripple cycle and the output shows 120 Hz hum. So the filter capacitor is sized not for a clean output (the regulator does that) but for enough valley headroom at full load.", "worked_example": "A 7812 needs 2 V of headroom. The bridge and capacitor give a 17 V peak. At 1 A load with C = 2,200 μF: V_ripple ≈ 1 / (120 × 0.0022) ≈ 3.8 V, so the valley is 17 − 3.8 = 13.2 V, below the 14 V the regulator needs, and hum appears. Raise C to 4,700 μF: V_ripple ≈ 1.8 V, valley = 15.2 V, regulation holds. The regulator then attenuates the 1.8 V ripple by about 70 dB to under 1 mV at the output. The capacitor's output clearly feeds the regulator, and the two are designed together.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the filter capacitor must produce clean DC on its own. Correction: the filter only needs to keep the ripple valley above the regulator's minimum input; the regulator that it feeds is what removes the remaining ripple.", "link": "section 4", "edge_cases": "The simple V_ripple = I / (f × C) estimate assumes the capacitor supplies the full load over the entire half-period; at heavy loads with large capacitors the rectifier conducts for a larger fraction of the cycle and the real ripple is somewhat less, but the formula is conservative for design."}

{"core": "A diode connected from the regulator output back to its input (cathode to input, anode to output) is reverse biased in normal operation and conducts only if the output ever rises above the input, which happens when the input is shorted or collapses quickly while the output capacitor still holds charge; it gives that charge a safe path and prevents reverse current from destroying the regulator's pass transistor.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A diode has no useful RF bypass function; bypassing is done with capacitors to ground, and the diode in question sits between input and output, not to ground.", "why_tempting": "Regulators often have small capacitors at input and output for stability, so the learner assumes the extra component is also about bypassing."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A diode adds no capacitance of consequence (a few pF of junction capacitance) and cannot store energy for the load.", "why_tempting": "The word capacity sounds like a supply benefit, and extra components across a regulator are often capacitors."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Primary-side voltage fluctuations are handled by the regulator's line regulation and by the filter capacitor's headroom; a diode from output to input cannot influence anything upstream of the regulator.", "why_tempting": "Protecting the regulator is the right theme, and line fluctuations are a real supply concern, so the learner picks the familiar disturbance rather than the specific reverse-voltage hazard."}], "concept": "A linear regulator's pass transistor is designed to conduct from input to output. If the input node falls below the output node, for example when the input is shorted, the input filter capacitor discharges faster than the output capacitor (large low-ESR output capacitors make this common), or the supply is switched off abruptly, the pass transistor's base-emitter or collector junction becomes reverse biased with the full output voltage across it. Many regulators tolerate only a few volts of reverse bias before the junction breaks down and the device is destroyed. The protection diode (typically a 1N4001 or similar rated above the output current for the discharge pulse) clamps V_out − V_in to about 0.7 V by conducting the output capacitor's charge back into the input node, where it dissipates harmlessly. The same idea applies to the adjust pin of an adjustable regulator when a large bypass capacitor sits on that pin: a second diode from adjust to output protects it. This is a specific instance of the general rule that any charge-storing element across a semiconductor needs a discharge path that does not run backwards through a junction.", "worked_example": "A 7812 has 1,000 μF at its input and 4,700 μF at its output, and the input is shorted by a fault. The input node drops to zero in microseconds; the output capacitor holding 12 V now sees the regulator's output pin at +12 V and input pin at 0 V, a 12 V reverse bias across the pass transistor, exceeding its roughly 7 V reverse rating. With a diode from output (anode) to input (cathode), the output capacitor discharges through the diode into the short, the reverse voltage across the regulator is clamped at about 0.7 V, and the 4,700 μF × 12 V = 56 mC of charge passes as a brief pulse well within a 1N4001's surge rating.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a regulator's output capacitor can never hurt the regulator because it is on the protected side. Correction: if the input collapses faster than the output, that capacitor drives current backwards through the pass transistor; the reverse-protection diode exists purely to carry that current around the regulator.", "link": "section 4", "edge_cases": "Fixed regulators with small output capacitors (under about 25 μF) and no large downstream reservoir usually do not need the diode; the hazard scales with output capacitance and with any low-impedance load that can hold the output up, such as a battery being charged."}

{"core": "A Hartley oscillator derives its feedback from a tapped inductor: the tank coil is split into two sections sharing a common tap (usually grounded or at the emitter), and the voltage across one section is returned to the active device's input in phase with the output, the inductive divider setting the feedback fraction.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A neutralizing capacitor is used in amplifiers to cancel internal plate-to-grid or collector-to-base feedback so the stage does not oscillate; it is the opposite of a deliberate feedback element and identifies no oscillator type.", "why_tempting": "Neutralization and oscillation are both about feedback through the device, so the term gets associated with oscillator circuits even though its purpose is suppression."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "A capacitive divider across the tank is the signature of the Colpitts oscillator; the two topologies are duals, with the Hartley tapping the inductor and the Colpitts tapping the capacitance.", "why_tempting": "The Hartley and Colpitts are taught together and their feedback schemes are mirror images, so they are easily swapped."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Link coupling is a separate small winding used to couple energy into or out of a tank for output or input matching, not to close the oscillator's own feedback loop in the Hartley configuration.", "why_tempting": "A separate feedback winding does exist in the Armstrong (tickler) oscillator, so the learner may generalize that to any transformer-like coupling."}], "concept": "Any LC oscillator needs a resonant tank to set frequency and a feedback path that returns a fraction β of the output to the input with zero net phase shift and loop gain A × β ≥ 1 at start-up (Barkhausen criterion). In the Hartley, the tank is L1 + L2 in series resonating with C: f = 1 / (2π × √((L1 + L2 + 2M) × C)), where M is the mutual inductance if the sections share a core. The tap between L1 and L2 is at AC ground; the two coil ends are then at opposite phases relative to the tap, which provides the 180 degree inversion needed around an inverting (common-emitter or common-cathode) device. The feedback ratio is roughly L2/L1 (with mutual coupling adjusting it), and is fixed by the tap position, which is both a strength (one coil, one adjustment) and a weakness (the tap carries circulating current and its position affects Q). Because the frequency-setting element is a single coil that can be tuned with one variable capacitor across the whole winding, the Hartley was historically popular in simple VFOs, though the Colpitts family generally gives better stability.", "worked_example": "Design a 7 MHz Hartley tank: choose total L = 2 μH. Required C = 1 / ((2π × 7e6)² × 2e-6) ≈ 258 pF. Tap the coil so that L2 (the feedback section, from tap to the input end) is 0.4 μH and L1 is 1.6 μH, giving a feedback fraction of about 0.4/1.6 = 0.25. With a transistor providing voltage gain of 10 the loop gain is 2.5 at start-up, comfortably above 1, and the amplitude grows until device non-linearity reduces the effective gain to exactly 1/0.25 = 4. If you flip to a Colpitts you would keep the same total C and L but obtain the 0.25 ratio from two series capacitors instead.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the feedback element is just whatever couples the output back, so coil, capacitor and link are interchangeable labels. Correction: the oscillator's name is defined by which tank element is tapped for feedback; a tapped coil is Hartley, a capacitive divider is Colpitts, a separate tickler winding is Armstrong.", "link": "Reactance & Resonance", "mnemonic": "Hartley has an L in it for the inductor tap; Colpitts has a C for the capacitor divider."}

{"core": "In a Colpitts oscillator the tank capacitance is split into two capacitors in series, and the junction between them is the common (ground or emitter) point; the voltage across one capacitor is fed back to the active device's input, so a capacitive voltage divider closes the feedback loop.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A tapped coil is the Hartley arrangement; in the Colpitts the inductor is a single untapped element and the division is done on the capacitive side.", "why_tempting": "Hartley and Colpitts are duals of each other and are taught in the same breath, so their feedback elements are easily transposed."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Neutralizing capacitors are added to amplifiers to cancel unwanted internal feedback and prevent oscillation; they are not part of any intentional oscillator feedback network.", "why_tempting": "Both oscillation and neutralization involve feedback capacitance through the device, so the term floats into oscillator questions."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Link coupling uses a separate low-impedance winding for input or output coupling to a tank; it is not how the Colpitts returns signal to its input.", "why_tempting": "A tickler-winding (Armstrong) oscillator does use a separate coil for feedback, so a learner may expect transformer-style coupling in general."}], "concept": "The Colpitts tank is L in parallel with the series combination C1 and C2: f = 1 / (2π × √(L × C_eq)) with C_eq = C1 × C2 / (C1 + C2). With the C1-C2 junction at AC ground, the two ends of the tank swing in opposite phase, which supplies the inversion needed around a common-emitter stage; alternatively, in the common-base or common-collector forms the divider provides a non-inverted fraction to a non-inverting stage. The feedback fraction is β ≈ C1/C2 (voltage across C2 relative to voltage across C1, since series capacitors divide voltage inversely to capacitance). Capacitive dividers have two advantages over the tapped coil: capacitors are cheaper to make stable and low-loss than tapped inductors, and making C1 and C2 large relative to the transistor's internal capacitances swamps those device capacitances, so temperature and bias changes in the transistor have less effect on frequency. That swamping is why the Colpitts, and its Clapp variant with a series tuning capacitor, are the usual choice for stable VFOs and for crystal oscillators.", "worked_example": "Build a 10 MHz Colpitts with C1 = 470 pF and C2 = 1,500 pF. C_eq = 470 × 1500 / 1970 ≈ 358 pF. Required L = 1 / ((2π × 10e6)² × 358e-12) ≈ 0.71 μH. Feedback fraction ≈ C1/C2 = 0.31, so a stage gain above 3.2 ensures start-up. If the transistor's input capacitance changes by 5 pF with temperature, it appears in parallel with C2 and shifts C_eq by only about 0.07 percent, roughly 7 kHz at 10 MHz; with a Hartley using small tank capacitance that same 5 pF could move the frequency ten times further.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: an oscillator with capacitors in its tank is a Colpitts regardless of where the feedback is taken. Correction: every LC oscillator has tank capacitance; the Colpitts is defined by taking feedback from the junction of two series tank capacitors (a capacitive divider), as opposed to a tapped inductor (Hartley).", "link": "Reactance & Resonance", "mnemonic": "Colpitts = Capacitor divider; Hartley = inductor (L) tap."}

{"core": "The Pierce oscillator uses the crystal itself as the feedback element between the active device's output and input, operating the crystal just above series resonance where it looks inductive; the feedback is therefore coupled capacitively, through the crystal's own equivalent circuit and the small capacitors at the device terminals, with no tapped coil or separate winding.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Link coupling implies a separate winding, and the Pierce has no coil at all; the crystal replaces the inductive branch of the tank.", "why_tempting": "Older crystal-oscillator circuits did use tank coils, so the learner assumes some inductive coupling must exist."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A tapped coil is the Hartley signature; the Pierce has no tapped inductor and its frequency is set by the crystal, not an LC tank.", "why_tempting": "The question asks about positive feedback coupling and the Hartley is the first oscillator most learners memorize, so its answer gets reused."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A neutralizing capacitor cancels unwanted internal feedback in an amplifier so that it does not oscillate; the Pierce uses the crystal as deliberate feedback and no neutralization is involved.", "why_tempting": "In the Pierce the crystal sits in the same collector-to-base position that an unwanted Miller capacitance would occupy, so the term neutralizing feels geometrically related."}], "concept": "A quartz crystal's equivalent circuit is a series R-L-C (the motional arm) in parallel with the holder capacitance C0. Between the series-resonant frequency f_s and the parallel-resonant frequency f_p, a few kilohertz apart, the crystal's reactance is inductive and rises steeply with frequency. The Pierce circuit is a Colpitts in disguise: the crystal plays the role of the tank inductor, and two small capacitors from each crystal terminal to ground form the capacitive divider. The crystal is connected from the inverting amplifier's output to its input (collector to base, drain to gate, or the output to input of a CMOS inverter), and together with the two shunt capacitors it provides the extra 180 degrees of phase shift required around an inverting stage. Because the crystal's reactance changes so rapidly with frequency (its Q is 10,000 to 100,000), the loop phase condition is satisfied only within a tiny band, which is what gives crystal oscillators their stability. The load capacitance C_L seen by the crystal, roughly C1 × C2 / (C1 + C2) plus strays, sets the exact operating frequency within the f_s to f_p window.", "worked_example": "A 10 MHz AT-cut crystal with motional L = 25 mH, motional C = 10 fF, and C0 = 5 pF. f_s = 1 / (2π × √(0.025 × 10e-15)) ≈ 10.066 MHz; f_p is about 0.1 percent higher. In a Pierce with 22 pF capacitors on each side, C_L ≈ 11 pF plus about 5 pF stray = 16 pF, and the oscillator runs at f_s × √(1 + C_m / (2 × (C0 + C_L))) ≈ f_s × (1 + 0.00024), about 2.4 kHz above series resonance. Changing one capacitor to 33 pF shifts C_L a few pF and moves the frequency only a few hundred hertz, which is the trimming range designers use.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a crystal oscillator needs an LC tank with the crystal somewhere in the loop. Correction: in the Pierce the crystal is the inductive element of the tank and the feedback path simultaneously; the loop is closed capacitively through the crystal and its two shunt capacitors, with no coil.", "link": "Reactance & Resonance", "edge_cases": "Overtone crystals (above about 30 MHz) will not start reliably in a plain Pierce because the fundamental mode has higher gain; an LC trap or tank must be added to suppress the fundamental, which reintroduces an inductor but not as the feedback element."}

{"core": "The Colpitts configuration is preferred for VFOs because its frequency is set by a capacitive divider whose large capacitances swamp the active device's internal capacitances and because its single untapped coil can be built with high Q; the result is a circuit whose frequency drifts little with temperature, supply voltage and device ageing, which is to say it is stable.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Crystal lock-in describes synchronizing an oscillator to a crystal reference; a VFO by definition is free-running and not locked, and while a Colpitts can be crystal-controlled, that is not why it is chosen for variable-frequency use.", "why_tempting": "The Pierce crystal oscillator is a Colpitts variant, so the learner recalls that connection and misreads it as a reason."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Load impedance pulling frequency is a defect, not a feature; good VFO design isolates the oscillator from the load with a buffer precisely so that frequency does not depend on load.", "why_tempting": "The phrase linear function sounds like a positive engineering property, masking that any dependence of frequency on load is undesirable."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "A VFO is deliberately run at low power to minimize heating and drift; high output power is neither a Colpitts property nor a VFO goal, and following stages provide amplification.", "why_tempting": "A Basic-level mental model treats the oscillator as the transmitter's power source, so more power sounds better."}], "concept": "Frequency stability of an LC oscillator comes down to how much the effective tank L and C move with environmental conditions. The frequency-determining capacitance in a Colpitts is C_eq = C1 × C2 / (C1 + C2) in parallel with the device's C_in and C_out, which appear across C2 and C1 respectively. If C1 and C2 are hundreds of picofarads while the device capacitances are a few picofarads, a 20 percent change in a device capacitance moves C_eq by a fraction of a percent, and since f ∝ 1/√C the frequency moves by half that again. In the Clapp refinement a small series capacitor C3 dominates C_eq and makes the device even less influential. Add NP0/C0G capacitors, a rigid air-wound or ceramic-form coil, a regulated supply, a buffer amplifier so the load cannot pull the tank, and light coupling, and the Colpitts delivers drift of a few hertz per hour at HF. The Hartley's tapped coil is harder to make with high Q and the inductive tap couples device capacitance more directly to the tank, which is why it is less favoured for stable VFOs.", "worked_example": "A 5 MHz Colpitts VFO with C1 = 1,000 pF, C2 = 1,000 pF (C_eq = 500 pF) and the transistor's 8 pF C_in across C2. Temperature raises C_in to 10 pF. C2 effective goes from 1,008 to 1,010 pF, C_eq from 502.0 to 502.5 pF, a change of 0.1 percent, so f changes by about 0.05 percent, 2.5 kHz. Now a Hartley at the same frequency with tank C = 100 pF and the same 2 pF device change directly across the tank: 2 percent capacitance change, 1 percent frequency change, 50 kHz. The capacitive divider's swamping gives the Colpitts a twentyfold advantage in this example.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: oscillator types differ mainly in power or convenience, and any LC circuit is equally stable. Correction: the Colpitts is chosen for VFOs specifically because its large divider capacitors swamp device capacitance changes, making the frequency far less sensitive to temperature and bias than tapped-coil circuits.", "link": "Reactance & Resonance", "edge_cases": "A Colpitts is only as stable as its passive parts: using X7R ceramic capacitors or a coil wound on a plastic form that expands with temperature will drift badly regardless of topology, and a VFO without a buffer stage will be pulled by the following amplifier's changing input impedance on keying."}

{"core": "A PLL multiplies its reference frequency by N to produce the output, and within the loop bandwidth it also multiplies the reference's phase deviations by N; any phase jitter on the reference therefore appears on the output as phase noise, scaled up by 20 × log10(N) dB, so the reference must be extremely clean.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Reference phase variations affect the synthesized carrier's phase, not the modulating audio; harmonic distortion of the modulating signal is an audio-chain or modulator-linearity problem unrelated to the reference oscillator.", "why_tempting": "Phase variation and distortion are both signal-quality terms, and in FM transmitters the synthesizer and the modulator are physically close, so the effects get attributed to the wrong block."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The phase detector responds to zero crossings or edges, so amplitude variations on the reference have little effect, and in any case the loop's ability to change frequency is set by the programmable divider and loop filter, not by reference amplitude.", "why_tempting": "An amplitude-modulated reference sounds like it would upset something, and frequency changing is what synthesizers do, so the two are joined without a mechanism."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Lock acquisition depends on the VCO tuning range, loop gain and filter, not on reference amplitude; a limiter or digital phase detector removes amplitude variation entirely.", "why_tempting": "Locking is the defining PLL behaviour, so any defect in the reference seems like it should threaten lock."}], "concept": "In a PLL synthesizer the VCO output at f_out is divided by N and compared in phase with the reference at f_ref; the loop forces f_out / N = f_ref, so f_out = N × f_ref. Phase is the integral of frequency, and the same relation holds for phase: within the loop bandwidth the VCO phase tracks N × φ_ref. A reference phase deviation of Δφ therefore appears at the output as N × Δφ, and since phase-noise power scales with the square of the deviation, the output phase noise is the reference phase noise plus 20 × log10(N) dB (plus phase-detector and divider noise, which are also multiplied). For a 2 m synthesizer with f_ref = 5 kHz and f_out = 146 MHz, N = 29,200 and the multiplication is 89 dB. Outside the loop bandwidth the VCO's own noise dominates instead. Phase noise on a transmitter spreads energy into adjacent channels; on a receiver it mixes strong nearby signals into the passband (reciprocal mixing), raising the noise floor and masking weak signals. That is why synthesizers use TCXO or OCXO references and why modern designs raise f_ref (fractional-N) to reduce N.", "worked_example": "A 10 MHz TCXO has phase noise of −150 dBc/Hz at 10 kHz offset. Used as a 5 kHz reference after division by 2,000 (division improves phase noise by 20 × log10(2000) = 66 dB, to about −216, but the divider's own floor of around −160 dBc/Hz dominates). Multiply to 146 MHz with N = 29,200: 20 × log10(29,200) ≈ 89 dB. Output phase noise inside the loop bandwidth ≈ −160 + 89 = −71 dBc/Hz at 10 kHz offset. A receiver with that local oscillator and a −30 dBm signal 10 kHz away sees reciprocal-mixing noise at −30 − 71 = −101 dBm/Hz, roughly 70 dB above thermal noise, which would bury a weak station. Every dB of reference jitter goes straight to the output.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the loop filter cleans up whatever reference you feed a PLL, so reference quality is not critical. Correction: inside the loop bandwidth the output faithfully tracks the reference phase multiplied by N; the loop cannot distinguish reference jitter from the signal it is supposed to track, so reference phase noise is amplified, not filtered.", "link": "Decibel Converter", "edge_cases": "The 20 × log10(N) penalty applies only inside the loop bandwidth; outside it the VCO's free-running phase noise dominates, so loop bandwidth is chosen at the crossover where reference-multiplied noise and VCO noise are equal."}

{"core": "Taking the feedback voltage from the junction of two series capacitors across the tank is the defining feature of the Colpitts oscillator; the capacitive divider both sets the feedback fraction and, with the coil, determines frequency.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "The Miller oscillator is a crystal circuit in which the crystal sits between the input (grid or gate) and ground and feedback occurs through the device's internal Miller capacitance with a tuned output circuit; there is no deliberate capacitive divider.", "why_tempting": "Miller capacitance is a capacitive feedback mechanism, so a learner who associates capacitance with Miller may choose it."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The Pierce uses a crystal as the series feedback element between output and input; although it is topologically a Colpitts relative, the question describes a generic capacitive divider across an LC tank, which is the Colpitts proper.", "why_tempting": "The Pierce does have two shunt capacitors that act as a divider, so it is a close call; the exam convention is that a plain capacitive divider identifies Colpitts, and a crystal in the feedback path identifies Pierce."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "The Hartley takes feedback from a tap on the tank inductor; its capacitor is a single element across the whole coil, not a divider.", "why_tempting": "It is the dual of the Colpitts and the most common swap in exam answers."}], "concept": "The oscillator family names encode where in the resonant network the feedback is sampled. In a parallel LC tank, the voltage across the inductor equals the voltage across the capacitance, so splitting either element into two series parts and grounding the junction produces a divider with the two ends in antiphase. Split the capacitor: Colpitts, with feedback fraction ≈ C1/C2 and f = 1/(2π√(L × C1C2/(C1+C2))). Split the inductor: Hartley, with fraction ≈ L2/L1. Replace the inductor with a crystal operating in its inductive region and keep the capacitive divider: Pierce. Use a separate tickler winding: Armstrong. Put the crystal at the input with a tuned output tank and let device capacitance close the loop: Miller. Being able to classify a schematic by this single question, where is the feedback taken from, is the skill the whole subsection tests.", "worked_example": "Thought experiment: start with a Colpitts at 3.5 MHz using L = 10 μH, C1 = 330 pF, C2 = 1,000 pF (C_eq ≈ 248 pF, f ≈ 3.2 MHz). Replace C1 and C2 with a single 248 pF capacitor and instead tap the 10 μH coil 25 percent from the grounded end: same frequency, same feedback fraction, but now it is a Hartley. Replace the 10 μH coil with a 3.5 MHz crystal and keep the two capacitors: the frequency is pinned by the crystal and it is now a Pierce. The feedback pickoff, not the component count, names the circuit.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: any oscillator using capacitors for feedback is a Miller or Pierce because those involve capacitance through the device. Correction: a capacitive voltage divider across the tank, with the junction grounded, is the Colpitts signature; Miller and Pierce are crystal-specific variants.", "link": "Reactance & Resonance", "mnemonic": "Colpitts = Capacitor divider; Hartley = inductor tap; Pierce = crystal in the Path."}

{"core": "The two series capacitors in a Colpitts-type feedback divider are part of the frequency-determining tank, so they must have very low temperature coefficient, low loss and no voltage or ageing drift; silver mica capacitors offer tempco near zero, high Q and excellent long-term stability, making them the traditional choice for high-stability RF oscillators.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Mylar (polyester film) has a tempco of several hundred ppm/°C, relatively high dielectric loss at RF and significant dissipation factor, so an oscillator built with it drifts noticeably and the tank Q suffers.", "why_tempting": "Film capacitors are accurate and stable at audio, and Mylar is a familiar quality film, so its audio reputation is transferred to RF."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Generic ceramic capacitors (X7R, Z5U) have tempcos of thousands of ppm/°C, strong voltage dependence and piezoelectric microphonics, all fatal for stability; only the NP0/C0G ceramic subclass is suitable, and the option does not specify it.", "why_tempting": "Ceramic capacitors are everywhere in RF circuits as bypass parts, and NP0 ceramics genuinely are used in modern VFOs, so the unqualified word ceramic seems acceptable."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Electrolytics are polarized, have microfarad values far too large for an RF tank, tolerance of −20/+80 percent, high ESR and ESL, and large tempco; they cannot function in an RF resonant circuit at all.", "why_tempting": "Electrolytics are the biggest and most visible capacitors in a transmitter, so a learner thinking in terms of robustness may pick them."}], "concept": "Oscillator frequency is f = 1/(2π√(LC)), so df/f = −½ (dL/L + dC/C). A capacitor tempco of α ppm/°C produces a frequency drift of −α/2 ppm/°C.
