Silver mica capacitors, made of mica sheets with fired-on silver electrodes, have tempco of roughly 0 to +70 ppm/°C, dissipation factor around 0.0005 (Q above 1,000 at HF), negligible voltage coefficient and almost no ageing, so they keep the tank Q high and the frequency fixed. Low loss also matters because tank Q sets the steepness of the phase-versus-frequency curve, and a steeper curve means a smaller frequency shift for a given phase disturbance from the device. In practice designers mix silver mica or NP0 ceramic with a small negative-tempco (N750) capacitor to cancel the coil's positive tempco, a technique called temperature compensation. Mylar's loss and drift, ordinary ceramic's wild tempco, and electrolytic's unsuitability for RF leave silver mica as the clear best of the four.", "worked_example": "A 7 MHz VFO uses 500 pF of divider capacitance. With silver mica at +50 ppm/°C and a 20 °C warm-up: ΔC/C = 1,000 ppm, Δf/f = −500 ppm, Δf = −3.5 kHz. With X7R ceramic at about −2,000 ppm/°C over the same range (and non-linear): ΔC/C ≈ −40,000 ppm, Δf ≈ +140 kHz, enough to move completely out of a band segment. With Mylar at +400 ppm/°C: Δf ≈ −28 kHz. Adding a 47 pF N750 capacitor in parallel with the silver mica shifts the net tempco toward zero and can bring the drift under 1 kHz.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: capacitance value is all that matters in a tank, so any capacitor type of the right value will do. Correction: tempco, dielectric loss and voltage/ageing stability of the dielectric directly become frequency drift and reduced Q; stable oscillators need silver mica or NP0 class dielectrics.", "link": "Reactance & Resonance", "edge_cases": "Modern designs usually substitute NP0/C0G ceramic for silver mica because it is cheaper, smaller and has an even tighter tempco (±30 ppm/°C); silver mica remains the exam answer and is still used where high RF current or high voltage ratings are needed."}

{"core": "An oscillator whose feedback path from output to input runs through a single capacitor in series with the crystal is the Pierce circuit; the crystal operating in its inductive region, together with the series and shunt capacitances, supplies the phase shift that makes the feedback positive.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "The Hartley uses a tapped inductor in an LC tank and has no crystal in the feedback path.", "why_tempting": "Hartley is the first oscillator name many learners memorize and gets picked when the circuit description is unfamiliar."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "In the Miller crystal oscillator the crystal is connected from the input terminal to ground, not in series with the feedback path; feedback flows through the device's internal capacitance to a tuned output circuit.", "why_tempting": "Miller is the other classic crystal oscillator and both use capacitance through the device, so distinguishing them requires remembering where the crystal sits."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A Colpitts uses an LC tank with a capacitive divider; although the Pierce is derived from it, a crystal in the series feedback path is what exam convention labels as Pierce.", "why_tempting": "The Pierce is literally a Colpitts with the inductor replaced by a crystal, so a learner who knows the derivation may over-generalize."}], "concept": "The Pierce places the crystal between the output and input of an inverting amplifier, often with a small series capacitor to fine-tune frequency or to block DC. The crystal's motional arm (series R, L, C) resonates at f_s; just above f_s and below f_p the net reactance is inductive, and the crystal together with the shunt capacitors C1 (input to ground) and C2 (output to ground) forms a pi network that contributes the 180 degrees of phase shift needed to turn the inverter's output back into positive feedback. The series capacitor adds to the load capacitance C_L that the crystal sees, so adjusting it pulls the frequency within the narrow f_s to f_p window, typically a few hundred ppm. Because the crystal's reactance slope is enormous (Q of 10⁴ to 10⁵), the phase condition can be met only at essentially one frequency, which is why crystal oscillators are so stable compared with LC types. The Miller circuit, by contrast, puts the crystal from input to ground operating near parallel resonance as a high-impedance element and relies on the tuned plate or collector circuit plus internal capacitance for feedback.", "worked_example": "Thought experiment: take a Pierce with a 7.030 MHz crystal, 33 pF shunt capacitors and a 100 pF series capacitor. Load capacitance seen by the crystal ≈ series combination of 100 pF with (33 pF × 33 pF / 66 pF ≈ 16.5 pF, plus strays): roughly 14 pF. The crystal was specified for 20 pF load, so the oscillator runs slightly high, perhaps 300 Hz above nominal. Replace the 100 pF series capacitor with a 30 pF trimmer and you can lower C_L further to raise frequency, or increase it toward 20 pF to hit nominal: that series capacitor is the frequency trim, and its presence in series with the crystal is the question's identifying clue.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: all crystal oscillators are the same circuit with the crystal somewhere in the loop. Correction: the Pierce has the crystal in the series feedback path from output to input (often with a series capacitor), whereas the Miller has it from input to ground; the location of the crystal names the circuit.", "link": "section 5", "edge_cases": "At high drive levels the series capacitor also limits crystal current; too much crystal dissipation (over a few hundred microwatts for small crystals) causes frequency drift and can fracture the quartz, so the series capacitor value sometimes serves as a power limiter as well as a trim."}

{"core": "A variable-frequency oscillator sustains its own output by returning a fraction of that output to its input in phase, so that the loop gain is at least unity and the signal regenerates each cycle; positive feedback is the defining requirement of any oscillator.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A mixer multiplies two input signals in a non-linear device to produce sum and difference frequencies; it has no feedback loop and produces no output without inputs.", "why_tempting": "Mixers are non-linear and often adjacent to oscillators in a block diagram (the LO feeds the mixer), so the association is strong."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A detector (demodulator) recovers the modulating information from a carrier by rectification, product detection or discrimination; it is a non-linear but open-loop process.", "why_tempting": "The regenerative detector of early receivers did use positive feedback, so a learner with historical knowledge may be drawn here, but a detector as a category does not depend on it."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "An audio amplifier uses negative feedback, if any, to lower distortion and flatten response; positive feedback in an amplifier is a fault that causes howling or motorboating.", "why_tempting": "Amplifiers and feedback are discussed together, and the learner may not distinguish the sign of the feedback."}], "concept": "The Barkhausen criterion states that a feedback loop oscillates when the loop gain magnitude |A × β| ≥ 1 and the total loop phase shift is 0 degrees (or a multiple of 360 degrees) at some frequency. An amplifier of gain A with a feedback network returning fraction β has closed-loop gain A / (1 − A × β); as A × β → 1 the gain goes to infinity, meaning an output exists with no input. The frequency-selective network (LC tank, crystal, RC ladder) ensures the phase condition is met at only one frequency, which is the oscillation frequency. At start-up A × β is deliberately greater than 1 so that noise at the resonant frequency grows exponentially; amplitude then stabilizes when the active device saturates or an AGC element reduces A until A × β = 1 exactly. Negative feedback, by contrast, returns the signal 180 degrees out of phase, giving gain A / (1 + A × β), which is smaller than A but more linear and stable, the opposite design goal. A VFO is thus the canonical positive-feedback circuit; the other three options are all open-loop or negative-feedback signal processors.", "worked_example": "Thought experiment: a common-emitter stage with gain 20 and a Colpitts divider returning β = 0.1 of the output. A × β = 2 > 1, so at power-up the thermal noise component at the tank frequency doubles every pass around the loop; from 1 μV it reaches 1 V in about 20 cycles, a few microseconds at 7 MHz. The transistor then clips, its average gain falls to 10, A × β = 1 and amplitude holds. Reverse the feedback phase (negative feedback): closed-loop gain = 20 / (1 + 2) = 6.7, no oscillation, just a well-behaved amplifier. The sign of the feedback is the whole difference between an amplifier and an oscillator.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: feedback is feedback, and any circuit with a feedback path could be the answer. Correction: only positive (in-phase) feedback with loop gain of at least one produces self-sustained oscillation; amplifiers use negative feedback and mixers and detectors have none.", "link": "section 5", "mnemonic": "Oscillators need Positive feedback and a Phase shift of zero: the two P's."}

{"core": "An oscillator generating the carrier followed by a class C amplifier boosting it to output power, with keying applied to turn the carrier on and off, is the minimal CW transmitter; class C is appropriate because a CW signal has a constant envelope and tolerates the amplifier's non-linearity.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "An FM transmitter also needs a modulator (reactance stage or varactor on the oscillator) and usually frequency multipliers; two stages of oscillator plus class C amplifier with no modulator produce only an unmodulated carrier.", "why_tempting": "Class C amplifiers are used in FM transmitters because FM is constant-envelope, so the amplifier class matches; the missing modulator is the catch."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A regenerative receiver uses a single detector stage with controlled positive feedback just below oscillation, followed by audio amplification; a class C RF power amplifier has no role in a receiver.", "why_tempting": "The regenerative receiver involves an oscillating stage, so oscillator plus another stage sounds superficially similar."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "SSB generation requires a balanced modulator and sideband filter or phasing network, and the resulting signal has a varying envelope that a class C amplifier would severely distort, generating splatter; SSB amplifiers must be linear (class AB or A).", "why_tempting": "Fixed-frequency hints at a crystal oscillator and the learner may assume any two-stage transmitter can carry any mode."}], "concept": "A class C amplifier is biased beyond cutoff so the active device conducts for less than 180 degrees of each RF cycle, typically 120 to 150 degrees. Current flows in short pulses that shock-excite the tuned output tank, and the tank's flywheel effect reconstructs a sine wave at the fundamental. Efficiency reaches 70 to 85 percent because the device is off most of the cycle, but the output amplitude is not proportional to input amplitude, so the amplifier is unusable for any signal whose envelope carries information (AM, SSB). CW, FM and FSK have constant envelopes, so class C is ideal for them. The simplest CW transmitter is therefore a crystal or VFO oscillator for the carrier, a class C power amplifier for the watts, and a key that interrupts either the oscillator supply or the amplifier bias. Keying shapes the envelope rise and fall over a few milliseconds to avoid key clicks, but between those edges the envelope is flat, exactly what class C delivers. Add a buffer between oscillator and PA to prevent chirp from load pulling and you have the classic three-stage design, but two stages is the minimal form.", "worked_example": "Thought experiment: feed a 1 W constant-amplitude 7 MHz carrier into a class C stage with 75 percent efficiency and 12 V supply drawing 1 A: output ≈ 0.75 × 12 = 9 W, a clean CW signal when keyed. Now feed the same stage a two-tone SSB signal whose envelope swings from zero to peak at 1 kHz: during low-envelope portions the drive falls below the conduction threshold and output drops to zero, during peaks it saturates; the output envelope becomes a distorted version of the input and the spectrum fills with intermodulation products tens of kHz wide. Same two stages, acceptable for CW, unacceptable for SSB.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: amplifier class is a matter of efficiency only, and any amplifier can follow any oscillator for any mode. Correction: class C is non-linear and works only for constant-envelope signals such as CW and FM; an oscillator plus class C stage with no modulator is specifically a CW transmitter.", "link": "section 5", "edge_cases": "A class C stage can be used for AM by plate or collector modulation (varying the supply voltage with the audio), which is how classic AM transmitters worked; the question's two-stage apparatus has no modulator, so that path is excluded."}

{"core": "A crystal in the series feedback path from the amplifier output back to its input, with a capacitor in series to set load capacitance and trim frequency, is the Pierce oscillator; the crystal's inductive reactance just above series resonance combined with the circuit capacitances provides the positive feedback phase shift.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "The Colpitts proper uses an LC tank with a capacitive divider; when the inductor is replaced by a crystal in the feedback path the circuit is named Pierce by convention, which is what the question describes.", "why_tempting": "The Pierce is topologically a Colpitts with a crystal, so a learner who understands the derivation may answer with the parent family."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The Hartley takes its feedback from a tap on an inductor and has no crystal in the loop.", "why_tempting": "It is the most frequently memorized oscillator name and appears in nearly every option set in this subsection."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "The Franklin oscillator uses two cascaded amplifier stages with very loose coupling to an LC tank so the tank is barely loaded; it is an LC circuit, not a crystal circuit, and there is no series feedback capacitor-crystal element.", "why_tempting": "Franklin is an obscure name that sounds authoritative, and obscure options attract guesses when the learner is unsure."}], "concept": "Crystal oscillators are classified by where the crystal sits relative to the active device. In the Pierce, the crystal connects output to input (collector to base, drain to gate, or across a CMOS inverter) and is operated as an inductor between f_s and f_p; two shunt capacitors to ground complete a Colpitts-style pi network, and a series capacitor is frequently added to set the total load capacitance C_L and thereby trim the exact frequency according to f = f_s × (1 + C_m / (2 × (C0 + C_L))), where C_m is the motional capacitance and C0 the holder capacitance. In the Miller, the crystal is from input to ground and feedback occurs through device capacitance to a tuned output. In the Butler, the crystal is in a series-resonant feedback path between two stages and operates at f_s. The Pierce is the overwhelmingly common choice in modern equipment because it needs no tuned circuit, works with a single inverter, and holds the crystal at low drive. Recognizing the capacitor-in-series-with-crystal feedback element is the identifying mark.", "worked_example": "A 14.318 MHz crystal with C_m = 20 fF and C0 = 6 pF is specified for C_L = 18 pF. In a Pierce with two 27 pF shunt capacitors (giving about 13.5 pF) and a series trimmer, the trimmer is set so that the total C_L is 18 pF and the oscillator lands on frequency. Reduce the trimmer so C_L drops to 12 pF: Δf/f ≈ (C_m / 2) × (1/(C0 + 12) − 1/(C0 + 18)) = 10 fF × (1/18 pF − 1/24 pF) ≈ 10e-15 × 1.39e10 ≈ 139 ppm, about 2 kHz upward. The series capacitor is both the clue in the question and the frequency adjustment.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the Pierce and Colpitts are different enough that a crystal circuit should be called Colpitts if it looks like one. Correction: exam and industry convention names any inverter-plus-crystal-in-the-feedback-path circuit a Pierce, with the capacitive elements completing the loop; Colpitts is reserved for the LC-tank version.", "link": "section 5", "edge_cases": "When the crystal is placed in a Colpitts where the LC tank is retained and the crystal is in series with the feedback from the emitter, some texts call it a Colpitts crystal oscillator; the exam's description of a single capacitor in series with the crystal as the feedback path is the Pierce."}

{"core": "The tune and load controls of a pi-network output tank adjust its two capacitors so that the network resonates at the operating frequency and transforms the antenna or feedline impedance (nominally 50 Ω) up to the much higher load impedance the tube or transistor needs; when both are set correctly, maximum power is transferred to the antenna with minimum loss and harmonic content.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Antenna switching is done with a relay or coaxial switch; the pi network's capacitors change impedance transformation and resonance, not which output connector is live.", "why_tempting": "Loading the amplifier to different antennas is a real operating task, so the learner associates the load control with the antenna selection itself."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Cross-modulation in nearby receivers results from the receiver's own front-end non-linearity under strong signal; the transmitter's tank controls do not change the receiver's overload behaviour, although a mistuned tank can raise harmonic output.", "why_tempting": "Reducing interference is a goal of good tank tuning (harmonic suppression), so interference-related options sound related."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Frequency multiplication happens in a previous stage by tuning that stage's tank to a harmonic of its drive; the PA output network is tuned to the final frequency and has no role in the multiplier.", "why_tempting": "In older multi-stage transmitters each stage had its own tuning control, and the learner may confuse the final's controls with those of the multiplier stages."}], "concept": "A pi network is C1 (tune, at the tube or transistor side) in shunt, L in series, and C2 (load, at the antenna side) in shunt. It behaves as two back-to-back L networks sharing the inductor, transforming a low antenna impedance R_L to a high source impedance R_P. For a tube with plate voltage V_p and plate current I_p delivering power P_out, the required plate load is approximately R_P = V_p² / (2 × P_out) for class B/C operation (sometimes written V_p / (1.8 × I_p) as a rule of thumb); values of 2 to 5 kΩ are typical versus 50 Ω at the antenna. The network's loaded Q (often 10 to 15) is set by the choice of C1 and L for a given transformation ratio: C1 ≈ Q / (2π f R_P), and the Q also determines harmonic attenuation, since a pi network is a low-pass filter. Tuning C1 for a dip in plate current finds resonance; adjusting C2 (load) sets how heavily the tank is coupled to the antenna and therefore the delivered power, after which C1 is re-dipped. The net effect of both controls being correctly set is a conjugate match between the amplifier's required load and the actual antenna, which is the condition for efficient power transfer.", "worked_example": "A triode PA at V_p = 2,000 V delivering 500 W wants R_P ≈ 2000² / (2 × 500) = 4,000 Ω. Antenna is 50 Ω. Choose Q = 12 at 7.1 MHz. X_C1 = R_P / Q = 333 Ω, so C1 = 1 / (2π × 7.1e6 × 333) ≈ 67 pF. The load-side reactance works out to X_C2 ≈ R_L × √(R_P / (R_L × (Q² + 1)) − 1)⁻¹ ... in practice about 90 Ω, so C2 ≈ 250 pF, and L ≈ 7 μH. With C1 and C2 set to these values the 50 Ω antenna looks like 4,000 Ω to the tube and all 500 W (minus a few percent in the coil) reaches the antenna. Detune C2 to 400 pF and the tube sees perhaps 2,000 Ω: plate current rises, efficiency falls, and dissipation climbs toward the tube's limit.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the tune and load knobs are just there to peak the output meter, like a volume control. Correction: they set the resonance and impedance transformation of a matching network; a correctly tuned pi presents the amplifier with the load impedance it was designed for, which is what makes the power transfer efficient and the harmonics low.", "link": "SWR & Impedance Match", "edge_cases": "Solid-state broadband amplifiers replace the adjustable pi network with fixed transformers and low-pass filters, so the operator sees no tune or load controls; the impedance transformation still happens, it is just not adjustable."}

{"core": "A directly heated cathode (filament) carries AC heating current, and the two ends of the filament sit at opposite instantaneous AC potentials; returning the cathode circuit to the centre tap of the filament winding places the effective cathode at the AC midpoint, so the heating voltage adds nothing to the grid-cathode signal and the output is not modulated at the mains frequency.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Filament transformer regulation is set by winding resistance and core design; a centre tap does not change the output voltage versus load relationship.", "why_tempting": "Centre taps on power transformers are associated with full-wave rectifiers and voltage splitting, so a learner reaches for a power-regulation explanation."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Power output is set by plate voltage, drive and load impedance; the filament centre tap affects hum, not the fundamental output power.", "why_tempting": "Any correctly configured transmitter detail might seem to contribute to optimum output in a vague sense."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Harmonic emissions are controlled by the output tank's low-pass characteristic, operating class and drive level; filament hum produces mains-frequency sidebands a few tens of hertz from the carrier, not RF harmonics.", "why_tempting": "Both hum sidebands and harmonics are unwanted emissions, so the learner may file them together."}], "concept": "In a directly heated tube the filament is the electron emitter. If the filament is run from 60 Hz AC, one end is +V_f/2 and the other −V_f/2 relative to the winding centre, alternating each half cycle. The grid signal and the cathode return must reference some point on that filament; if they reference one end, the effective grid-to-cathode bias swings by ±V_f/2 at 60 Hz (several volts for a big transmitting tube), which amplitude-modulates the RF output and produces hum sidebands at ±60 Hz and harmonics around the carrier. Returning to the centre tap (or to a centre-tapped resistor across the filament when the winding has none) makes the reference the average filament potential, which is constant, cancelling the first-order modulation. A second-order effect remains because emission density varies along the filament with the local potential, but it is much smaller. In a grounded-grid amplifier the filament additionally carries the RF drive, so the centre tap is returned through an RF choke, and the filament leads themselves are bifilar-wound chokes to keep the RF off the transformer. Indirectly heated cathodes avoid this problem entirely because the heater is insulated from the cathode sleeve.", "worked_example": "A 3-500Z has a 5 V, 15 A filament. With the cathode return at one filament end, the grid-cathode voltage sees a 2.5 V peak 60 Hz swing on top of, say, 50 V of RF drive, giving roughly 5 percent AM at 60 Hz: hum sidebands about 26 dB below the carrier, clearly audible on a receiver. Move the return to the centre tap and the first-order swing is zero; residual hum from emission non-uniformity might be 50 to 60 dB down, inaudible. Running the filament from DC would also cure it but is wasteful at 75 W of heater power.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the filament supply is just a heater and is isolated from the signal path. Correction: in a directly heated tube the filament is the cathode, so any AC on it appears in series with the grid signal unless the circuit is referenced to the filament winding's electrical centre.", "link": "section 5", "edge_cases": "Tubes with indirectly heated cathodes (most receiving tubes and many tetrodes such as the 4CX series) have the heater electrically separate from the cathode, so the centre-tap return is unnecessary there; the question applies to directly heated types such as the 3-500Z, 811A and 572B."}

{"core": "In a grounded-grid amplifier the control grid is held at RF ground and acts as a screen between input and output, so the drive signal must be injected at the cathode, which is the only remaining input electrode; the output is taken from the plate.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "In a directly heated tube the filament is the cathode, and drive is indeed applied to the filament/cathode structure through chokes; but the question asks which electrode receives the signal, and the electrode is the cathode, while filament leads is a description of the heater supply path.", "why_tempting": "In practice the RF drive does arrive via the filament leads of a directly heated tube, so this is a near-miss that confuses the wiring with the electrode function."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The plate is the output electrode in every tube amplifier configuration; applying input there would feed the drive directly into the output tank.", "why_tempting": "Grounded-grid flips the usual input electrode, so a learner may assume everything flips and the plate becomes the input."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "In grounded-grid the control grid is connected to ground (directly or through a bypass capacitor) specifically so it does not receive the signal; driving the grid describes the conventional grounded-cathode configuration.", "why_tempting": "The grid is the input in the basic grounded-cathode amplifier learned first, and that reflex overrides the name of the configuration."}], "concept": "A triode has three electrodes; whichever is common (grounded for RF) defines the configuration, exactly as with transistors. Grounded cathode (common emitter) drives the grid and has high input impedance, high voltage gain, and plate-to-grid capacitance that feeds output back to input, requiring neutralization. Grounded grid (common base) drives the cathode: input impedance is low, roughly 1/g_m plus the effect of plate loading, typically 50 to 200 Ω, which conveniently matches a 50 Ω exciter without much transformation. The grounded grid sits between cathode and plate as an electrostatic shield, so plate-to-cathode feedback capacitance is tiny and neutralization is seldom needed. The drive power is not wasted: it flows through the tube in series with the plate current and appears in the output (feed-through power), so a 100 W exciter driving a grounded-grid amplifier contributes most of that 100 W to the output. Voltage gain is lower than grounded-cathode (about 10 to 15 dB power gain), which is why these amplifiers need a full-power exciter. Cathode drive requires the cathode (or filament, for directly heated tubes) to be lifted above RF ground with chokes so the input signal can be impressed on it.", "worked_example": "A 3-500Z grounded-grid amplifier: g_m ≈ 4,000 μS at operating current, so input impedance ≈ 1/0.004 = 250 Ω in the simplest estimate, reduced to roughly 100 Ω by plate loading; a small pi or L input network matches it to 50 Ω. Drive 100 W into the cathode; the tube draws 400 mA at 3,000 V (1,200 W input) and at 60 percent efficiency puts 720 W into the tank, plus about 90 W of feed-through drive, for about 800 W output. Try to apply that 100 W to the grounded grid instead: the grid bypass capacitor shorts the drive to ground and nothing happens, confirming that the cathode is the input.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the control grid is always the input electrode of a tube. Correction: the input is whichever electrode is not grounded and not the plate; in the grounded-grid configuration the grid is the common (shield) electrode and the cathode receives the drive.", "link": "section 5", "mnemonic": "Name the configuration by the grounded electrode, drive the one that is left: grounded grid means drive the cathode."}

{"core": "The plate sits at the full B+ potential (thousands of volts DC) while the pi-network capacitors and the antenna must be at DC ground, so a high-voltage blocking capacitor couples the RF from plate to the pi network while keeping the DC off the tank and the output connector.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A bypass capacitor connects a node to ground to short RF while passing DC; placing one between the plate and the tank would shunt the RF output to ground rather than pass it along.", "why_tempting": "Bypass and blocking capacitors are both large-value capacitors found in the PA and both deal with separating RF from DC, so their roles get swapped."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The tuning capacitor is the variable shunt element at the input of the pi network (the tune control), connected from the hot end of the tank to ground; it is not the series element that couples plate to tank.", "why_tempting": "The tuning capacitor is physically the first capacitor the plate RF reaches after the blocking capacitor, so the learner may skip the blocking element."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Electrolytics are polarized, limited to a few hundred volts, have high ESL and ESR, and cannot carry RF current; they would fail instantly at kilovolts of DC plus RF.", "why_tempting": "Electrolytics are the largest capacitance values in the transmitter and high capacitance sounds like good coupling."}], "concept": "The plate is fed DC through an RF choke from the high-voltage supply; superimposed on that DC is the RF swing of nearly ±B+ volts. The pi network must see only the RF. A series blocking capacitor passes the RF with negligible reactance (X_C = 1/(2πfC) must be small compared with the plate load impedance) while standing off the full DC. For a 2 kΩ plate load at 3.5 MHz, a 2,000 pF capacitor has X_C ≈ 23 Ω, about 1 percent of the load, so it is transparent at RF; its voltage rating must exceed B+ plus the RF peak, so 3,000 V DC and 7 kV RF peak-capable parts (doorknob ceramics or mica) are used. The RF current through it equals the tank input current, which can be amperes, so low loss matters. If the blocking capacitor shorts, B+ appears on the tune capacitor (arcing) and on the antenna connector, a lethal fault, which is why a safety choke from the output to ground is often fitted to blow the HV fuse if that happens. The same DC-blocking principle appears in transistor amplifiers at low voltage and in receiver stages as coupling capacitors.", "worked_example": "B+ = 2,500 V, plate load 3,000 Ω, lowest band 1.8 MHz. Choose a blocking capacitor so that X_C ≤ 3 percent of R_P: X_C ≤ 90 Ω, so C ≥ 1/(2π × 1.8e6 × 90) ≈ 980 pF; use 1,500 pF rated 5 kV. At 28 MHz the same part has X_C ≈ 3.8 Ω, even more transparent. RF current at 1 kW output into 3,000 Ω is about √(1000/3000) ≈ 0.58 A rms, so a doorknob rated for several amperes RF is appropriate. A 1,500 pF electrolytic does not exist, and a 450 V one would vaporize.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: bypass and blocking capacitors are the same component with two names. Correction: a bypass capacitor shunts RF to ground around a DC node; a blocking capacitor passes RF in series while blocking DC. The plate-to-pi-network coupling element must pass RF and block DC, so it is a blocking capacitor.", "link": "Reactance & Resonance", "edge_cases": "In solid-state amplifiers the blocking function is often performed by the output transformer winding rather than a discrete capacitor, and in some tube designs the pi network is placed at DC potential (series-fed) with the blocking capacitor moved to the antenna side; the principle of separating DC from the output path is unchanged."}

{"core": "The plate radio-frequency choke is the DC feed path: one end connects to the plate and the other to the B+ high-voltage supply, so that plate current flows from the supply while the choke's high reactance keeps the RF from leaking back into the power supply.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Connecting the plate choke to ground would short the DC supply path and apply no plate voltage; the tube could not conduct and no amplification would occur.", "why_tempting": "Many chokes in a PA do return to ground (filament chokes in some designs), and the learner may assume all chokes do."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Bias is a negative voltage applied to the grid or a positive offset on the cathode; the plate needs positive high voltage, and connecting it to the bias supply would leave the tube without plate potential.", "why_tempting": "B− is a legitimate node in tube circuits (the negative return of the HV supply or the bias supply), so it looks like a plausible power connection."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Filament voltage is a few volts AC for heating; connecting the plate to it would provide no plate potential and would place the filament transformer across the output tank.", "why_tempting": "The filament winding is the other transformer in the amplifier and a learner may pick any supply node without checking its purpose."}], "concept": "The plate of a tube amplifier must be at high positive DC potential to attract electrons, yet it is also the point where the RF output voltage swings by nearly the full supply voltage. The plate RFC resolves this: it is a series inductor between B+ and the plate whose reactance at the operating frequency, X_L = 2πfL, is large compared with the plate load impedance so that essentially all the RF current goes into the tank via the blocking capacitor rather than into the supply. Typical values are 30 to 100 μH for HF, giving X_L of several kΩ at 3.5 MHz and higher above. Design constraints include avoiding series self-resonance within any amateur band (a series-resonant choke presents a short to RF and burns up) and handling the full DC plate current. A bypass capacitor at the supply end of the choke shunts any remaining RF to ground so it does not travel down the HV lead and radiate. The cathode choke in a grounded-grid amplifier does the analogous job for the input side, and the two questions together describe how DC enters the tube while RF is confined to the input and output networks.", "worked_example": "Plate load 2,500 Ω at 3.5 MHz. Choose the plate RFC so X_L ≥ 10 × R_P = 25 kΩ: L ≥ 25,000 / (2π × 3.5e6) ≈ 1.1 mH, which is large; practical designs accept X_L ≈ 3 to 5 × R_P, so about 50 to 100 μH with X_L ≈ 1.1 to 2.2 kΩ at 3.5 MHz, rising to about 9 to 18 kΩ at 28 MHz. The DC drop across a 90 μH choke with 3 Ω resistance at 400 mA is 1.2 V, negligible against 2,500 V. The choke's self-resonance must be checked, for example to ensure it does not fall near 21 or 24 MHz; a choke that resonates in-band will arc or burn.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a choke in a PA is a filter to ground like a bypass capacitor. Correction: the plate RFC is a series element in the DC feed from B+ to the plate; it blocks RF from the supply while delivering DC, which is why its far end goes to the high-voltage source.", "link": "Reactance & Resonance", "edge_cases": "At VHF the plate choke is often replaced by a quarter-wave stub or a very small inductor because large chokes have parallel resonances and excess capacitance; solid-state amplifiers use the output transformer's centre tap as the DC feed in place of a choke."}

{"core": "In a grounded-grid amplifier the cathode is the RF input and must be held above RF ground by a choke; the DC side of that cathode choke goes to the bias point, labelled B−, so that the cathode sits at the DC potential that sets the tube's idle current while the choke keeps the RF drive on the cathode and out of the bias supply.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "B+ is the plate supply; connecting the cathode to high voltage would reverse-bias the tube and apply lethal potential to the input connector and drive circuitry.", "why_tempting": "The previous question established that a choke goes to B+, and the learner may apply the same answer without noting it is now the cathode choke."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Connecting the cathode choke directly to ground would place the cathode at ground DC potential, leaving no way to set operating bias (except an unmanageable grid supply) and typically producing excessive idle plate current.", "why_tempting": "In a grounded-cathode amplifier the cathode is grounded, and in some zero-bias grounded-grid designs it returns to ground through a small resistor or Zener; the Zener or resistor is in fact the bias element, which is what B− represents."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Filament voltage is the AC heater supply; in directly heated tubes the filament is the cathode, but the choke's DC return still goes to the bias network, with the filament transformer feeding through separate bifilar chokes.", "why_tempting": "In directly heated tubes the cathode and filament are the same element, so the learner conflates the heater supply with the cathode's DC return."}], "concept": "A triode's operating point is set by the grid-to-cathode DC voltage. In grounded-grid operation the grid is at ground, so bias must be applied by raising the cathode positive relative to ground; a cathode a few volts positive is equivalent to a grid a few volts negative. The cathode choke therefore returns to the bias network: in practice a Zener diode (for example 5 to 10 V), a string of diodes, or a resistor between cathode and ground, which develops the bias from the plate current itself and is bypassed to keep RF off it. Together with the plate current flowing through it, this node is the negative return of the plate circuit, hence B−. The choke's reactance must be large compared with the cathode input impedance (roughly 50 to 200 Ω) so that the exciter's drive appears across the cathode and not across the bias element; a few tens of microhenries suffices. Cutoff bias for standby is often obtained by switching in a larger resistor or opening the cathode return through a relay, which raises the cathode potential until the tube stops conducting; this is why the cathode return is also where transmit/receive keying is applied in many amplifiers.", "worked_example": "A 3-500Z at 3,000 V wants about 100 mA of idle current in class AB2; its curves show this needs roughly −5 V grid relative to cathode. With the grid grounded, insert a 5.1 V Zener between the cathode-choke return and ground: the plate current flowing through it holds the cathode at +5.1 V, which the tube sees as −5.1 V of grid bias. Add a 50 μH cathode choke: at 3.5 MHz X_L ≈ 1.1 kΩ, about ten times the roughly 100 Ω cathode input impedance, so 90 percent of the drive voltage appears on the cathode. For standby, a relay opens the Zener and substitutes a 50 kΩ resistor; the cathode rises toward cutoff and idle current falls to nearly zero.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: both chokes in a grounded-grid PA return to the same supply. Correction: the plate choke goes to B+ to deliver plate voltage, and the cathode choke goes to the bias (B−) network so the cathode sits at the DC level that sets idle current while remaining free to carry RF drive.", "link": "section 5", "edge_cases": "Some high-mu triodes (811A, 572B) are run in true zero-bias grounded grid with the cathode choke returned directly to ground through only the metering shunt; the exam's B− answer describes the general case where a bias element sits in the cathode return."}

{"core": "The only transformer whose secondary connects directly to the tube is the filament transformer: it delivers the low-voltage, high-current AC that heats the directly heated cathode, and in grounded-grid service it does so through bifilar RF chokes so the filament can also carry the RF drive.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "B+ comes from the high-voltage supply through a rectifier, filter and the plate choke; the HV transformer secondary never connects directly to the tube because the tube needs DC, not AC, on its plate.", "why_tempting": "The plate transformer is the biggest transformer in the amplifier, so it seems like the obvious one to connect to the tube."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A triode has no screen grid, so there is no screen voltage; even in a tetrode the screen is fed regulated DC, not a transformer secondary.", "why_tempting": "Screen voltage is a real tube supply term from tetrode and pentode amplifiers, and the learner may not notice that the question specifies a triode."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Bias is a DC voltage, derived from a Zener, resistor or small rectified supply; no AC secondary feeds the tube directly for bias.", "why_tempting": "Bias supplies in some amplifiers do have their own small transformer, but it feeds a rectifier, not the tube."}], "concept": "A transmitting triode needs three things: a heated cathode to emit electrons, a positive plate supply to collect them, and grid-cathode bias to set the operating point. Of these, only the heater can be run on raw AC, because the thermal mass of the filament averages the 60 Hz power and emission is essentially constant (with the hum issue addressed by the centre-tap return). The filament transformer therefore connects straight to the tube's filament pins, supplying for example 5 V at 15 A for a 3-500Z or 7.5 V at 21 A for an 8877-class tube. The plate and bias paths both require DC and so pass through rectifiers and filters before reaching the tube. In a grounded-grid amplifier the filament is also the RF input, so each filament lead carries both heater current and RF; the bifilar-wound filament choke (two wires wound together on a ferrite rod) passes the heavy AC heating current with negligible drop while presenting high reactance to RF, keeping the drive on the cathode and out of the transformer. The transformer secondary is thus the one winding in intimate contact with the tube.", "worked_example": "Thought experiment: a 3-500Z filament is rated 5.0 V ± 0.25 V at 14.5 A. The filament transformer secondary is 5 V at 15 A, connected through a bifilar choke of about 30 μH per winding. At 15 A the choke's 0.02 Ω winding resistance drops 0.3 V, so the transformer must be chosen or tapped for about 5.3 V to deliver 5.0 V at the tube; running at 4.5 V shortens emission life, at 5.5 V shortens filament life. At 14 MHz the choke's X_L ≈ 2.6 kΩ, far above the 100 Ω cathode impedance, so essentially all the RF drive stays on the filament. No other transformer in the amplifier touches the tube without a rectifier in between.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the plate (HV) transformer connects to the tube because that is where the power goes. Correction: the plate needs DC and is fed through a rectifier-filter and choke; the only transformer secondary wired directly to the tube is the filament (heater) winding, because heating works fine on AC.", "link": "section 5", "edge_cases": "Tubes with indirectly heated cathodes (8877, 4CX series) also take their heater directly from a transformer secondary, but the cathode is a separate electrode, so the heater leads do not carry RF and need no bifilar choke; the question's triode with a directly connected secondary describes the directly heated case."}

{"core": "At 50 percent efficiency the DC input must be twice the RF output, 800 W; with 400 mA of plate current the plate voltage is V = P_in / I = 800 W / 0.4 A = 2,000 V.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "3,000 V at 400 mA is 1,200 W input, which at 50 percent efficiency would yield 600 W output, not 400 W; it overshoots by 50 percent.", "why_tempting": "3,000 V is a very common amplifier plate voltage for 3-500Z class tubes, so it is familiar from real hardware rather than from the arithmetic."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "1,000 V at 400 mA is only 400 W of DC input; at 50 percent efficiency that gives 200 W output, half the required value. This is the answer you get if you forget to divide by efficiency.", "why_tempting": "Dividing output power directly by current (400/0.4) gives 1,000 V, the classic error of ignoring that input power exceeds output power."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "500 V at 400 mA is 200 W input and 100 W output at 50 percent efficiency, a quarter of the target.", "why_tempting": "Extra steps of halving (perhaps applying the 50 percent twice) land here, and it is a plausible low-voltage tube supply."}], "concept": "Amplifier efficiency is η = P_out / P_in, where P_in is the DC power the plate circuit draws, P_in = V_plate × I_plate (treating the current as the average DC plate current the meter reads). Rearranging gives V_plate = P_out / (η × I_plate). The remaining (1 − η) × P_in is dissipated as heat in the plate: here 400 W, which must be within the tube's plate dissipation rating (a 3-500Z is rated 500 W, so this operating point is sustainable). The 50 percent figure is typical of class AB linear service for SSB; class B approaches 60 to 65 percent and class C 70 to 80 percent, so the same output at higher efficiency would need proportionally less plate voltage for the same current, or less current at the same voltage. The plate load impedance the pi network must present follows from the same numbers: R_P ≈ V_plate / (1.8 × I_plate) ≈ 2,000 / 0.72 ≈ 2,800 Ω, or from V_plate² / (2 × P_out) = 4,000,000 / 800 = 5,000 Ω with the idealized class B formula; real designs land between. The drive feed-through in grounded-grid service adds to the output but is conventionally ignored in this exam calculation.", "worked_example": "Step 1: required DC input P_in = P_out / η = 400 W / 0.50 = 800 W. Step 2: plate voltage V = P_in / I = 800 W / 0.400 A = 2,000 V. Step 3 (check): plate dissipation = P_in − P_out = 800 − 400 = 400 W, under a 500 W rating. Cross-check the distractors: 3,000 V × 0.4 A × 0.5 = 600 W out (too much); 1,000 V × 0.4 × 0.5 = 200 W (too little); 500 V × 0.4 × 0.5 = 100 W. Only 2,000 V gives 400 W.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: output power equals plate voltage times plate current. Correction: V × I is the DC input power; output is only the efficiency fraction of that, so the plate voltage needed for a given output is P_out / (η × I), not P_out / I.", "link": "Ohm's Law & Power", "edge_cases": "In a grounded-grid amplifier the exciter's drive power passes through to the output (feed-through), so measured output is slightly higher than η × V × I alone; the exam ignores this, but it explains why a real amplifier at these numbers might show 450 to 480 W on the wattmeter."}

{"core": "In a grounded-grid triode the cathode (here the directly heated filament) is the RF input electrode, so it must sit at a well-defined RF potential while still carrying the filament's low-frequency heating current. Capacitors from each filament lead to ground give the RF a low-impedance path to chassis without shorting the AC or DC heater supply: that is the definition of a by-pass capacitor.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A tuning capacitor is part of a resonant L-C network and is chosen to set a frequency; a filament by-pass is deliberately non-resonant and simply looks like a short at RF.", "why_tempting": "Grounded-grid amplifiers have tank and input tuning capacitors elsewhere, so 'capacitor to ground in an amplifier' pattern-matches to tuning."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Electrolytics have large ESL and ESR, are polarized, and are useless at HF; a filament by-pass is a ceramic or mica part of a few nF chosen for low impedance at the operating frequency, and in any case 'electrolytic' describes construction, not function.", "why_tempting": "Capacitors to ground that handle a supply rail evoke the big electrolytics in the HV power supply."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "A blocking capacitor is placed in series with the signal path to pass RF while stopping DC. Filament capacitors are in shunt to ground, which is the opposite topology and the opposite job.", "why_tempting": "Both blocking and by-pass capacitors separate DC from RF; learners mix up which one is series and which is shunt."}], "concept": "In a grounded-grid (cathode-driven) amplifier the grid is held at RF ground and the drive is applied between cathode and ground, so the cathode is the hot input terminal. A directly heated triode uses the filament itself as the cathode, so the filament must simultaneously carry heater current at 50/60 Hz or DC and be an RF node. The usual solution is a bifilar filament choke that presents high impedance to RF along the heater leads, plus capacitors from each filament lead to chassis on the supply side so the far end of the choke is an RF ground. The by-pass impedance is X_C = 1/(2πfC); a 0.01 μF part at 14 MHz is about 1.1 Ω, effectively a short compared with the few tens of ohms of cathode input impedance. Lead inductance matters: a capacitor with 10 nH of lead has a self-resonance near 16 MHz for 0.01 μF, above which it starts looking inductive, which is why VHF amplifiers use smaller values and feedthrough capacitors. The same by-pass principle appears at the screen grid of a tetrode and at the emitter of a solid-state stage.", "worked_example": "Take a 3-500Z grounded-grid amplifier at 7.1 MHz with 0.01 μF filament by-pass capacitors. X_C = 1/(2π × 7.1 × 10⁶ × 0.01 × 10⁻⁶) ≈ 2.2 Ω. At 60 Hz the same capacitor presents 1/(2π × 60 × 10⁻⁸) ≈ 265 kΩ, so essentially none of the 5 V, 15 A heater current is diverted. The filament choke, typically 20 to 30 μH, presents 2π × 7.1 MHz × 25 μH ≈ 1.1 kΩ to RF, isolating the hot cathode from the by-passed supply side. Remove the capacitors and the heater wiring becomes an uncontrolled RF path: drive leaks into the filament transformer, input impedance becomes unpredictable, and the stage can oscillate.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: any capacitor connected to ground in an RF stage is 'tuning' something. Correction: a by-pass capacitor is intentionally far below self-resonance and far below any circuit resonance; it exists to make a node an RF ground while leaving its DC or low-frequency function intact.", "link": "Reactance & Resonance", "mnemonic": "By-pass = shunt to ground (RF takes the bypass road around the DC). Blocking = series in the path (blocks DC, passes RF).", "edge_cases": "At VHF the lead inductance of a leaded disc capacitor dominates; feedthrough capacitors mounted on the chassis wall or multiple parallel small values are needed. With indirectly heated cathodes the heater is already isolated and the cathode gets its own by-pass; the filament-to-ground capacitors then serve only to keep heater leads from radiating or coupling RF."}

{"core": "A VHF power amplifier's shielding is part of its electrical design, not just a cover: it closes the RF return path, keeps output from feeding back to the input, and sets the stray capacitances the tuning was done against. Reinstalling and fastening every shield before power-up restores the amplifier to the condition it was tuned in and keeps RF and high voltage contained.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Removing shielding opens the enclosure to RF leakage and feedback paths, and cooling in these amplifiers is designed around forced air through the shielded compartment; an open chassis typically cools the tube or transistor worse, not better.", "why_tempting": "Heat is a real concern in power amplifiers, so 'more airflow' sounds like a safe instinct."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The interlock exists so the high-voltage supply cannot be energized with the cover off. Bypassing it exposes the operator to lethal plate or drain voltages and defeats the one safety device meant for exactly this situation.", "why_tempting": "Interlocks are inconvenient when you are iterating on adjustments, and 'bypass for testing' is a common shop shortcut."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Running an amplifier into no load leaves nowhere for the output power to go; the tank voltage rises until something arcs or the device fails. A dummy load or antenna must always be connected.", "why_tempting": "It sounds considerate toward interference, and learners confuse 'don't transmit on air during tests' with 'don't connect a load'."}], "concept": "At VHF the wavelength is short enough that the enclosure, partitions and covers are electrically significant structures. Shield walls between the input and output compartments keep the output-to-input isolation high; without them the feedback through stray capacitance and radiation can exceed the loop gain margin and the stage oscillates. The covers also complete the ground return for the tank circuit and set a few picofarads of stray capacitance that was present when the tuning was done, so the amplifier tuned with the lid off is detuned with it on. Shielding also contains harmonic radiation and limits operator RF exposure, and it ties into the interlock chain for the high-voltage supply. The ordering matters: shielding fastened, load connected, interlock intact, then power. Any 'adjust while open' work is done with HV off and bleeders discharged, then the amplifier is closed and the effect checked on an external meter or analyzer.", "worked_example": "Suppose the output compartment of a 2 m amplifier has a 10 pF tube output capacitance and the tank inductance was adjusted for resonance at 144.2 MHz with the cover on, where the cover adds 1.5 pF of stray. With the cover off, C drops from 11.5 pF to 10 pF, so f shifts by the factor √(11.5/10) ≈ 1.072, moving resonance to about 154 MHz. A tuning adjustment made in that state is wrong by about 10 MHz once the cover goes back on. The sound procedure is to make a small change, close the amplifier, then verify on a wattmeter or spectrum analyzer.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: shielding is only about preventing TVI and can be left off while bench-testing. Correction: at VHF the enclosure is part of the tuned circuit and the feedback isolation, and it is also the HV safety barrier; the amplifier is only in its designed state with all shields fastened.", "link": "section 5", "edge_cases": "Some amplifiers provide tuning holes with shielded access or use screwdriver-adjustable trimmers reachable with the cover on, precisely so that alignment can be done in the closed state. Where no such provision exists, expect to iterate: adjust, close, measure, repeat."}

{"core": "A tuned-circuit interstage coupling is a bandpass filter resonant at the fundamental; its impedance falls off above resonance, so harmonics generated upstream are attenuated relative to the wanted signal before they reach the next stage. Every tuned coupling adds another layer of harmonic rejection.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "More drive to the final pushes it harder into nonlinearity (class C conduction angle shrinks, or a linear stage saturates), which generates more harmonics, not fewer.", "why_tempting": "Learners associate 'more input' with 'more wanted signal' and assume the harmonics stay fixed in absolute terms."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Harmonic generation comes from the nonlinearity of the transfer characteristic and the conduction angle, not from whether the device is a transistor or a tube. Bipolar transistors are, if anything, more abruptly nonlinear.", "why_tempting": "Modern equals better is a general bias, and solid-state rigs often have cleaner spectra, but that is due to filtering and linearization, not the device itself."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A larger series coupling capacitor has lower reactance at all frequencies, so it passes harmonics at least as well as the fundamental; it is broadband coupling, which is exactly what you want to avoid when suppressing harmonics.", "why_tempting": "Capacitors are associated with filtering, so 'bigger capacitor, more filtering' feels plausible even though a series capacitor is a high-pass element."}], "concept": "Any stage driven into nonlinear operation produces harmonics at 2f, 3f and so on, and class C stages in particular have rich harmonic content because the collector or plate current flows in short pulses. A parallel L-C tank resonant at f presents a high impedance Z ≈ Q × X_L at the fundamental but, at the nth harmonic, the capacitor's reactance has fallen by n and the inductor's risen by n, so the tank impedance drops roughly as 1/(n − 1/n) scaled by the loaded Q. The voltage developed across the tank at a harmonic is therefore much smaller than at the fundamental, and the stage that follows is driven mainly by the fundamental. Link-coupled or capacitively tapped double-tuned transformers between stages behave as bandpass filters with a 3 dB bandwidth of about f/Q_L, and cascading two or three such couplings multiplies the attenuation in dB. This is complementary to the output low-pass filter: tuned couplings keep harmonics from being amplified in the first place, the output filter removes what remains.", "worked_example": "An interstage tank at 7 MHz with loaded Q_L = 10 has 3 dB bandwidth ≈ 7 MHz / 10 = 0.7 MHz. For a parallel resonant tank the magnitude of the impedance relative to resonance is roughly 1/√(1 + (Q_L × (f/f₀ − f₀/f))²). At the second harmonic f/f₀ − f₀/f = 2 − 0.5 = 1.5, so the factor is 1/√(1 + 225) ≈ 0.066, or about −23.6 dB. At the third harmonic the detuning term is 3 − 1/3 ≈ 2.67, giving 1/√(1 + 711) ≈ 0.037, about −28.5 dB. Two such couplings in cascade yield roughly −47 dB at 2f before the final stage even sees the signal.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: harmonics generated early in the chain are locked in and only the final output filter can remove them. Correction: each resonant interstage coupling attenuates harmonics in proportion to its loaded Q and the harmonic order, so narrowband coupling throughout the chain progressively cleans the spectrum.", "link": "Reactance & Resonance", "edge_cases": "The attenuation estimate assumes the tank is dominated by its lumped L and C. Stray capacitance and inductor self-resonance can create unintended high-frequency passbands, which is why broadband solid-state exciters rely on a switched low-pass filter bank at the output instead."}

{"core": "The RF transformer's primary (or secondary) is resonated with a capacitor so the coupling network is a tuned circuit at the operating frequency: it selects the fundamental from the oscillator, provides the impedance transformation into the class C base, and rejects harmonics. Beyond passing energy from one stage to the next, it is the tank of the interstage tuned circuit.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Oscillator feedback is arranged inside the oscillator stage, usually by a tapped coil or a capacitive divider, or a crystal in the feedback loop; the interstage transformer couples forward to the amplifier and is kept out of the oscillator's loop so loading the amplifier does not pull the frequency.", "why_tempting": "Transformers are used for feedback in Armstrong oscillators, so 'transformer in an oscillator circuit' triggers that memory."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A balanced mixer needs two inputs and a nonlinear element arranged so the inputs cancel at the output; a CW transmitter has no second input signal and nothing to mix.", "why_tempting": "Centre-tapped RF transformers appear in diode ring mixers, so the component looks familiar in that role."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A pi filter is a capacitor-inductor-capacitor low-pass at the output of the final stage, not an interstage transformer; it uses a single inductor, not two magnetically coupled windings.", "why_tempting": "The interstage network does provide some harmonic rejection, which is also what the pi network does, so the functions overlap conceptually."}], "concept": "In a crystal oscillator driving a class C final, the two stages are joined by a transformer whose primary is shunted by a capacitor to form a parallel L-C tank resonant at f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)). The oscillator transistor sees a high impedance at resonance, which maximizes voltage swing, while the secondary presents the low impedance the base of the class C transistor wants, with a turns ratio chosen so Z_pri/Z_sec = (N_pri/N_sec)². The loose magnetic coupling also provides DC isolation between collector and base, so each stage can be biased independently, and the tank's selectivity attenuates oscillator harmonics before they reach the amplifier. The class C stage then conducts only on the peaks of the drive, producing current pulses rich in harmonics, which its own output tank converts back into a clean sine wave at f₀. The coupling transformer's loaded Q is a design compromise: higher Q means better harmonic rejection but more sensitivity to drift and loading.", "worked_example": "A 7.030 MHz CW transmitter uses a 4 μH primary. For resonance, C = 1/((2π × 7.03 × 10⁶)² × 4 × 10⁻⁶) ≈ 128 pF, so a 100 pF fixed capacitor in parallel with a 10 to 60 pF trimmer is typical. If the oscillator collector wants to see about 2 kΩ and the class C base presents about 50 Ω, the turns ratio needed is √(2000/50) ≈ 6.3:1. The same winding set thus resonates, transforms impedance and isolates DC, three jobs in one component.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: an interstage RF transformer is only a signal-coupling device, like an audio transformer. Correction: in RF practice the transformer winding is resonated and the tank it forms is the selective element that defines the stage's bandwidth and harmonic rejection.", "link": "Reactance & Resonance"}

{"core": "A series inductor feeding the collector supply with capacitors shunted to ground on the supply side is a textbook L-C low-pass filter: the RFC presents high impedance to RF, the capacitors present low impedance, and together they keep RF out of the DC supply line while letting DC through.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Negative feedback requires a path from output back to input with the appropriate phase; a choke and bypass capacitors in the supply line are deliberately placed to block any signal path, which is the opposite of a feedback network.", "why_tempting": "Supply decoupling does prevent unintended feedback through the power rail, so there is a loose association with feedback control."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A key-click filter shapes the rise and fall of the keying waveform at the key or keyed stage, typically an R-C network with a time constant of a few milliseconds; an RF choke with small capacitors has a time constant far too short to shape keying envelopes.", "why_tempting": "Both involve filtering in a CW transmitter, and the collector supply line is where keying is sometimes applied."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "A tuned circuit requires L and C in series or parallel resonance at the operating frequency; an RFC is chosen so its reactance is far above the circuit impedance and the bypass capacitors far below, deliberately avoiding resonance at f₀.", "why_tempting": "An inductor plus capacitors is the ingredient list for a tank, so it is easy to assume any L-C combination is resonant."}], "concept": "The collector of a class C stage swings at RF with a large amplitude, and the DC supply must deliver average current without that RF leaking back onto the rail, where it could couple into the oscillator or other stages and cause instability or spurious outputs. The RFC in series with the supply has reactance X_L = 2πfL that is large at the operating frequency, so most of the RF voltage appears across the choke rather than across the supply. The capacitors from the supply side of the choke to ground have reactance X_C = 1/(2πfC) that is small, shunting whatever RF remains to ground. The network is an L-section low-pass with a cutoff at f_c = 1/(2π√(LC)) placed well below the operating frequency and well above DC. Attenuation above cutoff rises at 12 dB per octave for a single L-C section. This is the same decoupling idea as the filament by-pass in a tube amplifier and the Vcc decoupling on every digital board: isolate the RF node from the shared supply.", "worked_example": "A 7 MHz transmitter uses a 100 μH RFC and a 0.01 μF bypass. X_L = 2π × 7 × 10⁶ × 100 × 10⁻⁶ ≈ 4.4 kΩ. X_C = 1/(2π × 7 × 10⁶ × 0.01 × 10⁻⁶) ≈ 2.3 Ω. The voltage divider ratio is about 2.3/4400 ≈ 5 × 10⁻⁴, or roughly −66 dB of RF reaching the supply rail. The cutoff frequency is f_c = 1/(2π√(100 × 10⁻⁶ × 0.01 × 10⁻⁶)) ≈ 159 kHz, far below 7 MHz and far above DC, confirming the low-pass placement.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a choke and capacitors in an RF stage must be forming a resonant tank. Correction: when the inductor's reactance is much larger than the circuit impedance and the capacitor's is much smaller, the pair is operating far from resonance as a low-pass decoupling filter, not as a tuned circuit.", "link": "Reactance & Resonance", "edge_cases": "An RFC has a self-resonant frequency set by its winding capacitance; above it the choke looks capacitive and the decoupling degrades. Multi-band transmitters often use a choke with several winding sections or a ferrite bead in series with a smaller choke to keep the impedance high across the whole HF range."}

{"core": "In a two-stage CW transmitter the first stage generates the signal and the second stage raises its power to the level needed for the antenna. The second transistor, operated in class C and driven by the oscillator through a tuned coupling, is the power amplifier.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "The master oscillator is the first stage, which contains the crystal or L-C frequency-determining network; the second stage has no frequency-determining feedback loop and simply amplifies what it is fed.", "why_tempting": "Both stages contain a transistor and a tuned circuit, so the role has to be read from the circuit topology rather than the parts list."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A CW transmitter carries no audio; the keying simply turns the carrier on and off. An audio oscillator would belong in a sidetone circuit, not in the RF chain.", "why_tempting": "Many simple CW rigs include a sidetone oscillator, and the word 'oscillator' appears in the question's context."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A frequency multiplier is a class C stage whose output tank is tuned to a harmonic of the drive. In the simple two-stage design both tanks are tuned to the same frequency, so the stage amplifies rather than multiplies.", "why_tempting": "A class C stage with a tuned output is exactly the hardware used for multipliers; only the tank tuning distinguishes the two roles."}], "concept": "The minimal CW transmitter architecture is a master oscillator power amplifier (MOPA). The oscillator is run at low power so it stays stable; a crystal or high-Q tank sets the frequency and the stage is lightly loaded so that changes in the following stage do not pull it. The second stage is a class C amplifier: biased at or below cutoff so collector current flows for less than 180 degrees of each cycle, which gives efficiency in the 60 to 80 percent range because current flows only when the collector voltage is low. The output tank restores a sine wave from the current pulses by flywheel action and matches the collector to the antenna. Power gain of a single class C transistor stage is typically 10 to 15 dB, so an oscillator delivering tens of milliwatts can drive the final to a few watts. The same stage becomes a frequency multiplier only if its output tank is tuned to 2f or 3f, and becomes a buffer if its purpose is isolation rather than power.", "worked_example": "Thought experiment: the oscillator delivers 50 mW at 7.030 MHz into the class C base. With 13 dB of power gain the collector delivers 50 mW × 10^(13/10) ≈ 50 × 20 = 1 W to the tank. At 70 percent efficiency the DC input is 1/0.7 ≈ 1.43 W, so from a 12 V supply the average collector current is about 120 mA. Retune the output tank to 14.06 MHz and the same hardware becomes a doubler delivering perhaps 0.2 W at the second harmonic; keep it at 7.03 MHz and it is the power amplifier.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the stage closest to the antenna in a CW transmitter must be doing something special, such as multiplying or keying. Correction: in a MOPA design the final's only job is power gain; frequency determination lives entirely in the first stage.", "link": "section 5"}

{"core": "If the oscillator runs continuously and only the buffer stage is keyed, the oscillator never experiences the thermal and loading transients of being switched on and off, so its frequency stays put. Keying a stage after the oscillator avoids the chirp that results from keying the oscillator itself.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Key clicks come from the sharpness of the keying envelope, which is set by the rise and fall time of the keyed stage regardless of where it sits in the chain; eliminating them requires a shaping network, not a choice of stage.", "why_tempting": "Keying a lower-power stage does reduce the energy in the switched signal, which feels like it should reduce clicks."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Radiated bandwidth of a CW signal is set by the keying envelope's rise and fall time; a hard-keyed buffer produces exactly the same sideband spread as a hard-keyed final.", "why_tempting": "Restricting bandwidth is a real goal of keying design, and buffer keying is often done alongside envelope shaping."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The buffer runs at low power, so keying it does avoid switching high RF voltages, but that is a convenience for the key contacts, not the principal engineering advantage. The keyed answer identifies the reason the technique exists: frequency stability.", "why_tempting": "It is a true statement about buffer keying, making it a strong near-miss; the question asks for the advantage, and stability is the defining one."}], "concept": "An oscillator's frequency depends on its tank components, its supply voltage, its device junction capacitances and its load. Keying the oscillator switches all of those at once: the device heats and cools, the supply rail sags and recovers, and the tank sees a changing load. The result is chirp, a frequency slide during the first milliseconds of each element, which is heard as a 'yoop' on the received note. A buffer is a low-gain, lightly loaded stage whose input impedance barely changes between on and off, especially when it is a common-collector or high-impedance common-emitter stage. Keying the buffer leaves the oscillator running at constant temperature, constant supply and constant load, so the oscillator frequency is unchanged while the carrier still appears and disappears on command. The oscillator's residual output is then kept out of the antenna by the off-state isolation of the buffer and the following stages; backwave is the symptom when that isolation is inadequate.", "worked_example": "Suppose keying the oscillator directly causes a 60 Hz chirp over the first 20 ms of each dit because the transistor junction capacitance changes by 0.2 pF as it warms, against a 50 pF tank. The fractional change is 0.2/50 × 0.5 ≈ 0.2 percent of the frequency if applied directly, which at 7 MHz would be 14 kHz, but a crystal pulls far less; even a 10 ppm shift is 70 Hz, clearly audible. Move the key to the buffer: the oscillator's thermal and load conditions no longer change with keying, the shift drops to the drift of a free-running oscillator over seconds, and the note sounds clean.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the cleanest CW keying comes from stopping the oscillator, since nothing is generated between elements. Correction: stopping and restarting the oscillator is the source of chirp; keeping it running and keying a later isolating stage preserves frequency stability, with backwave managed separately by stage isolation.", "link": "section 5", "edge_cases": "Buffer keying with no envelope shaping still produces clicks; the practical design keys the buffer through an R-C network giving about 5 ms rise and fall. Where the oscillator must be keyed to avoid backwave, as in some QRP designs, a brief key-down lead time and a stabilized supply reduce chirp."}

{"core": "Grid current in a correctly neutralized stage depends only on the drive from the previous stage. If tuning the plate tank changes the grid current, energy is being fed back from output to input through unneutralized capacitance. The best neutralization is therefore the setting where grid current changes least as the output circuit is tuned through resonance.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Absolute grid current is set by drive level and bias; a low reading can simply mean low drive, and tells nothing about whether feedback is present.", "why_tempting": "Minimum readings sound like minimum error, a general instinct from nulling procedures."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Maximum grid current indicates heavy drive or a resonant input circuit, not an absence of feedback; a regenerative stage can show increased grid current because feedback adds to the drive.", "why_tempting": "Many tuning procedures peak the grid current when resonating the input tank, so 'peak grid current' is familiar from a different step."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "A large change in grid current with output tuning is the symptom of poor neutralization: feedback through the plate-to-grid capacitance varies strongly as the plate tank passes through resonance.", "why_tempting": "It is the exact inverse of the correct answer, and learners who remember 'watch the grid current change' may forget which direction indicates success."}], "concept": "In a grounded-cathode tube amplifier the plate-to-grid capacitance C_pg forms a feedback path from output back to input. When the plate tank is tuned slightly inductive, the phase of the fed-back voltage reinforces the grid drive (positive feedback); slightly capacitive and it opposes it. Sweeping the plate tuning through resonance therefore produces a characteristic dip-and-peak in grid current from the feedback alone. Neutralization adds an out-of-phase sample of the plate voltage, taken from a tap or a link on the tank, through a neutralizing capacitor C_n chosen so that the fed-back current through C_n cancels that through C_pg: in a bridge sense, C_n/C_pg equals the ratio of the tank voltages at the two sampling points. With the bridge balanced, the grid no longer sees the plate, and grid current becomes flat as the plate tank is tuned, which is exactly the observation the question describes. The usual procedure is to disable plate voltage, apply drive, tune the plate tank and adjust C_n for minimum RF at the output; the grid-current criterion is the in-operation check.", "worked_example": "Step by step on a tetrode final: apply normal drive and note grid current, say 10 mA. Tune the plate capacitor from well below resonance through to well above while watching the grid meter. With poor neutralization the reading might swing from 7 mA on one side of resonance to 13 mA on the other, a 6 mA change. Adjust C_n by a small amount and repeat; if the swing drops to 2 mA you are moving the right way. Continue until the swing is at its smallest, perhaps a fraction of a milliampere, which is the neutralization setting. Note that the final absolute reading, 10 mA, never mattered; only the variation did.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: neutralization is judged by the level of grid current. Correction: it is judged by how insensitive grid current is to plate-circuit tuning, because that insensitivity measures the degree to which output-to-input feedback has been cancelled.", "link": "section 5", "mnemonic": "Neutral means nothing changes: a well-neutralized grid meter does not care what the plate tank is doing.", "edge_cases": "Grounded-grid amplifiers rarely need neutralization because the grid shields the cathode from the plate; the grid-current method applies to grounded-cathode tetrode and triode stages. Modern solid-state finals do not use this test, but the same feedback mechanism through C_cb or C_rss appears in VHF transistor stages and is handled by layout and shielding."}

{"core": "A neutralizing circuit feeds a deliberately phase-inverted sample of the output back to the input so it cancels the unwanted positive feedback that occurs through the device's internal output-to-input capacitance. With that feedback nulled the stage cannot sustain self-oscillation.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Hum from the power supply is removed by filtering and regulation of the HV and filament supplies; a neutralizing capacitor passes RF only and has no effect on 60 or 120 Hz ripple.", "why_tempting": "Both are 'cleanup' functions in a transmitter, and both involve capacitors."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Incidental grid modulation would be a drive-level or bias-stability problem; neutralization cancels RF feedback and does nothing to stabilize bias or audio-rate variations in drive.", "why_tempting": "The grid is involved in neutralization, so anything with 'grid' in it sounds related."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Differential gain is a video-amplifier linearity specification describing how gain changes with signal level; it is unrelated to RF feedback paths in a power amplifier.", "why_tempting": "It is technical-sounding and vaguely about amplifier gain, which is enough to lure someone who does not recognize the term."}], "concept": "Every amplifying device has capacitance from its output electrode to its input electrode: plate-to-grid in a triode, collector-to-base in a BJT, drain-to-gate in a FET. The output tank voltage is large, so even a few picofarads of C_pg can push significant current back into the high-impedance input tank. When the input and output tanks are tuned near the same frequency, the loop phase can reach zero at some tuning condition and, if the loop gain exceeds unity, the stage oscillates (the tuned-plate tuned-grid oscillator is this same circuit used on purpose). Neutralization takes a voltage of opposite phase to the plate voltage, obtained from the far end of a centre-tapped tank or from a tap below ground on the input coil, and couples it to the input through C_n. Choosing C_n so the two feedback currents are equal and opposite makes the net feedback zero across the band of interest, since both paths are capacitive and scale the same way with frequency. The amplifier then has only its forward gain, and its stability no longer depends on tuning.", "worked_example": "Thought experiment: a tetrode has C_pg = 0.2 pF and its plate tank swings 2 kV peak. Current fed back through C_pg at 14 MHz is V × 2πfC = 2000 × 2π × 14 × 10⁶ × 0.2 × 10⁻¹² ≈ 35 mA peak. Into a grid tank impedance of 2 kΩ that is 70 V of unintended drive, comparable to the actual drive. Add a neutralizing capacitor of 0.2 pF from a point on the tank that swings −2 kV (the opposite end of a split tank with its centre at RF ground): it injects −35 mA, the sum at the grid is zero, and the stage no longer sees its own output.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: neutralization suppresses oscillation by reducing gain.
