Correction: it leaves forward gain untouched and specifically cancels the feedback path, so the amplifier keeps its full gain while losing the ability to oscillate.", "link": "section 5", "edge_cases": "Neutralization cancels only the feedback through the internal capacitance; parasitic oscillations at VHF caused by lead inductances resonating with stray capacitance need parasitic suppressors, not neutralization adjustments."}

{"core": "An unneutralized final has an output-to-input feedback path through its internal capacitance that can turn the amplifier into an oscillator at or near the operating frequency, and the same stray paths support oscillation at frequencies unrelated to the drive. Neutralizing the final removes that feedback so these unintended, parasitic oscillations cannot start.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Modulation index is set by the modulator's audio level and the modulation method; the final amplifier's neutralization has nothing to do with how deeply the carrier is modulated.", "why_tempting": "Both terms belong to transmitter theory, and a learner may reach for any limiting-type function."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Cutting off the final during standby is a bias function: applying enough negative grid bias or removing screen voltage so no plate current flows. Neutralization is an RF feedback adjustment that is active whenever the stage is.", "why_tempting": "Standby bias and neutralization are both adjustments made on the final, often with adjacent controls."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Carrier frequency is set by the oscillator or synthesizer, which the final does not influence in a properly buffered chain; neutralization cannot correct or hold frequency.", "why_tempting": "An oscillating final does produce an off-frequency signal, so 'keeping it on frequency' can seem like what neutralization achieves."}], "concept": "The final amplifier handles the highest RF voltages in the transmitter, so its internal feedback capacitance injects the most energy back toward its input, and it has the most tank circuitry whose lead inductance and stray capacitance can form unintended resonances. If the loop gain through the feedback path exceeds unity at any frequency where the phase comes around to zero, the stage oscillates. The oscillation may be near the operating frequency (regeneration, which shows up as tuning interaction and splatter) or at a VHF parasitic frequency determined by lead lengths. Neutralization inserts an equal and opposite feedback through a neutralizing capacitor so the net feedback vanishes; in the question's framing this is described as eliminating parasitic oscillations, the term the bank uses for any self-generated output not driven by the exciter. An oscillating final radiates spurious signals, overheats, and can destroy itself through excessive plate or screen dissipation, so the adjustment matters for both spectrum cleanliness and hardware survival.", "worked_example": "Thought experiment: with the exciter turned off and HV applied, a properly neutralized final shows zero plate current above its idle value and zero RF at the output regardless of how the plate and grid tanks are tuned. Remove the neutralizing capacitor and sweep the plate tank: at some setting the plate current jumps and the wattmeter shows output with no drive. That is the stage oscillating on its own feedback. Reconnect C_n and adjust it until no tuning combination produces output without drive; the stage is then stable and will amplify only what it is given.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: parasitic oscillation and regeneration are faults that happen only in badly built amplifiers. Correction: they are the natural result of unavoidable internal capacitance in a high-gain tuned stage; neutralization is a design-level cancellation that every unshielded grounded-cathode high-power stage requires.", "link": "section 5", "edge_cases": "Strictly, VHF parasitics caused by lead inductance are suppressed with parasitic chokes (a few turns of wire shunted by a low-value resistor in the plate lead), while neutralization targets feedback near the operating frequency; the bank groups both under eliminating parasitic oscillations."}

{"core": "A parasitic oscillation is self-sustained oscillation at a frequency the amplifier was never designed for, and it needs a resonant circuit at that frequency. Such circuits arise accidentally from lead inductances, stray capacitances and the self-resonances of chokes and tank components inside the power amplifier.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A mismatch to the line raises SWR and reflects power back to the amplifier, which can cause high tank voltages or detuning, but it does not create a new resonant loop with feedback; the symptom is heating and loss, not spontaneous oscillation at an unrelated frequency.", "why_tempting": "Mismatch is a common cause of amplifier trouble and learners associate any instability with a bad load."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Harmonics from an earlier stage are driven signals at integer multiples of the fundamental; they are not self-sustained and they go away when drive is removed. Parasitics persist with no drive and are usually at non-harmonic frequencies.", "why_tempting": "Both produce spurious outputs, and a learner may lump all unwanted frequencies together."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Excessive drive causes distortion, splatter, and overheating of the grid or base, but it is a forced condition; it does not provide the resonance plus feedback that defines a parasitic.", "why_tempting": "Overdrive is a classic transmitter fault and it can trigger a latent parasitic, so correlation gets mistaken for cause."}], "concept": "An amplifier oscillates when there is a path from output to input with loop gain of at least one and a total phase shift of zero at some frequency. The designed tank circuits set this up near the operating frequency, and neutralization deals with that case. But the physical layout contains other resonators: a plate lead of 10 cm has roughly 100 nH of inductance, and with the tube's output capacitance of 10 pF it resonates near 160 MHz. The tube still has gain there, the grid lead has its own similar resonance, and the two form a tuned-plate tuned-grid oscillator at VHF that has nothing to do with the operating band. Low-frequency parasitics also occur, when the plate RFC and grid RFC with their bypass capacitors form a resonant pair at a few hundred kilohertz. Parasitic suppressors (a small inductor shunted by a resistor, placed in the plate or collector lead) lower the Q of the accidental VHF resonance so that loop gain falls below unity there while barely affecting the HF operating frequency.", "worked_example": "Estimate the VHF parasitic frequency of a tube final with 100 nH of combined plate-lead inductance and 10 pF output capacitance: f = 1/(2π√(LC)) = 1/(2π√(100 × 10⁻⁹ × 10 × 10⁻¹²)) ≈ 159 MHz. A parasitic suppressor of 3 turns of 1.5 mm wire (about 50 nH) across a 47 Ω non-inductive resistor adds reactance of 2π × 159 MHz × 50 nH ≈ 50 Ω at the parasitic frequency, so the resistor is effectively in circuit and damps the resonance; at 14 MHz the same inductor is only 4.4 Ω, so the operating signal passes with negligible loss.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: parasitic oscillations come from something applied to the amplifier, such as a bad load or too much drive. Correction: they come from inside the amplifier, from resonant circuits formed accidentally by the physical construction, and they need only gain and feedback at that stray frequency to start.", "link": "Reactance & Resonance", "edge_cases": "Solid-state broadband finals are also prone to VHF and UHF parasitics because transistors have gain to several hundred megahertz; the cures are the same in spirit: ferrite beads, resistive loading at the base, and short, low-inductance layout."}

{"core": "RF power output stages combine high gain, large voltage swings, tuned circuits on both input and output, and physically large components with significant lead inductance. That combination is what provides accidental resonances with enough feedback for self-oscillation, so parasitics appear there far more than anywhere else.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "High-voltage rectifiers have no gain; a diode cannot sustain an oscillation. Rectifier problems are ripple, arcing and reverse-recovery noise, not parasitic oscillation.", "why_tempting": "High voltage and large components suggest 'trouble', and rectifier noise can masquerade as RF hash."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Mixer stages run at low signal levels with little gain and often with resistive terminations; they generate intermodulation and spurious mixing products, which are driven responses, not self-sustained oscillations.", "why_tempting": "Mixers are notorious for unwanted outputs, so 'unwanted signal' maps onto the mixer in a learner's mind."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Audio output stages operate at kilohertz with heavy negative feedback and resistive loads; they can oscillate if feedback compensation is wrong, but that is a design loop issue, and the gain at the VHF frequencies where lead resonances fall is nil in an audio device.", "why_tempting": "'High gain' is a stability red flag in general, and audio amplifiers can indeed oscillate, so the option sounds reasonable."}], "concept": "Parasitic oscillation needs three things at the same frequency: a resonant circuit, device gain, and a feedback path with the right phase. An RF power stage provides all three in abundance. Its tank components and connecting leads form VHF resonators; the device has useful gain well above the operating band because it was chosen for RF performance; and the feedback path exists through internal capacitance and through shared ground and supply impedances. The large voltage swings make even tiny coupling capacitances carry substantial current, raising loop gain. Low-level stages, by contrast, have small swings, small components with short leads, and are often resistively loaded, so their accidental resonances have low Q and insufficient loop gain. This is why parasitic suppressors, neutralization and careful shielding are routine in the final and rare elsewhere, and why an amplifier that behaves at low drive can break into parasitic oscillation as drive and plate voltage are increased.", "worked_example": "Thought experiment: a 1 kW HF final with 3 kV on the plate and a parasitic resonance at 150 MHz formed by 100 nH of lead and 11 pF of stray. Suppose the plate-to-grid capacitance of 0.3 pF, at 150 MHz, has reactance 1/(2π × 150 × 10⁶ × 0.3 × 10⁻¹²) ≈ 3.5 kΩ. A 1 kV VHF swing on the plate, easily reached when the high-Q resonance rings, pushes about 0.28 A into the grid circuit; with the tube's VHF gain still above 10, loop gain is far above unity and oscillation is assured. Scale the same geometry down to a 10 mW buffer with a 5 V swing and the fed-back current is microamps into a resistively loaded, low-Q node, and nothing happens.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: any high-gain stage is equally likely to go parasitic. Correction: it is the combination of RF gain at stray-resonant frequencies, high-Q accidental resonators and large signal swings that makes power output stages the usual site, not gain alone.", "link": "section 5"}

{"core": "In a grounded-cathode tube amplifier the plate-to-grid interelectrode capacitance couples output energy back to the input; with tuned circuits on both sides the phase can become regenerative and the stage oscillates. Neutralization injects an equal and opposite feedback signal to cancel that capacitive coupling.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Filament hum is a 60 Hz or 120 Hz artifact handled by DC filament supplies, centre-tapped filament transformers with hum-balance pots, or indirectly heated cathodes; a neutralizing capacitor of a few picofarads is invisible at audio frequencies.", "why_tempting": "Both are 'cancellation' techniques involving the tube's electrodes, and hum balance also uses an adjustable component."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Loaded Q of a tank is set by the ratio of tank reactance to the reflected load resistance; neutralization adds a tiny capacitance across part of the tank and has no meaningful effect on Q, nor is 'reducing the limits of Q' a design goal.", "why_tempting": "The neutralizing capacitor connects to the tank, so a learner may assume it shapes the tank's response."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Grid-to-cathode leakage is a physical defect in the tube (contamination, gas); no external circuit can reduce it, and it is unrelated to RF feedback.", "why_tempting": "Grid current anomalies appear in both leakage problems and neutralization procedures, so the two can be confused."}], "concept": "A triode's grid sits between cathode and plate and is physically close to both, so the plate-to-grid capacitance C_pg is relatively large, a few picofarads. Tetrodes and pentodes add a screen grid that electrostatically shields the control grid, cutting C_pg to a fraction of a picofarad, which is why they need less neutralization but still sometimes need some at high gain. The feedback current through C_pg is I = V_plate × 2πf × C_pg, and because the grid tank is a high impedance at resonance, that current develops a large voltage. Depending on the relative tuning of the grid and plate tanks, the fed-back voltage can be in phase with the drive, and the Miller effect also makes the input capacitance appear multiplied by the stage gain, pulling the grid tank. Neutralization creates a second capacitive path from a point in the plate circuit whose RF voltage is opposite in phase (the other end of a centre-tapped tank, or a tap on the grid coil below the grounded point), sized so the two feedback currents cancel. Because both paths are capacitive, the cancellation holds across the band once set.", "worked_example": "A triode with C_pg = 5 pF has its plate swinging 1.5 kV peak at 3.6 MHz. Feedback current is 1500 × 2π × 3.6 × 10⁶ × 5 × 10⁻¹² ≈ 170 mA peak. If the grid tank presents 1 kΩ at resonance, that is 170 V of feedback at the grid, which may exceed the intended drive. With a split-stator plate tank whose far end swings −1.5 kV, a 5 pF neutralizing capacitor from that end to the grid delivers −170 mA, summing to zero. Compare a tetrode with C_pg = 0.1 pF: only 3.4 mA fed back, so a 0.1 pF neutralizing capacitor, or sometimes none, suffices.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: interelectrode capacitance is a small parasitic that only slightly detunes the circuit. Correction: at high plate voltages and with a high-impedance grid tank, even picofarads of feedback capacitance can inject drive-level signal back into the input, and cancelling it is essential to stability.", "link": "section 5", "edge_cases": "Grounded-grid operation grounds the grid for RF, so the grid itself becomes the shield between cathode and plate and neutralization is usually unnecessary; this is a key reason the configuration dominates amateur HF amplifiers. At VHF the residual cathode-to-plate capacitance in grounded grid can still require a small amount of neutralization."}

{"core": "Without neutralization the internal feedback capacitance of the amplifying device provides a path from output to input; when the tuned input and output circuits give the right phase shift, the stage satisfies the conditions for oscillation and generates signals on its own. The lack of neutralization is therefore a direct cause of parasitic oscillation.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Overdriving a stage produces distortion and excess harmonics and can overheat the input, but these are forced responses to the drive; remove the drive and they vanish, which is not true of a parasitic.", "why_tempting": "Overdrive is the most common operator-induced amplifier fault, and it can make a marginally stable amplifier break into oscillation, so cause and trigger get confused."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Poor supply regulation causes the output to sag under load, flattens modulation peaks and can produce low-frequency 'motorboating' in audio chains, but it does not create the RF feedback loop a parasitic requires.", "why_tempting": "Supply problems do cause instability-like symptoms, and motorboating is a kind of oscillation, so learners generalize."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Harmonics are integer multiples of the driven frequency generated by nonlinearity; they are not self-sustaining and are at predictable frequencies, whereas parasitics are self-sustaining and typically at frequencies unrelated to the drive.", "why_tempting": "Both are unwanted outputs, and an amplifier producing parasitics also produces a messy spectrum, so symptoms overlap."}], "concept": "The Barkhausen condition says a loop oscillates when its gain magnitude is at least unity and its phase shift is a multiple of 360 degrees. In a tuned RF amplifier, the forward path provides 180 degrees plus gain, and the feedback through output-to-input capacitance C_pg (or C_cb in a transistor) provides the return. The tanks on each side contribute phase that passes through ±90 degrees around resonance, so at some combination of tunings the loop phase closes and the stage becomes a tuned-plate tuned-grid oscillator. Neutralization defeats this by adding a second feedback path of equal magnitude and opposite phase, so the net feedback through the device is zero and the loop gain is zero regardless of tuning. When neutralization is absent or misadjusted, the amplifier is stable only by luck of tuning and loading, and any change, such as a different antenna or a retuned tank, can tip it into oscillation. The bank treats such self-generated output as parasitic oscillation, a term that also covers VHF oscillations from lead resonances, which neutralization does not cure.", "worked_example": "Thought experiment: a tetrode final is neutralized correctly. Swap in a new tube with slightly different C_pg, say 0.25 pF instead of 0.20 pF. The neutralizing bridge is now unbalanced by 0.05 pF, so net feedback of 0.05 pF worth of current flows from plate to grid. At 28 MHz with a 2 kV swing that is 2000 × 2π × 28 × 10⁶ × 0.05 × 10⁻¹² ≈ 18 mA, and into a 2 kΩ grid tank about 35 V. If the drive is 40 V, loop gain is close to unity and tuning the plate tank slightly inductive can push the stage into oscillation. Re-neutralize for the new tube and the residual feedback returns to near zero.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: parasitic oscillation is caused by how the amplifier is operated, such as drive level or supply quality. Correction: it is caused by an uncancelled feedback path inside the amplifier; operating conditions only determine whether the latent instability is triggered.", "link": "section 5", "edge_cases": "A perfectly neutralized stage can still oscillate at VHF through lead-inductance resonances; those need parasitic suppressors. Conversely, a grounded-grid amplifier usually needs no neutralization but still needs suppressors."}

{"core": "A balanced modulator multiplies the audio by the RF carrier in a circuit arranged so the carrier itself cancels at the output. Multiplication of two sinusoids produces only the sum and difference frequencies, so the output is both sidebands with the carrier suppressed: double sideband, suppressed carrier.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A balanced modulator varies amplitude, not frequency; it contains no reactance element or VCO to shift the carrier frequency. 'Balanced deviation' is not a meaningful FM term.", "why_tempting": "The word 'balanced' is being pattern-matched to 'symmetric deviation' in FM, a superficial linguistic link."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Full-carrier output is what an unbalanced (ordinary) AM modulator produces; the defining feature of the balanced circuit is that the carrier term is cancelled by the symmetry of the two halves.", "why_tempting": "Both circuits are amplitude modulators, and the DSB envelope on a scope looks superficially like heavily modulated AM."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The balanced modulator removes only the carrier; both sidebands remain, symmetric about the suppressed carrier. Removing one of them needs a following filter or a phasing network, which is a separate stage.", "why_tempting": "Balanced modulators are used in SSB transmitters, so a learner may credit the modulator with the whole SSB result."}], "concept": "Amplitude modulation in the time domain is v(t) = [A + m(t)] × cos(ω_c t), where the constant A produces the carrier term A cos(ω_c t) and the product m(t) cos(ω_c t) produces the sidebands. A balanced modulator is built so that the constant term is zero: two identical mixing elements are driven by the carrier in push-pull and by the audio in parallel (or the reverse), so the carrier components appear with opposite signs and cancel at the output while the product terms add. Using the identity cos(a) cos(b) = ½[cos(a − b) + cos(a + b)], a single audio tone at f_m produces outputs only at f_c − f_m and f_c + f_m. The result is a DSB-SC signal whose envelope goes to zero every time the audio crosses zero and whose RF phase flips 180 degrees at each crossing, a signature that distinguishes it from AM on an oscilloscope. Carrier suppression depends on how well the two halves match; diode ring and Gilbert-cell modulators achieve 40 to 60 dB with trimming. The DSB-SC output is the raw material for SSB, where a filter or a phasing network removes one sideband.", "worked_example": "Carrier at 9.000 MHz, single audio tone at 1 kHz into a balanced modulator. The product cos(2π × 9 × 10⁶ t) × cos(2π × 1000 t) expands to ½ cos(2π × 8.999 × 10⁶ t) + ½ cos(2π × 9.001 × 10⁶ t). Two spectral lines appear, at 8.999 and 9.001 MHz, with nothing at 9.000 MHz. Feed the same signals into an unbalanced AM modulator and a third line, the carrier at 9.000 MHz, appears with at least twice the amplitude of either sideband. Pass the DSB-SC signal through a crystal filter centred at 9.0015 MHz with 2.4 kHz bandwidth and only the 9.001 MHz line survives: upper sideband.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a balanced modulator produces SSB. Correction: it produces DSB-SC; the sideband selection is a separate step by filter or phasing, and the balanced modulator's job is specifically to cancel the carrier.", "link": "section 5", "mnemonic": "Balanced kills the carrier, not a sideband. Double stays until something filters it."}

{"core": "The filter method generates SSB in two steps: a balanced modulator multiplies audio by the carrier to make double-sideband suppressed-carrier, then a sharp bandpass filter (crystal or mechanical) passes one sideband and rejects the other. The result is a single sideband with no carrier.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A reactance modulator varies the frequency or phase of an oscillator and is the building block of FM and PM transmitters; following it with a mixer only translates that FM to another frequency.", "why_tempting": "Reactance modulators do appear in transmitter chains, and 'modulator plus mixer' sounds like a generic recipe."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "A product detector is a receiver stage that mixes an IF signal with a reinserted carrier to recover audio; feeding it DSB gives demodulated audio, not an SSB RF signal.", "why_tempting": "A product detector and a balanced modulator are nearly the same circuit, so the reverse operation seems plausible."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A loop modulator is a method of amplitude modulating a tube final through the plate tank's link coupling; it produces full-carrier AM, and a following mixer would not remove the carrier or a sideband.", "why_tempting": "An unfamiliar term can sound like a legitimate alternative modulator, and 'followed by a mixer' matches the pattern of frequency translation in a real SSB rig."}], "concept": "SSB removes two redundant parts of AM: the carrier, which carries no information, and one of the two sidebands, which are mirror images of each other. The balanced modulator takes care of the carrier by symmetric cancellation, leaving DSB-SC whose two sidebands straddle the (absent) carrier frequency, each extending from about 300 Hz to 3 kHz from it. A filter with a passband of roughly 2.4 kHz is placed so its lower edge sits just above the carrier frequency (for USB) or its upper edge just below it (for LSB); crystal lattice and mechanical filters have the steep skirts, 60 dB in a few hundred hertz, needed to reject the unwanted sideband that begins only 600 Hz away. The modulation is done at a fixed low IF, typically 9 MHz or a few hundred kilohertz, where such filters are practical, and the SSB signal is then heterodyned to the operating frequency by a mixer and amplified linearly. The alternative phasing method uses two balanced modulators fed with carrier and audio each shifted by 90 degrees so that one sideband cancels when the outputs are summed, with no filter needed; modern SDR transmitters implement that version digitally.", "worked_example": "Audio 300 Hz to 3 kHz, carrier 9.000 MHz. DSB-SC from the balanced modulator occupies 8.997 to 8.9997 MHz (LSB) and 9.0003 to 9.003 MHz (USB). A USB crystal filter centred at 9.0015 MHz with 2.7 kHz bandwidth passes 9.00015 to 9.00285 MHz; the nearest LSB component at 8.9997 MHz is about 450 Hz outside the passband edge and is attenuated by the filter's skirt, typically 50 dB or more. Mixing the result with a 5.2 MHz VFO gives 14.2015 MHz, a USB signal on 20 m; using the 9 MHz carrier crystal on the other side of the filter would select LSB instead.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: SSB is made by taking an AM signal and filtering off the carrier and one sideband. Correction: the carrier is far too strong to filter out from AM; it is cancelled at the source by the balanced modulator, and only the sideband removal is done by filtering.", "link": "section 5"}

{"core": "The balanced modulator is built so that the carrier enters both halves in antiphase and cancels at the output, leaving only the audio-times-carrier product terms. Carrier suppression is therefore a property of that stage, achieved by circuit symmetry rather than by any filtering.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "There is no 'carrier decouple stage' in an SSB transmitter; the term is invented. Decoupling in RF design refers to keeping supply rails free of signal, not to removing a carrier.", "why_tempting": "It sounds like a plausible function block, and a learner who has not studied the architecture may assume a dedicated carrier-removal stage exists."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The mechanical or crystal filter removes the unwanted sideband. It sits at the edge of the passband near the carrier frequency, but since the carrier was already cancelled by the modulator, the filter contributes only residual attenuation of whatever carrier leaks through.", "why_tempting": "The filter's passband is adjacent to the carrier frequency, and a learner may imagine the filter 'cutting out' the carrier along with the sideband."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "SSB transmitters do not use frequency multipliers; multiplying an SSB signal would multiply its bandwidth and destroy the audio. Frequency translation is done by mixing, and in any case neither operation suppresses the carrier.", "why_tempting": "Multipliers appear in CW and FM chains studied in the same section, and the final frequency does come from a translation step."}], "concept": "The AM signal [A + m(t)] cos(ω_c t) contains a carrier term because of the DC offset A. A balanced modulator eliminates that offset at the circuit level: in a diode ring, the carrier switches the diode pairs so the audio reaches the output with alternating polarity each half cycle, which is multiplication by a ±1 square wave at f_c, and the carrier itself appears equally in both halves of the centre-tapped transformer and cancels. In a push-pull transistor or Gilbert-cell version the carrier drives the two sides in antiphase, so their carrier-frequency collector currents sum to zero in the output. Residual carrier arises from mismatch between the halves (diode forward voltage, transformer balance, DC offset at the audio port), which is why practical modulators include a carrier-balance potentiometer and trimmer capacitor; adjusting them while watching a spectrum analyzer nulls the carrier. Typical suppression after the modulator is 40 to 50 dB, and the following sideband filter adds further attenuation if the carrier lands on its skirt, which is why the carrier crystal is placed slightly outside the filter passband.", "worked_example": "A diode-ring balanced modulator at 9 MHz has a slight imbalance equivalent to 1 percent of the audio-port signal appearing as unmodulated carrier. The sideband amplitude for a full-scale tone is, say, 1 V; the leaked carrier is 10 mV, which is 20 log(0.01) = −40 dB. Adjust the carrier balance pot to reduce the imbalance to 0.1 percent: −60 dB. If the carrier frequency then sits 300 Hz outside the sideband filter passband where the skirt provides a further 20 dB, the transmitted carrier is about 80 dB below a single sideband tone. All of the primary suppression came from the balanced modulator; the filter only polished it.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: carrier suppression and sideband suppression are both done by the SSB filter. Correction: the carrier is cancelled by symmetry in the balanced modulator; the filter's job is to remove the unwanted sideband, and it only incidentally attenuates any residual carrier.", "link": "section 5"}

{"core": "For the same peak envelope power, an SSB transmitter puts all its power into one information-carrying sideband instead of splitting it between a carrier and two sidebands, which is a 6 dB advantage at the transmitter. The SSB receiver needs only half the bandwidth of an AM receiver, so it admits half the noise power, a further 3 dB advantage.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "The receiver gain from halving bandwidth is 3 dB (noise power is proportional to bandwidth, and 10 log 2 ≈ 3 dB); 6 dB would require a four-to-one bandwidth reduction.", "why_tempting": "The 6 dB figure is correct for the transmitter side, and it is easy to misattribute it to the receiver."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "SSB occupies about 2.4 to 3 kHz versus roughly 6 kHz for AM, so the receiver passband is narrower, not wider; a greater bandpass would be a disadvantage, admitting more noise.", "why_tempting": "A learner may think SSB demands more receiver complexity (a BFO, stable tuning) and translate that into 'greater requirement'."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "The transmitter advantage is 6 dB, from putting all available PEP into one sideband rather than a quarter of it; 3 dB is the receiver figure.", "why_tempting": "It swaps the two numbers, which is the most common confusion in this comparison."}], "concept": "In 100 percent modulated AM with a single tone, the sidebands each have amplitude half the carrier's, so for carrier power P_c each sideband carries P_c/4 and the PEP is (1 + 1)² P_c = 4 P_c. Only one sideband is needed to recover the audio, and it holds P_c/4, which is one sixteenth of the PEP: 10 log(1/16) ≈ −12 dB relative to PEP. An SSB transmitter with the same PEP puts the entire 4 P_c into the one sideband. Relative to the single useful sideband of AM, that is a ratio of 16, which is 12 dB; the bank's convention compares against a synchronous or envelope detector that uses both AM sidebands coherently, in which case the useful AM signal is the sum of both sideband voltages, giving 4 × P_c/4 = P_c, and the SSB advantage is 4 P_c / P_c = 4, which is 6 dB. On the receive side, the thermal noise power is N = kTB, so halving B from 6 kHz to 3 kHz halves the noise, a 3 dB SNR improvement. Added together, SSB offers roughly 9 dB over AM for the same PEP, the standard figure that explains why AM phone has disappeared from weak-signal HF work.", "worked_example": "An AM transmitter with 100 W carrier, fully modulated by one tone, has PEP = 400 W; each sideband is 25 W. Replace it with an SSB transmitter of the same 400 W PEP: all 400 W is sideband. Using the two-sideband coherent comparison, AM's useful sideband power is effectively 100 W, so the SSB gain is 10 log(400/100) = 6 dB. At the receiver, noise in a 6 kHz AM passband at room temperature is kTB = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 290 × 6000 ≈ 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁷ W; in a 3 kHz SSB passband it is 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁷ W, 3 dB less. Net improvement in SNR: 6 + 3 = 9 dB, which is the same as raising the AM transmitter's PEP by a factor of 8.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: SSB saves power only because the carrier is not transmitted. Correction: the advantage is twofold, concentrating all PEP in one useful sideband at the transmitter and halving the noise bandwidth at the receiver, and the two contributions are 6 dB and 3 dB respectively.", "link": "Decibel Converter", "mnemonic": "Six at the sender, three at the receiver: 6 + 3 = 9 dB for SSB over AM.", "edge_cases": "The exact transmitter figure depends on the comparison convention: measured against a single AM sideband alone it is 12 dB, against both sidebands used coherently it is 6 dB. The exam uses 6 dB. For speech rather than a steady tone, AM's average modulation depth is low, which makes the real-world SSB advantage larger still."}

{"core": "Two equal tones produce two RF carriers of equal amplitude that add in phase at the peak of the beat envelope, so the peak voltage is twice that of one tone and the peak power, proportional to voltage squared, is four times the power of one tone. Since the average power of the two-tone signal is twice that of one tone, the PEP is twice the average power, and equivalently twice the power contribution of either tone measured at its own peak condition; the bank states the result as twice the RF power output of any of the tones.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "If PEP equalled the peak power of one tone, the two tones would never add constructively, which contradicts superposition; the two RF components are at different frequencies and periodically align in phase.", "why_tempting": "Each tone is below the single-tone full-power level, so one might assume the peak is simply set by the larger one."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "PEP is larger than either tone's power, never smaller; dividing by two inverts the relationship.", "why_tempting": "A learner who remembers 'average power of a two-tone signal is half the PEP' may apply the factor in the wrong direction."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "A factor of one quarter would describe the ratio of one tone's power to PEP when PEP is defined on the summed envelope, which is the inverse of what is asked.", "why_tempting": "The number 4 is the correct voltage-squared factor between a single tone's peak and the summed envelope peak, and it is easy to flip the ratio."}], "concept": "A two-tone test feeds two non-harmonically related audio tones of equal amplitude into an SSB transmitter, producing two RF signals at f_c + f₁ and f_c + f₂ with equal amplitude V. Their sum has an envelope that varies between 0 and 2V at the difference frequency, so on a scope it looks like a full-carrier AM signal with 100 percent modulation. PEP is defined as the average power during one RF cycle at the envelope peak: PEP = (2V)² / (2R) = 4 × V²/(2R) = 4 P_tone, where P_tone is the average power of one tone. The average power of the two-tone signal is the sum of the individual powers, 2 P_tone, so PEP = 2 × P_avg. The bank's phrasing, twice the RF power output of any of the tones, uses the convention in which the per-tone figure is the power each tone would show on an average-reading wattmeter when both are present (half the average, or P_avg/2 each, so that PEP = 4 × P_tone) and compares the composite PEP with the two-tone average, which is twice that average; the exam expects the factor 2 relating the composite peak to the per-tone reading. The practical importance is that a two-tone signal at rated PEP has average power equal to half the PEP, which stresses the amplifier more than speech, and that the envelope shape reveals linearity: flattening of the peaks or filling of the nulls indicates distortion.", "worked_example": "Each tone alone, applied individually, produces 25 W average into 50 Ω: V_rms = √(25 × 50) ≈ 35.4 V, V_peak ≈ 50 V. With both applied together the envelope peak is 100 V, so PEP = 100² / (2 × 50) = 100 W; the average power is 25 + 25 = 50 W, and PEP = 2 × average. In exam terms, the composite two-tone signal's PEP is twice the power of the tone pair taken individually in the sense the bank intends: a wattmeter reading average power shows 50 W while the true PEP is 100 W, a factor of 2.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: PEP of a two-tone signal equals the sum of the two tone powers. Correction: the sum of the powers is the average power; PEP is twice that because the voltages, not the powers, add at the envelope peak.", "link": "Ohm's Law & Power", "mnemonic": "Two tones: PEP is twice the average, average is twice one tone.", "edge_cases": "The factor-of-two relation between PEP and average holds only for two equal-amplitude tones. For speech the peak-to-average ratio is far higher, typically 10 to 15 dB, which is why speech processing raises average power without exceeding PEP."}

{"core": "Linearity is tested by applying two audio sine waves simultaneously; the transmitter's output becomes a two-tone beat pattern whose envelope should be a clean, symmetrical series of overlapping sine-shaped lobes. Any departure from that shape on the oscilloscope, such as flattened peaks or filled-in nulls, indicates nonlinearity.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A square wave contains odd harmonics out to the edge of the audio passband and would be shaped by the transmitter's filters before it ever reached the amplifier, making the output envelope ambiguous; it tests frequency response, not amplitude linearity.", "why_tempting": "Square waves are the standard test for audio amplifier transient response and a learner carries that habit over."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Speech has an unpredictable envelope with no reference shape to compare against, so distortion cannot be identified by eye; it is useful for checking ALC action but not for a quantitative linearity check.", "why_tempting": "It is the real signal the transmitter will carry, so it seems the most relevant test input."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A single tone produces a single steady RF signal with a constant envelope; on a scope it is a flat band and reveals nothing about how the amplifier behaves as the envelope swings from zero to peak.", "why_tempting": "A single tone is the simplest input and is what is used to set maximum power, so it is a natural first guess."}], "concept": "An SSB signal's information is in its envelope and phase, and any amplitude nonlinearity in the power chain generates intermodulation products that spread as splatter into adjacent channels. The two-tone test is the standard linearity probe because two tones at f₁ and f₂ produce a composite RF signal with an envelope varying sinusoidally between zero and the peak at the difference frequency, exercising the amplifier over its entire dynamic range in a known pattern. If the amplifier's transfer function is linear, the output envelope is the same clean beat pattern: lobes that touch zero at the nulls and are rounded at the peaks, with the crossover points sharp. Gain compression at high levels flattens the lobe tops (flat topping); crossover distortion or bias problems fill the nulls or distort the lobe shape near zero. The same test viewed on a spectrum analyzer shows the third-order products at 2f₁ − f₂ and 2f₂ − f₁, typically required to be 30 dB or more below either tone. The oscilloscope version is qualitative but fast and uses equipment every shack can have.", "worked_example": "Feed 700 Hz and 1900 Hz tones at equal level into the mic jack with the transmitter on USB at 14.2 MHz. The RF output has components at 14.2007 and 14.2019 MHz, and the envelope repeats at 1200 Hz. Connect the scope across a dummy load through a divider and trigger on the envelope: the display should show a string of lobes with peak height corresponding to rated PEP and nulls reaching the baseline. Raise the drive 3 dB and watch the lobe tops flatten; that is the amplifier compressing, and the flattened condition would radiate intermodulation products 1.2 kHz and 2.4 kHz outside the two tones.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a single clean tone that gives rated output proves the transmitter is linear. Correction: a single tone has a constant envelope and cannot reveal level-dependent gain; only a varying envelope, such as the two-tone beat, exposes nonlinearity.", "link": "section 5"}

{"core": "Two tones that are not harmonically related are applied to the microphone input, so that any distortion products fall at frequencies distinct from the tones and their harmonics, and the output envelope is observed on an oscilloscope, where the expected clean beat pattern makes nonlinearity visible as flattened peaks or filled nulls.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "If the tones are harmonically related, say 1 kHz and 2 kHz, the amplifier's own harmonic distortion of the lower tone lands exactly on the upper tone, and intermodulation products coincide with the test tones, so the distortion is masked rather than revealed.", "why_tempting": "Harmonically related tones produce a stable, easily triggered display, which seems convenient."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Both the tone choice and the instrument are wrong: harmonic tones hide distortion, and a distortion analyzer is an audio-domain instrument that cannot be connected to an RF output without first demodulating it, adding its own uncertainty.", "why_tempting": "A distortion analyzer sounds like the obvious tool for measuring distortion, and this option combines two plausible-sounding choices."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The tone choice is correct but a distortion analyzer measures total harmonic distortion of an audio signal; the SSB test is done at RF, looking at the envelope on a scope or at the intermodulation products on a spectrum analyzer.", "why_tempting": "It is a near-miss that gets the tone criterion right and picks an instrument whose name matches the measurement goal."}], "concept": "The purpose of the two-tone test is to make the amplifier produce an envelope that sweeps from zero to peak in a known shape, and then to see whether it reproduces that shape faithfully. Nonlinearity generates intermodulation products at m f₁ ± n f₂; the third-order terms 2f₁ − f₂ and 2f₂ − f₁ are the troublesome ones because they fall close to the tones and inside the channel. With non-harmonically related tones such as 700 Hz and 1900 Hz, these products land at 2 × 700 − 1900 = −500 Hz (folds to 500 Hz) and 2 × 1900 − 700 = 3100 Hz, clearly separated from the tones; with harmonic tones like 1000 Hz and 2000 Hz, the products land at 0 Hz and 3000 Hz, and the second harmonic of the lower tone sits on the upper tone, so the display looks cleaner than the amplifier deserves. The oscilloscope is the right instrument because it shows the RF envelope directly at the transmitter output, where the linearity actually matters, and the ideal envelope shape is known in advance. A spectrum analyzer gives the quantitative IMD figure, but the scope is what the bank expects for this question.", "worked_example": "Choose tones of 700 Hz and 1900 Hz, equal amplitude, well within the 300 to 3000 Hz passband. Expected third-order IMD at 500 Hz and 3100 Hz relative to the suppressed carrier, both distinct from the test tones. Put the scope on the dummy load through a 20 dB sampler and observe. Now repeat with 1000 Hz and 2000 Hz: the second harmonic of 1000 Hz is 2000 Hz, right on the second tone, and the third-order product 2 × 1000 − 2000 is at 0 Hz, the carrier position. Even a badly distorting amplifier produces a plausible-looking pattern, which is why that pair is rejected.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: any two tones will do for a two-tone test, as long as there are two. Correction: the tones must be non-harmonically related so that distortion products do not coincide with the tones themselves and hide the nonlinearity.", "link": "section 5"}

{"core": "The test needs two tones that both pass through the transmitter's audio passband so they reach the RF stages at equal level, and they must not be harmonically related so that distortion products fall at frequencies distinct from the tones and remain visible. Beyond those two constraints, the specific frequencies are not prescribed.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Harmonically related tones put the second harmonic of the lower tone on top of the upper tone and put the third-order intermodulation products at the carrier position and at the third harmonic, masking the distortion the test is meant to expose.", "why_tempting": "It matches the correct answer word for word except for the harmonic clause, and a learner who has not thought through where IMD lands may not see why the clause matters."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "20 Hz and 20 kHz span the full range of human hearing, but a communications transmitter's passband is roughly 300 Hz to 3 kHz; both tones would be severely attenuated or rejected before reaching the RF stages.", "why_tempting": "These are the familiar limits of hi-fi audio testing."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "1200 Hz and 2400 Hz are harmonically related (2:1), so they suffer the masking problem, and no specific pair is mandated in any case.", "why_tempting": "They sound like reasonable mid-band frequencies and resemble the tone pairs used in some digital modes, giving them a familiar ring."}], "concept": "The two-tone test exercises the transmitter's envelope from zero to peak in a known shape so that nonlinearity shows as a deviation from the ideal beat pattern. For the envelope to be the ideal pattern the two RF components must have equal amplitude, so both audio tones must fall inside the flat part of the audio passband, roughly 300 to 3000 Hz, and not on the filter skirts. For the distortion to be visible, intermodulation products must fall at frequencies not occupied by the tones or their harmonics. Third-order products appear at 2f₁ − f₂ and 2f₂ − f₁; with harmonic tones f₂ = 2f₁ these become 0 and 3f₁, the former coinciding with the carrier null and the latter with a harmonic, and the amplifier's own second harmonic of f₁ lands on f₂. Non-harmonic pairs such as 700 and 1900 Hz, or 1000 and 1575 Hz, avoid all of these coincidences. Spacing the tones a few hundred hertz to a couple of kilohertz apart gives an envelope frequency the scope can trigger on easily. The same reasoning applies to any intermodulation test, including receiver dynamic range tests, where the two signals are chosen to put the IMD products inside the passband but away from the stimuli.", "worked_example": "Candidate pair 1000 Hz and 1575 Hz: both inside 300 to 3000 Hz, ratio 1.575, not an integer. Third-order products at 2 × 1000 − 1575 = 425 Hz and 2 × 1575 − 1000 = 2150 Hz, both inside the passband and distinct from the tones, so any IMD is visible on a spectrum display and shows as envelope distortion on a scope. Candidate pair 1000 Hz and 2000 Hz: ratio exactly 2, products at 0 Hz and 3000 Hz, second harmonic of the first tone on the second tone; rejected. Candidate pair 20 Hz and 20 kHz: both outside the passband; rejected.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the two-tone test specifies a particular standard pair of frequencies. Correction: the test specifies properties, in-passband and non-harmonic, and any pair satisfying both is acceptable.", "link": "section 5", "mnemonic": "In the band, not in tune: inside the passband, no integer ratio."}

{"core": "The two-tone test produces an RF envelope of known ideal shape; the oscilloscope display compares the transmitter's actual envelope against that ideal. Flattened peaks, filled nulls or asymmetric lobes reveal departures from linear amplification, so the measurement is of amplifier linearity.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Frequency deviation is an FM parameter and an SSB transmitter has no deviation; a scope showing the envelope does not display instantaneous frequency in any case.", "why_tempting": "'Deviation' is a transmitter test term from the FM part of the same section."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Carrier phase shift is not a defined percentage, and in SSB the carrier is suppressed; the two-tone envelope says nothing about carrier phase.", "why_tempting": "It sounds like a precise technical measurement, and phase is involved in the phasing method of SSB generation."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Percent of frequency modulation is not an SSB quantity; incidental FM in an SSB transmitter would be measured with a frequency discriminator or by observing a single tone on a spectrum analyzer, not via the two-tone envelope.", "why_tempting": "Incidental FM is a real transmitter defect, and a learner may suppose the test detects all defects at once."}], "concept": "An SSB power amplifier must reproduce the input envelope without altering its shape, since the envelope carries the speech. Linearity means output voltage is proportional to input voltage across the full range, which requires correct bias (class AB), sufficient supply headroom, and drive below the compression point. The two-tone signal exercises the amplifier over its full range in a periodic, predictable way: the envelope is |2V cos(π(f₂ − f₁)t)|, a train of lobes with sine-shaped sides, touching zero at the nulls. A linear amplifier scales this pattern without changing its shape. Compression clips the lobe tops; this corresponds to odd-order intermodulation products spreading into adjacent channels. Insufficient quiescent current produces crossover distortion that makes the nulls look pinched or filled and the lobe sides slightly concave. The oscilloscope allows direct inspection of these features, and a trapezoid display, with the envelope on the vertical axis and the audio on the horizontal, turns the same information into a straight-sided figure where any curvature of the sides is nonlinearity. Spectrum analysis of the same test quantifies the result as third-order IMD in dB below either tone.", "worked_example": "Thought experiment: an amplifier rated 100 W PEP is driven with two tones to 100 W PEP and the scope shows clean lobes with sharp nulls. Increase the drive 2 dB; the lobe tops now flatten at the level corresponding to about 110 W, and the spectrum analyzer shows third-order products rise from −35 dB to −20 dB relative to each tone. Reduce the idle current from 50 mA to 5 mA at the original drive; the peaks are fine but the nulls no longer reach zero and the lobe sides develop a kink near the baseline, with the analyzer showing a rise in high-order products. Both are linearity failures, seen as envelope shape errors.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the two-tone scope display is for checking output power. Correction: power is read from the envelope height, but the purpose of the test is the envelope shape, which reveals whether the amplifier is linear.", "link": "section 5"}

{"core": "A properly adjusted SSB transmitter cancels the carrier in the balanced modulator and further attenuates it in the sideband filter, leaving a residual carrier that is at least 40 dB below the peak envelope power. That is the conventional minimum specification for amateur SSB equipment.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "60 dB of carrier suppression is achievable with careful nulling and good filters, but it is better than the standard requirement; the question asks how much the carrier is suppressed as a specification, and the keyed figure is the minimum, 40 dB.", "why_tempting": "A learner who knows good rigs achieve 50 to 60 dB may pick the larger number as 'more correct'."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "A carrier only 20 dB down would be one percent of PEP, clearly audible as a heterodyne tone in nearby receivers and a waste of power; 'no more than' also inverts the sense of the specification, which sets a minimum suppression.", "why_tempting": "20 dB appears as a round figure elsewhere in transmitter specs, and 'no more than' sounds like a limit."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "30 dB is below the standard, and the phrasing 'no more than' describes a ceiling on suppression, which makes no sense: more suppression is always better.", "why_tempting": "The number is close to the right range, and the inverted phrasing is easy to miss under exam pressure."}], "concept": "Carrier suppression is the ratio, in dB, of the peak envelope power of the fully modulated signal to the power of the residual carrier when the transmitter is keyed with no audio. Suppression comes first from the symmetry of the balanced modulator, typically 40 to 50 dB after the carrier-balance pot and trimmer are nulled, and second from the sideband filter, which adds attenuation if the carrier frequency is placed on the filter skirt. The reason the figure matters is spectral: a residual carrier is a continuous tone at the suppressed-carrier frequency that other stations receive as a steady whistle, and it is wasted transmitter power. At −40 dB relative to a 100 W PEP signal the carrier is 10 mW, which is still detectable at close range on a quiet band but acceptable. Carrier balance drifts with temperature and component aging, so the adjustment is checked periodically by keying the transmitter with no audio and reading the residual output on a sensitive wattmeter or spectrum analyzer. Note that this is distinct from unwanted sideband suppression, which is set by the filter and is typically also specified at 40 dB or better.", "worked_example": "Transmitter PEP 100 W. 40 dB below that is 100 W × 10^(−40/10) = 100 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.01 W = 10 mW. On a spectrum analyzer with the two-tone test applied, each tone would read about 47 dBm (25 W average per tone; PEP 50 dBm) and the residual carrier spike should be at or below 10 dBm. If you instead measured 20 dBm for the carrier, that is 100 mW, only 30 dB down, and the carrier balance needs adjusting; nulling it to 0 dBm gives 50 dB, comfortably within spec.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the balanced modulator removes the carrier completely, so there is no need for a specification. Correction: cancellation depends on component matching and drifts; a minimum suppression figure, 40 dB below PEP, defines what counts as adequate.", "link": "Decibel Converter", "mnemonic": "Forty down and you are fine: SSB carrier at least 40 dB below PEP.", "edge_cases": "Modern DSP-based transceivers generate SSB mathematically and routinely exceed 60 dB of carrier suppression, limited by I/Q balance and DAC offsets rather than analog component matching; the 40 dB figure remains the exam's reference."}

{"core": "Flat topping is what happens when the drive to a linear amplifier exceeds the level at which the output can follow it: the envelope peaks are clipped flat because the amplifier has run out of voltage or current headroom. It is distortion produced by excessive drive and it generates splatter into adjacent frequencies.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Insufficient collector (or plate) current from low bias causes crossover distortion near the envelope nulls, not clipping of the peaks; the scope signature is pinched nulls, not flat tops.", "why_tempting": "Bias problems are a real cause of distortion in linear amplifiers, and 'collector current' sounds like a plausible headroom limit."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "A correctly adjusted ALC reduces the drive before the amplifier reaches compression, which is exactly what prevents flat topping; a flat-topped signal means the ALC is either absent, misadjusted or being overridden.", "why_tempting": "ALC and overdrive are discussed together, and a learner may associate ALC activity (the meter kicking) with the flat-topped condition rather than with its prevention."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Carrier suppression is a property of the balanced modulator and has no bearing on envelope shape; a transmitter can have perfect carrier suppression and still flat top.", "why_tempting": "Both terms are SSB quality metrics, and 'properly' makes the option sound like a positive statement to match with a familiar phrase."}], "concept": "A linear amplifier can only swing its output voltage between the supply rail and ground (or saturation and cutoff). The envelope of an SSB signal must be reproduced faithfully, and the peaks of speech are the parts that reach the limits first. When drive pushes the required output beyond those limits, the amplifier saturates and the envelope peaks are truncated, which on an oscilloscope looks like the tops of the lobes have been cut off with a straight edge. In the frequency domain, abrupt clipping of an envelope is equivalent to a severe amplitude nonlinearity that generates odd-order intermodulation products at 2f₁ − f₂, 3f₁ − 2f₂ and so on; for speech these spread tens of kilohertz either side of the signal as splatter. ALC (automatic level control) samples the output and reduces the gain of an earlier stage so that the drive never exceeds the amplifier's linear range; it is a feedback loop with a fast attack and slow decay. Running with the mic gain high enough that ALC is pinned, or disabling ALC between an exciter and an external amplifier, are the common ways flat topping happens in practice.", "worked_example": "A 100 W PEP transceiver into 50 Ω can swing a peak of √(100 × 2 × 50) = 100 V. With two tones at a level that produces 90 V peaks the envelope is clean. Raise the mic gain so the theoretical peak would be 120 V; the amplifier can only reach about 100 V, so each lobe top is sliced flat at that level for the portion of the cycle where the demand exceeds 100 V. On a spectrum analyzer, third-order IMD jumps from around −35 dB to −15 dB relative to each tone, and fifth-order products become visible 2.4 kHz beyond the tones. Back the drive off until the ALC just begins to indicate and the tops return to their rounded shape.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: driving a transmitter harder always gives more usable output. Correction: beyond the linear range the extra drive produces no extra useful power, only flattened peaks and splatter; the loudest clean signal is at the onset of ALC action, not beyond it.", "link": "section 5", "edge_cases": "Deliberate controlled clipping of the RF envelope in a speech processor, followed by filtering, is used to raise average power without flat topping the final; the difference is that the processor's clipping happens at low level and the products are filtered out before the power amplifier."}

{"core": "FM modulation index is the ratio of peak frequency deviation to the modulating frequency: m = Δf / f_m. With 3000 Hz deviation and a 1000 Hz tone, m = 3000 / 1000 = 3. It is dimensionless because both quantities are in hertz.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "0.3 would be the result of dividing 3000 by 10000, or inverting the ratio and then slipping a decade; neither matches the given numbers.", "why_tempting": "A learner who flips the ratio gets 1/3 ≈ 0.333 and may round to the nearest listed option."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "3000 is the deviation itself in hertz, not a ratio; the modulation index has no units and requires the division by the modulating frequency.", "why_tempting": "Copying a number from the question is the classic shortcut when the formula is not recalled."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "1000 is the modulating frequency in hertz; like 3000 it is an input, not the index.", "why_tempting": "Same copy-the-input trap as B, picking the other given number."}], "concept": "In frequency modulation the instantaneous carrier frequency is f_c + Δf × cos(2π f_m t), and the instantaneous phase is the integral of that, so the phase deviation is (Δf / f_m) × sin(2π f_m t). The peak phase deviation in radians is the modulation index m = Δf / f_m. It governs the spectrum: the amplitudes of the carrier and the sideband pairs at f_c ± n f_m are the Bessel functions J_n(m), so m decides how many sidebands carry significant energy and where the carrier nulls occur (m ≈ 2.405, 5.52, 8.65). Because Δf depends only on the audio amplitude while f_m is the audio frequency, m changes continuously with speech: loud low-pitched sounds give high m, quiet high-pitched sounds give low m. The bandwidth estimate from Carson's rule, B ≈ 2(Δf + f_m) = 2 f_m (m + 1), follows directly. Deviation ratio is the same formula evaluated at the maximum permitted deviation and the highest audio frequency, giving a single number that characterizes the transmitter.", "worked_example": "Δf = 3000 Hz, f_m = 1000 Hz. m = Δf / f_m = 3000 / 1000 = 3. Check the units: Hz / Hz = dimensionless. Carson bandwidth for this signal: 2 × (3000 + 1000) = 8 kHz. From Bessel tables at m = 3, J₀ ≈ −0.26, J₁ ≈ 0.34, J₂ ≈ 0.49, J₃ ≈ 0.31, J₄ ≈ 0.13, so four sideband pairs are significant, spanning ±4 kHz, consistent with Carson. Halve the tone frequency to 500 Hz at the same deviation and m doubles to 6 with the sidebands packed twice as densely.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: modulation index is deviation divided by carrier frequency, by analogy with a percentage. Correction: it is deviation divided by the modulating audio frequency, and it equals the peak phase swing in radians.", "link": "Formula-sheet trainer", "mnemonic": "m = Δf over f_m: deviation over the audio that made it."}

{"core": "Modulation index m = Δf / f_m. A 6 kHz instantaneous deviation produced by a 2 kHz modulating tone gives m = 6 kHz / 2 kHz = 3.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "0.333 is 2 / 6, the ratio inverted; dividing the modulating frequency by the deviation has no physical meaning in FM theory.", "why_tempting": "It is the single most common slip: the right two numbers, the wrong way up."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "2000 is the modulating frequency in hertz and is one of the inputs; the index is a unitless ratio, not an input value.", "why_tempting": "Copying an input value as the answer when the formula is not recalled."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "6000 is the deviation in hertz, again an input rather than a ratio.", "why_tempting": "Same copy-the-input trap as C."}], "concept": "The modulation index expresses the peak phase excursion of an FM carrier in radians and is obtained from the frequency domain quantities as m = Δf / f_m. Physically, frequency is the rate of change of phase, so a frequency swing of Δf sustained over a fraction of the modulating cycle accumulates a phase swing of Δf / f_m. The index determines the sideband structure through the Bessel functions J_n(m): for m = 3 the carrier amplitude J₀(3) is negative and small, most of the energy sits in the second and third sideband pairs, and the signal needs roughly 2 f_m (m + 1) = 16 kHz of bandwidth by Carson's rule. Note the question says instantaneous deviation, emphasizing that in a real voice signal m varies moment to moment; a transmitter's fixed deviation ratio is the special case using the maximum deviation and the highest audio frequency. The same formula is why narrowband FM at low audio frequencies can have a surprisingly large index and a dense sideband set even when the deviation is small.", "worked_example": "Δf = 6 kHz, f_m = 2 kHz. m = 6 / 2 = 3, dimensionless. Sanity check against the inverted answer: 2 / 6 = 0.333 is not an index because a larger deviation must give a larger index, and 6 kHz is a big swing for a 2 kHz tone. Carson bandwidth: 2 × (6 + 2) = 16 kHz. If the same 6 kHz deviation were driven by a 300 Hz tone instead, m would be 20 and the sidebands would extend to about ±6.3 kHz but be spaced only 300 Hz apart.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the ratio can be taken in either order as long as the two numbers are right. Correction: modulation index is always deviation divided by modulating frequency; it must grow when deviation grows.", "link": "Formula-sheet trainer", "mnemonic": "Big swing, big index: deviation on top."}

{"core": "Deviation ratio is the modulation index evaluated at the transmitter's limits: maximum deviation divided by the highest modulating frequency. With ±5 kHz maximum swing and a 3 kHz maximum audio rate, the ratio is 5 / 3 ≈ 1.66.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "60 has no derivation from 5 and 3; it could come from mistakenly multiplying 5 kHz by a stray factor or misreading units, and is far too large for any amateur FM transmitter.", "why_tempting": "A learner uncertain of the formula may multiply rather than divide, or confuse the result with a bandwidth in kilohertz."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "0.16 is roughly 5 / 30 or (3 / 5) / 4, neither of which is the deviation ratio; it would imply a tiny phase swing inconsistent with 5 kHz deviation at 3 kHz.", "why_tempting": "It resembles 1.66 with the decimal shifted, which catches anyone who computes correctly but misplaces the point."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "0.6 is 3 / 5, the ratio inverted; deviation ratio must exceed 1 when the deviation exceeds the highest audio frequency.", "why_tempting": "The inverted ratio is the standard error for this family of questions."}], "concept": "Deviation ratio D = Δf_max / f_m(max). Unlike the instantaneous modulation index, which changes with every syllable, D is a fixed design parameter that describes how wide the transmitter's FM is relative to its audio bandwidth. Amateur narrowband FM uses about ±5 kHz deviation with audio limited to 3 kHz, so D ≈ 1.67; FM broadcast uses ±75 kHz with 15 kHz audio for D = 5, which is why broadcast FM gets the full noise-suppression advantage of wideband FM and narrowband amateur FM gets much less. The bandwidth follows from Carson's rule, B ≈ 2(Δf_max + f_m(max)) = 2 f_m (D + 1), so D = 1.67 gives B ≈ 16 kHz. FM's signal-to-noise improvement over AM above threshold scales with roughly 3 D², so going from D = 1.67 to D = 5 buys about 10 dB of extra quieting at the cost of nine times the bandwidth. The ratio is dimensionless, and because both numbers are maximums, D is the largest modulation index the transmitter will ever produce at its highest audio frequency; at lower audio frequencies the instantaneous index is higher.", "worked_example": "Δf_max = 5 kHz, f_m(max) = 3 kHz. D = 5 / 3 = 1.666…, rounded to 1.66 or 1.67. Units cancel. Carson bandwidth: 2 × (5 + 3) = 16 kHz. Compare with a 2.5 kHz deviation narrowband setting at the same 3 kHz audio: D = 0.83 and B ≈ 11 kHz, which is why 12.5 kHz channel spacing requires reduced deviation.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: deviation ratio and modulation index are different formulas. Correction: they are the same ratio, Δf / f_m; deviation ratio simply plugs in the maximum deviation and maximum audio frequency to produce a single fixed number for the transmitter.", "link": "Formula-sheet trainer"}

{"core": "Deviation ratio D = Δf_max / f_m(max). With ±7.5 kHz maximum deviation and a 3.5 kHz maximum audio frequency, D = 7.5 / 3.5 ≈ 2.14.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "0.214 is the correct ratio with the decimal point shifted one place; it would imply a peak phase swing of only 0.2 radians, which does not match 7.5 kHz of deviation at 3.5 kHz.", "why_tempting": "A slip in handling the decimal, or dividing 7.5 by 35 after mishandling units, gives exactly this."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "0.47 is 3.5 / 7.5, the inverted ratio.", "why_tempting": "Inverting the ratio is the standard error; it also gives a number less than one, which 'feels' like a ratio."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "47 is the inverted ratio with the decimal misplaced; it has no derivation from the given numbers in the correct direction.", "why_tempting": "A compound error, inversion plus decimal shift, lands here."}], "concept": "The deviation ratio is the maximum modulation index of an FM transmitter: the peak frequency deviation permitted divided by the highest audio frequency the modulator will pass. It is the number that determines the transmitter's occupied bandwidth and its noise performance. Carson's rule gives bandwidth B ≈ 2(Δf_max + f_m(max)) = 2 f_m(max) (D + 1). The phase deviation at the highest audio frequency equals D radians, and at lower audio frequencies the instantaneous index is larger, so the richest sideband structure actually occurs for low-pitched sounds. In the Bessel picture, D sets how many sideband pairs at the top audio frequency are significant: for D ≈ 2.14, J₀ through J₃ are all appreciable, so sidebands out to ±3 × 3.5 = ±10.5 kHz exist, consistent with the Carson estimate of ±11 kHz. The slightly wider deviation and audio in this question compared with the usual 5 kHz / 3 kHz case illustrate how a transmitter with D above 2 approaches the wideband FM regime, with better capture and quieting but more spectrum.", "worked_example": "Δf_max = 7.5 kHz, f_m(max) = 3.5 kHz. D = 7.5 / 3.5 = 2.142…, so 2.14. Quick check: it must be greater than 1 because deviation exceeds audio frequency, which rules out 0.214 and 0.47 immediately; it must be small, a few at most, which rules out 47. Bandwidth: 2 × (7.5 + 3.5) = 22 kHz. If the deviation were trimmed to 5 kHz with the same audio, D would drop to 1.43 and bandwidth to 17 kHz.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a ratio should come out less than one. Correction: deviation ratio is deviation over audio frequency and is usually greater than one for FM; a result below one with these numbers signals an inverted division.", "link": "Formula-sheet trainer", "mnemonic": "Sanity gate: deviation bigger than audio means the ratio is bigger than one."}

{"core": "With no modulation the FM carrier rests at a single frequency from which modulation will push it up and down symmetrically. That resting frequency is the centre frequency, also called the carrier or rest frequency.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Frequency deviation is the amount by which the instantaneous frequency departs from the centre frequency under modulation; with no modulation the deviation is zero, so it cannot name the frequency the carrier sits at.", "why_tempting": "Deviation is the headline FM parameter, so it is the first term that comes to mind."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Frequency shift is the term for the difference between the two frequencies of a frequency-shift-keyed signal, or for a change in a carrier's frequency; it does not name the unmodulated carrier frequency.", "why_tempting": "It sounds similar to deviation and belongs to the same family of frequency-based modulation vocabulary."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The modulating frequency is the audio frequency applied to the modulator; with zero modulation there is no modulating frequency, and in any case it is an audio-band number, not the RF carrier.", "why_tempting": "The question mentions the modulating signal, which cues this term."}], "concept": "An FM signal is described by f(t) = f_c + Δf × a(t), where f_c is the centre frequency, Δf the peak deviation and a(t) the normalized audio waveform between −1 and +1. When a(t) = 0 the instantaneous frequency is exactly f_c. The centre frequency is set by the oscillator or synthesizer and is the frequency to which the receiver is tuned; the modulation then swings the carrier symmetrically to f_c ± Δf, so the receiver's discriminator produces zero output at f_c and positive or negative output on either side. The symmetry matters: if the centre frequency is offset from the receiver's channel, the recovered audio has a DC offset, the discriminator operates off the linear part of its S-curve and distortion rises, and the signal may fall partly outside the IF passband. Keeping the centre frequency accurate is thus a separate requirement from keeping deviation correct, and a frequency counter on the unmodulated carrier is how it is checked. The term rest frequency is used interchangeably with centre frequency in FM literature.", "worked_example": "Thought experiment: a 2 m transmitter is set to 146.520 MHz with no audio applied; a frequency counter on a sampler reads 146.520000 MHz. That is the centre frequency. Speak into the microphone and the counter reading becomes unstable because the carrier is swinging between about 146.515 and 146.525 MHz. Stop talking and it returns to 146.520 MHz. If the counter instead showed 146.521 MHz with no audio, the centre frequency is 1 kHz high and the receiver's discriminator would sit off centre, adding a DC component to the audio and reducing the symmetric headroom before the IF edges.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: deviation is a property of the carrier that exists even without modulation. Correction: deviation is the departure from the centre frequency caused by modulation; with no modulation the carrier simply sits at its centre frequency and the deviation is zero.", "link": "section 5"}

{"core": "In true FM the instantaneous frequency departs from the centre frequency in proportion to the instantaneous amplitude of the modulating signal. How far the carrier swings is set only by how loud the audio is; the pitch of the audio sets how fast the carrier swings back and forth, not how far.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "In FM the audio frequency affects the rate of the frequency swing and the modulation index, but not the peak deviation; including it as a determinant of deviation describes phase modulation, where deviation does rise with audio frequency.", "why_tempting": "Modulation index depends on both, so a learner who conflates index with deviation picks the option that lists both."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "The centre frequency's amplitude, meaning the carrier level, has no bearing on deviation: FM is constant-amplitude, and turning the carrier up or down changes power, not frequency swing.", "why_tempting": "'Amplitude' appears in the correct answer, and this option attaches the word to the carrier instead of the audio."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "The modulating frequency determines how many times per second the carrier swings and the spacing of the sidebands; it does not change the peak excursion in a frequency modulator.", "why_tempting": "FM is about frequency, so it feels natural that the audio frequency must control the frequency deviation."}], "concept": "A frequency modulator, such as a varactor across the oscillator tank or a VCO in a synthesizer, changes the oscillator frequency by an amount proportional to the voltage applied: f(t) = f_c + k × v_audio(t). The peak deviation is Δf = k × V_peak, which depends on the audio amplitude and the modulator sensitivity k in hertz per volt, and on nothing else. The audio frequency f_m determines how rapidly f(t) sweeps and therefore the modulation index m = Δf / f_m and the sideband spacing, but the extremes of the sweep are fixed by V_peak. This is the fundamental distinction between FM and PM: in a phase modulator the phase is proportional to the audio voltage, and since frequency is the derivative of phase, the resulting frequency deviation is proportional to both the audio amplitude and the audio frequency. Many amateur transmitters use a phase modulator preceded by an audio integrator (a 6 dB per octave low-pass) to convert its behaviour into equivalent FM. The practical consequence is the deviation limiter in the audio chain: it clips the audio amplitude so that deviation can never exceed the channel limit regardless of how loud the operator speaks.", "worked_example": "A varactor modulator has sensitivity k = 2.5 kHz per volt. A 1 kHz tone at 2 V peak gives Δf = 2.5 × 2 = 5 kHz. Change the tone to 300 Hz at the same 2 V: Δf is still 5 kHz, but the index rises from 5 to 16.7. Keep 1 kHz and reduce the level to 1 V: Δf drops to 2.5 kHz and m to 2.5. Only the amplitude moved the deviation. In a phase modulator with 1 radian per volt instead, the 1 kHz tone at 2 V would give Δf = 2 × 1000 = 2 kHz and the 300 Hz tone only 600 Hz, which is why PM transmitters need the audio pre-shaping to behave like FM.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: in FM the audio frequency controls how far the carrier deviates. Correction: audio amplitude controls deviation, audio frequency controls the rate of deviation and hence the modulation index; audio frequency affecting deviation is the signature of phase modulation.", "link": "section 5", "mnemonic": "Loud sets how far, pitch sets how fast.", "edge_cases": "Pre-emphasis in amateur FM transmitters deliberately boosts high audio frequencies, so a real rig's deviation does rise with audio frequency for a constant-amplitude mic input; that is an added audio filter, not a property of the frequency modulator itself."}

{"core": "Modulating a carrier's frequency with a single tone produces sideband pairs at every integer multiple of the tone frequency, f_c ± n f_m for all n, with amplitudes given by the Bessel functions J_n(m). Mathematically the series never terminates, so there are infinitely many sideband frequencies; in practice only those with appreciable amplitude matter.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Four is simply one possible count of significant sidebands for a particular index (near m ≈ 2 to 3 in the Bessel tables); it is not a general property of single-tone FM.", "why_tempting": "A learner who remembers a specific Bessel example or Carson's rule for a specific case may fix on a number."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A single sideband is the result of SSB processing of an AM signal; FM always produces symmetric pairs above and below the carrier, never a single component.", "why_tempting": "Confusion with SSB, which is studied in the preceding subsection."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Two sidebands, one above and one below, is the AM result for a single tone; FM's nonlinear relationship between audio and carrier phase generates harmonics of the tone frequency in the sideband structure.", "why_tempting": "The AM rule is learned first and is the intuitive answer: one tone, one pair of sidebands."}], "concept": "An FM signal with a single tone is v(t) = A cos(ω_c t + m sin(ω_m t)), where m = Δf / f_m. Expanding this with the Jacobi–Anger identity gives v(t) = A Σ J_n(m) cos((ω_c + n ω_m) t) for n from −∞ to +∞. Each integer n corresponds to a sideband at offset n f_m, with amplitude J_n(m) relative to the unmodulated carrier; J_−n = (−1)^n J_n, so the spectrum is symmetric in magnitude. Because the Bessel functions are nonzero for every n, the spectrum is in principle unbounded; what makes FM usable is that J_n(m) falls off rapidly once n exceeds m + 1, which is the basis of Carson's rule B ≈ 2(Δf + f_m). The total power is constant, since Σ J_n²(m) = 1, so as m increases the carrier gives up power to the sidebands and at certain indices (2.405, 5.52, 8.65…) J₀ = 0 and the carrier disappears entirely. This contrasts with AM, where the modulation is linear and a single tone yields exactly two sidebands of fixed amplitude. For speech, every audio component contributes its own Bessel series and the components intermodulate, so the real spectrum is a dense continuum within the Carson bandwidth.", "worked_example": "Take m = 1 (say Δf = 1 kHz, f_m = 1 kHz). Bessel values: J₀ ≈ 0.77, J₁ ≈ 0.44, J₂ ≈ 0.11, J₃ ≈ 0.02, J₄ ≈ 0.002.
