'Frequency clipping' is not a technique; you cannot clip a frequency, only an amplitude.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "RF clipping limits the envelope of the generated SSB signal at an IF, then filters the result; it is the preferred high-quality peak limiter because its distortion products fall outside the passband and are removed by the filter.", "why_tempting": "RF clipping is less familiar than audio clipping and harder to picture, so it may seem like the invented option."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Compression is a slow-acting peak limiter: it reduces gain as the envelope rises so peaks are held near a target level.", "why_tempting": "Compression reduces dynamic range rather than chopping peaks, so a strict reading of 'peak limiting' might seem to exclude it."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "AF clipping is the simplest peak limiter, a pair of diodes or a saturating amplifier in the audio chain followed by a low-pass filter.", "why_tempting": "Its known distortion problem might make it seem like a method 'not used' in a quality processor."}], "concept": "The purpose of peak limiting is to allow the average SSB power to be raised without exceeding the transmitter's PEP rating. The three real methods differ in where they act and what byproducts they create. AF clipping chops the audio; its harmonics of the clipped components fall within the audio band (2 kHz clipped produces 6 kHz, but 500 Hz clipped produces 1.5 kHz, in band) and intermodulation between speech components lands in band too, so audible distortion rises quickly. RF clipping generates the SSB signal at an IF, clips its envelope, and passes it through the same crystal filter again: the distortion products of clipping an SSB envelope fall mostly outside the 2.4 kHz passband and are filtered away, so 10 to 15 dB of clipping is possible with much less audible harm. Compression uses an envelope-following gain control, producing no harmonic distortion but acting too slowly to catch the fastest peaks on its own. The non-existent 'frequency clipping' conflates limiting amplitude with limiting bandwidth; the latter is filtering, not clipping.", "worked_example": "Speech with a 14 dB peak-to-average ratio into a 100 W PEP transmitter gives 4 W average. Apply 6 dB of AF clipping: average rises to about 16 W but in-band harmonic distortion reaches 15 to 20%. Apply 12 dB of RF clipping with the filter after it: average rises to perhaps 40 W with in-band distortion of only a few percent because the harmonics landed outside the crystal filter. Apply 3:1 compression first and 6 dB of RF clipping after: similar talk power with the smoothest sound. In none of these did the frequency of any speech component get 'clipped'; only amplitudes and gains were changed.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: clipping and filtering are interchangeable ways to limit a signal. Correction: clipping limits amplitude and creates new frequencies; filtering limits bandwidth and removes frequencies. A speech processor uses both, in that order, but 'frequency clipping' is a category error.", "link": "section 5", "mnemonic": "You can clip volts, not hertz.", "edge_cases": "Modern rigs implement both compression and clipping digitally in DSP, often at the IF, which gives RF-clipping quality with software-adjustable depth; the terminology survives even though no diode is involved."}

{"core": "Clipping the audio waveform replaces its rounded peaks with flat tops, abruptly changing the waveform shape. Any such shape change adds harmonics of the original frequencies (and intermodulation between them), and for audio the odd harmonics of low-frequency components land inside the speech band as audible distortion.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Clipping raises average power: once the clipped peaks are amplified back up to the PEP limit, everything below the clip level has been lifted, so average-to-peak ratio improves. Reduced average power is the opposite of the effect.", "why_tempting": "Removing the tops of the waveform intuitively seems to throw power away."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Increased average power is the desired result of clipping, not an undesirable one; the question asks for the drawback.", "why_tempting": "It is the true effect of clipping, so a learner who stops reading at 'result of AF clipping' selects it."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "The peak amplitude is reduced at the clipper itself, but that is the intended action and is immediately compensated by gain so the transmitter still reaches full PEP; it is not an undesirable consequence.", "why_tempting": "Clipping literally reduces peak amplitude at the clipping point."}], "concept": "A clipper is a hard nonlinearity: v_out = v_in for |v_in| < V_clip and ±V_clip beyond. Fourier analysis of a clipped sine wave shows odd harmonics at 3f, 5f, 7f and so on whose amplitudes grow with clipping depth; for speech containing many simultaneous components the nonlinearity also generates sum and difference products between them. Where these land determines whether they are heard. In AF clipping the input is baseband audio, so a 400 Hz vowel formant clipped at 6 dB produces harmonics at 1200 and 2000 Hz, squarely within the 300 to 3000 Hz band that the following low-pass filter must pass, and intermodulation between 400 Hz and 1800 Hz produces 1400 and 2200 Hz, also in band. The post-clipper low-pass removes only the products above about 3 kHz. The result is a harsher, more fatiguing sound and reduced intelligibility beyond a few dB of clipping. RF clipping avoids this because the products of clipping an SSB envelope at an IF fall largely outside the 2.4 kHz filter and are removed.", "worked_example": "Clip a 500 Hz sine at half its peak amplitude (6 dB clipping). The resulting waveform approximates a trapezoid; its third harmonic at 1500 Hz is roughly 20% of the fundamental (about −14 dB) and the fifth at 2500 Hz about 8% (−22 dB). Both lie inside a 300 to 3000 Hz speech filter and are transmitted. Total in-band harmonic distortion of roughly 22% is clearly audible. The same 6 dB of clipping applied to the SSB envelope at a 9 MHz IF yields products at 9 MHz ± 3 × audio and beyond, which the 2.4 kHz crystal filter attenuates by 60 dB or more.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a low-pass filter after the clipper cleans up all the distortion. Correction: the filter only removes products above the speech band; harmonics and intermodulation products of the lower speech frequencies fall inside the band and reach the air, which is why AF clipping depth must be modest.", "link": "section 5", "mnemonic": "Clip audio, hear harmonics; clip RF, filter them away.", "edge_cases": "Very light AF clipping (2 to 3 dB) that only catches rare peaks adds negligible distortion and is a cheap way to protect against overdeviation on FM, where the subsequent splatter filter does most of the work."}

{"core": "RF clipping requires generating the SSB signal at an IF, clipping its envelope, and refiltering it with a second crystal filter before further conversion, so it costs more parts and more alignment than a pair of diodes in the audio chain. Saying it is easier to implement is the incorrect statement.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "RF clipping genuinely produces less audible distortion than AF clipping because the clipping products of an SSB envelope fall outside the passband and are removed by the filter; this statement is true, so it is not the answer.", "why_tempting": "Hard clipping anywhere seems like it must be distorting, so 'less distortion' can read as the false claim."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "RF clipping needs an extra mixer or an IF tap, a second crystal filter or a loop back through the first, and a clipper with gain at IF; it is indeed more expensive than audio clipping. True statement.", "why_tempting": "Cost comparisons feel subjective, which makes this look like the arguable one."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The additional conversion, filtering and level management make RF clipping more difficult; this is true and is the direct opposite of the keyed answer.", "why_tempting": "It is nearly a paraphrase of option B, and a learner may think only one of two similar statements can be true."}], "concept": "The two clippers act on different signals. An AF clipper is a nonlinearity in the audio path followed by a low-pass filter; its products at odd harmonics and intermodulation frequencies of the speech components fall largely within the speech band and are audible. An RF clipper operates on the SSB signal after it has been generated at an IF: because an SSB signal is the audio translated up in frequency, clipping its envelope creates distortion products that are at the IF plus or minus multiples and combinations of the audio frequencies, most of which lie outside the narrow 2.4 kHz passband. A second pass through the crystal filter strips them, leaving a signal whose in-band distortion is low even at 10 to 15 dB of clipping. The price is complexity: the signal must be at an IF that the filter can handle, the clipper must have RF gain and flat response, the level into the second filter must be managed, and the regenerated signal must be mixed onward. In a design trade, AF clipping is cheap and modest; RF clipping is costlier, harder and better.", "worked_example": "Bill of materials thought experiment. AF clipper: two back-to-back diodes, one resistor, an op-amp buffer and a 3 kHz low-pass, perhaps a dozen parts and no alignment. RF clipper at a 9 MHz IF: a balanced modulator to produce DSB, a crystal filter to make SSB, an IF amplifier with a diode limiter, a second 9 MHz crystal filter (or a switched loop back through the first), gain blocks and level setting, then the existing mixer chain; a few dozen parts, two filters to match, and IF alignment. The outcome favours RF for quality but every practical measure of ease and cost favours AF.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the better-performing technique is also the simpler one. Correction: RF clipping wins on distortion because of extra filtering, and that extra filtering is exactly what makes it more complex and more expensive.", "link": "section 5", "mnemonic": "RF clipping: cleaner, costlier, more complicated.", "edge_cases": "In DSP-based transceivers the distinction nearly vanishes: envelope clipping of a digitally generated SSB signal and refiltering are a few lines of code, so 'RF' clipping has become the easy, cheap default in modern designs even though the exam's assumptions reflect analog hardware."}

{"core": "ALC samples the RF output envelope and reduces the gain of an earlier RF or IF stage to keep peaks at a set level. It is a gain-controlled (compressing) loop acting on the RF signal, which is what RF compression means.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "AF clipping is a hard nonlinearity in the audio path; ALC does not clip anything, it adjusts gain over milliseconds in response to the RF output.", "why_tempting": "Both limit peaks and the ALC meter kicks on peaks, so it can look like a peak clipper."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "AF compression acts on the audio voltage before modulation, using the audio level as its control input; ALC takes its control signal from the RF output and acts on RF or IF gain, not the audio stage.", "why_tempting": "ALC is a compressor, and most learners meet compression first as an audio process."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "RF clipping chops the SSB envelope at an IF and refilters it; ALC never flattens a waveform within a cycle, it only turns gain down.", "why_tempting": "'Automatic Level Control' and 'RF clipping' both act on RF and both hold peaks below a limit."}], "concept": "The defining feature of a compressor is that gain is a slowly varying function of signal level: a detector follows the envelope, a filter sets attack and release times, and the resulting DC adjusts a variable-gain stage. Clipping, by contrast, is instantaneous waveform truncation. ALC fits the compressor definition exactly, but its detector sits at the RF output (or on the final's drive current) and its controlled stage is the IF amplifier, so the compressed quantity is the RF envelope. Within its loop, an increase of several dB in drive produces only a fraction of a dB of change in output above threshold, which is a compression ratio in the same sense as an audio compressor. Because ALC acts on the RF envelope with fast attack and slow release, it holds the final amplifier at its PEP rating without creating in-band harmonics; its threshold is set at the rated output so that under normal speech it only trims peaks. The term 'RF compression' is therefore descriptive: compression (gain control, not clipping) applied to the RF signal (not audio).", "worked_example": "Thought experiment: speak into a transmitter at a constant level and watch the output. With audio gain set so the ALC meter just flickers on peaks, loud syllables push the final to 100 W PEP and the ALC trims the IF gain by 1 dB for 100 ms, then releases. Now triple the mic gain. The audio into the modulator is 10 dB hotter, but the output peaks still read 100 W: the ALC loop has reduced IF gain by nearly 10 dB on peaks, with release allowing quiet syllables through at higher gain, raising average power and background noise. That is the behaviour of a compressor with a high ratio, acting on the RF envelope.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: ALC is just an overload protector, unrelated to speech processing. Correction: ALC is a gain-control loop on the RF envelope, functionally an RF compressor; used lightly it protects the final, pushed hard it compresses speech, with the side effects of any compressor.", "link": "section 5", "mnemonic": "ALC: level control by gain, at RF. Gain control = compression.", "edge_cases": "Running mic gain high to make the ALC do heavy compression is a poor substitute for a real speech processor: the ALC time constants are tuned for protection, not sound quality, and the raised noise floor and pumping are audible on the receiving end."}

{"core": "Varicode, used by PSK31, assigns shorter bit patterns to common characters and longer ones to rare characters, so its code elements are of unequal length. ASCII, Baudot and the AX.25 frame format all use fixed-length character fields.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "ASCII is a fixed 7-bit code (8 with parity or in its extended forms); every character occupies the same number of bits.", "why_tempting": "ASCII has a large character set, which may suggest variable complexity."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "AX.25 is a link-layer packet protocol, not a character code; its frames carry fixed-length 8-bit octets with defined address, control and FCS fields.", "why_tempting": "Packet frames vary in overall length, which can be confused with elements of unequal length."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Baudot is a fixed 5-bit code; the only variability is the use of shift characters to select letters or figures, not unequal element lengths.", "why_tempting": "Baudot's LTRS and FIGS shifts mean a figure effectively costs more than 5 bits, which resembles variable length."}], "concept": "A variable-length prefix code assigns each symbol a bit pattern such that no pattern is the prefix of another, which allows the receiver to parse a continuous bit stream without separators. PSK31's Varicode uses patterns that never contain two consecutive zeros, and '00' marks the boundary between characters; the most frequent English characters (space, e, t, a) get the shortest codes of one to three bits, while capitals and punctuation get codes of up to ten bits. This is the same idea as Morse code, where E is a single dot and Q is four elements, and as Huffman coding in data compression. The payoff is throughput: at PSK31's 31.25 symbols per second, average English text runs at about 50 words per minute because common letters are cheap, whereas a fixed 7-bit code at the same symbol rate would be much slower. The cost is that a single bit error can shift the parsing and corrupt several characters until a '00' resynchronizes the decoder.", "worked_example": "Compare sending the word 'the' (three characters plus a space). Varicode: t is 101, h is 1111, e is 11, space is 1, and each is followed by the 00 separator: 3+2, 4+2, 2+2, 1+2 = 18 bits. Fixed 7-bit ASCII with a start and stop bit as used in RTTY-style asynchronous transmission: 4 characters × 9 bits = 36 bits. At 31.25 bits per second, Varicode sends it in 0.58 s versus 1.15 s for ASCII, a near doubling of throughput for ordinary text.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: all digital character codes are fixed-width because computers handle bytes. Correction: codes designed for transmission efficiency, like Varicode and Morse, deliberately use short patterns for common symbols and long ones for rare symbols, trading parsing complexity for speed.", "link": "section 5", "mnemonic": "Varicode varies: short for 'e', long for 'Q', just like Morse.", "edge_cases": "Varicode has no error correction, so PSK31 relies on the narrow bandwidth and high energy per bit for reliability; PSK63 and PSK125 trade bandwidth for speed with the same code, and FEC variants (QPSK31) add a convolutional code around it."}

{"core": "The physical layer defines the electrical and mechanical interface over which raw bits travel: voltage levels, connectors, pin assignments and signalling rates. The RS-232 or USB connection between a TNC and a terminal is exactly that interface, so it is layer 1.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "The network layer (layer 3) handles addressing and routing of packets across multiple links; it has nothing to do with the wire between a TNC and its terminal.", "why_tempting": "A TNC connects to a packet 'network', so the word matches."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "The transport layer (layer 4) provides end-to-end delivery, sequencing and flow control between applications; it is far above a serial cable.", "why_tempting": "A serial link does 'transport' bits, and the ordinary meaning of the word suggests it."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "The data link layer (layer 2) is where AX.25 lives, framing bytes into packets with addresses and a frame check sequence; the TNC implements it, but the cable to the terminal is below it.", "why_tempting": "The TNC's main job is the AX.25 link layer, so a learner who thinks about what the TNC does rather than what the cable does picks this."}], "concept": "The OSI model stacks seven layers, each using the services of the one below: physical (1), data link (2), network (3), transport (4), session (5), presentation (6) and application (7). Layer 1 concerns how bits are physically represented and moved: in the TNC-to-terminal case that is an asynchronous serial interface with defined voltage levels (RS-232 ±12 V or TTL), start and stop bits and a baud rate, or the USB equivalent; on the radio side it is the AFSK tones, the modem and the radio's modulation. Layer 2 (AX.25) takes bytes and builds frames with source and destination callsigns, a control byte, an information field and a 16-bit CRC, and handles retransmission on a point-to-point link. Layer 3 is where NET/ROM or TCP/IP routing sits in a packet network. The question isolates one connection, the cable to the terminal, and asks which layer governs it: that is the physical interconnection, which is layer 1 by definition. Distinguishing 'what the TNC implements' (layer 2) from 'how it is wired to the computer' (layer 1) is the whole point.", "worked_example": "Trace a keystroke. The terminal program sends the character 'K' as a byte over the serial port at 9600 baud with one start bit, 8 data bits and one stop bit; the voltage transitions on the TXD pin are the physical layer. The TNC accumulates characters, wraps them into an AX.25 UI frame with your callsign, the destination and an FCS; that is the data link layer. If the frame is a NET/ROM routed packet, the node address decisions are the network layer. Finally the TNC's modem converts the frame bits into 1200 and 2200 Hz tones for the radio, which is again the physical layer, this time on the RF side.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the TNC 'is' a link-layer device, so any connection to it is link layer. Correction: a device can implement one layer while its cables belong to another; the terminal cable is pure bit transport with no framing or addressing, hence physical layer.", "link": "section 5", "mnemonic": "Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away: Physical, Data link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application.", "edge_cases": "With a sound-card modem and software TNC the 'physical layer' to the computer is the audio interface (USB codec or line-level audio) and PTT control, and the AX.25 framing happens in software; the layer assignments are unchanged, only the hardware moved."}

{"core": "A CRC appends a short checksum, computed by polynomial division of the data, so the receiver can recompute it and detect whether the block arrived corrupted. It identifies errors with very high probability but carries no information about which bits were wrong, so it detects rather than corrects.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Lossy compression discards information to shrink data (as in audio codecs); a CRC adds bits and discards nothing.", "why_tempting": "'Redundancy' in the name sounds like something a compressor removes."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Error correction requires codes with enough structure to locate and fix errors (Hamming, Reed-Solomon, convolutional, LDPC); a 16- or 32-bit CRC can only report a mismatch, after which a protocol must request a repeat.", "why_tempting": "Detection and correction are both 'error control', and ARQ systems built on CRCs do end up delivering correct data, so the CRC gets the credit."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Lossless compression (Lempel-Ziv, Huffman) reduces size while preserving content; a CRC increases size slightly and has no compression function.", "why_tempting": "Same confusion as option A, with 'lossless' making it sound more respectable."}], "concept": "A CRC treats the message as the coefficients of a long binary polynomial M(x), multiplies it by x^n, and divides by a fixed generator polynomial G(x) of degree n using modulo-2 arithmetic (XOR, no carries). The remainder R(x), n bits long, is transmitted after the data. The receiver divides the whole received sequence (data plus CRC) by the same G(x); an uncorrupted block leaves a remainder of zero. Because division by a well-chosen generator spreads the influence of every bit across the remainder, the CRC catches all single-bit errors, all odd numbers of errors (if G(x) has a factor x + 1), all burst errors up to n bits long, and all but 1 in 2^n of longer random bursts. AX.25 uses the 16-bit CRC-CCITT as its frame check sequence, giving a 1 in 65 536 chance of an undetected random error burst. A detected failure causes the frame to be discarded and, in connected mode, the link layer requests a retransmission (ARQ). Detection is cheap in overhead and hardware; correction needs many more redundant bits.", "worked_example": "Tiny CRC with G(x) = x³ + x + 1 (binary 1011, n = 3). Message 1101. Append three zeros: 1101000. Divide by 1011 modulo 2: 1101 XOR 1011 = 0110, bring down → 1100 XOR 1011 = 0111, bring down → 1110 XOR 1011 = 0101, bring down → 1010 XOR 1011 = 0001. Remainder 001, so transmit 1101001. Receiver divides 1101001 by 1011 and gets remainder 000: accepted. Flip one bit in transit, 1111001: division leaves a non-zero remainder, so the frame is rejected and a repeat is requested. The CRC said 'bad', not 'bit 2 is wrong'.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a checksum that catches errors must also fix them. Correction: a CRC proves integrity but carries too little information to identify error positions; correction comes from either retransmission (ARQ) or a separate forward-error-correcting code.", "link": "section 5", "mnemonic": "CRC = Catch, Report, Can't fix.", "edge_cases": "A CRC is not a cryptographic hash: it is linear, so an adversary can forge data with a matching CRC trivially. It is intended for random channel errors, not for authentication, which is why protocols that need tamper resistance use SHA-family hashes or signatures instead."}

{"core": "ASCII has 7 information bits giving 128 codes, enough for separate upper- and lower-case letters, digits, punctuation and control characters. Baudot's 5 bits give only 32 codes per shift, so it has a single alphabet case.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Plain ASCII has no error correction; an optional eighth parity bit gives single-error detection only, and even that is not inherent to the code.", "why_tempting": "The parity bit in 8-bit ASCII transmission is often mentioned alongside error control, which gets inflated into 'built-in correction'."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "ASCII carries more information bits per character (7) than Baudot (5), not fewer; that is precisely why it has a larger character set.", "why_tempting": "Inverting the bit counts is an easy slip, and 'fewer bits' sounds like an advantage."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Store-and-forward is a function of a message-handling system (a mailbox or BBS) and works with any character code; the size of the character set has no bearing on it.", "why_tempting": "ASCII-based packet systems do offer store-and-forward, so the association is real but the causation is not."}], "concept": "The number of distinct characters a fixed-length code can represent is 2^N. Baudot (ITA2) uses N = 5, so 32 codes; to cover 26 letters plus digits and punctuation it uses two shift states, LTRS and FIGS, selected by dedicated shift characters, giving about 58 printable characters but no lower case. A missed shift character garbles everything until the next shift arrives, a familiar RTTY failure mode. ASCII uses N = 7, so 128 codes: 33 control characters (carriage return, line feed, bell and so on) plus 95 printable ones, including both cases, all digits and a full punctuation set, with no shift mechanism. The seven-bit structure also places upper and lower case 32 apart so that case conversion is a single-bit change. An eighth bit, when transmitted, is used for parity (error detection, not correction) or in extended code pages such as ISO-8859 for accented characters. In amateur RTTY, Baudot at 45.45 baud remains common for tradition and compatibility; ASCII at 110 baud is permitted but is mostly used inside packet and other computer-oriented modes.", "worked_example": "Count the capacity. Baudot: 2^5 = 32 patterns; subtract the two shift characters, space, CR, LF and blank, leaving 26 patterns in each of two shifts, 52 usable, all upper case. ASCII: 2^7 = 128 patterns; 95 printable, which includes A to Z (26), a to z (26), 0 to 9 (10) and 33 punctuation and symbols. To send 'Hello' in Baudot the receiver prints HELLO; in ASCII it prints Hello exactly. The text 'Call 2: 73' in Baudot costs extra FIGS and LTRS shift characters around '2:' and '73'; ASCII needs none.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: more bits per character is wasteful, so a shorter code is better. Correction: the extra two bits in ASCII quadruple the code space, eliminating shift characters and their failure mode and allowing mixed case; the per-character cost is small compared with the robustness and expressiveness gained.", "link": "section 5", "mnemonic": "Five bits, one case (Baudot); seven bits, both cases (ASCII).", "edge_cases": "Unicode (UTF-8) extends the same idea to variable-length multi-byte characters covering all writing systems and is what modern digital-mode software actually transmits in text fields; the exam's framing compares the two classic fixed-length codes."}

{"core": "AMTOR Mode A is an automatic repeat request (ARQ) system: the sender transmits three-character blocks, the receiver checks each block's character validity and replies with an acknowledge or a request-for-repeat code, and the sender repeats any block that was not acknowledged.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Sending every character twice is the Mode B (FEC) strategy, used for broadcasts where no return channel exists; Mode A relies on the return channel instead.", "why_tempting": "AMTOR has two modes and it is easy to attach the wrong error-control mechanism to each."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Mode A's entire purpose is error control; the handshaking is what makes AMTOR more reliable than plain RTTY.", "why_tempting": "The letter 'A' might be read as 'basic' rather than as 'ARQ'."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Frame check sequences are a packet (AX.25) technique applied to whole frames with a CRC; AMTOR uses a 7-bit constant-ratio code in which each character must contain exactly four 1s and three 0s, not an FCS.", "why_tempting": "FCS checking is the familiar error-detection method from packet radio, and ARQ systems in general often use one."}], "concept": "AMTOR (Amateur Teleprinting Over Radio, derived from the maritime SITOR system) uses a 7-bit code in which every valid character has exactly four marks and three spaces. A character received with any other ratio is known to be corrupted, which gives error detection without a separate checksum. In Mode A (ARQ) the two stations lock into a synchronous handshake: the information-sending station transmits a block of three characters (210 ms at 100 baud), then listens; the receiving station replies with one of two control characters, meaning 'received correctly, send next' or 'error, repeat that block'. The cycle is 450 ms, and the characteristic chirping sound of AMTOR is this rapid alternation. Because repeats are requested only when needed, throughput under good conditions approaches the raw rate, and under poor conditions the link slows rather than printing garbage. The system requires a full-duplex-like turnaround on both ends and a dedicated point-to-point link, which is why it cannot be used for broadcasting.", "worked_example": "Station X sends the block 'CQ ' (three characters). Station Y checks each character: 'C' has four 1s and three 0s, valid; 'Q' valid; space valid. Y sends the acknowledge control character. X sends the next block 'CQ '. Noise flips a bit in the first 'C', giving a five-ones pattern; Y detects the invalid ratio and sends the repeat request. X retransmits the same block. Y validates it, acknowledges, and the exchange continues. Each cycle takes 450 ms, so with no errors the link moves about 6.7 characters per second (about 67 words per minute); a 20% block error rate reduces this to roughly 5.3 characters per second but never prints a wrong character undetected (unless two bits flip in a compensating way).", "misconception": "Wrong belief: error control always means forward error correction added by the sender. Correction: ARQ puts the burden on the receiver to detect errors and ask for repeats; it needs a two-way link but spends no bandwidth on redundancy when the channel is clean.", "link": "section 5", "mnemonic": "Mode A = ARQ = Ask again. Mode B = Broadcast = send twice.", "edge_cases": "The 4-of-7 constant-ratio check cannot detect an error that flips one 1 to 0 and one 0 to 1 within the same character, so a small residual undetected error rate remains; PACTOR replaced this with a true CRC and adaptive data compression while keeping the ARQ handshake."}

{"core": "AMTOR Mode B is a forward-error-correction broadcast mode with no return channel, so it cannot ask for repeats. Instead each character is transmitted twice, separated in time, and the receiver prints whichever copy passes the 4-of-7 validity check.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Mode B does include error correction; FEC is literally in its name. The time-diversity double transmission combined with the constant-ratio code is the correction mechanism.", "why_tempting": "Because Mode B cannot request repeats, a learner may conclude it has no error control at all."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Requesting repeats is the Mode A (ARQ) mechanism and requires a two-way link; Mode B is one-to-many with listeners who cannot reply.", "why_tempting": "The two AMTOR modes are easily swapped."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "AMTOR characters are validated by their fixed 4-mark, 3-space ratio, not by a frame check sequence; FCS belongs to packet (AX.25).", "why_tempting": "FCS is the generic textbook answer for error detection in digital modes."}], "concept": "Forward error correction adds redundancy at the transmitter so the receiver can recover from errors on its own. AMTOR Mode B uses time diversity: each character is sent, then sent again a few character periods later (interleaved with other characters, so the stream reads DX, then the repeat of D, then the repeat of X, and so on, with a spacing of about 280 ms). HF noise bursts and fades are typically short compared with that interval, so the chance that both copies of the same character are hit is much lower than the chance that one is. Each received copy is checked against the 4-of-7 constant-ratio rule; the receiver prints the first copy that passes, and prints an error symbol only if both fail. The cost is halving the throughput compared with a single transmission at the same baud rate, since every character occupies two slots. This trade is appropriate for bulletins, CQ calls and net transmissions where many stations listen and none can talk back. Mode B is also used as the 'listen' mode for eavesdropping on an ARQ exchange, called Mode L, with the receiver using the repeats inherent in ARQ.", "worked_example": "Transmitter sends the text 'DE VE' in Mode B. On air the stream looks like: D, E, D(repeat), E(repeat), space, V, space(repeat), V(repeat), E, E(repeat)... with each original and its repeat separated by a fixed number of slots. A 150 ms noise burst corrupts the first copy of 'V' (its mark count becomes 5). The receiver flags that copy invalid, waits for the repeat slot, finds a valid 4-of-7 'V', and prints it. Text throughput at 100 baud drops from about 67 words per minute (Mode A on a clean channel) to about 33 words per minute, the price of redundancy.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: forward error correction must involve mathematically sophisticated codes like Reed-Solomon. Correction: the simplest FEC is repetition combined with a way to tell good copies from bad ones; AMTOR Mode B's repeat-after-a-delay plus the constant-ratio check is exactly that.", "link": "section 5", "mnemonic": "Mode B: Both copies sent, Best one kept.", "edge_cases": "Repetition FEC fails if the fade or interference lasts longer than the spacing between copies, which is why later modes (PACTOR, MFSK, FT8) use interleaving over longer spans and convolutional or LDPC codes that correct errors rather than just picking a clean copy."}

{"core": "APRS is a connectionless broadcast system built on AX.25 UI frames for position reports, telemetry, short messages and local bulletins. Automatic link establishment (ALE) is an HF selective-calling and channel-sounding system that negotiates a connected link, which is outside what APRS does.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "APRS supports short two-way text messages between stations, including acknowledgement and retry; messaging is one of its standard packet types.", "why_tempting": "APRS is thought of primarily as a position-beaconing system, so messaging may seem out of scope."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "APRS telemetry packets carry five analog and eight digital channels from remote sensors, weather stations and balloons; telemetry is a defined format in the protocol.", "why_tempting": "Telemetry sounds like a specialized feature beyond a tracking protocol."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Objects, items and bulletins are APRS formats for broadcasting local information such as net schedules, hamfest locations and repeater details to everyone in range.", "why_tempting": "The phrase 'amateur-specific local information broadcast' is clumsy, which can make it look like the odd one out."}], "concept": "APRS uses unconnected (UI) AX.25 frames, typically 1200 baud AFSK on a shared VHF channel, with a digipeater path such as WIDE1-1,WIDE2-1 so that fill-in and wide-area digipeaters relay each packet once. Because there is no connection, every packet is a fire-and-forget broadcast that any station, digipeater or internet gateway (iGate) can use; the data formats in the APRS specification cover position (with symbol, course and speed), weather, telemetry, status, objects and items, bulletins, and addressed messages with an acknowledgement scheme layered on top of UI frames. ALE, by contrast, is a channel-management protocol for HF: stations scan a set of frequencies, exchange sounding signals to measure link quality, and when one station calls another they automatically select the best channel and establish a two-way link before traffic flows. ALE is about finding and setting up a path; APRS assumes the path (a shared channel and digipeaters) and simply broadcasts. The two solve different problems and APRS has no mechanism for link negotiation.", "worked_example": "Thought experiment: a station wants to send the message 'QRV on 146.52' to a friend 40 km away. In APRS it addresses a message packet to the friend's callsign, sends it as a UI frame via WIDE2-1, and if no ack returns in a few seconds the software retries; a digipeater and an iGate both heard it and the friend's radio displays it. There was no link setup, no channel choice and no guarantee of delivery, just repeated broadcasts. An ALE system handling the same request would first sound several HF channels, pick the one with the best score, call the friend's address, wait for a handshake, and only then pass traffic over an established link, a wholly different architecture.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: any digital protocol with addressing must establish links between stations. Correction: APRS is deliberately connectionless so that one transmission serves every listener at once; it trades delivery guarantees for simplicity and reach, and link establishment is a foreign concept to it.", "link": "section 5", "mnemonic": "APRS: beacons, bulletins, bits of telemetry, brief messages; never a link.", "edge_cases": "The APRS messaging acknowledgement looks like a mini-ARQ but is implemented at the application layer over UI frames; it does not create an AX.25 connected-mode link, so even messaging stays within the connectionless model."}

{"core": "A CRC is a function that maps a block of data of any length to a short fixed-length value that changes unpredictably when any bit changes, which is the definition of a hash function. It is a non-cryptographic hash computed by polynomial division.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Lempel-Ziv is a dictionary-based lossless compression algorithm (the basis of ZIP, gzip and the compression in PACTOR); it reduces data size and produces no checksum.", "why_tempting": "Both LZ compression and CRC appear together in file formats and protocols, so they are associated."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Dynamic Huffman coding builds a variable-length code adapted to symbol frequencies for compression; it is not an integrity check.", "why_tempting": "Huffman codes are 'codes' and CRCs are 'codes', and both involve binary trees in some descriptions."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A convolutional code is a forward-error-correction scheme that generates redundant output bits from a sliding window of input bits, decoded with a Viterbi algorithm; it corrects errors rather than detecting them with a short tag.", "why_tempting": "Convolutional codes are error-control codes, like CRCs are, and the polynomial description of both makes them sound alike."}], "concept": "A hash function h(m) takes input of arbitrary length and produces a fixed-size digest such that small changes in m produce large, hard-to-predict changes in h(m). A CRC meets that definition: data bits are treated as a polynomial M(x), and the remainder of M(x)·x^n divided by a generator G(x) in modulo-2 arithmetic is an n-bit digest. The linear structure of the CRC is chosen so that specific error patterns (single bits, odd numbers of bits, bursts up to n bits) always change the remainder, which makes it an excellent channel-error detector. It is not a cryptographic hash: because the operation is linear over GF(2), anyone can compute what change to the data would preserve the CRC, so it offers no protection against deliberate tampering. Cryptographic hashes such as SHA-256 add nonlinearity to make that infeasible. In the amateur context, AX.25 frames end with the 16-bit CRC-CCITT remainder; PACTOR and many others use CRCs; and the term 'hash' is the general category to which CRC belongs, which is what the question is testing.", "worked_example": "Compute CRC-like digests of two messages with the tiny generator G(x) = x³ + x + 1 (1011). Message 1: 1101 → remainder 001 (worked earlier in this section). Message 2: 1100 (one bit different) → 1100000 ÷ 1011: 1100 XOR 1011 = 0111, bring down → 1110 XOR 1011 = 0101, bring down → 1010 XOR 1011 = 0001, bring down → 0010, remainder 010. A single-bit change produced a different 3-bit digest, as a hash should. Compare with Lempel-Ziv on the same 4 bits: there is nothing to compress and no digest emerges; the function categories are different.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: 'hash' means only the cryptographic hashes used in security. Correction: hash is the broad term for any fixed-length fingerprint of variable-length data; a CRC is a fast, linear hash specialized for detecting transmission errors.", "link": "section 5", "mnemonic": "CRC is a hash, not a squash: it fingerprints data, it does not compress it.", "edge_cases": "A CRC can be computed either by bitwise polynomial division or by a 256-entry lookup table one byte at a time; both give the same result and the table form is what most TNC firmware and software modems use."}

{"core": "AX.25 is the amateur adaptation of the X.25 link-layer protocol, defining how data is framed into packets with callsign addresses, control fields and a CRC. It is the protocol underlying amateur packet radio, including APRS and traditional connected-mode BBS and keyboard links.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Spread spectrum spreads a signal over a wide bandwidth with a pseudorandom code; it is a modulation technique and has no connection to the AX.25 framing protocol.", "why_tempting": "'AX' could be mistaken for an abbreviation related to an exotic mode."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "RTTY sends Baudot characters asynchronously with start and stop bits and no framing, addressing or error check; it does not use AX.25.", "why_tempting": "RTTY is the oldest keyboard digital mode, so a learner may attach any protocol name to it."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "ASCII is a character code, not a link protocol; AX.25 frames can carry ASCII text in their information field, but the designator refers to the framing, not the content.", "why_tempting": "Packet frames usually contain ASCII, so the two are seen together."}], "concept": "X.25 was an international standard for packet-switched data networks over wired links. Amateurs adapted its layer-2 component, LAPB, into AX.25 by extending the address field to carry up to two amateur callsigns plus up to eight digipeater callsigns, each with an SSID. A frame starts and ends with a flag byte (01111110), followed by the address field, a control byte (defining information, supervisory or unnumbered frames), an optional protocol ID, up to 256 bytes of information, and a 16-bit frame check sequence. Bit-stuffing inserts a 0 after any five consecutive 1s in the data so the flag pattern cannot appear inside the frame. Connected mode uses numbered frames and acknowledgements for reliable delivery (used by BBS and keyboard-to-keyboard links); unnumbered information (UI) frames provide a connectionless broadcast service that APRS exploits. The physical layer is usually 1200 baud AFSK (Bell 202 tones, 1200 and 2200 Hz) on VHF FM or 300 baud FSK on HF, with 9600 baud direct FSK also in use. AX.25 is thus the defining protocol of amateur packet radio.", "worked_example": "Anatomy of a short APRS packet on air. Flag; destination address 'APRS' padded to 6 characters with SSID; source 'VE6XYZ-9'; digipeater path 'WIDE1-1, WIDE2-1'; control byte 0x03 (UI frame); protocol ID 0xF0 (no layer 3); information field '!5103.00N/11404.00W>Mobile' (a position report); FCS computed over address through information; flag. The TNC bit-stuffs the stream, NRZI-encodes it and sends it as 1200 baud AFSK. Every element except the information text is defined by AX.25.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: 'packet' is a mode in the sense that RTTY or PSK31 are modes, with its own modulation. Correction: packet is a protocol layer, AX.25, that can ride on several modulations; the designator names the framing standard, not the tones on the air.", "link": "section 5", "mnemonic": "AX.25: Amateur X.25, the packet frame.", "edge_cases": "AX.25 has been extended with higher layers (NET/ROM, ROSE, TCP/IP over AX.25 via KISS) and newer protocols such as FX.25 add Reed-Solomon forward error correction around an AX.25 frame while staying backward compatible with existing decoders."}

{"core": "The Baudot code (ITA2) represents each character with 5 information bits, giving 32 patterns per shift state; LTRS and FIGS shift characters double the usable set. The start and stop bits added for asynchronous transmission are framing, not information.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "There is no 6-bit variant of Baudot in amateur use; six bits would give 64 codes and remove the need for the shift mechanism that defines Baudot.", "why_tempting": "Some learners count the start bit as a sixth bit."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Seven bits is ASCII (128 codes) or AMTOR's constant-ratio code; Baudot predates both and uses five.", "why_tempting": "Seven is the best-known 'information bits' figure from the ASCII question and gets reused."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Eight bits is a byte, used by extended ASCII and ISO-8859; Baudot teleprinters had five code bars and five bits, not eight.", "why_tempting": "Eight is the universal computer word size, so it is a reflex answer."}], "concept": "Information bits are the bits that distinguish one character from another; framing bits (start, stop, parity) are added for synchronization and detection and carry no character information. Baudot's five bits give 2^5 = 32 patterns. Two of these are reserved for LTRS and FIGS, which switch the receiver's interpretation of the other 30 between a letters table and a figures table, so the code reaches 26 letters, 10 digits, punctuation and a few controls (CR, LF, space, bell) with a single alphabet case. On the air, amateur RTTY sends each Baudot character as a start bit (space), five data bits, and a stop bit of 1.5 bit periods, at 45.45 baud: 7.5 bit periods or 165 ms per character, about 60 words per minute. Frequency-shift keying with a 170 Hz shift carries the mark and space states. The 5-bit limit is the root of RTTY's two main weaknesses: no lower case and the garbling that follows a missed shift character, both of which ASCII's 7 bits eliminated.", "worked_example": "Character timing at 45.45 baud: bit period = 1/45.45 = 22 ms. One character = 1 start + 5 data + 1.5 stop = 7.5 bits × 22 ms = 165 ms, so 6.06 characters per second, or about 61 words per minute at 6 characters per word. Only 5 × 22 = 110 ms of each 165 ms carries information, an efficiency of 67%. Sending 'RST 599' requires: R S T space FIGS 5 9 9, where the FIGS shift is an extra character carrying no text, then LTRS before the next letters.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the number of bits sent per character equals the information bits. Correction: RTTY transmits 7.5 bit periods per character, but only the 5 data bits select the character; start and stop bits exist so the receiver can find character boundaries.", "link": "section 5", "mnemonic": "Baudot: 5 fingers, 5 bits, 2 shifts.", "edge_cases": "Baudot has no error detection at all, which is why a single noise hit prints a wrong character silently; AMTOR's 7-bit 4-of-7 code was created specifically to add detection to the same 5-bit alphabet."}

{"core": "ISO-8859 extends 7-bit ASCII to a full 8-bit code: the first 128 codes are standard ASCII and the upper 128 add accented letters and symbols for various languages. All 8 bits are information bits, with no parity.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Five bits is Baudot, with only 32 codes; it cannot hold even the basic ASCII set, let alone an extension.", "why_tempting": "The bit-count questions in this subsection run together, and 5 is one of the memorized values."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Seven bits is the original ASCII; the whole purpose of ISO-8859 is to add an eighth bit for 128 more characters.", "why_tempting": "A learner who remembers 'ASCII is 7-bit' may miss that the question asks about the extension."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Six bits corresponds to no common character standard; it would give 64 codes, short of even basic ASCII.", "why_tempting": "It sits between the two familiar numbers and looks like a possible intermediate standard."}], "concept": "Seven-bit ASCII defines 128 codes, of which 95 are printable, serving English well but lacking accented letters. When 8-bit bytes became universal the eighth bit, originally reserved for parity in serial links, was repurposed for 128 additional codes. ISO-8859 is a family of such 8-bit single-byte encodings: ISO-8859-1 (Latin-1) covers Western European languages including French accents useful in Canada, while other parts cover Cyrillic, Greek, Hebrew and so on. Codes 0 to 127 are identical to ASCII in every part, which preserves compatibility, and codes 128 to 255 vary by part. Because all 8 bits carry character information, there is no built-in parity; integrity is left to the link layer (for example the AX.25 CRC). The successor, UTF-8, keeps ASCII in the first 128 codes but uses multi-byte sequences for everything else, covering all scripts with one encoding. In amateur digital modes the practical point is that 8-bit characters pass through packet and PACTOR unchanged, while older 7-bit paths strip or corrupt the upper half.", "worked_example": "Count the capacity. 7-bit ASCII: 2^7 = 128 codes. ISO-8859-1: 2^8 = 256 codes, of which 0 to 127 are ASCII and 160 to 255 are 96 extra printable characters (128 to 159 are control codes). The French word 'Québec': in ASCII the é has no code and must be approximated as 'Quebec'; in ISO-8859-1 é is code 233 (hex E9), one byte, and the word is sent exactly. In UTF-8 the same é becomes two bytes (C3 A9), illustrating the trade between single-byte simplicity and universal coverage.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the eighth bit in a byte of text is always a parity bit. Correction: parity is a transmission option, not part of the character code; in 8-bit encodings such as ISO-8859 the eighth bit is a character-selecting information bit.", "link": "section 5", "mnemonic": "ASCII 7, ISO-8859 8: the extension fills the byte.", "edge_cases": "Software that assumes 7-bit-plus-parity will strip the high bit and silently turn every accented character into a different ASCII character, a common source of garbled text when mixing old TNC firmware with modern terminal programs."}

{"core": "Spread spectrum deliberately spreads a signal over a bandwidth much wider than the information requires by varying the carrier according to a pseudorandom sequence known to both ends, either hopping among frequencies or multiplying the data by a fast spreading code. The receiver applies the same sequence to despread it.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "AMTOR is a narrowband HF teleprinter mode using 170 Hz FSK with ARQ or FEC error control; its carrier does not vary by any sequence and its bandwidth is a few hundred hertz.", "why_tempting": "AMTOR involves a predetermined sequence of block exchanges, and 'sequence' may trigger the association."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "'Time domain frequency modulation' is not a defined mode; FM varies carrier frequency with the audio waveform, not with a predetermined code, and is not wideband in the spread-spectrum sense.", "why_tempting": "It describes a carrier that varies over time, which superficially matches the question."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Amplitude-companded SSB is a narrowband voice mode that compresses the audio dynamic range before transmission and expands it after reception; it does not spread or hop the carrier.", "why_tempting": "It is a less familiar mode name and the compression process could be mistaken for 'predetermined' processing."}], "concept": "In frequency-hopping spread spectrum (FHSS) the carrier jumps among many channels in a pseudorandom order generated by a shift-register sequence; the receiver, synchronized to the same sequence, hops with it, while a narrowband listener sees only brief bursts on any one frequency. In direct-sequence spread spectrum (DSSS) the data bits are multiplied by a much faster pseudorandom chip sequence, spreading the spectrum by the ratio of chip rate to bit rate; the receiver multiplies by the same sequence, which collapses the wanted signal back to its original bandwidth while spreading any narrowband interferer out across the band where a filter removes most of it. The processing gain G_p = B_spread / B_info (in dB, 10·log10 of that ratio) quantifies the interference rejection. Spread spectrum signals have low power spectral density, so they coexist with narrowband users at the cost of slightly raised noise floors, resist jamming and multipath, and allow multiple users on one band with different codes (CDMA). The defining feature in the question is the predetermined sequence: without the key sequence the signal looks like noise.", "worked_example": "A 9.6 kbps data stream spread with a 1.2 Mchip/s DSSS code occupies about 2.4 MHz (main lobe width 2 × chip rate). Processing gain = 1 200 000 / 9600 = 125, or 10·log10(125) ≈ 21 dB. A narrowband carrier at −90 dBm lands in the band; after despreading it is smeared across 2.4 MHz, and the 9.6 kHz data filter passes only 9.6/2400 of its power, an attenuation of about 24 dB, leaving −114 dBm. Meanwhile the wanted signal despreads coherently with no loss. For FHSS with 50 channels, an interferer occupying one channel corrupts about 2% of the hops, which a modest error-correcting code recovers.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: wider bandwidth always means a stronger, more interfering signal. Correction: spreading divides the same transmit power across a much wider band, lowering the power in any narrow slice, and the receiver's despreading recovers the signal while rejecting narrowband interferers; the sequence, not the width, is what makes the mode work.", "link": "section 5", "mnemonic": "Spread spectrum: same key at both ends, wide on the air, narrow after despreading.", "edge_cases": "Spread spectrum on amateur bands is normally permitted only above certain frequencies and with constraints on the spreading codes and power, so check the current Canadian regulations before experimenting; the engineering here is general and the rules are not quoted."}

{"core": "Frequency hopping spread spectrum (FHSS) keeps a conventional narrowband carrier but retunes its centre frequency many times per second, with the channel order dictated by a pseudorandom sequence shared between transmitter and receiver. Over time the energy is spread across the whole hop set, which is what makes it spread spectrum.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Direct sequence does not move the carrier between channels at all; it stays on one centre frequency and the phase is flipped by a fast chip stream, spreading the energy continuously rather than by hopping.", "why_tempting": "It is the other major spread spectrum family, so a learner who knows there are two kinds may pick the one whose name is more familiar from Wi-Fi and GPS."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Time-domain frequency modulation is not a defined spread spectrum technique; FM in the ordinary sense is a modulation method whose deviation follows the baseband signal, not a pseudorandom channel list.", "why_tempting": "The phrase sounds technical and mentions frequency, and FHSS does change frequency over time, so the words loosely match the description."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Companding is a dynamic-range compression and expansion process applied to amplitude (as in some voice systems); there is no spread spectrum scheme that compands frequency.", "why_tempting": "The exam deliberately uses companded as a plausible-sounding invented term in several spread spectrum items; it pattern-matches to real jargon."}], "concept": "Spread spectrum means deliberately occupying far more bandwidth than the information rate requires, under control of a code known to both ends. In FHSS the transmitter is an ordinary narrowband signal at any instant, but a pseudorandom number (PN) generator drives the synthesizer to a new channel at the hop rate, so the long-term spectrum is the union of all channels in the hop set. The receiver runs an identical PN generator, synchronized in time, so it hops in step and sees a steady narrowband signal. Processing gain is roughly G_p = B_spread / B_info, so hopping over 50 channels of equal width gives about 17 dB of gain against a narrowband interferer that occupies only one channel. Slow hopping sends several symbols per hop; fast hopping changes channel more than once per symbol. The direct-sequence alternative spreads continuously by phase-chipping rather than by retuning.", "worked_example": "Suppose a 25 kHz wide voice-bandwidth signal hops over 80 channels spaced 25 kHz apart, so the hop set covers 2 MHz. Processing gain G_p = 2000 kHz / 25 kHz = 80, which is 10·log10(80) ≈ 19 dB. A narrowband jammer sitting on one channel corrupts only 1/80 of the hops, so the link loses about 1.25% of its symbols, which error-correcting coding can repair. Because the hop order comes from a PN sequence, a listener without the sequence cannot predict which channel is next.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a hopping signal is wideband at every instant. Correction: at any single moment the FHSS carrier is narrowband; only the time-averaged occupancy is wide, which is why a spectrum analyser in max-hold shows a comb of channels while a single sweep catches just one.", "link": "section 5", "mnemonic": "Hopping = the carrier HOPS between channels; Direct = the carrier stays put and is chipped DIRECTly.", "edge_cases": "Modern FHSS systems such as Bluetooth hop fast enough and over enough channels that regulators treat them as wideband emissions; the processing-gain formula assumes the interferer is narrowband and fixed, and gives little help against a wideband jammer covering the whole hop set."}

{"core": "Direct sequence spread spectrum (DSSS) multiplies the carrier by a high-rate pseudorandom binary chip stream, flipping the carrier phase by 180° on every chip transition. Because the chip rate is far higher than the data rate, the signal spectrum widens by the ratio of chip rate to bit rate.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Frequency hopping leaves the carrier phase alone and instead retunes the centre frequency to a new channel according to the PN sequence; the spreading is in the channel list, not in a fast phase modulation.", "why_tempting": "Both techniques use a pseudorandom sequence, so the learner may fix on the word pseudorandom and forget to check whether the sequence drives frequency or phase."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Phase companding is not a real spread spectrum technique; companding compresses and expands amplitude dynamic range and has nothing to do with spreading a carrier.", "why_tempting": "The question mentions shifting phase, and companded appears across these items as an invented term that sounds like it belongs."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "BPSK is the underlying modulation used inside DSSS, but BPSK alone, modulated by the data bits, is a narrowband mode; it becomes spread spectrum only when the modulating stream is the fast PN chip sequence rather than the data.", "why_tempting": "DSSS literally uses binary phase shifts, so BPSK is a technically accurate description of the mechanism but not the name of the spread spectrum system."}], "concept": "In DSSS each data bit is XORed with a PN chip sequence of N chips, and the result phase-modulates the carrier as BPSK. The main lobe of the transmitted spectrum extends to ±R_c around the carrier, where R_c is the chip rate, so the bandwidth is about N times wider than for the raw data. The receiver multiplies the incoming signal by a locally generated, time-aligned copy of the same PN sequence; for the wanted signal the chips cancel (PN × PN = 1) and the original narrowband BPSK data collapses back to bandwidth R_b, while anything not carrying that code gets multiplied by a random-looking sequence and is spread out to R_c. A narrowband filter after the despreader then keeps the data and rejects most of the spread interferer. Processing gain is G_p = R_c / R_b, often expressed in dB. The 180° phase flips are what distinguish it from FHSS, which spreads by moving the carrier between channels.", "worked_example": "A 9600 bit/s data stream is spread by a chip sequence running at 1.2288 Mchip/s. The spreading factor is N = 1 228 800 / 9600 = 128 chips per bit, so G_p = 10·log10(128) ≈ 21 dB. The null-to-null main lobe of the transmitted signal is about 2 × 1.2288 MHz ≈ 2.46 MHz wide, versus about 19.2 kHz for unspread BPSK at 9600 bit/s. After despreading, a narrowband interferer that was 10 dB above the wanted signal is spread to 2.46 MHz and only 1/128 of its power lands in the 19.2 kHz data filter, leaving the wanted signal roughly 11 dB above it.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: DSSS and BPSK are interchangeable names because both flip carrier phase. Correction: BPSK describes the modulation; DSSS describes using a PN chip stream, far faster than the data, as the thing doing the phase flipping, which is what spreads the spectrum.", "link": "section 5", "mnemonic": "Direct Sequence: the SEQUENCE is applied DIRECTly to the carrier phase.", "edge_cases": "Practical DSSS systems often use QPSK or offset-QPSK chipping rather than plain BPSK, and the despreader needs chip-level timing alignment within a fraction of a chip, which is why acquisition circuits search in time offsets before data can be recovered."}

{"core": "Frequency hopping is one of the two classic spread spectrum techniques: the carrier is moved rapidly between channels under control of a pseudorandom sequence so that the long-term signal occupies far more bandwidth than the data requires.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Packet radio is a data link protocol (framing, addressing, error checking) carried on a conventional narrowband modulation such as AFSK or FSK; it does not hop channels.", "why_tempting": "Packet is a digital mode with a pseudorandom-sounding vocabulary (scrambling, CRC), so a learner may lump all digital techniques together."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "RTTY uses two fixed tones (FSK with a shift such as 170 Hz) and the carrier alternates only between mark and space; its occupied bandwidth is a few hundred hertz and the frequency pattern is the data, not a PN sequence.", "why_tempting": "RTTY does shift frequency between two values, which superficially resembles hopping between channels."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "AMTOR is an ARQ or FEC variant of RTTY using the same narrowband FSK; adding handshaking does not change the carrier into a hopped wideband emission.", "why_tempting": "AMTOR is also a legacy digital mode with error control, and the exam groups these older modes together to test whether the learner can separate them from spread spectrum."}], "concept": "The defining property of spread spectrum is a transmitted bandwidth much larger than the information bandwidth, with the spreading controlled by a code independent of the data. FHSS achieves this by retuning the carrier to channels drawn from a PN sequence at the hop rate; DSSS achieves it by phase-chipping the carrier with a PN stream. The receiver needs the same code and synchronization to collapse the signal back to narrowband, which provides processing gain G_p = B_spread / B_info against narrowband interference and makes the signal hard to intercept. Packet, RTTY and AMTOR are all narrowband digital modes whose occupied bandwidth is set by the symbol rate and tone shift, typically a few hundred hertz to a few kilohertz, with no spreading code involved.", "worked_example": "Imagine a 300 baud RTTY signal with 170 Hz shift; it occupies roughly 500 Hz and sits on one frequency for the whole QSO, so any receiver tuned there copies it. Now take the same 300 baud data and hop it over 100 channels across 1 MHz under a PN sequence at 50 hops per second: a receiver parked on any one channel hears a burst only 1% of the time and cannot decode, while the synchronized receiver copies continuously with roughly 10·log10(1000 kHz / 0.5 kHz) ≈ 33 dB of processing gain against a single-channel interferer.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: any mode that changes frequency, such as FSK or RTTY, is a kind of frequency hopping. Correction: in FSK the frequency pattern is the data itself and the bandwidth stays narrow; in frequency hopping the pattern is an independent pseudorandom channel list and the long-term bandwidth is deliberately wide.", "link": "section 5", "edge_cases": "Some modern amateur digital modes use frequency diversity or multi-tone schemes, but unless the carrier is moved across a wide span under a PN code the emission is still classified as narrowband, not spread spectrum."}

{"core": "Direct sequence is the spread spectrum technique in which a fast pseudorandom chip stream phase-modulates the carrier, multiplying the occupied bandwidth by the ratio of chip rate to data rate. It belongs to the spread spectrum family, alongside frequency hopping.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Packet radio is a framing and error-checking protocol layered on narrowband FSK or AFSK modulation; its bandwidth is determined by the baud rate, not by a spreading code.", "why_tempting": "Packet carries sequences of bits and the word sequence in the question may suggest any serial data mode."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "RTTY is two-tone FSK at low baud rates occupying a few hundred hertz; there is no chip stream and no bandwidth expansion beyond what the data rate needs.", "why_tempting": "RTTY is a direct-printing teletype mode, and the word direct can be misread as a reference to it."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "AMTOR is RTTY with ARQ or FEC error control; it remains a narrowband FSK emission and uses no spreading sequence.", "why_tempting": "AMTOR sends data in short timed blocks with handshakes, which can sound like a sequence-driven system to someone unfamiliar with it."}], "concept": "Direct sequence spread spectrum takes the data bits, XORs them with a PN code running at chip rate R_c much greater than bit rate R_b, and BPSK-modulates the carrier with the result. The spectrum is a sinc-squared shape with main lobe width 2R_c, so the processing gain is G_p = R_c / R_b. At the receiver a time-aligned replica of the same PN code multiplies the signal; the wanted signal despreads to bandwidth R_b while everything else is spread to R_c and mostly rejected by the following narrowband filter. This is the mechanism behind GPS C/A code and CDMA cellular. Frequency hopping is the sibling technique that spreads by retuning the carrier; the older amateur digital modes in the other options are all narrowband and use no code independent of the data.", "worked_example": "If you changed a 1200 bit/s packet link into a DSSS link by chipping it at 1.2 Mchip/s, the spreading factor would be 1 000 and the bandwidth would grow from roughly 2.4 kHz to about 2.4 MHz, giving G_p = 10·log10(1000) = 30 dB. A conventional packet TNC listening on the channel would see only a noise-like hiss a few decibels above the floor, because the signal power is now spread thinly across 2.4 MHz, while a receiver with the matching PN code recovers the 1200 bit/s stream at full strength.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: direct sequence refers to any mode that sends bits directly one after another, such as packet or RTTY. Correction: direct sequence specifically means a pseudorandom chip sequence applied directly to the carrier phase to spread the bandwidth, which is a spread spectrum technique.", "link": "section 5", "edge_cases": "DSSS signals are often below the noise floor on a spectrum analyser, so a conventional band scope will not even show them; this near-invisibility is a feature for low probability of intercept but makes spectrum monitoring difficult."}

{"core": "Spread spectrum alters the carrier according to a pseudo-random sequence: a deterministic bit pattern that looks random statistically but is exactly reproducible by any receiver that knows the generator and its starting state. That reproducibility is what lets the receiver despread the signal.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Quantizing noise is the error introduced when an analogue signal is represented by a finite number of digital levels; it is a byproduct of A/D conversion, not a control signal for spreading a carrier.", "why_tempting": "It is a digital-signal term from the same syllabus area and contains the word noise, which the learner may associate with the noise-like appearance of a spread signal."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A truly random noise sequence cannot be regenerated at the receiver, so there would be no way to correlate and despread the signal; spread spectrum requires a sequence both ends can produce identically.", "why_tempting": "Spread signals do look like noise on the air, and the PN sequence has random-like statistics, so random seems like the right word until you ask how the receiver would ever synchronize."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Frequency companding is not a real signal type; companding refers to amplitude compression and expansion and has no role in generating a spreading code.", "why_tempting": "The exam uses companded as a recurring decoy that sounds like genuine jargon from the modulation chapter."}], "concept": "A pseudo-random (PN) sequence is typically produced by a linear feedback shift register whose output repeats after 2^n − 1 chips for an n-stage maximal-length register. Its autocorrelation is a sharp peak at zero offset and nearly flat elsewhere, which is exactly what a correlator needs to lock onto the right timing and reject misaligned copies. In DSSS the sequence chips the carrier phase; in FHSS it selects the next channel. Because the sequence is deterministic, a receiver with the same generator and synchronized state can reconstruct it and undo the spreading, recovering processing gain G_p = B_spread / B_info. The predetermined nature is the whole point: the alteration must be known in advance to the intended receiver and unknown to everyone else.", "worked_example": "A 7-stage maximal-length shift register with feedback taps at stages 7 and 6 produces a sequence 2^7 − 1 = 127 chips long before repeating. Chipping at 127 kchip/s, the sequence period is exactly 1 ms. A receiver running the same register compares its local output against the received chips at each possible offset; at 126 of the 127 offsets the correlation sum is −1, and at the one correct offset it is +127, a peak 42 dB above the sidelobes in power terms, so timing lock is unambiguous.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the spreading signal must be truly random to make the transmission secure. Correction: it must be pseudo-random, meaning deterministic and reproducible, because the receiver has to generate an identical copy to despread; true randomness would make reception impossible.", "link": "section 5", "mnemonic": "Pseudo = fake random: looks random on the air, but the receiver knows the recipe.", "edge_cases": "Short maximal-length sequences are easy for a third party to reverse-engineer from a few hundred received chips, so systems needing real security use long sequences or cryptographically generated codes; the physics of despreading is identical either way."}

{"core": "A spread spectrum receiver must generate the same pseudo-random sequence as the transmitter and stay locked to it in frequency and time; without that synchronization the receiver cannot follow the hops or despread the chips, and the signal appears as low-level noise.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Spread spectrum signals are typically constant-envelope; the carrier is varied in frequency or phase, not amplitude, so amplitude speed is not what defeats a casual listener.", "why_tempting": "The learner knows something is changing very rapidly and guesses amplitude, which is the parameter a Basic-level AM mindset reaches for first."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A properly despread signal is not distorted at all; the difficulty is that an unsynchronized receiver recovers nothing intelligible, not that it recovers a degraded copy.", "why_tempting": "An ordinary receiver tuned to a spread signal hears hiss or clicks, which could be mistaken for distortion rather than for a complete failure to despread."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Spread spectrum occupies far more bandwidth than conventional modes, not less; a narrowband receiver sees only a tiny slice of the energy at any moment.", "why_tempting": "This inverts the actual relationship, and a learner who recalls that spread signals are hard to see on a narrowband receiver may reason backwards about which bandwidth is narrower."}], "concept": "Spread spectrum reception is a correlation process. The receiver's local PN generator must produce the identical sequence, aligned in time to within a fraction of a chip for DSSS or synchronized to the hop timing and channel list for FHSS, and its local oscillator must track the transmitter's frequency so the despread product lands in the narrow data filter. Acquisition typically involves sliding the local code in time until the correlation peak appears, then a tracking loop holds the alignment. An eavesdropper without the sequence can only see energy spread across the full bandwidth B_spread, with power spectral density reduced by the processing gain G_p = B_spread / B_info, which may place the signal below the receiver noise floor. This synchronization requirement is also what gives the mode its interference rejection and low probability of intercept.", "worked_example": "A 1 W FHSS transmitter hops over 2 MHz with a 20 kHz channel width at 100 hops per second. An ordinary FM receiver on one 20 kHz channel receives a 10 ms burst once every second on average, roughly 1% duty, which the squelch mostly ignores. A synchronized receiver retunes in step, sees the signal 100% of the time, and decodes it as a continuous narrowband channel. If the synchronized receiver's clock drifts by half a hop period, it arrives on each channel late and loses half of every burst, so timing lock must be maintained continuously.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: you could monitor spread spectrum with a wide enough receiver. Correction: bandwidth alone is useless; the receiver must regenerate the spreading code and lock to it in time and frequency, because the information is recovered only through correlation with that code.", "link": "section 5", "edge_cases": "With enough signal-to-noise ratio and a known code family, a wideband SDR can in fact acquire and decode spread spectrum, which is how GPS receivers work on an open code; the difficulty is fundamental only when the sequence is unknown."}

{"core": "In frequency hopping spread spectrum the carrier frequency jumps between channels in an order given by a pseudo-random list; the receiver follows the same list in synchronism. Over time the signal spreads across the whole hop set even though it is narrowband at each instant.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Amplitude modulating a carrier over a wide range does not spread its spectrum under a code; AM bandwidth is twice the highest modulating frequency and the envelope carries the information, not a spreading sequence.", "why_tempting": "The phrase a wide range called the spread sounds like a definition and borrows the word spread directly from the question."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Frequency companding is not a real process; companding applies to amplitude dynamic range and there is no spread spectrum scheme based on it.", "why_tempting": "The term reappears throughout this subsection as an invented decoy that sounds like legitimate modulation vocabulary."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Phase shifting the carrier with a fast binary bit stream is direct sequence spread spectrum, the other major technique, not frequency hopping.", "why_tempting": "Both techniques use a pseudo-random sequence, so a learner who remembers the sequence but not which parameter it drives can confuse the two definitions."}], "concept": "FHSS uses a PN generator to select the synthesizer frequency at each hop interval. The instantaneous emission is a conventional narrowband modulated carrier (FM, FSK or similar) of bandwidth B_info; the long-term occupied bandwidth is the span of the hop set B_spread, and the processing gain against a narrowband interferer is G_p = B_spread / B_info, or in dB, 10·log10 of that ratio. Synthesizer settling time limits the hop rate, and the receiver's own synthesizer must retune in lockstep, which requires an identical PN generator and a time reference. Because a fixed-frequency interferer corrupts only the hops that land on its channel, forward error correction and interleaving across hops turn an occasional wiped hop into a recoverable error burst. Direct sequence achieves spreading by phase-chipping instead of retuning, and the two can be combined in hybrid systems.", "worked_example": "A system hops among 64 channels spaced 30 kHz apart, covering 1.92 MHz, at 200 hops per second with 5 ms dwell per hop. Processing gain is 10·log10(1920 / 30) = 10·log10(64) ≈ 18 dB. A 30 kHz wide jammer on one channel hits 1 hop in 64, about 3 hops per second, each costing 5 ms of data; with interleaving over 100 ms and a code that corrects a 5% erasure rate, the link runs error-free. If the synthesizer needed 2 ms to settle, 40% of each dwell would be lost, so faster synthesizers or slower hopping would be required.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the carrier in FHSS is modulated by the pseudo-random sequence in the same way voice modulates it. Correction: the sequence does not modulate the carrier at all; it selects which channel the normally modulated carrier sits on during each hop interval.", "link": "section 5", "mnemonic": "FH = Frequency Hops from a pseudo-random channel list.", "edge_cases": "At hop rates faster than the symbol rate the phase discontinuity at each hop forces non-coherent demodulation such as FSK, so fast FHSS trades some demodulator efficiency for its interference resistance."}
