{"core": "Direct-sequence spread spectrum phase-shifts the carrier with a fast binary pseudo-random chip stream, so the signal spectrum widens by the ratio of chip rate to data rate while the carrier frequency stays fixed.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Amplitude modulation over any range remains an envelope-carrying narrowband emission with bandwidth set by the modulating frequency; it is not spread by a code and the term the spread is not a defined quantity.", "why_tempting": "The answer reuses the word spread and reads like a plausible textbook definition."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Companding compresses and expands amplitude dynamic range and does not exist as a frequency operation; it is unrelated to spreading a carrier.", "why_tempting": "The decoy sounds like genuine jargon and appears in every item of this subsection."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Altering the carrier according to a pseudo-random list of channels is frequency hopping; DSSS keeps a single carrier frequency and spreads by phase chipping.", "why_tempting": "It correctly mentions a pseudo-random sequence, and the learner who has not sorted out which parameter each technique drives will accept it."}], "concept": "In DSSS the data bits at rate R_b are combined with a PN chip stream at rate R_c, where R_c may be tens to thousands of times R_b, and the result BPSK-modulates the carrier so its phase flips 180° at chip transitions. The spectrum takes the sinc-squared shape of the chip waveform with main lobe width 2R_c, giving processing gain G_p = R_c / R_b. The receiver multiplies by an aligned local replica of the code, collapsing the wanted signal to R_b and spreading any uncoded interferer to R_c, after which a narrow filter passes the data and rejects most of the interferer. Correlation also allows multiple users on the same frequency with different codes (CDMA). Frequency hopping is the alternative in which the same kind of PN sequence steers the carrier between channels rather than chipping its phase.", "worked_example": "A 2400 bit/s data link is chipped at 2.4 Mchip/s, so each bit becomes 1000 chips and G_p = 30 dB. The transmitted main lobe is about 4.8 MHz wide. A narrowband interferer 20 dB stronger than the wanted signal at the antenna is spread by the despreader to 4.8 MHz, and the 4.8 kHz data filter admits only 1/1000 of its power, so after despreading the wanted signal is 30 − 20 = 10 dB above the interferer. The carrier centre frequency never moved during this process.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: direct sequence means the carrier frequency is sequenced directly through a list of channels. Correction: that is frequency hopping; in direct sequence the carrier stays on one frequency and its phase is switched by the chip stream.", "link": "section 5", "mnemonic": "DS = Data Smeared by a chip stream on one frequency; FH = Frequency Hops between channels.", "edge_cases": "The sinc-squared spectrum has sidelobes only 13 dB below the main lobe, so practical DSSS transmitters apply pulse shaping or filtering to keep the emission inside its allocated bandwidth."}

{"core": "The despreading correlator in the receiver only collapses signals carrying the matching pseudo-random code back to narrowband; any signal without that code is spread out across the full bandwidth by the same process and mostly rejected by the following narrow filter. Interference is suppressed by the processing gain, not by any feedback or filter trick.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "No feedback channel is needed; the hop or chip sequence is fixed in advance and the receiver cannot and need not tell the transmitter to move. Interference rejection is a property of the correlation process itself.", "why_tempting": "Adaptive frequency selection does exist in some modern systems, and it sounds like a sensible engineering response to interference."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Spread spectrum transmitters usually run at the same or lower power than conventional ones; the signal is spread thinly and often sits below the noise floor, so brute-force power is not the mechanism.", "why_tempting": "Overpowering interference by raising transmitter power is the Basic-level instinct, and the question mentions resistance to interference."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A DSP interference filter is not a required component; the rejection comes from multiplying by the local code and then filtering, which can be done in analogue hardware. Even where DSP is used, it implements the correlation rather than a separate special filter.", "why_tempting": "Modern receivers do use DSP heavily and the learner may assume any clever interference rejection must be a DSP feature."}], "concept": "The receiver multiplies the incoming signal by a locally generated, synchronized copy of the spreading code. For the wanted signal, code × code = 1 at every chip, so the data reappears at its original narrow bandwidth B_info. For a narrowband interferer that is not coded, the multiplication acts as a spreading operation, smearing it across B_spread. A filter of bandwidth B_info after the correlator passes all of the wanted signal but only the fraction B_info / B_spread of the interferer, so the interferer is reduced by the processing gain G_p = B_spread / B_info. In FHSS the equivalent effect is that a fixed interferer collides with only a fraction 1/N of the hops, where N is the number of channels, and coding repairs those hops. Either way the suppression is built into the despreading, requires no negotiation with the transmitter, and works against any signal not using the correct code.", "worked_example": "Wanted DSSS signal: −100 dBm at the antenna, spread over 1 MHz, with 10 kbit/s data (G_p = 100 = 20 dB). A narrowband carrier at −90 dBm sits inside the band. Before despreading the interferer is 10 dB stronger. After multiplying by the local code the wanted signal collapses to 10 kHz and passes the 10 kHz filter intact at −100 dBm; the interferer is spread to 1 MHz and only 1/100 of it, −110 dBm, passes the filter. The wanted signal now leads by 10 dB, enough for a clean BPSK decode, with no change to the transmitter and no special DSP filter.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: spread spectrum resists interference because the receiver can detect and dodge it. Correction: the receiver dodges nothing; the correlation process inherently spreads and attenuates any signal not carrying the code, so the suppression is passive and automatic.", "link": "section 5", "mnemonic": "The code is the key: matching signals unlock, everything else gets smeared.", "edge_cases": "Processing gain has limits: a wideband interferer that already covers B_spread gains nothing from being spread further, and an interferer strong enough to overload the receiver front end before the correlator defeats the technique regardless of code."}

{"core": "Frequency hopping changes the carrier frequency very rapidly through a sequence of channels dictated by a pseudo-random sequence that both transmitter and receiver generate in step. The hop pattern is predetermined, not reactive.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "FHSS uses no feedback from the receiver; the hop sequence is fixed in advance by the PN generator, and the technique works even with no return path at all.", "why_tempting": "It describes a plausible adaptive scheme, and the learner may assume interference avoidance must involve detecting interference."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Waiting for a clear channel is a listen-before-talk or carrier-sense protocol, not spread spectrum; FHSS keeps transmitting on its scheduled sequence and relies on coding to cover hops that collide with interference.", "why_tempting": "It sounds like a courteous channel-sharing method and shares the interference-avoidance framing of the question."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "A pseudo-random bit stream shifting carrier phase is the definition of direct sequence spread spectrum, in which the carrier frequency stays fixed.", "why_tempting": "It correctly mentions a pseudo-random sequence and a rapid change, so a learner who has not separated phase-chipping from frequency-hopping will take it."}], "concept": "In FHSS a PN generator outputs an index at each hop interval, a frequency synthesizer jumps to the corresponding channel, and the information is sent on that channel using ordinary narrowband modulation until the next hop. The receiver's synthesizer follows the same index stream, so after mixing the signal appears at a constant IF. The occupied bandwidth is the hop set span B_spread while the instantaneous bandwidth is B_info, giving G_p = B_spread / B_info against narrowband interferers, each of which can corrupt at most the hops landing on its channel. Hop rate is limited by synthesizer settling time and by the need to resynchronize phase at each hop; fast hoppers use non-coherent modulation such as FSK for this reason. The predetermined sequence also makes the signal hard to intercept and allows several hoppers with orthogonal patterns to share one band.", "worked_example": "If you changed a conventional 12.5 kHz FM link into an FHSS link with 160 channels across 2 MHz, hopping 50 times per second, the processing gain would be 10·log10(2000 / 12.5) = 10·log10(160) ≈ 22 dB. A jammer on one channel would hit 1 hop in 160, about one 20 ms burst every 3.2 seconds, and the receiver would never signal the transmitter about it; the PN schedule simply carries on and error correction fills the gap. A receiver whose PN generator started one state late would land on every channel one hop behind and hear nothing but noise.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: frequency hopping is a reactive scheme that moves away from interference when it is detected. Correction: hopping follows a predetermined pseudo-random schedule regardless of interference; its resistance comes from statistical avoidance and coding, not from sensing and responding.", "link": "section 5", "mnemonic": "FHSS hops on a schedule, not on a complaint.", "edge_cases": "Adaptive frequency hopping, as used in Bluetooth, does blacklist bad channels based on measured error rates, but it layers that on top of the basic PN-scheduled hop and is not what the syllabus means by the technique."}

{"core": "Converting every incoming signal to a fixed intermediate frequency lets the designer build the selective filtering and most of the gain at one frequency where tuned circuits and crystal filters can be optimized once, rather than trying to keep a tunable filter sharp across a whole band. The result is high, consistent selectivity and well-designed tuned circuits.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Soft limiting and squelch are functions added in the IF or audio chain for FM and are not produced by the act of frequency conversion; a superhet without them works perfectly well.", "why_tempting": "Both terms appear in receiver block diagrams, so they can be mistaken for inherent features of the architecture."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Sensitivity is set by the noise figure of the front end, mainly the RF amplifier and first mixer; conversion itself adds loss and noise rather than sensitivity, and squelch is an unrelated audio-muting feature.", "why_tempting": "Superhets are more sensitive than TRF sets in practice, but that comes from the gain being easier to realize at a fixed IF, not from conversion as such."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Detection takes place in the detector after the IF amplifier, never in the RF amplifier; an RF amplifier that detected would destroy the signal before it reached the mixer.", "why_tempting": "It mentions a real stage and the word sensitivity, which the learner associates with good receivers."}], "concept": "In a superheterodyne receiver the mixer multiplies the incoming signal at f_RF with a local oscillator at f_LO, producing sum and difference products; the IF filter selects f_IF = |f_LO − f_RF| (or the sum in up-converting designs). Because f_IF is fixed, the designer can use high-Q crystal, mechanical or ceramic filters whose shape factor (60 dB bandwidth divided by 6 dB bandwidth) can approach 1.5 to 2, something impossible with a gang of variable LC circuits tracked across a band. Gain is also easier to make stable at one frequency, since each stage's stray feedback is predictable and neutralization can be set once. The price is image response: a signal at f_RF ± 2f_IF also mixes to the same IF, so front-end preselection must reject it. Selectivity, image rejection and the choice of IF are the interlocking design decisions of the whole receiver chapter.", "worked_example": "A tunable LC preselector at 14.2 MHz with a loaded Q of 50 has a 3 dB bandwidth of 14 200 / 50 = 284 kHz, nowhere near enough to separate SSB signals 3 kHz apart. Converting to a 9 MHz IF and inserting an 8-pole crystal filter with a 2.4 kHz passband and a 1.8 shape factor gives a 60 dB bandwidth of only 4.3 kHz. Every station on every band enjoys that same filter after conversion, which is the optimization the question points to.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the superhet's advantage is more sensitivity because of the extra stages. Correction: the advantage is selectivity and consistent tuned-circuit performance, because filtering and gain are done once at a fixed IF; sensitivity is governed by the front-end noise figure, which conversion does nothing to improve.", "link": "section 6", "mnemonic": "Fixed IF = filter once, filter well.", "edge_cases": "Direct-sampling SDRs digitize at RF and do their selectivity in software, so the fixed-IF argument no longer applies to them; they trade the image problem for anti-aliasing and ADC dynamic range constraints instead."}

{"core": "The IF frequency sets where the image lies (2 × f_IF away from the wanted signal) and where other spurious responses such as IF feedthrough, LO harmonic mixes and half-IF products fall, so image rejection and responses to unwanted signals are the governing factors in choosing it.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Noise figure is set by the RF amplifier and mixer design, and distortion by stage linearity and signal levels; neither depends meaningfully on the numeric value of the IF.", "why_tempting": "They are genuine receiver performance parameters from the same chapter, so they look like reasonable things to weigh."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "A receiver IF radiates only through LO or IF leakage, which is a shielding and layout issue; interference to other services is not what drives the IF choice, although a few IFs are avoided because strong broadcast signals sit there.", "why_tempting": "Choosing an IF that coincides with a strong broadcast band is a known pitfall, and the learner may reverse the direction of the interference."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Cross-modulation is a front-end linearity problem caused by strong adjacent signals in the RF amplifier and mixer; it occurs before the IF and is not controlled by the IF frequency.", "why_tempting": "Cross-modulation and interference are real receiver issues, and the learner may think a cleverly chosen IF could avoid them."}], "concept": "A mixer produces outputs at |m·f_LO ± n·f_RF| for all integer m and n, and the IF filter accepts whatever lands at f_IF. The desired product is |f_LO − f_RF| = f_IF, but a signal at the image frequency f_RF ± 2f_IF (on the far side of the LO) produces exactly the same difference. Image rejection must therefore come from front-end selectivity ahead of the mixer, and a high IF places the image far from the wanted signal where the preselector can attenuate it. A low IF makes narrow, high-Q filtering easier and cheaper but puts the image close to the wanted signal. Other unwanted responses include direct IF feedthrough (a strong signal at f_IF itself passing through the mixer), the half-IF response at f_RF ± f_IF/2 from second-order mixing, and LO harmonic mixes. Choosing the IF is a trade between image separation, filter availability and avoiding bands full of strong signals; double conversion resolves the trade by using a high first IF and a low second IF.", "worked_example": "Receiver tuned to 7.100 MHz. With a 455 kHz IF and high-side LO at 7.555 MHz, the image is at 8.010 MHz, only 910 kHz away; a front-end tuned circuit with Q of 50 gives roughly 15 dB of image rejection there. With a 9 MHz IF and LO at 16.100 MHz, the image is at 25.100 MHz, 18 MHz away, where the same preselector gives more than 60 dB. The high IF wins on image rejection but needs a crystal filter for selectivity, which is why 9 MHz became a standard amateur IF.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the IF is chosen for best noise figure and lowest distortion. Correction: those are front-end properties; the IF value matters because it positions the image and other spurious responses, and that is what governs its selection.", "link": "section 6", "mnemonic": "IF choice = Image Free (as far as possible) and spur free.", "edge_cases": "Modern HF receivers often up-convert to a first IF above the highest received frequency (for example 40 to 70 MHz) so a fixed low-pass filter rejects all images without any tracked preselector, then convert down to a low IF for roofing and crystal filtering."}

{"core": "Double conversion uses a high first IF so the image sits far from the wanted signal where the front-end tuned circuits can reject it easily, then a low second IF where narrow selectivity is cheap. For the same front-end selectivity the image rejection is therefore much better than in a single-conversion set that must compromise on one IF.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Output loudness is just audio gain and has nothing to do with the number of conversions; any receiver can have as much AF gain as desired.", "why_tempting": "More stages intuitively suggests more gain and therefore a louder output."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Adding a second local oscillator adds a second source of drift, so double conversion is if anything slightly less stable unless both oscillators are crystal controlled; stability is not its purpose.", "why_tempting": "Double conversion sets are usually higher-end receivers that also happen to be stable, so the learner attributes the stability to the architecture."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Sensitivity is set by the noise figure of the RF amplifier and first mixer; a second mixer behind them adds noise rather than removing it and does not improve the minimum detectable signal.", "why_tempting": "Better receivers are often described as more sensitive, and more conversion stages sound like more amplification."}], "concept": "In any superhet the image is at f_RF ± 2f_IF and can only be rejected by selectivity ahead of the mixer. Front-end LC circuits have modest Q, so the attenuation they provide depends on how far away the image is in relative terms: roughly, attenuation in dB rises with 20·log10 of the ratio of image offset to preselector bandwidth for a single tuned circuit. A high first IF (several MHz or tens of MHz) moves the image far out, giving large rejection from ordinary tuned circuits. But narrow filters at a high IF are hard to make with LC parts, so a second mixer converts to a low IF (455 kHz or similar) where high-Q selectivity is simple. The two conversions divide the labour: the first conversion handles image rejection, the second handles adjacent-channel selectivity. Single conversion must pick one IF and accept weakness on one side of the trade.", "worked_example": "Receiver tuned to 28.500 MHz, preselector a single tuned circuit with Q of 40 (bandwidth about 712 kHz). Single conversion at 455 kHz: image at 29.410 MHz, 910 kHz away, about 1.3 bandwidths, giving roughly 8 dB of rejection. Double conversion with a 10.7 MHz first IF: image at 49.900 MHz, 21.4 MHz away, about 30 bandwidths, giving on the order of 35 dB from that same tuned circuit, before the second conversion to 455 kHz provides the narrow selectivity. Same front end, vastly better image rejection.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: double conversion gives better selectivity or sensitivity. Correction: its distinctive gain is image rejection for a given front end; the narrow selectivity is achieved at the low second IF and would be equally achievable in a single-conversion set using that IF, which would then have poor image rejection.", "link": "section 6", "mnemonic": "High first IF pushes the image away; low second IF pulls the selectivity in.", "edge_cases": "Each extra mixer and oscillator introduces new spurious mixing products, so a double conversion receiver with poorly chosen frequencies can have more internal birdies than a single conversion set; the image advantage is real but not free."}

{"core": "A crystal filter provides the receiver's narrow passband, and it only works at one fixed frequency, so it belongs in the IF chain where every received signal has already been converted to that frequency. There it defines the adjacent-channel selectivity for SSB or CW.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "The local oscillator may use a crystal as its frequency-determining element, but that is an oscillator crystal, not a crystal filter; the LO generates a single tone and has no passband to shape.", "why_tempting": "Crystals and local oscillators are strongly associated, so the learner conflates a crystal-controlled oscillator with a crystal filter."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The audio stage operates at a few hundred to a few thousand hertz, far below the frequencies at which quartz crystals resonate, and audio filtering is done with RC, LC or DSP filters instead.", "why_tempting": "Audio filters do exist for CW and the learner may think any selectivity filter can be placed at the audio end."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "The detector converts the IF signal to audio; selectivity ahead of it has already been set by the IF filter, and placing a filter inside the detector would serve no purpose and would be at the wrong impedance and frequency.", "why_tempting": "The detector is adjacent to the IF chain in the block diagram, so it is a near-miss choice."}], "concept": "A quartz crystal behaves as a series RLC resonator with an extremely high Q (10 000 to 100 000) shunted by a small holder capacitance, giving a series resonance and a slightly higher parallel resonance. Several crystals arranged in a ladder or lattice form a bandpass filter whose bandwidth is set by the crystal spacing and coupling capacitors, typically 250 Hz to 500 Hz for CW and 2.1 to 2.8 kHz for SSB, with shape factors around 1.5 to 2 for 8-pole designs. Because such a filter is fixed-frequency and narrow, it is only useful where the signal frequency is constant, which in a superhet is the IF. A roofing filter near the first mixer protects later stages from strong off-channel signals; the main selectivity filter further down the IF chain sets the final passband. Filter bandwidth B relates to Q by B = f_0 / Q, and the high Q of quartz is what makes narrow bandwidths at MHz frequencies practical.", "worked_example": "To get a 2.4 kHz SSB passband at a 9 MHz IF, the required filter Q is 9 000 000 / 2 400 = 3 750. A good LC tank manages a loaded Q of perhaps 100, so it would need to be 37 times better; quartz crystals with unloaded Q near 50 000 make the design straightforward. Four matched 9.000 MHz crystals in a Cohn ladder with 100 pF coupling capacitors produce roughly that 2.4 kHz passband, and because every band converts to 9 MHz, the same filter serves 160 m through 10 m.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a crystal filter goes wherever the receiver needs its sharpest tuning, which might be the front end. Correction: a crystal filter cannot be tuned, so it must sit at the one frequency that does not change as you tune the receiver, the IF.", "link": "section 6", "mnemonic": "Crystals are fixed; the IF is fixed; they live together.", "edge_cases": "Crystal filters have passband ripple and can ring on CW at very narrow bandwidths (under 250 Hz), and their shape degrades if the terminating impedances are wrong; modern rigs often follow a wider crystal roofing filter with DSP filtering at a low IF or baseband for the final shaping."}

{"core": "Every additional conversion adds another local oscillator and another mixer, and each mixer generates products at all combinations m·f_LO ± n·f_signal; with more oscillators there are more such combinations, including harmonic mixes between the oscillators themselves, that can land inside an IF passband as spurious responses or birdies.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "AGC workload depends on signal level range, not on the number of conversions, and AGC acting on a strong signal reduces gain rather than overloading stages.", "why_tempting": "Overload does cause spurious products, so a learner who knows that may attach it to the wrong cause."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Multiple conversion generally improves IF selectivity by allowing a low second IF with narrow filters; the frequency changes do not degrade the filter shape.", "why_tempting": "It inverts the real relationship, and the learner may assume that more mixing stages must smear the passband somehow."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Sensitivity is a front-end property unchanged by adding later conversions, and higher RF levels would come from the antenna and RF amplifier, not from the conversion scheme.", "why_tempting": "Strong RF in the front end does produce intermodulation, which sounds like a spurious-response mechanism."}], "concept": "A mixer is a nonlinear multiplier; besides the wanted product it produces outputs at |m·f_1 ± n·f_2| for integers m and n, with amplitude falling as the orders rise. A single conversion receiver has one LO, so the spurious set involves the LO, its harmonics and incoming signals. A double or triple conversion receiver adds a second and third LO, each with harmonics, and any combination such as 3·f_LO1 − 5·f_LO2 that happens to equal an IF will be heard as a steady tone (birdie) whether or not an antenna is connected. Signals at the second image (f_IF1 ± 2·f_IF2) must also be rejected by the first IF filter, and leakage of one LO into another mixer creates further crossings as the receiver tunes. Careful frequency planning, shielding and balanced mixers minimize these, but the count of possible spurious combinations grows combinatorially with the number of oscillators, so more conversions means more opportunities for trouble.", "worked_example": "A receiver with a 10.7 MHz first IF and 455 kHz second IF uses a second LO at 10.245 MHz. The second mixer's image is at 10.7 − 0.91 = 9.79 MHz, which the first IF filter must reject. The 7th harmonic of the second LO is 71.715 MHz; if the first LO passes through 61.015 MHz or 82.415 MHz while tuning, the difference is exactly 10.7 MHz and a birdie appears at those dial settings. A single conversion receiver with one 10.7 MHz IF has no second LO and therefore none of these crossing points.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: more conversions means more filtering and therefore fewer unwanted signals. Correction: more conversions means more oscillators and mixers, and every added nonlinear stage multiplies the number of possible spurious products that can fall into a passband.", "link": "section 6", "mnemonic": "Every extra LO is a new birdie factory.", "edge_cases": "Modern up-converting designs with a first IF well above the tuning range, plus DSP-based final selectivity, have reduced but not eliminated this issue; direct-sampling SDRs avoid it entirely by having no analogue mixers at all, at the cost of ADC aliasing and overload constraints."}

{"core": "The first conversion to a high IF places the image far from the wanted signal so the front end can reject it; the second conversion to a low IF is where narrow, high-Q filters give adjacent-channel selectivity. Image rejection first, selectivity second.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Dynamic range is a property of front-end linearity and the AGC range, not something a conversion stage is designed to provide, and selectivity is the job of the second, low IF rather than the first.", "why_tempting": "Both are real receiver specifications and the learner may assign them to the two stages arbitrarily."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Noise figure is set by the stages ahead of and including the first mixer; the second conversion happens after the noise figure has already been determined and cannot improve it.", "why_tempting": "The first half, image rejection, is correct, which makes the option look right at a glance."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "This reverses the order: a low first IF would put the image close to the wanted signal where the front end cannot reject it, and a high second IF would make narrow filtering hard again.", "why_tempting": "A learner who remembers the two purposes but not which IF is high and which is low will pick the inverted pairing."}], "concept": "The image of a superhet lies at f_RF ± 2·f_IF, on the opposite side of the LO from the wanted signal, and the only defence is selectivity before the mixer. Front-end tuned circuits of modest Q reject the image well only when 2·f_IF is large compared to their bandwidth, so the first IF is chosen high (for example 9 MHz, 10.7 MHz, 45 MHz or 70 MHz). At that frequency a narrow passband would need a very high Q filter, which is expensive or impossible with LC parts, so a second mixer converts to a low IF (455 kHz or 50 kHz) where filters of a few hundred hertz are practical. The first IF filter also serves as a roofing filter that must reject the second image at f_IF1 ± 2·f_IF2. The division of labour is the entire rationale for double conversion: each IF is optimized for one job.", "worked_example": "Tuning 21.200 MHz. First IF at 45 MHz (up-conversion), LO1 at 66.200 MHz; image at 111.200 MHz, 90 MHz away, rejected by a simple 30 MHz low-pass filter by well over 70 dB. Second IF at 455 kHz, LO2 at 45.455 MHz; second image at 45.910 MHz, which the 15 kHz wide 45 MHz crystal roofing filter rejects. A 455 kHz ceramic or mechanical filter with a 2.4 kHz passband then sets the SSB selectivity. Swap the order (455 kHz first) and the image would be at 22.110 MHz, inside the front-end passband.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: both conversions serve the same purpose and simply add selectivity cumulatively. Correction: they serve different purposes; the first is for image rejection via a high IF, the second is for selectivity via a low IF, and reversing them defeats both.", "link": "section 6", "mnemonic": "First Far (image far away), Second Sharp (narrow filter).", "edge_cases": "Some high-performance HF receivers now do the opposite in a sense: a single conversion to a low first IF around 9 MHz with a narrow crystal roofing filter, relying on tight band-pass preselectors for image rejection, because this gives better close-in dynamic range than up-conversion."}

{"core": "The RF amplifier is the only stage whose input and output tuned circuits are both tuned to the incoming signal frequency; it provides preselection and a little gain before the mixer. Every stage after the mixer works at the IF, and the local oscillator runs offset from the signal by the IF.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "The local oscillator is tuned to f_RF ± f_IF, deliberately offset from the received frequency so that mixing produces the IF; if it were on the signal frequency the output would be at DC and audio, not at the IF.", "why_tempting": "The LO tracks the received frequency as the dial turns, so the learner may think it is tuned to it."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "The audio amplifier handles baseband frequencies below about 3 kHz after detection and has no RF tuned circuits.", "why_tempting": "It is a stage with input and output, and a learner guessing structurally might pick it."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The detector receives the IF signal and converts it to audio; its input is at the IF, not the received frequency, and its output is audio.", "why_tempting": "The detector is where the signal is finally recovered, so it feels like the stage most tied to the signal."}], "concept": "A superhet's signal path is antenna, RF amplifier, mixer, IF amplifier, detector, audio amplifier, with the LO feeding the mixer. The RF amplifier sits ahead of frequency conversion, so both its input tank and its output tank resonate at f_RF; they are ganged with the LO tuning so that f_LO − f_RF (or f_RF − f_LO) stays equal to f_IF as the receiver tunes. These tuned circuits form the preselector, whose job is to attenuate the image at f_RF ± 2·f_IF and to limit the total signal power reaching the mixer, and whose gain sets the receiver noise figure. The mixer's input is also at f_RF but its output is at f_IF, so it is the transition stage. Everything downstream is fixed-tuned at the IF, which is where crystal filters and most of the gain live.", "worked_example": "Receiving 14.200 MHz with a 9 MHz IF and high-side LO at 23.200 MHz. The RF amplifier's input and output tanks both resonate at 14.200 MHz, each with Q around 50 giving about 284 kHz bandwidth. The mixer's input sees 14.200 MHz and 23.200 MHz; its output tank is at 9.000 MHz. The image at 32.200 MHz is 18 MHz from the RF amplifier's resonance and is attenuated by both of its tuned circuits, roughly 35 dB each for a single-tuned circuit at that offset, which is why two tuned circuits in the RF stage matter.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the local oscillator is tuned to the received frequency because it moves with the dial. Correction: it moves with the dial but is always offset by the IF; the only stage actually resonant at the received frequency on both input and output is the RF amplifier.", "link": "section 6", "mnemonic": "RF amp: RF in, RF out. Mixer: RF in, IF out.", "edge_cases": "Many modern receivers replace the tracked RF amplifier with fixed band-pass filters per band and sometimes no RF amplifier at all on the low HF bands, where atmospheric noise exceeds mixer noise; the principle that preselection happens at f_RF before conversion still holds."}

{"core": "The mixer takes its input from the tunable RF stage (or antenna preselector) at the received frequency and delivers its output to the fixed-tuned IF amplifier, so it is the stage that sits between tunable and fixed-tuned circuits.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "The RF amplifier has tunable circuits on both its input and output, both at the received frequency; it sits before the frequency change, not at it.", "why_tempting": "It is the first stage with tuned circuits and the learner may think of it as the boundary between antenna and receiver."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "The IF amplifier is fixed-tuned on both input and output; it lies entirely on the fixed side of the boundary.", "why_tempting": "It is the stage immediately after the frequency change and might be read as the one adjacent to the tunable section."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The local oscillator is tunable but it feeds the mixer rather than lying in the signal path between two stages; it has no fixed-tuned output stage after it.", "why_tempting": "The LO is tunable and connects to the mixer, so a learner may think of it as bridging the tunable and fixed sections."}], "concept": "The superhet divides into a tunable front end (preselector, RF amplifier, LO) that follows the dial, and a fixed-tuned back end (IF filter, IF amplifier, detector) that always operates at f_IF. The mixer is the interface: it multiplies the signal at f_RF by the LO at f_LO and its output tank is tuned to f_IF = |f_LO − f_RF|. Its input circuit is part of the tracked preselection, its output circuit is the first element of the fixed IF chain. Because the mixer handles the full spectrum admitted by the preselector, its linearity sets the receiver's intermodulation performance, and its noise figure, together with any RF amplifier gain ahead of it, sets sensitivity. Understanding the mixer as the boundary also explains why the image problem exists: anything the tunable side lets through that differs from the LO by f_IF gets converted into the fixed side.", "worked_example": "Tune the dial from 7.000 to 7.300 MHz on a receiver with a 9 MHz IF. The RF amplifier tanks move from 7.000 to 7.300 MHz, the LO moves from 16.000 to 16.300 MHz, and the mixer's input follows them; but the mixer's output tank, the crystal filter and the IF amplifier stay at exactly 9.000 MHz throughout. The mixer is the one stage with a moving input and a stationary output.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the IF amplifier is where the receiver transitions from tunable to fixed because it is the first fixed stage. Correction: the transition happens inside the mixer, whose input is tunable and whose output is fixed; the IF amplifier is already fully on the fixed side.", "link": "section 6", "mnemonic": "The mixer is the doorway: variable on the way in, fixed on the way out.", "edge_cases": "In up-converting receivers with a fixed first IF above the band and a synthesized LO, the front end may have only switched band-pass filters rather than tracked tuning, but the mixer still forms the boundary between the frequency-dependent and frequency-independent halves of the signal path."}

{"core": "The IF is the difference between the LO and the received signal, so the receiver is tuned to either 16 − 9 = 7 MHz or 16 + 9 = 25 MHz; only 7 MHz is among the options, and it is the conventional high-side-LO arrangement.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "9 MHz is the IF itself, the frequency the mixer output is converted to, not the received frequency; a 9 MHz signal would pass only by direct IF feedthrough.", "why_tempting": "The IF is the most prominent number in the question and is easily confused with the tuned frequency."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "16 MHz is the LO frequency; a signal at 16 MHz would mix with the LO to produce zero difference, not 9 MHz, and would never reach the IF filter.", "why_tempting": "The LO tracks the dial, so a learner may assume the LO frequency equals the tuned frequency."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "21 MHz is 16 + 5, not 16 ± 9; it does not satisfy |f_LO − f_RF| = f_IF and would produce a 5 MHz product that the 9 MHz IF filter rejects.", "why_tempting": "It is a familiar amateur band and sits above the LO, which might appeal to someone who recalls that the sum product also exists but computes it wrongly."}], "concept": "A mixer produces outputs at f_LO + f_RF and |f_LO − f_RF|, and the IF filter selects the one equal to f_IF. For a difference IF, the received frequency is f_RF = f_LO − f_IF (high-side injection, LO above the signal) or f_RF = f_LO + f_IF (low-side injection). Both satisfy the mixer equation, and the one the designer does not want is the image, separated from the wanted signal by 2·f_IF. Preselection ahead of the mixer must attenuate it. High-side injection is common on HF because the LO tuning ratio across a band is smaller, which makes tracking easier, and because it places the image above the signal where it is often less congested. The simple arithmetic f_RF = f_LO ± f_IF underpins every LO, IF and image question in this section.", "worked_example": "f_LO = 16 MHz, f_IF = 9 MHz. Candidates: f_LO − f_IF = 16 − 9 = 7 MHz (high-side injection) and f_LO + f_IF = 16 + 9 = 25 MHz (low-side injection). Check: 16 − 7 = 9 MHz, correct. The receiver is tuned to 7 MHz, and 25 MHz is its image, 18 MHz away, which the 7 MHz preselector rejects strongly. Of the listed options only 7 MHz satisfies the equation.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the LO runs on the received frequency, or the IF is what the dial reads. Correction: the dial frequency, the LO and the IF are three different numbers linked by f_IF = |f_LO − f_RF|; given any two, the third follows.", "link": "section 6", "mnemonic": "LO minus RF equals IF: dial = LO − IF for a high-side oscillator.", "edge_cases": "With low-side injection the answer would be 25 MHz, and some receivers switch injection side by band; the question is unambiguous only because 25 MHz is not offered. With high-side injection the sidebands are inverted at the IF, which matters for SSB and is why the BFO must be placed on the correct side of the filter."}

{"core": "A double conversion receiver converts twice, so it needs two mixers driven by two local oscillators and has two IF chains; for SSB it also needs a BFO at the final IF to reinsert the suppressed carrier at the product detector.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "One IF stage and one local oscillator describes a single conversion receiver; a second conversion requires a second LO and a second IF.", "why_tempting": "It is the simplest superhet configuration and the one most often drawn in Basic-level diagrams."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Three oscillators would be correct only if the BFO were counted as a local oscillator, but the question already lists the BFO separately, so only the two conversion oscillators remain.", "why_tempting": "Counting every oscillator in the set (LO1, LO2, BFO) gives three, and the learner who overlooks the and in the question double-counts the BFO."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Two IF stages cannot exist with only one LO, because the second IF is produced by a second mixing operation that needs its own oscillator (unless a harmonic of the first is used, which is not a standard design).", "why_tempting": "The learner may think a single oscillator can somehow serve both conversions, or may confuse IF amplifier stages with IF frequencies."}], "concept": "Each frequency conversion requires a mixer and an oscillator. In double conversion, LO1 (usually tunable) mixes the received signal down or up to IF1, and LO2 (usually crystal controlled) mixes IF1 to IF2, so there are two LOs and two IFs with their own filters and amplifiers. SSB has no carrier, so the product detector at the end of IF2 needs a locally generated carrier substitute: the BFO, placed at the edge of the IF2 passband so that the recovered audio is f_IF2 ± f_BFO. The BFO is not a conversion oscillator; it is part of detection. Counting therefore gives LO1, LO2 and BFO as three oscillators in total, with the BFO named separately in the question, leaving two IFs and two LOs. Frequency stability of all three matters because any drift appears directly as a pitch shift in the recovered audio.", "worked_example": "Receiving 14.200 MHz USB. LO1 at 23.200 MHz gives IF1 = 9.000 MHz (sideband inverted to LSB at IF1). LO2 at 8.545 MHz gives IF2 = 455 kHz (inverted again, back to USB). The 455 kHz filter passes 455.3 to 457.7 kHz; the BFO at 455.0 kHz beats with it in the product detector to recover 300 to 2700 Hz audio. Inventory: two IFs (9 MHz, 455 kHz), two LOs (23.200 MHz, 8.545 MHz), one BFO (455 kHz).", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the BFO is one of the receiver's local oscillators and should be counted among them. Correction: local oscillators drive mixers that shift the signal to a new IF; the BFO drives the product detector to recover audio and is a separate function, so a double conversion SSB receiver has two LOs plus the BFO.", "link": "section 6", "mnemonic": "Two conversions = two mixers = two LOs = two IFs, plus one BFO to put the carrier back.", "edge_cases": "Some designs use a single master oscillator with a synthesizer that derives LO1, LO2 and BFO from it, but functionally there are still three distinct injection frequencies; and some receivers detect at IF1 by making the BFO operate there, which does not change the LO count."}

{"core": "Double conversion's distinctive advantage is image rejection: a high first IF moves the image far from the wanted signal so the front end rejects it, while a low second IF supplies the selectivity. For the same front end (the question's phrase for the same preselector performance), image interference is much lower than in a single conversion design.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Sensitivity depends on the noise figure of the RF amplifier and first mixer, which are the same in either architecture; a second mixer behind them cannot lower the noise floor.", "why_tempting": "Double conversion sets are typically premium receivers and sensitivity is the specification learners associate with quality."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Audio volume is a matter of audio gain and is unrelated to how many times the signal is converted.", "why_tempting": "More stages suggests more amplification to someone thinking of a receiver as a chain of gain blocks."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A second local oscillator is a second potential source of drift, so double conversion does not inherently cure drift; stability comes from crystal control or synthesis, which can be applied to either design.", "why_tempting": "Drift-free operation is desirable and receivers with double conversion often use crystal-controlled second LOs, so the association is natural but not causal."}], "concept": "In a superhet the image at f_RF ± 2·f_IF reaches the IF with the same conversion efficiency as the wanted signal, and the only defence is attenuation by tuned circuits before the mixer. A front end of given selectivity rejects the image better the further away it is, so raising the IF improves image rejection directly. But a high IF makes narrow filtering difficult, so double conversion follows the high first IF with a low second IF for selectivity. Single conversion is forced to compromise: a low IF for selectivity with poor image rejection, or a high IF with good image rejection but broad filtering. Sensitivity, loudness and drift are governed by other parts of the design and are not changed by the conversion count. The question wording front end sensitivity should be read as the capability of the front-end tuned circuits; the answer that follows from the physics is the reduction of image interference.", "worked_example": "Single conversion with 455 kHz IF, tuned to 3.800 MHz, LO at 4.255 MHz: image at 4.710 MHz, 910 kHz away. A two-stage preselector with 100 kHz bandwidth attenuates it by about 38 dB. Double conversion with 9 MHz first IF: image at 21.800 MHz, 18 MHz away, attenuated by more than 80 dB by the same preselector. Both receivers then have identical sensitivity if their RF amplifiers and first mixers are identical, and identical selectivity if both end at a 455 kHz filter. The only difference is 40-plus dB of image rejection.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: double conversion is a general upgrade that improves sensitivity, stability and loudness along with everything else. Correction: it specifically solves the image-versus-selectivity trade-off; all its other characteristics depend on the individual stage designs, not on the number of conversions.", "link": "section 6", "mnemonic": "Double conversion buys image rejection, nothing more and nothing less.", "edge_cases": "The item's phrase front end sensitivity is loosely worded; in A-006-001-003 the same idea is stated as front end selectivity, which is the physically accurate term, since it is the preselector's selectivity that determines how much the image offset helps."}

{"core": "The mixer multiplies the incoming signal with the local oscillator and produces sum and difference frequencies; the IF filter selects the difference (or sum) equal to the fixed IF, so the mixer's job is to translate the received signal frequency to the intermediate frequency.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A receiver uses one IF per conversion, chosen at design time; the mixer does not offer a choice of IFs and cannot change the frequency the following filter is built for.", "why_tempting": "The mixer does produce many products, and a learner may think that means several IFs are available."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "The mixer converts the image to the IF just as efficiently as the wanted signal; image removal must be done before the mixer by the preselector, and the mixer itself is the reason the image exists.", "why_tempting": "Image rejection is discussed alongside the mixer and IF choice, so the learner may attribute the solution to the stage that causes the problem."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Audio is produced by the detector after IF amplification; the mixer's output is at radio frequency (the IF), typically hundreds of kHz to tens of MHz.", "why_tempting": "A product detector is also a mixer, so a learner who knows that may generalize that mixers produce audio."}], "concept": "Mixing is multiplication of two signals; by the trigonometric identity cos(a)·cos(b) = ½[cos(a − b) + cos(a + b)], a signal at f_RF multiplied by an LO at f_LO yields components at f_LO − f_RF and f_LO + f_RF, and the modulation on the signal is carried intact to both. A tuned circuit or filter at the mixer output picks the one equal to f_IF. In practice the mixer is a nonlinear or switching device (diode ring, FET, Gilbert cell) whose transfer characteristic contains a second-order term that performs the multiplication; higher-order terms produce unwanted products. Translating to a fixed IF is what allows the rest of the receiver to be fixed-tuned with high-performance filters. The product detector at the end of the chain is another mixer, with the BFO as its LO, translating the IF down to audio; the principle is identical but the stage and purpose differ.", "worked_example": "Signal at 3.600 MHz carrying SSB voice, LO at 12.600 MHz, IF filter at 9.000 MHz. Mixer output contains 12.600 − 3.600 = 9.000 MHz and 12.600 + 3.600 = 16.200 MHz, both carrying the voice modulation. The 9 MHz crystal filter passes the difference and rejects the sum. Retune the dial to 3.700 MHz and the LO to 12.700 MHz; the difference is still exactly 9.000 MHz, so the filter and IF amplifier need no adjustment. That constancy is the point of the mixer.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the mixer blends the signal with the oscillator to make it stronger or cleaner. Correction: the mixer changes the signal's frequency to the IF; it adds no useful gain or filtering on its own, and in fact introduces some loss and noise.", "link": "section 6", "mnemonic": "Mixer = frequency mover, not frequency improver.", "edge_cases": "In direct-conversion receivers the LO is set at the signal frequency itself and the mixer output is audio, so the mixer and detector functions merge into one stage; that is a distinct architecture from the superhet described here."}

{"core": "An SSB transmitter suppresses the carrier, leaving only one sideband; an envelope or product detector cannot recover intelligible audio from a sideband alone, so the receiver must reinsert a locally generated carrier at the BFO frequency to beat against the sideband and reproduce the original audio frequencies.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "The IF passband is set by the IF filter; the BFO is injected at the detector and has no effect on the bandwidth of the stages ahead of it.", "why_tempting": "The BFO is placed at the edge of the filter passband, and a learner may think it shapes the passband rather than merely sitting beside it."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "There is no received carrier to beat with in SSB, and the missing sideband is never reconstructed; the BFO supplies the carrier, not the other sideband, and demodulation needs only one sideband plus a carrier.", "why_tempting": "It contains plausible SSB vocabulary and sounds like it is restoring something that was removed at the transmitter."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Unwanted sideband rejection is done by the IF filter (or by phasing in some designs) before the detector; the BFO cannot phase out anything because it is a single tone injected into the detector.", "why_tempting": "The phasing method of SSB generation involves oscillators and phase shifts, and the learner may confuse that transmitter technique with the receiver's BFO."}], "concept": "An SSB signal at the IF is a band of frequencies f_c + f_a (USB) or f_c − f_a (LSB), where f_c is the suppressed carrier position and f_a the audio frequencies, with no energy at f_c. An envelope detector responds to the envelope of the sum of all components, which for a single-sideband voice signal is not the original audio and sounds like unintelligible mush. A product detector multiplies the IF signal by a local carrier at f_BFO, producing difference frequencies |f_c ± f_a − f_BFO|; if f_BFO = f_c the output is exactly f_a, the original audio. The BFO therefore replaces the carrier the transmitter removed. Its frequency must sit at the correct edge of the IF filter passband for the sideband in use, and any error between f_BFO and the true carrier position shifts every audio frequency by that error, which is why SSB tuning is so critical.", "worked_example": "USB signal at IF: filter passes 9.0003 to 9.0027 MHz (audio 300 to 2700 Hz above a 9.0000 MHz carrier point). With the BFO at 9.0000 MHz the product detector outputs 300 to 2700 Hz, correct audio. Offset the BFO to 9.0001 MHz and every voice component shifts down 100 Hz, giving a slightly deep but readable voice. Remove the BFO entirely and an envelope detector produces only the beats between voice harmonics, which is unintelligible. The BFO is the carrier the transmitter threw away.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the BFO filters or selects the sideband. Correction: the IF filter selects the sideband; the BFO supplies the missing carrier so a product detector can convert the sideband back to baseband audio.", "link": "section 6", "mnemonic": "BFO = Bring the carrier back, Friend Of the product detector.", "edge_cases": "AM can be received with the BFO switched on too (synchronous or exalted-carrier detection), which improves reception under selective fading; and in SDRs the BFO is a numerical oscillator in software, but its purpose is unchanged."}

{"core": "The first mixer multiplies the incoming RF signal by the local oscillator and its output tank selects the difference (or sum) product that equals the design intermediate frequency, so its output is the IF.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "The input to the mixer is a radio frequency; its purpose is to change that to the IF. Strictly the IF is also an RF-range frequency, but the exam's intent is the functional label, and the stage's output is defined as the IF.", "why_tempting": "The IF is often in the MHz range, and the learner may reason that any such frequency is a radio frequency."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "The high frequency oscillator is another name for the local oscillator itself; it is an input to the mixer, not its output.", "why_tempting": "The HFO term appears in older receiver literature and sounds like a product rather than a source."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Audio is produced by the detector at the end of the IF chain; the first mixer's output is far above audio frequencies and still carries the modulated signal.", "why_tempting": "A product detector is a mixer producing audio, so the learner may generalize that any mixer produces audio."}], "concept": "The first mixer realizes the identity cos(ω_RF t)·cos(ω_LO t) = ½cos((ω_LO − ω_RF)t) + ½cos((ω_LO + ω_RF)t), carrying the signal's modulation onto both products. The IF filter at its output passes the product equal to f_IF, giving a signal at a fixed frequency regardless of where the receiver is tuned. In older terminology the local oscillator was called the HFO, and the stage combining it with the signal was the first detector or converter. The IF then feeds the fixed-tuned amplifier chain and ultimately the detector, which produces audio. The chain is RF in, IF after the mixer, audio after the detector; each step is a frequency translation and recognizing which stage produces which frequency is the backbone of this subsection.", "worked_example": "Incoming signal 7.150 MHz, LO (HFO) at 16.150 MHz. Mixer output contains 9.000 MHz (difference) and 23.300 MHz (sum); the 9 MHz IF filter passes the difference. The 9 MHz IF then passes through two amplifier stages and reaches a product detector with a 9 MHz BFO, which outputs 300 to 2700 Hz audio. Three stages, three frequencies: 7.150 MHz (RF), 9.000 MHz (IF), 0.3 to 2.7 kHz (AF).", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the mixer output is still at the received radio frequency, just combined with the oscillator. Correction: the mixer output is a new frequency, the IF, equal to the difference (or sum) of signal and LO; the received frequency is left behind.", "link": "section 6", "mnemonic": "RF + LO into the mixer, IF out.", "edge_cases": "In up-converting receivers the first IF is the sum product and may be higher than the received frequency, so an IF can be numerically larger than the RF signal; it is still called the IF because it is the fixed frequency the following stages are built for."}

{"core": "The LO must differ from the signal by the IF: f_LO = f_RF + f_IF = 3.6 + 9 = 12.6 MHz or f_LO = f_IF − f_RF = 9 − 3.6 = 5.4 MHz. Of the options only 5 400 kHz satisfies |f_LO − f_RF| = 9 MHz, with the mixer's sum product 3.6 + 5.4 = 9 MHz producing the IF.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "21 600 kHz minus 3 600 kHz is 18 000 kHz, double the IF; 21.6 MHz would be the LO for an 18 MHz IF, not 9 MHz.", "why_tempting": "A learner who adds the IF twice or confuses 2·f_IF (the image spacing) with f_IF arrives here."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "3 400 kHz is only 200 kHz from the signal, so the difference product would be 200 kHz, not 9 MHz.", "why_tempting": "A learner might subtract wrong digits or think the LO must be near the signal, as in a direct-conversion receiver."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "10 600 kHz minus 3 600 kHz is 7 000 kHz, not 9 000 kHz; it would require a 7 MHz IF.", "why_tempting": "A learner who adds 7 MHz instead of 9 MHz, or confuses the IF with a band edge, lands here."}], "concept": "A mixer produces f_LO + f_RF and |f_LO − f_RF|, and the IF filter selects whichever equals f_IF. Two LO frequencies therefore always work: f_RF + f_IF (high-side injection, difference product used) and |f_RF − f_IF| (low-side injection, or in this case the sum product, since the LO at 5.4 MHz plus the signal at 3.6 MHz gives 9 MHz). The choice affects where the image falls and whether the sideband is inverted. When the sum product is used (f_RF + f_LO = f_IF), the image is the signal that reaches the IF by the difference product, at f_IF + f_LO = 14.4 MHz here; with high-side injection at 12.6 MHz the image would instead be at 21.6 MHz. Either way the image is 2·f_IF from the wanted signal. This question simply tests the arithmetic: find the LO value for which signal and LO combine to 9 MHz.", "worked_example": "f_RF = 3 600 kHz, f_IF = 9 000 kHz. High-side candidate: 3 600 + 9 000 = 12 600 kHz (not offered). Low-side candidate: 9 000 − 3 600 = 5 400 kHz (option B). Verify: mixer output includes 3 600 + 5 400 = 9 000 kHz, which the IF filter passes. Check the distractors: 21 600 − 3 600 = 18 000 kHz; 3 600 − 3 400 = 200 kHz; 10 600 − 3 600 = 7 000 kHz; none equals 9 000 kHz.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the LO must always be above the signal, so the only valid LO is f_RF + f_IF. Correction: any LO for which a sum or difference with the signal equals the IF works; when f_IF > f_RF, as in this up-conversion case, the LO at f_IF − f_RF uses the sum product.", "link": "section 6", "mnemonic": "Signal ± LO = IF; test each option by adding and subtracting.", "edge_cases": "With a 9 MHz IF the 80 m and 20 m bands are symmetrical: an LO near 5.2 to 5.5 MHz converts both 3.5 to 3.8 MHz (sum) and 14.0 to 14.3 MHz (difference) to 9 MHz, which is why classic 9 MHz IF transceivers covered those two bands with one VFO range; each band is the other's image."}

{"core": "The BFO is a local carrier injected into the product detector so it can beat (heterodyne) with the incoming IF signal; the difference between them is the recovered audio. For CW the offset of 500 to 1 500 Hz is the audible note; for SSB the BFO sits at the carrier point beside the filter passband so the sideband beats down to baseband.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "The BFO adds no signal gain; a product detector's output level depends on the IF signal and the injection level, but the BFO's purpose is frequency translation to audio, not amplification.", "why_tempting": "Injecting a strong local signal might seem like it boosts the weak one."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A single injected tone provides no protection against interference; interference rejection comes from the IF filter and front end.", "why_tempting": "Narrow CW reception with a BFO does sound cleaner, which may be misattributed to the BFO rather than to the narrow filter."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Passing the signal through unchanged is the opposite of what a detector does; the BFO exists precisely so the signal is changed from IF to audio.", "why_tempting": "The phrase without interruption sounds like a continuity or stability goal, and the learner may think the BFO keeps the signal flowing."}], "concept": "A product detector multiplies the IF signal by the BFO tone, giving an output at the difference frequency. For an unmodulated CW carrier at f_IF, a BFO at f_IF + Δ produces an audio tone at Δ, typically set to 500 to 1 000 Hz for comfortable copy; with Δ = 0 the output is DC and nothing is heard, which is why the offset is required. For SSB, the signal at the IF occupies f_c + 300 Hz to f_c + 2700 Hz (USB), and the BFO is placed at f_c, the suppressed carrier point, so that each component beats down to its original audio frequency; the apparent offset from the signal energy is then roughly the same 300 to 1500 Hz range the question cites. Heterodyning is the same multiplication used in the first mixer, applied one last time to reach baseband. The BFO must be stable to a few hertz, because any drift shifts the CW note or the SSB voice pitch directly.", "worked_example": "CW carrier arrives at the IF at exactly 455.000 kHz. BFO at 455.000 kHz: product detector output is 0 Hz, silence. BFO at 455.700 kHz: output is 700 Hz, a clear CW note. BFO at 456.500 kHz: 1 500 Hz, a higher pitch some operators prefer for weak-signal work. For an SSB signal whose carrier point is 455.000 kHz and whose sideband spans 455.3 to 457.7 kHz, a BFO at 455.000 kHz recovers 300 to 2700 Hz; moving it to 455.200 kHz would lower every voice frequency by 200 Hz.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the BFO should be tuned exactly onto the incoming signal for best reception. Correction: a BFO exactly on a CW carrier produces zero beat and no sound; it must be offset so the beat note falls in the audio range, and for SSB it sits at the carrier position beside, not inside, the sideband energy.", "link": "section 6", "mnemonic": "Beat Frequency Oscillator: the beat IS the audio, so there must be an offset.", "edge_cases": "Receivers with a CW pitch control vary this offset, and modern rigs shift the IF filter centre with it so the signal stays in the passband; older designs with a fixed filter required the operator to retune the main dial when changing pitch."}

{"core": "Oscillator drift shifts every received signal and the recovered audio pitch, and any harmonics, phase noise or spurs on the LO or BFO are mixed onto the signal path as spurious responses and reciprocal mixing. So the two essential properties are frequency stability and spectral purity.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Sensitivity is a receiver-level property describing weak-signal detection; an oscillator generates a signal rather than receiving one, so the term does not apply to it.", "why_tempting": "Stable is correct, and sensitive is the receiver virtue most learners recall, so the pairing looks right."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Selectivity describes a filter's ability to pass one frequency and reject others; an oscillator produces a single tone and has no selectivity in that sense.", "why_tempting": "Spectrally pure is correct, and selective sounds like a near-synonym for pure in casual usage."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Both terms describe the receiver as a whole, not its oscillators; neither sensitivity nor selectivity is a property of a signal source.", "why_tempting": "These are the two words most associated with receiver performance in the Basic syllabus."}], "concept": "The LO sets the received frequency through f_RF = f_LO ± f_IF, so a drift of Δf in the LO moves the receiver by Δf; for SSB a drift of 50 Hz is audible as a pitch change and a few hundred hertz makes speech unintelligible. The BFO must be equally stable for the same reason. Spectral purity matters because mixing is multiplication: any component on the LO (harmonics, sidebands, phase noise) also mixes with incoming signals. LO harmonics create spurious responses where n·f_LO ± f_signal = f_IF; phase noise spreads the LO into a skirt, and a strong signal near the wanted one mixes with that skirt into the IF passband, raising the noise floor in a process called reciprocal mixing, which can be the limiting factor in close-in dynamic range. Phase noise is specified in dBc/Hz at a given offset; a value of −130 dBc/Hz at 10 kHz is good for an HF receiver. Crystal control, low-noise synthesizer design and clean power supplies serve both requirements.", "worked_example": "A receiver with LO phase noise of −120 dBc/Hz at 5 kHz offset and a 2.4 kHz SSB filter is tuned 5 kHz from a signal that is S9+40 dB (about −33 dBm). Reciprocal mixing noise in the passband is −33 dBm − 120 dBc/Hz + 10·log10(2400) ≈ −33 − 120 + 34 = −119 dBm, roughly 15 dB above a good HF noise floor of −134 dBm, so a weak station 5 kHz from the strong one is buried. Improve the LO to −135 dBc/Hz and the reciprocal noise drops to −134 dBm, level with the floor. Stability and purity are not decorative specifications.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: an oscillator only needs to be on the right frequency; its waveform quality does not matter because the IF filter cleans everything up. Correction: the IF filter cannot remove products created by LO impurity, because those products are generated at the IF itself by mixing; purity has to be designed into the oscillator.", "link": "section 6", "mnemonic": "Oscillators must be steady and clean: stable in frequency, pure in spectrum.", "edge_cases": "Direct digital synthesis gives excellent stability but can produce discrete spurs from quantization; modern receivers combine DDS or fractional-N synthesis with filtering to get both properties, and in SDRs the ADC clock's jitter plays the same role as LO phase noise."}

{"core": "A tuned circuit before the IF amplifier with a main variable capacitor, a parallel trimmer and an inductor, in the stage that is ganged with the dial, is the local oscillator tank; the variable capacitor tunes the LO across the band while the trimmer sets its tracking at the high-frequency end.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "The BFO operates at the fixed IF and is never ganged to the main tuning; and an antenna circuit tunes at the signal frequency, so one capacitor could not serve both.", "why_tempting": "Combining two tuned functions on one capacitor sounds economical, and the BFO is a real oscillator in the set."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The BFO is fixed at the IF (or has only a small pitch adjustment) and sits at the detector after the IF amplifier, not before it; it does not use a ganged tuning capacitor with a trimmer.", "why_tempting": "Both LO and BFO are oscillators, and the learner may not distinguish which one tracks the dial."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "The antenna (RF) circuit and the LO resonate at frequencies differing by the IF, so a single capacitor section cannot tune both; they use separate ganged sections, and the question describes one stage with one circuit.", "why_tempting": "In a ganged capacitor the sections are mechanically linked, so a learner may think of them as one capacitor tuning everything."}], "concept": "In a classic superhet the main tuning capacitor has two or three ganged sections: one for the RF or antenna tuned circuit at f_RF and one for the LO at f_RF + f_IF. The LO section must track so the difference stays at f_IF across the band, which requires its tank to cover a different frequency ratio than the RF section. Tracking is adjusted with a parallel trimmer (small capacitance, effective at the high end where the main capacitor is nearly unmeshed) and a series padder (effective at the low end where the main capacitor is fully meshed), giving exact tracking at two or three points and small errors between. The question describes the parallel-trimmer-plus-variable arrangement typical of an LO tank. The resonant frequency follows f = 1/(2π√(LC)), with C the sum of the variable, trimmer and strays. The BFO, by contrast, is fixed at the IF and lives after the IF amplifier, so it is excluded by both position and function.", "worked_example": "Broadcast receiver covering 540 to 1 600 kHz with a 455 kHz IF: the RF tank must cover a 2.96:1 frequency range (8.8:1 capacitance ratio), while the LO must cover 995 to 2 055 kHz, only 2.07:1 (4.3:1 capacitance ratio). With identical 365 pF gang sections, the LO needs a series padder of roughly 400 pF to compress its range and a parallel trimmer of about 20 pF to align the high end. Adjusting the trimmer at 1 400 kHz and the padder at 600 kHz brings the LO to within a few kHz of f_RF + 455 kHz across the dial.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the BFO is tuned by the main dial like the LO because both are oscillators. Correction: only the LO tracks the dial; the BFO stays at the fixed IF, so a ganged variable capacitor with a tracking trimmer in a pre-IF stage belongs to the LO.", "link": "Reactance & Resonance", "mnemonic": "Trimmer trims the top end; padder pads the bottom; both belong to the LO.", "edge_cases": "Synthesized receivers have no mechanical gang at all; the LO is set digitally and the preselector is either switched band-pass filters or electronically tuned with varactors driven from a lookup table, which performs the same tracking function in software."}

{"core": "With no RF amplifier, the tuned circuit at the mixer input is the receiver's only preselector; its variable capacitor tunes that circuit to the reception frequency so the wanted signal is passed and the image and other off-frequency signals are attenuated before mixing.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "The BFO is a fixed oscillator at the IF located at the detector; it is not tuned by a front-end capacitor and cannot share a tank with the antenna circuit, which resonates at a completely different frequency.", "why_tempting": "A single capacitor doing two jobs sounds plausible, and the BFO is a familiar name."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The BFO does not sit at the mixer input and is not tuned across the band; a tank at the mixer input resonates at the signal frequency, not at the IF.", "why_tempting": "The learner may confuse the two oscillators or assume any tuned circuit near the mixer is an oscillator tank."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "The LO tank resonates at f_RF ± f_IF, not at f_RF, so the antenna circuit and the LO require separate tuned circuits even though their capacitors are ganged on one shaft.", "why_tempting": "Ganged capacitors are mechanically one unit, and the learner may think of the shared shaft as one capacitor tuning both."}], "concept": "Preselection is the selectivity applied before the mixer. Its two jobs are image rejection (attenuating signals at f_RF ± 2·f_IF, which would otherwise convert to the IF) and limiting the total signal power delivered to the mixer, which protects against intermodulation and cross-modulation from strong out-of-band stations. In a receiver with an RF amplifier the preselector includes that stage's input and output tanks; without one, the single LC circuit at the mixer input is all the preselection there is, so its Q and its correct tuning matter even more. The capacitor is ganged with the LO section so that as the dial moves, the preselector resonance follows f_RF while the LO follows f_RF + f_IF. Resonance is f = 1/(2π√(LC)), and the image attenuation of a single tuned circuit is approximately 20·log10(Q·(f_img/f_RF − f_RF/f_img)) dB for large offsets. Omitting the RF amplifier is common on the lower HF bands, where atmospheric noise dominates and the mixer's own noise figure is adequate.", "worked_example": "Receiver tuned to 3.750 MHz with a 455 kHz IF and no RF amplifier; the mixer input tank has a loaded Q of 60. Image at 3.750 + 0.910 = 4.660 MHz. Attenuation ≈ 20·log10(60 × (4.660/3.750 − 3.750/4.660)) = 20·log10(60 × (1.243 − 0.805)) = 20·log10(26.3) ≈ 28 dB. If the capacitor were mis-set and the tank resonated at 3.950 MHz instead, the wanted signal would lose roughly 10 dB and the image would be attenuated only about 20 dB, so correct preselector tuning is what this capacitor provides.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the tuned circuit at the mixer input is part of the LO or BFO because oscillators use LC tanks. Correction: it is the signal-frequency preselector; the oscillator tanks are separate circuits at different frequencies.", "link": "Reactance & Resonance", "mnemonic": "No RF amp? The mixer-input tank is your whole front end: tune it to the signal.", "edge_cases": "Some direct-conversion and simple regenerative receivers also use a single input tank; in a direct-conversion set there is no image in the superhet sense, but the tank still rejects strong broadcast signals that would otherwise overload the mixer."}

{"core": "Combining a 14.25 MHz signal with a 13.795 MHz oscillator to yield their 455 kHz difference is frequency conversion, which is the mixer's function; 14.25 − 13.795 = 0.455 MHz confirms the arithmetic.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A multiplier produces harmonics of a single input (2f, 3f, and so on); it does not combine two inputs to form a difference frequency.", "why_tempting": "Mixing is mathematically multiplication, and a learner who knows that may pick the stage literally named multiplier."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The BFO is the oscillator injected at the product detector at the IF; 13.795 MHz is the first LO, and the stage that combines signals is the mixer, not either oscillator.", "why_tempting": "The question mentions an oscillator signal, and the BFO is the oscillator most associated with producing an audible beat."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "The VFO generates the 13.795 MHz oscillator signal; it is a source feeding the mixer, not the stage where the two signals combine.", "why_tempting": "13.795 MHz is plausibly the VFO's output, so a learner may name the oscillator instead of the stage that uses it."}], "concept": "The mixer is the stage that performs frequency conversion by multiplying two inputs: cos(ω_1 t)·cos(ω_2 t) = ½[cos((ω_1 − ω_2)t) + cos((ω_1 + ω_2)t)]. Feeding it a 14.25 MHz signal and a 13.795 MHz LO yields 0.455 MHz and 28.045 MHz, and the IF filter keeps 455 kHz. Here the LO is below the signal (low-side injection), so the image is at 13.795 − 0.455 = 13.340 MHz and the sideband is not inverted. The VFO (or synthesizer) generates the LO; the multiplier, if present, raises a crystal frequency to a harmonic for VHF LO chains; the BFO reinserts a carrier at the product detector. Each of these is a distinct block, and the question tests whether the learner can map a described operation to its block name.", "worked_example": "Signal 14.250 MHz, LO 13.795 MHz. Difference: 14.250 − 13.795 = 0.455 MHz = 455 kHz, the IF. Sum: 28.045 MHz, rejected by the IF filter. Image: 13.795 − 0.455 = 13.340 MHz, 910 kHz below the wanted signal, to be rejected by the preselector. Stage performing this: the mixer. If the LO were instead 14.705 MHz (high-side), the difference would still be 455 kHz but the image would move to 15.160 MHz and the sidebands would invert.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the oscillator that supplies the 13.795 MHz signal is where the conversion happens. Correction: oscillators only generate; the mixer is the stage that combines the oscillator output with the signal to produce the IF.", "link": "section 6", "mnemonic": "Two in, difference out: that is a mixer.", "edge_cases": "A product detector is also a mixer (signal plus BFO gives audio), and in a direct-conversion receiver the mixer and detector are the same stage; the question's 455 kHz output identifies this one as the first mixer rather than the detector."}

{"core": "The RF amplifier and the first mixer both receive the signal before conversion, so their input tuned circuits are both tuned to the received frequency f_RF; the LO is offset by the IF and the IF stages are at the fixed IF.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "The IF stages are tuned to f_IF and the LO to f_RF ± f_IF; these are two different frequencies by construction.", "why_tempting": "Both are internal to the receiver and the learner may lump them as the fixed stages."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "The RF amplifier is tuned to f_RF and the IF amplifier to f_IF; they coincide only in the degenerate case of a zero-IF receiver, which is not a superhet in the sense asked.", "why_tempting": "RF and IF are the two amplifier chains that carry the signal, so pairing them is natural if the learner forgets that the mixer changes the frequency between them."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The LO must be offset from the RF signal by exactly the IF; if its tank were tuned to f_RF the mixer difference output would be zero and no IF would be produced.", "why_tempting": "The LO and RF tanks are ganged on the same shaft and move together, which gives the impression they are tuned alike."}], "concept": "The signal path before the mixer, comprising the antenna tuned circuit, the RF amplifier and the mixer input, is all resonant at the received frequency f_RF, and these circuits together form the preselector that sets image rejection and limits strong out-of-band signals. The LO tank is resonant at f_RF + f_IF (or f_RF − f_IF) and is ganged with the preselector so the difference stays constant. After the mixer everything is at f_IF. The two stages whose inputs share f_RF are therefore the RF amplifier and the first mixer; in a receiver with two RF stages, those would share it too. The question also implicitly tests the tracking idea: multiple tuned circuits at f_RF, moved together, give a sharper combined preselector response because their attenuations in dB add.", "worked_example": "Receiver tuned to 21.300 MHz with a 9 MHz IF and high-side LO. RF amplifier input tank: 21.300 MHz. Mixer input tank (fed from the RF amplifier output): 21.300 MHz. LO tank: 30.300 MHz. Mixer output tank, crystal filter and IF amplifier: 9.000 MHz. Image at 39.300 MHz; with two tuned circuits at 21.3 MHz each giving 30 dB at that offset, the preselector gives about 60 dB total, which is why having both the RF and mixer inputs tuned to f_RF matters.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the LO and RF circuits are tuned to the same frequency because they are on the same tuning shaft.
