Correction: they are ganged so they move together but are offset by the IF; the circuits actually sharing the received frequency are the RF amplifier and mixer inputs.", "link": "section 6", "mnemonic": "Everything before the mixer's output is at the dial frequency, except the LO.", "edge_cases": "In up-converting designs with a fixed high first IF, the RF and mixer inputs may use broadband band-pass filters rather than tracked tanks, but they are still passing the same received frequency; the LO alone runs offset."}

{"core": "The mixer combines the received signal with the local oscillator and produces the intermediate frequency, the fixed frequency at which the rest of the receiver provides selectivity and gain. Producing the IF is its defining purpose.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "SSB demodulation is done by the product detector using the BFO after the IF chain; the first mixer only translates the still-modulated signal to the IF.", "why_tempting": "A product detector is itself a mixer, so a learner who knows that may credit the mixer stage with demodulation."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Mixers do generate unwanted products as a side effect, but that is a flaw the designer minimizes, not the purpose of the stage; the question asks what the mixer stage does in the receiver's design.", "why_tempting": "It is technically true that mixers produce spurious outputs, so a learner reading literally may select it."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A buffer isolates one stage from another without changing frequency; the mixer changes frequency and is deliberately nonlinear, the opposite of a buffer.", "why_tempting": "The mixer sits between the front end and the IF and might be imagined as an isolating stage between them."}], "concept": "In a superhet, the mixer takes the signal at f_RF and the LO at f_LO and outputs their sum and difference; the IF filter passes the one at f_IF = |f_LO − f_RF|. Because this output is fixed regardless of tuning, the IF chain can use fixed, high-Q filters and stable gain. The mixer should ideally be a pure multiplier; real mixers have higher-order terms that produce intermodulation and spurious responses, and designers choose balanced topologies (diode ring, Gilbert cell, switching FET) to suppress LO feedthrough and even-order products. The mixer's conversion loss or gain and its noise figure, combined with any RF amplifier ahead of it, set receiver sensitivity; its third-order intercept point sets strong-signal performance. Demodulation happens later in the detector, which for SSB is another mixer (the product detector) driven by the BFO.", "worked_example": "If you removed the mixer from a superhet and connected the RF amplifier straight to the 9 MHz IF filter, a 14.2 MHz signal would simply be rejected by the filter and nothing would be heard; the receiver would only respond to signals already at 9 MHz. Reinsert the mixer with a 23.2 MHz LO and the 14.2 MHz signal is translated to 9 MHz, passes the filter, and reaches the detector. Nothing about the signal's modulation has changed, only its centre frequency.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the mixer is where the signal is detected, since it is where the oscillator meets the signal. Correction: the first mixer only moves the signal to the IF; detection, including the mixing of the BFO for SSB, happens at the end of the IF chain in the detector.", "link": "section 6", "mnemonic": "Mixer makes the IF; detector makes the audio.", "edge_cases": "In a direct-conversion receiver the single mixer does produce audio because the LO is at the signal frequency, which collapses the superhet's two mixing operations into one; the question refers to the superhet, where the mixer's output is the IF."}

{"core": "The noise floor is the level of the receiver's own internally generated noise referred to its input, and therefore the weakest signal that can be detected above it; it is set by thermal noise in the bandwidth plus the receiver's noise figure.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "LO noise contributes to reciprocal mixing but is only one of several internal noise sources; the noise floor is the total noise from all stages, dominated by the front end.", "why_tempting": "Oscillator phase noise is a real receiver noise mechanism discussed in the same section."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Atmospheric noise is external to the receiver and varies with band, time and location; the noise floor is a property of the receiver alone, measured with a resistive termination in place of the antenna.", "why_tempting": "In practice external noise often exceeds the receiver's floor on HF, so the learner may define the floor by what they actually hear."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Overload is a strong-signal limit at the top of the dynamic range; the noise floor is the weak-signal limit at the bottom.", "why_tempting": "Both are limits of receiver performance, and the learner may invert which end of the range noise floor refers to."}], "concept": "Thermal noise power available from any resistance at temperature T in bandwidth B is P_n = k·T·B, which at 290 K is −174 dBm per hertz. A receiver adds its own noise, quantified by noise figure NF in dB, so the input-referred noise floor is P_floor = −174 dBm + 10·log10(B) + NF. This is the minimum discernible signal (MDS) when a signal equal to the noise is taken as just detectable. Narrower bandwidth lowers the floor, which is why CW with a 500 Hz filter digs deeper than SSB with 2.4 kHz. Noise figure is set almost entirely by the first stages, per the Friis formula F_total = F_1 + (F_2 − 1)/G_1 + ..., so a low-noise RF amplifier with enough gain makes the later stages' noise negligible. On HF the external noise usually exceeds the receiver floor, so a very low NF matters mostly at VHF and above; the floor also anchors the bottom of the dynamic range, which runs up to the intermodulation or blocking limit.", "worked_example": "Receiver with NF = 8 dB and a 2.4 kHz SSB filter: P_floor = −174 + 10·log10(2400) + 8 = −174 + 33.8 + 8 ≈ −132 dBm. Switch to a 500 Hz CW filter: −174 + 27 + 8 = −139 dBm, 7 dB better. Add a preamplifier with NF = 2 dB and 15 dB gain ahead of it: F_total ≈ 1.58 + (6.31 − 1)/31.6 ≈ 1.75, NF ≈ 2.4 dB, floor ≈ −138 dBm in the SSB bandwidth. A 0.05 μV signal into 50 Ω is −133 dBm, so it would be at the floor of the original receiver and 5 dB above it with the preamp.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the noise floor is the band noise heard when no station is transmitting. Correction: that is external noise; the receiver noise floor is the internally generated noise, measured with the antenna replaced by a dummy load, and it defines the weakest signal the receiver itself can detect.", "link": "Decibel Converter", "mnemonic": "−174 dBm/Hz + 10·log(B) + NF = the floor you cannot hear below.", "edge_cases": "Below about 20 MHz atmospheric and man-made noise typically exceeds a good receiver's floor by 10 to 30 dB, so improving NF there buys nothing; at VHF and UHF, where external noise is low, the receiver floor is the real limit and preamplifiers pay off."}

{"core": "The first IF amplifier works at the fixed intermediate frequency where high-Q filtering is practical, so it both sharpens selectivity (through its filters and tuned circuits) and supplies a large part of the receiver's total gain at a frequency where stable amplification is easy.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Dynamic response is not a defined receiver function; dynamic range is set by front-end linearity and the AGC system, and the IF amplifier is not where it is created.", "why_tempting": "It sounds like dynamic range, a real specification, and the IF stage is where AGC is applied."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Noise figure is determined by the stages ahead of the IF amplifier; by the Friis formula, gain in the front end makes the IF amplifier's noise contribution negligible, so the IF stage cannot improve NF.", "why_tempting": "The IF amplifier is a low-noise stage in a well-designed receiver, and the learner may think any low-noise stage improves NF."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Cross-modulation occurs in nonlinear front-end stages when a strong signal modulates a weak one; once it has happened the modulation is on the wanted signal and no later filter can remove it.", "why_tempting": "The IF filter does remove adjacent signals, so a learner may think it also removes the effects those signals caused earlier."}], "concept": "After conversion the signal sits at the fixed IF, so the IF amplifier can be built with crystal, mechanical or ceramic filters having bandwidth B = f_0/Q far narrower than tunable front-end circuits could achieve. Selectivity is specified by the −6 dB bandwidth and the shape factor (−60 dB bandwidth divided by −6 dB bandwidth). The IF chain also provides most of the receiver's gain, typically 60 to 100 dB, because at a fixed frequency the stages can be neutralized and shielded once, and feedback paths do not shift as the receiver tunes. AGC is applied here to hold the detector input roughly constant across a wide input range. The first IF stage in particular sits right after the mixer and roofing filter and sets the gain distribution: enough to overcome detector and later-stage noise, not so much that strong signals overload the following filter. Noise figure and cross-modulation are decided earlier in the front end.", "worked_example": "A receiver needs about 100 dB of total gain to bring a 1 μV (−107 dBm) signal to the 1 V level a detector wants. The RF amplifier gives 15 dB, the mixer 5 dB of conversion loss, so 90 dB must come from the IF chain across two or three stages at 9 MHz, each with a crystal filter contributing selectivity. The first IF stage with 30 dB gain and an 8-pole 2.4 kHz filter (shape factor 1.8) attenuates a signal 5 kHz away by over 60 dB, so the later stages see only the wanted signal. Had that same gain been attempted at the tuned RF frequency, the broad front-end tanks would pass neighbouring signals at nearly full strength.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the IF amplifier is just a gain block and selectivity comes from somewhere else. Correction: the IF amplifier is where selectivity is deliberately built in, because the fixed frequency allows narrow filters; it is the home of both selectivity and gain.", "link": "section 6", "mnemonic": "IF = where the receiver gets Sharp and Strong (selectivity and gain).", "edge_cases": "In modern rigs the later IF stages are often replaced by an ADC and DSP filtering; the first IF amplifier and roofing filter remain analogue and still determine how much strong-signal energy reaches the ADC, so their gain and bandwidth choices are now about ADC dynamic range as much as about selectivity."}

{"core": "The RF amplifier's job is to provide just enough low-noise gain that weak signals arrive at the mixer well above the mixer's own noise contribution, setting a good overall noise figure; excess gain beyond that only pushes strong signals toward mixer overload and intermodulation.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Maximum gain degrades dynamic range: strong signals drive the mixer into intermodulation and cross-modulation long before self-oscillation becomes the issue, so gain must be limited deliberately.", "why_tempting": "More gain intuitively means more sensitivity, which was an acceptable Basic-level view but ignores strong-signal behaviour."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "The IF amplifier comes after the mixer and its gain is irrelevant to the noise contribution of the mixer; by the Friis formula only the gain ahead of a stage affects how much that stage's noise matters.", "why_tempting": "Gain distribution across stages is a real design issue, and the IF stage does carry most of the receiver's gain."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Keeping weak signals below the mixer noise would make them undetectable; the purpose of RF gain is the opposite, to lift them above that noise.", "why_tempting": "It is the inverse of the correct statement and reads similarly at a glance."}], "concept": "The Friis noise formula F_total = F_1 + (F_2 − 1)/G_1 + (F_3 − 1)/(G_1·G_2) + ... shows that the RF amplifier (stage 1) with gain G_1 divides the mixer's excess noise (F_2 − 1) by G_1. A modest G_1 of 10 to 15 dB is enough to make a mixer with NF of 8 to 10 dB contribute only a fraction of a dB. Beyond that, each extra dB of RF gain raises the level of every signal at the mixer by 1 dB, which raises third-order intermodulation products by 3 dB and lowers the input-referred third-order intercept point by 1 dB. The design goal is therefore the minimum gain that achieves the required noise figure, which maximizes the spurious-free dynamic range SFDR = (2/3)·(IIP3 − P_floor). On lower HF bands, where atmospheric noise is far above the receiver floor, the optimum RF gain can be zero and the amplifier is switched out or replaced by an attenuator.", "worked_example": "Mixer with NF = 9 dB (F = 7.9) and input IP3 of +20 dBm. RF amplifier with NF = 3 dB (F = 2.0). With G_1 = 10 dB (×10): F_total = 2.0 + 6.9/10 = 2.69, NF = 4.3 dB. With G_1 = 25 dB (×316): F_total = 2.0 + 6.9/316 = 2.02, NF = 3.05 dB, only 1.25 dB better, but the system IIP3 falls from about +10 dBm to −5 dBm, a 15 dB loss in strong-signal handling. The 10 dB design overcomes the mixer noise adequately and keeps 15 dB more dynamic range.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: RF amplifier gain should be as high as possible because sensitivity is the measure of a good receiver. Correction: gain beyond what is needed to override the mixer's noise buys almost no sensitivity and costs dynamic range directly; the right amount is sufficient, not maximal.", "link": "Decibel Converter", "mnemonic": "Enough RF gain to beat the mixer's noise, and not one dB more.", "edge_cases": "At VHF and UHF, where external noise is low, a high-gain low-noise preamplifier at the antenna is justified and feedline loss ahead of it would otherwise add directly to the noise figure; the same Friis reasoning gives a different numeric answer because the noise environment is different."}

{"core": "The RF amplifier sits ahead of the mixer, and by the Friis cascade formula the first stage's noise figure and gain dominate the whole receiver's noise figure. A low-noise RF stage with modest gain masks the much noisier mixer behind it, which is why its primary job is to set (improve) the receiver noise figure rather than to supply bulk gain.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Image rejection is set by the preselector's filtering relative to the IF and the LO choice, not by varying anything with AGC. AGC changes gain, not the frequency selectivity that decides image response.", "why_tempting": "Both AGC and image rejection are front-end-adjacent topics, and AGC is often applied to the RF stage, so it is easy to conflate 'AGC controls the RF amp' with 'AGC controls what the RF amp rejects'."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "AGC voltage is derived after the IF chain or detector, where the signal is large and easily rectified; the RF amplifier is a recipient of AGC control, not its source.", "why_tempting": "The RF amplifier is a stage whose gain the AGC loop adjusts, so a learner may reverse the direction of the control signal."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Most receiver gain (typically 60 to 100 dB) is delivered in the IF strip where the fixed frequency makes high, stable gain cheap. Piling gain into the RF stage would overload the mixer and wreck dynamic range.", "why_tempting": "It is intuitive that an 'amplifier' exists to amplify, and at Basic level the RF stage is described simply as boosting the weak antenna signal."}], "concept": "Friis' formula for a cascade is F_total = F1 + (F2 − 1)/G1 + (F3 − 1)/(G1·G2) + …, with noise factors and gains as linear ratios. Because every later stage's contribution is divided by the gain ahead of it, the first stage sets the floor: a 1.5 dB-NF LNA with 15 dB gain in front of a 10 dB-NF mixer gives a system NF only slightly above 1.5 dB, whereas the mixer alone would give 10 dB. That is the entire engineering purpose of a receiver RF amplifier. Its gain is deliberately kept modest (10 to 20 dB) because every dB of pre-mixer gain raises the signal level hitting the mixer, which lowers the input intercept point and blocking dynamic range by the same amount. The trade-off is minimum detectable signal versus strong-signal handling, which is why many HF receivers can switch the RF amplifier out entirely and why VHF/UHF receivers, where external noise is low, almost always need one.", "worked_example": "Take an RF amplifier with NF = 2 dB (F1 = 1.58) and gain 12 dB (G1 = 15.8) feeding a mixer with NF = 9 dB (F2 = 7.94). F_total = 1.58 + (7.94 − 1)/15.8 = 1.58 + 0.44 = 2.02, i.e. about 3.0 dB. Without the RF amplifier the receiver NF would be the mixer's 9 dB, so the stage bought 6 dB of sensitivity. Doubling its gain to 24 dB would only trim the NF to about 2.1 dB while costing 12 dB of overload margin at the mixer, which shows why gain is not the point.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the RF amplifier is where the receiver gets its gain. Correction: it is where the receiver gets its noise figure; the gain is kept just high enough to swamp the mixer's noise, and the IF strip does the heavy amplification.", "link": "Decibel Converter", "edge_cases": "On HF below roughly 20 MHz, atmospheric and man-made noise usually exceeds receiver noise by 10 dB or more, so a low NF buys nothing and a good receiver may run with the RF amplifier bypassed to protect dynamic range. The RF amplifier's value is greatest at VHF and above."}

{"core": "FM receivers are specified by the RF input level, in microvolts or dBm, that produces 12 dB SINAD, where SINAD is the ratio of (signal + noise + distortion) to (noise + distortion) at the audio output. A typical figure is around 0.25 μV for 12 dB SINAD, and this test captures the demodulator's threshold behaviour that a bare noise figure does not.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Noise figure describes only the front-end's added noise; it says nothing about how the FM limiter and discriminator convert carrier-to-noise ratio into usable audio, so it is not the usual sensitivity spec for an FM set.", "why_tempting": "Noise figure is the general-purpose sensitivity metric for receivers, and the previous question in this subsection ties NF directly to sensitivity."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Overall gain is unrelated to sensitivity: an infinitely high gain receiver with a poor noise floor still cannot recover a weak signal because it amplifies its own noise along with the signal.", "why_tempting": "Beginners equate 'more gain' with 'hears weaker signals', a confusion that persists from Basic-level thinking."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Bit error rate is the sensitivity metric for digital receivers (data, DMR, P25, GPS). It needs a defined bitstream and modulation scheme and does not apply to analog FM voice.", "why_tempting": "Modern UHF handhelds are often digital, and BER is a legitimate sensitivity measure in those modes."}], "concept": "SINAD = 10·log10[(S + N + D)/(N + D)], measured at the audio output with a standard test tone (1 kHz at 3 kHz deviation for narrowband FM). The RF generator level is reduced until the audio SINAD falls to 12 dB, which corresponds to roughly 25 percent distortion-plus-noise, about the point where speech is still intelligible. The resulting RF level is the sensitivity. This matters for FM because the limiter and discriminator exhibit a threshold effect: above the threshold the audio signal-to-noise improves faster than the RF carrier-to-noise, below it the audio collapses abruptly. Noise figure alone cannot capture that nonlinearity, so a direct output-quality test is used. Other FM metrics in the same family are 20 dB quieting (how much RF is needed to drop the no-signal noise by 20 dB) and, for AM/SSB, the 10 dB (S+N)/N method. The lower the required RF level for 12 dB SINAD, the more sensitive the receiver.", "worked_example": "A receiver spec reads 0.2 μV for 12 dB SINAD. In power terms across 50 Ω: P = V²/R = (0.2×10⁻⁶)²/50 = 8×10⁻¹⁶ W = −121 dBm. For a 12 kHz noise bandwidth, thermal noise is −174 + 10·log10(12000) ≈ −133 dBm, so the receiver achieves 12 dB SINAD about 12 dB above kTB, consistent with a few dB of noise figure plus the FM threshold margin.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: FM sensitivity is given as a noise figure or simply as microvolts with no condition. Correction: the number is only meaningful with its quality criterion attached, and the standard criterion for analog FM is 12 dB SINAD.", "link": "Decibel Converter", "mnemonic": "SINAD: Signal In, Noise And Distortion out. 12 dB is the magic number for FM voice.", "edge_cases": "Wideband versus narrowband FM test conditions differ (deviation and audio bandwidth), so two radios quoted at 12 dB SINAD are only comparable if measured under the same deviation and filter settings."}

{"core": "Dynamic range is the span, expressed in dB, between the weakest signal the receiver can discern (the minimum discernible signal, set by noise) and the strongest signal it can accept before the front end produces audible distortion products. It is the single number that describes how well a receiver copes with simultaneous weak and strong signals.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Design parameter is a generic phrase, not a defined receiver specification; it names nothing measurable.", "why_tempting": "It sounds plausibly technical and the question is phrased as a definition, inviting a vague catch-all."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Stability refers to the receiver holding its tuned frequency and gain constant over time and temperature; it says nothing about the amplitude span it can handle.", "why_tempting": "Stability and dynamic range are both receiver-quality attributes listed in the same subsection, so they blur together."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Noise figure defines only the bottom of the range (how much noise the receiver adds, which sets the MDS); it does not say anything about the strong-signal ceiling.", "why_tempting": "The question mentions the minimum discernible signal, which is directly set by noise figure, so a learner may latch onto half the definition."}], "concept": "Dynamic range (DR) = P_max − MDS in dB. The floor, MDS, is MDS(dBm) = −174 + 10·log10(B) + NF, where B is the noise bandwidth in Hz and NF the noise figure in dB; a 500 Hz CW filter and 8 dB NF give about −139 dBm. The ceiling depends on which impairment you measure: blocking dynamic range uses the level of an off-channel signal that compresses gain by 1 dB, while two-tone third-order IMD dynamic range uses the level of two equal tones whose third-order products just reach the MDS. For third-order IMD the ceiling is tied to the input intercept point by IMD DR = (2/3)·(IIP3 − MDS). Because the floor depends on bandwidth, dynamic range figures must always quote the filter used. In practice a good HF receiver reaches 90 to 110 dB of IMD dynamic range; a poor one can drop to 70 dB, at which point a nearby strong signal generates phantom signals that mask weak ones.", "worked_example": "A receiver has NF = 10 dB in a 2.4 kHz SSB bandwidth: MDS = −174 + 10·log10(2400) + 10 = −174 + 33.8 + 10 = −130 dBm. Its third-order input intercept point is IIP3 = +20 dBm. IMD dynamic range = (2/3)·(20 − (−130)) = (2/3)·150 = 100 dB. Two equal signals at −30 dBm will therefore just produce IMD products at the noise floor; anything stronger makes false signals appear.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a receiver with a very low noise figure automatically has good dynamic range. Correction: NF fixes only the floor; the ceiling is set by front-end linearity, and adding gain to lower NF usually lowers the ceiling by the same amount.", "link": "Decibel Converter", "edge_cases": "Phase noise of the local oscillator imposes another ceiling, reciprocal mixing, that can be lower than the IMD limit at close spacings (2 to 5 kHz); modern specs quote dynamic range at several spacings for this reason."}

{"core": "Noise figure is the amount of noise the receiver adds above the thermal floor; lowering it lowers the minimum discernible signal, which by definition means greater sensitivity. Sensitivity is bounded by noise, not gain, so NF and sensitivity move inversely.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Rejection of unwanted signals is a filtering and linearity property (selectivity, image rejection, IMD performance) and is independent of how much noise the active stages add.", "why_tempting": "Both describe 'hearing the signal you want', so noise and unwanted signals get mentally lumped together as 'interference'."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Selectivity is set by the filter shape factor and bandwidth, which are passive properties untouched by amplifier noise.", "why_tempting": "A quieter receiver subjectively seems cleaner, and learners may credit that to selectivity rather than sensitivity."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Stability is about oscillator drift and freedom from regeneration; a low-noise device does nothing for either.", "why_tempting": "It is one of the standard receiver quality words from this subsection and is easily swapped in without a mechanism in mind."}], "concept": "Noise figure NF = 10·log10(F), where the noise factor F = (S/N)_in / (S/N)_out, the degradation of signal-to-noise ratio through the stage. A perfect amplifier has F = 1 (0 dB). The minimum discernible signal is MDS = −174 dBm/Hz + 10·log10(B) + NF, so each dB shaved off NF lowers the MDS by one dB and the receiver can resolve a signal one dB weaker. Equivalent noise temperature gives the same information: T_e = 290·(F − 1) K, used at microwave where fractional-dB NFs are common. NF is dominated by the first active stage per Friis, so 'lower NF' in practice means a better low-noise amplifier or less loss ahead of it. Note that loss before the first amplifier adds directly to NF: 3 dB of coax loss in front of a 1 dB LNA gives a 4 dB system NF, which is why mast-mounted preamps exist.", "worked_example": "Receiver A has NF = 12 dB, receiver B has NF = 4 dB, both with a 500 Hz CW filter. MDS_A = −174 + 27 + 12 = −135 dBm; MDS_B = −174 + 27 + 4 = −143 dBm. Receiver B can copy a signal 8 dB weaker (about 2.5 times less voltage) than receiver A. At 2 metres with quiet-site external noise around NF-equivalent 2 to 3 dB, that 8 dB is the difference between hearing a weak EME echo or not.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: sensitivity is about gain, so add an amplifier to make the receiver more sensitive. Correction: sensitivity is noise-limited; an amplifier only helps if its own NF is lower than what follows and the gain is enough to mask the next stage's noise.", "link": "Decibel Converter", "edge_cases": "Below about 20 MHz the external band noise usually exceeds the receiver's own noise, so improving NF from 8 dB to 2 dB yields no audible gain in sensitivity; the rule 'lower NF = more sensitive' holds for the receiver in isolation but not always for the system on the air."}

{"core": "In a well-designed receiver the dominant noise is generated in the RF amplifier and the first mixer, because these are the first active stages and every later stage's noise is divided by the gain ahead of it (Friis). The signal is weakest here, so noise added at this point has the largest effect on output signal-to-noise ratio.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "By the time the signal reaches the IF amplifier and detector it has typically been amplified 20 to 40 dB, so the noise those stages add is swamped by the already-amplified front-end noise.", "why_tempting": "The IF strip contains the most gain stages, so it seems like the most noise should come from there."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Detector and audio stages operate on signals of millivolts to volts; their microvolt-level noise contributions are negligible in comparison.", "why_tempting": "Audio hiss is what you hear, so it is natural to blame the audio section for producing it."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "The BFO is a signal source injected at the detector for CW/SSB demodulation; its phase noise can matter in special cases but it is not the origin of receiver noise in a good design.", "why_tempting": "The BFO is an oscillator and oscillators are known noise sources, inviting a guess."}], "concept": "Friis: F_total = F1 + (F2 − 1)/G1 + (F3 − 1)/(G1·G2) + … Every stage after the first contributes its excess noise (F − 1) attenuated by the cumulative gain preceding it. With a front end giving 20 dB (×100) of gain, an IF amplifier with F = 10 (10 dB NF) adds only (10 − 1)/100 = 0.09 to the noise factor, roughly 0.4 dB. The mixer is important because diode-ring and many active mixers have conversion loss or poor NF (6 to 12 dB) and come right after the RF amplifier where the gain budget is still small. Hence receiver designers spend their effort on the LNA and mixer: low-noise devices, optimum source impedance for minimum NF, and minimal loss (filters, relays, attenuators) ahead of them. Everything downstream is designed for linearity and selectivity, not for noise.", "worked_example": "Chain: RF amp NF 3 dB gain 10 dB, mixer NF 8 dB gain −6 dB, IF amp NF 6 dB gain 40 dB, detector/AF NF 20 dB. Linear: F1 = 2.0, G1 = 10; F2 = 6.3, G2 = 0.25; F3 = 4.0, G3 = 10⁴; F4 = 100. F_total = 2.0 + 5.3/10 + 3.0/(10×0.25) + 99/(10×0.25×10⁴) = 2.0 + 0.53 + 1.2 + 0.004 = 3.73 → 5.7 dB. The RF amp and mixer together account for 3.73 − 0.004 of the total; the detector and AF stages are invisible.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: noise accumulates equally from every stage, so the stage with the most gain makes the most noise. Correction: noise added early is amplified by everything after it, so the first two stages set the noise performance and later stages barely register.", "link": "Decibel Converter", "edge_cases": "If the mixer has high conversion loss and the RF amplifier is bypassed (common on HF), the mixer's noise and the loss of the first IF filter dominate instead; the principle is the same, only the identity of 'first active stage' changes."}

{"core": "On HF the antenna delivers atmospheric (lightning), galactic and man-made noise that is typically 10 to 40 dB above the thermal floor, so the receiver's own noise is already buried. Lowering NF further cannot improve the signal-to-noise ratio because external noise, not the receiver, sets the floor.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Succeeding stages are no noisier on HF than elsewhere, and by Friis their noise is divided by the front-end gain anyway; this reverses the real reason.", "why_tempting": "It acknowledges the Friis idea that later stages exist but misapplies it by implying they dominate."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The ionosphere causes fading, multipath and Doppler smear, not broadband noise; it distorts the signal rather than adding noise power.", "why_tempting": "Propagation effects are an HF-specific phenomenon and learners may assume any HF-specific degradation is 'noise'."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Narrow modes help by reducing noise bandwidth but they do not change where the noise comes from; they are a mitigation, not a reason NF is unimportant.", "why_tempting": "SSB and CW are indeed the dominant HF modes and are narrower than FM, so the statement contains a true fact attached to the wrong conclusion."}], "concept": "The system noise temperature is T_sys = T_ant + T_rx, where T_rx = 290·(F − 1). At 7 MHz a typical residential site has T_ant on the order of 10⁵ to 10⁶ K (ITU-R P.372 figures put man-made noise 30 to 40 dB above kT₀B at 40 metres), whereas a receiver with NF = 10 dB has T_rx = 290·(10 − 1) ≈ 2600 K. Reducing NF to 3 dB drops T_rx to 290 K, but T_sys barely moves because T_ant dominates. The practical rule is that the receiver should be no more than a few dB quieter than the band: you can verify this by listening for the noise rising when the antenna is connected. External noise falls roughly with frequency, crossing the receiver's floor somewhere between 30 and 100 MHz depending on site, which is why VHF and especially UHF receivers do care about NF while HF receivers prioritise dynamic range instead. Many HF rigs provide an input attenuator or a bypassable preamp precisely because reducing gain on HF costs no sensitivity but buys overload margin.", "worked_example": "Antenna noise at 14 MHz measured 25 dB above kT₀B. Receiver NF = 8 dB. Convert to temperatures: T_ant = 290 × 10^(2.5) ≈ 91,700 K; T_rx = 290 × (6.3 − 1) ≈ 1540 K. T_sys ≈ 93,200 K. Replace the receiver with NF = 2 dB: T_rx = 290 × (1.58 − 1) ≈ 170 K, T_sys ≈ 91,900 K. The improvement is 10·log10(93,200/91,900) ≈ 0.06 dB, inaudible.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a lower noise figure always means better weak-signal reception. Correction: it only helps when receiver noise is the limiting noise; on HF the antenna noise dominates, so NF improvements are wasted and dynamic range is what matters.", "link": "section 6", "edge_cases": "The rule weakens at 10 m and 6 m, at very quiet rural sites, or with very small or lossy receiving antennas (a short whip or small loop with low efficiency) where antenna-delivered noise can fall near or below the receiver floor and a preamp becomes worthwhile."}

{"core": "Dynamic range is specifically the span of signal amplitudes, from the weakest discernible to the strongest tolerable, that the receiver can handle simultaneously without one signal degrading reception of another. It is the metric about accommodating multiple signals of differing levels.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Noise figure sets only the weak-signal floor and says nothing about tolerance of strong signals present at the same time.", "why_tempting": "It defines the bottom edge of the dynamic range, so it is half the right idea."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "AGC is a control loop that reduces gain as the desired signal gets stronger; it extends the range of a single signal the audio can present but does not stop a strong adjacent signal from generating IMD or blocking in the front end.", "why_tempting": "AGC is the mechanism that visibly manages signal levels, so it looks like the thing that 'accommodates amplitude levels'."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Cross-modulation is one specific failure mode when dynamic range is exceeded (a strong signal's modulation transferring onto a weaker one), not the general term for the range itself; 'cross-modulation index' is not a standard receiver specification.", "why_tempting": "It involves multiple signals and strong-signal effects, which matches the wording of the question."}], "concept": "Dynamic range (dB) = strongest tolerable input − minimum discernible signal. The floor is noise-limited: MDS = −174 + 10·log10(B) + NF dBm. The ceiling is linearity-limited and depends on the test: blocking (1 dB gain compression from an off-channel signal), two-tone third-order IMD (products reaching the MDS), or reciprocal mixing (LO phase noise converting a strong signal into noise on-channel). The reason multiple signals matter is that a real band presents dozens of signals spanning 100 dB; the receiver must amplify a −120 dBm signal linearly while a −20 dBm signal 10 kHz away passes through the same front end. Any nonlinearity in that front end lets the strong signal's amplitude modulate the gain seen by the weak one (cross-modulation), compress the gain (desensitization), or create new frequencies (intermodulation). All three are symptoms of insufficient dynamic range, so the single parameter that captures 'how many amplitude levels can coexist' is dynamic range.", "worked_example": "A receiver with MDS −130 dBm and a blocking level of −20 dBm has a 110 dB blocking dynamic range. During a contest, a neighbour's station delivers −25 dBm to your antenna terminal while you are trying to copy a −125 dBm DX station. The difference is 100 dB, inside the 110 dB range, so copy is possible. If an RF preamp adds 15 dB of gain, the strong signal becomes −10 dBm referred to the mixer, exceeding the ceiling, and the DX station vanishes under desensitization even though the preamp 'improved sensitivity'.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: receiver quality is about sensitivity, so the most sensitive receiver is best. Correction: in a crowded band the limiting spec is the amplitude span the receiver can handle at once, which is dynamic range, and excess sensitivity (gain) often reduces it.", "link": "Decibel Converter"}

{"core": "The tuned circuits that bracket the RF amplifier, selecting a band-limited slice of spectrum before the mixer, are collectively called the preselector. Its job is to pass the wanted band while attenuating the image frequency and strong out-of-band signals ahead of the nonlinear mixer.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A preamplifier is the active gain device alone; the question explicitly asks about the resonant networks before and after it, which are passive selectivity elements.", "why_tempting": "The RF amplifier is in the middle of the section described, and 'preamp' is common amateur shorthand for the whole front end."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Pass-selector is not a term used in receiver design; it is a plausible-sounding coinage built from 'bandpass' and 'selector'.", "why_tempting": "It mixes two correct words (bandpass and select) into a near-miss of the real term."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A preamble is a synchronization sequence at the start of a data packet; it has nothing to do with analog front-end filtering.", "why_tempting": "It shares the 'pre-' prefix and is a familiar word from digital modes and packet radio."}], "concept": "A superheterodyne converts the wanted frequency f_RF to a fixed IF via the mixer, but the mixer equally converts the image at f_RF ± 2·f_IF (on the far side of the LO). The IF filter cannot distinguish the two after conversion, so rejection of the image must happen before the mixer: that is the preselector's main role. It also limits the total power reaching the mixer, improving effective dynamic range, and reduces direct IF breakthrough. A preselector is a bandpass filter made of one or more LC resonators, either tracked with the LO (older ganged-capacitor sets) or switched per band (modern rigs, with half-octave filter banks). Its selectivity is modest because its Q is limited by practical component losses: Q = f₀/BW, so a Q of 50 at 14 MHz gives a 280 kHz bandwidth, fine for rejecting an image 910 kHz away with a 455 kHz IF but useless against an adjacent-channel signal 5 kHz away. That is why final selectivity lives in the IF filter and the preselector only handles coarse, image-level filtering.", "worked_example": "A 20 m receiver tunes 14.200 MHz with a 455 kHz IF and LO above the signal at 14.655 MHz. The image is at 14.655 + 0.455 = 15.110 MHz, 910 kHz away. A two-section preselector with loaded Q = 40 at 14.2 MHz has a 3 dB bandwidth of 355 kHz; 910 kHz is about 2.6 bandwidths off centre, and two cascaded resonators attenuate roughly 20·log10(2·Δf·Q/f₀) ≈ 20·log10(5.1) ≈ 14 dB each, around 28 dB total. Modest, which is why modern designs use a higher IF to push the image further away.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the preselector provides the receiver's channel selectivity. Correction: it provides band-level selectivity for image and overload protection; the narrow adjacent-channel selectivity comes from the IF filter.", "link": "Reactance & Resonance", "mnemonic": "Pre-SELECT-or: it selects the band before the mixer gets a chance to mis-select the image."}

{"core": "FM transmitters boost higher audio frequencies with pre-emphasis (a +6 dB/octave rising response) to lift them above the triangular FM noise spectrum; the receiver must apply the inverse, a de-emphasis network with a −6 dB/octave roll-off, which restores the original proportion by effectively bringing the lows back up relative to the highs.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Pre-emphasis is the transmitter-side network that boosts the highs; applying it again at the receiver would double the tilt and make audio shrill, not restore it.", "why_tempting": "The two networks are mirror images and are always discussed together, so the names are easily swapped, especially since the question mentions lower frequencies being 'attenuated'."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A prescaler is a frequency divider used ahead of a counter or PLL to bring a high frequency into range; it has no role in audio shaping.", "why_tempting": "The 'pre-' prefix and the word 'scaler' suggest proportional scaling, which loosely matches the question wording."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "There is no standard 'heterodyne suppressor' audio network; heterodynes (beat notes) are an RF/IF phenomenon, not an audio frequency-response correction.", "why_tempting": "It sounds like a legitimate receiver circuit and heterodyne is a familiar term from this section."}], "concept": "In FM the demodulated noise power density rises with audio frequency (triangular noise spectrum) because the discriminator output is proportional to frequency deviation, and noise deviation grows linearly with offset from the carrier. To keep signal-to-noise flat across the audio band, the transmitter applies pre-emphasis: a network with a zero at f₁ = 1/(2π·τ) that rises at 6 dB per octave above it, so a 3 kHz tone is transmitted with much more deviation than a 300 Hz tone. The receiver applies de-emphasis, a single-pole RC low-pass with the same time constant, H(f) = 1/(1 + j·2π·f·τ), which rolls the highs back down and with them the high-frequency noise, giving a net SNR gain of several dB on voice. Narrowband amateur FM uses τ = 750 μs (corner about 212 Hz) in the usual implementation, and broadcast FM uses 75 μs (corner 2.1 kHz). The question's phrasing, 'restore proportionally attenuated lower frequencies', describes the same thing from the lows' perspective: relative to the boosted highs, the lows were attenuated, and de-emphasis puts the proportions back.", "worked_example": "De-emphasis with R = 75 kΩ and C = 10 nF gives τ = RC = 750 μs, corner f₁ = 1/(2π × 750×10⁻⁶) = 212 Hz. At 2.12 kHz, ten times the corner, |H| = 1/√(1 + 10²) ≈ 0.0995, a 20 dB cut, exactly cancelling the +20 dB the transmitter's pre-emphasis applied at that frequency. Replace the de-emphasis with a second pre-emphasis by mistake and the 2 kHz region ends up 40 dB above the 200 Hz region: harsh, sibilant audio.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: de-emphasis is a treble cut that degrades audio fidelity. Correction: it is the exact inverse of the transmitter's pre-emphasis, restoring flat response while removing the high-frequency noise that FM detection emphasises.", "link": "section 5", "edge_cases": "Digital modes and packet over FM often bypass de-emphasis (taking audio from the discriminator directly) because the flat 9600-baud data spectrum must not be tilted; and if a transmitter runs 'flat' (no pre-emphasis) into a receiver with de-emphasis, the audio sounds muffled."}

{"core": "A product detector is a mixer used as a demodulator: it multiplies the IF signal by a locally generated carrier (the BFO) so that the difference frequencies land at audio. This reinserts the carrier that SSB suppressed, or beats a CW carrier against the BFO to create an audible tone.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Cross-modulation products are an interference symptom in an overloaded front end; nothing in a receiver is designed to 'detect' them, and the product detector's output is the wanted audio, not a diagnostic.", "why_tempting": "The word 'products' appears in both, inviting a literal reading that a product detector detects 'products'."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Supplying local oscillations is the job of the LO or BFO; the product detector consumes an oscillator signal rather than generating one.", "why_tempting": "The BFO and product detector are always drawn together, so the oscillator's role can be misattributed to the detector."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Amplifying and narrowing the passband is what the IF amplifier and crystal/mechanical filter do before the detector; the product detector is a frequency-translation stage, not a filter.", "why_tempting": "The IF strip is immediately upstream, and 'narrowing' is a strongly receiver-flavoured phrase."}], "concept": "Multiplying two sinusoids gives sum and difference frequencies: cos(ω_IF·t)·cos(ω_BFO·t) = ½[cos((ω_IF − ω_BFO)·t) + cos((ω_IF + ω_BFO)·t)]. With the BFO placed at the IF where the suppressed carrier would have been, each sideband component at f_IF + f_audio is translated to f_audio, exactly recovering the original modulation; the sum term is filtered off. For CW, the BFO is offset from the IF by the desired pitch (typically 600 to 800 Hz), so the carrier becomes a tone at that offset. The detector is 'product' because its output is the product of the two inputs, in contrast to an envelope (diode) detector that follows the peak of the IF waveform and only works when a carrier is present. Implementations include diode-ring mixers, dual-gate MOSFETs, Gilbert-cell ICs (NE602 family) and, in SDR, a digital multiplier with a numerically controlled oscillator. The same block, with the oscillator locked to the incoming carrier, becomes a synchronous AM detector with far better performance than a diode in selective fading.", "worked_example": "An SSB signal at a 9.000 MHz IF carries an upper-sideband voice component at 9.001500 MHz (1.5 kHz above the suppressed carrier). The BFO is set to 9.000000 MHz. Product detector output: difference = 9.001500 − 9.000000 = 1.500 kHz (the recovered audio), sum = 18.0015 MHz (filtered away). If the BFO drifts to 9.000100 MHz, the audio appears at 1.400 kHz and every voice component shifts down 100 Hz together, giving the familiar 'Donald Duck' mistuned-SSB sound.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: any detector can demodulate SSB if the IF filter is narrow enough. Correction: SSB has no carrier, so an envelope detector produces garbled audio; the carrier must be re-inserted by mixing with a BFO, which is what a product detector does.", "link": "section 6", "mnemonic": "Product = multiply. IF times BFO equals audio.", "edge_cases": "A product detector handles AM too if the BFO is tuned exactly to the carrier (synchronous detection); tune it off by a few hertz and you hear a low-frequency flutter, which is why AM receivers that use one need a carrier-locking PLL."}

{"core": "The AGC loop exists specifically to reduce gain on strong signals so later stages stay in their linear region; if it fails or is misadjusted, strong signals drive the IF amplifier and detector into clipping while weak signals, which never needed gain reduction, sound normal. Distortion that appears only on strong signals therefore points at the AGC.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A faulty IF amplifier (wrong bias, bad filter alignment) distorts or attenuates all signals regardless of level, not just strong ones.", "why_tempting": "The IF amplifier is where the clipping physically happens when AGC fails, so a learner may blame the stage that distorts rather than the control that should have prevented it."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "AF amplifier faults depend on the audio drive level, which the volume control and AGC hold roughly constant; a defective AF stage distorts at any RF level once the volume is turned up.", "why_tempting": "Distortion is heard at the audio output, so the audio stage is the intuitive first suspect."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "RF amplifier problems typically show as lost sensitivity, instability or front-end overload with multiple signals; a single strong on-channel signal distorting cleanly is more characteristic of a gain-control failure than an RF stage fault.", "why_tempting": "Strong-signal overload is a well-known RF front-end issue (desensitization, IMD), so 'strong signal' plus 'distortion' seems to point at the RF stage."}], "concept": "The AGC loop samples the signal level (at the IF or the detected audio), compares it with a threshold, and feeds back a control voltage that lowers the gain of the RF and IF stages by tens of dB. Its purpose is level compression: a 100 dB range of inputs becomes perhaps a 10 dB range at the detector. If the AGC is defective (open loop, stuck control line, wrong time constants, or switched off while the RF gain is fully up), the IF stages receive the full dynamic range of the input. Weak signals are handled fine, but a strong one, which the loop should have throttled, swings the last IF stage past its linear range and overdrives the detector, producing clipped, splattery audio. Symptom-based diagnosis in receivers works by asking what the failed block's job was: a fault that only shows up under the condition the block was designed to manage identifies that block. A related but distinct symptom, distortion on all signals, points to a stage that is always in the path at a fixed operating point, such as a mis-biased IF or audio amplifier.", "worked_example": "A receiver sounds clean on a S3 signal but a S9+40 dB signal is badly distorted. Turning the RF gain control down restores clean audio on the strong signal. That manual gain reduction is exactly what AGC should have done automatically, confirming an AGC fault, likely a lost AGC voltage or a hang-time circuit stuck at zero. If instead both the S3 and the S9+40 signals were distorted, the RF gain test would not help and the IF or AF stage would be the suspect.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: distortion on strong signals means the receiver's front end is being overloaded. Correction: front-end overload affects reception of other signals near the strong one; distortion of the strong signal itself, while weak signals stay clean, indicates the gain-control loop is not reducing gain as it should.", "link": "section 6"}

{"core": "AGC is a negative-feedback loop: a larger detected signal produces a larger control voltage that lowers the gain of the RF and IF amplifiers, holding the level at the detector approximately constant. Stronger input therefore means less receiver gain.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Limiting is hard clipping of amplitude, used deliberately in FM receivers ahead of the discriminator; AGC avoids clipping by reducing gain smoothly before the stages saturate.", "why_tempting": "Both limiting and AGC prevent large signals from overdriving later stages, so the two mechanisms get confused."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Increasing gain with increasing signal would be positive feedback and would drive the receiver into saturation on any strong signal; it is the opposite of the loop's design.", "why_tempting": "A learner might reason that AGC 'responds' to signal strength and pick the direction that sounds like a bigger response."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A correctly operating AGC prevents distortion by keeping stages linear; distortion arises when AGC fails, not when it acts.", "why_tempting": "The previous question associates AGC with distortion symptoms, so the association can be misread as cause rather than failure mode."}], "concept": "The AGC detector rectifies the IF (or uses the audio) to produce a DC proportional to signal amplitude. This control voltage is applied to the gain-control inputs of the RF and IF stages: reverse bias on a dual-gate MOSFET's second gate, reduced current in a variable-transconductance IC stage, or a PIN-diode attenuator. Gain falls as control voltage rises, so the loop equation is V_det = G(V_agc)·V_in with G decreasing in V_agc; the loop settles where the detected level matches the AGC threshold. The result is a compressed transfer characteristic: an input change of 60 dB may change the output by only 3 dB above threshold. Below threshold (delayed AGC) the gain stays at maximum so weak signals are not penalised. The loop has an attack time (fast, so the first syllable of a strong signal does not blast), and a decay or hang time (slower, so gain does not pump between syllables). The S-meter typically reads the AGC voltage itself, which is why S-meter readings are a gain-reduction measure.", "worked_example": "A receiver has 90 dB of IF gain available and an AGC threshold of 2 μV at the antenna. A 2 μV signal: AGC inactive, full gain, detector input is 2 μV × 10^(90/20) ≈ 63 mV. A 2 mV signal (60 dB stronger): to keep the detector at about 63 mV the loop must reduce gain by about 60 dB, to 30 dB. The S-meter, reading the control voltage, shows roughly S9+40 dB relative to the threshold point.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: AGC amplifies weak signals more. Correction: AGC does nothing below threshold, where the gain is already at maximum; its only action is to cut gain as signals get stronger.", "link": "section 6", "mnemonic": "AGC = Automatic Gain CUT. Louder in, less gain."}

{"core": "In the superheterodyne signal path the IF amplifier delivers the selected, amplified signal to the detector, which is the stage that recovers the modulation (audio) from the IF carrier. The detector is the boundary between the RF/IF part of the receiver and the audio part.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "The local oscillator feeds the mixer at the front of the chain; it does not receive the IF signal and nothing from the IF is routed to it.", "why_tempting": "The LO is one of the standard superhet blocks and connects to the mixer right where the IF is created, so proximity in a block diagram can mislead."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The RF amplifier is the first stage, before the mixer, operating at the signal frequency; the IF signal is produced after it and flows forward, not back.", "why_tempting": "A learner who has the block order confused may think amplification happens after conversion in an 'RF' stage."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "The audio output stage handles the detected audio at low frequencies; the IF signal (hundreds of kHz to tens of MHz) must first be demodulated before anything at audio exists.", "why_tempting": "Skipping the detector is a natural error if one thinks of the receiver as RF in, audio out, without the demodulation step in between."}], "concept": "The canonical superhet chain is antenna → preselector/RF amplifier → mixer (with LO) → IF filter and IF amplifier → detector → AF amplifier → speaker, with AGC fed back from the detector or IF to the RF and IF stages. The IF amplifier runs at a fixed frequency, which lets its filter be sharp and its gain high and stable; it contributes the bulk of the receiver's gain, typically 60 dB or more. Its output is a large (tens to hundreds of millivolts) replica of the received signal translated to the IF. The detector converts that to baseband: an envelope detector for AM, a product detector with BFO for SSB/CW, a discriminator or PLL for FM. Only after detection does the signal exist at audio frequencies for the AF stage. The order matters when reasoning about faults, noise and overload: the IF-to-detector interface is where AGC is usually sampled, where the signal level is largest before demodulation, and where S-meter drive is taken.", "worked_example": "Trace a 14.250 MHz SSB signal: the LO at 23.250 MHz converts it to a 9.000 MHz IF. The 2.4 kHz crystal filter and IF amplifier raise it from microvolts to about 100 mV at 9 MHz. This 9 MHz signal is applied to the product detector, where a 9 MHz BFO translates it to 300 to 2700 Hz audio. If you probed the IF amplifier output with a scope you would see a 9 MHz waveform, not audio; audio first appears at the detector output.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the IF amplifier output is audio because it is the last amplifier before the volume control. Correction: the IF output is still an RF carrier at the intermediate frequency; the detector must demodulate it before audio exists.", "link": "section 6"}

{"core": "The detector's output is small (millivolts) and cannot drive a loudspeaker or headphones directly; it is fed to the audio-frequency amplifier, which raises it to the watt level needed for the speaker. The AF amplifier is the only stage after the detector in the forward signal path.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Grounding the detector output would discard the recovered audio entirely; only the RF/IF residue is filtered to ground through a bypass capacitor, not the audio.", "why_tempting": "Detector circuits do include an RF bypass capacitor to ground, and the DC component is sometimes used for AGC, so 'to ground' has a surface plausibility."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "A typical diode or product detector produces a few millivolts into a high impedance; a speaker needs volts into 4 to 8 Ω, a power mismatch of many orders of magnitude.", "why_tempting": "Crystal sets drive high-impedance earphones directly from a diode detector, so a learner may generalise that to all receivers."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Feeding audio back into the RF amplifier would serve no purpose and in practice would be ignored by the tuned RF stage, which only passes the signal band; the RF stage receives AGC DC, not audio.", "why_tempting": "AGC voltage derived from the detector does go back to the RF amplifier, so the detector-to-RF connection exists, but it carries a filtered DC control, not the audio."}], "concept": "After demodulation the signal is at baseband (roughly 300 Hz to 3 kHz for communications audio) at a level of perhaps 1 to 100 mV, with a source impedance of kilohms set by the detector load. The AF amplifier chain provides voltage gain (a preamp stage, after the volume control) and then power gain (a class AB or class D output stage) to deliver 0.5 to 3 W into a speaker, 30 to 50 dB of total gain. Between detector and AF amplifier sit the audio filtering (a low-pass to remove residual IF, sometimes a CW audio filter or noise blanker), the volume control, and in SSB/CW rigs often the audio-derived AGC pickoff. Separating detection from power amplification lets the detector operate at a small-signal, low-distortion level while the power stage is optimised for efficiency. In an SDR the 'detector' is a DSP demodulator and the 'AF amplifier' is a DAC and audio power IC, but the architecture is identical: demodulate at low level, then amplify to drive the transducer.", "worked_example": "A product detector delivers 20 mV RMS into the volume pot. The speaker needs 1 W into 8 Ω, i.e. V = √(P·R) = √8 ≈ 2.83 V RMS. Required voltage gain = 2.83/0.020 ≈ 141, about 43 dB. A single op-amp preamp (×10) followed by a power amplifier IC (×14) covers it; neither the detector nor any RF stage could supply that swing into 8 Ω.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the detector is the final stage and its output goes to the speaker. Correction: the detector produces a low-level audio signal that must be amplified by a dedicated AF stage before it can drive a speaker.", "link": "Ohm's Law & Power"}

{"core": "Automatic gain control (AGC) is the circuit that automatically adjusts the receiver's gain in response to signal strength so that the detected output stays roughly constant; it does automatically what the manual RF gain control does by hand.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Automatic load control is not a receiver circuit; the only similar term, automatic level control (ALC), belongs to the transmitter, where it limits drive to the final amplifier.", "why_tempting": "ALC is a real and closely related feedback loop (it controls gain to limit output), and the acronym and purpose look alike."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Automatic frequency control locks the receiver to the incoming signal's frequency to correct drift; it adjusts the LO, not the gain, and does not affect output level.", "why_tempting": "AFC is another 'automatic' receiver loop listed in the same breath as AGC, and in FM sets the two are often adjacent on the panel."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Inverse gain control is not a standard term; it is a distractor built to sound like 'gain is reduced as signal increases'.", "why_tempting": "AGC does act inversely to signal strength, so the word 'inverse' feels like a description of the mechanism."}], "concept": "AGC closes a loop around the RF/IF chain: detector or IF level → rectifier and filter → control voltage → gain-control element in the RF and IF amplifiers. The loop forces the detected level toward a set point, which both keeps the audio volume steady as signals fade and protects the detector and later stages from overload on strong signals. The characteristic is described by the threshold (the input level at which gain reduction starts) and the time constants (attack and decay/hang), and by the loop's compression slope, commonly a few dB of output change per 60 dB of input change above threshold. The manual RF gain control sets the same gain-control line by hand and is often arranged so turning it down raises the AGC threshold, letting the operator deliberately desensitise the receiver in noisy conditions. In AM/CW/SSB receivers the AGC can be IF-derived or audio-derived; FM receivers typically do not need AGC for level because the limiter removes amplitude variation, though some use it to protect the front end.", "worked_example": "An SSB signal fades between 5 μV and 500 μV over a minute (40 dB QSB). Without AGC the speaker output would swing by 40 dB, from a whisper to painful. With an AGC slope of 3 dB per 40 dB above a 2 μV threshold, the output changes by only about 3 dB over the whole fade, perceptible but comfortable. Turning the manual RF gain down 20 dB shifts the threshold to about 20 μV so the 5 μV troughs now drop below threshold and the band noise falls away with them.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: AGC and ALC are the same loop. Correction: AGC lives in the receiver and controls RF/IF gain to keep output constant; ALC lives in the transmitter and reduces drive to prevent the final from being overdriven.", "link": "section 6"}

{"core": "The AGC control voltage is applied to the gain-controlled stages ahead of the detector, the RF and IF amplifiers, so that signal level is reduced before it reaches the detector and later stages. Controlling the audio stage would be too late, since the overload it is meant to prevent happens in the IF and detector.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Reducing AF gain would not prevent the IF amplifier and detector from being overdriven by a strong signal; the distortion would already be present in the audio by the time it was turned down.", "why_tempting": "Volume is perceived at the audio stage, so controlling it there seems the obvious way to keep loudness constant."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Including the AF stage has the same flaw as option A, and omitting the IF leaves out the stage that supplies most of the gain and so has the most gain to give up.", "why_tempting": "It contains the RF amplifier, which is correct, paired with the wrong second stage."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The detector is where the AGC voltage is generated, not where it is applied; feeding it back into the detector and AF stages would form a loop that does nothing to protect the gain stages.", "why_tempting": "The detector is central to the AGC circuit, so its role as source of the control voltage can be confused with being a controlled stage."}], "concept": "AGC must act on the stages whose gain can be reduced without harming the signal-to-noise ratio and whose reduction protects everything downstream. The IF amplifier is the main gain-controlled element: it has the most gain (60 dB or more) and operates at a fixed frequency, so its gain-control characteristic is easy to make smooth and stable. The RF amplifier is controlled too, usually with a delayed or reduced AGC so that it stays at full gain for weak signals (preserving noise figure) and only backs off for very strong ones, protecting the mixer from overload. Applying control to the RF stage last and least is important: cutting gain ahead of the mixer raises the system noise figure per Friis, so a well-designed loop reduces IF gain first and RF gain only when the signal is so strong that noise figure no longer matters. The control itself is a DC voltage from the AGC rectifier and its RC filter, routed to the bias of the controlled devices. Signal flow and control flow therefore run in opposite directions: signal goes RF → IF → detector, AGC goes detector → IF → RF.", "worked_example": "A loop with 90 dB of total controllable gain splits as 70 dB in the IF and 20 dB in the RF amplifier, with the RF amplifier's AGC delayed by 30 dB above the IF threshold. A 30 dB-above-threshold signal: the IF drops 30 dB, the RF amp stays at full gain, the noise figure is unchanged. A 70 dB-above-threshold signal: the IF has given up 60 dB and the RF amp 10 dB, and the mixer sees 10 dB less drive than it would with an unreduced front end, protecting its intercept point. The AF amplifier's gain never changed; its level stayed constant because the stages ahead of it did the work.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: AGC controls the audio amplifier because that is where loudness is set. Correction: AGC controls the RF and IF amplifiers so the signal is tamed before detection; the audio stage simply receives an already-levelled signal.", "link": "section 6", "mnemonic": "AGC goes back where the Gain is: RF and IF, never AF."}

{"core": "AGC voltage can be developed by rectifying the IF signal (IF-derived AGC) or by rectifying the recovered audio after the detector (audio-derived AGC). The two names describe where the loop samples the level, and each has a characteristic response to SSB and CW signals.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "RF-derived AGC is not a practical scheme: the signal at the RF stage is microvolts, far too small to rectify reliably, and sampling before the IF filter would let off-channel signals pump the gain.", "why_tempting": "The RF amplifier is one of the stages AGC controls, so sampling there feels symmetric with the control point."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "This pairs the correct IF-derived option with the impractical RF-derived one; the second real method is audio-derived, not RF-derived.", "why_tempting": "It includes IF-derived, which is correct, and RF and IF are the two stages AGC controls, which is a different fact."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "'Detector derived' and 'audio derived' both describe sampling after demodulation, so the pair does not offer two distinct methods; the actual alternative to audio-derived is IF-derived.", "why_tempting": "The detector does produce the DC used for AGC in AM receivers, so 'detector-derived' is a natural phrase."}], "concept": "IF-derived AGC takes a sample from the last IF stage, amplifies and rectifies it, and filters it to DC. Because the IF carries the full selected signal (carrier plus sidebands for AM, sidebands only for SSB), it works for all modes and can respond quickly, limited only by the AGC filter time constants. Audio-derived AGC rectifies the output of the detector; it is simpler, needs no extra IF amplifier for the AGC path, and in SSB/CW rigs the audio already represents the signal envelope. Its drawbacks are that the response is slower (audio must be present for at least a cycle or two to develop a voltage) and that for SSB the envelope is a function of the speech waveform, so the loop needs a fast attack to avoid a loud first syllable and a hang circuit to avoid pumping between words. In AM receivers the detector's DC component is a direct carrier-level measurement, which blurs the line between the two methods, but in CW/SSB sets the distinction matters: there is no carrier, so the AGC must follow the sideband energy either at IF or at audio. Modern SDRs implement IF-derived AGC digitally on the complex baseband signal's magnitude, which is equivalent to IF-derived with ideal time constants.", "worked_example": "A CW signal keyed at 25 WPM has dot durations of about 48 ms. An audio-derived AGC with a 10 ms attack and 500 ms decay: the first dot of a strong string causes a brief loud 'thump' before gain falls, then the gain holds during the 500 ms decay so inter-element gaps do not let the gain recover and noise surge. An IF-derived AGC with a 1 ms attack removes the thump because gain is reduced before the audio reaches full amplitude.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: AGC is always derived from the detector's DC output as in a simple AM set. Correction: in CW/SSB receivers there is no carrier to provide a DC, so the loop samples either the IF signal amplitude or the recovered audio, giving IF-derived and audio-derived AGC.", "link": "section 6"}

{"core": "An AGC loop's behaviour is defined by its threshold, the input level at which it begins reducing gain, and its decay time, how quickly gain recovers after a strong signal disappears. Together these set how weak signals are treated and how the receiver sounds between syllables or after a strong station stops.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Blanking level belongs to a noise blanker, which gates the IF off during impulse noise; slope is an AGC property but blanking is not.", "why_tempting": "Noise blankers and AGC are both IF-chain level-management circuits with a 'level' adjustment, so the vocabularies mix."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Bandwidth is a filter property that does not define the AGC loop; slope (output change per input change) is a secondary AGC characteristic but on its own does not describe when the loop engages or how it recovers.", "why_tempting": "Slope is genuinely part of AGC behaviour, and bandwidth sounds like it could refer to the loop's response speed."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Clipping level describes a limiter or speech processor, not a gain-control loop; hang time is a real AGC parameter but it is a variant of decay behaviour and is paired here with an irrelevant term.", "why_tempting": "Hang time is a familiar AGC control on many rigs, so this option contains one correct-sounding half."}], "concept": "The AGC loop generates a control voltage proportional to signal level above a reference. The threshold is that reference: below it, the receiver runs at full gain (delayed AGC) so the noise floor and weak signals are not penalised; above it, gain reduction begins. The time behaviour is governed by two RC constants. Attack time (typically 1 to 10 ms) is fixed short so that a sudden strong signal is caught before it overloads. Decay time (or release time) is the operator-visible choice, fast (around 100 to 300 ms) or slow (1 to 3 s). Fast decay lets gain recover quickly between CW elements or during pauses, letting noise come up in the gaps; slow decay holds gain down, giving a quieter but less responsive receiver. Hang AGC is a refinement: gain holds constant for a hang period and then decays rapidly, which avoids both pumping and the prolonged deafness after a strong burst. The loop's slope, how many dB the output changes per dB of input above threshold, follows from the loop gain and matters for S-meter calibration but is not what the operator tunes. Threshold and decay are therefore the two parameters that primarily shape the loop's audible behaviour.", "worked_example": "Threshold set at 3 μV, decay 2 s (slow). A S9+30 signal (about 1.6 mV) stops transmitting. The gain recovers along an exponential with τ ≈ 2 s; a weak 5 μV station calling right after will be buried for roughly 2 to 3 seconds while the gain climbs back 55 dB. Switch to fast decay (τ = 0.2 s) and the weak station is audible within a quarter second but the band noise pumps up and down between the strong station's words. Raise the threshold to 30 μV and the 5 μV station never engages the AGC at all, so it is heard at full gain along with the noise.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: AGC attack time is the main adjustment. Correction: attack is kept fast and fixed; the operator-relevant parameters are the threshold, which decides which signals get levelled, and the decay time, which decides how the receiver recovers.", "link": "section 6"}

{"core": "The stage that multiplies the IF signal with a BFO to translate the sidebands down to audio is the product detector. It is the demodulator for CW and SSB, where no carrier is transmitted and one must be supplied locally.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "The AGC circuit generates a slow DC control voltage from signal level; it does not combine the BFO with the IF and does not produce audio.", "why_tempting": "AGC is often derived from the IF stage, so 'takes a signal from the IF amplifier' matches the first half of the question."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The power supply converts mains or battery to DC rails; it is not in the signal path at all.", "why_tempting": "It is a pure guess option, attractive only if the other names are unfamiliar."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A VFO is the variable oscillator that tunes the receiver (the LO); it feeds the first mixer at the front of the receiver, not the detector, and it does not produce audio.", "why_tempting": "A VFO and a BFO are both oscillators, and the BFO feeds the circuit in question, so oscillator terms get mixed up."}], "concept": "For SSB the transmitter removed the carrier, leaving only one sideband; the received IF signal is thus a set of components at f_IF + f_audio (for USB) with nothing at f_IF itself. An envelope detector cannot recover the audio because the envelope of a pure sideband bears no simple relation to the original modulation. A product detector multiplies the IF by a BFO sinusoid at f_IF: (f_IF + f_a) × f_IF → difference f_a (wanted) and sum 2f_IF + f_a (filtered away). For CW, the BFO is set a few hundred hertz from the IF so the unmodulated carrier appears as an audible tone of that offset. The BFO must be stable to a few hertz because any drift shifts every audio component equally, altering voice pitch. Practical product detectors are balanced mixers, which cancel the BFO and IF feedthrough so that only the product reaches the audio stage. In a direct-conversion receiver the same multiplication is done at the signal frequency with the LO acting as BFO, which is why DC receivers are sometimes described as 'a product detector at RF'.", "worked_example": "IF = 455 kHz. A CW signal at the IF is 455.000 kHz; set the BFO to 455.700 kHz. Product detector difference: 455.700 − 455.000 = 0.700 kHz, a 700 Hz sidetone-pitch note. Sum: 910.7 kHz, removed by the audio low-pass. Move the BFO to 454.300 kHz and the note is again 700 Hz (|455.000 − 454.300|), which is why a CW signal can be heard on either side of zero beat.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the BFO is the detector. Correction: the BFO only supplies the reinserted carrier; the product detector is the mixing stage that combines it with the IF to produce audio.", "link": "section 6"}

{"core": "The image frequency is converted to the IF just as efficiently as the wanted signal, so once both reach the mixer nothing downstream can separate them; image rejection is set entirely by how much the RF amplifier's preselector attenuates the image before the mixer. Its selectivity relative to the image spacing of 2·f_IF decides the image rejection ratio.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "AGC adjusts gain in response to level; it applies equally to the wanted signal and its image and cannot discriminate by frequency.", "why_tempting": "AGC is a front-end-related control, and a strong image producing gain reduction is a plausible-sounding mechanism."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "After mixing, the image and the wanted signal are both at exactly the IF, so the IF filter passes them equally; its narrowness is irrelevant to image rejection.", "why_tempting": "The IF filter is the receiver's main selectivity, so it is natural to credit it with rejecting any unwanted signal."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "The product detector is at the end of the chain and demodulates whatever the IF delivers; by then the image has already been converted and is indistinguishable.", "why_tempting": "It is the only other block with 'detector' in it, and image response is sometimes first noticed as a spurious signal in the audio."}], "concept": "A mixer produces |f_LO ± f_in| outputs. For LO above the signal, f_RF = f_LO − f_IF is wanted, but f_image = f_LO + f_IF = f_RF + 2·f_IF also yields the IF. The image rejection ratio (IRR) is the ratio, in dB, of the receiver's response to the wanted signal versus its response to an equal-level signal at the image, and it equals the preselector's attenuation at f_image relative to f_RF. For a tuned circuit of loaded Q, the attenuation at a frequency offset Δf is approximately 20·log10(2·Q·Δf/f₀) dB per resonator when Δf is well outside the passband, so IRR grows with Q, with the number of resonators, and with 2·f_IF/f_RF. Thus a low IF at a high signal frequency (455 kHz at 28 MHz) gives poor image rejection, while a high first IF (45 to 70 MHz for an HF rig) places the image far above the HF range where a simple low-pass filter kills it. Double-conversion designs use a high first IF for image rejection and a low second IF for cheap sharp selectivity. The engineering lesson: wherever a nonlinear process creates ambiguity, the rejection must occur before that process.", "worked_example": "Receiver tuned to 28.500 MHz, IF 455 kHz, LO at 28.955 MHz. Image = 28.955 + 0.455 = 29.410 MHz, only 910 kHz away (3.2 percent of the tuned frequency). A single preselector resonator with Q = 50: attenuation ≈ 20·log10(2 × 50 × 0.91/28.5) = 20·log10(3.19) ≈ 10 dB. Raise the IF to 9 MHz: image at 46.5 MHz, Δf = 18 MHz, attenuation ≈ 20·log10(2 × 50 × 18/28.5) = 20·log10(63) ≈ 36 dB from the same single resonator.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a sharper IF filter improves image rejection. Correction: the IF filter sees the image at the same frequency as the wanted signal; only front-end selectivity before the mixer, or a higher IF that moves the image further away, improves image rejection.", "link": "Reactance & Resonance", "edge_cases": "Image-reject (quadrature) mixers and SDR I/Q demodulation cancel the image by phase rather than filtering, achieving 30 to 60 dB of rejection without preselection; in those architectures the 'preselector' is effectively the I/Q balance of the mixer and the DSP correction."}

{"core": "Desensitization (blocking) is the loss of sensitivity to a wanted weak signal when a strong signal near the tuned frequency drives the front end toward gain compression, or triggers AGC via the wideband IF, so that the weak signal is amplified less.
