With the far end open, Z_L → ∞, so Z_in → 0 and the source sees a very low impedance, equivalent to a series resonant circuit.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A very high input impedance is the result for an open half-wave line or a shorted quarter-wave line; the quarter-wave section does not repeat the open, it inverts it.", "why_tempting": "An open circuit is high impedance, and it is natural to expect the input to look like the load."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "The line's input impedance is determined entirely by Z₀, electrical length and the load; the generator's output impedance plays no part in what the line presents.", "why_tempting": "Source impedance appears in many matching questions, so it feels like a relevant quantity whenever the source is mentioned."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Only a line terminated in its characteristic impedance presents Z₀ at the input regardless of length; an open termination has an infinite reflection coefficient magnitude, the opposite of a matched load.", "why_tempting": "Students associate every transmission line question with its Z₀ and pick it as a safe default."}], "concept": "From Z_in = Z₀ (Z_L + jZ₀ tan βl)/(Z₀ + jZ_L tan βl), set βl = π/2 so tan βl → ∞ and the expression becomes Z_in = Z₀²/Z_L; let Z_L → ∞ and Z_in → 0. In standing-wave terms the open end forces a current node and a voltage antinode; a quarter wavelength back the pattern has swapped to a current antinode and a voltage node, so a tiny voltage drives a large current, which is a very low impedance. An open quarter-wave stub therefore behaves like a series-resonant trap across whatever it is connected to: it shorts out its design frequency and its odd harmonics, while remaining an open circuit at DC and at even harmonics. Shorter than λ/4 the open stub is capacitive (X = −Z₀ cot βl); longer it is inductive. The quarter-wave open stub is also the reason a coax patch cord with nothing on the far end can wreck a measurement at the right frequency: it is a near short across the port.", "worked_example": "50 Ω coax, velocity factor 0.66, open at the far end, 3.51 m long. Electrical quarter wave: 3.51 m / 0.66 = 5.32 m physical-equivalent in free space, so λ = 21.3 m and f = 300/21.3 ≈ 14.1 MHz. At 14.1 MHz, Z_in = Z₀²/Z_L with Z_L large, say the 100 kΩ of a slightly leaky open: Z_in = 2500/100000 = 0.025 Ω, effectively a short. At 7.05 MHz the same stub is only λ/8: Z_in = −jZ₀ cot(45°) = −j50 Ω, a modest capacitive reactance. The difference between −j50 Ω and 0.025 Ω is the quarter-wave inversion.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: an open-ended cable is harmless because nothing is connected to it. Correction: at the frequency where it is an electrical quarter wavelength, an open cable looks like a short circuit at its input, so a forgotten tee with an open stub can kill a signal entirely.", "link": "SWR & Impedance Match", "mnemonic": "Open at the far end, quarter wave back: a short.", "edge_cases": "The stub's end effect (fringing capacitance at the open end) makes an open stub electrically slightly longer than its cut length, so open stubs are trimmed a little short of the calculated quarter wave; shorted stubs do not have this correction."}

{"core": "A half-wavelength line reproduces its load impedance at the input: Z_in = Z_L regardless of Z₀, because tan βl = 0 at βl = π. An open far end is therefore seen as an open, a very high impedance, at the source.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A line presents Z₀ only when terminated in Z₀; an open end has a reflection coefficient of +1 and the half-wave section passes that mismatch straight through to the input.", "why_tempting": "The characteristic impedance is the first number associated with any line, so it gets chosen whenever the question mentions impedance."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The input impedance of a passive line depends only on its own Z₀, its electrical length and the load; the source's output impedance does not enter the equation.", "why_tempting": "Source impedance is part of the broader matching discussion and sounds relevant whenever the source is named."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A very low impedance is what an open quarter-wave line or a shorted half-wave line shows; a half wave repeats rather than inverts, so the open stays an open.", "why_tempting": "Students who have just learned that a quarter-wave line inverts the load may over-apply the inversion to every length."}], "concept": "The lossless line equation Z_in = Z₀ (Z_L + jZ₀ tan βl)/(Z₀ + jZ_L tan βl) has tan βl = 0 whenever βl is a multiple of π, i.e. whenever the line is a whole number of half wavelengths. Then Z_in = Z_L exactly: the half-wave line is a one-to-one impedance repeater, and this is independent of its characteristic impedance. In standing-wave terms the voltage and current patterns repeat every half wavelength, so a voltage antinode at the open end is again a voltage antinode at the input. The practical consequences are large: a half-wave (or multiple) feedline lets you measure the antenna's feedpoint impedance from the shack end, and a half-wave open stub is a parallel-resonant trap at its design frequency, just like a shorted quarter-wave stub. On a Smith Chart a half wavelength is a full rotation back to the same point.", "worked_example": "Thought experiment at 14.1 MHz with 75 Ω coax of velocity factor 0.66: a half wave is 0.66·(300/14.1)/2 ≈ 7.02 m. Terminate it in 100 + j30 Ω and the shack end reads 100 + j30 Ω even though the line is 75 Ω. Leave it open and the shack end reads an open (a few kΩ in practice because of line loss). Cut it to 3.51 m (a quarter wave) and the open end instead reads 75²/∞ ≈ 0 Ω. Same cable, same termination, opposite result, because the electrical length changed from half to quarter wavelength.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a transmission line always transforms the load, so you can never trust the impedance at the shack end. Correction: at exact multiples of a half wavelength the line transforms nothing; what you see at the input is the load itself, which is why half-wave lines are used as measuring and repeating sections.", "link": "SWR & Impedance Match", "mnemonic": "Half wave, same wave: the load repeats.", "edge_cases": "The repetition is exact only at one frequency and its harmonics; a line that is λ/2 on 20 m is λ/4 on 40 m and inverts the load there, so a half-wave feedline for a multiband antenna only behaves as a repeater on bands where it is a multiple of λ/2."}

{"core": "A half-wave line repeats its load at the input because tan βl = 0 when βl = π, giving Z_in = Z_L for any Z₀. A short at the far end is therefore seen as a short, a very low impedance, at the source.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A line shows Z₀ at its input only when it is terminated in Z₀; a short produces total reflection, and the half-wave section delivers that short unchanged to the input.", "why_tempting": "The characteristic impedance is the reflex answer for any question mentioning a transmission line."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "The line is a passive two-port whose input impedance is fixed by Z₀, electrical length and the load; the generator's own output impedance has no influence on what the line presents.", "why_tempting": "Source impedance matters for power transfer and appears throughout the matching material, so it looks relevant."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A very high input impedance results from a shorted quarter-wave line (or an open half-wave line); the half-wave line does not invert, so the short does not become an open.", "why_tempting": "Having just learned that a shorted quarter-wave stub looks open, learners apply the inversion rule to the half-wave case as well."}], "concept": "The lossless line equation Z_in = Z₀ (Z_L + jZ₀ tan βl)/(Z₀ + jZ_L tan βl) collapses to Z_in = Z_L whenever βl is a multiple of π, because tan βl = 0. The line's own impedance drops out entirely. Physically the standing wave repeats every half wavelength: the short forces a voltage node and current antinode at the far end, and a half wave back the pattern is again a voltage node and current antinode, i.e. a short. A shorted half-wave stub therefore acts as a series-resonant short across its attachment point at the design frequency and at every harmonic, which makes it a good broadband-ish notch at a repeater site but a poor choice where you want to pass the even harmonics. The quarter-wave and half-wave cases together form the whole rule set: quarter-wave inverts, half-wave repeats, and every other length is reactive, which the Smith Chart shows as half a turn versus a full turn around the centre.", "worked_example": "50 Ω coax with velocity factor 0.66 at 7.1 MHz: free-space half wave = 300/7.1/2 ≈ 21.1 m, physical length 0.66·21.1 ≈ 13.9 m. Short the far end. Z_in = 50 (0 + j50 tan π)/(50 + 0) = 0 Ω in theory; with 0.3 dB of matched line loss the measured input is a few ohms, still effectively a short. Now trim the line to 6.97 m, a quarter wave: Z_in = 50²/0 → ∞, and a real stub reads several kilohms. The termination never changed; halving the length turned a short into an open.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: once a line is long enough, its termination stops mattering and the input impedance settles toward Z₀. Correction: on a low-loss line the termination matters at every length; a shorted line reads a short at every multiple of a half wavelength no matter how many wavelengths long it is, and only loss slowly pulls the input toward Z₀.", "link": "SWR & Impedance Match", "mnemonic": "Half wave repeats, quarter wave inverts: short stays short at λ/2.", "edge_cases": "On lossy line or at UHF, a long shorted line's input impedance does creep toward Z₀ because the reflected wave is attenuated on its round trip; the ideal repeat assumes loss is negligible over the line length."}

{"core": "Velocity factor is defined as the ratio of the speed at which a signal propagates along the line to the speed of light in a vacuum, VF = v/c. It is a dimensionless number less than one because the dielectric between the conductors slows the wave.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Multiplying a velocity by c would give units of m²/s² and a value on the order of 10¹⁶, not a dimensionless factor between 0 and 1; the definition is a ratio (division), not a product.", "why_tempting": "The option contains the right two quantities and only swaps the operation, which is easy to misread under exam pressure."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Shielding effectiveness of coax (how well the braid confines fields) is measured in decibels of leakage and is unrelated to propagation speed; a solid-copper-jacket hardline and a loose-braid cable can share the same velocity factor.", "why_tempting": "Both shielding and velocity factor are cable specifications listed on the same data sheet."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The ratio of characteristic impedance to load impedance is related to SWR (SWR = Z_L/Z₀ or its inverse for resistive loads), which describes mismatch, not how fast the wave travels.", "why_tempting": "It is a legitimate ratio that appears in the same chapter, and ratio is the keyword the question hints at."}], "concept": "In a line whose conductors are separated by a dielectric of relative permittivity ε_r, the electromagnetic wave travels at v = c/√ε_r, so VF = 1/√ε_r. This is the same physics as refractive index in optics, n = √ε_r at RF. The velocity factor matters because the wavelength on the line is shortened by the same factor, λ_line = VF·λ_free, so every length that is specified electrically (a quarter-wave stub, a half-wave repeater section, a phasing line) must be cut to VF times the free-space length. It also sets the propagation delay, t = l/(VF·c), which is how time-domain reflectometers locate faults. Solid polyethylene gives VF ≈ 0.66, foam polyethylene 0.78 to 0.85, PTFE about 0.70, and open-wire or ladder line, which is mostly air, 0.90 to 0.98. Characteristic impedance, by contrast, depends on both ε_r and the conductor geometry, which is why two 50 Ω cables can have different velocity factors.", "worked_example": "RG-213 (solid polyethylene, ε_r ≈ 2.3): VF = 1/√2.3 ≈ 0.66, so v ≈ 0.66 × 3.0×10⁸ ≈ 2.0×10⁸ m/s. A 30 m run therefore delays a signal by 30/(2.0×10⁸) = 150 ns, versus 100 ns in free space. On 14.1 MHz the free-space wavelength is 21.3 m but inside the cable it is 0.66 × 21.3 ≈ 14.0 m, so a quarter-wave stub must be cut to about 3.5 m rather than 5.3 m.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a signal travels at the speed of light in any cable, so electrical and physical length are the same thing. Correction: the dielectric slows the wave to VF·c; electrical length (in wavelengths) is physical length divided by VF·λ, and ignoring this makes every stub and phasing line too long.", "link": "Wavelength ↔ Frequency", "mnemonic": "VF = v over c: the velocity factor is how much of lightspeed the cable keeps.", "edge_cases": "Velocity factor is nearly frequency-independent for good dielectrics at HF through UHF, but foam cables can vary a few percent between production lots, so stubs cut from a data-sheet value should be checked with an analyzer."}

{"core": "The quantity v_line/c, the fraction of lightspeed at which a signal actually travels in a line, is by definition the velocity factor. It is a property of the line's dielectric and is independent of the load or the signal.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Surge impedance is another name for characteristic impedance, the ratio of voltage to current for a travelling wave; it has units of ohms and does not describe speed.", "why_tempting": "Surge sounds dynamic, like something to do with wave motion, and the term is less familiar so it reads as a possible technical synonym."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Standing wave ratio is the ratio of maximum to minimum voltage along a mismatched line, a measure of how well the load matches Z₀; it says nothing about propagation velocity.", "why_tempting": "SWR is a ratio and it is the most-discussed line parameter, so it is a reflexive choice when the question says ratio."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Characteristic impedance is √(L/C) per unit length, the impedance a travelling wave sees; it depends on the dielectric too but describes voltage-to-current, not speed-to-lightspeed.", "why_tempting": "Both Z₀ and velocity factor depend on the dielectric constant, so they are often listed together and can be confused."}], "concept": "A transmission line can be modelled as distributed series inductance L and shunt capacitance C per unit length. Two quantities fall out: the characteristic impedance Z₀ = √(L/C), and the phase velocity v = 1/√(LC). For a line whose fields are entirely in a dielectric of relative permittivity ε_r, the capacitance per unit length scales by ε_r while the inductance does not, so v = c/√ε_r and VF = 1/√ε_r. Velocity factor and Z₀ are therefore siblings that share a parent (the dielectric) but describe different things: Z₀ is about the ratio of V to I in the wave, VF about how fast the wave moves. SWR is a third, unrelated quantity, set by the load. Keeping these three straight is the core of the subsection: VF converts between physical and electrical length, Z₀ determines matching, SWR measures the result.", "worked_example": "Thought experiment with three cables all carrying a 28 MHz signal: RG-8X (foam, VF 0.80), RG-213 (solid PE, VF 0.66), and 450 Ω window line (VF 0.91). Free-space wavelength is 10.7 m. On the three lines a wavelength occupies 8.6 m, 7.1 m and 9.7 m respectively. Terminate all three in a perfect match and the SWR is 1:1 on each, regardless of VF; change the load to 100 Ω and the SWR is 2:1 on the 50 Ω cables but 4.5:1 on the window line, again regardless of VF. Velocity factor changed the wavelength and the delay, nothing else.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: all the named transmission-line ratios are versions of the same idea. Correction: SWR is about mismatch (load vs Z₀), Z₀ is about the wave's V/I ratio, and velocity factor is about speed relative to light; only the last answers how fast a signal travels.", "link": "Wavelength ↔ Frequency", "mnemonic": "Velocity factor: velocity, as a factor of c.", "edge_cases": "Surge impedance is sometimes used specifically for the impedance a line presents to a fast transient (a lightning surge) before any reflections return; it is numerically the same Z₀ but the name hints at the time-domain picture."}

{"core": "Solid polyethylene has a relative permittivity of about 2.3, and VF = 1/√ε_r = 1/√2.3 ≈ 0.66. That is the familiar figure for RG-58, RG-8, RG-213 and similar solid-dielectric coax.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A VF of 0.1 would require ε_r = 100, far beyond any plastic; it would also make a 20 m quarter-wave stub only 0.5 m long and make cable loss enormous. No practical RF cable is anywhere near this slow.", "why_tempting": "It is a small round number, and a learner who remembers only that VF is less than one might grab the smallest option."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A velocity factor greater than 1 would mean the signal outruns light in a vacuum, which is physically impossible for a signal in a dielectric; VF is always between 0 and 1.", "why_tempting": "2.7 is close to a plausible dielectric constant (ε_r of polyethylene is about 2.3), so a learner may confuse ε_r with the VF derived from it."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A VF of 0.33 would need ε_r ≈ 9, roughly that of alumina ceramic, not polyethylene; no common flexible coax is this slow.", "why_tempting": "It is exactly half of 0.66, and the quarter-wave stub formula involves dividing by 4 and by VF, so factors of two get scrambled in memory."}], "concept": "The velocity factor follows directly from the dielectric: VF = 1/√ε_r, because the wave's phase velocity is v = 1/√(LC) and the capacitance per unit length scales with ε_r while the inductance does not. Polyethylene's ε_r ≈ 2.26 gives VF ≈ 0.665, which rounds to the 0.66 used in every stub and phasing calculation. Foam polyethylene mixes air into the dielectric, lowering the effective ε_r to about 1.5 to 1.7 and raising VF to 0.78 to 0.85; PTFE (ε_r ≈ 2.1) gives about 0.69; air-spaced hardline approaches 0.9 or better; and window line is 0.91 to 0.95 depending on how much plastic remains between the wires. Knowing the family values lets you sanity-check a data sheet and spot a mislabelled cable: if an analyzer measures a quarter-wave resonance at a length implying VF = 0.80 on cable sold as RG-213, it is foam, not solid.", "worked_example": "Cut a quarter-wave stub for 7.15 MHz from RG-213. Free-space wavelength: λ = 300/7.15 ≈ 42.0 m, quarter wave 10.5 m. Physical length = 0.66 × 10.5 ≈ 6.93 m. If you mistakenly used foam RG-8X at VF 0.80 with the same cut length, its electrical length would be 6.93/(0.80 × 42.0) = 0.206 λ, about 17° short of a quarter wave, and the stub would be inductive rather than a clean open or short.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: coax is coax, and the standard velocity factor is 0.66 for all of it. Correction: 0.66 is specific to solid polyethylene; foam and air dielectrics are noticeably faster, so always check the dielectric type (or measure) before cutting electrical lengths.", "link": "Wavelength ↔ Frequency", "mnemonic": "Solid poly, two-thirds of light.", "edge_cases": "Some data sheets quote 0.659 or 0.67 for solid PE depending on the exact resin and the measurement frequency; the 1 percent spread rarely matters for a stub at HF but can shift a VHF phasing line by a few degrees."}

{"core": "The wave's speed on a line is v = c/√ε_r, set by the relative permittivity of the insulating material between the conductors. The dielectric therefore determines the velocity factor; conductor resistivity, load and length do not change it.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Conductor resistivity affects attenuation (loss) through skin-effect resistance, but the phase velocity of a low-loss line is 1/√(LC), and neither L nor C per unit length depends on resistivity in any significant way.", "why_tempting": "Copper versus copper-clad steel is a real cable difference that affects performance, so it feels like it should affect everything about the cable."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "The terminating impedance sets the reflection coefficient and SWR, not how fast the wave propagates; velocity factor is a property of the line itself and is the same whether the load is matched, open or shorted.", "why_tempting": "Students lump all the line parameters together and assume the load influences each of them."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Velocity factor is a per-unit-length property; a 1 m piece and a 100 m piece of the same cable have identical VF. Length affects delay (t = l/v) and electrical length, not the speed.", "why_tempting": "Longer lines do have longer delay, and delay and velocity are easy to conflate."}], "concept": "Model a line as distributed series inductance L and shunt capacitance C per metre. Phase velocity is v = 1/√(LC). The inductance depends only on conductor geometry, but the capacitance is multiplied by the relative permittivity ε_r of whatever fills the space between the conductors. The result is v = c/√ε_r, i.e. VF = 1/√ε_r. Air (ε_r ≈ 1.0) gives VF ≈ 1; solid polyethylene (ε_r ≈ 2.3) gives 0.66; foam dielectric is a mixture of plastic and gas with an effective ε_r of about 1.5, giving 0.8 or more. The same dielectric also affects Z₀ = √(L/C), lowering it by √ε_r for a given geometry, which is why a solid-dielectric cable needs a larger centre conductor than an air-spaced one to hit 50 Ω. Loss, by contrast, comes from conductor resistance and from the dielectric's loss tangent, and SWR comes from the load; each parameter has its own owner.", "worked_example": "Compare two 50 Ω cables with identical outer diameter. Solid PE: ε_r = 2.3, VF = 1/√2.3 = 0.66, v = 1.98×10⁸ m/s. Foam PE: ε_r ≈ 1.56, VF = 1/√1.56 = 0.80, v = 2.40×10⁸ m/s. A 100 m run delays the signal 505 ns in the solid cable but 417 ns in the foam cable. Swap the copper centre conductor for copper-clad steel in either cable: attenuation rises slightly at low HF, delay and VF are unchanged. Terminate either cable in 25 Ω: SWR becomes 2:1, VF unchanged.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the conductors carry the signal, so the conductor material sets the speed. Correction: the energy travels in the electromagnetic field between the conductors, and the field is slowed by the insulating material it passes through; the conductors merely guide it.", "link": "Wavelength ↔ Frequency", "mnemonic": "The signal lives in the gap: the stuff in the gap sets the speed.", "edge_cases": "At frequencies where the dielectric's ε_r itself varies (notably in polar plastics such as PVC at UHF and above), VF drifts with frequency; polyethylene and PTFE are nearly flat, which is one reason they dominate RF cable."}

{"core": "Inside coax the wave travels at only VF·c, so a given number of wavelengths fits into a shorter physical distance than it would in air. A cable that is electrically one wavelength is therefore physically only VF times the free-space wavelength, typically about two thirds.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Surge (characteristic) impedance describes the V/I ratio of a travelling wave and has no bearing on how many wavelengths fit in a metre; parallel line's higher Z₀ is a separate consequence of its geometry.", "why_tempting": "Parallel line does have a higher Z₀ than coax, so the statement is true but irrelevant, which makes it a good distractor."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Skin effect governs conductor loss, not phase velocity; it is present in both coax and parallel line and does nothing to shorten the wavelength.", "why_tempting": "Skin effect is a transmission-line topic covered nearby, and less pronounced sounds like an advantage worth selecting."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Characteristic impedance (another name for surge impedance) is not what sets wavelength on a line; the velocity factor does, and parallel line's higher Z₀ is a geometric fact that does not explain anything about coax length.", "why_tempting": "It repeats the true-but-irrelevant comparison from option B in different words, which doubles the chance a guesser lands on it."}], "concept": "Electrical length is measured in wavelengths at the operating frequency; physical length is measured in metres. They are tied by the wavelength on the line, λ_line = v/f = VF·c/f = VF·λ_free. Because the polyethylene dielectric slows the wave to about 0.66c, λ_line is only 0.66 λ_free, and a cable that is, say, one electrical wavelength long is only 0.66 of a free-space wavelength in physical length. Equivalently, a given physical length of coax is electrically longer (more degrees) than the same length of wire in air: l_electrical(λ) = l_physical/(VF·λ_free). Open-wire line, whose field is mostly in air, has VF near 0.95 and so is physically nearly as long as free space. The statement in the question is really a statement about velocity factor, which in turn is a statement about dielectric constant: VF = 1/√ε_r.", "worked_example": "At 21.2 MHz the free-space wavelength is 300/21.2 ≈ 14.15 m. A half-wave repeater section in air would be 7.08 m. In RG-213 (VF 0.66) it is 0.66 × 7.08 ≈ 4.67 m. In 450 Ω window line (VF 0.91) it is 0.91 × 7.08 ≈ 6.44 m. Conversely, a 10 m length of RG-213 at 21.2 MHz is 10/(0.66 × 14.15) ≈ 1.07 wavelengths, i.e. about 385°, whereas the same 10 m of air-spaced line would be 0.71 wavelengths, about 254°.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a quarter-wave stub is a quarter of the free-space wavelength, the same as a quarter-wave antenna element. Correction: antenna elements sit in air (VF close to 1, with only a small end-effect shortening), but a coax stub carries the wave inside polyethylene, so it must be cut about one third shorter than the free-space quarter wave.", "link": "Wavelength ↔ Frequency", "mnemonic": "Slower wave, shorter wavelength: coax packs more degrees per metre.", "edge_cases": "The effect is purely about propagation inside the cable; the cable's length as a radiating common-mode conductor on the outside of the braid is governed by free-space velocity, which is why choke placement and coax-as-counterpoise calculations use VF ≈ 1."}

{"core": "The phase velocity on a line filled with a dielectric of relative permittivity ε_r is v = c/√ε_r, so the velocity factor is VF = v/c = 1/√ε_r. Taking the reciprocal of the square root of the dielectric constant gives the velocity factor directly.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "VSWR depends on the ratio of load impedance to characteristic impedance, not on the dielectric constant; a perfectly matched line has VSWR 1:1 whatever its dielectric.", "why_tempting": "VSWR is the most-discussed transmission-line quantity and it is a ratio, so it gets attached to any formula involving a ratio."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Characteristic impedance does depend on ε_r, but as Z₀ = (geometry term)/√ε_r, e.g. Z₀ = (138/√ε_r)·log(D/d) for coax; it is not simply 1/√ε_r, and it has units of ohms rather than being dimensionless.", "why_tempting": "Z₀ and VF both scale with 1/√ε_r, so the fragment of the formula looks like it could be either; only the dimensionless result matches VF."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Hermetic refers to an airtight seal and is not an electrical loss mechanism; dielectric loss is governed by the loss tangent, not by √ε_r.", "why_tempting": "It sounds like a technical cable term and loss is a real dielectric property, so a guesser may accept the unfamiliar word."}], "concept": "In a medium with relative permittivity ε_r and relative permeability 1, Maxwell's equations give a wave speed v = 1/√(μ₀ ε₀ ε_r) = c/√ε_r, exactly as a refractive index n = √ε_r slows light in glass. On a transmission line this appears through the distributed constants: capacitance per unit length is multiplied by ε_r, inductance is unchanged, so v = 1/√(LC) drops by √ε_r. Hence VF = 1/√ε_r: polyethylene (2.3) → 0.66, PTFE (2.1) → 0.69, foam (about 1.5) → 0.82, air (1.0) → 1.0. The same √ε_r appears in Z₀, which for coax is Z₀ ≈ (138/√ε_r) log₁₀(D/d), but Z₀ also carries the geometry; VF does not. Where the dielectric fills only part of the field (window line, microstrip) the formula uses an effective ε_r between 1 and the bulk value.", "worked_example": "Polyethylene, ε_r = 2.3: √2.3 = 1.517, VF = 1/1.517 = 0.659 ≈ 0.66. PTFE, ε_r = 2.1: √2.1 = 1.449, VF = 0.69. A foam cable with VF 0.80 must have ε_r = 1/0.80² = 1.56. Now Z₀ for a coax with D/d = 3.3: in air, 138 × log₁₀(3.3) ≈ 138 × 0.519 ≈ 71.6 Ω; filled with polyethylene, 71.6/1.517 ≈ 47 Ω. The √ε_r shows up in both, but only the pure 1/√ε_r number is the velocity factor.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: dielectric constant only matters for capacitors. Correction: the dielectric constant of the insulation sets both the velocity factor and (with geometry) the characteristic impedance of a transmission line, because the line is itself a distributed capacitor and inductor.", "link": "Wavelength ↔ Frequency", "mnemonic": "VF = 1/√ε_r: root the dielectric, flip it.", "edge_cases": "The simple formula assumes a non-magnetic dielectric; a line loaded with ferrite (μ_r > 1) slows the wave by √(ε_r μ_r), which is why ferrite-loaded delay lines are much slower than their ε_r alone suggests."}

{"core": "Velocity factor is the dimensionless ratio v_line/v_free-space, where v_free-space is c. It tells you what fraction of lightspeed a signal travels at inside the line.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "The speed of a signal in free space is c, about 3×10⁸ m/s, a fixed constant; velocity factor is the ratio of the line's speed to that constant, not the constant itself.", "why_tempting": "The option contains free space and speed, two words from the correct definition, and omits only the ratio."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Reflected waves travel at the same velocity as forward waves on the line; there is no separate reflection speed, and the amount of reflection is described by the reflection coefficient and SWR, not by velocity factor.", "why_tempting": "Standing waves and reflections are the other major topic in this subsection, and the sentence sounds like plausible jargon."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "The impedance of the line is its characteristic impedance Z₀ in ohms; velocity factor is dimensionless and describes propagation speed, not impedance.", "why_tempting": "50 and 75 Ω are the two numbers everyone knows about coax, so impedance is the reflex association with any cable property."}], "concept": "A transmission line is a distributed LC structure whose wave speed is v = 1/√(LC) per unit length; filling the space between conductors with a dielectric of relative permittivity ε_r raises C by ε_r and leaves L alone, so v = c/√ε_r. Velocity factor is defined as VF = v/c = 1/√ε_r. It is the single conversion between physical length and electrical length: λ_line = VF·λ_free, and electrical length in degrees = 360°·l/(VF·λ_free). This is why the same formula sheet entry that gives a quarter-wave antenna as 71.3/f (metres, MHz) gives a quarter-wave coax stub as 71.3·VF/f. The reflected wave in a standing-wave pattern propagates at the same v; what differs between forward and reflected waves is amplitude and phase, captured by Γ and SWR, not speed.", "worked_example": "RG-213 at 50.1 MHz: VF = 0.66. Free-space wavelength λ = 300/50.1 = 5.99 m. Wavelength in the cable = 0.66 × 5.99 = 3.95 m. A phasing line that must be 90° long for a two-element phased array is therefore 3.95/4 = 0.99 m of cable, not 1.50 m. Delay through that 0.99 m: t = 0.99/(0.66 × 3×10⁸) = 5.0 ns, which is exactly one quarter of the 20 ns period at 50.1 MHz, confirming the 90° phase shift.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: velocity factor is one of the line's impedance-related ratings, like 50 Ω or SWR. Correction: it has nothing to do with impedance or mismatch; it is purely the propagation speed as a fraction of c, and it is the quantity you need whenever a length must be specified in wavelengths or degrees.", "link": "Wavelength ↔ Frequency", "mnemonic": "VF: velocity fraction of free space.", "edge_cases": "For a mismatched line the standing-wave pattern's nodes are spaced λ_line/2 apart, so VF can be measured directly by sliding a probe along an open line; this is the basis of slotted-line and TDR measurements of unknown cable."}

{"core": "The T match taps the driven element at two symmetric points either side of centre, connecting each feedline conductor to one tap through a short parallel rod. Because impedance along a dipole rises away from the centre, choosing the tap spacing lets a higher-impedance balanced line be matched to the lower centre impedance, and the symmetry keeps the feed balanced.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A stub match uses a short length of transmission line hung off the feeder near the antenna to cancel reactance and transform resistance; it does not connect the feeder to the element at two spaced points.", "why_tempting": "Stub matching is in the same subsection and also involves adjusting a length to achieve a match."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The gamma match is the single-sided half of a T match: braid to the element centre and centre conductor to one tap through a series capacitor; it is unbalanced and uses only one tap.", "why_tempting": "The gamma and T are mechanically similar (rods parallel to the element with sliding shorting bars), so students recall the look and pick the more familiar name."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "The omega match is a gamma match with an added shunt capacitor at the feedpoint so the rod can be shorter; it is still a one-sided unbalanced arrangement, not a symmetric two-tap feed.", "why_tempting": "The omega match is the least familiar name and attracts guesses when the learner knows the answer is one of the Greek-letter matches."}], "concept": "On a half-wave element the current is maximum at the centre and falls toward the ends, so the impedance Z(x) ≈ R_centre / cos²(βx) rises as you move out from centre. The T match exploits this: two short rods run parallel to the element, one on each side, with sliding shorting straps at distance x from centre; the balanced feedline connects to the inner ends of the rods. The rods and the element form a short section of transmission line, and the combination behaves like a shorted stub in series with the tapped-up feedpoint resistance, which adds inductive reactance. Series capacitors (one per rod) cancel that reactance. Adjusting x sets the resistance (further out = higher R), adjusting the capacitors sets reactance to zero. Because the driven element can be a continuous, grounded-at-centre tube, the T match suits Yagis with a boom-grounded driven element and provides DC grounding for static. A gamma match is the T match cut in half for coax; a delta match is the same idea with the rods splayed into a triangle and no capacitors.", "worked_example": "Thought experiment: a Yagi driven element whose centre impedance has been pulled down to about 20 Ω by the parasitic elements, to be fed with 200 Ω balanced line through a 4:1 balun from 50 Ω coax. Start with the T taps close to centre: the feedpoint reads roughly 20 Ω plus a lot of inductive reactance, SWR high. Slide the shorting straps outward in small steps; the resistance climbs through 50, 100, toward 200 Ω because the taps now sit where element current is lower. At each step retune the two series capacitors to null the reactance. When the analyzer shows 200 + j0 Ω at the balun's balanced side (50 Ω on the coax side), the straps and capacitors are locked. Moving the straps inward again would drop the resistance back toward 20 Ω.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the feedpoint impedance of a dipole is a fixed property, so you can only match it with a separate network. Correction: impedance varies along the element, and tapping it off-centre is itself a transformation; the T, gamma and delta matches are all ways of choosing a feed position where the impedance is what the line wants.", "link": "section 7", "mnemonic": "T has two arms, gamma has one: the symmetric two-tap feed is the T.", "edge_cases": "Because the T rods lengthen the effective element and add inductance, the driven element is usually cut slightly short of resonance before the T is applied; the series capacitors then tune it, so a T-matched element does not measure resonant on its own."}

{"core": "A gamma match connects the coax braid to the electrical centre of the driven element and the centre conductor, through a series capacitor, to a tap a fraction of a wavelength out on one side via the gamma rod. One tap only, with the centre grounded, makes it inherently unbalanced and therefore suited to coax feed.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A T match uses two symmetric taps, one on each side of centre, and is a balanced arrangement for balanced line; the question specifies feed at the centre and at only one off-centre point.", "why_tempting": "The T and gamma look alike mechanically and both involve sliding bars on a rod parallel to the element; the T is the more complete-looking version."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "An omega match is a gamma variant with an extra shunt capacitor, used when the gamma rod would otherwise be too long; it is still fed one-sided but the question describes the basic arrangement, and omega is the special case, not the general term.", "why_tempting": "Omega is the obscure option that learners pick when they know the answer is a Greek letter but cannot place which one."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A stub match works on the transmission line near the antenna with a length of line, not by tapping the element itself at an off-centre point.", "why_tempting": "It is the other named matching method in this group, and a gamma rod can be thought of as a kind of stub, which blurs the distinction."}], "concept": "The current on a half-wave element peaks at the centre and falls toward the ends, so the impedance seen between the centre and a point x out along the element rises with x. The gamma match feeds exactly that: the braid goes to the centre (which, being a current maximum and a voltage null, can be bonded to a metal boom without disturbing the antenna) and the centre conductor goes out along a rod parallel to the element to a shorting strap at distance x. The rod and the adjacent element segment form a short-circuited two-wire transmission line, which contributes inductive reactance; a series capacitor in the centre conductor cancels it. Two adjustments, strap position for resistance and capacitor for reactance, let the gamma bring a 15 to 30 Ω Yagi driven element up to 50 Ω resistive. Because only one side of the element is driven asymmetrically, the current distribution is slightly skewed and the pattern can tilt a degree or two; this asymmetry is the price of a direct coax feed with no balun. The T match is the symmetric, balanced twin; the omega adds a shunt capacitor to shorten the rod.", "worked_example": "Thought experiment on a 3-element 20 m Yagi whose driven element shows about 22 Ω at the centre. Install a gamma rod 1 m long, 5 cm from the element, with a 150 pF variable in series. Strap at 40 cm: the analyzer reads about 35 + j60 Ω. Rotate the capacitor to cancel the +j60: now 35 + j0, SWR 1.4. Slide the strap out to 55 cm: resistance rises to about 50 Ω but reactance returns (the longer shorted rod section is more inductive); retune the capacitor and the reading is 50 + j0, SWR 1.0. The strap sets R, the capacitor sets X, and the braid never leaves the centre of the element.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a dipole must always be fed at its centre, so the only way to match it is with a transformer. Correction: feeding at centre plus one off-centre point is a legitimate transformation in itself; the gamma match exploits the rising impedance along the element to step a low centre impedance up to 50 Ω with nothing but a rod and a capacitor.", "link": "section 7", "mnemonic": "Gamma (Γ) has one arm sticking out: one tap, one side, unbalanced.", "edge_cases": "The gamma's series capacitor must handle the full feed current and considerable RF voltage; at high power a trombone-style coaxial capacitor made from the rod itself is used instead of an air variable, and water ingress into that capacitor is the most common gamma failure."}

{"core": "A stub match uses a short piece of transmission line, open or shorted at its far end, connected to the main feedline a calculated distance from the antenna and branching off at right angles. At the attachment point the main line's admittance has the right conductance, and the stub's susceptance cancels the remaining reactive part, leaving a match.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A gamma match attaches a rod and capacitor to the antenna element itself, not a length of transmission line to the feeder; the matching happens at the driven element, not on the line.", "why_tempting": "Gamma is the most familiar name in the subsection, and a gamma rod resembles a short stub running alongside the element."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The omega match is a gamma match with an extra shunt capacitor; like the gamma it works on the element with hardware, not with a section of transmission line hung off the feeder.", "why_tempting": "The unfamiliar Greek-letter name invites guessing when the learner is unsure which named match is which."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A delta match fans the two feedline wires out to two points on the element, forming a triangle; it is an element-tap method with no stub.", "why_tempting": "The delta match does use a section of wire shaped like a transmission line, so it can be confused with a stub."}], "concept": "The single-stub match is the classic transmission-line matching technique, and the Smith Chart in admittance form explains it. Moving along the line from the load toward the generator rotates the normalized admittance y around the chart at constant SWR; at some distance d the point crosses the g = 1 circle, meaning the conductance is exactly 1/Z₀ and only a susceptance jB remains. A shorted stub of length l presents a pure susceptance B_stub = −(1/Z₀) cot βl (an open stub gives +(1/Z₀) tan βl), so a stub of the right length placed in shunt at that point cancels jB, and the line from there back to the transmitter sees y = 1, a perfect match. Two lengths, d and l, are the two unknowns that cancel reactance and set resistance, the same two jobs every matching network does. Shorted stubs are preferred because they are less sensitive to end effects and provide a DC path to ground; the stub must branch perpendicular to the main line so it does not couple to it or to the antenna. The match is narrow-band because both d and l are frequency-dependent.", "worked_example": "Load 100 + j0 Ω on 50 Ω line (SWR 2:1), normalized z = 2, y = 0.5. Rotating toward the generator, the admittance point reaches the g = 1 circle at y = 1 + j0.707 after about 0.152 λ. A shorted stub must supply −j0.707: cot βl = 0.707·1 → βl = 54.7°, so l ≈ 0.152 λ. With solid-PE coax (VF 0.66) at 14.1 MHz (λ_free 21.3 m, λ_line 14.0 m), both d and l come out to about 2.1 m. Attach a 2.1 m shorted stub 2.1 m from the antenna and the input reads 50 + j0 Ω.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a mismatch can only be corrected at the antenna or at the transmitter. Correction: because the line transforms the impedance continuously, there is always a point along it where the resistive part is right; a stub attached there fixes the reactive part, so the match can be made on the line itself.", "link": "SWR & Impedance Match", "mnemonic": "Stub: a short branch off the line that cancels what is left.", "edge_cases": "The single-stub match requires the stub position to be adjustable, which is awkward on installed coax; a double-stub tuner with two fixed-position stubs trades that for a small range of unmatched loads, and quarter-wave shorted stubs are also used purely as harmonic traps or lightning drains rather than for matching."}

{"core": "A free-space quarter wave at 14.1 MHz is 300/(4 × 14.1) ≈ 5.32 m; multiplying by the velocity factor 0.66 gives the physical cable length of 0.66 × 5.32 ≈ 3.51 m (11.5 ft).", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "20 m is nearly a full free-space wavelength at 14.1 MHz (21.3 m); a stub that long would be about 1.4 wavelengths of cable, not a quarter wave.", "why_tempting": "14 MHz is the 20 metre band, so the band name itself is sitting in the question as a decoy."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "2.33 m is the quarter wave with the velocity factor applied twice (5.32 × 0.66 × 0.66 ≈ 2.32 m) or roughly the eighth-wave with VF; it is too short by a factor of 0.66.", "why_tempting": "Applying VF to a figure that already included it, or confusing eighth and quarter wave, both land near this number."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "0.25 m is just the fraction one quarter written as a length; it would be a quarter wave at about 790 MHz in this cable, not at 14.1 MHz.", "why_tempting": "The number 0.25 appears in the phrase quarter wavelength and a rushed reader may copy it as the answer."}], "concept": "Electrical length and physical length differ by the velocity factor: λ_line = VF·λ_free, where λ_free = c/f. For a quarter-wave stub, l = VF·c/(4f). With c = 3×10⁸ m/s and f in MHz, that is l(m) = 75·VF/f(MHz), or in feet l(ft) = 246·VF/f(MHz). The velocity factor enters because the wave inside polyethylene-filled coax travels at only 0.66c, so a quarter of a cable wavelength is only 0.66 of a free-space quarter wave. The same calculation governs half-wave repeater sections (150·VF/f) and phasing lines. For an open quarter-wave stub a further small shortening for end effect is sometimes applied, and in practice the cut is made a little long and trimmed while watching an analyzer for the frequency where the shorted stub shows a high-impedance peak or the open stub shows a null.", "worked_example": "f = 14.1 MHz. λ_free = 300/14.1 = 21.28 m. Quarter wave in free space = 21.28/4 = 5.32 m. Apply VF: 5.32 × 0.66 = 3.51 m. Check with the shortcut: 75 × 0.66/14.1 = 49.5/14.1 = 3.51 m. In feet: 246 × 0.66/14.1 = 162.4/14.1 = 11.5 ft. Cross-check by delay: 3.51 m at 0.66c takes 3.51/(1.98×10⁸) = 17.7 ns, and one period at 14.1 MHz is 70.9 ns, so the stub is 17.7/70.9 = 0.25 of a period, exactly 90°.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a quarter-wave stub is cut to a quarter of the free-space wavelength like an antenna element. Correction: the wave in coax is slowed by the dielectric, so the stub must be shortened by the velocity factor; forgetting VF makes the stub about 50 percent too long.", "link": "Wavelength ↔ Frequency", "mnemonic": "75 × VF over f in MHz gives the quarter-wave coax length in metres.", "edge_cases": "The result depends on VF being accurate: foam coax at 0.80 would make the same stub 4.26 m, so a stub cut to 3.51 m from foam cable would resonate near 17 MHz instead of 14.1 MHz."}

{"core": "Braid bonded to the centre of the driven element, centre conductor going through a series variable capacitor to an adjustable rod tapped onto one side of the element: that is the exact definition of a gamma match, the standard one-sided unbalanced feed for a coax-fed Yagi.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A T match is symmetric, with rods and capacitors on both sides of centre and the two feedline conductors going to the two taps; the question describes only one rod on one side with the braid at centre.", "why_tempting": "The T match is the balanced twin of the gamma and uses the same sliding-bar hardware, so the mechanical description sounds like either."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "There is no zeta match in antenna practice; the name is a fabricated Greek-letter distractor.", "why_tempting": "Gamma, delta and omega are all real match names, so any Greek letter sounds plausible to a learner who has not memorized which ones exist."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Lambda is the symbol for wavelength, not the name of a matching system; no lambda match exists.", "why_tempting": "Lambda appears constantly in antenna work, so it looks like a term the learner has seen before."}], "concept": "A Yagi's parasitic elements lower the driven element's centre impedance well below 50 Ω, often to 15 to 30 Ω, and the element is usually a continuous tube bolted to a grounded boom. The gamma match feeds such an element with coax without a balun. The braid lands on the element centre, a voltage null that can be grounded without effect. The centre conductor runs through a series capacitor to a rod a few centimetres from and parallel to the element, with a sliding shorting strap connecting rod to element some distance out. Between centre and strap the rod and element act as a shorted two-wire line, contributing inductive reactance, while the tap position picks up a higher resistive impedance because current there is lower than at centre, roughly R(x) ≈ R₀/cos²(βx). The capacitor cancels the inductance. Two knobs, strap distance for resistance and capacitor for reactance, yield 50 + j0 Ω. The asymmetry means slightly more current flows on one half of the element, and some common-mode current may flow on the coax, so a choke near the feedpoint is still good practice.", "worked_example": "Thought experiment during tune-up: with the strap close to centre and capacitor mid-range the analyzer shows 25 + j40 Ω. Moving the strap outward raises the resistive part: at a certain point it reads 50 + j55 Ω. The reactance is positive (inductive), so the series capacitor must be reduced (less capacitance means more negative reactance) until the reading is 50 + j0 Ω. If instead the reading had gone to 50 − j20 Ω, the capacitor would need more capacitance. If the strap were moved too far out, R would overshoot to 70 Ω and no capacitor setting could fix it, because the capacitor only adjusts X.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the variable capacitor in a gamma match is what sets the impedance level. Correction: the tap position along the element sets the resistance; the capacitor only cancels the inductive reactance of the rod section, and the two must be adjusted alternately to converge on a match.", "link": "section 7", "mnemonic": "Braid to the middle, rod to one side, capacitor in the hot lead: gamma.", "edge_cases": "At VHF and UHF the gamma capacitor is often a sleeve of PTFE-insulated rod sliding inside a tube, and the rod-to-element spacing becomes critical because the rod section is a significant fraction of a wavelength."}

{"core": "A free-space quarter wave at 15 MHz is 300/(4 × 15) = 5 m; scaled by the velocity factor of 0.8 the physical cable length is 0.8 × 5 = 4 m (13.1 ft).", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "12 m is more than a full cable wavelength at 15 MHz (0.8 × 20 = 16 m per wavelength, so 12 m is 0.75 λ); it is a three-quarter-wave stub, which does invert like a quarter wave but is not what was asked.", "why_tempting": "Confusing the 300/f free-space wavelength formula with a quarter-wave calculation, or multiplying by 0.6 instead of dividing by 4, lands near this figure."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "8 m is a half wavelength of cable (0.8 × 10 m); a half-wave stub repeats its termination instead of inverting it, so it is the wrong electrical length.", "why_tempting": "Dividing the free-space wavelength by 2 instead of 4, or forgetting that the question asks for a quarter wave, produces this number."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "7.5 m is 0.8 × 300/(2 × 15) with an extra 0.75 factor, or 5 m × 1.5; it corresponds to no standard electrical length in this cable (it is 0.47 λ).", "why_tempting": "Applying 0.8 upside down (5 m/0.8 = 6.25) or mixing in a 0.75 factor from a three-quarter wave both produce figures in this neighbourhood."}], "concept": "The physical length of an electrical quarter wave in any line is l = VF·λ_free/4 = VF·c/(4f). In convenient units, l(m) = 75·VF/f(MHz) and l(ft) = 246·VF/f(MHz). The velocity factor enters because the signal travels at VF·c inside the dielectric, so the wavelength inside the cable is shorter than in free space by the same factor. A VF of 0.8 is typical of foam-dielectric coax (effective ε_r ≈ 1.56); solid polyethylene would be 0.66 and would give a shorter stub (3.3 m). The same method with 150·VF/f gives the half-wave length. Being able to run this calculation quickly matters for stub traps, phasing harnesses for stacked antennas, and quarter-wave transformers (Z₀ = √(Z_in·Z_L)) made from odd-impedance cable.", "worked_example": "f = 15 MHz. λ_free = 300/15 = 20 m. Quarter wave in free space = 20/4 = 5 m. Physical length = VF × 5 m = 0.8 × 5 = 4.0 m. Shortcut: 75 × 0.8/15 = 60/15 = 4.0 m. In feet: 246 × 0.8/15 = 196.8/15 = 13.1 ft. Delay check: 4.0 m at 0.8 × 3×10⁸ = 2.4×10⁸ m/s takes 16.7 ns, and the period at 15 MHz is 66.7 ns, so the stub is one quarter period, 90°, as required.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: velocity factor is applied by dividing, because the cable is slower so the stub must be longer. Correction: a slower wave has a shorter wavelength in the cable, so the stub must be shorter; multiply the free-space length by VF, never divide.", "link": "Wavelength ↔ Frequency", "mnemonic": "Quarter-wave coax: 75 times VF, divided by MHz.", "edge_cases": "If the stub is open-ended, the fringing field at the cut end makes it electrically a little longer than its physical length, so builders trim open stubs slightly below the computed 4 m while a shorted stub is cut to the calculated value."}

{"core": "A single rod with a sliding strap (the mechanical adjustment) plus a single series capacitor (the capacitive adjustment), both on one side of the driven element, is the gamma match. One rod and one capacitor is the defining feature; the T match needs two of each.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "An omega match uses the gamma rod plus a second, shunt capacitor at the feedpoint so that the rod can be shorter; it has two capacitive adjustments, not one.", "why_tempting": "The omega is a close relative of the gamma and the learner may not remember that its distinguishing feature is the extra capacitor."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "There is no Y match in standard antenna practice; the closest real device is the delta (triangular) match, which splays the feeder wires to two taps and has no capacitor at all.", "why_tempting": "A fanned-out feed looks like a Y, and the delta match's shape invites a letter-name guess."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A T match has two rods, two straps and two series capacitors arranged symmetrically on both sides of centre, feeding a balanced line; the question specifies a single arrangement.", "why_tempting": "T and gamma matches are built from the same hardware and tuned the same way, so the only distinction is the count of parts, which is easy to overlook."}], "concept": "All of the element-tap matches use the fact that impedance along a half-wave element rises from the centre outward (approximately R₀/cos²(βx)), so a tap at distance x sees a higher resistance than the centre. The gamma match is the minimal unbalanced version: braid to centre, centre conductor through one series capacitor to one rod, strap at distance x. The rod-element pair forms a shorted stub that is inductive, hence the capacitor. The T match doubles everything for a balanced feed. The omega match keeps the single rod but adds a shunt capacitor between the rod's feed end and the element centre; this lets the rod be shorter than a gamma rod would need to be and makes tuning less interactive, at the cost of a second adjustment. The delta match has no capacitor because its splayed wires are chosen so the inductive reactance is small, and it is used mostly on wire antennas with open-wire feed. Recognizing each by part count (gamma: 1 rod, 1 C; omega: 1 rod, 2 C; T: 2 rods, 2 C; delta: 2 wires, 0 C) is the fastest way through this family of questions.", "worked_example": "Thought experiment: you are handed three Yagis to identify. The first has a single rod along the driven element with a cylindrical capacitor in the coax lead: gamma. The second has the same rod but also a small variable capacitor across the feedpoint to the boom: omega. The third has rods on both sides of centre with a ladder-line feed and a balun at the boom: T match. In each case ask how many rods and how many capacitors; the gamma is the one-and-one answer.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the Greek-letter match names are interchangeable labels for the same rod-and-capacitor device. Correction: each name specifies a distinct part count and balance; the gamma is uniquely the one-rod, one-capacitor, unbalanced feed.", "link": "section 7", "mnemonic": "One rod, one cap: gamma. Two of each: T. One rod, two caps: omega.", "edge_cases": "Some commercial Yagis use a hairpin (beta) match instead, which is a shunt inductor across the split feedpoint with the element cut short to supply series capacitance; it has no rod and no capacitor and is not in this question's family but is often confused with it."}

{"core": "In a gamma match the coaxial braid (shield) is bonded to the centre of the driven element, which is a voltage null and is usually also bonded to the boom. The centre conductor goes to the capacitor and rod; the braid provides the ground reference at the element's midpoint.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "The variable capacitor is in series with the centre conductor and the gamma rod, carrying the hot side of the feed; connecting the braid to it would short the capacitor out of the circuit.", "why_tempting": "The capacitor is the most visible component at the feedpoint, so it attracts any connection the learner is unsure about."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "The gamma rod is the hot conductor fed from the centre conductor through the capacitor; it taps the element at the shorting strap, and grounding it to the braid would collapse the match.", "why_tempting": "The rod runs along the element and looks like it could be a ground return, especially since its far end is strapped to the element."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The reflector is a parasitic element that is not connected to the feedline at all; it is excited only by coupling through space, and tying the coax to it would convert it into a second driven element and destroy the pattern.", "why_tempting": "The reflector is usually bonded to the boom too, so a learner reasoning that the braid goes to ground might reach for any grounded element."}], "concept": "The gamma match has four connections in a fixed chain: coax braid → centre of the driven element; coax centre conductor → series variable capacitor; capacitor → gamma rod; gamma rod → shorting strap → tap point on one half of the driven element. The braid's landing point is chosen because at the centre of a half-wave element the current is maximum and the voltage is at a null, so it is the one place that can be bonded to the boom, to the coax shield and to ground without disturbing the antenna. The hot side then taps the element off-centre where the impedance is higher, with the rod-and-element section acting as a shorted stub whose inductance the capacitor cancels. Because the braid is at the element's electrical centre and the rod is on one side only, the arrangement is unbalanced, which is exactly what coax wants, so no balun is needed in principle; in practice a choke is still used to suppress common-mode current induced by the asymmetry.", "worked_example": "Thought experiment: trace a signal leaving the transmitter. On the centre conductor it reaches the feedpoint, passes through the series capacitor (which removes the inductive reactance of what follows), travels out along the gamma rod, crosses the shorting strap into the driven element at distance x from centre, flows through the element and returns to the braid at the element's centre. Measuring with an analyzer at the coax end gives 50 + j0 Ω when x and C are right. If the braid were instead moved to the strap, the braid and centre conductor would both land at the same point and the feed would be shorted.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the coax braid in a gamma match should connect to the end of the gamma rod or the strap, since that is where the element is tapped. Correction: the tap is the hot connection; the braid belongs at the element centre, the voltage null, and the rod is what carries the hot side out to the tap.", "link": "section 7", "mnemonic": "Shield to the centre, hot to the side.", "edge_cases": "On elements that are insulated from the boom (plastic insulators, split elements) the braid still goes to the electrical centre of the element; grounding to the boom is a convenience for lightning and static, not a requirement of the match."}

{"core": "The centre of the driven element in a gamma match is the ground reference: the coaxial braid bonds there (often along with the boom). The centre conductor does not touch the element centre; it goes through the capacitor and rod to an off-centre tap.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "The gamma rod connects to the element only at its far end via the shorting strap, some distance out from centre; its near end goes to the capacitor, not to the element centre.", "why_tempting": "The rod runs parallel to and very close to the element from the centre outward, so it looks as if it should be attached at the centre."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "The variable capacitor sits between the coax centre conductor and the gamma rod; connecting it to the element centre would place it from hot to ground across the feedpoint, which is the omega match's extra shunt capacitor, not the gamma's series element.", "why_tempting": "The omega variant does have a capacitor to the centre, and the two matches are easily confused."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "The centre conductor is the hot side and must feed the off-centre tap through the capacitor and rod; landing it at the element centre would bypass the whole matching arrangement and present the raw low centre impedance to the coax.", "why_tempting": "In a plain centre-fed dipole the centre conductor does go to one half of the element at the centre, so Basic-level feed habits leak in."}], "concept": "At the centre of a half-wave driven element the standing-wave current is maximum and the voltage is at a null, so that point is at ground potential for RF and can be bonded to the braid and the boom without changing the antenna. The gamma match exploits this: the braid lands at the centre, and the whole element, boom and mast are at the same RF ground. The hot centre conductor then reaches out through a series capacitor and a rod to a tap at distance x, where the impedance between tap and centre is higher than the centre impedance. The chain is always braid → element centre; centre conductor → capacitor → rod → strap → element at x. Tracing current, the transmitter's current flows out the rod, into the element at the strap, through the element and back to the braid at centre, with the half of the element on the other side of centre excited by the common current path. The result is an unbalanced, coax-compatible feed with the element continuous and grounded, which is why most commercial HF and VHF Yagis with grounded elements use it.", "worked_example": "Thought experiment: imagine wiring it wrong, with the centre conductor and braid both landed at the element centre as for a split dipole. Because the element is continuous and grounded to the boom, the coax would be shorted across the element centre: the analyzer reads near 0 Ω, and the transmitter sees a dead short. Now move the centre conductor to the capacitor, run it along the rod and strap it 50 cm out: the analyzer reads a finite resistance that rises as the strap moves out, and the capacitor trims the reactance to zero at 50 Ω. The element centre still shows the braid, and only the braid.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the driven element's centre is the feedpoint, so both coax conductors must connect there. Correction: in a gamma-matched grounded element the centre is only the ground connection; the feedpoint is the asymmetric pair of points, centre for the braid and the off-centre tap for the hot conductor.", "link": "section 7", "mnemonic": "Centre of the element is cold: braid only.", "edge_cases": "Some VHF Yagis use a split, insulated driven element with a gamma on one half only; the braid still goes to the centre of the half that carries the rod, and the other half is bonded to the boom, keeping the same electrical arrangement."}

{"core": "The gamma rod's inner end connects to the series variable capacitor, which in turn connects to the coax centre conductor; its outer end is strapped to the driven element at the tap point. The capacitor is in series between the coax and the rod to cancel the rod section's inductive reactance.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "The rod is strapped to the element at the off-centre tap, not at the centre; the centre of the element is where the braid lands, and connecting the hot rod there would short the feed.", "why_tempting": "The rod begins physically beside the element centre and runs outward, so its near end seems to belong at the centre."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The rod does not connect directly to the centre conductor; the series capacitor sits between them, and bypassing it would leave the rod section's inductive reactance uncancelled.", "why_tempting": "The rod is electrically on the hot side, and a learner who forgets the capacitor's position will wire it straight to the coax."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "The reflector is a parasitic element with no feedline connection of any kind; the gamma match hardware is entirely on the driven element.", "why_tempting": "Both elements are mounted on the same boom and both are often grounded to it, so a learner might imagine a connection running between them."}], "concept": "The gamma match chain is coax braid → driven element centre; coax centre conductor → series capacitor → gamma rod → shorting strap → driven element at distance x from centre. The rod, running parallel to the element at a few centimetres spacing and shorted to it at the strap, is a length of two-wire transmission line terminated in a short, so looking into it from the capacitor end it presents an inductive reactance X_L = Z₀_rod·tan(βl), in series with the transformed element resistance R(x). The capacitor supplies −jX_C = −1/(2πfC) to cancel X_L, leaving R(x) ≈ 50 Ω. Adjusting the strap changes both R(x) and l (and so X_L), which is why the capacitor must be retuned after every strap move. The capacitor must be in series with the hot lead to do this; placed anywhere else it cannot subtract reactance from the rod. The rod diameter relative to the element diameter and the spacing also matter: a fatter rod closer to the element has a lower Z₀_rod, less reactance per unit length, and a longer required length, which gives the designer another handle on the geometry.", "worked_example": "A 20 m Yagi gamma: rod spacing gives Z₀_rod ≈ 150 Ω, strap 0.6 m out at 14.2 MHz (λ_free 21.1 m, βl = 360° × 0.6/21.1 ≈ 10.2°). The shorted rod section contributes X_L ≈ 150 × tan(10.2°) ≈ 27 Ω, plus the element's own detuning adds more; suppose the analyzer sees 50 + j60 Ω. The series capacitor must supply −j60 Ω: C = 1/(2π × 14.2×10⁶ × 60) ≈ 187 pF. A 250 pF variable set near 187 pF brings the reading to 50 + j0 Ω. Shortening the strap distance to 0.5 m lowers R toward 42 Ω and reduces X_L, so the capacitor must be increased to re-null.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the capacitor and rod are independent adjustments that each do one job and can be set once. Correction: they interact because the strap position changes both the resistance and the rod's inductive reactance, and the capacitor is wired in series with the rod precisely so it can track that reactance each time the strap moves.", "link": "section 7", "mnemonic": "Coax hot → capacitor → rod → strap → element: four hops out, braid straight to centre.", "edge_cases": "On high-power HF gammas the rod itself often doubles as the capacitor: an insulated inner rod slides inside an outer tube to form a coaxial capacitor, so the rod connects to the capacitor by being one of its plates."}

{"core": "The gamma match's series capacitor sits between the coax centre conductor and the gamma rod. Its job is to cancel the inductive reactance of the shorted rod-and-element section, so it must be in series with the hot lead feeding the rod.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Directors are parasitic elements with no electrical connection to the feed system; nothing from the gamma match reaches them.", "why_tempting": "A learner who has memorized that something connects to an adjustable point on an element may misplace which element that is."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The element centre is the braid's connection; a capacitor from the hot lead to the centre would be a shunt capacitor across the feedpoint, which is the extra component of an omega match, not the single series capacitor of a gamma.", "why_tempting": "The omega match does put a capacitor to the element centre, and the two matches are routinely confused."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "The braid is the ground side; a capacitor from the centre conductor to the braid would simply shunt the feedpoint and could not cancel series inductance in the rod.", "why_tempting": "Many matching networks (L, pi) have a shunt capacitor across the input, so a capacitor to ground is a familiar shape."}], "concept": "In a gamma match the hot path is coax centre conductor → series capacitor → gamma rod → shorting strap → driven element at the tap, and the braid goes to the element centre. The rod and the parallel segment of element form a short-circuited two-wire line, which presents X_L = Z₀_rod·tan(βl) in series with the tapped element resistance R(x). Adding a series capacitor with X_C = X_L makes the net reactance zero: Z_in = R(x) + j(X_L − X_C) = R(x). The capacitor must therefore be in series, directly on the rod; a shunt capacitor would add susceptance in parallel and could not subtract series reactance. {"core": "On a half-wave dipole the ends are open circuits, so current must be zero there while charge piles up, producing the voltage maximum. {"core": "The ends of a dipole are open circuits, so no current can flow there; the current standing wave has nodes at the tips and its single antinode at the centre. {"core": "The centre of a half-wave antenna is the current antinode: the open ends force the current to zero there, and a quarter wavelength in from each end the current reaches its maximum. Feeding at the current maximum has three advantages: the impedance is low and resistive, which matches coax directly; the current is largest where the drive is applied, which makes efficient use of the feed; and the feed is symmetric, so a balanced current distribution is maintained with a balun. Moving the feedpoint toward a tip raises the impedance by roughly 1/cos²(βx), which is the principle behind off-centre-fed dipoles (about 200 Ω at the one-third point) and end-fed half waves (a few kΩ at the tip).", "worked_example": "Thought experiment: 100 W into a resonant dipole. {"core": "On a half-wave dipole the voltage standing wave is V(x) = V₀ sin(βx) measured from the centre, which is zero at the middle and peaks at the tips. The centre is thus a voltage null, which has two practical consequences. First, the feedpoint impedance V/I is minimum there, about 73 Ω, so coax can drive it. Second, the centre of a continuous half-wave element (as in a Yagi driven element with a gamma match) can be bonded directly to a grounded boom with no effect on the antenna, because there is no RF voltage to short out. {"core": "The open ends of a half-wave dipole force the current to zero at the tips, and the current standing wave rises as a cosine toward the middle, where it reaches its single maximum. Written from the centre, I(x) = I₀ cos(βx), V(x) = V₀ sin(βx). The centre is the one point where current is maximum, and because radiation is driven by current, the central portion of the dipole does most of the radiating. This has a chain of consequences: the feedpoint resistance at the centre is the radiation resistance, about 73 Ω; the far-field pattern is determined by the cosine current distribution, giving the familiar figure-eight with 2.15 dBi gain; and current-measuring devices such as RF ammeters or a current-sensing SWR bridge belong at the centre. The field radiated from each metre of wire is proportional to the current in that metre, so the central 3.5 m contributes more to the far field than the outer 7 m combined. {"core": "A half-wave dipole is normally fed at its centre because that is the current maximum: the current standing wave peaks there and the voltage is at a null, giving the lowest and purely resistive feedpoint impedance, about 73 Ω, which coax can drive directly.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Maximum voltage occurs at the open tips; feeding there is end-feeding, which requires a high-ratio transformer because the impedance is several thousand ohms.", "why_tempting": "A transmitter applies voltage, so the feedpoint intuitively seems like the voltage point of the antenna."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Resistance (V/I) is minimum at the centre and maximum at the ends; a maximum-resistance feedpoint would be the tip, which is the hardest place to match to coax.", "why_tempting": "Maximum power transfer theorems and radiation resistance both use the word resistance, and a learner may assume a bigger number is better."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Resonance is a property of the whole antenna's length at a given frequency, not of a point along it; the antenna is resonant everywhere or nowhere, so resonance cannot define a feed location.", "why_tempting": "A resonant dipole is the usual goal, and the option is true in spirit but answers a different question (when to feed, not where)."}], "concept": "The current on a half-wave element is I(x) = I₀ cos(βx), maximum at the centre and zero at the tips; the voltage is V(x) = V₀ sin(βx), the reverse. Feeding at the current maximum therefore gives the low, resistive impedance that 50 or 75 Ω coax can drive with low SWR and no transformer, delivers the drive where the current (and hence the radiation) is greatest, and keeps the two halves symmetric so a simple 1:1 balun maintains balance. Every other feed point trades this simplicity for something: an off-centre feed (about 200 Ω) buys multiband operation with a 4:1 transformer; an end feed (2 to 4 kΩ) buys a single support point with a 49:1 transformer and a counterpoise. Only the centre feed, the current maximum, matches coax without hardware.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: resonant and matched mean the same thing, so a dipole is fed at the centre because it is resonant there. {"core": "The ends of a half-wave dipole are open circuits: current must fall to zero there, and the charge that cannot flow past the end accumulates, producing the voltage maximum. {"core": "The ends of a half-wave dipole are open circuits where current must be zero and voltage is maximum; a quarter wavelength inward at the centre the standing wave has swapped roles, giving the voltage minimum and current maximum at the feedpoint.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A resonant element carries a standing wave, so voltage varies sinusoidally along its length rather than being uniform.
