A quarter wavelength of line transforms an open into a short-like condition, so at the centre (λ/4 from each end) the voltage is minimum and current maximum. The local impedance Z = V/I is therefore lowest at the centre and highest at the ends. This single picture explains why a dipole is current-fed at its centre with low-impedance coax, why end-fed half waves need a 49:1 or similar transformer, and why RF burns and corona happen at antenna tips rather than at the feedpoint.", "worked_example": "Suppose a 40 m dipole with a free-space centre Z of 73 Ω runs 1 kW. Centre: I = √(1000/73) ≈ 3.7 A, V ≈ 270 V. Moving outward, I follows cos(2πx/λ): at x = λ/8 from centre it is 3.7 × 0.707 ≈ 2.6 A and V has risen toward its peak. At the tips current is essentially zero and the voltage, limited only by end capacitance and losses, can reach several kV. The minimum voltage point is unambiguously the centre.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the feedpoint is where the antenna is most electrically active, so it must have the highest voltage. Correction: the feedpoint is the current maximum and voltage minimum; power is delivered there efficiently precisely because the voltage is low and the current is high.", "link": "section 7", "mnemonic": "Voltage Vaults at the ends; Current Collects in the Centre.", "edge_cases": "The voltage minimum at the centre is not zero because the antenna radiates (it has 73 Ω of radiation resistance, not a dead short). On a full-wave element the centre becomes a voltage maximum instead, so the rule is specific to odd multiples of a half wave."}

{"core": "The tips of a dipole are open circuits, and current cannot flow into an open end, so the current standing wave must be zero at both ends. The maximum is a quarter wave inward at the centre.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A centre-fed dipole is symmetric; both ends present the same open-circuit boundary condition. Current is minimum at both ends equally, not at one end only.", "why_tempting": "Thinking of current as flowing from one end toward the other suggests a source end and a sink end, but it is a standing wave, not a one-way flow."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The centre is the current maximum, which is exactly why a dipole is fed there and why the feed impedance is low. It is the voltage minimum, not the current minimum.", "why_tempting": "Confusing the voltage and current distributions, which are mirror images of each other in position."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A resonant element supports a standing wave with sinusoidal variation; uniform current only approximates on a very short loaded antenna or a terminated travelling-wave antenna.", "why_tempting": "At DC or on a short wire the current is the same at every point, so the standing-wave picture is easy to skip."}], "concept": "Current distribution on a half-wave dipole is approximately I(x) = I_max cos(2πx/λ) with x from the centre, falling to zero at x = ±λ/4. The physics is a boundary condition: an open end can store charge but cannot pass current, so charge piles up at the tips (high voltage) while current goes to zero. The reflected wave from each tip adds to the outgoing wave to form the standing-wave envelope. Because radiated power is proportional to the square of current, the centre region does most of the radiating; the last fraction of each end contributes little except to set the resonant length. This is why capacity hats at the ends can shorten an antenna with little loss, and why a loading coil placed near the centre of a shortened vertical is more lossy than one placed where the current is already small in terms of radiation but less efficient overall, a trade-off that is explored in the loaded-antenna material.", "worked_example": "A 20 m dipole is 10.1 m long, so each half is about 5.05 m. With 100 W into 73 Ω, I_max ≈ 1.17 A at the centre. At 2.5 m from the centre (half way to the tip) the current is 1.17 × cos(2π × 2.5/20.3) ≈ 1.17 × 0.71 ≈ 0.83 A. At 4.5 m it is 1.17 × cos(2π × 4.5/20.3) ≈ 1.17 × 0.17 ≈ 0.20 A, and at 5.05 m it reaches zero. Both tips are current minima.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: RF current flows along the whole wire the way DC does, so it should be the same at every point. Correction: the open ends reflect the wave and a standing wave forms; the ends are current nodes and the centre is the antinode.", "link": "section 7", "edge_cases": "The cosine law assumes a thin element. Real wire has end capacitance, so the physical zero-current point lies slightly beyond the wire tip; that end effect is why practical dipoles are cut about 5% shorter than a free-space half wavelength."}

{"core": "Impedance at a point is the local V/I ratio. The centre of a half-wave dipole is the only point where voltage is at its minimum while current is at its maximum, so that is where impedance is lowest, roughly 73 Ω in free space.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Because voltage and current vary sinusoidally and in quadrature along the element, their ratio changes continuously from about 73 Ω at the centre to a few kΩ at the tips. It is nowhere near constant.", "why_tempting": "A transmission line has a single characteristic impedance along its length, and the antenna is wrongly imagined the same way."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Both ends are high-impedance voltage maxima; a symmetric dipole cannot have a special right end. The highest impedance, not the lowest, is found at either tip.", "why_tempting": "Asymmetric answers exploit the idea that current flows from one end to the other."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "The ends are open circuits with near-zero current and maximum voltage, so Z = V/I is maximum there, typically 2 to 5 kΩ. That is the end-fed condition, the opposite of minimum impedance.", "why_tempting": "Confusing the current minimum (which is at the ends) with the impedance minimum."}], "concept": "The impedance seen at any point along a resonant antenna follows Z(x) = V(x)/I(x) where V ∝ sin(2πx/λ) and I ∝ cos(2πx/λ) measured from the centre. At the centre this ratio bottoms out at the radiation resistance plus loss resistance, about 73 Ω for a thin free-space dipole, which is why a centre-fed dipole is a direct match to coax. Moving the feedpoint outward raises the impedance smoothly: feeding about 0.14 λ off centre gives roughly 300 Ω (the Windom principle), and feeding at the very end gives several kΩ, requiring a step-down transformer. The relationship also tells you which feed is current-fed (low Z, centre) and which is voltage-fed (high Z, end), and therefore where to expect high RF voltages and where losses in a matching network will be dominated by current (I²R) versus voltage (dielectric stress).", "worked_example": "Model a dipole running 100 W. At the centre, I ≈ 1.17 A and V ≈ 85 V so Z ≈ 73 Ω. Move 0.125 λ toward one end: current drops by cos(45°) to 0.83 A and the voltage has risen by sin(45°) of its maximum. Taking the end voltage as roughly 2 kV, V there is about 1.4 kV, so Z ≈ 1400/0.83 ≈ 1.7 kΩ. At the tip, current is a few mA and voltage about 2 kV, giving several kΩ. Impedance rises monotonically from the centre, so the minimum is at the centre.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: an antenna has one impedance that you can measure anywhere on it. Correction: the feedpoint impedance depends entirely on where you break the element; the centre of a half-wave dipole is the minimum because that is where current peaks and voltage dips.", "link": "SWR & Impedance Match", "edge_cases": "Ground proximity perturbs the centre value: a dipole at about 0.15 λ high can dip toward 50 Ω, and at 0.25 λ it rises toward 90 Ω before settling near 73 Ω above a wavelength. A folded dipole multiplies the centre impedance by about four."}

{"core": "A circularly polarized wave has an electric field vector whose direction rotates through a full 360° once per RF cycle while its magnitude stays constant. It is the sum of two equal linear components at right angles, 90° apart in phase.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A small or full-wave circular loop radiates linear polarization; the shape of the antenna does not set the polarization of the wave. Circular polarization requires two orthogonal field components in phase quadrature.", "why_tempting": "The word circular is read as describing the antenna instead of the field behaviour."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The electric field at any point is a vector, not a shape; it cannot be bent. Circular polarization describes how that vector rotates over time, with the tip of the vector tracing a circle.", "why_tempting": "Picturing field lines as physical wires that could be curved into a ring."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Propagation around the Earth is a path question (ionospheric or ground-wave), unrelated to polarization. Polarization describes field orientation, not the route the wave takes.", "why_tempting": "Long-path and round-the-world echoes are real phenomena, so the phrase sounds plausible."}], "concept": "Any plane wave can be decomposed into two orthogonal linear components, E_x = E₀ cos(ωt) and E_y = E₀ cos(ωt + φ). With φ = 0 or 180° the resultant is linear at 45°; with φ = ±90° and equal amplitudes the resultant vector has constant magnitude E₀ and its angle advances as ωt, so the tip traces a circle: this is circular polarization, right- or left-handed depending on the sign of φ. Unequal amplitudes or other phase differences give elliptical polarization, the general case. Circular polarization is produced by crossed dipoles fed in quadrature, by axial-mode helices, and by Lindenblad or patch antennas. Its practical value is that a circularly polarized antenna receives a linear signal of any orientation with the same 3 dB loss, which removes the deep cross-polarization fades seen on satellite links where the spacecraft tumbles. Matching the sense of rotation matters: an RHCP antenna receiving LHCP suffers a large loss, in theory total.", "worked_example": "Feed two identical dipoles mounted at right angles with equal currents, the second delayed by 90° (a quarter wave of extra coax). At t = 0 the x-dipole field is maximum and the y-dipole field is zero: the net E points along x. A quarter cycle later x has fallen to zero and y is at maximum: E points along y. Another quarter cycle and E points along −x, then −y, then back to x. The vector swept a full circle in one RF period at constant length, which is the definition of circular polarization.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: polarization is a fixed property set by the antenna shape (a loop gives circular, a straight wire gives linear). Correction: polarization describes the time behaviour of the E-field vector; circular polarization needs two orthogonal components in phase quadrature regardless of what geometry produces them.", "link": "section 7", "mnemonic": "Two fields, ninety apart, equal size, makes the arrow spin.", "edge_cases": "Perfect circularity is a free-space ideal. Real CP antennas have an axial ratio of 1 to 3 dB on boresight that degrades off-axis, and Faraday rotation in the ionosphere, which ruins linear polarization on VHF satellite paths, is exactly what CP is immune to."}

{"core": "Two orthogonal dipoles driven with equal currents 90° apart in phase radiate E-field components in space and time quadrature; their vector sum has constant magnitude and rotates once per cycle, which is circular polarization along the axis perpendicular to both elements.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Orthogonal field components cannot cancel because they are at right angles; cancellation requires collinear fields in antiphase. The two components add as vectors to a rotating field of constant magnitude.", "why_tempting": "A 90° phase shift sounds like it might produce destructive interference, confusing phase quadrature with antiphase (180°)."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Cross-polarization is a mismatch condition between two antennas (for example horizontal versus vertical), not a type of polarization an antenna produces.", "why_tempting": "The antennas are physically crossed, so the term sounds like a literal description."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Perpendicular is a geometric relationship between the elements, not a recognized polarization. Polarization types are linear, circular and elliptical.", "why_tempting": "Again the physical arrangement of the elements is mistaken for the resulting wave property."}], "concept": "The field broadside to a turnstile (crossed dipoles) is E = E₀[x̂ cos(ωt) + ŷ cos(ωt ± 90°)] = E₀[x̂ cos(ωt) ∓ ŷ sin(ωt)]. The magnitude is √(cos² + sin²) × E₀ = E₀ regardless of time, and the angle is ∓ωt, so the field rotates at the carrier frequency. The sign of the phase lead sets right- or left-hand sense; swapping which dipole leads reverses it. Off the main axis the two components no longer appear equal in projection, so the polarization becomes elliptical, and in the plane of the dipoles it degenerates to linear. The 90° shift is usually obtained with a quarter-wave section of coax feeding one dipole, or by making one dipole slightly long and the other slightly short so their reactances produce ±45° current phase shifts (the self-phased turnstile). The same principle in different clothing is the Lindenblad (four tilted dipoles) and the patch antenna fed at two points in quadrature.", "worked_example": "Build a 2 m turnstile: two 1 m dipoles at right angles. Feed dipole A directly and dipole B through an extra 0.25 λ × velocity factor of coax, about 0.34 m of RG-8X (VF 0.66) at 146 MHz. Dipole B's current now lags A's by 90°. Looking down the axis from above, at successive quarter-cycles the net E points along A, then along B, then along −A, then along −B: a rotating vector, hence circular polarization. Swap the delay line to dipole A instead and the rotation reverses from RHCP to LHCP.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: 90° out of phase means partially cancelling, so the result must be weaker or null. Correction: cancellation needs the same axis and 180°; orthogonal fields in quadrature combine into a constant-magnitude rotating field.", "link": "section 7", "edge_cases": "The turnstile is circular only on its axis. In the plane of the elements it is linear, and the sense of rotation flips between the two axial directions (up versus down), which matters when you feed a turnstile over a reflector for satellite work."}

{"core": "A loaded helically-wound antenna (a normal-mode helix such as a rubber duck or a helically wound shortened vertical) is just an electrically short monopole with distributed inductance; it radiates linear polarization along its axis orientation. The other three are classic circular-polarization antennas.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Crossed dipoles in phase quadrature are the textbook turnstile, which produces circular polarization on its axis by vector addition of two orthogonal fields 90° apart.", "why_tempting": "Learners who have not yet connected quadrature feeding with rotating fields may doubt this one."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "The Lindenblad uses four dipoles tilted about 30° and spaced around a circle, fed so that their combined field rotates; it is a well-known omnidirectional circularly polarized satellite antenna.", "why_tempting": "It is the least familiar name on the list, so it is easy to assume it is the odd one out."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "An axial-mode helix with circumference near one wavelength radiates a beam along its axis whose field rotates with the winding sense; it is the canonical CP antenna for satellite and EME work.", "why_tempting": "Both C and D contain the word helical, which is precisely the trap: the two helix modes have nothing in common electrically."}], "concept": "A helix operates in two radically different modes depending on size. When the circumference is near one wavelength (C ≈ λ) and the pitch is around 12° to 14°, a travelling wave runs along the wire and the antenna radiates in axial mode: a beam along the axis, circularly polarized in the sense of the winding, with gain of roughly 10 to 15 dBi for 10 to 20 turns. When the helix is tiny compared with a wavelength (circumference a few percent of λ), it operates in normal mode: the current is essentially in phase along the whole length, the winding is just a way of packing inductance into a short conductor, and it radiates broadside like a short vertical with linear polarization parallel to the axis. The rubber duck on a handheld and the helically wound mobile whip are normal-mode, loaded helices. Their radiation resistance is low and their bandwidth narrow, but their polarization is plainly linear. The question tests whether you can distinguish the mode by electrical size rather than by the word helical.", "worked_example": "At 146 MHz, λ ≈ 2.05 m. An axial-mode helix needs a diameter of about λ/π ≈ 0.65 m per turn; that is a satellite antenna. A rubber duck wound on a 6 mm former has a circumference of about 19 mm, or 0.009 λ, three orders of magnitude smaller. Nothing about such a winding can create a rotating field; it is a lumped inductor stretched along a short radiator, and its polarization follows the axis of the whip: vertical on a handheld held upright.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: anything wound in a spiral radiates circular polarization. Correction: circular polarization from a helix requires the axial mode, with circumference near a wavelength; a small loaded helix is a linearly polarized short monopole with its inductance distributed along the element.", "link": "section 7", "mnemonic": "Big helix, beam and spin; small helix, just a loaded pin.", "edge_cases": "Between the two regimes the helix behaves unpredictably, which is why practical designs sit firmly at C ≈ 0.75 to 1.3 λ (axial) or C < 0.1 λ (normal). An axial helix over a ground reflector also only has good axial ratio within its main lobe."}

{"core": "Doppler shift Δf = f × v_radial/c is proportional to carrier frequency and to the line-of-sight velocity. Only a low-earth-orbit satellite moves fast enough (about 7.5 km/s) for the shift to reach several kilohertz at VHF/UHF, enough to push a signal out of an SSB or narrow FM passband.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A hilltop repeater is fixed, so radial velocity is zero and there is no Doppler shift at all; any error is just the station's own frequency tolerance.", "why_tempting": "Repeaters involve offsets and tones that feel like frequency manipulation, but those are deliberate, not Doppler."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Two walking or stationary operators have radial velocities of a metre or two per second, giving a shift of under 1 Hz at 440 MHz, far below any receiver's channel width.", "why_tempting": "Line-of-sight sounds like a direct-path condition where effects are strongest, but the velocity term is what matters."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A car at 100 km/h (28 m/s) produces only about 14 Hz of shift at 146 MHz and 40 Hz at 440 MHz, negligible against a 12 kHz FM channel.", "why_tempting": "A vehicle is clearly moving, so it seems like the obvious Doppler candidate, but it is two orders of magnitude too slow."}], "concept": "For a source and observer with relative radial velocity v, the received frequency is f_r ≈ f_t (1 + v/c) when closing and f_t (1 − v/c) when receding, so Δf = f × v/c. The shift scales linearly with carrier frequency, which is why it matters far more at UHF than at HF, and linearly with velocity, which is why only orbital speeds are significant. A LEO satellite at about 7.5 km/s has a radial component that swings from positive at acquisition to negative at loss, passing through zero at closest approach, so the received frequency slides steadily downward across a pass. The total swing is about 2 × f × v_radial,max/c. On a linear transponder the downlink shift and uplink shift combine, and for inverting transponders they partly cancel, which is the basis of the 'one-true-rule' Doppler correction used by satellite software. Modern practice is to let a tracking program tune the radio in real time from the Keplerian elements, holding the transponder-centred frequency constant.", "worked_example": "Downlink at 435 MHz, satellite approaching with a radial velocity of 6 km/s near the horizon. Δf = 435 × 10⁶ × 6000 / 3 × 10⁸ ≈ 8.7 kHz above nominal. At closest approach the radial velocity is zero. As it recedes at 6 km/s the shift is 8.7 kHz below nominal, so the whole pass spans about 17 kHz, several SSB bandwidths. On the 145 MHz uplink the same geometry gives only 2.9 kHz each way, which is why many operators let the VHF side ride and track only the UHF side.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: anything moving causes meaningful Doppler shift on VHF/UHF. Correction: at radio frequencies the shift is f × v/c, and only kilometres-per-second relative velocity (orbital speed) makes it comparable to a channel width.", "link": "Wavelength ↔ Frequency", "mnemonic": "Doppler needs speed and frequency: satellites have both.", "edge_cases": "Aircraft scatter at 300 m/s can produce a few hundred hertz of shift at 1296 MHz, audible as a chirp during aeronautical scatter, and EME has a small shift from the Moon's radial motion plus Earth rotation (up to about 300 Hz at 144 MHz). These are nuisances, not pass-shaping effects like LEO Doppler."}

{"core": "The coupling between two linearly polarized antennas is proportional to cos²θ of the angle between their polarization planes. At 90° the ideal loss is infinite; in practice antenna imperfections and ground effects leave a residual coupling, so the realistic figure on a VHF/UHF line-of-sight path is 20 dB or more.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "6 dB corresponds to a quarter of the power, which is what you get at about 60° of misalignment (cos² 60° = 0.25), not at 90°.", "why_tempting": "6 dB is a familiar number from doubling voltage or halving distance, and learners reach for it as a moderate penalty."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "10 dB is one tenth of the power, roughly a 71° misalignment. Fully crossed antennas are much worse than this on a clean line-of-sight path.", "why_tempting": "A round-number intermediate loss feels safe when the true value is remembered as somewhere between 3 dB and infinity."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "3 dB is the polarization loss between a circularly polarized antenna and any linear one, or between two linear antennas at 45°. It is not the cross-polarized case.", "why_tempting": "The 3 dB linear-to-circular rule is in the same syllabus block and is easily confused with the linear-to-linear 90° case."}], "concept": "The polarization loss factor between two linear antennas misaligned by angle θ is PLF = cos²θ, or in decibels 20 log(cos θ) because the E-field projection is cos θ and power is the square of field. At θ = 0 the loss is 0 dB, at 45° it is 3 dB, at 60° it is 6 dB, and at 90° cos θ = 0 so the ideal loss is unbounded. Real antennas are not perfectly pure: a Yagi has some cross-polarized component from its feed and boom, a vertical over real ground develops a horizontal component, and multipath reflections rotate polarization. Those leakage paths typically cap the measured penalty at 20 to 30 dB on a direct path. On an HF skywave path the ionosphere scrambles polarization so the issue largely disappears, which is why the question specifies VHF/UHF over a fixed path. The rule of thumb drives practical decisions: FM mobile and repeater work standardises on vertical, weak-signal SSB/CW on horizontal, and satellite work uses circular to avoid the problem entirely at a fixed 3 dB cost.", "worked_example": "A 50 W station with a horizontal Yagi talks to a vertical collinear 40 km away. With matched polarization the path delivers, say, S9 + 10 dB. Switching the far end to vertical gives θ = 90°: ideal loss infinite, real loss about 20 to 25 dB, dropping the signal to roughly S5 to S6. By comparison a 45° misalignment would only cost 20 log(0.707) = 3 dB, and 60° would cost 20 log(0.5) = 6 dB. The jump from 6 dB at 60° to 20-plus dB at 90° shows how steeply cos²θ falls near the null.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: polarization mismatch is a modest fixed penalty of a few decibels. Correction: the loss follows cos²θ and goes to a deep null at 90°; the only 3 dB rule is for circular-to-linear, not crossed linear antennas.", "link": "Decibel Converter", "mnemonic": "Forty-five is three, sixty is six, ninety is twenty-plus.", "edge_cases": "On HF skywave, Faraday rotation and multiple ionospheric modes randomise polarization, so cross-polarized HF antennas work fine most of the time. On VHF/UHF, terrain reflections and buildings can partly refill the null, sometimes reducing the penalty to 10 to 15 dB in urban multipath."}

{"core": "Newtonian describes an optical telescope that uses a flat diagonal mirror to fold the focus out of the side of the tube; it is not a recognised way of feeding a parabolic antenna. Front (prime) feed, Cassegrain and offset feed are the three standard dish illumination geometries.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Offset feed is a valid and very common arrangement: the dish is a section of a larger paraboloid cut away from the axis, so the feed and its supports sit outside the beam, eliminating aperture blockage. Most consumer satellite TV dishes are offset-fed.", "why_tempting": "The dish looks asymmetric and tilted, which can make it seem like a non-standard or improper configuration."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Cassegrain is a classic two-reflector arrangement: a hyperbolic sub-reflector at the prime focus redirects energy back to a feed at the dish vertex, shortening the feed line and reducing spillover toward the warm ground.", "why_tempting": "It is borrowed from optical telescopes just as Newtonian is, so a learner may assume both are optics-only terms."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Front feed, also called prime-focus feed, places the feed horn or dipole directly at the focal point of the paraboloid. It is the simplest and most common amateur arrangement.", "why_tempting": "It sounds informal next to the named designs, so it may seem invented."}], "concept": "A paraboloid reflects any ray arriving parallel to its axis through a single focal point at distance f from the vertex, where the surface satisfies z = r²/(4f). A dish antenna is illuminated by placing a feed at that focus (prime or front feed) or by relaying the focus elsewhere. Cassegrain uses a convex hyperboloid sub-reflector whose one focus coincides with the paraboloid's focus and whose other focus is at the vertex, where the feed sits; Gregorian does the same with a concave ellipsoid beyond the prime focus. Offset feed uses an off-axis slice of a larger paraboloid so that the feed is outside the aperture and does not shadow it. Each geometry trades aperture blockage, spillover (energy from the feed that misses the dish and sees warm ground, raising noise temperature), feed-line length and mechanical convenience. Aperture efficiency, typically 50 to 65% for amateur dishes, depends on how well the feed's pattern tapers toward the rim (about 10 dB edge taper is a common optimum). A Newtonian telescope's flat secondary mirror would simply block and scatter a radio beam; it has no equivalent in antenna practice.", "worked_example": "Consider a 1.2 m dish with f/D = 0.4, so the focal length is 0.48 m. Front feed: a 10 GHz horn at 0.48 m in front of the vertex, held by three struts that shadow a few percent of the aperture. Cassegrain: a 12 cm hyperbolic sub-reflector near that focus bounces energy back to a horn mounted through the centre of the dish, keeping the waveguide short and pointing the horn's spillover at cold sky instead of warm ground. Offset: cut the dish as a section from a larger paraboloid so the feed sits below the aperture edge, with zero blockage. All three put a feed at a focus; none uses a flat side-exit mirror.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: any optical telescope configuration has a radio-antenna equivalent because both are focusing reflectors. Correction: only configurations that deliver a focus a feed can occupy without blocking the beam are used; Newtonian folding is pointless at radio wavelengths.", "link": "section 7", "mnemonic": "Front, Cassegrain, Offset: FCO. Newtonian stays with the stargazers.", "edge_cases": "Gregorian (concave sub-reflector) is a fourth valid geometry omitted from the question. Cassegrain only pays off when the dish is large in wavelengths, because the sub-reflector must itself be several wavelengths across; on small amateur dishes its blockage outweighs the benefit."}

{"core": "A paraboloid has the geometric property that every ray arriving parallel to its axis is reflected through the same focal point with the same path length, so the whole aperture's energy is coherently concentrated on the feed. Gain scales with aperture area, G ≈ η(πD/λ)², which is why dishes are the most efficient way to get very high gain.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A dipole can indeed serve as a prime-focus feed, but that is a convenience, not the reason for the dish's efficiency. The gain comes from the reflector's collecting area, not from what sits at the focus.", "why_tempting": "Learners know a simple dipole-plus-splash-plate feed is common on amateur dishes and confuse feed choice with efficiency."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Impedance matching is always required; the feed must present the correct impedance to its line, and reflections from the dish back into the feed actually complicate the match. The reflector does not remove this need.", "why_tempting": "Because the dish is a passive metal surface, it seems like it should not have any impedance concerns."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A horn is the usual feed for a dish, but horns do not trap energy; they are matched launchers between waveguide and free space. The dish's gain would exist with any suitable feed.", "why_tempting": "Horns look like funnels, and the word trap suggests they capture more energy than a wire would."}], "concept": "The surface z = r²/(4f) ensures that an incoming plane wave reflected from any point on the paraboloid reaches the focus with the same total path length. Equal path length means equal phase, so the contributions from the entire aperture add in phase at the feed; this coherent summation is what converts a large physical area into gain. The directivity of any aperture antenna is D = 4πA_e/λ², and for a circular dish of diameter D with aperture efficiency η that becomes G = η(πD/λ)². Efficiency η (typically 0.5 to 0.65) accounts for feed spillover, non-uniform illumination taper, surface errors, blockage by the feed, and cross-polarization. In transmit the picture reverses: the spherical wave from the feed is turned into a plane wave across the aperture. The half-power beamwidth is roughly 70 λ/D degrees, so the same geometry that gives gain gives a narrow beam that must be aimed accurately.", "worked_example": "A 1.2 m dish at 10.368 GHz: λ = 0.0289 m, so D/λ ≈ 41.5. With η = 0.55, G = 0.55 × (π × 41.5)² = 0.55 × 17 000 ≈ 9350, or 39.7 dBi. Beamwidth ≈ 70/41.5 ≈ 1.7°. The same dish at 1296 MHz (λ = 0.231 m, D/λ ≈ 5.2) gives G = 0.55 × (π × 5.2)² ≈ 147, about 21.7 dBi: the focusing geometry is identical, but the aperture is far fewer wavelengths across, so less energy is collected relative to a wavelength-sized element.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the dish's performance comes from the special feed antenna placed in front of it. Correction: the feed merely couples to the focus; the gain is a property of the reflector's aperture area in wavelengths and the in-phase focusing of the paraboloid.", "link": "Decibel Converter", "edge_cases": "A dish only behaves as described when it is many wavelengths across; below about 10 λ edge diffraction and feed blockage erode efficiency badly, which is why dishes are uncommon below 1296 MHz in amateur use and Yagis dominate on 2 m and 70 cm."}

{"core": "A circularly polarized antenna responds fully only to a wave whose field rotates in the same sense; an RHCP helix receives an RHCP signal with no polarization loss, receives any linear signal with a 3 dB loss, and in theory rejects LHCP entirely.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A horizontal signal is linear; it projects onto only one of the two orthogonal components that make up the circular response, giving a 3 dB polarization loss. It is received, but not best.", "why_tempting": "Horizontal is the usual weak-signal VHF polarization and might seem like the general-purpose match."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Left-hand circular is the orthogonal polarization to right-hand circular. Ideally the coupling is zero; practical helices give 15 to 25 dB of rejection. This is the worst case, not the best.", "why_tempting": "The two circular senses sound like near-equivalents, and a learner may assume any circular signal couples well into any circular antenna."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Vertical is just another linear orientation and suffers the same 3 dB loss as horizontal when received on a circular antenna; nothing about it is preferred.", "why_tempting": "The word only makes it sound exclusive, which can read as authoritative."}], "concept": "Polarization matching is a vector inner product between the incoming field and the antenna's polarization state. Represent RHCP as (1, −j)/√2 and LHCP as (1, +j)/√2 in a two-component basis; they are orthogonal, so the ideal coupling between them is zero. A linear state such as horizontal (1, 0) has an inner product of magnitude 1/√2 with either circular state, giving a power coupling of one half, or −3 dB. The polarization loss factor for matched circular is 0 dB, for circular-to-linear 3 dB, and for opposite-sense circular limited only by axial-ratio imperfections. An axial-mode helix radiates in the sense of its winding, and a reflection from a flat conductor reverses the sense, which is why a dish fed by a helix must use the opposite-hand feed to produce the desired far-field sense. Satellites use the same reasoning: the ground station antenna sense must match what the spacecraft transmits after accounting for any reflectors in the chain.", "worked_example": "An RHCP helix with an axial ratio of 1 dB receives three test signals of equal power. RHCP signal: coupling ≈ 0 dB, full signal. Horizontal dipole signal: coupling = 10 log(0.5) = −3 dB. LHCP signal: with a 1 dB axial ratio the rejection is about 25 dB, so the signal is down 25 dB. Ranking: same-sense circular is best, linear is 3 dB behind, opposite-sense circular is almost gone.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: circular polarization accepts anything equally, so the sense does not matter. Correction: circular antennas are indifferent to linear orientation (always 3 dB), but strongly selective between RHCP and LHCP; the matched sense wins by 3 dB over linear and by 20-plus dB over the opposite sense.", "link": "section 7", "mnemonic": "Same hand, full strength; any line, lose three; wrong hand, nearly nothing.", "edge_cases": "Each reflection flips circular sense: a helix feeding a dish must be wound opposite to the sense you want in the far field. Real helices have axial ratios that worsen off-axis, so the opposite-sense rejection drops sharply away from boresight."}

{"core": "An axial-mode helical beam is circularly polarized, meaning its response contains equal vertical and horizontal components in phase quadrature. It therefore receives a vertically or horizontally polarized signal with the same 3 dB polarization loss, so it responds to both at once.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A ground plane is a vertical monopole and is linearly, vertically polarized; a horizontal signal is cross-polarized and heavily attenuated.", "why_tempting": "The radials are horizontal, which can suggest a horizontal response, but radials carry balanced currents that cancel in the far field."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A quad loop fed at the centre of one side is linearly polarized, horizontal or vertical depending on feed position. It responds to one orientation at a time unless deliberately fed at two points in quadrature.", "why_tempting": "The loop has both horizontal and vertical wires, so it looks like it should pick up both orientations."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A folded dipole is a linear antenna with the same polarization as its orientation; the fold only changes the feed impedance by a factor of four, not the polarization.", "why_tempting": "Two parallel conductors might suggest two polarizations, but they are parallel, not orthogonal."}], "concept": "Polarization of an antenna is fixed by the direction of the current that radiates. A single straight conductor, whether a monopole, dipole or folded dipole, produces a linear field aligned with that conductor. A quad loop's two side segments carry currents that add while the top and bottom segments carry currents that cancel (or vice versa), so it too is linear. The axial-mode helix is different: its current rotates around the axis as it travels along the wire, so the radiated field has two orthogonal components with a 90° phase relationship, which is circular polarization. Expressed in a horizontal/vertical basis the response is (1, ±j)/√2, giving an inner product of magnitude 1/√2 with any linear state and therefore a constant 3 dB coupling to either vertical or horizontal. This is why helices and other circularly polarized antennas are favoured for satellite work, where the arriving polarization is unpredictable, and why a circularly polarized antenna can be seen as deliberately trading 3 dB for immunity to the 20-plus dB cross-polarization fade.", "worked_example": "Imagine a 2 m helix pointed at a satellite whose linear antenna is tumbling. When the satellite's polarization happens to be vertical, the helix response is 10 log(cos² 45°) = −3 dB. When it rotates to horizontal: still −3 dB. At 30° from vertical: the linear projection onto the helix's rotating field is still 1/√2 in magnitude, so still −3 dB. A horizontal Yagi on the same path would go from 0 dB to −20 dB or worse as the satellite rotates. The helix responds to every orientation equally, which is the property the question is after.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: an antenna with wires in both the vertical and horizontal planes will receive both polarizations. Correction: polarization is set by the net radiating current, not by wire geometry; a quad or a ground plane is linear, and only an antenna with two orthogonal, quadrature-phased current components (circular polarization) responds to both.", "link": "section 7", "edge_cases": "Crossed Yagis fed in quadrature and Lindenblads also respond to both orientations. A circular antenna's 3 dB penalty against a matched linear link is real, so for fixed terrestrial paths with known polarization a linear antenna of the right orientation outperforms a helix by 3 dB."}

{"core": "Surface deviations on a reflector cause phase errors in the aperture that reduce gain. The amateur rule of thumb is to hold surface error to no more than about 0.1 λ at the operating frequency; beyond that the loss grows rapidly because phase error scales with the error in wavelengths, not in millimetres.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A 0.25 λ surface error produces a 180° round-trip phase error (the wave travels to the surface and back, doubling the path error), which means parts of the aperture cancel each other outright. That is a ruined reflector, not an upper limit.", "why_tempting": "A quarter wavelength is a familiar tolerance in antenna work (matching sections, stubs), so it sounds reasonable."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "A fixed metric tolerance ignores that the penalty depends on error relative to wavelength. 5 mm is negligible at 1296 MHz (0.02 λ) but is 0.17 λ at 10 GHz and 0.4 λ at 24 GHz, so it cannot be a universal limit.", "why_tempting": "Workshop thinking naturally expresses tolerances in millimetres."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Diameter has nothing to do with the phase error a bump introduces; 1% of a 3 m dish is 30 mm, which would be hopeless at any microwave band. The tolerance must be referenced to wavelength.", "why_tempting": "Diameter sets the gain, so it feels like it should also set the acceptable error."}], "concept": "A reflector works by giving every ray the same path length to the focus. A surface displaced by δ along the axis changes the round-trip path by about 2δ, producing a phase error of φ = 2π × 2δ/λ = 4πδ/λ. Random errors across the aperture reduce gain by the Ruze relation G/G₀ = exp[−(4πε/λ)²], where ε is the RMS surface error. The loss is tiny for ε below about λ/50 (0.1 dB class), reaches roughly 0.7 dB at λ/25, about 2.7 dB at λ/12.5 (0.08 λ), and becomes severe approaching 0.1 λ. The keyed amateur limit of 0.1 λ therefore marks the edge beyond which a dish stops being worth using; practical builders aim well inside it. Because the tolerance is in wavelengths, a given mesh or spun-aluminium dish has a highest usable frequency: a surface that is fine on 2.3 GHz may be useless on 24 GHz. Mesh adds a second criterion, that hole size be small compared with λ (under about λ/10) to keep leakage through the surface low.", "worked_example": "A surplus 1 m dish has measured surface errors of about 3 mm peak. At 2.4 GHz (λ = 125 mm) that is 0.024 λ, well inside the 0.1 λ limit; Ruze with ε ≈ 1.5 mm RMS gives exp[−(4π × 1.5/125)²] = exp(−0.023) ≈ 0.98, a loss of about 0.1 dB. At 10 GHz (λ = 28.9 mm) the 3 mm peak is 0.10 λ, right at the limit, and 1.5 mm RMS gives exp[−(4π × 1.5/28.9)²] = exp(−0.43) ≈ 0.65, a 1.9 dB loss. At 24 GHz the same dish is at 0.24 λ and essentially useless. The usable ceiling for this dish is roughly 10 GHz.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a dish that looks smooth is good at any frequency. Correction: acceptable surface error is a fraction of the wavelength, roughly 0.1 λ as an outer bound, so the same dish degrades steadily as frequency rises and has a maximum useful band.", "link": "Wavelength ↔ Frequency", "mnemonic": "A tenth of a wave or walk away.", "edge_cases": "Professional practice uses the Ruze formula with RMS error and targets λ/16 to λ/20 (about 0.05 to 0.06 λ) for under 1 dB loss; the 0.1 λ figure is a generous amateur ceiling for peak error, and a dish right at that limit is already a few dB down. Systematic errors (a warped rim) behave worse than random ones of the same size because they do not average out."}

{"core": "The gain of an aperture antenna is G = η(πD/λ)², set by the diameter expressed in wavelengths and the aperture efficiency. Doubling D/λ quadruples the gain (+6 dB), so diameter in wavelengths is the controlling variable for a surplus dish you are repurposing.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Focal length (or f/D ratio) sets where the feed sits and how wide the feed's pattern must be to illuminate the dish; it affects efficiency slightly but not the fundamental gain, which is fixed by aperture area.", "why_tempting": "Changing the dish band means rebuilding the feed at the focal point, so focal length feels central to the conversion."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Any good conductor (aluminium, steel, copper mesh with fine enough holes) reflects essentially 100% of the energy; material only matters through surface accuracy and mesh leakage, not through a gain term.", "why_tempting": "Conductivity and loss matter in feedlines and loading coils, and that intuition is wrongly transferred to the reflector."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "The feed's polarization determines the polarization of the beam, not its gain; a dish fed with a linear horn or a circular helix has the same gain for the same illumination efficiency.", "why_tempting": "Polarization mismatch causes loss on a link, so it feels like a gain parameter, but it is a matching loss between two antennas, not a property of one."}], "concept": "Any aperture antenna has directivity D = 4πA_e/λ² where A_e is the effective area. For a circular reflector of physical diameter D the effective area is η × πD²/4, giving G = η(πD/λ)². This is why dish gain rises 6 dB for each doubling of frequency with the same dish: the dish is twice as many wavelengths across. Efficiency η, typically 0.5 to 0.65, bundles illumination taper (the feed should be about 10 dB down at the rim), spillover past the rim, feed and strut blockage, surface error (Ruze loss) and feed cross-polarization. The f/D ratio chooses the feed design: a deep dish (f/D ≈ 0.25 to 0.35) needs a feed with a very broad pattern, a shallow one (f/D ≈ 0.5 to 0.8) a narrower horn, but a correctly matched feed delivers nearly the same η either way. When repurposing a surplus dish the first calculation is D/λ at your band, then beamwidth ≈ 70 λ/D degrees to judge whether your mount can point it.", "worked_example": "A surplus 90 cm offset dish from a satellite TV installation. At 10.368 GHz: λ = 2.89 cm, D/λ = 31.1, so with η = 0.6 the gain is 0.6 × (π × 31.1)² ≈ 5730, or 37.6 dBi; beamwidth about 2.2°. At 5.76 GHz: D/λ = 17.3, G ≈ 0.6 × (π × 17.3)² ≈ 1770, or 32.5 dBi. At 2.4 GHz: D/λ = 7.2, G ≈ 0.6 × (π × 7.2)² ≈ 307, or 24.9 dBi. Each halving of frequency costs 6 dB because the dish is half as many wavelengths across; nothing about the metal, focal length or polarization entered the calculation.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a dish has a gain figure stamped on it the way a Yagi does. Correction: a reflector's gain depends on how many wavelengths it spans, so the same dish gains 6 dB per octave of frequency; quote dish gain only together with the frequency.", "link": "Decibel Converter", "mnemonic": "Gain goes with (pi D over lambda) squared: double the wavelengths, four times the gain.", "edge_cases": "Below about 10 wavelengths across, edge diffraction and blockage drop η well under 0.5 and the formula becomes optimistic. An offset dish from satellite TV is a section of a larger paraboloid; its effective aperture is the projected area normal to the beam, slightly smaller than the physical dish."}

{"core": "Net system gain is the algebraic sum of decibel terms: −3 dB (line) + 6 dBd (antenna) = +3 dB, which is a power ratio of 2. ERP = 100 W × 2 = 200 W.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "400 W would require a net gain of +6 dB, which ignores the 3 dB of feedline loss entirely and applies only the antenna gain.", "why_tempting": "Taking the 6 dBd at face value without subtracting the line loss."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "300 W is not a decibel-consistent result; it would be a net gain of 4.8 dB, which no combination of the given figures produces. It comes from treating dB as if they combined linearly with power (100 × 3).", "why_tempting": "Multiplying the output by the number 3 that appears in the question."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "350 W (net +5.4 dB) likewise matches nothing in the problem; it looks like 100 W plus some fraction of a wrongly computed 400 W.", "why_tempting": "A mid-range guess between the attractive wrong answers."}], "concept": "Effective Radiated Power is the power that a half-wave dipole would need to be fed with to produce the same field strength in the antenna's favoured direction. The chain is transmitter output, minus every loss between transmitter and antenna (coax, connectors, tuner, filters), plus antenna gain referenced to a dipole (dBd). Because the quantities are decibels, they add: G_net(dB) = Σ gains − Σ losses, and ERP = P_tx × 10^(G_net/10). The useful anchors are 3 dB = ×2, 6 dB = ×4, 10 dB = ×10, and negative values invert them. Losses expressed in watts rather than dB must be subtracted before applying antenna gain. If the antenna gain is quoted in dBi, subtract 2.15 dB first to get dBd, because ERP is defined against a dipole; the isotropic equivalent is EIRP. ERP is the regulator's figure of merit because it captures the actual field strength a station puts into the air regardless of how it was achieved.", "worked_example": "Step 1: convert the chain to dB. Line and connectors: −3.0 dB. Antenna: +6.0 dBd. Net = +3.0 dB. Step 2: convert to a ratio: 10^(3/10) = 1.995 ≈ 2. Step 3: ERP = 100 W × 2 = 200 W. Cross-check in watts: 100 W through 3 dB of loss leaves 50 W at the antenna; 6 dBd (×4) gives 50 × 4 = 200 W. Both routes agree.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: antenna gain is applied to the transmitter's rated output. Correction: the antenna only amplifies what actually reaches it, so line loss must come off first; equivalently, add all the dB terms (with losses negative) before converting to a ratio.", "link": "Decibel Converter", "mnemonic": "Losses out, gain in, then convert: 3 dB is double, 6 dB is four, 10 dB is ten.", "edge_cases": "If the antenna gain were quoted in dBi, 6 dBi is only 3.85 dBd and the ERP would be 100 × 10^(0.085) ≈ 122 W. SWR-related extra loss is not in the stated 3 dB unless the question says so."}

{"core": "Line loss is heating: I²R in the conductors and V²/R_dielectric (plus dielectric hysteresis) in the insulation. Standing waves raise the peak current and peak voltage at points along the line above their matched values, so these ohmic and dielectric heat losses increase with SWR.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Antenna current is set by the power delivered and the antenna's radiation resistance; it is not the mechanism of loss inside the line. The extra loss occurs in the cable, at the current maxima of the standing wave.", "why_tempting": "High current does raise loss, but the question asks about loss in the transmission line, so the current that matters is in the line conductors, not the antenna."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "High antenna voltage is similarly a property of the load, not a loss mechanism in the cable. Voltage maxima on the line stress the dielectric, but it is the resulting dielectric heating that is the loss.", "why_tempting": "High SWR does produce high voltage points, so the answer is adjacent to the truth but names the symptom rather than the loss."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Coax has a shield; there is no meaningful leakage path to ground through the dielectric. Insulation resistance of polyethylene is enormous and does not change with SWR.", "why_tempting": "Leakage is a familiar failure mode for capacitors and old insulation, and the dielectric is mentioned by name."}], "concept": "Matched-line attenuation α (dB per 100 m) comes from two terms: conductor loss, proportional to √f because of skin effect, and dielectric loss, proportional to f and to the loss tangent of the insulation. Both are heating. When the load is mismatched, a reflected wave travels back and interferes with the forward wave to form a standing-wave envelope with voltage maxima of V_f(1 + |Γ|) and current maxima of I_f(1 + |Γ|). Because loss goes as the square of current and voltage, the extra heating at the maxima exceeds the reduction at the minima, so total dissipation rises. The additional loss also comes from the reflected power making a second and third trip through the lossy line as it is re-reflected at the transmitter. The standard approximation for total loss with SWR is L_total = 10 log[(a² − |Γ|²) / (a(1 − |Γ|²))] where a = 10^(L_matched/10). Low matched loss means SWR costs little; high matched loss (thin coax, UHF) means SWR costs a lot. This is why open-wire line tolerates enormous SWR: its matched loss is tiny.", "worked_example": "RG-58 at 146 MHz, 30 m run, matched loss about 5.4 dB. With a 3:1 SWR, |Γ| = 0.5 and a = 10^0.54 = 3.47: L = 10 log[(12.0 − 0.25)/(3.47 × 0.75)] = 10 log(4.52) ≈ 6.5 dB, about 1.1 dB extra. Now a 30 m run of 450 Ω ladder line with 0.2 dB matched loss at the same 3:1: a = 1.047, L = 10 log[(1.096 − 0.25)/(1.047 × 0.75)] = 10 log(1.078) ≈ 0.33 dB, only 0.13 dB extra. The extra loss in both cases is heat generated at the standing-wave current and voltage maxima.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the reflected power on a high-SWR line is lost or goes back and damages the transmitter. Correction: reflected power is re-reflected at the transmitter and eventually radiated; what is lost is the extra I²R and dielectric heating it causes on each pass through the line.", "link": "SWR & Impedance Match", "mnemonic": "SWR hurts in proportion to how lossy the line already is.", "edge_cases": "At HF with short low-loss runs, even 3:1 SWR adds only a fraction of a dB; the real SWR hazards there are tuner losses and transmitter foldback, not line heating. At UHF with long thin coax the same SWR can add several dB."}

{"core": "Subtract the line loss given in watts first: 200 − 5 = 195 W reaching the antenna. A 3 dBd gain is a factor of 2, so ERP = 195 × 2 = 390 W.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "178 W is below the transmitter output and would need a net loss; it corresponds roughly to 195 W less about 0.4 dB, a sign error that treats the antenna term as a loss.", "why_tempting": "Subtracting both terms as if gain and loss were the same kind of penalty."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "197 W is just 200 − 5 + 2, treating 3 dB as if it added 2 or 3 watts rather than doubling the power.", "why_tempting": "Confusing a logarithmic gain with an additive wattage."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "228 W would be 195 W × 1.17, about +0.7 dB, matching nothing in the problem. It results from misreading the gain or mixing dBi/dBd conversions in error.", "why_tempting": "A plausible-looking modest increase for a learner who is unsure how much 3 dB is worth."}], "concept": "ERP is the dipole-equivalent power: P_tx, minus all losses between transmitter and antenna, times antenna gain relative to a dipole. When losses are stated in watts you subtract them linearly; when they are in dB you add them (negative) to the gain and convert the net dB to a ratio with 10^(dB/10). Mixing the two forms is where errors happen, so convert everything to one domain before combining. 3 dB is exactly a factor of 1.995, close enough to 2 for exam work. A watt-stated loss of 5 W on 200 W is 10 log(195/200) = −0.11 dB; expressed that way the net gain is +2.89 dB and ERP = 200 × 10^0.289 = 389 W, consistent with the linear route. Note that ERP uses dBd; if an antenna is rated in dBi you subtract 2.15 dB first.", "worked_example": "Step 1: power at antenna = 200 W − 5 W = 195 W. Step 2: 3 dBd → ratio 10^(3/10) = 1.995. Step 3: ERP = 195 × 1.995 = 389 W ≈ 390 W. Alternative all-dB route: line loss = 10 log(200/195) = 0.11 dB; net = 3.0 − 0.11 = 2.89 dB; ERP = 200 × 10^0.289 = 200 × 1.946 = 389 W. Same answer, option B.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: dB values can be added to or subtracted from watts directly. Correction: dB is a ratio; convert it to a multiplier (3 dB ≈ ×2) and apply it to the power that actually reaches the antenna.", "link": "Decibel Converter", "edge_cases": "The exam keys 3 dB as exactly ×2; strictly 10^0.3 = 1.995, so 389 W. Real transmission line loss scales with power and is quoted in dB; a fixed 5 W loss is an exam simplification."}

{"core": "ERP is defined as the power a half-wave dipole would have to radiate to produce the same field in the main lobe: transmitter output, less every loss on the way to the antenna, times (or plus, in dB) the antenna's gain referenced to a dipole.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Power before modulation is just the carrier power at the transmitter; it ignores feedline loss and antenna gain and has nothing to do with the dipole-referenced radiated figure.", "why_tempting": "Carrier power is a familiar transmitter specification and is easy to mistake for a radiated figure."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Power supplied to the transmission line is the transmitter output, not the power at the antenna; this definition leaves out the line loss that ERP explicitly accounts for.", "why_tempting": "It is almost right, missing only the loss term, so it reads as a reasonable summary."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "A ratio of output to input power is a gain, a dimensionless number in dB. ERP is a power in watts.", "why_tempting": "Gain is involved in computing ERP, and the word ratio sounds technical."}], "concept": "Regulators care about how much field a station produces, not how much its transmitter is rated for, so they define ERP as the dipole-equivalent radiated power: ERP = P_tx × L_line × G_dBd in linear terms, or ERP(dBW) = P_tx(dBW) − losses(dB) + G(dBd). Losses include coax attenuation, connector loss, tuner or filter insertion loss and any power splitter. The gain reference is a half-wave dipole; the same concept referenced to an isotropic radiator is EIRP, which is always 2.15 dB (×1.64) larger. ERP applies in the direction of maximum radiation, so a directional antenna has a high ERP in one direction and a low one elsewhere. The definition matters practically because a modest transmitter into a high-gain antenna with short low-loss feed can have the same ERP as a kilowatt into a lossy system feeding a dipole; the first is cheaper and generates less RF exposure near the shack.", "worked_example": "Station A: 100 W into 30 m of RG-213 at 146 MHz (about 2.5 dB loss) feeding a 10 dBd Yagi. Net = −2.5 + 10 = +7.5 dB → ×5.6, ERP = 560 W. Station B: 500 W into the same coax feeding a dipole (0 dBd). Net = −2.5 dB → ×0.56, ERP = 280 W. Station A puts twice the field into its favoured direction with one fifth the transmitter, which is exactly what the ERP definition is built to capture.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: ERP is just another name for transmitter output. Correction: ERP includes the feedline losses and the antenna's directional gain over a dipole; it describes what leaves the antenna in its best direction, not what leaves the radio.", "link": "section 7", "mnemonic": "Transmitter, minus the line, plus the beam, versus a dipole.", "edge_cases": "ERP versus EIRP: identical concept, different reference antenna, differing by 2.15 dB. Some specification sheets quote dBi, so check the reference before computing ERP."}

{"core": "Net gain = −3 dB + 9 dBd = +6 dB, which is a power ratio of 4. ERP = 200 W × 4 = 800 W.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "1600 W is 200 × 8, a net gain of 9 dB, which ignores the 3 dB of line loss and applies the antenna gain alone.", "why_tempting": "Forgetting to subtract the feedline loss before applying the antenna gain."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "400 W is 200 × 2, a net of only 3 dB; it results from subtracting 3 from 9 and then treating the remaining 6 dB as a factor of 2 instead of 4.", "why_tempting": "Mixing up the 3 dB = ×2 and 6 dB = ×4 anchors."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "3200 W is a net gain of 12 dB, which would require adding the 3 dB loss as if it were a gain: 9 + 3 = 12.", "why_tempting": "A sign error that treats every dB figure in the problem as a gain."}], "concept": "ERP = P_tx × 10^((G_ant − L_line)/10) where G_ant is in dBd and L_line is the sum of all losses in dB between transmitter and antenna. Because dB are logarithmic, the whole chain reduces to one addition before a single conversion. The anchors to memorise: 3 dB ≈ ×2, 6 dB ≈ ×4, 9 dB ≈ ×8, 10 dB = ×10, and 1 dB ≈ ×1.26; any other value is 10^(dB/10). Losses subtract in the exponent, never in watts, unless the question explicitly gives the loss in watts. ERP is referenced to a dipole, which is why the antenna gain is given in dBd; a dBi figure would need 2.15 dB removed first. The result represents the field strength in the main lobe, so the same transmitter with the same coax produces a different ERP depending only on the antenna's directional gain.", "worked_example": "Step 1: sum the dB chain: −3 (coax and connectors) + 9 (antenna, dBd) = +6 dB. Step 2: ratio = 10^(6/10) = 3.98 ≈ 4. Step 3: ERP = 200 W × 4 = 800 W. Watt-by-watt check: 200 W through 3 dB loss leaves 100 W at the antenna; 9 dBd is ×7.94, so 100 × 7.94 = 794 W, which rounds to 800 W.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the 9 dBd antenna gain acts on the full 200 W. Correction: only 100 W survives the 3 dB of line loss, so the antenna multiplies 100 W, giving roughly 800 W; always net the dB terms first.", "link": "Decibel Converter", "mnemonic": "3, 6, 9, 10: times 2, 4, 8, 10.", "edge_cases": "The exact figure is 794 W; the question says approximate. If the 9 dB were dBi instead of dBd the ERP would be 200 × 10^((9 − 2.15 − 3)/10) ≈ 485 W."}

{"core": "Sum the chain in dB: −1.30 (line) − 0.20 (tuner) + 4.50 (antenna, dBd) = +3.00 dB. {"core": "A 3 dB change is a power ratio of 10^(3/10) ≈ 2. The 3 dB change might come from any element in the chain: doubling transmitter power, halving line loss in dB terms (for example replacing 3 dB of coax with 0 dB of coax would be a 3 dB improvement), or swapping an antenna for one with 3 dB more gain. {"core": "Net gain = −0.8 − 0.2 + 10 = +9.0 dB, a power ratio of 10^0.9 ≈ 7.94. The tenths-of-a-dB losses show how the chain is typically populated: a short low-loss coax run at HF (0.8 dB), a well-matched tuner (0.2 dB). {"core": "Swapping a 3 dBd antenna for a 9 dBd antenna raises net system gain by 6 dB. 6 dB is a power ratio of 10^0.6 ≈ 3.98, so ERP increases by a factor of 4.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A factor of 2 corresponds to a 3 dB change, which is only half of the 6 dB difference between the two antennas.", "why_tempting": "Reading 3 dBd as the change rather than as the starting gain."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "A factor of 6 would be about 7.8 dB; the mistake is treating the 6 dB difference as a linear multiplier.", "why_tempting": "The difference is 6 and the option says 6."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A factor of 1.5 is only 1.76 dB. {"core": "Net gain = −1 dB + 10 dBd = +9 dB, a ratio of 10^0.9 ≈ 7.94. {"core": "Net gain = −1 dB + 10 dBd = +9 dB → ratio 10^0.9 ≈ 7.94. ERP = 1000 W × 7.94 ≈ 7940 W PEP, which rounds to the 8000 W option.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "10 000 W applies the 10 dBd gain (×10) and ignores the 1 dB composite loss, which removes about 21% of the power before the antenna.", "why_tempting": "Discounting the 1 dB loss as negligible."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "9000 W is 1000 × 9, using the net dB value of 9 as a linear multiplier. 9 dB is a ratio of 7.94, not 9.", "why_tempting": "The net dB figure coincidentally looks like a plausible multiplier."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "1009 W is 1000 + 10 − 1, adding dB values as if they were watts. {"core": "A horizontal antenna over ground forms an interference pattern with its ground reflection. The lowest lobe peaks where the direct and reflected rays add in phase, at an elevation angle θ with sin θ = λ/(4h), so raising the antenna (larger h in wavelengths) lowers the main-lobe takeoff angle.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "The ionospheric layer height determines which takeoff angles reach a given distance, not which angle the antenna radiates most strongly. The antenna's lobe structure is purely a function of height above ground and element pattern.", "why_tempting": "Both the E-region height and the antenna's angle feature in propagation planning, so the two get tangled together."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "The relationship is inverse: sin θ = λ/(4h) means higher h gives a smaller θ. A low antenna fires its main lobe at a high angle, nearly straight up at λ/4.", "why_tempting": "Intuition that a higher antenna sees more sky and therefore radiates more upward."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Height is the dominant factor in the vertical pattern of any horizontal antenna; the Yagi's own free-space pattern is multiplied by the ground-reflection factor, which changes completely with height.", "why_tempting": "A Yagi has a fixed free-space pattern, and learners forget that the ground modifies it."}], "concept": "A horizontal antenna at height h over a conducting ground has an image antenna at depth h carrying current reversed in phase (the horizontal E-field must vanish at the conductor). At elevation angle θ the direct and reflected rays differ in path by 2h sin θ, plus the 180° reflection phase shift. Constructive interference occurs when 2h sin θ = λ/2, 3λ/2, ..., so the lowest lobe is at sin θ₁ = λ/(4h) and nulls appear at sin θ = nλ/(2h). The ground-reflection factor is F(θ) = |2 sin(2πh sin θ/λ)|, with a maximum of 2 (a 6 dB gain over free space) in the lobe directions. At h = λ/4 the first lobe peaks at 90° (straight up, NVIS); at λ/2 it is at 30°; at one wavelength at about 14.5°; at two wavelengths at about 7°. The Yagi's directivity multiplies this ground factor, so raising a Yagi both lowers its takeoff angle and sharpens the lobe. This is the engineering basis for the rule that DX antennas want to be at least half a wavelength up, and ideally a full wavelength or more.", "worked_example": "A 20 m three-element Yagi (λ = 21.4 m). Each doubling of height roughly halves the takeoff angle in this range, moving the main lobe from a useful-for-Europe 32° toward the 10° angles that work long multi-hop paths.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the antenna's radiation angle is a property of the antenna design. Over poor ground the reflection is weaker and shifted, filling the nulls and raising the effective lobe slightly. Vertical antennas obey a different rule because their image is in phase."}

{"core": "Below about half a wavelength the ground image of a horizontal antenna is so close that the ground-reflection factor dominates and the pattern collapses toward a single high-angle, nearly omnidirectional blob. Only at half a wavelength or more does the lowest lobe drop enough and the azimuth pattern separate enough for the antenna's inherent directivity to show.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "At λ/8 the direct and reflected waves nearly cancel at all low angles and the antenna radiates mainly straight up with very poor efficiency; there is no usable directivity at this height.", "why_tempting": "Any height above ground sounds like it should help, but an eighth wave is deep in the cancellation region."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "At λ/4 the main lobe points at the zenith (NVIS), the azimuth pattern of a dipole is nearly circular, and the figure-eight is almost gone. Directivity is minimal.", "why_tempting": "Quarter wavelength is the magic number for many other antenna rules (verticals, matching sections) and is wrongly applied here."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "At 3λ/8 the first lobe peaks at about 42°, still a high angle, and the ground factor still washes out most of the azimuth pattern. The transition to visible directivity is generally placed at λ/2.", "why_tempting": "Three-eighths is between quarter and half, and the pattern is indeed starting to improve, so it sounds like a reasonable threshold."}], "concept": "The far-field of a horizontal antenna over ground is its free-space pattern multiplied by the ground-reflection factor F(θ) = 2 sin(2πh sin θ/λ). At low heights this factor is small at every low elevation angle and only becomes large near the zenith, so whatever directivity the antenna has in azimuth is masked: a dipole at λ/4 is nearly omnidirectional, and a Yagi at λ/4 shows little front-to-back ratio at useful angles. At h = λ/2, the first lobe is at 30° elevation and the ground factor at that angle reaches its full value of 2, so the free-space pattern of the antenna is reproduced with a 6 dB ground gain and its azimuth shape, the figure-eight of a dipole or the forward lobe of a Yagi, appears clearly. This is why the half-wavelength figure is the widely quoted minimum height for a directional HF antenna to behave as designed. Above that the antenna becomes progressively more directive at lower angles and acquires additional lobes.", "worked_example": "A 40 m dipole (λ ≈ 41 m). At 5 m (λ/8): the pattern is a single lobe at the zenith, roughly 10 dB down from a free-space dipole in gain, with no discernible broadside null. At 10 m (λ/4): still a zenith-pointing lobe, azimuth almost round, ends of the dipole only about 2 dB weaker than broadside at 45° elevation. At 20 m (λ/2): main lobe at 30°, broadside gain about 8 dBi, with the off-the-ends radiation 10 dB or more down at that angle. The figure-eight has returned. Raising the antenna by another λ/2 lowers the lobe to about 15° and sharpens it.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: an antenna's directivity is intrinsic and shows up at any height. Correction: ground reflection multiplies the pattern; below about λ/2 the ground factor smears the pattern into a high-angle, near-omnidirectional lobe, so the designed directivity only appears from λ/2 upward.", "link": "section 7", "mnemonic": "Half a wave up before the pattern shows up.", "edge_cases": "The rule is for horizontally polarized antennas. On 160 m and 80 m, λ/2 is 80 m and 40 m respectively, which is why low-band directional antennas are usually verticals or vertical arrays rather than Yagis."}

{"core": "Real soil is a lossy dielectric that RF penetrates before it is effectively reflected, so the apparent reflecting plane lies below the physical surface by an amount depending on conductivity and permittivity: from a few centimetres over wet, conductive ground to around two metres over dry, rocky or sandy soil at HF.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A reflecting plane above the surface would require a conductor floating in the air; vegetation and surface clutter scatter energy but do not form an elevated reflector.", "why_tempting": "Tall grass or crops sometimes seem to raise the effective ground, but that is scattering and loss, not reflection."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Only a perfect conductor reflects exactly at its surface. Earth has finite conductivity (typically 1 to 30 mS/m) and a relative permittivity of 4 to 30, so the wave penetrates to a skin depth that at HF is well below the surface.", "why_tempting": "Textbook antenna diagrams draw the ground as a flat mirror at the surface."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Six centimetres is at the shallow end of the range; it may hold over salt marsh or very wet clay, but dry or rocky soils push the effective plane far deeper, so 6 cm is not a general upper figure.", "why_tempting": "Picking the smallest non-zero number to acknowledge penetration without accepting that it can be large."}], "concept": "Reflection from ground is governed by the complex relative permittivity ε_r' = ε_r − j σ/(ωε₀). For a good conductor the second term dominates and the wave is reflected within a skin depth δ = √(2/(ωμσ)); for poor ground the real permittivity dominates and the wave refracts into the soil, reflecting from a distributed region. In both cases the apparent plane from which the image antenna should be measured is below the surface, at roughly the skin depth or the equivalent penetration depth. At 7 MHz with σ = 5 mS/m the skin depth is about 2.7 m; with σ = 30 mS/m it is about 1.1 m, and over seawater (σ ≈ 5 S/m) it is only about 8 cm. The practical consequence is that the effective antenna height in the ground-reflection formula sin θ = λ/(4h_eff) is the physical height plus this depth, which lowers the takeoff angle slightly and shifts the resonant frequency of a low antenna. It also explains why ground conductivity and frequency, not just the physical height, determine the vertical pattern.", "worked_example": "A 40 m dipole 10 m above average soil (σ = 5 mS/m). Skin depth at 7.1 MHz: δ = √(2/(2π × 7.1 × 10⁶ × 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 0.005)) = √(2/280) ≈ 2.7 m, so the effective reflecting plane is of order 1 to 2 m down and the effective height is about 11 to 12 m rather than 10 m. The first lobe moves from sin θ = 41/40 (which is above 1, meaning a zenith lobe) to sin θ = 41/46 ≈ 0.89, θ ≈ 63°. The same dipole over seawater reflects from 8 cm below the surface, so effective height is essentially 10 m and the lobe stays at the zenith.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: the ground acts as a mirror at the soil surface, so antenna height is measured from the dirt. Correction: lossy soil is penetrated before it reflects, so the effective plane is below the surface by centimetres to a couple of metres depending on conductivity, frequency and moisture.", "link": "section 7", "edge_cases": "At VHF the skin depth shrinks to centimetres even over poor soil, so the effect is negligible and the surface itself is the reflector. Frozen ground (as in a Calgary winter) has very low conductivity and acts almost like a dry dielectric, pushing the effective plane deeper and increasing ground loss for low antennas and verticals."}

{"core": "A dipole at λ/4 height radiates its main lobe almost straight up because of ground-reflection cancellation at low angles. A ground-mounted quarter-wave vertical has an in-phase image, so its pattern peaks at low elevation angles, and low-angle radiation is what reaches distant stations via long ionospheric hops.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Omnidirectional azimuth coverage is a convenience, not an advantage for distance; a low dipole is also nearly omnidirectional. Reaching far stations depends on elevation angle, not on covering all compass directions.", "why_tempting": "Omnidirectional sounds like it reaches everywhere, including far away."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Polarization is scrambled by the ionosphere on skywave paths, so vertical versus horizontal makes no direct difference to DX. The vertical's advantage comes from its low radiation angle, which is a consequence of geometry, not of polarization itself.", "why_tempting": "Vertical polarization and low-angle radiation go together on a ground-mounted vertical, and the cause gets attributed to the polarization."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Lower radiation resistance (about 36 Ω for a quarter-wave vertical versus 73 Ω for a dipole) is a disadvantage: it makes ground losses a larger fraction of the total and reduces efficiency. It has nothing to do with takeoff angle.", "why_tempting": "A number specific to verticals that learners remember, mistaken for the reason they work."}], "concept": "Over a conducting ground, a horizontal antenna's image is anti-phase, so at low angles the direct and reflected rays nearly cancel and the lowest lobe sits at sin θ = λ/(4h); at h = λ/4 that lobe is at the zenith. A vertical antenna's image is in phase, because the vertical E-field is not reversed by a horizontal conductor; direct and reflected rays add at low angles, and over perfect ground a quarter-wave vertical radiates most strongly at the horizon with the pattern falling to zero at the zenith. Long-distance HF paths require takeoff angles below about 30°, often under 10° for multi-hop, which the low dipole simply cannot supply but the vertical does. The price is that real ground is lossy: the Fresnel reflection coefficient for vertical polarization drops sharply at the pseudo-Brewster angle (typically 10° to 20° at HF over average soil), so the vertical's actual low-angle lobe peaks a bit higher and loses several dB compared with perfect ground. Good radials and proximity to saltwater restore much of this. The comparison in the question therefore holds in reasonably open surroundings with decent ground, which is the stated condition.", "worked_example": "On 40 m, a dipole at 10 m (λ/4) has its lobe at 90° with maybe 2 dB of gain remaining at 30° and essentially nothing below 15°. A quarter-wave ground-mounted vertical with 32 radials over average soil peaks at about 20° to 25° elevation with roughly 0 dBi there and still radiates usefully at 10°. For a 3000 km single-hop F-layer path needing a takeoff angle of about 10° to 15°, the vertical delivers perhaps 10 dB more signal than the low dipole, despite the dipole being the higher-gain antenna in free space.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a dipole always beats a vertical because it has more gain and no ground loss. Correction: a dipole's advantage exists only when it is high enough to fire at low angles; at λ/4 it radiates upward, and a vertical's low-angle lobe wins for distance.", "link": "section 7", "mnemonic": "Low dipole looks up; ground vertical looks out.", "edge_cases": "Over very poor ground or with few radials the vertical's low-angle advantage can disappear and a low dipole may equal it. For short-range (under about 500 km) NVIS work the high-angle dipole at λ/4 is the better antenna; the question is specifically about long distance."}

{"core": "At λ/2 height the ground-reflected ray toward the zenith travels an extra full wavelength (2h = λ) and picks up a 180° reflection phase reversal, so it arrives in antiphase with the direct ray and the straight-up radiation cancels. The energy instead goes into a lobe at about 30° elevation.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "A dipole at λ/2 has a single lobe per side peaking at 30° with nulls at 0° and 90°; there are no distinct side lobes at 15° and 50°, which are just points on the slopes of that one lobe.", "why_tempting": "Specific numbers lend false authority, and higher antennas do develop multiple lobes."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Ground reflection creates lobes and nulls in the vertical plane; it does not cancel azimuth side lobes, which for a dipole barely exist anyway. The cancellation at λ/2 is specifically at the zenith.", "why_tempting": "The word cancelled is right, but the direction is wrong."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Ground is a strong reflector, and the pattern of any horizontal antenna within a few wavelengths of it is radically altered; at λ/2 the free-space doughnut becomes a 30° lobe with a zenith null.", "why_tempting": "Treating the free-space pattern as the real pattern."}], "concept": "The ground-reflection factor for a horizontal antenna is F(θ) = 2 sin(2πh sin θ/λ), with the sine arising from the 180° phase reversal at reflection and the path difference 2h sin θ. Nulls occur when 2h sin θ = nλ, and lobe peaks when 2h sin θ = (2n − 1)λ/2. Put h = λ/2: at θ = 90° the argument is 2π × 0.5 = π, F = 0, a null at the zenith; at θ = 30° the argument is π/2, F = 2, the lobe maximum with 6 dB of ground gain over free space; at θ = 0° F = 0 again. So a dipole at half a wavelength pours its energy into a 30° lobe, which is the first height at which a horizontal antenna becomes a credible medium-distance DX antenna. Compare h = λ/4: F(90°) = 2 sin(π/2) = 2, maximum at the zenith, the NVIS configuration. The two heights are complementary: λ/4 for radiating straight up, λ/2 for cancelling the zenith and radiating at 30°.", "worked_example": "20 m band, λ = 21.4 m, dipole at 10.7 m. Direct ray to the zenith: reference phase 0°. Reflected ray: path is 2 × 10.7 = 21.4 m = 1 λ, contributing 360°, plus 180° from the reflection, total 540° ≡ 180°. The two rays are antiphase and cancel. At 30°: path difference = 21.4 × sin 30° = 10.7 m = λ/2 = 180°, plus 180° reflection = 360°, in phase, fields add to double the free-space value (+6 dB). Lower the antenna to 5.35 m (λ/4): zenith path difference = 10.7 m = 180°, plus 180° = 360°, in phase, maximum straight up.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: raising a dipole simply makes it radiate more in all directions. Correction: height changes the interference between direct and ground-reflected rays; at λ/2 the zenith is a null and the 30° lobe is the maximum, whereas at λ/4 the zenith is the maximum.", "link": "section 7", "mnemonic": "Quarter wave: up. Half wave: zenith shut, thirty degrees out.", "edge_cases": "Over real ground the zenith null is partial rather than complete, because the reflection coefficient is less than 1 and the effective plane is below the surface.
