Correction: one ground plane under the trace defines the line but leaves the top side open, so microstrip couples and radiates; coax encloses the field on all sides.", "link": "section 7", "mnemonic": "Coax is a tube, microstrip is a table: one side is always open.", "edge_cases": "Microstrip with a tightly fitted conductive lid and via fences along the edges approaches a shielded structure, but the lid then alters the impedance and must be included in the design; such 'suspended' or 'boxed' microstrip is a different design case."}

{"core": "A waveguide passes energy only above its cutoff frequency, which is fixed by its cross-sectional dimensions, and attenuates signals below cutoff exponentially; that is exactly the behaviour of a high-pass filter.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "A band-stop filter passes both low and high frequencies and rejects a band in the middle; waveguide rejects everything below cutoff, with no low-frequency passband.", "why_tempting": "Waveguide does have an upper practical limit (higher-order modes), so a learner may picture a rejected band."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Waveguide is rigid, heavy and must be installed with precise bends and flanged joints, and in any case this is a mechanical description, not a frequency response.", "why_tempting": "It is a true-or-false style distractor about properties, inserted among filter answers to catch guessers."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "A low-pass filter would pass DC and low frequencies and block high ones; waveguide does the opposite, blocking DC and all frequencies below cutoff.", "why_tempting": "The learner who remembers 'waveguide has a cutoff' but inverts its direction picks low-pass, the more familiar filter type."}], "concept": "The propagation constant in a waveguide is β = (ω/c)·√(1 − (f_c/f)²). For f > f_c, β is real and the wave propagates; for f < f_c the radicand is negative, β becomes jα and the field decays as e^(−αz) with no net power flow. The transfer function versus frequency is therefore zero (strongly attenuated) below f_c and near unity above it: a high-pass characteristic with a very steep skirt. The corner is set by geometry alone, f_c = c/(2a) for TE₁₀ in rectangular guide, and no reactive components are involved; it is a consequence of the boundary conditions, not of an LC network. In practice the guide's useful passband is bounded above as well, by the onset of the next mode at about 2 f_c, but that upper limit is a moding problem, not attenuation, so the filter analogy that matters is high-pass. The same physics is exploited in 'waveguide below cutoff' attenuators, which use a tube deliberately operated below f_c to produce a precise, calculable attenuation.", "worked_example": "A rectangular guide with a = 40 mm has f_c = 3×10⁸ / (2 × 0.040) = 3.75 GHz. Sweep a signal from 2 to 6 GHz: at 2 GHz, (f_c/f)² = 3.5, α = (2π·2×10⁹/3×10⁸)·√2.5 ≈ 66 Np/m ≈ 575 dB/m, so nothing emerges. At 3.75 GHz the attenuation drops sharply. At 5 GHz the signal passes with about 0.1 dB/m. Plotting attenuation versus frequency gives a brick-wall high-pass response with its corner at 3.75 GHz.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: a waveguide's cutoff is an upper limit, like the bandwidth of coax or an amplifier. Correction: cutoff is a lower limit; waveguide blocks everything below it and passes everything above, so it behaves as a high-pass filter.", "link": "section 7", "mnemonic": "Guide passes high, cuts off low.", "edge_cases": "Strictly, waveguide below cutoff is reactive rather than dissipative: power is reflected, not absorbed, so a source feeding it sees a large mismatch rather than a resistive loss. The high-pass label describes the transmission response, not the mechanism."}

{"core": "Stripline is a printed-circuit transmission line in which a flat conductor is embedded in dielectric between two parallel ground planes; it is the fully shielded sibling of microstrip and is fabricated as part of a multilayer board.", "distractors": [{"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Stripline is a passive conductor geometry, not a semiconductor device family; no junctions or active elements are involved.", "why_tempting": "The '-line' suffix and the small size of microwave parts might suggest a device series name."}, {"option": "C", "why_wrong": "Stripline is a guided-wave structure designed to confine fields between ground planes; it is specifically not an antenna and radiates very little.", "why_tempting": "'Strip' evokes a patch or strip antenna, and both are planar microwave structures."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "This is a nonsense distractor; stripline has nothing to do with chemicals or coating removal.", "why_tempting": "The word 'strip' as in stripping paint; a pure word-association trap."}], "concept": "Stripline consists of a centre trace sandwiched symmetrically between two ground planes with dielectric filling the whole space, so the field is entirely within one homogeneous medium. That makes stripline a true TEM line, with velocity c/√ε_r, no dispersion of the microstrip kind, and no top-side fringing: it is essentially a flattened coax. Characteristic impedance depends on trace width w, the ground-plane spacing b, trace thickness and ε_r; a useful approximation for thin traces is Z₀ ≈ (60/√ε_r)·ln(4b/(0.67·π·(0.8w + t))). Because the fields are enclosed, stripline has excellent isolation between adjacent lines and negligible radiation, which makes it the preferred structure for filters, couplers and distribution networks in dense RF boards. Its costs are a multilayer board, higher dielectric loss because 100% of the field is in the substrate, and the difficulty of mounting components on an internal layer; microstrip, with its surface trace, is the trade-off in the other direction.", "worked_example": "Thought experiment: take a 50 Ω microstrip trace on a 0.8 mm substrate and add a second 0.8 mm dielectric layer plus a ground plane on top, making stripline with b = 1.6 mm. The field that previously fringed into air is now captured in the dielectric, ε_eff rises from about 3.0 to the full 4.4, and the impedance drops; to restore 50 Ω the trace must be narrowed from about 1.5 mm to roughly 0.7 mm. Crosstalk to a parallel trace 1 mm away falls by roughly 10 to 15 dB, and radiation from an open stub essentially vanishes.", "misconception": "Wrong belief: stripline and microstrip are interchangeable names for any PCB trace. Correction: microstrip has one ground plane and an air-exposed trace; stripline buries the trace between two ground planes and is fully shielded, with different impedance equations and velocity.", "link": "section 7", "mnemonic": "Stripline is a strip in a sandwich; microstrip is a strip on a plate.", "edge_cases": "Asymmetric or 'offset' stripline, where the trace is nearer one plane than the other, is common in multilayer digital boards and needs its own impedance formulas; the symmetric case is the textbook definition."}

{"core": "Microwave feed horns and waveguides concentrate RF power density at the aperture, and even a few watts at 10 GHz can exceed exposure limits within centimetres, so before any hands-on work the transmitter must be switched off and its power source disconnected so it cannot be keyed while you are in the beam.", "distractors": [{"option": "A", "why_wrong": "Tropospheric ducting affects how far your signal travels, not whether the feed horn is safe to touch; propagation has no bearing on local RF exposure.", "why_tempting": "Ducting is a microwave-relevant propagation term, so it looks like the 'microwave-specific' answer."}, {"option": "B", "why_wrong": "Clothing and gloves offer no protection against RF energy at microwave frequencies; the hazard is tissue heating from the field, not cuts, and gloves may actually hide a burn until it is severe.", "why_tempting": "It sounds like sensible workshop safety and sharp waveguide flanges are real, but it addresses the wrong hazard."}, {"option": "D", "why_wrong": "Weather has no effect on RF exposure from an energized feed; dry conditions might even reduce the incidental attenuation of the beam.", "why_tempting": "Outdoor work on a dish is more pleasant in fair weather, but that is comfort, not the required safety precaution."}], "concept": "RF exposure limits are expressed as power density in W/m² or mW/cm², and the near-field density at a horn or open waveguide can be enormous because the full transmitter power is passing through an aperture of a few square centimetres. Power density at the aperture is approximately P/A: 10 W through a 2 cm × 3 cm WR-90 opening is 10 W / 6 cm² ≈ 1.7 W/cm² = 1700 mW/cm², three orders of magnitude above typical controlled-environment limits in the low-GHz range, where the body absorbs microwave energy efficiently and the eyes and testes are especially vulnerable because they have poor blood-flow cooling. The guide and horn also look like ordinary metal with no visible indication of energization, and the transmitter may be remote or under automatic control (beacon, repeater, software keying).
